author: أبو المظفر مؤيد الدولة مجد الدين أسامة بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ الكناني الكلبي الشيزري (المتوفى: 584هـ)
notes: Poems are in text order. id numbers the index entries by print page, then text order. Unmatched poems have id null. Hemistichs are h1/h2; separator is "..." or "=" as in the source, null if absent. intro is all prose between the previous poem (or heading) and this one; after is prose following the last poem before a heading or the end; interludes are prose inside a merged poem, placed after_verse n, with refers_to_verse set when a glossed word is found in a verse.

paragraphs.text: قال أسامة بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ الكناني - غفر الله له، ولجميع أمة محمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: "الحمد لله وإن تنقلت بنا الدنيا تنقل الظلال، وتقلب بنا الدهر من حال إلى حال، وعفت رسوم آثارنا، واستولت يد الاعتداء على ديارنا، وتصدع شملنا أيدي سبا، وتشعبت بنا سبل المذاهب، وأخنت الحوادث على معشري وآلي، وأفنى الموت أسودي وأشبالي، كل ذلك بقدر جرى به القلم في القدم، وقضاء سبقت به المشيئة قبل الخروج إلى الوجود من العدم، ألقى ما سر من ذلك وساء بالتسليم والرضا، وافوض إليه جل وعلا فيما قدر وقضى، واقر بأن ابتلاءه بعدله، ومعافاته بفضله، وأرجو من رحمته أن يكون ذلك كفارة لذنوب سلفت، وموعظة دعت عن المعاصي وصرفت، وأن ما نالنا من الدنيا وآفاتها، بذنوب اقترفناها فرحمنا بتعجيل مكافاتها، وصلى الله على رسوله الأمين، محمد خاتم النبيين، الذي وصفه في كتابه الكريم، فقال: (وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم) وعلى آله الطيبين الطاهرين، وأصحابه البررة المتقين، وأزواجه الطاهرات أمهات المؤمنين، صلاة دائمة إلى يوم الدين.

وبعد: - جعلك الله بنجوة من النوائب، وأصفى لك الحياة من كدر الشوائب، ولا راعك بحادثة تنسى ما قبلها، وتصغر ما بعدها، وتفتح من النكبات أبوابا لا تستطيع سدها - فإني دعاني إلى جمع هذا الكتاب، ما نال بلادي وأوطاني من الخراب؛ فإن الزمان جر عليها ذيله، وصرف إلى تعفيتها حوله حيله، فأصبحت "كأن لم تعن بالأمس" موحشة العرصات بعد الأنس، قد دثر عمرانها، وهلك سكانها، فعادت مغانيها رسوما، والمسرات بها حسرات وهموما، ولقد وقفت عليها بعدما أصابها من الزلازل ما أصابها، وهي "أول أرض مس جلدي ترابها"، فما عرفت داري، ولا دور والدي وإخوتي، ولا دور أعمامي وبني عمي وأسرتي، فبهت متحيرا مستعيدا بالله من عظيم بلائه، وانتزاع ما خوله من نعمائه.

وقد عظمت الرزية حتى غاضت بوادر الدموع، وتتابعت الزفرات حتى أقامت حنايا الضلوع، وما اقتصرت حوادث الزمان على خراب الديار دون هلاك السكان، بل كان هلاكهم أجمع، كارتداد الطرف أو أسرع، ثم استمرت النكبات تترى، من ذلك الحين وهلم جرا، فاسترحت إلى جمع هذا الكتاب، وجعلته بكاء للديار والأحباب، وذلك لا يفيد ولا يجدي، ولكنه مبلغ جهدي، وإلى الله عز وجل أشكو ما لقيت من زماني وانفرادي من أهلي وإخواني، واغترابي عن بلادي وأوطاني:
وإليه — عز وجل — أرغب في أن يمن علي وعليهم بغفرانه، ويعوضنا برحمته في دار رضوانه، إنه لا يرد دعاء من دعاه، ولا يخيب رجاء من رجاه.

وقد جعلت هذا الكتاب فصولا؛ فافتتحت كل فصل بما يوافق حالي، ثم أفضت فيما يوافق ذا القلب الخالي، ليلا يأتي الكتاب وهو كله عويل ونياحة، ليس فيه لسوى ذي البث راحة، على أن رزايا الدنيا كالأجل؛ تمهل ولا تمهل، فإن تولت اليوم فغدا تقبل:
وتتبع هذا المعنى صعب وحصره لا يمكن، وقد أوردت منه ما يبرد اللوعة، ويسكن الروعة، والعذر إلى من وقف عليه مبذول، وهو عند الكرام مقبول.

items.text: فصل في ذكر المساكن والمحل والمعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات
فصل في ذكر بكاء الأهل والإخوان

paragraphs.text: Usāma ibn Murshid ibn ʿAlī ibn Muqallad ibn Naṣr ibn Munqidh al-Kinānī—may God forgive him and the entire community of Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace—said: “Praise be to God, though this world shifts us about as shadows shift, and time turns us from one condition to another; though the vestiges of our traces have been effaced, the hand of aggression has seized our dwellings, our company has scattered like the people of Sabaʾ, and diverging paths have carried us apart; though calamities have laid waste my people and my family, and death has destroyed my lions and my cubs. All this is by a decree that the Pen inscribed in eternity, and an ordinance willed before we passed from nonexistence into existence. Whatever of this brings joy or sorrow, I meet with submission and acceptance. To Him, exalted and sublime, I entrust whatever He has decreed and ordained. I acknowledge that His affliction is by His justice, and His preservation from affliction by His bounty. I hope, through His mercy, that this may atone for sins committed in the past and serve as an admonition calling us away from disobedience and turning us aside from it; and that whatever we have suffered from this world and its scourges is for sins we committed, so that He has shown us mercy by hastening their requital. May God bless His faithful Messenger, Muḥammad, the Seal of the Prophets, whom He described in His noble Book, saying, ‘Indeed, you are of an exalted character’; and his good and pure family, his righteous and God-fearing Companions, and his pure wives, the Mothers of the Believers—with a blessing enduring until the Day of Judgment.”

To proceed: may God keep you safe from calamities, make your life clear of the turbidity of troubles, and never terrify you with a disaster that makes you forget what came before it, belittles whatever follows it, and opens doors of misfortune that you cannot close. What prompted me to compile this book was the devastation that befell my lands and homelands. Time dragged its train over them and turned its strength and stratagems to effacing them, until they became ‘as though they had not flourished yesterday,’ their courtyards desolate after being companionable. Their buildings have crumbled and their inhabitants perished; their dwelling places have become mere vestiges, and the joys once found there have turned to regrets and sorrows. I stood among them after the earthquakes had done what they did to them—and this was ‘the first land whose dust touched my skin.’ Yet I could not recognize my own house, nor the houses of my father and brothers, nor those of my paternal uncles, my cousins, and my family. I stood bewildered and confounded, seeking refuge in God from His terrible affliction and the withdrawal of the blessings He had bestowed.

The calamity was so great that the first rush of tears dried up, and sigh followed sigh until they straightened the curves of my ribs. The disasters of time did not stop at destroying the dwellings while sparing their inhabitants: rather, they all perished in the twinkling of an eye, or sooner. Then calamities continued to follow one another, from that time onward. I sought solace in compiling this book and made it a lament for dwellings and loved ones. That neither helps nor avails, but it is the utmost I can do. To God, mighty and majestic, I complain of what I have suffered from my times, of being left alone without my family and brothers, and of my exile from my lands and homelands:

To Him, mighty and majestic, I pray that He may graciously grant His forgiveness to me and to them, and through His mercy recompense us in the abode of His good pleasure. He does not reject the prayer of one who calls upon Him, nor disappoint the hope of one who places hope in Him.

I have arranged this book in chapters, opening each chapter with what accords with my own condition, then ranging more widely over what suits someone whose heart is free of care, lest the book consist entirely of wailing and lamentation, offering comfort to none but the grief-stricken. Yet the calamities of this world are like the appointed hour of death: they may delay, but they grant no reprieve. If they turn away today, tomorrow they return:

To pursue this theme is difficult, and to encompass it is impossible. I have included enough of it to cool the burning anguish and calm the terror. I offer my apology to whoever reads it, and among the generous it will be accepted.

verses.h1: ثم انصرفت فلا أبثك حيبتي
verses.h2: رعش القيام أميس ميس الأصور

verses.h1: Then I turned away—I will not pour out my grief to you—
verses.h2: trembling as I stood, swaying like a man bent to one side.

verses.h1: لو كانت الأحلام ناجتني بما
verses.h2: ألقاه يقظان لأصماني الردى

verses.h1: Had dreams whispered to me what
verses.h2: I would encounter waking, death would have struck me down.

verses.h1: فما أحد من ريبهن سليم
No one is safe from their vicissitudes.

poems.intro: عن ابن أبي مريم قال: مررت بسويقة عبد الوهاب وقد خربت، وعلى حائط. منها مكتوب:

verses.h1: هذي منازل أقوام عهدتهم
verses.h2: في خفض عيش وعز ماله خطر

verses.h1: صاحت بهم نائبات الدهر فانقلبوا
verses.h2: إلى القبور، فلا عين ولا أثر

verses.h1: These are the dwellings of people I once knew
verses.h2: living in ease and matchless honor.

verses.h1: Time’s calamities cried out against them, and they passed
verses.h2: into their graves—not a soul remains, not a trace.

prose_translation.intro: On the authority of Ibn Abī Maryam, who said: I passed through Suwayqat ʿAbd al-Wahhāb after it had fallen into ruin, and on one of its walls was written:

verses.h1: ماذا أرجى بعد آل محرق
verses.h2: درست منازلهم، وبعد إياد

verses.h1: أهل الخورنق والسدير وبارق
verses.h2: والقصر ذي الشرفات من سنداد

verses.h1: جرت الرياح على محل ديارهم
verses.h2: فكأنما كانوا على ميعاد

verses.h1: فإذا النعيم وكل ما يلهى به
verses.h2: يوما يصير إلى بلى ونفاد

verses.h1: ولقد غنوا فيها بأنعم عيشة
verses.h2: في ظل ملك ثابت الأوتاد

verses.h1: What can I hope for after the house of Muḥarriq—
verses.h2: their dwellings effaced—and after Iyād?

verses.h1: The people of al-Khawarnaq, al-Sadīr, and Bāriq,
verses.h2: and the palace with battlements at Sindād.

verses.h1: The winds swept over the site of their dwellings,
verses.h2: as though they had an appointed time to keep.

verses.h1: And behold, luxury and all that gives diversion
verses.h2: one day come to decay and an end.

verses.h1: They once dwelt there in the greatest ease,
verses.h2: in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes were firmly planted.

verses.h1: أي المنازل بعد الحول تعترف
verses.h2: أم هل صباك وقد حكمت منصرف؟

verses.h1: أم ما بكاؤك في دار عهدت بها
verses.h2: عهدا، فأخلف، أم في أيها تقف؟

verses.h1: كأنها بعد عهد العاهدين بها
verses.h2: من الذنوب وخرمى واحف صحف

verses.h1: أضحت خلاء قفارا لا أنيس بها
verses.h2: إلا الجوازي والظلمان تختلف

verses.h1: فأصبحوا بعد نعماهم بمبأسة
verses.h2: والدهر يخدع أحيانا فينصرف

verses.h1: تبكي لهم أعين من شجو غيرهم
verses.h2: وإن بكى لهم باك فقد لهفوا

interludes.text: قوله: يخدع، أي يخالف ما تريد، يقال للرجل إذا وعد ثم أخلف: خدع، وإذا أطلع الضب رأسه ثم أدخله يقال: خدع الضب، وخدع الريق، إذا تغير وفسد، وخدعت السوق؛ إذا كسدت، وقوله: "فينصرف" أي ينقلب ويحول.

verses.h1: Which dwellings do you recognize after a year?
verses.h2: Or will your youthful folly leave you, now that you have grown wise?

verses.h1: Or why do you weep in a dwelling where you once knew
verses.h2: a familiar life, now changed—or at which of them will you stop?

verses.h1: As though, since those who knew them last were there,
verses.h2: the dwellings at al-Dhanūb and the two passes of Wāḥif were written pages.

verses.h1: They have become empty wilderness, with no companions there
verses.h2: except wild cattle and male ostriches coming and going.

verses.h1: After their prosperity, they found themselves in misery;
verses.h2: time sometimes deceives, then turns away.

verses.h1: Eyes weep for them out of grief for others;
verses.h2: and if anyone weeps for them, they themselves have known anguish.

notes.note: The construction «عهدت بها عهداً فأخلف» is uncertain. I take it to mean a remembered way of life that has changed; «عهد» can also mean a pledge, with «أخلف» indicating its failure.
I tentatively read «خرمى واحف» as «خَرْمَيْ واحف», ‘the two passes of Wāḥif,’ rather than as separate place names. The identification and vocalization of al-Dhanūb and Wāḥif are uncertain.

«من شجو غيرهم» literally appears to mean ‘out of grief for others,’ though its connection to weeping for these people is unclear. Another possible reading takes «غيرهم» as «غِيَرهم», referring to their changes of fortune.

interludes: [Al-Dhanūb and Kharmā Wāḥif]: place names.

His word [Yakhdaʿ]: acts contrary to what you wish. Of a man who makes a promise and then breaks it, one says khadaʿa. When a lizard pokes its head out and then draws it back in, one says khadaʿa al-ḍabb. One says khadaʿa al-rīq when saliva changes and becomes foul, and khadaʿat al-sūq when the market becomes stagnant. His expression [fa-yanṣarif]: it turns about and changes.

poems.intro: (لهفوا) : أي الحق ذلك وقال ابن أبي طاهر:

verses.h1: يا منزلا لعب الزمان بأهله
verses.h2: طورا يفرقهم، وطورا يجمع

verses.h1: أين الذين عهدتهم بك مرة
verses.h2: كان الزمان بهم يضر وينفع

verses.h1: أصبحت تفزع من رآك، وطالما
verses.h2: كنا إليك من الحوادث نفزع

verses.h1: أيام لا أغشى لأهلك مربعا
verses.h2: إلا وفيه للمسرة مربع

verses.h1: لهفي عليك، لو أن لهفا ينفع
verses.h2: أو أن دهرا راحم من يجزع

verses.h1: ما كان ذاك العيش إلا خلسة
verses.h2: خطفا كرجع الطرف أو هو أسرع

verses.h1: O dwelling whose people time has toyed with,
verses.h2: now scattering them, now gathering them together.

verses.h1: Where are those I once knew within you,
verses.h2: through whom time dealt harm and benefit?

verses.h1: You now frighten whoever sees you; yet how long
verses.h2: we sought refuge in you from misfortunes!

verses.h1: In those days I never visited a dwelling of your people
verses.h2: without finding that joy, too, had a dwelling there.

verses.h1: My grief for you—if only grief could avail,
verses.h2: or time had mercy on those who lament!

verses.h1: That life was nothing but a stolen moment,
verses.h2: snatched like the blink of an eye, or swifter still.

notes.note: The force of بهم is ambiguous: ‘through whom’ suggests that these people were agents of harm and benefit; alternatively, the phrase may indicate that they themselves experienced time’s harm and benefit.

prose_translation.intro: [Lahfū]: that is, “Add that.” And Ibn Abī Ṭāhir said:

verses.h1: يا ليت أن ديارنا كانت كذا
verses.h2: طورا تفرقنا وطورا تجمع

verses.h1: لكنها درست وأوحشها الردى
verses.h2: من أهلها فهي القفار البلقع

verses.h1: لا يرتجى لهم إياب جامع
verses.h2: لشتاتهم حتى يضم المجمع

verses.h1: Would that our dwellings had been like this:
verses.h2: at times parting us, at times bringing us together.

verses.h1: But they have fallen into ruin, and death has emptied them
verses.h2: of their people: they are now a barren wilderness.

verses.h1: There is no hope of a return that would reunite
verses.h2: their scattered company, until the Gathering brings them together.

notes.note: I understand al-majmaʿ (“the gathering” or “place of assembly”) as the gathering at the Resurrection, though this is not explicitly stated.

poems.poet_from_text: عبد الله بن الزبعري في العاص بن وائل
poems.intro: وقال عبد الله بن الزبعري في العاص بن وائل:

poet.from_text: عبد الله بن الزبعري في العاص بن وائل

verses.h1: وأصبحت المنازل وهي قفر
verses.h2: مخلاة عليهن القتام

verses.h1: كأن الناس بعدك نظم سلك
verses.h2: تقطع لا يقوم له نظام

verses.h1: And the dwellings have become desolate,
verses.h2: abandoned, with dust upon them.

verses.h1: After you, the people are like beads strung on a thread
verses.h2: that has snapped: no order holds them together.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā said of al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil:

poems.poet_from_text: المتنبي أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين
poems.intro: وقال المتنبي أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين:

poet.from_text: المتنبي أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين

verses.h1: أبنى أبينا نحن أهل منازل
verses.h2: أبدا غراب البين فينا ينعق

verses.h1: نبكي على الدنيا وما من معشر
verses.h2: جمعتهم الدنيا فلم يتفرقوا

verses.h1: أين الأكاسرة الجبابرة الألى
verses.h2: جمعوا الكنوز فما بقين ولا بقوا

verses.h1: من كل من ضاق الفضاء بجيشه
verses.h2: حتى توى فحواه لحد ضيق

verses.h1: خرس إذا نودوا، كأن لم يعلموا
verses.h2: أن الكلام لهم حلال مطلق

verses.h1: O sons of our father, we are dwellers in abodes;
verses.h2: among us the raven of parting forever croaks.

verses.h1: We weep for this world, yet there is no company
verses.h2: the world has gathered that has not parted.

verses.h1: Where are the Khusraws, those tyrants who
verses.h2: amassed treasures? Neither the treasures nor they endured.

verses.h1: Each one for whose army the wide earth was too narrow,
verses.h2: until he perished and a narrow grave enclosed him.

verses.h1: Mute when called, as though they did not know
verses.h2: that speech was freely permitted them.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Mutanabbī, Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn, said:

verses.h1: وما أهل المنازل غير ركب
verses.h2: مناياهم رواح وابتكار

verses.h1: لنا في الدهر آمال طوال
verses.h2: نرجيها، وأعمار قصار

verses.h1: The people of these dwellings are but travelers;
verses.h2: their deaths are departures at evening and at dawn.

verses.h1: In this life we have far-reaching hopes,
verses.h2: whose fulfillment we await—and lives that are short.

verses.h1: يا منزلا نسجت له أيدي الصبا
verses.h2: من حوكهن سبائبا وبرودا

verses.h1: هل كنت إلا منزلا عمدت له
verses.h2: عقب الزمان فغادرته عميدا؟

verses.h1: O dwelling, for which the east wind’s hands have woven
verses.h2: fine cloths and striped cloaks of their own weaving!

verses.h1: Were you anything but a dwelling assailed
verses.h2: by time’s vicissitudes, which left it stricken?

verses.h1: قفا نعط المنازل من جفون
verses.h2: لها في الشوق أحشاء غزار

verses.h1: عفت آياتهن، وأي ربع
verses.h2: يكون له على الزمن الخيار؟

verses.h1: Stop, you two: let us offer the dwellings tears from eyes
verses.h2: whose depths overflow with longing.

verses.h1: Their traces have been effaced—and what abode
verses.h2: can have its way against time?

notes.note: أحشاء غزار, literally ‘copious innards,’ is an unusual and uncertain description of the eyes. I have understood it as depths overflowing with tears in longing; ‘tears’ is implicit rather than explicit in the Arabic.

poems.intro: وقال أبو تمام، حبيب بن أوس الطائي:

verses.h1: يا منزلا أعطى الحوادث حكمها
verses.h2: لا مطل في عدة ولا تسويفا

verses.h1: أرسى بناديك الندى وتنفست
verses.h2: نفسا بعقوتك الرياح ضعيفا

verses.h1: شعف الغرام بعقوتيك، وربما
verses.h2: روت رباك الهائم المشعوفا

verses.h1: ولئن نرى بك ملقيا أجرانه
verses.h2: ضيف الخطوب، لقد أصاب مضيفا

verses.h1: وهي الفجائع لم تزل نكباتها
verses.h2: يألفن ربع المنزل المألوفا

verses.h1: خلفت بعقوتك الشؤون وطالما
verses.h2: كانت بنات الدهر عنك خلوفا

verses.h1: أيام لا تسطو بأهلك نكبة
verses.h2: إلا تراجع صرفها مصروفا

verses.h1: O dwelling that granted its consent to Time’s changes,
verses.h2: with no delay in a promise, no postponement.

verses.h1: Generosity settled in your gathering-place, and the winds breathed
verses.h2: a faint breath in your courtyard.

verses.h1: Passion is smitten with your two courtyards; how often
verses.h2: your hills quenched the thirst of the love-stricken wanderer!

verses.h1: Though we see it settling down within you—
verses.h2: calamity, your guest—it has indeed found a host.

verses.h1: Such are disasters: their blows have always
verses.h2: haunted the precincts of the familiar home.

verses.h1: Troubles have moved into your courtyard, though for so long
verses.h2: the daughters of Time had kept away from you,

verses.h1: in the days when no calamity assailed your people
verses.h2: but that its assault was recoiled, repelled.

notes.note: الندى can mean either generosity or dew. I have chosen generosity, in keeping with the gathering-place and the imagery of hospitality in line 4.
ملقيا أجرانه appears to evoke a camel laying its neck on the ground to settle down. The form أجرانه is unusual; I have taken it as a plural referring to necks and rendered the apparent sense.
I read خلفت as meaning that troubles have succeeded the former occupants, and الشؤون as adverse events. The unvocalized wording leaves the precise reading uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Tammām, Ḥabīb ibn Aws al-Ṭāʾī, said:

verses.h1: وأبى المنازل إنها لشجون
verses.h2: وعلى الصبابة إنها لتبين

verses.h1: فاعقل بنضو الدار نضوك نقتسم
verses.h2: فيها الصبابة: مسعد، ومعين

verses.h1: لا تمنعني وقفة أشفى بها
verses.h2: داء الصبابة إنها ماعون

verses.h1: واسق الأثافي من شؤونك ريها
verses.h2: إن الضنين بدمعه لضنين

verses.h1: By my father, these dwellings are sorrows indeed,
verses.h2: and they plainly reveal longing.

verses.h1: Tether your worn-out mount beside the wasted dwelling; let us share
verses.h2: the longing there, as consoler and helper.

verses.h1: Do not deny me a halt with which to heal
verses.h2: the sickness of longing: it is a small kindness.

verses.h1: Give the hearthstones their fill from your tear ducts:
verses.h2: whoever is miserly with his tears is miserly indeed.

notes.note: I read «وأبى» as «وأبي», the oath ‘by my father.’ The construction «وعلى الصبابة إنها لتبين» is unclear, particularly the preposition «على»; the translation tentatively takes the dwellings as revealing or expressing longing.

poems.intro: وقال أبو نواس الحسن بن هانئ:

verses.h1: عفا المصلى فأقوت الكثب
verses.h2: مني فالمربدان فاللبب

verses.h1: فالمسجد الجامع المروءة والمج
verses.h2: د عفا فالصمان فالرحب

verses.h1: منازل قد عمرتها زمنا
verses.h2: حتى بدا في عذارى الشهب

verses.h1: في فتية كالسيوف هزهم
verses.h2: شرخ شباب وزانهم أدب

verses.h1: ثم أراب الزمان فاقتسموا
verses.h2: أيدي سبا في البلاد فانشعبوا

verses.h1: لن يخلف الدهر مثلهم أبدا
verses.h2: علي، هيهات شأنهم عجب!

verses.h1: Al-Muṣallā has faded away; the dunes lie empty
verses.h2: of me, then al-Mirbadān, then al-Labab.

verses.h1: Then the mosque that gathered manly virtue and glory
verses.h2: fell into ruin, then al-Ṣammān, then al-Raḥb.

verses.h1: Dwellings I inhabited for a time,
verses.h2: until gray appeared at my temples.

verses.h1: Among young men like swords, stirred
verses.h2: by the vigor of youth and adorned with refinement.

verses.h1: Then time turned treacherous, and they scattered,
verses.h2: like the people of Sabaʾ, dispersing across the lands.

verses.h1: Time will never bring forth their like again
verses.h2: for me—never! Their story is a marvel!

notes.note: Al-Muṣallā, al-Mirbadān, and al-Labab are treated as place-names, though their precise locations here are uncertain. Al-kuthub, translated as ‘the dunes,’ may also be a place-name.
The precise locations intended by al-Ṣammān and al-Raḥb are uncertain; the vocalization of al-Raḥb is also uncertain.
عذارى is understood as عذاري, ‘the hair at my temples/cheeks,’ with a final-letter spelling variation or transcription error.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Nuwās al-Ḥasan ibn Hāniʾ said:

verses.h1: فيء إليك، فقد تخون أسرتي
verses.h2: حتف الردى وتحامل النكبات

verses.h1: تلك المنازل ما تمتع واقفا
verses.h2: بزهى الشخوص، ولا وغى الأصوات

verses.h1: ولن تخلف الأيام لي بدلا بهم
verses.h2: أيهات من بدل بهم أيهات

verses.h1: ومعيري بالدهر يعلم في غد
verses.h2: أن الحصاد وراء كل نبات

verses.h1: Come to your senses: my family has been ravaged
verses.h2: by deadly doom and the onslaught of calamities.

verses.h1: Those dwellings no longer delight anyone standing there
verses.h2: with the splendor of human forms or the clamor of voices.

verses.h1: The days will never give me others in their stead—
verses.h2: far beyond reach is any replacement for them, far beyond reach!

verses.h1: He who mocks what Time has done to me will learn tomorrow
verses.h2: that the harvest follows every growth.

notes.note: فيء إليك is unusual as printed. The translation assumes فِئْ إليك, an injunction to return to oneself or recover one’s composure.
بزهى الشخوص is obscure as printed and may contain a textual error. ‘The splendor of human forms’ is tentative, taking زهى as related to زهو, ‘splendor’ or ‘pride.’

poems.poet_from_text: كاسب بن غياث أحد بني حن
poems.intro: وقال كاسب بن غياث أحد بني حن:

poet.from_text: كاسب بن غياث أحد بني حن

verses.h1: هل منزل دارس يبين
verses.h2: سؤال من ما له معين؟

verses.h1: أقوى وأودت به الليالي
verses.h2: وصرف دهر له فنون

verses.h1: فما بربعيه من أنيس
verses.h2: كأن من فيه لم يكونوا

verses.h1: صاح بمن حله زمان
verses.h2: واخترمتهم به المنون

verses.h1: فكل عهد لهم محيل
verses.h2: وكل ربع لهم دفين

verses.h1: سوى الذي حل في فؤادي
verses.h2: من حبهم فهو لا يبين

verses.h1: وكل حي إلى افتراق
verses.h2: تشعبهم نية شطون

verses.h1: Can a ruined dwelling answer
verses.h2: the questions of one who has no helper?

verses.h1: It lies deserted; the nights have destroyed it,
verses.h2: and time’s vicissitudes, which take many forms.

verses.h1: Neither of its two quarters holds a companion,
verses.h2: as though those who lived there had never been.

verses.h1: Time cried out to those who dwelt there,
verses.h2: and death cut them down within it.

verses.h1: Every place once theirs lies desolate,
verses.h2: and every encampment of theirs is buried.

verses.h1: Except what has settled in my heart
verses.h2: of love for them: that does not depart.

verses.h1: Every tribe is bound for separation;
verses.h2: a far-off destination scatters them.

notes.note: The construction يبين سؤال is unclear. The translation takes it as answering a question; understanding or making the question clear may instead be intended.
عهد is taken here as a formerly familiar abode, with محيل meaning altered or desolate. عهد can also mean a bond or remembered acquaintance, so the first hemistich remains somewhat ambiguous.

prose_translation.intro: And Kāsib ibn Ghiyāth, one of the Banū Hann, said:

verses.h1: دعني وتسكاب دمعي في منازلهم
verses.h2: فللشؤون ولي من بعدهم شان

verses.h1: أحبابنا ما الديار اليوم بعدكم
verses.h2: تلك الديار ولا الأوطان أوطان!

verses.h1: Leave me to pour out my tears in their dwellings;
verses.h2: for since they left, my tear ducts and I have known distress.

verses.h1: Our loved ones, since you left, the dwellings today are not
verses.h2: those same dwellings, nor are our homes still home!

opening.note: verse found inside a longer poem of the text

verses.h1: أحبابنا ما الديار اليوم بعدكم
verses.h2: تلك الديار ولا الأوطان أوطان!

verses.h1: Our loved ones, since you left, the dwellings today
verses.h2: are not those dwellings, nor are our homelands home!

poems.poet: محمد بن عبدالله بن سليمان المعري
poems.poet_from_text: القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان
poems.intro: وقال القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان رحمه الله:

poet.expected: محمد بن عبدالله بن سليمان المعري
poet.from_text: القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان

verses.h1: يا معشر الأحباب قد
verses.h2: أضحت منازلهم قبورا

verses.h1: كنت الصغير فليتني
verses.h2: لم أدع بعدهم كبيرا

verses.h1: O company of loved ones—
verses.h2: their dwellings have now become graves.

verses.h1: I was the youngest; if only I
verses.h2: had not been left to grow old after them.

notes.note: The Arabic addresses the loved ones directly, then refers to ‘their dwellings’ in the third person; this shift is retained.
The unvowelled أدع is read here as ‘be left,’ though ‘be called’ is also possible. الصغير and كبيرا may contrast the youngest with the eldest, rather than youth with old age.

prose_translation.intro: And the judge Abū al-Majd Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulaymān, may God have mercy on him, said:

poems.intro: عن زنام الزامر قال: لما اشتد بالمعتصم المرض - في مرضه الذي مات فيه - أفاق في بعض الأيام، فقال: هيئوا لي الزلال؛ لأركب فيه في دجلة غدا، فعملوه، فركب وركبت معه، فمر في دجلة بإزاء منازله، فقال: يا زنام ازمرلي:

verses.h1: يا منزلا لم تبل أطلاله
verses.h2: حاشا لأطلالك أن تبلى

verses.h1: لم أبك أطلالك، لكنني
verses.h2: بكيت عيشي فيك إذ ولى

verses.h1: والعيش أولى ما بكاه الفتى
verses.h2: لا بد للمخزون أن يسلى

verses.h1: قد كان لي فيك هوى مرة
verses.h2: غيره الدهر وما ملا

verses.h1: O dwelling whose traces have not faded,
verses.h2: far be it from your traces to fade!

verses.h1: I did not weep for your traces; rather,
verses.h2: I wept for my life within you when it passed away.

verses.h1: The life one has lived is worthiest of a young man’s tears;
verses.h2: the sorrowful must one day find consolation.

verses.h1: Once I had a love within you;
verses.h2: time changed it, and never wearied.

notes.note: المخزون (‘stored up’) appears to be a misprint for المحزون (‘the sorrowful’), which is the reading translated here.
وما ملا is read as وما مَلَّا (‘and did not weary’), with a rhyme-lengthening final alif. The translation takes ‘time’ as its subject, though the reference is not entirely certain.

prose_translation.intro: From Zunām the piper, who said: When al-Muʿtaṣim’s illness grew severe—the illness from which he died—he regained consciousness one day and said, “Prepare the pleasure boat for me, so that I may ride in it on the Tigris tomorrow.” They made it ready, and he boarded it, and I boarded with him. As he passed along the Tigris opposite his residences, he said, “Zunām, play this for me on your pipe:”

poems.intro: فما زال ينتحب حتى عاد على منزله. مات المعتصم رحمه الله لثماني عشرة بقيت من ربيع الأول سنة سبع وعشرين ومائتين. وحدثني من أثق به، أنه لما وقع بمصر الغلاء العظيم في أيام المستنصر بالله، واستولت كتامة والجند على الدولة، واستنفدوا ما في الخزائن من الأموال، وتضعضعت الدولة، أمر المستنصر بإحضار ابن الجوهري الواعظ، فحضر، ونصب له كرسي، فلما صعد على الكرسي تلفت يمينا وشمالا على نواحي القصر، ثم أنشد:

verses.h1: يا منزلا لم تبل أطلاله
verses.h2: حاشا لأطلالك أن تبلى

verses.h1: O dwelling whose traces have not faded,
verses.h2: may your traces never fade!

prose_translation.intro: He continued sobbing until he returned to his home. Al-Muʿtaṣim, may God have mercy on him, died with eighteen days remaining in Rabīʿ al-Awwal in the year 227. Someone whom I trust told me that when the great famine struck Egypt in the days of al-Mustanṣir bi-llah, and the Kutāma and the troops took control of the state, exhausted the wealth in its treasuries, and left the state weakened, al-Mustanṣir ordered that Ibn al-Jawharī the preacher be brought before him. He came, and a chair was set up for him. When he mounted the chair, he looked right and left around the palace, then recited:

poems.intro: الأبيات، فارتفع البكاء والضجيج في القصر، وما زاد على ذلك، يستعاد منه ويكرره حتى انقضى المجلس. وقال آخر:

verses.h1: أحب منازل الأحبا
verses.h2: ب إن غابوا وإن حضروا

verses.h1: وأسقيها دموع العي
verses.h2: ن إن لم يسقها المطر

verses.h1: بقدر كرامة الأحبا
verses.h2: ب يكرم بعدها الأثر

verses.h1: ولولا راحة الشكوى
verses.h2: لكان القلب ينفطر

verses.h1: I love the dwellings of loved ones,
verses.h2: whether they are absent or present.

verses.h1: I water them with my tears
verses.h2: if the rain does not water them.

verses.h1: As dearly as loved ones are esteemed,
verses.h2: so are their traces honored after they are gone.

verses.h1: Were it not for the relief of lamenting,
verses.h2: the heart would break.

notes.note: The text reads بعدها (‘after her/it’), with no clear feminine singular antecedent. The translation takes this as referring to the loved ones’ departure; the wording may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro: the verses, whereupon weeping and clamor rose in the palace. He added nothing more, but was asked to repeat them and kept doing so until the gathering ended. Another poet said:

verses.h1: أيا منزلا بالدير أصبح خاليا
verses.h2: تلاعب فيه شمال ودبور

verses.h1: كأنك لم تسكنك بيض نواعم
verses.h2: ولم تتبختر في فنائك حور

verses.h1: وأبناء أملاك كرام وسادة
verses.h2: صغيرهم بين الأنام كبير

verses.h1: إذا لبسوا أدراعهم فضراغم
verses.h2: وإن لبسوا تيجانهم فبدور

verses.h1: O dwelling at al-Dayr, now deserted,
verses.h2: where north and west winds play!

verses.h1: As though no fair, tender women had dwelt in you,
verses.h2: nor wide-eyed beauties strutted in your courtyard,

verses.h1: Nor sons of noble kings, nor lords—
verses.h2: even their youngest is great among men.

verses.h1: When they don their coats of mail, they are lions;
verses.h2: when they don their crowns, they are full moons.

notes.note: Al-Dayr literally means ‘the monastery’; it is unclear whether this is a place-name or a reference to a particular monastery. The location is unidentified.

poems.intro: وقال الحارث بن شداد، أخو بني كعب بن عمرو:

verses.h1: إلى الله أشكو ما أرى من عشيرتي
verses.h2: وما كنت فيما قد مضى استزيدها

verses.h1: تذكرنيهم وحدتي، ومنازل
verses.h2: سواء علينا رثها وجديدها

verses.h1: أرى الناس راعوا للديار وللحيا
verses.h2: وكعب بن عمرو لا يريع شريدها

verses.h1: To God I complain of what I see from my clan,
verses.h2: though in days gone by I never asked more of them.

verses.h1: My solitude reminds me of them, as do dwellings
verses.h2: whose worn and new are all alike to us.

verses.h1: I see people returning to their dwellings and rain-watered lands,
verses.h2: but the wanderers of Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr do not return.

notes.note: استزيدها can mean asking more of the clan, with the implication of finding their conduct wanting or reproaching them. The precise sense intended here is uncertain.
الحيا literally means rain; ‘rain-watered lands’ takes it as referring to places offering pasture after rainfall.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Ḥārith ibn Shaddād, a member of Banū Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr, said:

poems.intro: أنشدني الخطيب العالم قدوة الشريعة "أبو زكريا يحيى بن سلامة الحصكفي - حرمه الله - عند اجتماعي به بميافارقين في سنة سبع وعشرين وخمسمائة لبعض أهل المعرة، وقد اجتاز بقرية من أعمال المعرة يقال لها: "سياث" وفيها علوج من الإفرنج يهدمون من جدرانها الحجارة، ويكسرونها بالمعاول؛ ليخف عليهم حملها، فوقف كالمتأسف، وقال:

verses.h1: مررت بربع من سياث فهاجني
verses.h2: بها زجل الأحجار تحت المعاول

verses.h1: تصدى لها عبل الذراع، كأنما
verses.h2: جنى الدهر فيما بينهم حرب وائل

verses.h1: فقلت له: شلت يمينك خلها
verses.h2: لمستخبر أو واقف أو مسائل

verses.h1: منازل قوم حدثتنا حديثهم
verses.h2: ولم أر أجلى من حديث المنازل

verses.h1: I passed a dwelling-site in Siyāth, and was stirred
verses.h2: by the clamor of stones there beneath the pickaxes.

verses.h1: A burly-armed man set upon them, as though
verses.h2: time had kindled between them the war of Wāʾil.

verses.h1: I said to him: “May your right hand wither! Leave them
verses.h2: for one seeking tidings, one pausing here, or one asking questions.”

verses.h1: The dwellings of a people have told us their story;
verses.h2: I have seen no account clearer than the account of dwellings.

notes.note: The place-name سياث is unvocalized; its rendering as Siyāth is tentative.
The “war of Wāʾil” probably refers to the Basus War between Bakr and Taghlib, tribes descended from Wāʾil. The comparison apparently casts the man and the stones as hereditary enemies.

prose_translation.intro: The learned preacher, an exemplar of the Sacred Law, Abū Zakariyyā Yaḥyā ibn Salama al-Ḥaṣkafī—may God protect him—recited to me, when I met him in Mayyāfāriqīn in the year 527, some verses by a man of al-Maʿarra. He had passed through a village in the district of al-Maʿarra called Siyāth, where Frankish infidels were tearing stones from its walls and breaking them with pickaxes to make them easier to carry. He stopped, seemingly grief-stricken, and said:

verses.h1: إذا أنت لم ترع العهود لمنزل
verses.h2: فلست براع عهد أهل المنازل

verses.h1: ولا سيما دار ولدت بربعها
verses.h2: وكنت بها جذلان في خير آهل

verses.h1: If you do not keep faith with a dwelling,
verses.h2: you will not keep faith with those who dwell there.

verses.h1: Especially a home within whose grounds you were born,
verses.h2: where you lived joyful among the finest people.

poems.intro: وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة المخزومي:

verses.h1: هاج ذا القلب منزل
verses.h2: بالبليين محول

verses.h1: غيرت آيه الصبا
verses.h2: وجنوب وشمأل

verses.h1: فلئن بان أهله
verses.h2: لبما كان يؤهل

verses.h1: قد أرانا بغبطة
verses.h2: فيه نلهو ونجذل

verses.h1: A dwelling has stirred this heart,
verses.h2: desolate at al-Baliyyayn.

verses.h1: The east wind has altered its traces,
verses.h2: and the south wind and the north.

verses.h1: Though its people have departed,
verses.h2: it was indeed once inhabited.

verses.h1: I can still see us in happiness,
verses.h2: playing there and rejoicing.

notes.note: البليين is treated as a place name, provisionally transliterated al-Baliyyayn; its vocalization and location are uncertain.
The construction لبما is unclear to me. It is rendered as an emphatic recollection, ‘indeed once,’ contrasting the dwelling’s former habitation with its present abandonment.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī said:

poems.intro: وقال جرير بن عطية بن الخطفي:

verses.h1: ذم المنازل بعد منزلة اللوى
verses.h2: والعيش بعد أولئك الأقوام

verses.h1: ضربت معارفها الروامس بعدنا
verses.h2: وسجال كل مجلجل سجام

verses.h1: ولقد أراك
verses.h2: وأنت جامعة الهوى يثنى بعهدك خير دار مقام

verses.h1: فإذا أتيت على المنازل باللوى
verses.h2: فاضت دموعي غير ذات نظام

verses.h1: Scorn all dwellings after the dwelling at al-Liwā,
verses.h2: and life after those people.

verses.h1: The effacing winds battered its landmarks after we left,
verses.h2: as did the torrents of every thundering, rain-laden cloud.

verses.h1: Indeed, I once saw you
verses.h2: gathering all my love within you; your former days were praised, O finest dwelling-place.

verses.h1: Whenever I come upon the dwellings at al-Liwā,
verses.h2: my tears overflow in no ordered stream.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the first hemistich probably ends after وأنت جامعة الهوى. The supplied division is preserved here. The syntax of يثنى بعهدك خير دار مقام is uncertain; the translation tentatively takes it as praise of the dwelling’s former days, followed by an address, ‘O finest dwelling-place.’

prose_translation.intro: And Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn al-Khaṭafā said:

verses.h1: ألا حييا قصرا رسوم المنازل
verses.h2: بسلان سلمانين أو ميث عاقل

verses.h1: خلت من أنيس صالحين فأصبحت
verses.h2: مرادا لوحدان النعاج الخواذل

verses.h1: بما قد أرى الحي الجميع بغبطة
verses.h2: بها، والنوى قطاعة للوسائل

verses.h1: Come, you two, briefly greet the traces of the dwellings
verses.h2: in the watercourses of Salmānayn or the soft plains of ʿĀqil.

verses.h1: They stand empty of good companions, and have become
verses.h2: a haunt for solitary wild cows that have left the herd.

verses.h1: Once I would see the whole tribe living happily
verses.h2: there—but separation severs ties.

notes.note: The function of قصرا is uncertain; ‘briefly’ is a provisional reading. The precise locations of Salmānayn and ʿĀqil are uncertain.
The opening بما is syntactically unclear. The translation takes the line as recalling the tribe’s former happiness in these dwellings.

verses.h1: أأبكاك رسم المنزل المتقادم
verses.h2: بأمراش أقوى من حلول الأخارم

verses.h1: فأمرت به عيناك لما عرفتها
verses.h2: بمبتدر نظم الفريدين ساجم

verses.h1: لعرفانك الربع الذي صدع العصا
verses.h2: به البين صدعا ليس بالمتلائم

verses.h1: فقد كنت أدرى أن للبين صيحة
verses.h2: على الحي في يوم لنفسك ضائم

verses.h1: Has the trace of the age-old dwelling made you weep,
verses.h2: at Amrāsh, deserted by the dwellers of al-Akhārim?

verses.h1: So your eyes, when you recognized it, overflowed there
verses.h2: with streaming tears, rushing like two strings of pearls.

verses.h1: Because you recognized the campsite where the staff was split
verses.h2: by parting—a split that will never mend.

verses.h1: For I had known that parting has a cry
verses.h2: over the tribe, on a day cruel to your soul.

notes.note: Amrāsh and al-Akhārim are unidentified; their vocalization is uncertain. I take حلول as ‘dwellers,’ but whether al-Akhārim names a place or a group is unclear.

The construction مبتدر نظم الفريدين is uncertain. The translation takes it as an image of tears rushing like strung pearls; مبتدر may more specifically mean ‘outpacing,’ and the precise reference of the dual الفريدين is unclear.
I read أدرى as أدري, ‘I knew,’ giving a shift from second-person address to first-person speech. As written, it could instead be أدرى, ‘better aware,’ allowing ‘you knew better.’

interludes: [Amrāsh]: a place.

poems.intro: وقال الراعي، وهو عبيد بن حصين النميري - وكان قومه ارتحلوا، فصار بعضهم إلى العراق، وبعضهم إلى الشام:

verses.h1: تذكرت فاستبكاك رسم المنازل
verses.h2: بقارة أقوى أو بسوقة حائل

verses.h1: خلت من جميع ساكن وتبدلت
verses.h2: ظباء السليل بعد خال وجامل

verses.h1: ذكرت بها من لن أبالي بعده
verses.h2: تفرق حي في النوى متزايل

verses.h1: وإن امرأ بالسيف أكبر همه
verses.h2: وبطنان ليس الشوق عنه بغافل

verses.h1: You remembered, and the traces of the dwellings made you weep,
verses.h2: at Qārah, now deserted, or at Sūqah, now altered.

verses.h1: They stand empty of all inhabitants, and have received in their place
verses.h2: the gazelles of al-Salīl, instead of horses and camel herds.

verses.h1: There I remembered one after whose loss I would not care
verses.h2: if a tribe scattered far and wide in separation.

verses.h1: A man whose chief concern lies at al-Sīf
verses.h2: and Baṭnān—longing never leaves him alone.

notes.note: I take Qārah and Sūqah as place names, and aqwā and ḥāʾil as descriptions of the deserted and altered traces. Their precise locations, and this parsing of the unvocalized text, are uncertain.
The rare word khāl is tentatively rendered as ‘horses’; its intended sense here is uncertain. Al-Salīl appears to be a place name, but I cannot identify it securely.
Al-Sīf and Baṭnān are taken as place names. The introduction suggests locations associated with Iraq and Syria respectively, but their precise identification is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Rāʿī—ʿUbayd ibn Ḥuṣayn al-Numayrī—said, after his people had departed, some going to al-ʿIrāq and others to al-Shām:

verses.h1: شعفت بعهد ذكرته المنازل
verses.h2: وكيف تناسى الحلم والشيب شامل

verses.h1: لعمرك لا أنسى ليالي منعج
verses.h2: ولا عاقلا، إذ منزل الحي عاقل

verses.h1: فيا حبذا أيام يحتل أهلها
verses.h2: بذات الغضا والحي في الدار آهل

verses.h1: وإذ نحن ألاف لدى كل منزل
verses.h2: ولم تتفرق للطيات الحمائل

verses.h1: I am enthralled by a time the dwellings recalled—
verses.h2: yet how can one forget good sense when gray hair has spread?

verses.h1: By your life, I shall not forget the nights at Munʿij,
verses.h2: nor ʿĀqil, when ʿĀqil was the tribe’s dwelling-place.

verses.h1: How lovely were the days when her people encamped
verses.h2: at Dhāt al-Ghaḍā, and the tribe thronged the dwelling-place!

verses.h1: When we were close companions at every stopping-place,
verses.h2: and the clans had not scattered to their separate destinations.

notes.note: The syntax of وكيف تناسى الحلم is uncertain. The translation takes الحلم as ‘good sense’ and تناسى as forgetting or disregarding it; a second-person reading would require understanding تناسى as shortened from تتناسى.
The feminine pronoun in أهلها (‘her/its people’) has no explicit antecedent. It may refer to a beloved, as translated, or to an abode.

verses.h1: حي المنازل إذ لا نبتغي بدلا
verses.h2: بالدار دارا، وبالجيران جيرانا

verses.h1: نهدي السلام لأهل الغور من ملح
verses.h2: هيهات من ملح بالغور مهدانا

verses.h1: أحبب إلي بذاك الجزع منزلة
verses.h2: بالطلح طلحا وبالأعطان أعطانا

verses.h1: Greet the dwellings, where once we sought no exchange—
verses.h2: no home for our home, no neighbors for our neighbors.

verses.h1: We send greetings from Milḥ to the people of al-Ghawr;
verses.h2: how far from Milḥ, in al-Ghawr, lies our greeting’s destination!

verses.h1: How dear to me is that valley bend as a dwelling,
verses.h2: those acacias as acacias, those camel-watering grounds as watering grounds!

notes.note: The identification and vocalization of ملح, provisionally transliterated Milḥ, are uncertain. Al-Ghawr means the lowlands; the particular region intended is unclear.
مهدانا is ambiguous here. ‘Our greeting’s destination’ is a tentative interpretation; it may instead refer to the greeting being sent.
The repeated nouns in the second hemistich are syntactically compressed. I take them as continuing the exclamation, specifying the acacias and camel-watering grounds as further objects of affection.

poems.intro: روى أن أبا عمرو بن العلاء - رحمه الله - غاب عن البصرة عشرين سنة، ثم عاد فجلس مجلسه في الجامع، ففقد إخوانه وأصحابه الذين كانوا يقعدون إليه، فبكى، وأنشأ يقول:

verses.h1: يا منزل الحي الذي
verses.h2: ن تفرقت بهم المنازل

verses.h1: أصبحت بعد عمارة
verses.h2: قفرا تهب بك الشمائل

verses.h1: فلئن رأيتك موحشا
verses.h2: فبما رأيت وأنت آهل

verses.h1: O dwelling of the people
verses.h2: whose abodes have scattered them,

verses.h1: After being inhabited, you have become
verses.h2: a wasteland where the north winds blow.

verses.h1: Though I now see you desolate,
verses.h2: how often I have seen you full of people!

prose_translation.intro: It is related that Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ’—may God have mercy on him—was away from al-Basra for twenty years. Then he returned and took his usual seat in the congregational mosque. Finding his friends and companions, who used to sit with him, no longer there, he wept and began to recite:

verses.h1: هل أنت منصرف فتنظر ما ترى
verses.h2: أبقى الحوادث من رسوم المنزل؟

verses.h1: دار بإحدى الرجلتين كأنها
verses.h2: قد عفيت حججا، ولما تحلل

verses.h1: فسقيت من دار
verses.h2: وإن لم تسمعي أصواتنا قطر الربيع المسبل

verses.h1: قد كان أهلك مرة لك زينة
verses.h2: فاستبدلوا بدلا ولم تستبدلي

verses.h1: فابكي إذا بكت المنازل أهلها
verses.h2: معذورة، وظلمت إن لم تفعلي

verses.h1: أهلا كراما لن يحلك مثلهم
verses.h2: في ذا الزمان ولا الزمان المقبل

verses.h1: Will you turn back and see what you can discern
verses.h2: of the dwelling’s traces left by time’s upheavals?

verses.h1: A dwelling at one of al-Rijlatayn, as though
verses.h2: effaced for years, though not yet settled anew.

verses.h1: May you, dwelling, be watered—
verses.h2: though you cannot hear our voices—with spring’s streaming rain.

verses.h1: Your people were once your adornment;
verses.h2: they found a dwelling in your place, but you found none in theirs.

verses.h1: So weep when dwellings weep for their people,
verses.h2: blameless in your grief; you would do wrong not to.

verses.h1: For noble people, whose like will never dwell in you
verses.h2: in this age or the age to come.

notes.note: Al-Rijlatayn is unidentified; the unvocalized name’s pronunciation is uncertain.
ولما تحلل is unclear in context. The translation tentatively reads تُحلَل, ‘be inhabited,’ taking the phrase to mean that the dwelling has not yet been inhabited anew.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAdī ibn al-Riqāʿ al-ʿĀmilī said:

verses.h1: لمن المنازل أقفرت بعباء؟
verses.h2: لو شيت هيّجتِ الغداةَ بكائي

verses.h1: لولا التجلد، واعترافي أنه
verses.h2: لا قوم إلا عقرهم لفناء

verses.h1: لرثيت أصحابي الذين توجهوا
verses.h2: ودعوت أخرس لا يجيب دعائي

verses.h1: وفراق ذي حسب وروعة فاجع
verses.h2: داويته بتجمل وعزاء

verses.h1: ليرى الرجال الشامتون صلابتي
verses.h2: وأكف ذاك بعفة وحياء

verses.h1: Whose are the dwellings, deserted at ʿAbāʾ?
verses.h2: Had I wished, they would have stirred my tears this morning.

verses.h1: Were it not for fortitude, and my acknowledgment that
verses.h2: no people’s dwelling-place escapes destruction,

verses.h1: I would have mourned my companions who departed,
verses.h2: and called to something mute that does not answer my call.

verses.h1: Parting from a man of noble lineage, and the shock of calamity—
verses.h2: I have treated these with dignified composure and patience,

verses.h1: so that gloating men might see my firmness,
verses.h2: while I hold that grief in check with restraint and modesty.

notes.note: ʿAbāʾ (عباء) appears to be a place name, but its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

شيت probably represents شئت, with the hamza omitted or misprinted. The translation reads شئت and هيجت as first-person verbs; the unvocalized text also permits other readings, including taking the dwellings as the subject of هيجت: ‘they would have stirred my tears.’
‘That grief’ interprets ذاك (‘that’) as referring to the mourning or distress described earlier; its precise referent is not explicit.

verses.h1: منازل أضحت للرياح منازلا
verses.h2: تردد فيها بين نؤي ورمدد

verses.h1: شجدت صاحبي أطلالها فتهللت
verses.h2: مدامعه فيها، وما قلت: أسعد

verses.h1: وقلت لعيني في المنازل عبرة
verses.h2: من الشوق لم تملك بصبر فتردد

verses.h1: Dwellings that have become dwellings for the winds,
verses.h2: which wander through them between a tent-trench and scattered ashes.

verses.h1: Their ruins grieved my companion, and there welled up
verses.h2: his tears among them, though I had not said, “Weep with me.”

verses.h1: I said: “My eye has a tear for these dwellings,
verses.h2: born of longing, which patience could neither restrain nor turn back.”

notes.note: شجدت appears corrupt; translated as شجت, “grieved,” with أطلالها (“their ruins”) as its subject.
The syntax and vocalization are uncertain. The translation takes وقلت as “I said,” followed by a statement beginning لعيني, and reads لم تملك ... فتردد as passive verbs referring to the tear.

verses.h1: سألت الغوادي ملحفا في سؤالها
verses.h2: وناشدتها في سقى برقة ثهمد

verses.h1: منازل ما أبقى البلى من عراصها
verses.h2: سوى أرسم معفوة الآى همد

verses.h1: I begged the morning rainclouds, pressing my plea,
verses.h2: and implored them to water Burqat Thahmad.

verses.h1: Dwellings—of their open grounds, decay has spared
verses.h2: only lifeless outlines, their markings effaced.

verses.h1: تزافر صحبي يوم ذي الأثل زفرة
verses.h2: تذوب قلوب من لظاها وأضلع

verses.h1: منازل لم تسلم عليهن مقلة
verses.h2: ولا جم بعد البين فيهن مدمع

verses.h1: فدمع على رسم الديار مفرق
verses.h2: وقلب على أهل الديار مروع

verses.h1: My companions heaved a sigh that day at Dhū al-Athl,
verses.h2: whose blaze melts hearts and ribs.

verses.h1: Dwellings at whose sight no eye escaped unharmed,
verses.h2: nor, since the parting, has any well of tears there filled again.

verses.h1: So tears are scattered over the traces of the dwellings,
verses.h2: and the heart is distraught for their people.

notes.note: Dhū al-Athl appears to be a place name; its location is uncertain.

The phrase «ولا جم ... مدمع» is ambiguous. I take جم to mean ‘filled again,’ with مدمع as a source or well of tears, continually drained by weeping. A sense closer to ‘no tearful eye found rest’ may also be intended.

poems.intro: وقال عبيد الله بن قيس الرقيات:

verses.h1: يا سند الظاعنين من أحد
verses.h2: حييت من منزل ومن سند

verses.h1: ما إن بمثواك غير راكدة
verses.h2: سفع وهاب كالفرخ ملتبد

verses.h1: استبدلت بالظباء والبقر العي
verses.h2: ن خلاف العقائل الخرد

verses.h1: فساخط أنت أم رضيت بما اس
verses.h2: تبدلت بالحي بعدهم فقد

verses.h1: بدلت غير الرضا وشط بهم عن
verses.h2: ك صروف المنون والأبد

verses.h1: O hillside of those who departed from Uḥud,
verses.h2: hail to you, dwelling place and hillside.

verses.h1: Nothing remains at your dwelling but motionless hearthstones,
verses.h2: soot-darkened, and ash clumped like a huddled chick.

verses.h1: You have taken gazelles and wide-eyed wild cattle
verses.h2: in place of bashful, noble women.

verses.h1: Are you displeased, then, or content with what
verses.h2: you took in exchange for the tribe after they left? Indeed,

verses.h1: you were given little cause for contentment; far from you
verses.h2: the turns of fate and time have carried them.

notes.note: The word هاب is uncertain. I tentatively understand it as referring to ash, from هبا, used of dust or ash rising or scattering. ‘Hearthstones’ is inferred from راكدة سفع, literally ‘motionless, darkened [things].’

The construction استبدلت بالظباء ... خلاف العقائل is unusual: the preposition would normally mark what was relinquished. The translation follows the apparent sense that wild animals have replaced the women.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUbayd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى أبو القاسم علي بن الحسين بن موسى بن محمد بن موسى بن إبراهيم بن موسى بن جعفر بن محمد بن علي بن الحسين بن علي بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليهم -:

verses.h1: أعلى العهد منزل بالجناب
verses.h2: كان فيه متى أردت طلابي؟

verses.h1: المغاني تلك المغاني فهل في
verses.h2: هن ما قد عهدت من إطرابي؟

verses.h1: ليست الدار بعد أن توحش الد
verses.h2: ار نوى غير جندل وتراب

verses.h1: فإذا لم يعد حنيني على الدا
verses.h2: ر حبيبا فليس يغني انتحابي

verses.h1: Does the dwelling at al-Janāb remain as I knew it,
verses.h2: where, whenever I wished, I found what I sought?

verses.h1: The abodes are those same abodes; but is there still
verses.h2: within them what used to stir my delight?

verses.h1: The dwelling, once it has been left desolate
verses.h2: by separation, is nothing but stones and dust.

verses.h1: So if my longing for the dwelling cannot bring back
verses.h2: a loved one, my sobbing is of no avail.

notes.note: I take al-Janāb as a place name; its precise identification is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā Abū al-Qāsim ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Mūsā ibn Muḥammad ibn Mūsā ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with them all—said:

poems.poet_from_text: الشريف نظام الملك أبو الحسن على الفاطمي
poems.intro: وقال الشريف نظام الملك أبو الحسن على الفاطمي، أحد شعراء الدولة بمصر - إذ أنا بها - ويعرف بالأخفش:

poet.from_text: الشريف نظام الملك أبو الحسن على الفاطمي

verses.h1: أحبابنا لم تذق عيناي مذ بعدت
verses.h2: عني منازلكم غمضا ولا وسنا

verses.h1: ولا وجدت لقلبي من يسر به
verses.h2: ولم تر العين شيئا بعدكم حسنا

verses.h1: Our beloved, my eyes have tasted—since your dwellings grew
verses.h2: far from me—neither sleep nor drowsiness.

verses.h1: Nor have I found anyone to gladden my heart,
verses.h2: nor has my eye seen anything beautiful since you left.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf Niẓām al-Mulk Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī al-Fāṭimī, known as al-Akhfash, one of the court poets in Egypt when I was there, said:

poems.intro: وقال البكاء - واسمه أرطاة بن كعب (جاهلي) :

verses.h1: لمن المنازل قد عفون سنينا
verses.h2: أقفرن بعد تحدد وبلينا

verses.h1: بقنان ودعة والبقيل تغيرت
verses.h2: بعدي تحن بها الرياح حنينا

verses.h1: وبدارة السلم التي شوقتها
verses.h2: دمن يظل حمامها يبكينا

verses.h1: ما كنت أول من تفرق شمله
verses.h2: ورأى الغداة من الفراق يقينا

verses.h1: Whose dwellings are these, effaced over the years,
verses.h2: Left desolate after their freshness, and worn away?

verses.h1: At Qinān Wadʿa and al-Buqayl, they have changed
verses.h2: Since I left; the winds moan mournfully through them.

verses.h1: And at Dārat al-Salam, for which I yearned,
verses.h2: Are traces of dwellings whose doves keep making us weep.

verses.h1: I was not the first whose company was scattered,
verses.h2: Who saw that morning the certainty of parting.

notes.note: تحدد is unclear here. The translation provisionally assumes تجدد, ‘renewal’ or ‘freshness,’ with a possible dotting error in the source.
The locations and their vocalizations are uncertain. قنان ودعة is rendered as Qinān Wadʿa, but could mean ‘the peaks of Wadʿa’; البقيل is provisionally vocalized al-Buqayl.
شوقتها is interpreted as passive شُوِّقْتُها, ‘I was made to yearn for it.’ The unvocalized form is ambiguous. يبكينا is read as يُبكينا, ‘makes us weep,’ though ‘weeps for us’ is also possible.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Bakkāʾ—whose name was Arṭāʾa ibn Kaʿb (a pre-Islamic poet)—said:

poems.intro: وقال الرماح بن ميادة، وميادة أمه سندية، وأبوه الأبرد بن ثوبان بن سراقة بن سلمى، ابن ظالم:

verses.h1: منازل أما أهلها فتحملوا
verses.h2: فساروا، وأما خيمها فمقيم

verses.h1: كأني بها لما عرفت رسومها
verses.h2: ثقيل لدى أيدي الرقاة سليم

verses.h1: ولم تر عيني مربعا مثل مربع
verses.h2: بذي العش لو أن النعيم يدوم

verses.h1: Dwelling places—their people have packed up
verses.h2: and gone away, but their tents remain.

verses.h1: There, when I recognized their traces, I was like
verses.h2: a snakebitten man, gravely ill in the hands of charm-healers.

verses.h1: My eyes have never seen a spring encampment like the one
verses.h2: at Dhū al-ʿIshsh—if only bliss would last.

notes.note: The location and precise vocalization of Dhū al-ʿIshsh (ذي العش) are uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rammāḥ ibn Mayyadah said—Mayyadah was his mother, a woman from Sind, and his father was al-Abrad ibn Thawbān ibn Suraqah ibn Salmā ibn Ẓālim:

poems.poet_from_text: عباس بن كبير بن جابر بن عمرو بن غيظ بن السبد
poems.intro: وقال عباس بن كبير بن جابر بن عمرو بن غيظ بن السبد:

poet.from_text: عباس بن كبير بن جابر بن عمرو بن غيظ بن السبد

verses.h1: سقى الصفرات العفر حول تبالة
verses.h2: إلى رحب بالوشم غيث مطبق

verses.h1: منازل من حيي ذؤيب بن مازن
verses.h2: وغيظ وكعب قبل أن يتفرقوا

verses.h1: عصائب في بر البلاد وبحرها
verses.h2: فمنهم شآم غائر ومشرق

verses.h1: ديار من الحي الذين رماحهم
verses.h2: معاقل في الهيجا وبالوتر تسبق

verses.h1: عظام مقاريهم جماع فدورهم
verses.h2: يد الدهر تنتاب النهار وتطرق

verses.h1: بهم تتقى الحرب العوان وفيهم
verses.h2: حفاظ على جل الأمور ومصدق

verses.h1: May the dust-colored al-Ṣafarāt around Tabālah be watered,
verses.h2: as far as Raḥb in al-Washm, by an all-enveloping rain.

verses.h1: Abodes of the clans of Dhuʾayb ibn Māzin,
verses.h2: Ghayẓ, and Kaʿb, before they scattered—

verses.h1: Bands across the country’s land and sea,
verses.h2: some bound for al-Shām, some for the lowlands, and some eastward.

verses.h1: Homes of a people whose spears
verses.h2: are strongholds in battle and take the lead in avenging blood.

verses.h1: Great are their guest-bowls, capacious their cooking pots,
verses.h2: sought out forever by day and visited by night.

verses.h1: Through them recurrent warfare is warded off, and in them
verses.h2: are steadfastness in weighty matters and proven valor.

notes.note: Al-Ṣafarāt and Raḥb appear to be place-names; their precise identification and vocalization are uncertain.
حيي appears to be the construct dual, ‘the two clans,’ but three names follow. The grouping or wording is unclear; the translation uses ‘clans.’
The compressed phrase بالوتر تسبق is understood as taking precedence in exacting blood vengeance; its precise construction is uncertain.
فدورهم appears to be a misprint for قدورهم, ‘their cooking pots,’ adopted here. جماع is understood as ‘capacious,’ describing pots large enough to hold a whole slaughtered animal.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAbbās ibn Kabīr ibn Jābir ibn ʿAmr ibn Ghayẓ ibn al-Sabad said:

poems.intro: عن سنان بن يزيد الديلمي قال: كنت مع مولاي جرير بن سهم التيمي، وهو يسير أمام أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليه - إلى الشام، فلم انتهى إلى مدائن كسرى، وقف مولاي ينظر، ثم تمثل:

verses.h1: جرت الرياح على محل ديارهم
verses.h2: فكأنما كانوا على ميعاد

verses.h1: The winds swept over the site of their dwellings,
verses.h2: as though they had an appointed time to depart.

prose_translation.intro: From Sinān ibn Yazīd al-Daylamī, who said: I was with my master, Jarīr ibn Sahm al-Taymī, as he traveled ahead of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with him—toward al-Shām. When he reached Madāʾin Kisrā, my master stopped to look, then quoted this verse:

poems.intro: الأبيات التي تقدمت للأسود بن يعفر، فقال له علي - رضوان الله عليه -: أي شيء قلت؟ فأنشده الشعر، فقال: هلا قلت: "كم تركوا من جنات وعيون" ثم قال: يا ابن أخي إن هؤلاء كفروا النعم، فحلت بهم النقم، فإياكم وكفر النعم، فتحل بكم النقم. وقال الشريف البياضي:

verses.h1: مالي أعلل نفسي بالوقوف على
verses.h2: منازل أقفرت منكم وأطلال؟

verses.h1: وأبتغي البرء منها وهي بالية
verses.h2: هيهات! كيف يداوي باليا بال؟

verses.h1: Why do I console myself by standing before
verses.h2: dwellings empty of you, and ruined remains?

verses.h1: And seek healing from them, though they are worn away?
verses.h2: Far from it! How can the worn-out heal the worn-out?

prose_translation.intro: The foregoing verses are by al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur. ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—said to him, “What did you say?” So he recited the verses to him. He said, “Why did you not say, ‘How many gardens and springs they left behind’?” Then he said, “My nephew, these people were ungrateful for their blessings, so calamities befell them. Beware of ingratitude for blessings, lest calamities befall you.” al-Sharīf al-Bayāḍī said:

verses.h1: يذكرني لمع البروق منازلي
verses.h2: بنجد وأهليها، فأضنى بها وجدا

verses.h1: وهذي النوى حكم من الله نازل
verses.h2: وما كنت ممن يستطيع له ردا

verses.h1: The flashing lightning reminds me of my homes
verses.h2: in Najd and their people, and I waste away with longing for them.

verses.h1: This separation is a decree sent down by God,
verses.h2: and I was never one who could avert it.

verses.h1: حي المنازل بين حمة فاللوى
verses.h2: إن كنت مشتغلا بهن عميدا

verses.h1: يا برق حمة ما فعلت على البلى
verses.h2: لا زلت يصحبك الغمام سديدا

verses.h1: فلئن بكيت لأبكين صبابة
verses.h2: ولئن صبرت لأصبرن جليدا

verses.h1: Greet the dwellings between Ḥumma and al-Liwā,
verses.h2: if you are absorbed in them, stricken with love.

verses.h1: O Barq Ḥumma, how have you fared amid decay?
verses.h2: May the clouds ever attend you, unerring in their course.

verses.h1: If I weep, I shall surely weep from longing;
verses.h2: and if I endure, I shall surely endure with fortitude.

notes.note: The identification and vocalization of حمة, rendered here as Ḥumma, are uncertain.

برق حمة is taken as a place designation, Barq Ḥumma; برق may refer to rocky ground rather than lightning. The precise sense of سديدا is also uncertain; it is rendered as describing clouds that do not miss their destination.
The unvocalized بكيت and صبرت can mean either ‘I wept/endured’ or ‘you wept/endured.’ Both are taken here as first person.

poems.intro: وقال عبيد الله بن قيس الرقيات:

verses.h1: ما هاج من منزل بذي العلم
verses.h2: بين لوى المنجنون فالسلم

verses.h1: لم تبق منه الرياح معلمة
verses.h2: إلا بقايا الثمام والحمم

verses.h1: وقفت بالدار ما أبينها
verses.h2: إلا إدكارا، توهم الحلم

verses.h1: بادت وأقوت من الإنيس كما
verses.h2: أقوت محاريب دارس الأمم

verses.h1: واستبدل الحي بعدها إضما
verses.h2: هيهات غمر الفرات من إضم

verses.h1: What longing a dwelling at Dhū al-ʿAlam stirred,
verses.h2: between Liwā al-Manjanūn and al-Salam!

verses.h1: The winds have left no recognizable trace of it,
verses.h2: save remnants of thumām grass and charcoal.

verses.h1: I stood at the dwelling, unable to recognize it
verses.h2: save through memory, like the dim recollection of a dream.

verses.h1: It fell to ruin, emptied of human company, as
verses.h2: the sanctuaries of long-vanished peoples lay deserted.

verses.h1: After leaving it, the tribe chose Iḍam instead—
verses.h2: how far the deep waters of al-Furāt are from Iḍam!

notes.note: The precise locations of Dhū al-ʿAlam, Liwā al-Manjanūn, and al-Salam are uncertain; their vocalizations are provisional. The opening is understood as an exclamation, with longing implied rather than explicitly named.
The compressed phrase توهم الحلم is understood as comparing recognition of the dwelling to the indistinct recollection of a dream; its exact grammatical relation to إدكارا is uncertain.
The unusual expression دارس الأمم is taken to mean peoples or nations that have long vanished.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUbayd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:

poems.intro: قيل لأعرابية أصيبت بابنها: ما أحسن عزاءك! قالت: إن فقدي إياه أمنى كل فقد سواه، وإن مصيبته هونت على المصائب من بعده، ثم قالت:

verses.h1: من شاء بعدك فليمت
verses.h2: فعليك كنت أحاذر

verses.h1: كنت السواد لناظري
verses.h2: فعليك يبكي الناظر

verses.h1: ليت المنازل والديار
verses.h2: حضائر ومقابر

verses.h1: Let whoever wishes die after you;
verses.h2: it was for you that I feared.

verses.h1: You were the pupil of my eye;
verses.h2: for you my eye now weeps.

verses.h1: Would that the dwellings and homes
verses.h2: were enclosures and graves.

notes.note: حضائر is uncertain here. I have provisionally translated it as ‘enclosures,’ reading it as a possible variant or misprint of حظائر.

prose_translation.intro: A Bedouin woman who had lost her son was told, “How well you bear your grief!” She replied, “Losing him has left me unafraid of any other loss, and the calamity of his death has made all calamities after him easier for me to bear.” Then she said:

poems.intro: كان الرقاشي يجتمع إليه جماعة من أصحابه وإخوانه يتحدثون ويتذاكرون، فغاب في بعض أحواله، ثم رجع بعد مدة، فوجد بعضهم قد مات، وبعضهم قد غاب، فوقف على مجلسهم وبكى، وقال:

verses.h1: لولا التطير قلت غيركم
verses.h2: ريب الزمان فخنتم عهدي

verses.h1: درست منازل كنت آلفها
verses.h2: من بعدكم، وتغيرت بعدي

verses.h1: Were it not for fear of ill omens, I would say: you have been changed
verses.h2: by time’s vicissitudes, and so have broken faith with me.

verses.h1: The dwellings I used to frequent have fallen into ruin
verses.h2: after your departure, and have changed since mine.

prose_translation.intro: A group of al-Raqāshī’s companions and friends used to gather around him to converse and reminisce. On one occasion he went away, then returned after some time to find that some of them had died and others had gone away. He stood at their gathering place, wept, and said:

poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء (أحمد بن عبد الله) بن سليما المعري:

verses.h1: أعفى المنازل قبر يستراح به
verses.h2: وأفضل اللبس فيما أعلم الكفن؟

verses.h1: إن الذين على وجه الثرى وطئوا
verses.h2: يشابهون أناسا في الثرى دفنوا

verses.h1: The most trouble-free dwelling is a grave in which one rests;
verses.h2: and the finest clothing, so far as I know, is the shroud.

verses.h1: Those who have trodden the surface of the earth
verses.h2: resemble people buried within it.

notes.note: أعفى is an unusual comparative here; I understand it as ‘most free from trouble or burdens.’ The source’s final question mark has no clear grammatical basis and may be a transcription error.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ (Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah) ibn Sulaymā al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: دعني وتسكاب دمعي في منازلهم
verses.h2: فللشؤون ولي من بعدهم شان

verses.h1: أحبابنا ما الديار اليوم بعدكم
verses.h2: تلك الديار، ولا الأوطان أوطان

verses.h1: Leave me to pour out my tears amid their dwellings,
verses.h2: for since they left, my tear ducts and I have our own sorrow.

verses.h1: Our loved ones, now that you are gone, these dwellings are not
verses.h2: the dwellings they were, nor are our homelands home.

verses.h1: أبكى إلى الشوق أن كانت منازلكم
verses.h2: بجانب الغرب خوف القيل والقال

verses.h1: أقول: بالخد خال حين أذكره
verses.h2: خوف الرقيب، وما بالخد من خال

verses.h1: I weep toward [the east], though your dwellings lay
verses.h2: on the western side—for fear of gossip.

verses.h1: I say, “There is a mole on his cheek,” when I mention him,
verses.h2: for fear of the watcher, though there is no mole on his cheek.

notes.note: The opening أبكى إلى الشوق is obscure as written. I tentatively read إلى الشرق (‘toward the east’) instead of إلى الشوق (‘toward longing’), giving a contrast with الغرب (‘the west’) and suggesting that the speaker conceals the direction of the beloved’s dwelling.
The referent of ‘him’ in أذكره is not explicit; I take it to be the beloved. The Arabic says simply ‘the cheek,’ without an explicit possessive.

verses.h1: يا منزلا لعبت به أيدي البلى
verses.h2: لعب الشكوك، وقد بدا بتيقن

verses.h1: إما تناشدني العهود فإنها
verses.h2: خيست فكانت بين ذخر المقتنى

verses.h1: نفض الصبي أوراقه، وأعادني
verses.h2: خوط اليراعة، كيف تغمز تنحني

verses.h1: إني لأعلم قبل فضى ختمه
verses.h2: ما في كتاب بالمشيب معنون

verses.h1: O dwelling, the hands of decay have played with you
verses.h2: as doubts play, though once you stood beyond doubt.

verses.h1: If you call on me to remember the pledges, they
verses.h2: were broken, and became part of the treasures laid away.

verses.h1: Youth shook off its leaves and left me
verses.h2: a slender reed: however you press it, it bends.

verses.h1: I know, before I break its seal,
verses.h2: what is in a book whose heading is gray hair.

notes.note: The construction «لعب الشكوك، وقد بدا بتيقن» is compressed and somewhat unclear. I take it to contrast the dwelling’s former unmistakable presence with the uncertainty produced by its decay.

The second hemistich is obscure and may be corrupt. «خيست» can suggest that the pledges were violated, but its connection with «فكانت بين ذخر المقتنى» (‘and became among stored-up treasures’) is unclear. The translation is tentative.
I read «الصبي» as «الصبا» (‘youth’), apparently a transcription error, in keeping with the imagery of aging.

verses.h1: أمزمعة للبين ليلى ولم تمت
verses.h2: كأنك عما قد أظلك غافل؟

verses.h1: ستعمل إن شطت بهم غربة النوى
verses.h2: وزالوا بليلي أن لبك زائل

verses.h1: وأنك مسلوب التصبر والأسى
verses.h2: إذا بعدت ممن تحب المنازل

verses.h1: Is Laylā resolved to depart, and you have not died?
verses.h2: It is as though you are heedless of what looms over you!

verses.h1: You will learn, if distant exile carries them far away,
verses.h2: and they depart with Laylā, that your reason will depart,

verses.h1: and that you will be stripped of patience and consolation
verses.h2: when your dwellings lie far from the one you love.

notes.note: للبيت (‘for the house’) appears to be a misprint for للبين (‘to depart’), the reading adopted here.
ستعمل (‘you will act/work’) appears to be a transposition error for ستعلم (‘you will learn’). بليلي is read as بليلى (‘with Laylā’).
الأسى is taken here as al-usā, ‘consolations’ (plural of uswa). The unvocalized text can also mean ‘grief’; the intended sense is uncertain.

verses.h1: تطوى المنازل عن حبيبك دائبا
verses.h2: وتظل تبكيه بدمع ساجم

verses.h1: ألا أقمت ولو على جمر الغضا
verses.h2: قلبت، أوحد الحسام الصارم؟

verses.h1: كذبتك نفسك لست من أهل الهوى
verses.h2: تشكو الفراق وأنت عين الظالم؟

verses.h1: You tirelessly cover the stages, away from your beloved,
verses.h2: yet keep weeping for him with streaming tears.

verses.h1: Why did you not stay, even if on embers of ghaḍā wood
verses.h2: you were tossed—or on the edge of a keen sword?

verses.h1: Your soul has deceived you: you are not among true lovers.
verses.h2: You complain of separation, yet you are the very wrongdoer?

notes.note: Read تطوى as تطوي, ‘you traverse,’ rather than the passive ‘are traversed’; the following second-person address supports this reading.
The translation tentatively reads قلبت as قُلِّبْتَ, ‘you were tossed/turned about,’ and separates أوحد into أو حدّ, ‘or the edge of.’ The printed spacing and punctuation appear faulty.

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ
poems.intro: قلت: لي على من تقدم ذكره من الشعراء فضل المزية؛ إذ كنت دونهم صاحب الرزية فكان شعري أولى أني قدم على أشعارهم، وإن قصرت بي البلاغة عن اقتفاء آثارهم، لكن للمتقدم السبق، وهو بالتقدمة أولى وأحق، وإن كنت وهم كما قال ذر لأبيه: يا أبه. مالك إذا تكلمت أبكيت الناس، وإذا تكلم غيرك لم يبكهم؟ قال: يا بني. ليست النائحة المستأجرة كالثكلى. وأنا ذاكر شيئا من شعر أخي - رحمه الله - وشعري مما يدخل في هذا الفصل: قال أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ - رضي الله عنه -:

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

verses.h1: يا منزلا لعب البلى برسومه
verses.h2: شعفا ببهجته فليس يريم

verses.h1: لا تبعدن وجاد ربعك وابل
verses.h2: يروى ثراك أتيه ويسيم

verses.h1: فاسق الربوع من الدموع سجالها
verses.h2: إن الرسوم لها عليك رسوم

verses.h1: O dwelling whose traces decay has toyed with,
verses.h2: enamored of your beauty, unwilling to depart.

verses.h1: May you never perish; may a downpour drench your grounds,
verses.h2: its floodwaters soaking your soil and providing pasture.

verses.h1: So water the dwelling-sites with bucketfuls of tears:
verses.h2: the traces have their rightful claims upon you.

notes.note: The intended sense and construction of ويسيم are uncertain. It ordinarily means ‘lets graze’; ‘providing pasture’ interprets it here as the rain enabling grazing.

prose_translation.intro: I say: I have a distinction over the poets mentioned above, for I, unlike them, am the one who suffered the calamity. My poetry therefore had a better claim to be placed before theirs, even if my eloquence fell short of following in their footsteps. Yet those who came before have precedence, and are more entitled to be placed first—even though my case and theirs is like what Dharr said to his father: “Father, why is it that when you speak, you make people weep, but when others speak, they do not?” He replied: “My son, a hired mourner is not like a bereaved mother.” I shall now relate some of my brother’s poetry—may God have mercy on him—and my own that belongs in this chapter. My brother, ʿIzz al-Dawla Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Murshid ibn ʿAlī ibn Muqallad ibn Naṣr ibn Munqidh—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

verses.h1: سل المنازل عمن كان يسكنها
verses.h2: من الأحبة والإخوان ما صنعوا؟

verses.h1: تخبرك وعظا بلا لفظ فقد نظرت
verses.h2: آمالهم والمنايا كيف تصطرع

verses.h1: وهكذا بعد نفخ الصور خاوية
verses.h2: تضحى المنازل أعلاهن متضع

verses.h1: بنى أبي إن عدا دهر ففرقنا
verses.h2: فهم نفسي بكم ما عشت مجتمع

verses.h1: نزحتم أدمعي حتى لقد محلت
verses.h2: جفون عيني، ومات اليأس والطمع

verses.h1: وإن دهرا رمى عن جيده دررا
verses.h2: أمثالكم لزمان عاطل ضرع

verses.h1: Ask the dwellings about those who once inhabited them—
verses.h2: the loved ones and brothers: what became of them?

verses.h1: They will admonish you without a word, for they have seen
verses.h2: how their hopes and death wrestle with one another.

verses.h1: And so, after the Trumpet is blown, desolate
verses.h2: the dwellings will become, their loftiest brought low.

verses.h1: Sons of my father, though time assail us and scatter us,
verses.h2: my soul’s concern remains centered on you as long as I live.

verses.h1: You drained my tears until no moisture remained
verses.h2: in the lids of my eyes; despair and hope both died.

verses.h1: An age that cast from its neck pearls
verses.h2: such as you is indeed a time unadorned and abased.

notes.note: The unvocalized نظرت can mean either ‘they [the dwellings] have seen’ or ‘you have seen.’ The translation takes the dwellings as its subject.

poems.poet: علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد
poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

poet.expected: علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد
poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

verses.h1: يا منزلا أضحى كجسمي باليا
verses.h2: حزن القلوب، وحسرة للناظر

verses.h1: لي كل يوم في ربوعك زفرة
verses.h2: يرمى لظاها بالشرار الطائر

verses.h1: غربت شموسك والذين عهدتهم
verses.h2: بك في ملمات الزمان الغابر

verses.h1: فعليهم مني سلام نشره
verses.h2: متضوع كثنائهم في الحاضر

verses.h1: O dwelling, worn away like my body,
verses.h2: a sorrow to hearts, a grief to the beholder.

verses.h1: Each day amid your grounds I heave a sigh
verses.h2: whose blaze sends sparks flying.

verses.h1: Your suns have set, and so have those I knew
verses.h2: within you through the trials of bygone days.

verses.h1: To them I send a greeting whose fragrance
verses.h2: wafts abroad like the praise of them today.

notes.note: يرمى is taken as يرمي, ‘casts’ or ‘sends forth,’ with a likely spelling or transcription error in the final letter. Read literally as a passive, it would mean that the blaze ‘is pelted with’ sparks.
في الحاضر is taken to mean ‘in the present,’ hence ‘today’; it could also mean ‘among those present.’

poems.intro: قلت: كان رحمه الله تأخر عنا، وخرجت أنا وأخواي إلى دمشق، ثم إلى مصر، فكان يتأسف لبعدنا عنه، وخلو منازلنا منا. وهذا شيء من شعري في هذا المعنى، بعد ما أصابنا من الزلازل ما أصابنا، قلت:

verses.h1: إلى الله أشكو روعتي لمنازل
verses.h2: خلت، وجوى قلبي لأهل المنازل

verses.h1: سيوفي إذا ما نازلتني ملمة
verses.h2: حصوني إذا خفت الردى ومعاقلي

verses.h1: مضوا سلفا قبلي فلم أحظ بعدهم
verses.h2: من العيش والعمر الطويل بطائل

verses.h1: To God I lament my anguish over dwellings
verses.h2: left empty, and my heart’s burning grief for their people.

verses.h1: They were my swords whenever calamity assailed me,
verses.h2: my fortresses and strongholds whenever I feared death.

verses.h1: They passed on before me, and after them I gained
verses.h2: nothing of worth from life and its long years.

prose_translation.intro: I said: He—may God have mercy on him—had stayed behind, while my two brothers and I went to Dimashq, then to Miṣr. He grieved at our being far from him and at our dwellings standing empty of us. Here are some verses of mine on this theme, composed after the earthquakes had inflicted upon us what they did. I said:

verses.h1: هذي منازلهم عفت وتفرقوا
verses.h2: فسل المنازل عنهم ماذا لقوا؟

verses.h1: تخبرك أن الأرض قد وارتهم
verses.h2: وأبت لهم أن يسمعوا أو ينطقوا

verses.h1: وبقيت بعدهم لهم فادح
verses.h2: وكآبة تضنى، وخطب يطرق

verses.h1: أرجو اللحاق بهم، ودون لحاقهم
verses.h2: باب من الأجل المؤقت مغلق

verses.h1: فإذا نهاني عن رجاء لقائهم
verses.h2: يأسى هفا قلب إليهم شيق

verses.h1: These are their dwellings, now effaced; their people have scattered.
verses.h2: Ask the dwellings what befell them.

verses.h1: They will tell you that the earth has buried them
verses.h2: and refuses to let them hear or speak.

verses.h1: I remained after them, prey to crushing sorrow,
verses.h2: wasting grief, and calamity that comes knocking.

verses.h1: I hope to join them, but between me and that reunion
verses.h2: stands a locked gate—the allotted term of life.

verses.h1: Whenever I am restrained from hoping to meet them
verses.h2: by my despair, my longing heart flutters toward them.

verses.h1: قل للذي فقد الأحبة وانثنى
verses.h2: يسقى منازلهم دموعا تسجم:

verses.h1: ماذا وقوفك في الديار مسائلا
verses.h2: عن أهلها، ومتى يجيب الأبكم؟

verses.h1: سل عنهم صرف الزمان فإنه
verses.h2: بهم من الدار المحيلة أعلم

verses.h1: أفناهم ريب المنون، وهذه
verses.h2: آثارهم عظة لمن يتوسم

verses.h1: هي شيمة الأيام: كف تبتنى
verses.h2: مذ كانت الدنيا وكف تهدم

verses.h1: وإذا رأيت محسدين فقلما
verses.h2: ترجيهم الأيام حتى يرحموا

verses.h1: وترى تقلب هذه الدنيا بنا
verses.h2: وكأننا فيها سكارى نوم

verses.h1: Say to the man who lost his loved ones and turned
verses.h2: to water their dwellings with streaming tears:

verses.h1: Why do you stand among the dwellings, asking
verses.h2: about their people? When does the mute give an answer?

verses.h1: Ask time’s vicissitudes about them, for time
verses.h2: knows more of them than the desolate dwelling does.

verses.h1: The ravages of death destroyed them; these
verses.h2: traces of theirs are a lesson for those who discern.

verses.h1: Such is the way of days: one hand builds—
verses.h2: ever since the world began—and another hand destroys.

verses.h1: If you see men much envied, the days scarcely
verses.h2: give them respite before they become objects of pity.

verses.h1: You see how this world turns us about,
verses.h2: while we are as though drunk and asleep within it.

notes.note: The reading ترجيهم is uncertain. I take it as an unhamzated form of ترجئهم, meaning ‘give them respite’ or ‘leave them be’: those now envied are soon reduced to being pitied.

verses.h1: يعنفني في الدار صحبي على البكا
verses.h2: فيا ويح قلبي من خلي وجاهل؟

verses.h1: وقالوا: أتبكي للمنازل؟ قلت: لا
verses.h2: ولكنما أبكى لأهل المنازل

verses.h1: At the dwelling, my companions rebuke me for weeping;
verses.h2: alas for my heart, beset by the carefree and the unknowing!

verses.h1: They said, “Do you weep for the dwellings?” I said, “No—
verses.h2: I weep only for those who dwelt there.”

verses.h1: حيي ربوعك من ربى ومنازل
verses.h2: ساري الغمام بكل هام هامل

verses.h1: وسقتك يا دار الهوى بعد النوى
verses.h2: وطفاء تسفح بالهتون الهاطل

verses.h1: حتى تروض كل ماح ما حل
verses.h2: عاف، وتروى كل ذاو ذابل

verses.h1: أبكيك، أم أبكى زماني فيك، أم
verses.h2: أهليك، أم شرخ الشباب الزائل

verses.h1: ما قدر دمعي إن تقسمه الجوى
verses.h2: والوجد بين أحبة ومنازل؟

verses.h1: أنفقته سرفا وهأنا ماثل
verses.h2: في ماحل أبكى بجفن ما حل

verses.h1: وإذا فرغت إلى العزاء دعوت من
verses.h2: لا يستجيب، ورمت نصرة خاذل

verses.h1: May your haunts—hills and dwellings—be greeted
verses.h2: by clouds passing in the night, with every pouring shower.

verses.h1: And may you, dwelling of love, be watered after our separation
verses.h2: by a heavy cloud spilling copious rain,

verses.h1: until it greens every effaced and barren tract,
