notes.note: The grammatical form of the final عينا is unclear as written. The translation follows the apparent sense of the idiom قرت العين, meaning that the eye is gladdened or content.

prose_translation.intro: He also said—may God have mercy on him:

poems.intro: وهذه الأبيات من شعري في هذا المعنى قلت:
poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: هذي ديار بني أبي ومعاشري
verses.h2: قفر عليها وحشة وظلام

verses.h1: درست محافظة لهم، وتوحشت
verses.h2: من بعدهم، وتعفت الأعلام

verses.h1: فإذا مرتت بها فقل
verses.h2: متمثلا

verses.h1: These are the dwellings of my brothers and companions,
verses.h2: empty, shrouded in desolation and darkness.

verses.h1: They have fallen into ruin, keeping faith with them, and grown forlorn
verses.h2: after their departure; the landmarks have been effaced.

verses.h1: And when you pass by them, say,
verses.h2: quoting a verse:

notes.note: The unusual phrase محافظة لهم is rendered as ‘keeping faith with them’; its precise force here is uncertain.
مرتت appears to be a misprint for مررت, ‘you pass.’ The line appears incomplete, and متمثلا (‘quoting a verse or saying’) introduces a quotation that is not supplied.

prose_translation.intro: These verses are from my own poetry on this theme. I said:

poems.intro: : "يا دار ما صنعت بك الأيام" [نصف المصراع مضمن لأبي نواس] . وقلت:
poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: إذا أنا شارفت الديار تحدثت
verses.h2: بمكنون أسراري الدموع الذوارف

verses.h1: وماذا انتفاعي بالديار وقربها
verses.h2: إذا أقفرت من كل من أنا آلف

verses.h1: When I draw near the dwellings, they speak—
verses.h2: the streaming tears—of my innermost secrets.

verses.h1: What good are the dwellings and their nearness to me,
verses.h2: when they stand empty of everyone I hold dear?

prose_translation.intro: : “O dwelling, what have the days done to you?” [Half the hemistich is borrowed from Abū Nuwās.] And I said:

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: تقول لي الأشواق: هذي ديارهم
verses.h2: فقلت: نعم، لكنها منهم قفر

verses.h1: وما كنت أهوى الدار إلا لأهلها
verses.h2: وبعدهم لا جاد ساكنها القطر

verses.h1: فما الدار تلك الدار بعد قطينها
verses.h2: ولا الدهر فيها بعدهم ذلك الدهر

verses.h1: My longing says to me, “These are their dwellings.”
verses.h2: I say, “Yes, but they are empty of them.”

verses.h1: I loved the dwelling only for its people;
verses.h2: now they are gone, may rain never bless whoever dwells there.

verses.h1: The dwelling is not the same dwelling since its people left,
verses.h2: nor is time there, without them, the time it was.

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: ديار خلت من أهلها وتوحشت
verses.h2: فليس بها مرعى لعين ولا خصب

verses.h1: علاها البلى حتى تعفت رسومها
verses.h2: وأنكرها طرفي فأثبتها القلب

verses.h1: Dwellings emptied of their people and grown desolate:
verses.h2: there is no pasture there for the eye, no verdure.

verses.h1: Decay overtook them until their traces were effaced;
verses.h2: my eyes did not recognize them, but my heart knew them.

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: بنو منقذ ما أنقذوا من زمانهم
verses.h2: وكم أنقذوا من مرهق وأسير

verses.h1: أجاروا على الأيام فاضطغنتهم
verses.h2: وما استمسكوا من جورها بمجير

verses.h1: فلم يبق منهم غير حي كميت
verses.h2: أخي حسرة ما تنقضي وزفير

verses.h1: فقد أقفرت منهم ديار عهدتها
verses.h2: غياثا لملهوف، وذخر فقير

verses.h1: وما أقفرت من ساكن بل من العلى
verses.h2: ومن نائل هامي السحاب غزير

verses.h1: The Banū Munqidh were not saved from Time,
verses.h2: though how many a hard-pressed man and captive they saved!

verses.h1: They offered protection against the days, and the days bore them a grudge;
verses.h2: yet against their tyranny they had no protector to cling to.

verses.h1: None remains of them but a living man like one dead,
verses.h2: a companion of unending grief and sighs.

verses.h1: Their dwellings stand desolate without them—dwellings I once knew
verses.h2: as succor for the distressed and a resource for the poor.

verses.h1: They are empty not of inhabitants, but of greatness,
verses.h2: and of copious bounty, pouring down like rainclouds.

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: ديار الهوى حيي معالمك القطر
verses.h2: وإن لم يدع إلا تذكرك الدهر

verses.h1: عهدتك أفقا للسعود، وساكنو
verses.h2: ربوعك في أرجائك الأنجم الزهر

verses.h1: وعصرهم فصل الربيع نضارة
verses.h2: فهل يرجعن لي ذلك الزمن النضر

verses.h1: إذا مر في فكري الديار وأهلها
verses.h2: فيالي من وجد يجدده الذكر

verses.h1: إذا أوحشتني وحدتي بعد فقدهم
verses.h2: ولهت، كأني قد أصابني السحر

verses.h1: فكيف التسلي والتأسي فيهم
verses.h2: ولا عوض منهم، ولا عنهم صبر

verses.h1: لقد ساءني الدهر الذي سرني بهم
verses.h2: وما ظلموا ساءوا قصاصا بما سروا

verses.h1: Abodes of love, may rain greet your landmarks,
verses.h2: though time has left nothing but the memory of you.

verses.h1: I knew you as a horizon of good fortune; the dwellers
verses.h2: in your quarters were the shining stars within your bounds.

verses.h1: Their time was spring itself in freshness—
verses.h2: will that flourishing time ever return to me?

verses.h1: When those abodes and their people cross my mind,
verses.h2: oh, the longing that remembrance renews in me!

verses.h1: When my solitude leaves me desolate after losing them,
verses.h2: I grow distraught, as though a spell had fallen upon me.

verses.h1: How can I find solace or consolation for their loss,
verses.h2: when none can replace them, and I cannot endure their absence?

verses.h1: Time, which gladdened me through them, has indeed grieved me;
verses.h2: yet they did no wrong: they grieved me in requital for the joy they gave.

notes.note: The plural verbs in the second hemistich apparently refer to the departed loved ones, although the first hemistich makes Time the agent. I read ظلموا as active, ‘they did wrong’; without vowel marks it could also be passive, ‘they were wronged.’

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: لا جاد ربعك من ديار أقفرت
verses.h2: من أهلها صوب الغمام الماطر

verses.h1: لم يبق منك الدهر إلا حسرة
verses.h2: للذاكرين، وعبرة للناظر

verses.h1: يا حسن أول ذلك الدهر الذي
verses.h2: قد كان فيك وقبح هذا الآخر!

verses.h1: May your dwelling, among abodes deserted
verses.h2: by their people, never be watered by the downpour of rain-laden clouds.

verses.h1: Time has left nothing of you but sorrow
verses.h2: for those who remember, and a lesson for whoever looks.

verses.h1: How fair the beginning of that time
verses.h2: that once passed in you, and how ugly this latter time!

notes.note: The unvocalized عبرة can mean either ‘a lesson’ (ʿibra) or ‘a tear’ (ʿabra); both fit the context.

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: إذا بكى لديار باد ساكنها
verses.h2: ذو وحدة ساءه في داره الزمن

verses.h1: بكيت أهلي وأوطاني وآسفني
verses.h2: أن ليس لي بعدهم دار ولا سكن

verses.h1: أخنى الزمان على قومي وملك أو
verses.h2: طاني سواي، فلا أهل ولا وطن

verses.h1: ولم تدع لي المنايا مشتكى حزن
verses.h2: أبثه كمدى إن عادني حزن

verses.h1: When a man weeps for dwellings whose inhabitants have perished,
verses.h2: a lonely man whom time has afflicted in his own home,

verses.h1: I weep for my family and my homelands, and it grieves me
verses.h2: that after them I have neither home nor refuge.

verses.h1: Time laid waste my people, and my homelands
verses.h2: fell into another’s possession: no kin, no homeland.

verses.h1: Death has left me no one to hear my lament,
verses.h2: to whom I might pour out my anguish when sorrow visits me.

notes.note: Sakan, rendered as “refuge,” can mean a dwelling or someone in whom one finds comfort; either sense is possible here.

poems.intro: (آخر ما أثبته من شعر قومي وشعري) وقال الشريف المرتضى، أبو القاسم علي بن الحسين الموسوي - رضي الله عنه -:
poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: ديار كرعن الضيم وهو مصرف
verses.h2: ونادى بهن الموت أهلا فأسمعا

verses.h1: كأن قطين الحي بعد تفرق
verses.h2: جنته الليالي ساعة ما تجمعا

verses.h1: ولو كان يدري بالذين تفرقوا
verses.h2: توجع من فقدانهم وتفجعا

verses.h1: Dwellings that drank deep of oppression as it was dealt out;
verses.h2: death summoned the folk within them and made itself heard.

verses.h1: It is as though the encampment’s people, after a scattering
verses.h2: wrought by the nights, had never gathered for even an hour.

verses.h1: Had the encampment known of those who had scattered,
verses.h2: it would have grieved at their loss and lamented.

notes.note: مصرف is uncertain here; provisionally read as مُصَرَّف, ‘dealt out’ or ‘dispensed.’
أهلاً is taken as the object of ‘summoned,’ meaning inhabitants. It could instead represent death’s cry of ‘Welcome!’
The subject is unstated. The translation takes it to refer to الحي, ‘the encampment,’ in line 2; the antecedent is not certain.

prose_translation.intro: (Here ends what I have recorded of my kinsmen’s poetry and my own.) al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, Abū al-Qāsim ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Mūsawī—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: ولما مررنا بالديار التي خلت
verses.h2: فهن لفقدان الأنيس نواحل

verses.h1: فإشراقها بعد الذين تحملوا ظلام، وضحوات النهار أصائل
أثار الجوى عرفانها، وتبادرت
verses.h2: على أهلها منا الدموع الهوامل

verses.h1: When we passed the dwellings that lay deserted,
verses.h2: they were wasted away for lack of familiar company.

verses.h1: After their people departed, their radiance is darkness, and their bright forenoons are late afternoons.
Recognizing them stirred our burning grief, and there came rushing
verses.h2: our freely flowing tears for their people.

poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: يا ديار الأحباب لا أبصرتك الع
verses.h2: ين من بعد أن حللت رسوما

verses.h1: إن عيشا لنا خلسناه من أي
verses.h2: دي الرزايا لديك كان نعيما

verses.h1: من عذيري من الزمان أخي عوجا
verses.h2: ء أعيا علي أن يستقيما

verses.h1: ليس يعطي البقاء إلا لمن يس
verses.h2: لبه ذلك البقاء حميما

verses.h1: O dwellings of loved ones, may my eye never see you
verses.h2: now that you have become mere traces.

verses.h1: The life we snatched from the hands
verses.h2: of calamities there with you was bliss.

verses.h1: Who will take my side against wayward Time,
verses.h2: which has defied my efforts to set it straight?

verses.h1: It grants long life only to one
verses.h2: whom that long life robs of a loved one.

notes.note: أخي عوجاء is elliptical: literally, ‘brother of a crooked [thing or course].’ I take it to characterize Time as wayward, though the implied noun is uncertain.

poems.intro: كتب إلى الملك الصالح ناصر الأئمة، وكاشف الغمة، أمير الجيوش، سيف الإسلام، غياث الأنام، كافل قضاة المسلمين، وهادي دعاة المؤمنين، أبو الغارات طلائع بن رزيك فتى أمير المؤمنين عزيز مصر - رحمه الله - قصيدة من نظمه، يعزيني عن أهلي الذين هلكوا في الزلازل - رحمهم الله - منها:
poems.subchapter: أبيات من شعر والدي وأخي - رضي الله عنهما - مما يوافق المعنى المقصود

verses.h1: لهف نفسي على ديار من السك
verses.h2: ان أقوت، فليس فيها عريب

verses.h1: ولكم حلها فأنسته أوطا
verses.h2: ن صباه والأهل يوما غريب

verses.h1: فاحتسب ما أصاب قومك مجد الد
verses.h2: ين واصبر فالحادثات ضروب

verses.h1: هكذا الدهر، حكمه الجور والع
verses.h2: دل، وفيه المكروه والمحبوب

verses.h1: إن تخصصكم نوائب مازا
verses.h2: لت لكم دون من سواكم تنوب

verses.h1: فكذاك القناة تكسر يوم الرو
verses.h2: ع منها صدور وتبقى كعوب

verses.h1: My soul grieves for dwellings
verses.h2: emptied of their inhabitants, with not a soul remaining.

verses.h1: How many a stranger once lodged there, and it made him forget
verses.h2: the homes of his youth and his family.

verses.h1: Seek God’s reward for what has befallen your people, Majd al-Dīn,
verses.h2: and be patient, for calamities come in many forms.

verses.h1: Such is time: its rule is injustice and justice,
verses.h2: and in it are both what is hated and what is loved.

verses.h1: If calamities single you out, they have always
verses.h2: befallen you rather than anyone else.

verses.h1: So too, on the day of battle, spears
verses.h2: have their upper shafts broken, while their joints remain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ, champion of the imams, dispeller of distress, commander of the armies, sword of Islam, succor of mankind, guardian of the judges of the Muslims, and guide of the missionaries of the believers, Abū al-Ghārāt Ṭalāʾiʿ‘ ibn Ruzzīk, retainer of the Commander of the Faithful and mighty lord of Miṣr—may God have mercy on him—sent me a poem of his own composition, consoling me for the loss of my family who perished in the earthquakes—may God have mercy on them. Among its verses are:

poems.intro: قال كثير بن عبد الحرمن الخزاعي:

verses.h1: أشاقك بالعبوقرة الديار
verses.h2: نعم منا منازلها قفار

verses.h1: أحب الأرض أرض دموها
verses.h2: وكان لهم بها يوما قرار

verses.h1: فما عندي لواش في هواكم
verses.h2: رضى حتى يموت ولا اعتذار

verses.h1: Have the dwellings at al-ʿAbūqara stirred your longing?
verses.h2: Yes—their abodes are empty of us.

verses.h1: The land I love best is the land they [dwelt in],
verses.h2: where once they had a settled home.

verses.h1: For any slanderer concerning my love for you,
verses.h2: I offer no appeasement till he dies, and no apology.

notes.note: العبوقرة appears to be a place name; its identification and vocalization are uncertain. It is provisionally transliterated al-ʿAbūqara.
دموها is unclear and appears corrupt. The bracketed ‘dwelt in’ is a conjectural rendering suggested by the following hemistich; the intended Arabic wording is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khuzāʿī said:

poems.poet_from_text: محمد بن عبد الملك بن حبيب بن تمام بن معبد بن فقعس بن طريف
poems.intro: وقال محمد بن عبد الملك بن حبيب بن تمام بن معبد بن فقعس بن طريف:

poet.from_text: محمد بن عبد الملك بن حبيب بن تمام بن معبد بن فقعس بن طريف

verses.h1: وإن مروري بالديار التي بها
verses.h2: سليمى ولم ألمم بها لجفاء

verses.h1: وما بالهوى يا أم عمرو ولا الذي
verses.h2: تحملت من وجد عليك خفاء

verses.h1: على أنني يا أم عمرو تهيجني
verses.h2: ديار لكم بالأبرقين خلاء

verses.h1: Indeed, to pass the dwellings where
verses.h2: Sulaymā lives without stopping there is cold neglect.

verses.h1: My love, Umm ʿAmr, and the longing
verses.h2: I have borne are no secret to you.

verses.h1: And yet, Umm ʿAmr, I am stirred
verses.h2: by your deserted dwellings at al-Abraqayn.

notes.note: The precise location of al-Abraqayn is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ḥabīb ibn Tammām ibn Maʿbad ibn Faqʿas ibn Ṭarīf said:

poems.poet: صالح بن عبد الله بن الحجاج
poems.poet_from_text: صالح بن عبد الله بن الحجاج
poems.intro: وقال صالح بن عبد الله بن الحجاج:

poet.expected: صالح بن عبد الله بن الحجاج
poet.from_text: صالح بن عبد الله بن الحجاج

verses.h1: كفى حزنا يا سعد إن بنت أن أرى
verses.h2: ديارك يفليها الحمام المطوق

verses.h1: وأن يسجع القمري فيها إذا بدا
verses.h2: لركبانها قرن من الشمس أورق

verses.h1: وألا أرى يا سعد أهلك جيرة
verses.h2: وأهلي إلا ريثما نتفرق

verses.h1: It is sorrow enough, Saʿd, if you depart, that I should see
verses.h2: ring-necked doves combing through your dwellings;

verses.h1: And that the turtle-dove should coo within them when there appears
verses.h2: to riders there a gray rim of the sun;

verses.h1: And that I should not see, Saʿd, your people as neighbors
verses.h2: to mine, except for the brief span before we part.

notes.note: أورق usually means gray or ash-colored; its precise force here as a description of the sun’s rim is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥajjāj said:

verses.h1: حي الديار إذ الزمان زمان
verses.h2: وإذ السماك جري لنا ومعان

verses.h1: يا حبذا سفوان من متربع
verses.h2: ولربما جمع الهوى سفوان

verses.h1: فإذا مررت على الديار مسلما
verses.h2: فلغير دار أميمة الهجران

verses.h1: Salute the dwellings of the days when life was truly life,
verses.h2: when al-Simāk was our emissary and was granted aid.

verses.h1: How lovely Safwān was as a springtime abode!
verses.h2: How often Safwān brought lovers together!

verses.h1: When you pass the dwellings, offering greetings,
verses.h2: reserve your neglect for dwellings other than Umayma’s.

notes.note: The phrase «السماك جري لنا ومعان» is uncertain. I provisionally read جري as جَرِيّ, ‘emissary’ or ‘agent,’ and معان as مُعان, ‘aided.’ al-Simāk is a star name, but the precise celestial allusion and the sense of ‘aided’ here are unclear; the text may be faulty.
«جمع الهوى سفوان» literally says that Safwān ‘gathered love’; ‘brought lovers together’ is an interpretive rendering.

verses.h1: قل لديار حييتها درس
verses.h2: من صمم ما عييت أم خرس؟

verses.h1: هاجر عنهن سكنهن فما
verses.h2: فيهن من جنة ولا أنس

verses.h1: إلا شبيه بها لبعضهم
verses.h2: في حور المقلتين واللعس

verses.h1: Say to the ruined dwellings you have greeted:
verses.h2: “Is it deafness that keeps you from answering, or muteness?”

verses.h1: Their inhabitants have departed, and now
verses.h2: neither jinn nor humans remain within,

verses.h1: except one there resembling some of them
verses.h2: in its dark eyes with their clear whites, and its dusky lips.

notes.note: The unnamed creature resembling former inhabitants is presumably a gazelle or wild antelope, but the animal is not explicitly identified.

verses.h1: أتعرف رسما كاطراد المذاهب
verses.h2: لعمرة وحشا غير موقف راكب

verses.h1: ديار التي كادت
verses.h2: ونحن على منى تحل بنا، لولا نجاء الركائب

verses.h1: تبدت لنا كالشمس تحت غمامة
verses.h2: بدا حاجب منها وضنت بحاجب

verses.h1: ولم أرها إلا ثلاثا على نمى
verses.h2: وعهدي بها عذراء ذات ذوائب

verses.h1: Do you recognize traces like the coursing of streams,
verses.h2: ʿAmra’s, desolate save where a rider stops?

verses.h1: The dwellings of her who nearly—
verses.h2: while we were at Minā—undid us, had our mounts not sped away.

verses.h1: She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud:
verses.h2: one brow of hers appeared, but she withheld the other.

verses.h1: I saw her only three times, [at Minā?],
verses.h2: and I remember her as a maiden with braided locks.

notes.note: المذاهب is tentatively understood as streams or watercourses; the precise sense of the comparison is uncertain.

The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: ونحن على منى probably belongs with the first hemistich. تحل بنا literally suggests descending upon or alighting with us; ‘undid us’ interprets it as bringing ruin through love, but the intended sense is uncertain.

على نمى is unclear and may be corrupted. The translation tentatively conjectures على منى, ‘at Minā,’ as in line 2. ثلاثا is taken as ‘three times,’ though ‘three nights’ is also grammatically possible.

verses.h1: أراجعة يا ليل أيامنا الألى
verses.h2: بذي الرمث، أم لا مالهن رجوع؟

verses.h1: وخيماتك اللاتي بمنعرج اللوى
verses.h2: بلين بلى لم تبلهن ربوع

verses.h1: ولو لم يهجني الظاعنون لهاجني
verses.h2: حمائم ورق في الديار وقوع

verses.h1: تداعين فاستبكين من كان ذا هوى
verses.h2: نوائح لم تذرف لهن دموع

verses.h1: Will our former days return, O Laylā,
verses.h2: at Dhū al-Rimth—or is there no returning for them?

verses.h1: And your little tents at the bend of al-Liwā—
verses.h2: they have worn away as no dwellings ever have.

verses.h1: Had those departing not stirred my grief, it would have been stirred
verses.h2: by gray doves perched among the dwellings.

verses.h1: They called to one another, making everyone who loved weep—
verses.h2: mourners who shed no tears.

notes.note: I take يا ليل as a shortened vocative form of Laylā; it could alternatively mean “O night.”
The wording بلى لم تبلهن ربوع is difficult, particularly the pronoun ending in تبلهن. The translation tentatively understands a comparison with the decay of other dwellings; the text may be corrupt.

verses.h1: بدا لي وللتيمي قلة صامع
verses.h2: على بعدها مثل الحصان المجلل

verses.h1: فقلت: أرى تلك الديار التي بها
verses.h2: أميمة، يا شوق الأسير المكبل!

verses.h1: The peak of Ṣāmiʿ appeared to me and al-Taymī,
verses.h2: despite its distance, like a caparisoned stallion.

verses.h1: I said: “I see those dwellings where
verses.h2: Umayma lives—oh, the longing of a shackled captive!”

notes.note: Ṣāmiʿ appears to be a mountain name, but its identification is uncertain. Al-Taymī, the speaker’s companion, is unidentified.

verses.h1: أريتك إن نجدا ألظ بأهله
verses.h2: وحرته العليا الغيوث الرواجس

verses.h1: وعاد نبات الأرض رطبا كأنه
verses.h2: إذا اطردت فيه الرياح الطيالس

verses.h1: أمطلع تلك الديار فناظر
verses.h2: إلى أهلها، أم أنت من ذاك آيس؟

verses.h1: Tell me: if there linger over Najd’s people
verses.h2: and its upper lava plain the rumbling rainclouds,

verses.h1: And the earth’s vegetation turns lush again, resembling,
verses.h2: when winds sweep through it, mantles,

verses.h1: Will you visit those dwellings and gaze
verses.h2: upon their people, or have you given up hope of that?

notes.note: I read إن as conditional (‘if’), with the question in line 3 completing the sense. The construction إن نجداً ألظ بأهله ... الغيوث is syntactically awkward as transmitted, so this reading is uncertain.

verses.h1: إن الذين نسوا برامة عهدنا
verses.h2: سعدوا وأشقانا به أوفانا

verses.h1: ظعنوا وشبت وما كبرت وإنما سار الشباب يودع الأظعانا
أجد الديار كما عهدت، وإنما
verses.h2: شكواي أني أفقد الجيرانا

verses.h1: Those who forgot our pledge at Rāma found happiness;
verses.h2: the most faithful to it among us was the most wretched.

verses.h1: They departed, and I turned gray, though I had not grown old; my youth had merely gone to bid the departing caravans farewell.
I find the dwellings just as I knew them; my only
verses.h2: complaint is that I find the neighbors gone.

verses.h1: أمر على الديار ديار ليلى
verses.h2: أقبل ذا الجدار وذا الجدارا

verses.h1: وما من حبي الجدران لكن
verses.h2: محبة كل من سكن الديارا

verses.h1: I pass by the abodes—the abodes of Laylā—
verses.h2: and kiss this wall and that.

verses.h1: It is not out of love for the walls, but
verses.h2: out of love for all who dwelt in those abodes.

verses.h1: كأن ابنة البكري يوم اجتليتها
verses.h2: عبيدة مكحول الدامع مرشق

verses.h1: وذكرنيها بعد ما قد نسيتها
verses.h2: ديار عليها وابل متبعق

verses.h1: وقفت بها والشمس دون مغيبها
verses.h2: قريبا، فهاج الشوق من يتشوق

verses.h1: قليلا، فلما استعجمت عن جوابنا
verses.h2: تعزيت عنها، والدموع ترقرق

verses.h1: فلا الدار تدنيها لنا غير فينة
verses.h2: ولا حبها عن شاحط النأي يخلق

verses.h1: It was as though the daughter of al-Bakrī, the day I beheld her,
verses.h2: ʿUbayda, were a kohl-eyed gazelle, its neck outstretched.

verses.h1: And what reminded me of her, after I had forgotten her,
verses.h2: was a dwelling-place beneath a torrential downpour.

verses.h1: I stood there, the sun not yet set,
verses.h2: but close to it; longing stirred one who longs.

verses.h1: Briefly I stayed; then, when the dwellings gave us no answer,
verses.h2: I sought consolation for her loss, while tears welled up.

verses.h1: The dwelling brings her near to us only now and then,
verses.h2: yet love for her does not wear out through distant separation.

notes.note: I take عبيدة (ʿUbayda) as the daughter’s name, in apposition to ابنة البكري. الدامع looks like a corruption of المدامع, ‘the eyes’ or ‘tear ducts.’ The gazelle is implicit in the descriptive phrase مكحول ... مرشق, rendered ‘kohl-eyed ... its neck outstretched.’
قليلا (‘briefly’) appears to refer back to ‘I stood’ in line 3. The pronoun in عنها could refer either to the beloved or to the abandoned dwelling-place; the translation takes it as the beloved.

verses.h1: لمن الديار ببرقة الروحان
verses.h2: إذ لا نبيع زماننا بزمان

verses.h1: أصبحت بعد نعيم عيش مونق
verses.h2: قفرا، وبعد نواعم أخدان

verses.h1: هل رام جو سويقتين مكانه
verses.h2: أم حل بعد محلنا البردان

verses.h1: هل تؤنسان، ودير أروى دوننا
verses.h2: بالأعزلين، بواكر الأظعان

verses.h1: راجعت بعد سلوهن صبابتي
verses.h2: وعرفت رسم منازل أبكاني

verses.h1: Whose are the dwellings at Barqat al-Rawḥān,
verses.h2: from when we would not trade our days for any other time?

verses.h1: They have become, after the pleasures of a delightful life,
verses.h2: a wasteland, after the presence of tender companions.

verses.h1: Has the hollow of Suwayqatayn departed from its place,
verses.h2: or has al-Bardān settled there after our stay?

verses.h1: Can you two discern—with Dayr Arwā before us—
verses.h2: at al-Aʿzalayn, the caravans departing at dawn?

verses.h1: I returned to my yearning after forgetting those women,
verses.h2: and recognized traces of dwellings that made me weep.

notes.note: The vocalization of الروحان, rendered al-Rawḥān, is uncertain.

The second hemistich is unclear as transmitted. The translation takes حل as active ḥalla, ‘settled,’ with al-Bardān as its subject. A passive reading, ‘has al-Bardān been inhabited,’ is also possible; alternatively, حل may be a misprint for حال, ‘changed.’
راجعت is read here as rājaʿtu, ‘I returned to.’ It could instead be rājaʿat, with صبابتي as the subject: ‘My yearning returned after I had forgotten them.’

verses.h1: هل بالديار الغداة من صمم
verses.h2: أم هل بعهد الأنيس من قدم

verses.h1: أم ما تحيي من ماثل درج الس
verses.h2: يل عليه، كالحوض منهدم

verses.h1: تسأله العهد وهو عهدك واس
verses.h2: تجمع من حله، ولم يرم

verses.h1: إنك أنت المخزون في أثر ال
verses.h2: قوم فإن تنو نيهم تقم

verses.h1: كان بها بعض من هويت ومن
verses.h2: يلق سرورا في العيش لم يدم

verses.h1: يسألني صاحبي بدائي وقد
verses.h2: نام عشاء، وبت لم أنم

verses.h1: إن شفائي واصل دائي لشي
verses.h2: ء واحد وهو أكبر السقم

verses.h1: من عهد ما أورثت حبيبة
verses.h2: والشر يوافي مطالع الأكم

verses.h1: أكنى بغير اسمها وقد يعلم الل
verses.h2: ه خفيات كل مكتتم

verses.h1: مخافة الكاشح المكثر أن
verses.h2: يطرح فيها عوائر الكلم

verses.h1: Are the dwellings deaf this morning,
verses.h2: or have the days of their companions grown remote?

verses.h1: Or what standing remnant do you greet, over which
verses.h2: the flood has passed, leaving it like a collapsed basin?

verses.h1: You ask it about the old days, though it is as you knew it;
verses.h2: those who dwelt there have gathered together, but it has not moved.

verses.h1: You are the one who grieves in the wake
verses.h2: of those people; if you resolve to go their way, you will rise.

verses.h1: Some whom you loved once dwelt there; and whoever
verses.h2: finds joy in life finds that it does not last.

verses.h1: My companion asks me about my ailment, though he
verses.h2: slept that evening, while I passed the night without sleep.

verses.h1: My cure and the root of my ailment are
verses.h2: one and the same—and that is the greatest sickness.

verses.h1: Ever since Ḥabība left me this legacy—
verses.h2: and evil comes upon the hilltops.

verses.h1: I call her by another name, though
verses.h2: God knows the secrets of all who conceal them.

verses.h1: For fear that the spiteful, much-talking man
verses.h2: should cast wounding words against her.

notes.note: The wording is difficult. وهو عهدك is taken as ‘it is as you knew it.’ واستجمع من حله literally appears to say that those who inhabited it gathered together; whether this implies their departure is uncertain.

المخزون (‘stored away’) appears to be a misprint for المحزون (‘grief-stricken’), which is translated here. The phrase تنو نيهم تقم is also uncertain; نيهم is provisionally understood as their intended direction, and تقم as ‘you will rise [to go].’

The syntax of من عهد ما أورثت حبيبة and its connection to the preceding line are unclear. The translation provisionally understands a legacy of love or sickness left by Ḥabība. حبيبة could instead mean ‘a beloved woman’; the person’s identity and any particular allusion in the second hemistich are uncertain.

verses.h1: لأسماء محتل بظاهرة البشر
verses.h2: قديم، ولما يعفه سالف الدهر

verses.h1: يكاد من العرفان يضحك رسمها
verses.h2: ولكم من ليال للديار ومن شهر

verses.h1: Asmāʾ has a campsite on the open ground of al-Bishr,
verses.h2: an ancient one, not yet effaced by time gone by.

verses.h1: The traces of her dwelling almost smile in recognition—
verses.h2: and how many nights and months these dwellings have known!

notes.note: “In recognition” (من العرفان) may suggest the traces recognizing the poet, or their familiarity to him.

verses.h1: قف بالديار التي لم يعفها القدم
verses.h2: بلى، وغيرها الأرواح والديم

verses.h1: لا الدار غيرها بعد الأنيس ولا
verses.h2: بالدار لو كلمت ذا حاجة صمم

verses.h1: دار لأسماء بالغمرين ماثلة
verses.h2: كالوحي ليس بها من أهلها إرم

verses.h1: كأن عيني وقد سال التليل بهم
verses.h2: وعبرة ما هم، لو أنهم أمم

verses.h1: غرب على بكرة، أو لؤلؤ قلق
verses.h2: في السلك جاربه رباته النظم

verses.h1: Stand by the dwellings that age has not effaced—
verses.h2: but yes, the winds and steady rains have changed them.

verses.h1: The absence of its people has not changed the dwelling;
verses.h2: nor is the dwelling deaf—if only it could speak to one in need.

verses.h1: A dwelling of Asmāʾ at al-Ghamrayn, still standing,
verses.h2: like writing, with not one of its people remaining.

verses.h1: It is as though my eye, as al-Talīl flowed with them—
verses.h2: and what neighbors they were, if only they were near!—

verses.h1: were a great bucket on a pulley, or trembling pearls
verses.h2: on a thread whose stringing has failed the women who own them.

notes.note: The syntax and sense are uncertain. The translation takes لا as negation and بعد الأنيس as بُعد الأنيس, ‘the absence of its people.’ Initial لا could instead be corrective: ‘No—it is the absence of its people that changed the dwelling.’ The force of لو كلمت ذا حاجة is also unclear.
التليل is retained as the unidentified name al-Talīl. It may be a textual error for السليل, ‘the valley.’
وعبرة ما هم is difficult to construe and appears corrupt. The translation assumes وجيرة ما هم, ‘and what neighbors they were.’ أُمَم is understood as ‘near.’
جاربه رباته النظم is obscure as printed. The translation tentatively reads جار به رباته النظم as describing stringing that has gone awry for the pearls’ owners; the exact wording may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro: And Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā said:
interludes: [Iram]: anyone.
[Al-Talīl]: a valley.

verses.h1: عوجا على الطلل المحيل لعلنا
verses.h2: نبكي الديار كما بكى ابن خذام

verses.h1: دار لهم إذ هم لأهلك جيرة
verses.h2: إذ تستبيك بواضح بسام

verses.h1: فظللت في دمن الديار كأنني
verses.h2: نشوان باكره صبوح مدام

verses.h1: Turn aside, you two, to the time-worn ruins, that we may
verses.h2: weep for the dwellings as Ibn Khidhām wept.

verses.h1: A dwelling of theirs, when they were neighbors to your people,
verses.h2: when she captivated you with a bright, smiling mouth.

verses.h1: So I lingered among the dwellings’ traces, as though I were
verses.h2: a drunken man greeted at dawn by a morning draught of wine.

notes.note: The source spells the name خذام, rendered here as Khidhām; it is also transmitted as حذام (Ḥidhām). The allusion is to an earlier poet who wept over abandoned dwellings, but his identity and the vocalization of his name are uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Ḥujr said:

verses.h1: طال الوقوف على رسوم ديار
verses.h2: قفر، أسائلها وما استخباري؟

verses.h1: دار تعفت، لا أنيس بجوها
verses.h2: إلا بقايا دمنة وأوراي

verses.h1: جادت عليها
verses.h2: فاضمحل رسومها هزج الرياح بديمة مدرار

verses.h1: دار لمية إذ هم لك جيرة
verses.h2: هيهات منك منازل الزوار

verses.h1: Long have I stood over the traces of dwellings,
verses.h2: deserted, questioning them—but what can my questioning yield?

verses.h1: A dwelling effaced, with no companion in its grounds
verses.h2: save remnants of a darkened campsite and tethering-stakes.

verses.h1: Upon it poured
verses.h2: the roaring winds with steady, copious rain, and its traces vanished.

verses.h1: The dwelling of Mayya, when her people were your neighbors—
verses.h2: far, far from you are the dwellings of those who used to visit!

notes.note: أوراي appears to be a transposition error for أواري, meaning tethering-places or tethering-stakes; the latter is adopted here.

The hemistich division appears displaced, probably belonging after رسومها. The wording هزج الرياح and its syntax are uncertain; the translation provisionally takes it as ‘roaring winds,’ the delayed subject of جادت.

poems.intro: وقال ذو الرمة، غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود:

verses.h1: كأن ديار الحي بالزرق خلفة
verses.h2: من الأرض أو مكتوبة بمداد

verses.h1: إذا قلت: يعفو، لاح منها مهيج
verses.h2: على الهوى من طارف وتلاد

verses.h1: وما أنا في دار لمى عرفتها
verses.h2: بجلد، ولا دمعي بها بجماد

verses.h1: إذا قلت بعد النأي يا مي نلتقي
verses.h2: عدتني بكره أن أراك عواد

verses.h1: As though the tribe’s dwellings at al-Zurq were fresh growth
verses.h2: from the earth, or words written in ink.

verses.h1: Whenever I say, “It is fading,” something appears there to stir
verses.h2: my longing, both new and old.

verses.h1: In a dwelling of Mayy’s that I recognized, I am not
verses.h2: steadfast, nor do my tears there refuse to flow.

verses.h1: Whenever I say after separation, “O Mayy, we shall meet,”
verses.h2: hindrances keep me, against my will, from seeing you.

notes.note: The sense of خلفة is uncertain here; it is provisionally rendered as “fresh growth,” a possible botanical meaning. The location and vocalization of الزرق (al-Zurq) are unverified.
لمى is read as لمي, “of Mayy,” referring to the woman addressed in line 4; the final letter appears to be a typing or OCR variation.

prose_translation.intro: And Dhū al-Rumma, Ghaylān ibn ʿUqba ibn Masʿūd, said:

verses.h1: أما والذي حج الملبون بيته
verses.h2: شلالا ومولى كل باق وهلك

verses.h1: ورب القلاص البدني تدمي نحورها
verses.h2: بمكة والساعين حول المناسك

verses.h1: لقد كنت آتي الأرض ما يستفزني
verses.h2: لها الشوق إلا أنها من ديارك

verses.h1: By Him whose House the pilgrims visit, chanting the pilgrimage call,
verses.h2: in scattered bands—the Master of all who live and perish—

verses.h1: and by the Lord of the young sacrificial she-camels whose throats bleed
verses.h2: at Makka, and of those who hasten about the sacred sites:

verses.h1: I would indeed visit the land, though no longing stirred me
verses.h2: toward it, save that it was among your abodes.

notes.note: البدني appears to be a misprint for البدن, referring to sacrificial camels; the translation follows that reading.

verses.h1: ألا تسأل اليوم الرسوم الدوارس
verses.h2: بحزوى وهل تدري القفار البسابس؟

verses.h1: متى العهد ممن حلها، أم كم انقضى
verses.h2: من الدهر مذ جرت عليها الروامس

verses.h1: ديار لمى ظل من دون صحبتي
verses.h2: لنفسي مما هيجت لي وساوس

verses.h1: ولم تنسني ميا نوى ذات غربة
verses.h2: شطون، ولا المستطرفات الأوانس

verses.h1: إذا قلت أسلو عنك يا مي لم يزل
verses.h2: محل لدائي من ديارك ناكس

verses.h1: Will you not question today the effaced traces
verses.h2: at Ḥazwā? Yet can the vast, barren wastes know?

verses.h1: How long since those who dwelt there were last here—or how much
verses.h2: time has passed since the sand-burying winds swept over them?

verses.h1: Mayy’s abodes! Apart from my companions, there lingered
verses.h2: in my soul troubled thoughts from what they stirred in me.

verses.h1: Nor did separation in a strange land make me forget Mayy,
verses.h2: however far-flung, nor charming women newly met.

verses.h1: Whenever I say, ‘I shall forget you, Mayy,’ there is always
verses.h2: a dwelling among your abodes that brings my sickness back.

notes.note: The phrase من دون صحبتي may mean physically apart from his companions, or that these troubled thoughts affected him alone, not his companions.

poems.intro: وقال المرقش الأصغر، واسمه عمرو بن سعد بن مالك بن ضبيعة:

verses.h1: هل بالديار أن تجيب صمم
verses.h2: لو كان رسم ناطقا كلم

verses.h1: الدار قفر والرسوم كما
verses.h2: رقش في ظهر الأديم قلم

verses.h1: دار لأسماء التي تبلت
verses.h2: قلبي، فعيني ملؤها يسجم

verses.h1: بل هل شجاك الظعن باكرة
verses.h2: كأنهن النخل من ملهم

verses.h1: النشر مسك والوجوه دنا
verses.h2: نير، وأطراف الأكف عنهم

verses.h1: Are the dwellings too deaf to answer?
verses.h2: If a ruined trace had speech, it would speak.

verses.h1: The dwelling is deserted, its traces like
verses.h2: patterns a pen has drawn upon leather.

verses.h1: The dwelling of Asmāʾ, who ravaged
verses.h2: my heart; my eye pours out its fill of tears.

verses.h1: Or did the women departing in their litters at dawn grieve you,
verses.h2: as though they were the palm trees of Mulham?

verses.h1: Their fragrance is musk, their faces gold
verses.h2: coins, and their fingertips red as ʿanam.

notes.note: The source reads عنهم, which appears to be a misprint for عنم (ʿanam), a plant whose red blossoms, fruit, or branches are compared to dyed fingertips. Its precise botanical identity is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Muraqqish al-Aṣghar, whose name was ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Ḍubayʿa, said:
interludes: (It was from this verse that he was called Muraqqish.)

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري
poems.intro: وقال أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري:

poet.from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

verses.h1: ما أنت للكلف المشوق بصاحب
verses.h2: فاذهب على مهل فلست بذاهب

verses.h1: عرف الديار وقد سئمن من البلى
verses.h2: ومللن من سقيا السحاب الصائب

verses.h1: فأراه جهل الشوق بين معالم
verses.h2: فيها وجد الوجد بين ملاعب

verses.h1: ما كان أحسن هذه من وقفة
verses.h2: لو كان ذاك السرب سرب كواعب

verses.h1: You are no companion to one love-stricken and yearning;
verses.h2: go, then, at your leisure, for I am not going.

verses.h1: He recognized the dwellings, grown weary of decay,
verses.h2: and tired of being watered by the pouring clouds.

verses.h1: I see him, in the folly of yearning, amid their landmarks,
verses.h2: and in love’s earnestness amid their haunts of play.

verses.h1: How lovely a halt this would have been,
verses.h2: had that herd been a company of full-breasted maidens!

notes.note: The syntax of فأراه جهل الشوق ... فيها is unclear, and the wording may be corrupt. Tentatively, I take أراه as ‘I see him’ and جهل الشوق as ‘the folly of yearning.’ I read وجد الوجد as ‘and the earnestness of love,’ contrasting earnestness with the places of play.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū ʿUbāda al-Walīd ibn ʿUbayd al-Buḥturī said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

poet.from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

verses.h1: كيف أغدو من الصبابة خلوا
verses.h2: بعد ما أضحت الديار خلاء

verses.h1: قف بها وقفة ترد عليها
verses.h2: أدمعا ردها الجوى أنضاء

verses.h1: How can I become free of longing
verses.h2: now that the dwellings have become empty?

verses.h1: Stand there a while, giving back to them
verses.h2: tears that anguish has worn thin.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

poet.from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

verses.h1: قد وقفنا على الديار وفي الرك
verses.h2: ب حريب من الغرام ومثري

verses.h1: ولو أني أطيع آمر حلمي
verses.h2: كان شتى أمر الديار وأمري

verses.h1: We stopped at the dwellings; among the riders
verses.h2: was one despoiled by passion, and another rich.

verses.h1: Had I obeyed the dictates of my reason,
verses.h2: the dwellings’ concerns and mine would have been far apart.

notes.note: Ḥarīb means someone despoiled of possessions, contrasted here with muthrī, ‘wealthy.’ It is uncertain whether the latter means enriched by love or spared its ravages.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

poet.from_text: أبو عبادة الوليد بن عبيد البحتري

verses.h1: أقام كل ملث الودق رجاس
verses.h2: على ديار بعلو الشام أدراس

verses.h1: فيها لعلوة مصطاف ومرتبع
verses.h2: من بانقوسا وبابيلا وبطياس

verses.h1: منازل أنركتنا بعد معرفة وأوحشت من هوانا بعد إيناس
Every thunderous cloud of lingering rain has settled
verses.h2: over effaced dwellings in the heights of al-Shām.

verses.h1: There ʿAlwa had a summer home and a spring abode,
verses.h2: at Bānqūsā, Bābīlā, and Baṭyās.

verses.h1: Dwellings that disowned us after knowing us, and grew desolate, bereft of our love, after intimacy.

notes.note: The precise identifications and vocalizations of the place names بانقوسا، بابيلا، بطياس are uncertain.

أنركتنا appears to be a typographical error for أنكرتنا, ‘disowned us’ or ‘no longer recognized us.’ The construction أوحشت من هوانا is somewhat unclear; ‘grew desolate, bereft of our love’ is a tentative rendering.

poems.poet_from_text: بيهس بن صهيب بن عامر بن عبد الله بن نائل
poems.intro: وقال بيهس بن صهيب بن عامر بن عبد الله بن نائل:

poet.from_text: بيهس بن صهيب بن عامر بن عبد الله بن نائل

verses.h1: هل بالديار وهل بالقاع من أحد
verses.h2: باق فيسمع صوت المدلج الساري؟

verses.h1: تلك المنازل من صفراء ليس بها
verses.h2: نار تضيء، ولا أصوات سمار

verses.h1: عفت معالمها هوج مغيرة
verses.h2: تسفي عليها تراب الأبطح الهار

verses.h1: حتى تنكرت منها كل معرفة
verses.h2: إلا الرماد، وإلا دمعي الجاري

verses.h1: إن أصبح اليوم لا أهل ذوو لطف
verses.h2: ألهو إليهم، ولا صفراء في الدار

verses.h1: أرعى بعيني نجوم الليل مرتفقا
verses.h2: يا طول ذلك من ليل وإسهار

verses.h1: فقد يكون بها الأهل الجميع وقد
verses.h2: ألهو بصفراء ذات المنظر الواري

verses.h1: كذلك الدهر، إن الدهر ذو غير
verses.h2: على الأنام، وذو نقض وإمرار

verses.h1: Is there anyone in the dwellings, anyone on the plain,
verses.h2: still there to hear the voice of the night traveler?

verses.h1: Those are Ṣafrāʾ’s dwellings; there is no
verses.h2: fire shining there, nor voices of evening companions.

verses.h1: Fierce, onrushing winds have effaced their landmarks,
verses.h2: sweeping over them the loose earth of the streambed,

verses.h1: until everything familiar there became unrecognizable,
verses.h2: except the ashes, and my flowing tears.

verses.h1: If today I have no kindly kin
verses.h2: whose company I can enjoy, nor Ṣafrāʾ in the dwelling,

verses.h1: I watch the stars of night, propped on my elbow—
verses.h2: how long that night, how long the sleeplessness!

verses.h1: Yet once the kin would all be gathered there, and I
verses.h2: would delight in Ṣafrāʾ, radiant to behold.

verses.h1: Such is Time: Time brings changes
verses.h2: upon humankind, unraveling and binding fast.

notes.note: Ṣafrāʾ is treated as the woman’s name here and in lines 5 and 7. It could instead be an epithet referring to her fair complexion.
The precise sense of al-wārī, rendered as ‘radiant’ in the description of her appearance, is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Bayhas ibn Ṣuhayb ibn ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Nāʾil said:

poems.intro: وقال بشر بن أبي خازم، أخو بني والبة بن الحارث:

verses.h1: ديار أقفرت من آل سلمى
verses.h2: رعى سلمى بحسن الوصل راع

verses.h1: ذكرت بهن من سلمى وداعا
verses.h2: فشاقك منهم قرب الوداع

verses.h1: فإن تك قد نأتك اليوم سلمى
verses.h2: فكل قوى قرين لانقطاع

verses.h1: Dwellings deserted by Salmā’s people;
verses.h2: may one who cherishes Salmā keep faith with her in love.

verses.h1: There you recalled a farewell to Salmā,
verses.h2: and the nearness of parting from them stirred your longing.

verses.h1: Though Salmā has gone far from you today,
verses.h2: every bond of companionship is destined to break.

notes.note: I take رعى سلمى بحسن الوصل راع as a wish or blessing. It could instead be a past-tense statement: someone cherished Salmā with faithful affection. The identity of this راع, literally a keeper or guardian, is unspecified.
The compressed phrase قوى قرين is uncertain. I understand قوى as rope-strands, used figuratively for the bonds joining companions.

prose_translation.intro: And Bishr ibn Abī Khāzim, a member of the Banū Wāliba ibn al-Ḥārith, said:

verses.h1: ألا حي الديار بسعد إني
verses.h2: أحب لحب فاطمة الديارا

verses.h1: أراد الظاعنون ليحزنوني
verses.h2: فهاجوا صدع قلبي فاستطارا

verses.h1: Come, greet the dwellings at Saʿd, for I
verses.h2: love the dwellings for love of Fāṭima.

verses.h1: Those departing meant to grieve me;
verses.h2: they reopened the rift in my heart, and it spread.

notes.note: Saʿd appears to be a place-name; its location is uncertain.

verses.h1: غشيت الديار بالبقيع فثهمد
verses.h2: دوارس قد أقوبن من أم معبد

verses.h1: أربت بها الأرواح كل عشية
verses.h2: فلم يبق إلا آل خيم منضد

verses.h1: وغير ثلاث كالحمام خوالد
verses.h2: وهاب محيل هامد متلبد

interludes.text: (الآل، جمع آله، وهو عود له شعبتان يعرض عليه عود آخر، ويلقي عليه ثمام يستظل به)

verses.h1: I visited the dwellings at al-Baqīʿ and Thahmad,
verses.h2: their traces effaced, now empty of Umm Maʿbad.

verses.h1: The winds lingered there every evening,
verses.h2: leaving only the remnants of tents, laid in rows,

verses.h1: and three enduring hearthstones like doves,
verses.h2: and weathered ash, cold and caked.

notes.note: أقوبن appears to be a misprint for أقوين, ‘became deserted’; the translation follows that reading.
آل خيم may refer specifically to surviving tent frames or poles rather than to remnants generally.
هاب is understood as هابٍ, referring to fine ash or dust. ‘Ash’ fits the hearthstones, but the word’s precise sense here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā said:
interludes: (Āl: the plural of ālah, a forked piece of wood across which another piece is laid, with thumām grass spread over it to provide shade.)

verses.h1: أهاجك
verses.h2: أم لا بالستارين مربع ورسم بأجراع الغديرين بلقع

verses.h1: ديار لليلى إذ نحل بها معا
verses.h2: وإذ نحن منها بالموادة نطمع

verses.h1: فيارب حببني إليها وأعطني ال
verses.h2: مودة منها، أنت تعطي وتمنع

verses.h1: وإلا فصبرني وإن كنت كارها
verses.h2: فإني بها ياذا المعارج مولع

verses.h1: وفي الصبر عن بعض المطامع راحة
verses.h2: إذا لم يكن في الشيء ترجوه مطمع

verses.h1: وقد قرع الواشون فيها لك العصا
verses.h2: قديما، كما كانت لذي الحلم تقرع

verses.h1: Has it stirred your longing
verses.h2: or not—a spring encampment at al-Sitārayn, and a desolate trace in the sandy tracts of al-Ghadīrayn?

verses.h1: Dwellings of Laylā, where we once dwelt together,
verses.h2: when we hoped for affection from her.

verses.h1: O Lord, make me beloved to her, and grant me
verses.h2: her affection: You give and withhold.

verses.h1: Otherwise, grant me patience, though I am unwilling,
verses.h2: for I am infatuated with her, O Lord of the ways of ascent.

verses.h1: In patiently forgoing some desires there is relief,
verses.h2: when there is no prospect of attaining what you hope for.

verses.h1: The talebearers tapped the staff for you concerning her
verses.h2: long ago, as it used to be tapped for the man of discernment.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the likely division is after مربع, with ورسم beginning the second hemistich. The translation preserves the supplied division.
The precise locations of al-Sitārayn and al-Ghadīrayn are uncertain.

Tapping the staff alludes to a proverbial warning or reminder given to a discerning man. The proverb is commonly associated with the judge ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib, but whether he is specifically intended here is uncertain.

verses.h1: بكت للفراق وقد راعها
verses.h2: بكاء الحبيب لبعد الديار

verses.h1: كأن الدموع على خدها
verses.h2: بقية طل على جلنار

verses.h1: She wept at parting, distressed
verses.h2: by her beloved’s weeping over distant homes.

verses.h1: The tears upon her cheek were like
verses.h2: dew lingering on a pomegranate blossom.

verses.h1: إن جرى بيننا وبينك عتب
verses.h2: وتناءت منا ومنك الديار

verses.h1: فالعليل الذي عهدت مقيم
verses.h2: والدموع التي شهدت غزار

verses.h1: If reproach has come between us,
verses.h2: and our homes lie far apart,

verses.h1: the lovesick man you knew is still here,
verses.h2: and the tears you witnessed still flow abundantly.

verses.h1: أما الديار فقلما لبثوا بها
verses.h2: بعد اشتياق العيس والركبان

verses.h1: وضعوا سياط الشوق في أعناقها
verses.h2: حتى طلعن بهم على الأوطان

verses.h1: As for the dwellings, they lingered there but little
verses.h2: once longing stirred in the pale camels and their riders.

verses.h1: They laid the whips of longing upon the camels’ necks
verses.h2: until the camels bore them back to their homelands.

notes.note: “Ishtiyāq al-ʿīs wa-l-rukbān” is grammatically ambiguous: it may mean longing felt by the camels and riders, as translated, or longing for them.

poems.intro: وقال قيس بن الخطيم، وقيل: هي للربيع بن أبي الحقيق الأوسي:

verses.h1: وما بعض الإقامة في ديار يهان بها الفتى إلا عناء
وبعض خلائق الأقوام داء
verses.h2: كداء البطن ليس له دواء

verses.h1: وكل شديدة نزلت بقوم
verses.h2: سيأتي بعد شدتها رخاء

verses.h1: يريد المرء أن يعطي مناه
verses.h2: ويأتي الله إلا ما يشاء

verses.h1: Even a brief stay in dwellings where a man is humiliated is nothing but hardship.
Some traits of men are a sickness,
verses.h2: like a sickness of the belly for which there is no cure.

verses.h1: Every hardship that befalls a people
verses.h2: will, after its severity, be followed by ease.

verses.h1: A man desires to be granted his wishes,
verses.h2: yet God permits nothing but what He wills.

notes.note: بعض الإقامة literally means ‘some staying’; it is understood here as a limited duration, hence ‘even a brief stay.’

The translation assumes two likely textual errors: يعطي for يُعطى (‘be granted’), and ويأتي (‘and comes’) for ويأبى (‘but refuses’). The latter, with إلا ما يشاء, means that God allows only what He wills.

prose_translation.intro: Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said—and it is also said that these verses are by al-Rabīʿ ibn Abī al-Ḥuqayq al-Awsī:

verses.h1: تدنو الديار وأنت تبعد جاهدا
verses.h2: فالدهر ينصفني وأنت الظالم

verses.h1: فمتى ينال العدل عندك طالب
verses.h2: أنت المسيء به، وأنت الحاكم

verses.h1: The dwellings draw near, yet you strive to keep your distance;
verses.h2: time treats me fairly, while you do me wrong.

verses.h1: When, then, can one seeking justice obtain it from you,
verses.h2: when you are both the one who wrongs him and the judge?

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: أروح بفتيان خماص من السرى
verses.h2: لهم أنة في كل دار وأدمع

verses.h1: فدمع على نأي الديار مفرق
verses.h2: وقلب على أهل الديار مروع

verses.h1: هل أنت معين للغليل بعبرة
verses.h2: فنبكي على تلك الديار ونجزع؟

verses.h1: ألا ليت شعري كل دار مشتة
verses.h2: ألا منزل يدنو بشمل فيجمع؟

verses.h1: ألا سلوة تنهى الدموع فتنتهي
verses.h2: ألا مورد يصفو لشرب فينقع؟

verses.h1: فصبرا على قرع الزمان وغمزه
verses.h2: وهل ينكر الحمل الذلول الموقع؟

verses.h1: I journey at evening with young men gaunt from night travel;
verses.h2: at every abode they have a groan and tears.

verses.h1: Tears are scattered over the remoteness of the abodes,
verses.h2: and a heart is distraught over those who dwelt there.

verses.h1: Will you lend a tear to ease this burning grief,
verses.h2: so we may weep over those abodes and lament?

verses.h1: Would that I knew! Every abode scatters us;
verses.h2: is there no dwelling that draws our company close and reunites it?

verses.h1: Is there no solace to bid the tears cease, so they cease?
verses.h2: No watering place clear to drink from, to quench our thirst?

verses.h1: Patience, then, under Time’s blows and prods:
verses.h2: does the docile, saddle-galled beast refuse its load?

notes.note: I take مشتة to describe an abode that disperses its people, though the unvocalized form leaves some uncertainty about its precise sense.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.intro: قرأت على حائط مسجد "بفنك" هذا البيت مفردا:

verses.h1: تجنبت غشيان الديار وليس في
verses.h2: تجنبها بعد الفراق ملام

verses.h1: I have avoided visiting the dwellings, and there is no
verses.h2: blame in avoiding them after parting.

prose_translation.intro: I read this single verse on the wall of a mosque in Fanak:

verses.h1: وما كنت أهوى الدار إلا لأهلها
verses.h2: على الدار بعد الظاعنين سلام

verses.h1: I loved the dwelling only for its people;
verses.h2: farewell to the dwelling now that they have departed.

prose_translation.intro: So I answered him with this verse and wrote it beneath his:

poems.intro: ذكر أبو عمرو الشيباني أن عروة بن الورد أصاب امرأة من كنانة بكرا يقال لها: سلمى، وتكنى أم وهب، فأعتقها، واتخذها لنفسه، فمكثت عنده بضع عشرة سنة، فولدت له أولا وهو لا يشك في أنها أرغب الناس فيه، وهي تقول له: لو حججت بي، فأمر على أهلي وأراهم؟ فحج بها، فأتى مكة، ثم أتى المدينة، وكان يخالط من أهل يثرب بني النضير، فيقر ضونه إن احتاج. ويبايعهم إذا غنم، وكان قومها يخالطون بني النضير، فأتوهم وهو عندهم، فقالت لهم سلمى: إنه خارج بي قبل أن يحرج الشهر الحرام، فتعالوا إليه، وأخبروه أنكم تستحيون أن تكون امرأة منكم معروفة النسب صحيحته سبية، وافتدوني منه، فإنه لا يرى أني أفارقه، ولا أختار عليه أحدا، فأتوه، فسقوه الخمر، فلما ثمل قالوا له: فادنا بصاحبتنا، فإنها وسيطة النسب فينا معروفة، وإن علينا سبة أن تكون سبية، فإذا صارت إلينا، وأردت معاودتها، فاخطبها إلينا، فإنها تنكحك، فقال لهم: ذاك لكم، ولكن لي شرط فيها، أن تخيروها، فإن اختارتني انطلقت معي إلى ولدها، وغن اختارتكم انطلقتم بها، قالوا: ذاك لك، قال: دعوني أله بها الليلة وأفاديها غدا، فلما كان الغد جاءوه فامتنع من فدائها، فقالوا له: قد فاديتها منذ البارحة، وشهد عليه جماعة ممن حضر، فلم يقدر على الامتناع، وفادوها، فلما فادوها خيرها، فاختارت أهلها، ثم أقبلت عليه: فقالت له: يا عروة. أما إني أقول فيك - وإن فارقتك - الحق: والله ما أعلم امرأة من العرب ألقت سترها على بعل خير منك، أغرض طرفا، وأقل فحشا، وأعوذ يدا، وأحمى لحقيقة، وما مر علي يوم منذ كنت عندك إلا والموت فيه أحب إلي من الحياة بين قومك، لأني لم أكن أشاء أن أسمع امرأة من قومك تقول: أمة عروة وكذا وكذا، إلا سمعته، والله لا أنظر في وجه غطفانية أبدا، فارجع راشدا إلى ولدك، وأحسن إليهم، فقال عروة في ذلك:

verses.h1: أرقت وصحبتي بمضيق عمق
verses.h2: لبرق من تهامة مستطير

verses.h1: سقى سلمى، وأين ديار سلمى
verses.h2: إذا كانت مجاورة السدير

verses.h1: إذا حلت بأرض بني علي
verses.h2: وأهلي بين زامرة وكير

verses.h1: ذكرت منازلا من أم وهب
verses.h2: محل الحي أسفل من ثبير

verses.h1: وأحدث معهد من أم وهب
verses.h2: معرسنا بدار بني النضير

verses.h1: وقالوا: ما تشاء؟ فقلت: ألهو
verses.h2: إلى الإصباح آثر ذي أثير

verses.h1: بآنسة الحديث رضاب فيها
verses.h2: بعيد النوم كالعنب العصير

verses.h1: سقوني الخمر ثم تكنفوني
verses.h2: عداة الله من كذب وزور

verses.h1: وقالوا: لست بعد فداء سلمى
verses.h2: بمغن ما لديك ولا فقير

verses.h1: فلا والله لو ملكت أمري
verses.h2: ومن لي بالتدبر في الأمور؟

verses.h1: إذن لعصيتهم في حب سلمى
verses.h2: على ما كان من حسك الصدور

verses.h1: فيا للناس كيف ملكت أمري
verses.h2: على شيء ويكرهه ضميري

verses.h1: I lay sleepless, my companions at the pass of ‘Amq,
verses.h2: watching lightning spread across the sky from Tihamah.

verses.h1: May it bring Salmā rain! But where are Salmā’s dwellings,
verses.h2: now that she lives beside al-Sadīr?

verses.h1: She has settled in the land of Banū ʿAlī,
verses.h2: while my people are between Zamirah and Kīr.

verses.h1: I remembered dwellings of Umm Wahb,
verses.h2: the tribe’s campsite below Thabīr.

verses.h1: The last place I knew with Umm Wahb
verses.h2: was our overnight halt in the land of Banū al-Naḍīr.

verses.h1: They asked, “What do you desire?” I said, “To take my pleasure
verses.h2: until morning—before all else—

verses.h1: with a woman of delightful conversation, whose mouth’s moisture,
verses.h2: just after sleep, is like freshly pressed grapes.”

verses.h1: They gave me wine, then hemmed me in,
verses.h2: God’s enemies—with lies and deceit.

verses.h1: They said, “After Salmā’s ransom, you will be
verses.h2: neither rich through what you possess nor poor.”

verses.h1: No, by God! Had I controlled my own affairs—
verses.h2: but who could grant me sound judgment in such matters?—

verses.h1: then I would have defied them for love of Salmā,
verses.h2: despite the rancor lodged in their hearts.

verses.h1: O people, how could I surrender control of my affairs
verses.h2: over something my heart detests?

notes.note: The location and vocalization of عمق, provisionally rendered ‘Amq, are uncertain.
The precise location intended by al-Sadīr is uncertain.
The identification and vocalization of Banū ʿAlī are uncertain; Zamirah and Kīr have not been securely identified.
بمغن ما لديك is grammatically awkward. The translation tentatively understands it as ‘rich through what you possess’; the exact construction and sense remain uncertain.
ملكت is unvocalized. The translation reads it as mallaktu, ‘I handed over control,’ with the recipient unstated, rather than malaktu, ‘I possessed/controlled.’

prose_translation.intro:
Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī related that ‘Urwah ibn al-Ward captured a virgin from Kinanah named Salmā, whose kunyah was Umm Wahb. He freed her and took her for himself. She remained with him for more than ten years and bore him children, while he had no doubt that she desired him more than anyone else did. She would say to him, “Why not take me on pilgrimage, so that I may visit my people and see them?” So he took her on pilgrimage, going first to Makkah and then to al-Madinah. Among the people of Yathrib, he had dealings with Banū al-Naḍīr: they would lend him money if he was in need, and he would trade with them when he acquired booty. Her people also had dealings with Banū al-Naḍīr, and they came to them while he was staying among them. Salmā told her people, “He will take me away before the sacred month ends. Go to him and tell him that you are ashamed to have a woman of your people, of known and unblemished lineage, held captive, and ransom me from him. He cannot imagine that I would leave him or choose anyone over him.”

They went to him and gave him wine to drink. When he was drunk, they said, “Let us ransom our woman from you, for she is a woman of well-known and honorable lineage among us, and it is a disgrace to us that she should be a captive. Once she has returned to us, if you wish to be with her again, ask us for her hand, and she will marry you.” He said to them, “You may do that, but I have one condition concerning her: you must give her the choice. If she chooses me, she will go with me to her children; if she chooses you, you may take her away.” They said, “You shall have that.” He said, “Let me take my pleasure with her tonight, and tomorrow I will let you ransom her.”

The next day they came to him, but he refused to let her be ransomed. They said to him, “You agreed to her ransom last night,” and a number of those who had been present testified against him. He could no longer refuse, and they ransomed her. Once they had done so, he gave her the choice, and she chose her people. Then she turned to him and said, “O ‘Urwah, though I am leaving you, I will speak the truth about you. By God, I know of no Arab woman who has drawn her veil over a husband better than you: more modest in his gaze, less foul in his speech, more ready with a helping hand, or more protective of what honor requires him to defend. Yet not a day has passed since I came to live with you when death was not dearer to me than life among your people. Whenever I might have wished to hear a woman of your people say, ‘‘Urwah’s slave woman,’ and suchlike, I would hear it. By God, I will never look upon the face of a woman of Ghaṭafān again. Return in safety to your children and treat them well.” Concerning this, ‘Urwah said:

opening.note: verse found inside a longer poem of the text

verses.h1: سقوني الخمر ثم تكنفوني
verses.h2: عداة الله من كذب وزور

verses.h1: They gave me wine to drink, then closed in on me—
verses.h2: God’s enemies—with lies and falsehood.

poems.intro: قلت: ذكرت هذا الخبر لما في الشعر من ذكر الديار. وقال يزيد بن عبد المدان:

verses.h1: عفا من سليمى بطن غول فيذبل
verses.h2: فغمرة فيف الريح، فالمتنخل

verses.h1: ديار التي صاد الفؤاد دلالها
verses.h2: وأغرت به يوم النوى حين نرحل

verses.h1: فإن هي صدت عن هواي وراعها
verses.h2: نوازل أحداث وشيب مجلل

verses.h1: فيا رب خيل قد هديت بشطبة
verses.h2: يعارضها عبل الجزارة هيكل

verses.h1: تواغل جردا كالقنا حاثية
verses.h2: عليها قنان والحماس ورعبل

verses.h1: معاقلهم في كل يوم كريهة
verses.h2: صدور العوالي والصفيح المصقل

verses.h1: Deserted since Sulaymā left are the valley of Ghawl and Yadhbul,
verses.h2: and Ghamrat Fayf al-Rīḥ, and al-Mutanakhkhil.

verses.h1: The dwellings of her whose coquetry ensnared my heart,
verses.h2: and who tempted it on the day of separation, as we departed.

verses.h1: If she has turned away from loving me, frightened by
verses.h2: the calamities of time and the gray hair that shrouds me,

verses.h1: then many a troop of horsemen have I led on a slender mare,
verses.h2: with a mighty steed, stout of limb, keeping abreast of her.

verses.h1: They press onward, lean as spear-shafts, scattering dust,
verses.h2: bearing Qanān, al-Ḥamās, and Raʿbal.

verses.h1: Their strongholds on every day of battle
verses.h2: are the points of lofty spears and burnished blades.

notes.note: The grouping of «غمرة فيف الريح» is uncertain; it is provisionally treated as the compound place name Ghamrat Fayf al-Rīḥ. Al-Mutanakhkhil is unidentified, and its vocalization is uncertain.
«وأغرت به» is ambiguous without vowels, and its implied object or referent is unclear. ‘Who tempted it’ provisionally takes the woman as the subject and the heart as the referent.
«شطبة» is interpreted as a long, slender mare; the following description is taken to designate another horse keeping alongside her.

The construction «تواغل جردا كالقنا حاثية» is difficult and may contain a transcription error. The translation provisionally understands the horses as pressing onward and «حاثية» as scattering dust, although dust is not explicitly mentioned.
Qanān, al-Ḥamās, and Raʿbal are unidentified; they may designate individuals or tribal groups. Their vocalizations, particularly those of the latter two names, are uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: I said: I have mentioned this account because the verse contains mention of dwellings. And Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Madān said:

poems.intro: عن الأصمعي قال: دخلت خضراء روح، فإذا أنا برجل من ولده على فاحشة يؤتى، فقلت: قبحك الله، هذا موضع كان أبوك يضرب فيه الأعناق، ويعطي فيه اللهى، وأنت تفعل فيه ما أرى! فالتفت إلي من غير أن يزول عنها، وقال:

verses.h1: ورثنا المجد عن آباء صدق
verses.h2: أسأنا في ديارهم الصنيعا

verses.h1: إذا الحسب الرفيع تواكلته
verses.h2: بناة السوء أوشك أن يضيعا

verses.h1: We inherited glory from honorable forefathers;
verses.h2: we have behaved badly in their abodes.

verses.h1: When lofty ancestral honor is left for others to uphold
verses.h2: by unworthy builders, it is soon lost.

prose_translation.intro: On the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: I entered Khaḍrāʾ’ Rūḥ, and there I found one of his descendants being sodomized. I said, “May God disgrace you! This is a place where your father used to strike off heads and bestow lavish gifts, yet here you are doing what I see!” He turned toward me, without ceasing what he was doing, and said:

poems.intro: والشعر لمعن بن أوس. وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة:

verses.h1: يا خليلي قد مللت ثوائي
verses.h2: بالمصلى، وقد شنئت البقيعا

verses.h1: بلغاني ديار هند وسعدى
verses.h2: وارجعاني، فقد هويت الرجوعا

verses.h1: My two friends, I have tired of staying
verses.h2: at al-Muṣallā, and have come to loathe al-Baqīʿ.

verses.h1: Take me to the dwellings of Hind and Suʿdā,
verses.h2: and bring me back, for I have longed to return.

prose_translation.intro: The verses are by Maʿn ibn Aws. And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:

verses.h1: لمن الديار كأنها لم تحلل
verses.h2: بجنوب أسنمة فقف العنصل

verses.h1: درست معالمها فباقي رسمها
verses.h2: خلق كعنوان الكتاب المحول

verses.h1: دار لسعدى، إذ سعاد كأنها
verses.h2: رشأ غضيض الطرف رخو المفصل

verses.h1: Whose are these abodes, as though never inhabited,
verses.h2: south of Asnima and at Quff al-ʿUnṣul?

verses.h1: Their landmarks have vanished; what remains of their traces
verses.h2: is worn, like the heading of a faded letter.

verses.h1: An abode of Saʿdā, when Suʿād was like
verses.h2: a gazelle fawn, downcast of eye and supple of limb.

notes.note: The locations and exact vocalizations of Asnima and Quff al-ʿUnṣul are uncertain.
المحول, rendered as “faded,” is uncertain: it may describe writing that has been altered or effaced, or a document that has aged a year.
The text switches from Saʿdā to Suʿād within the same hemistich. These may be variant names for the same woman; a textual error is also possible.

verses.h1: ولم أر هندا بعد موقف ساعة
verses.h2: بأنعم في وسط الديار تطوف

verses.h1: أتت بين أتراب تمايس إن مشت
verses.h2: دبيب القطا أوهن منهن أقطف

verses.h1: أشارت إلينا في حياء وراعها
verses.h2: سراة الضحى مني على الحي موقف

verses.h1: وقالت: تباعد يا ابن عم، فإنني منيت بذي صول يغار ويعنف
I have not seen Hind since a brief encounter
verses.h2: at Anʿam, as she wandered among the dwellings.

verses.h1: She came among girls her age, swaying as she walked,
verses.h2: with a sandgrouse’s tread, more languid than they and shorter-stepped.

verses.h1: She gestured to us shyly, and was alarmed
verses.h2: by my standing before the tribe in broad morning light.

verses.h1: She said, “Keep your distance, cousin: I am afflicted with a violent man, jealous and harsh.”

notes.note: أنعم is taken as the place-name Anʿam; its location is uncertain.
The compressed phrase «أوهن منهن أقطف» is taken to describe Hind as more languid and shorter-stepped than her companions. The comparison might instead be with the sandgrouse.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAbd Allah ibn al-ʿAjlān said:

verses.h1: عرفت ديار الحي خالية قفرا
verses.h2: كأن بها لما توهمتها سطرا

verses.h1: وقفت بها كيما ترد جوابها
verses.h2: فما بينت لي الدار عن أهلها خبرا

verses.h1: I recognized the tribe’s dwellings, empty and desolate,
verses.h2: as though, when I made them out, a line of writing lay there.

verses.h1: I stood there, hoping the dwelling would answer,
verses.h2: but it disclosed no news of its people to me.

verses.h1: ديار للجمانة مقفرات
verses.h2: بلين، وهجن للقلب ادكارا

verses.h1: فلم أملك دموع العين مني
verses.h2: ولا النفس التي جاشت مرارا

verses.h1: فقلت لصاحبي: عرج قليلا
verses.h2: نذكر شوقنا الدرس القفارا

verses.h1: كأن لم أغن في العرصات منها
verses.h2: ولم أذعر بقاعتها صوارا

verses.h1: The deserted dwellings of al-Jumāna
verses.h2: have worn away, stirring memories in the heart.

verses.h1: I could not hold back the tears in my eyes,
verses.h2: nor my soul, which surged time and again.

verses.h1: So I said to my companion, “Turn aside a little;
verses.h2: let us remind our longing of the worn, deserted ruins.”

verses.h1: As though I had never dwelt in their courts,
verses.h2: nor startled a herd of wild cattle on their open ground.

notes.note: I read نذكر as nudhakkir, “remind.” The relationship between its objects is uncertain: the phrase could instead mean “let us remind the worn, deserted ruins of our longing.”

verses.h1: عفت الديار فما بها أهل
verses.h2: حزانها ودماثها السهل

verses.h1: إني وما نحروا غداة مني
verses.h2: عند الجمار تئودها العقل

verses.h1: لو بدلت أعلى منازلها
verses.h2: سفلا، وأصبح سفلها يعلو

verses.h1: فيكاد يعرفها الخبير بها
verses.h2: فيرده الإقواء والمحل

verses.h1: لعرفت مغناها بما احتملت
verses.h2: مني الضلوع لأهلها قبل

verses.h1: The dwellings are effaced; no inhabitants remain,
verses.h2: on their rugged ground or their smooth, level stretches.

verses.h1: I swear by the beasts they slaughtered one morning at Minā,
verses.h2: beside al-Jimār, weighed down by their hobbles:

verses.h1: if the highest parts of those dwellings were made
verses.h2: low, and their lowest parts rose high,

verses.h1: so that one who knew them well would almost recognize them,
verses.h2: only to be thwarted by their desolation and barrenness,

verses.h1: I would recognize their dwelling-place by the feelings borne
verses.h2: within my breast for its people long ago.

notes.note: I read تئودها as تؤودها, ‘weigh them down,’ taking العقل to mean the sacrificial animals’ hobbles. The supplied spelling appears irregular.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Ḥārith ibn Khālid al-Makhzūmī said:

verses.h1: هل بالديار على لومي ومعذرتي
verses.h2: عدوى تقام على وجدي وتذكاري

verses.h1: أم كنت تعذل فيما لا تزيد به
verses.h2: إلا مداواة حر النار بالنار

verses.h1: Is there among the dwellings, despite my reproach and my excuses,
verses.h2: a plea for redress against my longing and remembrance?

verses.h1: Or were you reproaching me, accomplishing nothing thereby
verses.h2: but treating the heat of fire with fire?

notes.note: The construction is uncertain. I take عدوى in its sense of a plea for assistance or redress, rather than contagion. على لومي ومعذرتي is also ambiguous: لومي may mean either reproach I utter or reproach directed at me, while معذرتي may mean my excuse or the justification offered for me.

poems.intro: قال كثير بن عبد الرحمن الخزاعي:

verses.h1: وقفت عليه ناقتي فتنازعت
verses.h2: شعوب الهوى لما عرفت المغانيا

verses.h1: فما أعرف الآيات إلا توهما
verses.h2: وما أعرف الأطلال إلا تماريا

verses.h1: وما خلف منكم بأطلال دمنة
verses.h2: تنكرن فاستبدلن منك السوافيا

verses.h1: I halted my she-camel there, and contending
verses.h2: strands of longing stirred within me when I recognized the dwelling places.

verses.h1: I recognize the signs only by conjecture,
verses.h2: and recognize the ruins only with doubt.

verses.h1: The ruins of a campsite are no replacement for you;
verses.h2: they have grown unrecognizable, taking the sand-bearing winds in your place.

notes.note: The first hemistich is syntactically uncertain. I read خلف as khalaf, ‘a replacement,’ rather than as a verb. السوافي can denote sand-bearing winds or the sand and dust they carry.

prose_translation.intro: Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khuzāʿī said:

verses.h1: عفا رابغ من أهله فالظواهر
verses.h2: فأكناف هرشي قد عفت فالأصافر

verses.h1: مغان يهيجن الحليم إلى الهوى
verses.h2: وهن قديمات العهود دوائر

verses.h1: بما قد أرى تلك الديار وأهلها
verses.h2: وهن جميعات الأنيس عوامر

verses.h1: Rābigh lies deserted of its people, and al-Ẓawāhir;
verses.h2: the outskirts of Harshā lie effaced, and al-Aṣāfir.

verses.h1: Abodes that stir even the sober-minded to longing,
verses.h2: though their days are long past and their traces effaced.

verses.h1: For once I would see those dwellings and their people,
verses.h2: with their inhabitants gathered together, flourishing.

notes.note: Al-Ẓawāhir and al-Aṣāfir appear to be place names; their precise locations are uncertain.
The opening بما قد أرى is syntactically uncertain. I take it as recalling the dwellings’ former condition and explaining why they awaken longing.

verses.h1: أناشد الغيث أن تهمي غواديه
verses.h2: على العقيق وإن أقوت مغانيه

verses.h1: على محل أرى الأيام تضحك عن
verses.h2: أيامه، والليالي عن لياليه

verses.h1: عهد من اللهو لم تذمم معاهده
verses.h2: يوما فينسى ولم تقدم بواديه

verses.h1: I implore the rain to let its morning showers pour down
verses.h2: upon al-ʿAqīq, though its dwelling places lie deserted.

verses.h1: Upon a dwelling: I see the days smile to reveal
verses.h2: its days, and the nights its nights.

verses.h1: A time of pleasure whose haunts were never found wanting
verses.h2: for a single day, that it should be forgotten; its beginnings have not grown old.

notes.note: بواديه is taken as “its beginnings” or “its earliest manifestations,” and لم تقدم as “have not grown old.” The wording is unusual, and this reading is uncertain.

verses.h1: شهدت لقد أقوت مغانيكم بعدي
verses.h2: ومحت كما محت وشائع من برد

verses.h1: فأنجدتم من بعد إتهام داركم
verses.h2: فيا دمع أنجدني على ساكني نجد

verses.h1: لعمري لقد أبليتم جدة البكا
verses.h2: بلاى، وجددتم على بلى الوجد

verses.h1: I bear witness: your dwellings have stood empty since I left,
verses.h2: and faded as the woven stripes of a cloak fade.

verses.h1: You went up to Najd after your home had been in Tihāmah;
verses.h2: O tears, come to my aid against those who dwell in Najd.

verses.h1: By my life, you have worn out the freshness of weeping,
verses.h2: as you wore me out, and made my faded longing new again.

notes.note: The form «بلاى» is uncertain. I take it as «بِلايَ», ‘my wearing away,’ with an implied comparison: ‘as you wore me out.’ I read «على» here as «عليّ», ‘upon me.’

verses.h1: تجرع أسى قد أقفر الجرع الفرد
verses.h2: ودع جفه عين يحتلب ماءها الوجد

verses.h1: إذا انصرف المحزون قد فل صبره
verses.h2: سؤال المغاني، فالبكاء له رد

verses.h1: هوى كانقضاض النجم كان نتيجة
verses.h2: من الهزل يوما إن هزل الهوى جد

verses.h1: Swallow sorrow: the lone sandy tract lies deserted,
verses.h2: and let the eye be: longing wrings its tears from it.

verses.h1: When the grieving man turns away, his patience worn down
verses.h2: by questioning the old dwellings, weeping is his answer.

verses.h1: A love like a falling star arose
verses.h2: one day from jest: indeed, love’s jest is earnest.

notes.note: جفه is unclear and may be a misprint for جفن (‘eyelid’). The second hemistich is translated tentatively, taking ودع as ‘and leave be.’
الجرع الفرد is rendered descriptively as ‘the lone sandy tract’; it may instead designate a particular site, al-Jarʿ al-Fard.
فالبكاء له رد is ambiguous: besides ‘weeping is his answer,’ it may mean that weeping brings the grieving man back after he turns away.

poems.poet: محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان المعري
poems.poet_from_text: القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان المعرى
poems.intro: وقال القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان المعرى:

poet.expected: محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان المعري
poet.from_text: القاضي أبو المجد محمد بن عبد الله بن سليمان المعرى

verses.h1: يا مغاني الصبي بباب حناك
verses.h2: لا برمل الغضا ووادي الأراك

verses.h1: وعزيز علي أن حكم الده
verses.h2: ر على رغم ناظري ببلاك

verses.h1: O haunts of youth at Bāb Ḥanāk,
verses.h2: not at Raml al-Ghaḍā or Wādī al-Arāk!

verses.h1: It grieves me that Time has decreed
verses.h2: your decay, to my eyes’ distress.

notes.note: الصبي appears to stand for الصبا, ‘youth,’ which is the reading translated here.
I could not identify باب حناك; the vocalization ‘Bāb Ḥanāk’ is tentative.
على رغم ناظري literally suggests ‘in defiance of my eye(s).’ The unvocalized ناظري permits either singular or dual.

prose_translation.intro: And the judge Abū al-Majd Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:
interludes: [Hanak]: a village in the district of Maʿarra.

verses.h1: لله در أناس قد عهدتهم
verses.h2: بالشام دهرا سقى مغناهم الديم

verses.h1: لو قيل لي
verses.h2: وهجير الصيف متقد وفي الحشا غلة كالنار تضطرم

verses.h1: هم أحب إليك اليوم تبصرهم
verses.h2: أو شربة من زلال الماء؟ قلت: هم

verses.h1: God bless the people I once knew
verses.h2: for a time in al-Shām; may steady rains water their dwelling.

verses.h1: If I were asked—
verses.h2: with summer’s midday heat ablaze and a thirst in my breast flaring like fire—

verses.h1: “Would you rather see them today
verses.h2: or drink a draught of pure water?” I would say, “Them.”

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: وهجير الصيف متقد likely belongs with h1, leaving وفي الحشا غلة كالنار تضطرم as h2. The supplied division has been preserved.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو الشعر موسى بن سحيم الضبي
poems.intro: وقال أبو الشعر موسى بن سحيم الضبي:

poet.from_text: أبو الشعر موسى بن سحيم الضبي

verses.h1: فيا صاح المم بالمغاني فحيها
verses.h2: مغان لهند عطلت وملاعب

verses.h1: مغان خلت من غبطة ونضارة
verses.h2: مغاني الغواني، والغني والرغائب

verses.h1: ولكم زايلتها من فتاة ومن فتى
verses.h2: ومن قرح منسوبة ونجائب

verses.h1: وقفت فأبكاني وهيج عبرتي
verses.h2: علي وقوفي في ديار الحبائب

verses.h1: بكى صاحبي لما بكيت من الهوى
verses.h2: فما كاد يقضي عبرة الحزن صاحبي

verses.h1: جرت عبرة منه فهم بردها
verses.h2: فلم يستطع رد الدموع السواكب

verses.h1: فلو أن فيها أهلها يوم زرتها
verses.h2: لقضيت حاجاتي بها، ومآربي

verses.h1: My friend, visit the dwelling places and greet them—
verses.h2: Hind’s dwellings and playgrounds, now deserted.

verses.h1: Dwellings emptied of happiness and splendor,
verses.h2: the dwellings of fair women, wealth, and all one could wish for.

verses.h1: How many a maiden and young man have left them,
verses.h2: and full-grown steeds of noble pedigree and choice camels.

verses.h1: I stopped; what made me weep and stirred my tears
verses.h2: was my standing in the dwellings of loved ones.

verses.h1: My companion wept when I wept for love;
verses.h2: my companion could scarcely finish shedding his tears of grief.

verses.h1: A tear flowed from him, and he sought to hold it back,
verses.h2: but he could not stem the streaming tears.

verses.h1: Had their people been there the day I visited,
verses.h2: I would have fulfilled my needs and wishes there.

notes.note: الغني is understood as الغنى, “wealth,” rather than الغنيّ, “the wealthy man”; the final letter may reflect a typographical or transcription variation.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Shaʿr Mūsā ibn Suḥaym al-Ḍabbī said:

verses.h1: أهاجك من سعداك مغنى المعاهد
verses.h2: بروضة نعمي فذات الأساود؟

verses.h1: تعاورها الأرواح ينسفن تربها
verses.h2: وكل ملث ذي أهاضيب راعد

verses.h1: عهدت بها سعدى وسعدى غريرة
verses.h2: عروب تهادى في جوار خرائد

verses.h1: Has your Saʿdā’s familiar dwelling-place stirred your longing,
verses.h2: at Rawḍat Nuʿmā and on to Dhāt al-Asāwid?

verses.h1: Winds assail it in turn, scattering its dust,
verses.h2: and every lingering thundercloud pouring down torrents.

verses.h1: There I once knew Saʿdā, when Saʿdā was innocent,
verses.h2: affectionate, walking with a swaying gait among bashful maidens.

notes.note: The locations of Rawḍat Nuʿmā and Dhāt al-Asāwid are uncertain. The spelling نعمي has been read as نعمى (Nuʿmā); its vocalization is not certain.

verses.h1: ابكيا هذه المغاني التي أخ
verses.h2: لقها بعد عهدها بالغواني

verses.h1: أسعدا الغيث إذ بكاها وإن كا
verses.h2: ن خليا من كل ما تجدان

verses.h1: جاد فيها بنفسه فاستجدت
verses.h2: حللا منه جمة الألوان

verses.h1: Weep, you two, for these dwellings, worn away
verses.h2: by the long lapse since lovely women dwelt there.

verses.h1: Join the rain as it weeps for them, though it is
verses.h2: untouched by all that you two feel.

verses.h1: It lavished itself upon them, and they gained fresh
verses.h2: robes from it in a wealth of colors.

poems.intro: وقال أبو القاسم بن هانئ المغربي:

verses.h1: قد مررنا على مغانيك تلك
verses.h2: ورأينا فيها مشابه منك

verses.h1: عارضتنا المها الخواذل أس
verses.h2: رابا بأجراعها، فلم نسل عنك

verses.h1: لا يرع للمها هنالك سرب
verses.h2: فلقد أشبهتك إن لم تكنك

verses.h1: We passed those former haunts of yours
verses.h2: and saw in them likenesses of you.

verses.h1: The oryx that had left their herds crossed our path,
verses.h2: in bands upon their sandy stretches; we did not forget you.

verses.h1: May no herd of oryx there be frightened,
verses.h2: for they resembled you—if they were not you.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Qāsim ibn Hāniʾ al-Maghribī said:

verses.h1: أي مرعى عين وواد قشيب
verses.h2: لحيته الأيام في ملحوب

verses.h1: ند عنك العزاء فيه وقاد الد
verses.h2: مع من مقلتيك قود الجنيب

verses.h1: وبما قد أراه ريان مكسو
verses.h2: المغاني من كل حسن وطيب

verses.h1: لسقيم الجفون من غير سقم
verses.h2: ومريب الألحاظ غير مريب

verses.h1: فعليه السلام لا أشرك الأط
verses.h2: لال في لوعتي ولا في نحيبي

verses.h1: فسواء إجابتي غير داع
verses.h2: ودعائي بالقفر غير مجيب

verses.h1: What a pasture for the eye, what a fresh valley
verses.h2: time has scraped bare at Malḥūb!

verses.h1: There solace fled you, and the place led
verses.h2: tears from your eyes as one leads a spare horse.

verses.h1: How often I saw it lush, its haunts clothed
verses.h2: in every beauty and delight,

verses.h1: For one with languid eyelids, though not ill,
verses.h2: whose glances raise suspicion, though above suspicion.

verses.h1: Peace be upon him! I give the ruins no share
verses.h2: in my burning grief or my sobbing.

verses.h1: For answering one who does not call is just the same
verses.h2: as calling, in the wilderness, to one who does not answer.
