notes.note: لحيته appears corrupt, probably an OCR error for لحبته, ‘scraped it bare’ or ‘wore it away,’ which is the reading followed here. Malḥūb is a place name; its precise location is uncertain.
The pronoun in عليه is taken to refer to the beloved described in line 4; a reference to the dwelling-place is also possible.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو محمد القاسم بن علي الحريري العالم
poems.intro: وقال أبو محمد القاسم بن علي الحريري العالم:

poet.from_text: أبو محمد القاسم بن علي الحريري العالم

verses.h1: عرج
verses.h2: لك الخير صدور الركاب على ربا كن مغاني الرباب

verses.h1: وقف بها وقفة مستعبر
verses.h2: يسح فيها الدمع سح الرباب

verses.h1: فسنة العشاق أن يعولوا
verses.h2: في منزل الحب إذا الحب غاب

verses.h1: يا حبذا تلك الربا من ربا
verses.h2: ظباؤها أفتك من ليث غاب

verses.h1: Turn
verses.h2: —may good be yours—the mounts toward hills that were once al-Rabāb’s abodes.

verses.h1: And stand there as one who weeps,
verses.h2: pouring out tears there as rain clouds pour.

verses.h1: For lovers’ custom is to wail
verses.h2: in love’s dwelling when the beloved is gone.

verses.h1: How fair those hills among hills!
verses.h2: Their gazelles are deadlier than a lion of the thicket.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the first hemistich likely ends after الركاب, with the second beginning على ربا. The translation preserves the supplied division. صدور الركاب literally means ‘the breasts of the mounts,’ rendered idiomatically as ‘the mounts.’
The unvocalized الحب permits both ḥubb (‘love’) and ḥibb (‘beloved’). The translation reads the first occurrence as ‘love’ and the second as ‘beloved’; both could refer to the beloved.

prose_translation.intro: And the scholar Abū Muḥammad al-Qāsim ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥarīrī said:

poems.poet_from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: مغاني اللوى من شخصك اليوم أطلال
verses.h2: وفي النوم مغنى من خيالك محلال

verses.h1: معانيك شتى، والعبارة واحد
verses.h2: فطرفك مغتال، وزندك مغتال

verses.h1: متى سألت بغداد عني وأهلها
verses.h2: فإني عن أهل العواصم سال

verses.h1: إذا جن ليلي جن لبى وزائد
verses.h2: خفوق فؤادي كلما خفق الآل

verses.h1: وماء بلادي كان أنجع مشربا
verses.h2: ولو أن ماء الكرخ صهباء جريال

verses.h1: The dwellings of al-Liwā are ruins today, bereft of your presence;
verses.h2: but in sleep there is a dwelling much frequented by your phantom.

verses.h1: Your qualities are varied, though the expression is one:
verses.h2: your glance is deadly, and your wrist is full and rounded.

verses.h1: Should Baghdad and its people ask after me,
verses.h2: I have ceased to yearn for the people of al-ʿAwāṣim.

verses.h1: When my night grows dark, my mind goes mad;
verses.h2: and my heart beats harder whenever the mirage shimmers.

verses.h1: The water of my homeland was a more wholesome draught,
verses.h2: even were the water of al-Karkh golden-red wine.

notes.note: Al-ʿAwāṣim may name the northern Syrian frontier districts or mean ‘capital cities’ generally. The unvocalized سألت also permits ‘you ask Baghdad and its people about me,’ rather than making Baghdad and its people the subjects.

prose_translation.intro: And Shaykh Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: مغاني الشعب طيبا في المغاني
verses.h2: بمنزلة الربيع من الزمان

verses.h1: ولكن الفتى العربي فيها
verses.h2: غريب الوجه واليد واللسان

verses.h1: إذا غنى الحمام الورق فيها
verses.h2: أجابته أغاني القيان

verses.h1: ومن بالشعب أحوج من حمام
verses.h2: إذا غنى وناح إلى البيان

verses.h1: The dwellings of al-Shiʿb, in their loveliness, are among dwellings
verses.h2: what spring is among the seasons.

verses.h1: Yet the Arab youth among them
verses.h2: is a stranger in face, hand, and tongue.

verses.h1: When the gray doves sing there,
verses.h2: the songs of singing girls answer them.

verses.h1: And those in al-Shiʿb have greater need than a dove—
verses.h2: when it sings and laments—of making themselves understood.

notes.note: The intended sense of ‘hand’ (Al-yad) is not explicit; it may refer to handwriting. The literal wording is retained.

verses.h1: المغاني أحفى بقلبي من العد
verses.h2: ل وإن هجن لوعة وزفيرا

verses.h1: أفهمتني على نحول رباها
verses.h2: فكأني قرأت منها سطورا

verses.h1: يا معيري أجفانه أنا أغنى
verses.h2: بجفوني الغزار أن أستعيرا

verses.h1: The old dwelling sites are kinder to my heart than reproach,
verses.h2: though they stir anguish and sighing.

verses.h1: They made their meaning clear to me, despite their wasted knolls,
verses.h2: as though I had read lines of writing in them.

verses.h1: You who lend me your eyelids, I have no need—
verses.h2: with my own so overflowing—to borrow.

notes.note: العدل, split across the hemistichs, appears to be a misprint for العذل, here translated as ‘reproach.’ Without vowel marks, the corrected form could also mean ‘reproachers’ (العُذَّل).

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي
poems.intro: وقال أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي - رحمه الله -:

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي

verses.h1: مغناهم أضحى صموتا ناطقا
verses.h2: يهدي الهموم إلى القلوب بيانه

verses.h1: غشيت ديارهم المحول، وريها
verses.h2: دون السحاب على العيون ضمانه

verses.h1: قد ألبسته يد البلى عفر الثرى
verses.h2: فعفا، ومح، فأخمدت نيرانه

verses.h1: وتنكب العافون لاحب سبله
verses.h2: لما عفا، وتهدمت أركانه

verses.h1: ولقد أراه وفيه مجتمع الهوى
verses.h2: يهدي السرور إلى القلوب عيانه

verses.h1: فرجا لمكروب، ونضرة ثائر
verses.h2: وملاذ من تنبو به أوطانه

verses.h1: والدهر مثل الطيف لا تبقى على
verses.h2: حال إساءته ولا إحسانه

verses.h1: Their dwelling has fallen silent, yet speaks;
verses.h2: its eloquence brings sorrow to hearts.

verses.h1: Droughts have overtaken their dwellings; their watering
verses.h2: is guaranteed by eyes, not clouds.

verses.h1: The hand of decay has clothed it in the dust of the earth;
verses.h2: it has faded and worn away, and its fires have been quenched.

verses.h1: Those seeking bounty have shunned its well-trodden paths
verses.h2: since it faded away and its pillars crumbled.

verses.h1: I once beheld it as a gathering-place of love,
verses.h2: its very sight bringing joy to hearts:

verses.h1: relief for the distressed, support for an avenger,
verses.h2: and a refuge for those whose homelands cast them out.

verses.h1: Time is like a dream: neither remains
verses.h2: unchanged—its cruelty or its kindness.

notes.note: The source reads نضرة ثائر, literally something like “freshness of an avenger,” which is unclear here. The translation tentatively assumes نصرة ثائر, “support for an avenger,” with نضرة a possible typing or OCR error. ثائر can also mean a rebel or insurgent.

prose_translation.intro: And my brother, ʿIzz al-Dawla Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī—may God have mercy on him—said:

verses.h1: شجاني مغاني الحي وانشقت العصا
verses.h2: وصاح غراب البين أنت مريض

verses.h1: ففاضت دموعي عند ذاك صبابة
verses.h2: وفيهن خود كالمهاة غضيض

verses.h1: ووليت محزون الفؤاد مروعا
verses.h2: كئيبا ودمعي في الرداء يفيض

verses.h1: The tribe’s dwelling places stirred my sorrow; our bond was broken,
verses.h2: and the raven of parting cried, “You are sick.”

verses.h1: Then my tears overflowed with longing,
verses.h2: and among them was a young beauty, like an oryx, demure.

verses.h1: I turned away, grieving at heart, distraught,
verses.h2: despondent, my tears streaming onto my cloak.

notes.note: The referent of فيهن (“among them”) is uncertain; it may mean “in those dwelling places.” غضيض, rendered “demure,” may suggest downcast eyes or softness and delicacy.

verses.h1: هل هيجتك مغاني الحي والدور
verses.h2: فاشتقت، إن الغريب الدار معذور

verses.h1: وقد نحل بها إذ عيشنا أنق
verses.h2: بيض أوانس أمثال الدمى حور

verses.h1: Have the tribe’s old haunts and dwellings stirred you
verses.h2: to longing? One far from home may be excused.

verses.h1: We once dwelt there, when our life was pleasant,
verses.h2: with fair, companionable maidens, like statues, with wide, dark eyes.

notes.note: The syntax is uncertain: نحل means ‘we dwell,’ but بيض (‘fair women’) appears grammatically disconnected from it. ‘With’ is supplied provisionally. نحل may be a misprint for تحل, which would make the sense ‘Fair, companionable maidens once dwelt there, when our life was pleasant.’

poems.index_hemistich: ألا حيّ من أجل الحبيب الليالي

opening.expected: ألا حيّ من أجل الحبيب الليالي
opening.actual: ألا حي من أجل الحبيب المغانيا

verses.h1: ألا حي من أجل الحبيب المغانيا
verses.h2: لبسن البلى مما لبسن اللياليا

verses.h1: إذا ما تقاضى المرء يوم وليلة
verses.h2: تقاضاه شيء لا يمل التقاضيا

verses.h1: Ah, greet the dwelling places for the beloved’s sake;
verses.h2: they have put on decay from all the nights they have worn.

verses.h1: Whenever a day and a night demand their due from a man,
verses.h2: he faces a creditor that never tires of demanding.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: ومن سفه وقوفك في المغاني
verses.h2: تسائل عن فريق فارقونا

verses.h1: سقين غداة بينهم دموعا
verses.h2: وكفن فما وقفن ولا روينا

verses.h1: It is folly for you to stand among the dwellings,
verses.h2: asking after a company who parted from us.

verses.h1: The dwellings were watered with tears on the morning of their departure;
verses.h2: the tears streamed and never ceased, yet our thirst was not quenched.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: أنا يا دار أخو وحش الفلا
verses.h2: فيك، من خان فعزمي لم يخني

verses.h1: ولئن غال مغانيك البلى
verses.h2: عادة الدهر فشخص منك يغني

verses.h1: إن خبت نار فهذي كبدي
verses.h2: أو جفا الغيث، فهذا لك جفني

verses.h1: I, O dwelling, am a brother to the beasts of the wastes
verses.h2: within you; whoever else proves faithless, my resolve has not failed me.

verses.h1: Though decay has ravaged your abodes,
verses.h2: as is time’s way, a single remnant of you suffices.

verses.h1: If a fire has gone out, here is my liver;
verses.h2: or if rain forsakes you, here is my eyelid for you.

verses.h1: يا مغاني الحمى سقيت، وما ين
verses.h2: فعني الغيث أن يجودك قطرا

verses.h1: أي عين أصابت الدار أق
verses.h2: ذى الله بعدي أجفانها وأضرا

verses.h1: لا ثراها يطيل بعد النوى غص
verses.h2: نا، ولا جوها يتمم بدرا

verses.h1: غير حم مثل القطا جاثمات
verses.h2: كن جونا فعدن بالريح كدرا

verses.h1: وبقايا مواقد تصف الجو
verses.h2: د أباديد في يد الريح تذرى

verses.h1: قلبوا ذلك الرماد تصيبوا
verses.h2: فيه قلبي إن لم تصيبوا الجمرا

verses.h1: O dwellings of al-Ḥimā, may you be watered! Yet what
verses.h2: good does it do me if rain lavishes its drops on you?

verses.h1: What evil eye struck the dwelling after I left? May God
verses.h2: fill its lids with grit and do it harm!

verses.h1: Since our parting, its soil no longer lengthens a branch,
verses.h2: nor does its sky bring a moon to fullness.

verses.h1: Nothing but blackened stones crouching like sandgrouse,
verses.h2: once jet-black, now turned dusty by the wind;

verses.h1: and remnants of hearths that speak
verses.h2: of generosity—scattered, blown about in the wind’s grasp.

verses.h1: Turn over those ashes, and you will find
verses.h2: my heart there, if you find no embers.

notes.note: Al-Ḥimā can mean a protected pasture or reserved grazing ground; it is unclear whether a particular named locality is intended here.
The placement of بعدي (‘after I left’) makes its attachment uncertain. It is taken here with the eye’s striking the dwelling, rather than with the ensuing curse.
حم denotes black objects, presumably the blackened hearthstones left at the campsite; the noun ‘stones’ is supplied.

verses.h1: عابوا وفائي لمن أهوى وقد علموا
verses.h2: أن الخيانة ذنب لا أواقعه

verses.h1: كأنني أول العشاق طالله
verses.h2: مغنى الأحبة فارفضت مدامعه

verses.h1: They faulted my faithfulness to the one I love, though they knew
verses.h2: that betrayal is a sin I do not commit.

verses.h1: As though I were the first lover before whom appeared
verses.h2: the loved ones’ dwelling, so that his tears streamed forth.

notes.note: The reading طالله is unclear and may be a transcription error. The translation provisionally understands it as طلّ له, ‘appeared to him.’

poems.intro: قال جرير بن عطية بن الخطفي:

verses.h1: حي الغداة برامة الأطلالا
verses.h2: رسما تحمل أهله فأحالا

verses.h1: إن السواري والغوادي غادرت
verses.h2: للريح منخرقا به ومجالا

verses.h1: لم نلق مثلك بعد عهدك منزلا
verses.h2: فسقيت من سبل السماك سجالا

verses.h1: أصبحت بعد جميع أهلك دمنة
verses.h2: قفرا، وكنت محلة محلالا

verses.h1: ولقد عجبت من الديار وأهلها
verses.h2: والدهر كيف يبدل الأبدالا

verses.h1: Greet this morning the ruins at Rāma—
verses.h2: a trace whose people departed, leaving it changed.

verses.h1: The night rains and the morning rains have left
verses.h2: a passage there for the wind, and room to roam.

verses.h1: Since your days, we have found no dwelling like you;
verses.h2: may you be watered with bucketfuls of al-Simāk’s rain.

verses.h1: After your people’s gathering, you have become a remnant,
verses.h2: deserted—once you were an abode where many stayed.

verses.h1: I have indeed marveled at dwellings and their people,
verses.h2: and at time—how it replaces one with another.

notes.note: Al-Simāk is a star-name associated here with seasonal rain. The unqualified name can designate Spica (Al-Simāk al-Aʿzal) or Arcturus (Al-Simāk al-Rāmiḥ); the verse does not specify which.

prose_translation.intro: Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn al-Khaṭafā said:

verses.h1: قفا حييا الأطلال من مسقط اللوى
verses.h2: وهل في تحيات الرسوم جداء

verses.h1: وماذا نحيي من عراص تبدلت
verses.h2: شعوب النوى عنا فهن قواء

verses.h1: كأن لم يكن فيها الجميع، ولم تصح
verses.h2: بهم نية تعري الديار خلاء

verses.h1: تذكرت عصرا قد مضى وصحابة
verses.h2: ولم يك عما قد ذكرت عزاء

verses.h1: Stop, you two, and greet the ruins at the foot of al-Liwā;
verses.h2: but is there any gain in greeting the traces?

verses.h1: What is there to greet in courtyards that have exchanged us
verses.h2: for the sundering paths of separation, and now lie desolate?

verses.h1: As though the whole company had never dwelt there, nor been summoned
verses.h2: by a resolve to depart, leaving the dwellings bare and empty.

verses.h1: I remembered a time gone by, and companions,
verses.h2: and there was no solace for what I recalled.

notes.note: Al-Liwā may be a place-name or a descriptive term for a curving tract of sand. I understand مسقط اللوى as its foot or lower slope.

شعوب النوى is uncertain. The translation takes شعوب as branching or sundering paths, figuratively belonging to separation; شعوب can also denote death, which would suggest a personification of separation as death.
I take نية as a resolve to depart, personified as calling the company away. It can also mean an intended destination or direction of travel.

verses.h1: إن شئت ألا ترى صبرا لمصطبر
verses.h2: فانظر على أي حال أصبح الطلل

verses.h1: كأنما جاد مغناه
verses.h2: فغيره دموعنا يوم بانوا، وهي تنهمل

verses.h1: If you wish to see a patient man bereft of patience,
verses.h2: look at the state the ruined campsite has come to.

verses.h1: As though its dwelling-place had been watered
verses.h2: and altered by our tears, streaming down the day they departed.

notes.note: The hemistich division appears misplaced: فغيره (“and altered it”) likely belongs at the end of h1. I take دموعنا (“our tears”) as the delayed subject of both جاد (“watered”) and غيّر (“altered”).

verses.h1: أسقى طلولهم أجش هزيم
verses.h2: وغدت عليهم نضرة ونعيم

verses.h1: جادت معاهدهم عهاد سحابة
verses.h2: ما عهدها عند الديار ذميم

verses.h1: سفه الفراق عليك يوم رحيلهم
verses.h2: وبما أراه عنك وهو حليم

verses.h1: May a deep-rumbling, thundering cloud water their ruins,
verses.h2: and may freshness and bliss dawn upon them.

verses.h1: May a cloud’s returning showers drench their old haunts—
verses.h2: a cloud whose faithfulness to the dwellings is beyond reproach.

verses.h1: Parting behaved rashly toward you on the day they left,
verses.h2: though often I have found it forbearing toward you.

notes.note: The construction «وبما أراه عنك» is uncertain. I take «بما» in the sense of «ربما», ‘often,’ and understand «عنك» as completing «حليم», ‘forbearing toward you.’

verses.h1: يقول زميلي يوم سابقة النقى
verses.h2: وعيناي من فرط الأسى تكفان:

verses.h1: أمن أجل دار بين لوذان فالنقى
verses.h2: غداة النوى عيناك تبتدران؟

verses.h1: فقلت له: لا، بل قذيت، وإنما
verses.h2: قذى العين مما هيج الطللان

verses.h1: My companion says, on the day at Sābiqat al-Naqā,
verses.h2: while my eyes stream with overwhelming grief:

verses.h1: “Is it for a dwelling between Lawdhān and al-Naqā
verses.h2: that your eyes race to shed tears on the morning of departure?”

verses.h1: I told him, “No—a mote has got into my eye; it is only that
verses.h2: the mote in my eye comes from what the two ruined camps stirred up.”

notes.note: سابقة النقى is unclear. Provisionally treated as the place name Sābiqat al-Naqā, but I could not identify it; the wording may be corrupt.
Lawdhān (لوذان) is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain.

verses.h1: ثوى ماثلا بين الطلول المواثل
verses.h2: فهل بل من داء الجوى والبلابل

verses.h1: معنى قضى دين الغرام مدامعا
verses.h2: يقسمها في دراسات المنازل

verses.h1: تسائل عن أحبابه كل دمنة
verses.h2: سوائل من عينيه غير سوائل

verses.h1: He lingered, standing among the ruins still standing;
verses.h2: was he then cured of love’s anguish and turmoil?

verses.h1: A tormented man, he paid passion’s debt in tears,
verses.h2: distributing them among the dwellings’ faded traces.

verses.h1: Every ruined dwelling is questioned about his loved ones
verses.h2: by streams from his eyes, though they are no questioners.

notes.note: The printed دراسات appears to be a transposition error for دارسات, meaning effaced or faded remains; the translation follows that reading.

verses.h1: سقى الله أطلالا بأكثبة الحمى
verses.h2: وإن كن قد أبدين للناس ما بيا

verses.h1: منازل لو مرت بهن جنازتي
verses.h2: لقال الصدى يا حاملي أربعا بيا

verses.h1: May God water the ruins among the dunes of al-Ḥimā,
verses.h2: though they have revealed to everyone what ails me.

verses.h1: Dwellings—were my bier to pass by them,
verses.h2: my spirit would cry, “You two who bear me, pause here with me!”

notes.note: Al-Ḥimā literally means a protected pasture or reserve; the particular location is uncertain.

Ṣadā, translated as “my spirit,” can mean an echo or the bird associated in old Arab belief with a dead person’s spirit. The funeral setting suggests the latter, but “the echo would say” is also possible.

prose_translation.intro: And Muḥammad ibn Bashīr al-Khārijī said:

verses.h1: أشاقتك المعارف والطلول
verses.h2: عفون وخف منهن الحمول

verses.h1: نعم وذكرت دنيا قد تولت
verses.h2: وأي نعيم دنيا لا يزول؟

verses.h1: Have the familiar landmarks and ruins stirred your longing,
verses.h2: now effaced, with the camel caravans gone?

verses.h1: Yes, and I remembered a life gone by—
verses.h2: and what earthly bliss does not pass away?

verses.h1: ومن جزعي
verses.h2: والشيب إحكام ذي النهى بكاء على الأطلال يوم الرواكس

verses.h1: أسائل أطلالا عفت بعد أهلها
verses.h2: وغيرها سهك الرياح الروامس

verses.h1: فما أبقت الأيام من عرصاتها
verses.h2: لمن جاءها غير الرسوم الدوارس

verses.h1: And one sign of my anguish
verses.h2: —though gray hair gives the discerning self-command—is weeping over the ruins on the day of al-Rawākis.

verses.h1: I question ruins effaced since their people left,
verses.h2: altered by the scouring of winds that bury all traces.

verses.h1: The days have left nothing of their open grounds
verses.h2: for anyone who comes there but fading traces.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the likely division is after «ذي النهى». The translation preserves the supplied division.
«الرواكس» (Al-Rawākis) is unidentified; it may be a place name. The reference in «يوم الرواكس», ‘the day of al-Rawākis,’ is uncertain.

verses.h1: هل تعرف اليوم
verses.h2: أم لا تعرف الطللا بلى، فهيج لي الأحزان والوجلا

verses.h1: وقد أراني بها في عيشة عجب
verses.h2: والدهر بينا له حال إذ انفتلا

verses.h1: Do you recognize today—
verses.h2: or do you not recognize—the ruined campsite? Yes; it has stirred my sorrows and dread.

verses.h1: Once I saw myself there, living a wondrous life;
verses.h2: but time, just when it holds one course, turns aside.

notes.note: The hemistich division appears misplaced: the first hemistich likely ends with الطللا, and the second begins with بلى. The translation preserves the supplied division.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAdī ibn al-Riqāʿ al-ʿĀmilī said:

verses.h1: لمن طلل بذي خيم قديم
verses.h2: يلوح كأن باقيه وشوم

verses.h1: محا معروفه قدم الليالي
verses.h2: ووكاف عزاليه سجوم

verses.h1: وآونة عجاج الصيف حتى
verses.h2: تنكرت المعالم والرسوم

verses.h1: وقفت به أسائله ودمعي
verses.h2: يفيض كأنه شن هزيم

verses.h1: Whose ancient ruins are these at Dhū Khaym,
verses.h2: still visible, their remnants like tattoos?

verses.h1: The long passage of nights has erased their familiar features,
verses.h2: and a rain-cloud whose spouts stream down,

verses.h1: and, at times, summer’s swirling dust, until
verses.h2: the landmarks and traces grew unrecognizable.

verses.h1: I stood there questioning them, while my tears
verses.h2: overflowed like a worn, split waterskin.

notes.note: Dhū Khaym is a place-name; its precise location is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Ṭufayl ibn ʿAwf al-Ghanawī said:

poems.intro: (الشن: القربة الخلقة، والإداوة الخلق، هزيم: منكسر) . وقال حاتم بن عبد الله الطائي:

verses.h1: أتعرف أطلالا ونويا تهدما
verses.h2: كخطك في رق كتابا منمنما

verses.h1: أذاعت به الأرواح بعد أنيسها
verses.h2: شهورا وأياما وحولا محرما

verses.h1: دوارج قد غيرن ظاهر تربه
verses.h2: وغيرت الأيام ما كان معلما

verses.h1: وغيرها طول التقادم والبلى
verses.h2: فما أعرف الأطلال إلا توهما

verses.h1: Do you recognize ruins and a crumbled encircling bank,
verses.h2: like an ornate text you trace on parchment?

verses.h1: The winds have scattered it since its inhabitants departed,
verses.h2: for months and days and a full year.

verses.h1: Sweeping winds have altered the surface of its soil,
verses.h2: and the days have altered what once was clearly marked.

verses.h1: The long passage of time and decay have changed them,
verses.h2: so I recognize the ruins only by conjecture.

notes.note: Read نويا as نؤيًا: a trench or earthen bank surrounding a tent to keep out rainwater, rendered here as ‘encircling bank.’
محرما is unclear here and may be a misprint for مجرما, ‘completed,’ in the expression حولا مجرما, ‘a full year.’ The translation follows that probable reading.
دوارج is taken as describing the winds, ‘sweeping’ or ‘passing’; it could instead describe the passing periods of time mentioned in the preceding line.

prose_translation.intro: (Al-shann: a worn-out waterskin or a worn-out small water vessel; Hazīm: broken.) Ḥātim ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ṭāʾī said:

poems.intro: وقال رقيع بن عبيد بن صيفي:

verses.h1: يا صاحبي ألما بي على الطلل
verses.h2: وحييا قبل طول البين والشغل

verses.h1: وما تحية دار بعد ما درست
verses.h2: إلا معارف رسم هاج من خبلي

verses.h1: My two companions, stop with me at the ruins,
verses.h2: and greet them before long separation and cares.

verses.h1: What greeting can a dwelling offer once it has been effaced,
verses.h2: but familiar traces that stir my distracted grief?

notes.note: The construction «إلا معارف رسم هاج من خبلي» is compressed and uncertain. I take the recognizable traces as the dwelling’s answering greeting; «خبلي» can mean my madness, mental disturbance, or distraction.
The poet’s lineage is inconsistent in the supplied context: the poet field gives Ṣīnī (صيني), while the introduction gives Ṣayfī (صيفي).

prose_translation.intro: And Ruqayʿ ibn ʿUbayd ibn Ṣayfī said:

poems.poet_from_text: ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود
poems.intro: وقال ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود:

poet.from_text: ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود

verses.h1: خليلي عوجا اليوم حتى نسلما
verses.h2: على طلل بين النقا والأخارم

verses.h1: كأن لم يكن إلا حديثا وقد أتى
verses.h2: له ما أتى للمزمن المتقادم

verses.h1: وهل يرجع التسليم ربع كأنه
verses.h2: بسائفة قفرا ظهور الأراقم؟

verses.h1: My two friends, turn aside today, that we may greet
verses.h2: a ruined campsite between al-Naqā and al-Akhārim.

verses.h1: It is as though it were only yesterday, yet it has undergone
verses.h2: what the aged and timeworn undergo.

verses.h1: Can an encampment return a greeting, when it seems,
verses.h2: desolate on a sandy fringe, like the backs of speckled snakes?

notes.note: Al-Naqā and al-Akhārim are treated as place-names, but their locations are unidentified here. The words can also describe terrain: a sand dune and clefts or mountain passes.
I take sāʾifa (سائفة) as a sandy fringe or tract rather than a place-name; its precise topographical sense here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Dhū al-Rumma, Ghaylān ibn ʿUqba ibn Masʿūd, said:

verses.h1: يأبى الخلي بكاء المنزل الخالي
verses.h2: والنوح في أرسم أقوت وأطلال

verses.h1: وذو الصبابة ما ينفك ينصبه
verses.h2: وجدا تأبد آي المنزل الخالي

verses.h1: The man untroubled by love refuses to weep for the empty dwelling,
verses.h2: or to lament among deserted traces and ruins.

verses.h1: Yet the lovesick man is forever worn down
verses.h2: with longing by the desolation of the empty dwelling’s traces.

prose_translation.intro: [Al-sāʾifa]: the edge of a stretch of sand. Al-Buḥturī said:

verses.h1: أشاقتك من أرض العراق طلول
verses.h2: تحمل منها جيرة وحلول

verses.h1: فكيف ألذ العيش بعد معاشر
verses.h2: بهم كنت عند النائبات أصول

verses.h1: Have ruins in the land of al-ʿIrāq stirred your longing—
verses.h2: ruins from which neighbors and dwellers have departed?

verses.h1: How can I savor life after those companions are gone,
verses.h2: with whose help I used to stand against calamities?

verses.h1: طلل الجميع لقد عفوت حميدا
verses.h2: وكفى على رزئي بذاك شهيدا

verses.h1: دمن كأن البين أصبح طالبا
verses.h2: دمنا لدى آرامها وحقودا

verses.h1: أمواقف الفتيان تطوى لم تذب
verses.h2: شوقا، ولم تندب لهن صعيدا؟

verses.h1: O ruins of the gathered clan, you have faded, yet remain praised;
verses.h2: that alone is witness enough to my loss.

verses.h1: Traces—as though separation had come seeking
verses.h2: our blood among their gazelles, full of rancor.

verses.h1: Are the young men’s haunts swept away, while you have not melted
verses.h2: with longing, nor lamented their bare ground?

notes.note: The construction «ولم تندب لهن صعيدا» is unclear. «صعيدا» ordinarily means bare or level ground; ‘lamented their bare ground’ is tentative. The wording may contain a transcription error.

verses.h1: تطل الطلول الدمع في كل موقف
verses.h2: وتمثل بالدمع الديار المواثل

verses.h1: دوارس لم يجف الربيع ربوعها
verses.h2: ولا مر في أغفالها وهو غافل

verses.h1: فقد سحبت فيها السحائب ذيلها
verses.h2: وقد أخملت بالنور فيها الخمائل

verses.h1: The ruins squander tears at every stopping place,
verses.h2: and the dwellings still standing wreak havoc on tears.

verses.h1: Effaced abodes—spring has not shunned their grounds,
verses.h2: nor passed heedlessly through their unmarked wastes.

verses.h1: The clouds have trailed their skirts through them,
verses.h2: and their thickets have grown lush with blossom.

notes.note: تمثل بالدمع is unusual and possibly misprinted. I have taken تمثل بـ to mean ‘mutilate’ or ‘maltreat,’ giving ‘wreak havoc on tears’; the intended image is uncertain.

verses.h1: أثلث، فإنا أيها الطلل
verses.h2: نبكي، وترزم تحتنا الإبل

verses.h1: لو كنت تنطق قلت
verses.h2: معتذرا بي غير ما بك أيها الرجل

verses.h1: أبكاك أنك بعض من شعفوا
verses.h2: ولم أبك أني بعض من قتلوا

verses.h1: إن الذين أقمت وارتحلوا
verses.h2: أيامهم لديارهم دول

verses.h1: Be the third, O ruined dwelling, for we
verses.h2: weep, and the camels moan beneath us.

verses.h1: If you could speak, you would say
verses.h2: in apology: “My affliction is not yours, O man.

verses.h1: You weep because you are among those consumed by love;
verses.h2: I have not wept, though I am among those slain.”

verses.h1: Those who departed while you remained—
verses.h2: their days bring changing fortunes to their dwellings.

verses.h1: لمن طلل لم أشجه وشجاني
verses.h2: وهاج الصبي، لو هاجه لأوان!

verses.h1: بلى، فازدهتني للصبي أريحية
verses.h2: يمانية إن السماح يماني

verses.h1: Whose are these ruins? I did not grieve them, yet they grieved me;
verses.h2: they stirred youthful passion—if only they had stirred it in its season!

verses.h1: Yes, a generous impulse toward youthful passion swept me away—
verses.h2: a Yemeni one: generosity is Yemeni.

notes.note: الصبي, here and in line 2, appears to represent الصبا, ‘youthful passion,’ rather than ‘the boy.’ I take the compressed phrase لو هاجه لأوان as a wish: ‘if only they had stirred it at the proper time.’

poems.intro: وقال آخر، وهو ذو الرمة غيلان:

verses.h1: ما هاج عينيك من الأطلال
verses.h2: المزمنات بعدك الخوالي

verses.h1: كالوحي في سواعد الحوالي
verses.h2: غيرها تناسخ الأحوال

verses.h1: وغير الأيام والليالي
verses.h2: فاستبدلت والدهر ذو استبدال

verses.h1: من ساكنيها فرق الآجال
verses.h2: فانظر إلى صدرك ذا بلبال

verses.h1: صبابة للأزمن الخوالي
What in the ruins has stirred your eyes to tears—
verses.h2: long-weathered, deserted since you left?

verses.h1: Like writing on the forearms of adorned women—
verses.h2: the succession of years has changed them,

verses.h1: And the vicissitudes of days and nights;
verses.h2: they have exchanged—for time brings change—

verses.h1: Their inhabitants for bands of wild cattle.
verses.h2: Consider, then, your heart, so full of turmoil,

verses.h1: In longing for times gone by.

notes.note: الأحوال can mean either “years” or “conditions”; “years” is adopted here.

prose_translation.intro: Another poet, Dhū al-Rumma, Ghaylān, said:

verses.h1: مألف موحش من الآلاف
verses.h2: هاج عافية لي جوي غير عاف

verses.h1: أحرام صفو الليالي لصب
verses.h2: ذكرته الأطلال عهد التصافي؟

verses.h1: عاج يمحو بعض الصبابة ما بي
verses.h2: ن مغان ممحوة وأثاف

verses.h1: كم ترى شمل أهلها في افتراق
verses.h2: وترى شمل دمعه في ائتلاف!

verses.h1: A familiar haunt, desolate of companions:
verses.h2: Its fading traces stirred in me a grief that does not fade.

verses.h1: Is the serenity of nights forbidden to a lovesick man
verses.h2: whom the ruins remind of a time of mutual affection?

verses.h1: He turned aside to efface some of his longing, among
verses.h2: effaced dwellings and hearthstones.

verses.h1: How often you see its people scattered apart,
verses.h2: and see his tears gathered together!

notes.note: The second hemistich appears to contain transcription errors. I tentatively read «عافية» as «عافيه» (‘its effaced traces’) and «جوي» as «جوى» (‘grief’ or ‘love-sorrow’).

verses.h1: عوجا على الطلل المحيل لعلنا
verses.h2: نبكي الديار كما بكى ابن خذام

verses.h1: فظللت في دمن الديار كأنني
verses.h2: نشوان باكره صبوح مدام

verses.h1: Turn aside, you two, to the timeworn ruins, that we may
verses.h2: weep for the dwellings as Ibn Khidhām wept.

verses.h1: I lingered among the dark traces of the dwellings, as though I were
verses.h2: a drunken man plied at dawn with a draught of aged wine.

notes.note: The identity of Ibn Khidhām, invoked as a predecessor in weeping over abandoned dwellings, is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Ḥujr said:

poems.intro: روى ابن حبيب أنه "ابن حمام" وقال ابن الكلبي: "هو امرؤ القيس بن حمام بن مالك بن عبيدة بن هبل الكلبي، وكذا روى ابن الأعرابي، وأبو عمرو، والمفضل، وخالد. وقلت - من قصيدة -:

verses.h1: نعم هذه الأطلال قفر كما ترى
verses.h2: فما عذر أجفاني إذا لم تفض دما؟

verses.h1: ولليوم أعددت الدموع وصنتها
verses.h2: وما يستجم الدمع إلا ليسجما

verses.h1: وفي منزل الأحباب عذر لذي الهوى
verses.h2: فلا لوم إلا أن تجور وتظلما

verses.h1: Yes, these ruins are desolate, as you see;
verses.h2: what excuse have my eyelids, then, if they do not pour forth blood?

verses.h1: For this day I readied my tears and kept them in reserve;
verses.h2: tears gather only to stream forth.

verses.h1: In the loved ones’ dwelling lies an excuse for one in love;
verses.h2: so there is no ground for blame, unless you would be unjust and do wrong.

prose_translation.intro: Ibn Ḥabīb reported that he was “Ibn Ḥumām.” Ibn al-Kalbī said: “He is Imruʾ’ al-Qays ibn Ḥumām ibn Mālik ibn ʿUbayda ibn Hubal al-Kalbī.” Ibn al-Aʿrābī, Abū ʿAmr, al-Mufaḍḍal, and Khālid reported likewise. And I said, in a passage from a qasida:

poems.poet: سعيد بن حميد، الدوقلة أو غيره
poems.poet_from_text: سعيد بن حميد المنبجي المذحجي المعروف بالدوقلة
poems.intro: وقال سعيد بن حميد المنبجي المذحجي المعروف بالدوقلة:

poet.expected: سعيد بن حميد، الدوقلة أو غيره
poet.from_text: سعيد بن حميد المنبجي المذحجي المعروف بالدوقلة

verses.h1: هل بالطلول لسائل رد
verses.h2: أم هل لها بتكلم عهد؟

verses.h1: درس الجديد جديد معهدها
verses.h2: وكأنما هي ريطة جرد

verses.h1: من طول ما تبكي الغيوم على
verses.h2: عرصاتها، ويقهقه الرعد

verses.h1: وتلث سارية وغادية
verses.h2: ويكر نحس خلفه سعد

verses.h1: تلقى شآمية يمانية
verses.h2: لهما بمور ترابها سرد

verses.h1: فوقفت أسألها وليس بها
verses.h2: إلا ألمها ونقانق ربد

verses.h1: فتناثرت درر الشؤون على
verses.h2: خدي كما يتناثر العقد

verses.h1: Have the ruins an answer for one who asks,
verses.h2: or have they ever been acquainted with speech?

verses.h1: Time has worn away the freshness of their site,
verses.h2: and they seem a threadbare cloth,

verses.h1: so long have the clouds wept over
verses.h2: their courtyards, while thunder laughs aloud.

verses.h1: Night showers and morning showers linger,
verses.h2: and ill fortune comes round, with good fortune following.

verses.h1: A wind from al-Shām meets one from al-Yaman;
verses.h2: the two weave with the ruins’ swirling dust.

verses.h1: I stood questioning them, though they held nothing
verses.h2: but oryx and dusky male ostriches.

verses.h1: Then pearls spilled from my tear ducts
verses.h2: over my cheeks, as a necklace’s beads scatter.

notes.note: الجديد is understood here as time renewing itself, which wears away the site’s former freshness; the precise sense of the singular expression is uncertain.
نحس and سعد may refer specifically to successive unlucky and lucky stars or periods, rather than to ill and good fortune in general.
شآمية and يمانية are understood as winds from al-Shām and al-Yaman. سرد appears to describe their weaving or interlacing the moving dust, but its exact sense here is uncertain.
ألمها appears to be a typing or OCR error for المها, ‘oryx,’ adopted in the translation.

prose_translation.intro: Saʿīd ibn Ḥumayd al-Manbijī al-Madhḥijī, known as al-Dawqalah, said:
interludes: He means al-Dabarān and al-ʿAqrab:

verses.h1: خبرني أيها الطلل
verses.h2: الألى حدوك ما فعلوا؟

verses.h1: لا علم لي بهم
verses.h2: أيها المشتاق مذ رحلوا

verses.h1: فأبكهم؛ ثم أبكني معهم
verses.h2: بدموع ماؤها خضل

verses.h1: تنسج النكباء في دمني
verses.h2: للبلى ثوبا وتغتزل

verses.h1: فإذا ما أخلقت حلل
verses.h2: جددت لي بعدها حلل

verses.h1: قلت: إن القلب بعدهم
verses.h2: من عزاء عنهم عطل

verses.h1: عصفت فيه رياح هوى
verses.h2: فكلانا بعدهم طلل

verses.h1: Tell me, O ruined dwelling:
verses.h2: those who dwelt in you—what became of them?

verses.h1: “I have no knowledge of them,
verses.h2: O yearning one, since they departed.

verses.h1: So weep for them, then weep for me along with them,
verses.h2: with tears flowing abundantly.

verses.h1: The crosswind weaves among my remnants
verses.h2: a garment for decay, and spins.

verses.h1: Whenever garments wear out,
verses.h2: it makes me fresh garments in their stead.”

verses.h1: I said: “Since their departure, my heart
verses.h2: has been bereft of solace for their absence.

verses.h1: Winds of longing have swept through it;
verses.h2: so since they left, we are both ruins.”

notes.note: حدوك appears to be a misprint for حلوك, ‘dwelt in you,’ which is the reading translated here.

interludes: It said to me:

verses.h1: هل عند هذا الطلل الماحل
verses.h2: إجابة تجدي على سائل؟

verses.h1: أصم، بل يسمع، لكنه
verses.h2: من البلى في شغل شاغل

verses.h1: وقفت فيها شبحا ماثلا
verses.h2: مرتفدا من شبح ماثل

verses.h1: ولا ترى أعجب من ناحل
verses.h2: يشكو ضنى الجسم إلى ناحل

verses.h1: لهفك يا دار، ولهفي على
verses.h2: قطينك المرتحل الزائل

verses.h1: قلبي للأحزان بعد النوى
verses.h2: وأنت للسافي وللناخل

verses.h1: مثلان في السقم، ولي فضلة
verses.h2: بالعقل، والبلوى على العاقل

verses.h1: Does this barren ruin have
verses.h2: an answer that might help a questioner?

verses.h1: It is deaf—no, it hears, but
verses.h2: decay keeps it wholly occupied.

verses.h1: I stood there, a figure upright,
verses.h2: seeking support from another upright figure.

verses.h1: You will see nothing stranger than a wasted man
verses.h2: complaining of his body’s weakness to another wasted form.

verses.h1: Your grief, O dwelling, and mine are for
verses.h2: your inhabitants, who have departed and gone.

verses.h1: My heart is left to sorrows after separation,
verses.h2: and you to drifting sand and fine, sifting rain.

verses.h1: We are alike in sickness, but I surpass you
verses.h2: in understanding—and affliction weighs upon those who understand.

notes.note: I take al-sāfī as wind-driven sand and al-nākhil as fine, sifting rain. The latter is uncertain here; it may instead describe a wind that sifts or scatters dust.

verses.h1: ألا أنعم صباحا أيها الطلل البالي
verses.h2: وهل ينعمن من كان في العصر الخالي؟

verses.h1: وهل ينعمن إلا سعيد مخلد
verses.h2: قليل الهموم، لا يبيت بأوجال؟

verses.h1: ديار لسعدى عافيات بذي الخال
verses.h2: ألح عليها كل أسحم هطال

verses.h1: Ah, a happy morning to you, O timeworn ruins!
verses.h2: But can one who lived in an age gone by be happy?

verses.h1: And who can be happy but a fortunate man who lives forever,
verses.h2: with few cares, never passing the night in fear?

verses.h1: Dwellings of Saʿdā, effaced at Dhū al-Khāl,
verses.h2: on which every dark, rain-laden cloud has poured relentlessly.

notes.note: Dhū al-Khāl is a place-name; its precise location is uncertain.

verses.h1: لهند بحزان الشريف طلول
verses.h2: تلوح وأدنى عهدهن محيل

verses.h1: وبالسفح آيات كأن رسومها
verses.h2: يمان وشته ريدة وسحيل

verses.h1: فغيرن آيات الديار مع البلى
verses.h2: وليس على ريب الزمان كفيل

verses.h1: بما قد أرى الحي الجميع بغبطة
verses.h2: إذ الحي حي، والحلول حلول

interludes.text: (ريدة: قرية باليمن، وسحيل: ريح تسحل، أي تقشر)

verses.h1: Hind has ruined camps on the rugged ground of al-Sharīf,
verses.h2: still visible, though a year has passed since their last occupation.

verses.h1: At the foot of the slope are traces, their outlines like
verses.h2: a Yemeni cloth embroidered by Rayda and Saḥīl.

verses.h1: So the marks of the dwellings were altered as they decayed;
verses.h2: and against time’s vicissitudes there is no guarantor

verses.h1: for what I once saw—the whole tribe together in prosperity,
verses.h2: when the tribe was a tribe, and the dwellers were dwellers.

notes.note: I take محيل to mean ‘a year old’ or ‘having passed through a year’; the reference to the camps’ last occupation is implicit rather than explicit.

Saḥīl (سحيل) appears to be a place associated with Yemeni textiles, but its identification is uncertain. The spelling may be related to, or a corruption of, Saḥūl (سحول), a name associated with such cloth.

The unvocalized فغيرن is difficult in context. I tentatively read it as passive, فَغُيِّرْنَ, with ‘the marks of the dwellings’ explaining the feminine plural pronoun. An active reading, ‘they altered,’ would leave the subject unidentified in the supplied text.

interludes: (Rayda: a village in Yemen; Saḥīl: a wind that scrapes away, that is, strips off the surface.)

verses.h1: ألم تر للأطلال يوم سويقة
verses.h2: عفت بعد عهد الحي فهي قفور؟

verses.h1: تحمل منها بعد طول إقامة
verses.h2: حسان نقيات المدامع حور

verses.h1: دعاهن سير بعد خفض ورفعت
verses.h2: لهن على بزل الجمال خدور

verses.h1: فأصبحت لا أدري لدن أن رأيتهم أتى حدب دون الجميع وقور
وحتى رأيت الحي تعفو عراصهم
verses.h2: يمانية تسدي البلى وتنير

verses.h1: ونفح جنوب أو شمال ملثة
verses.h2: تعارضها بالمعصفات دبور

verses.h1: Did you not see the ruins that day at Suwayqa,
verses.h2: effaced since the tribe dwelt there, now desolate?

verses.h1: From them departed, after a long stay,
verses.h2: beautiful, clear-eyed women, their eyes vividly black and white.

verses.h1: Travel summoned them after ease, and there were raised
verses.h2: curtained litters for them upon full-grown camels.

verses.h1: Now I know nothing of them since I saw them; a ridge and hills have come between me and the company.
And until I saw the tribe—their open grounds being effaced
verses.h2: by a wind from Yaman, laying decay’s warp and weaving it.

verses.h1: And gusts of a south wind, or a persistent north wind,
verses.h2: crossed by a west wind with its tempestuous blasts.

notes.note: The syntax of لدن أن رأيتهم أتى حدب دون الجميع وقور is unclear, and the text may be defective. The translation tentatively takes أتى حدب ... وقور to mean that a ridge and hills intervened; ‘of them’ and ‘between me and’ are supplied to make the inferred sense readable.

The opening وحتى (‘and until’) does not connect clearly with the preceding line as transmitted. يمانية is understood as a wind from Yaman. تنير is taken as a weaving term associated with threading the loom, continuing the image introduced by تسدي (‘lays the warp’).

verses.h1: بقيت طلولك يا أمام على البلى
verses.h2: لا مثل ما بقيت عليه طلول

verses.h1: عفت الجنوب مع الشمال رسومها
verses.h2: وصبا مزمزمة الحنين عجول

verses.h1: أعذرت في طلب النوال إليكم
verses.h2: لو كان من ملك النوال ينيل

verses.h1: إن كان دهركم الدلال فإنه
verses.h2: حسن دلالك يا أميم جميل

verses.h1: لا يبعدن أنس تقادم بعدهم
verses.h2: طلل ببرقة رامتين محيل

verses.h1: ولقد نكون إذا يحل بغبطة
verses.h2: أيام أهلك للديار حلول

verses.h1: ولقد تساعفنا الديار وعيشنا
verses.h2: لو دام ذاك كما نحب ظليل

verses.h1: فسقى ديارك حيث كنت مجلجل
verses.h2: هزج، ومن غر السحاب هطول

verses.h1: Your ruins, O Umām, have endured amid decay;
verses.h2: no other ruins have endured as they have.

verses.h1: The south wind and the north have effaced their traces,
verses.h2: and a rushing east wind, murmuring its lament.

verses.h1: I have spared no effort in seeking favor from you—
verses.h2: if only the one who possessed that favor would bestow it!

verses.h1: If coyness is your constant way, then indeed
verses.h2: your coyness, O Umaym, is fine and lovely.

verses.h1: May that fellowship never perish! Since they left, time has aged
verses.h2: a desolate ruin at Burqat Rāmatayn.

verses.h1: Indeed, we once lived in happiness when we camped,
verses.h2: in the days when your people dwelt in those abodes.

verses.h1: The dwellings once favored us, and our life—
verses.h2: if only it had lasted as we wished!—was sheltered.

verses.h1: May a rumbling cloud water your dwellings, wherever you are,
verses.h2: a pealing cloud, and a downpour from the bright clouds.

notes.note: عجول is rendered as ‘rushing,’ but it can also describe a bereaved mother or she-camel. Alongside الحنين (‘plaintive yearning’), it may instead personify the wind as grieving.
The syntax is compressed. I take لا يبعدن أنس as an independent blessing on past fellowship, and طلل in the second hemistich as the delayed subject of تقادم (‘has grown old’).
إذا يحل (‘when he settles’) is awkward beside نكون (‘we were/would be’). The translation provisionally reads إذا نحل (‘when we settle’), a possible correction of a dotting or transcription error.

poems.poet_from_text: عمارة بن بلال بن جرير بن عطية
poems.intro: وقال عمارة بن بلال بن جرير بن عطية:

poet.from_text: عمارة بن بلال بن جرير بن عطية

verses.h1: ألا يا اسلما يا أيها الطللان
verses.h2: وإن هجتما عيني على الهملان

verses.h1: وهل دمع عيني اللجوجين راجع
verses.h2: ليالي حل الحي هضب عران

verses.h1: كأن زمانا حله الحي باللوى
verses.h2: لوى ترمذاء لم يكن بزمان

verses.h1: ولم تغن في أيامه أحسن الغنى
verses.h2: وشعبا جميع الشمل متفقان

verses.h1: إذا قلت: أنسى ذكر أسماء هيبت
verses.h2: بقلبي دواعي حبها فعصاني

verses.h1: Peace to you both, O two ruined camps,
verses.h2: though you have stirred my eyes to streaming tears.

verses.h1: Can the tears of my unrelenting eyes bring back
verses.h2: the nights when the tribe camped among the hills of ʿArān?

verses.h1: It is as though the time the tribe spent at the sandy bend—
verses.h2: the bend of Tarmadhāʾ—had never been.

verses.h1: As though its days had not been lived in utmost happiness,
verses.h2: with our two clans gathered together in harmony.

verses.h1: Whenever I say, ‘I shall put Asmāʾ from my mind,’ love calls
verses.h2: to my heart with its promptings, and my heart disobeys me.

notes.note: The place عران has not been securely identified; the vocalization ʿArān is tentative.
ترمذاء is unidentified, and its vocalization as Tarmadhāʾ is tentative. The spelling may be corrupted, possibly for ثرمداء (Tharmadāʾ).

The subject of تغن (‘you/she dwelt or lived’) is unclear; the translation leaves it implicit. The compressed phrase وشعبا جميع الشمل متفقان is taken provisionally to describe two clans gathered in unity.
هيبت بقلبي is unusual. It is provisionally understood as ‘called to my heart,’ with دواعي حبها (‘the promptings of her love’) as its subject; the wording may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmāra ibn Bilāl ibn Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyya said:

poems.intro: روى عن مويلك عن أبيه قال: قال لي سائب خاثر يوم الحرة: ألا أسمعك شيئا قد صنعت؟ قلت: نعم، فغناني:

verses.h1: لمن طلل بين الكراع إلى القصر
verses.h2: يغيب عنا آيه سبل القطر

verses.h1: إلى خالدات ما تريم، وهامد
verses.h2: وأشعث ترسيه الوليدة بالفهر

verses.h1: Whose are the ruins between al-Kurāʿ and al-Qaṣr?
verses.h2: The streaming rain conceals their traces from us,

verses.h1: save for enduring hearthstones that never shift, and cold ashes,
verses.h2: and a splintered tent peg the young girl drives firmly in with a handstone.

notes.note: The precise locations of al-Kurāʿ and al-Qaṣr are uncertain.
The source reads إلى (‘to’), but إلا (‘except for’) appears required by the sense and is followed here.

The objects are described rather than explicitly named: خالدات (‘enduring things’) probably means hearthstones, هامد (‘extinguished, lifeless’) ashes, and أشعث (‘shaggy, disheveled’) a weathered or splintered tent peg. These identifications, especially the last, are interpretive.

prose_translation.intro: It is related from Muwaylik, from his father, who said: Sāʾib Khāthir said to me on the day of al-Ḥarra, “Shall I let you hear something I have composed?” I said, “Yes,” and he sang to me:

poems.poet_from_text: ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود
poems.intro: فسمعت عجبا معجبا، ثم ذكر أهله وولده، فبكى، فقلت له: فما يمنعك منهم؟ قال: أما بعد شيء سمعته من يزيد بن معاوية فلا، ثم تقدم فقاتل بسيفه حتى قتل، وسائب خاثر: مولى بني ليث، اشترى عبد الله بن جعفر - رضي الله عنهما - ولاءه من مواليه، وقيل: اشتراه وأعتقه، فانقطع إلى عبد الله ولزمه، وهو أول من عمل العود بالمدينة، وغنى به. وقال ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود:

poet.from_text: ذو الرمة غيلان بن عقبة بن مسعود

verses.h1: لمية أطلال بحزوي دواثر
verses.h2: عفتها السوافي بعدنا والمواطر

verses.h1: كأن فؤادي
verses.h2: هاض عرفان ربعها بها وهي ساق أسلمتها الجبائر

verses.h1: عشية مسعود يقول
verses.h2: وقد جرى

verses.h1: على لحيتي من دمع عيني ماطر
أفي الدار تبكي أن تفرق أهلها
verses.h2: وأنت امرؤ قد حلمتك العشائر؟

verses.h1: فلا ضير أن تسعبر العين إنني
verses.h2: على ذاك إلا جولة الدمع صابر

verses.h1: فيامي هل يجزي بكائي بمثله
verses.h2: إليك، وأنفاسي عليك زوافر

verses.h1: وإني متى أشرف إلى الجانب الذي
verses.h2: به أنت من بين الجواب ناظر

verses.h1: وأن لا ينال الركب تهويم وقعة
verses.h2: من الليل إلا اعتادني منك زائر

verses.h1: Mayya’s crumbling traces lie at Ḥazwā;
verses.h2: windblown sands and rainstorms have effaced them since we left.

verses.h1: As though my heart—
verses.h2: broken anew by recognizing her campsite there—were a weakened leg abandoned by its splints.

verses.h1: That evening Masʿūd said—
verses.h2: as there streamed

verses.h1: down my beard a shower of tears from my eyes—
“Do you weep over the dwelling because its people have dispersed,
verses.h2: though you are a man the clans deem sober-minded?”

verses.h1: There is no harm if the eye sheds tears, for I,
verses.h2: despite all this, am steadfast, save for a surge of tears.

verses.h1: O Mayy, is my weeping answered with the like
verses.h2: by you, while my breaths are sighs for you?

verses.h1: Whenever I look out, it is toward the quarter
verses.h2: where you are, of all quarters, that I gaze.

verses.h1: No brief spell of dozing overtakes the riders
verses.h2: at night without a visitor from you returning to me.

notes.note: The syntax of هاض عرفان ربعها بها وهي ساق is unclear and may be corrupt. The translation tentatively understands recognition of the campsite as breaking the heart anew, followed by a comparison with an injured leg abandoned by its splints. The supplied hemistich division also appears misplaced.
Lines 3–4 appear to constitute a single bayt divided incorrectly in the supplied text; their supplied divisions have been retained. Masʿūd’s identity is uncertain.

The construction يجزي بكائي بمثله إليك is awkward. The translation tentatively understands a question about whether Mayy reciprocates the speaker’s tears; إليك literally means ‘toward you,’ rather than ‘by you.’
الجواب appears to be a misprint for الجوانب, ‘quarters’ or ‘directions,’ which is the reading translated.
The opening وأن لا is syntactically uncertain and may be misprinted. The unusual phrase تهويم وقعة has been rendered tentatively as ‘a brief spell of dozing.’

prose_translation.intro: I heard something truly astonishing. Then he spoke of his family and children and wept. I said to him, “What keeps you from joining them?” He replied, “After something I heard from Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya—no.” Then he advanced and fought with his sword until he was killed. Sāʾib Khāthir was a client of the Banū Layth. ʿAbd Allah ibn Jaʿfar—may God be pleased with them both—purchased the rights of patronage over him from his patrons; it is also said that he bought him and set him free. He then devoted himself to ʿAbd Allah and remained in his company. He was the first to make an oud in al-Madīna and sing to its accompaniment. Dhū al-Rumma, Ghaylān ibn ʿUqba ibn Masʿūd, said:

poems.intro: وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة المخزومي:

verses.h1: بوجرة أطلال تعفت رسومها
verses.h2: وأقفر من بعد الأنيس قديمها

verses.h1: تلوح على طول الزمان عراصها
verses.h2: كما لاح في كف الفتاة وشومها

verses.h1: وقفت بها والعين شاملة القذى
verses.h2: كعين طريف ما يجف سجومها

verses.h1: فذلك هاج الشوق من أم نوفل
verses.h2: وذكرى لنفس جمة ما تريمها

verses.h1: فقد أدركت عندي من الود فوق ما
verses.h2: تمنت بغيب أو تمنى حميمها

verses.h1: At Wajra are ruins whose traces have faded,
verses.h2: their ancient dwellings deserted since their people left.

verses.h1: Their open grounds remain visible through the long years,
verses.h2: as tattoos show on a young woman’s palm.

verses.h1: I stood there, my eye beset with grit,
verses.h2: like an injured eye whose streaming tears never dry.

verses.h1: That stirred my longing for Umm Nawfal,
verses.h2: and a host of memories that never leave my soul.

verses.h1: She has indeed gained from me more affection than
verses.h2: she wished in secret, or her close companion wished.

notes.note: شاملة القذى is an unusual expression, rendered literally as an eye beset with grit. I take طريف to mean someone struck or injured in the eye.
The syntax of وذكرى لنفس جمة ما تريمها is compressed. I take جمة (‘abundant’) to describe the memories, which do not leave the soul.
بغيب may mean ‘in secret’ or ‘in [my] absence’; the former is used here.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī said:

verses.h1: عفا من آل بلجاء الطلول
verses.h2: وجد البين وانقطع الوسيل

verses.h1: وصاح بصرمها من بطن قو
verses.h2: غداة البين شحاج حجول

verses.h1: من اللائي لعن بكل أرض
verses.h2: فليس لهن في بلد قبول

verses.h1: يباصرن النوى فإذا اشمعلت
verses.h2: بأهل الدار واقلولى الحمول

verses.h1: تبادرن الديار يمسن فيها
verses.h2: وبئس من المليحات البديل

verses.h1: The traces of Baljāʾ’s folk have faded;
verses.h2: separation has grown earnest, and the bond is severed.

verses.h1: From the hollow of Qaww, her breaking with us was proclaimed
verses.h2: on the morning of parting by a harsh-voiced, hopping crow.

verses.h1: One of those cursed in every land,
verses.h2: welcome in no country.

verses.h1: They watch for departure; when it hastens away
verses.h2: with the dwellings’ people, and the laden camels move off,

verses.h1: they race to the dwellings and strut about within them—
verses.h2: a wretched substitute for the lovely women!

notes.note: Baljāʾ appears to be a woman’s name; her identity is unknown.
Qaww is a place name, but its precise location is uncertain. The feminine pronoun in bi-ṣarmihā (‘her breaking off’) is taken to refer to Baljāʾ.
The rare verb iqlawlā is rendered ‘move off’; its precise force here may be ‘rise’ or ‘hasten away.’

verses.h1: ألا يا اسلما بالنير من أم واصل
verses.h2: ومن أم جبر أيها الطللان

verses.h1: وهل يسلم الربعان يجرى عليهما
verses.h2: صباح مساء دائم الهطلان

verses.h1: كفى حزنا أني تطاللت كي أرى
verses.h2: ذرى علمي دمخ فما تريان

verses.h1: كأنهما والآل يجري عليهما
verses.h2: من البعد عينا برقع خلقان

verses.h1: ألا حبذا والله
verses.h2: لو تعلمانه

verses.h1: ظلالكما يأيها العلمان
وماؤكما العذب الذي لو شربته
verses.h2: وبي صالب الحمى إذا لشفاني

verses.h1: Hail to you both at al-Nīr, remnants of Umm Wāṣil
verses.h2: and Umm Jabr, O you two ruined dwellings!

verses.h1: But can the two dwelling sites survive, when over them pours,
verses.h2: morning and evening, unceasing rain?

verses.h1: It is grief enough that I stretched upward to see
verses.h2: the crests of Damkh’s two heights, yet you two cannot be seen.

verses.h1: With the mirage flowing over them, the two seem
verses.h2: from afar like the eyeholes of a worn-out veil.

verses.h1: Ah, how lovely, by God—
verses.h2: if only you two knew it—

verses.h1: is your shade, O you two heights!
And your sweet water, which, if I drank it
verses.h2: while a fierce fever gripped me, would surely cure me.

notes.note: I read تريان as passive تُرَيان, ‘you two are seen,’ taking the phrase as a direct address to the two heights. The unvowelled wording is ambiguous; يُريان, ‘they are seen,’ may instead have been intended.
Lines 5–6 appear to be one bayt split incorrectly in the digitized text: ألا حبذا والله لو تعلمانه / ظلالكما يأيها العلمان. The supplied segmentation has been retained.

poems.intro: وقال أبو الصفى رفاعة بن قيس:

verses.h1: سفى الله أطلالا لبلجاء بالغضا
verses.h2: كساها البلى والنأي لبدا على لبد

verses.h1: وأيامنا اللاتي مضين بعاقل
verses.h2: فغير ذميمات مضين ولا نكد

verses.h1: لقد كان لي ليل ببلجاء مرة
verses.h2: قصير إذا ما الليل طال على الرمد

verses.h1: May God water Baljāʾ’s ruined dwellings at al-Ghaḍā,
verses.h2: which decay and distance have clothed in matted layer upon layer.

verses.h1: And our days that passed at ʿĀqil—
verses.h2: they passed neither blameworthy nor unhappy.

verses.h1: Indeed, I once spent a night with Baljāʾ,
verses.h2: a short one, though the night drags on for those with sore eyes.

notes.note: The source reads سفى الله, probably a misprint for سقى الله, the conventional prayer ‘May God water …’; the translation follows that reading.
لبدا على لبد literally suggests felt or matted coverings piled one upon another; the precise material or image intended is uncertain.
Baljāʾ is interpreted as a woman’s name, though a place-name is also possible. The precise locations of al-Ghaḍā and ʿĀqil are uncertain here.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Ṣafā Rifāʿa ibn Qays said:

verses.h1: لمن طلل برامة لا يريم
verses.h2: عفا، وخلا له حقب قديم

verses.h1: تحمل أهله منه فبانوا
verses.h2: وفي عرصاته منهم رسوم

verses.h1: يلوح كأنه كفا فتاة
verses.h2: ترجع في معاصمها الوشوم

verses.h1: Whose is the remnant at Rāma, still unmoving,
verses.h2: worn away, with a long age passed over it?

verses.h1: Its people packed up and departed,
verses.h2: leaving traces of themselves in its open grounds.

verses.h1: It gleams like a young woman’s two hands,
verses.h2: the tattoos on her wrists traced afresh.

notes.note: The unvocalized ترجع is taken here as turajjaʿu, meaning that the tattoos are retraced or renewed; ‘return/reappear’ is also a possible reading.

prose_translation.intro: And Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā said:

verses.h1: أمن طلل أقوى من الحي ماثله
verses.h2: تهيج أحزان الطروب منازله

verses.h1: بكيت وما يبكيك من رسم دمنة
verses.h2: أضر به جود الشمال ووابله؟

verses.h1: وحبك ينسيني من الشيء في يدي
verses.h2: ويذهلني عن كل شيء أزاوله

verses.h1: سيهلك في الدنيا شفيق عليكم
verses.h2: إذا غاله من حادث الدهر غائله

verses.h1: كريم يميت السر حتى كأنه
verses.h2: إذا استخبروه عن حديثك جاهله

verses.h1: Was it for a ruin whose standing remains the tribe has deserted—
verses.h2: its dwellings stirring the lovesick man’s sorrows—

verses.h1: that you wept? What makes you weep over a campsite’s traces,
verses.h2: worn away by the north wind’s abundant rain and downpours?

verses.h1: Love for you makes me forget what is in my hand
verses.h2: and distracts me from everything I undertake.

verses.h1: One tenderly devoted to you will perish in this world
verses.h2: when a deadly stroke of time’s misfortunes takes him.

verses.h1: A noble man who buries the secret so thoroughly that he seems,
verses.h2: when they ask him for news of you, to know nothing of it.

notes.note: The construction من الشيء في يدي is awkward, particularly the function of من. I have understood it as referring to what the speaker holds in his hand; the wording may contain a textual error.

verses.h1: خليلي عوجا عوجة ناقتيكما
verses.h2: على طلل بين الربنة والحبل

verses.h1: بجرعائها من سامر الحي ملعب
verses.h2: وآرى أفراس كجرثومة النمل

verses.h1: كأن لم يكنها الحي إذ أنت مرة
verses.h2: بها ميت الأهواء مجتمع الشمل

verses.h1: بكيت على مي بها إذ عرفتها
verses.h2: وهجت البكا حتى بكى القوم من أجلي

verses.h1: وهل هملان العين راجع ما مضى
verses.h2: من العيش أو مدنيك يا مي من أهلي؟

interludes.text: شبه ما تهدم من مرابط الخيل بما يخرجه النمل من التراب عند بيوته:

verses.h1: My two friends, turn your she-camels aside
verses.h2: toward a ruined campsite between ar-Rabnah and al-Ḥabl.

verses.h1: On its sandy flat is a place where the tribe made merry at night,
verses.h2: and a tethering-place for horses, like an anthill.

verses.h1: As though the tribe had never dwelt there—though once you were
verses.h2: there, your yearnings stilled, your loved ones gathered together.

verses.h1: I wept for Mayy there when I recognized the place,
verses.h2: and stirred such weeping that my companions wept on my account.

verses.h1: But can streaming tears bring back the life
verses.h2: that has passed, or bring you, Mayy, nearer to my kin?

notes.note: The places الربنة and الحبل are not securely identified; ar-Rabnah and al-Ḥabl are provisional vocalizations.
I read آرى as آريّ, a tethering-place or stall for horses; the intended spelling and form are uncertain.
ميت الأهواء literally means ‘dead in desires/passions.’ I have interpreted this unusual expression as yearnings stilled through fulfillment, but its precise force is uncertain.

interludes: He likened the crumbled remains of the horses’ tethering-places to the earth that ants bring out beside their nests:

verses.h1: قف العيش في أطلال مية فاسأل
verses.h2: رسوما كأخلاق الرداء المسلسل

verses.h1: أظن الذي يجدي عليك سوالها
verses.h2: دموعا كتبذير الجمان المفصل

verses.h1: وما يوم حزوي إن بكيت صبابة
verses.h2: لعرفان ربع أو لعرفان منزل

verses.h1: بأول ما هاجت لك الشوق دمنة
verses.h2: بأجراع محلال مرب محلل

verses.h1: عفت غير آري وأعضاد مسجد
verses.h2: وسفع مناخات رواحل مرجل

verses.h1: تجر بها الدقعاء هيف كأنها
verses.h2: تسح التراب من خصاصات منخل

verses.h1: دعت مية الأعداد واستبدلت بها
verses.h2: خناطيل آجال من العين خذل

verses.h1: Halt the pale camels among Mayya’s ruins, and question
verses.h2: the traces, like the tatters of a threadbare cloak.

verses.h1: I think all your questioning of them will bring you
verses.h2: is tears, like pearls scattered from a necklace.

verses.h1: And the day at Hazwa—if you wept with longing
verses.h2: on recognizing a campsite or a dwelling—

verses.h1: was not the first time a deserted site stirred your yearning
verses.h2: among sandy flats where people often halted and stayed.

verses.h1: It has faded, save for a tethering stake and the posts of a prayer enclosure,
verses.h2: and blackened stones, kneeling mounts that bore a cooking pot.

verses.h1: Hot, parching winds drag the fine dust across it,
verses.h2: as though pouring earth through the holes of a sieve.

verses.h1: The perennial waterholes parted with Mayya and took in her stead
verses.h2: scattered herds of wide-eyed wild cows, lingering with their calves.

notes.note: العيش (‘life’) appears to be a misprint for العيس (‘pale camels’), which is translated here. The precise textile sense of المسلسل is uncertain; ‘threadbare’ is provisional.
The closely grouped epithets محلال مرب محلل appear to describe a frequently occupied stopping place; their precise individual senses are uncertain.
I take سفع مناخات رواحل مرجل as blackened hearthstones likened to kneeling riding beasts supporting a cooking pot. The compressed construction is uncertain.

The opening دعت is unclear as transmitted. The translation takes الأعداد (‘perennial waterholes’) as the subject of both verbs and understands the first as releasing or parting with Mayya; a defective form or misprint involving ودعت may be involved.

poems.intro: (يقول: لما نصبت مياه منازلهم ارتحلوا إلى الأعداد، وهي المياه التي لها مادة في الصيف والشتاء، فكأنها دعتها، والخناطيل: أقاطيع الظباء والبقر، الواحدة خنطلة، وإجل، والعين: البقر الوحشي، وخذلت الظبية ونحوها: أقامت وتخلفت عن قطعانها، والواحدة خاذل) وقال جميل بن معمر العذري:

verses.h1: ألم تربع فتخبرك الطلول
verses.h2: وقد ساءت لو نفع السؤول

verses.h1: وكيف سؤال خيمات بوال
verses.h2: ونوى عهد أحدثه محيل؟

verses.h1: لئن أمسى خلاء بعد جمل
verses.h2: لقد يغني به الأنس الحلول

verses.h1: Did you not halt, so the ruins might tell you,
verses.h2: though they have decayed—if questioning could avail?

verses.h1: But how can one question worn-out tents
verses.h2: and an old encampment ditch, its newest trace a year old?

verses.h1: Though it now lies empty since Juml departed,
verses.h2: once a company of people dwelt there.

notes.note: وقد ساءت is awkward here. It is translated as referring to the ruins’ deterioration, but it may be a misprint for وقد سألت, ‘though you have asked.’

The second hemistich appears defective. The translation tentatively reads نوى as نؤي, an encampment’s drainage ditch, and أحدثه محيل as ‘its newest trace is a year old.’ The wording عهد and the construction as a whole remain uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: (He means: when the waters at their dwelling places dried up, they moved to the aʿdād—watering places supplied with water in summer and winter—as though these had called them. Al-khanāṭīl: scattered herds of gazelles and wild cattle; a single herd is called a khinṭilah or an ijl. Al-ʿīn: wild cattle. Khadhalat, said of a gazelle or the like: she stayed behind, apart from her herds; one such animal is called a khādhil.) And Jamīl ibn Maʿmar al-ʿUdhrī said:

verses.h1: هلا سألت بجو ثهمد
verses.h2: طللا لمية قد تأبد؟

verses.h1: درست عهاد الغيث من
verses.h2: ه فحال عما كنت تعهد

verses.h1: ولقد يساعف ذا الهوى
verses.h2: بأوانس كالوحش خرد

verses.h1: Why did you not question, in the hollow of Thahmad,
verses.h2: the ruins of Mayya’s dwelling, now desolate?

verses.h1: Successive rains have effaced its traces,
verses.h2: and it has changed from what you used to know.

verses.h1: Once it would favor the lover
verses.h2: with bashful maidens, like wild gazelles.

notes.note: The syntax of درست عهاد الغيث منه is compressed and somewhat uncertain. I take the successive rains as the agent effacing the dwelling’s traces. The word منه is split across the two hemistichs.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: ليس بجدي يا صاحبي وقوف
verses.h2: بطلول ولا يرد سؤال

verses.h1: إنما الربع بالمقيمين فيه
verses.h2: وهو خلوا من ساكنيه مثال

verses.h1: It avails nothing, my friend, to linger
verses.h2: at ruins; nor does questioning bring back what is gone.

verses.h1: A dwelling is only what its inhabitants make it;
verses.h2: empty of those who lived there, it is a mere likeness.

notes.note: بجدي appears to be a misprint for يجدي (‘avail’). I read يرد as ‘bring back’; its object is unstated, so ‘what is gone’ is supplied.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: خليلي قوما في عطالة فانظرا
verses.h2: أنارا ترى من آل يبرين أم برقا؟

verses.h1: فإن تك نارا فهي في مشمخرة
verses.h2: من الربح تذروها وتصفقها صفقا

verses.h1: لأم علي أوقدتها طماعة
verses.h2: لأوبة سفر أن تكون لهم وفقا

verses.h1: وحطا على الأطلال رحلي فإنها
verses.h2: لأول أطلال عرفت بها العشقا

verses.h1: My two friends, rise at ʿAṭālah and look:
verses.h2: is it a fire you see from the folk of Yabrīn, or lightning?

verses.h1: If it is a fire, it stands on a towering height;
verses.h2: the wind scatters it and lashes it fiercely.

verses.h1: It belongs to Umm ʿAlī, who lit it in hope
verses.h2: of travelers returning, that it might serve them well.

verses.h1: And set down my saddle upon the ruins, for they are
verses.h2: the first ruins where I came to know love.

notes.note: ʿAṭālah appears to be a place-name, but its location is uncertain. I take آل يبرين as ‘the folk of Yabrīn’; آل can also mean ‘mirage,’ making the phrase ambiguous.
الربح (‘profit’) appears corrupt, probably for الريح (‘wind’). The translation follows that reading, though the syntax of من الريح remains awkward. مشمخرة is understood as an elevated peak or height.
Umm ʿAlī is unidentified. The final phrase is understood to mean that the fire would be useful to the returning travelers.

prose_translation.intro: And Suwayd ibn Kurāʿ al-ʿUklī said:

verses.h1: أتعرف أطلالا بوهبين فالخضر
verses.h2: لمي كأنيار المفوفة الخضر

verses.h1: فلما عرفت الدار واغترني الهوى
verses.h2: تذكرت، هل لي إن تصابيت من عذر؟

verses.h1: فلم أر عذرا بعد عشرين حجة
verses.h2: مضت لي وعشر قد مضين إلى عشر

verses.h1: فأخفيت شوقي من رفيقي وإنه
verses.h2: لذو نسب دان إلي وذو حجر

verses.h1: محل الحواءين الذي لست رائيا
verses.h2: محلهما إلا غلبت على الصبر

verses.h1: فهاجت عليك الدار ما لست ناسيا
verses.h2: من الحاج إلا أن تنسى على ذكر

verses.h1: إذا قلت: يسلو ذكر مية قلبه
verses.h2: أبى حبها إلا بقاء على الدهر

verses.h1: Do you recognize ruins at Wahbayn and al-Khaḍr,
verses.h2: Mayy’s, like the bands of green striped cloth?

verses.h1: When I recognized the dwelling and passion beguiled me,
verses.h2: I reflected: have I any excuse for indulging in youthful passion?

verses.h1: I could see no excuse after twenty years
verses.h2: of my life had passed, and ten more added to another ten.

verses.h1: So I hid my longing from my companion, though he
verses.h2: is a close kinsman of mine and a man of good sense.

verses.h1: The site of the two encampments—I never see
verses.h2: their dwelling place without losing command of my patience.

verses.h1: The dwelling stirred in you what you will never forget
verses.h2: of your longings—unless you forget despite remembrance.

verses.h1: Whenever you say, “His heart will leave Mayya’s memory behind,”
verses.h2: love for her insists on enduring for all time.

notes.note: The places وهبين and الخضر are not securely identified here; their vocalizations as Wahbayn and al-Khaḍr are tentative.

The qualification إلا أن تنسى على ذكر is obscure. Translated literally as “unless you forget despite remembrance,” it may refer to forgetting despite reminders or to deliberately suppressing recollection.
The unvocalized قلت can mean “I say” or “you say.” The latter is adopted here, retaining the third-person “his heart” in the quoted thought. Mayya is a variant of Mayy in line 1.

verses.h1: عليكن يا أطلال مي بشارع
verses.h2: على ما مضى من عهدكن سلام

verses.h1: علام سألناكن عن أم سالم
verses.h2: ومي فلم يرجع لكن كلام

verses.h1: هوى لك لا ينفك يدعو كما دعا
verses.h2: حماما بأجراع العقيق حمام

verses.h1: إذا هملت عيني له قال صاحبي:
verses.h2: بمثلك هذا فتنة وغرام

verses.h1: Upon you, O ruins of Mayy at Shāriʿ,
verses.h2: though your days are long past, be peace.

verses.h1: Why did we ask you about Umm Sālim
verses.h2: and Mayy, when no words came back from you?

verses.h1: A longing for you keeps calling, as
verses.h2: one dove called to others on the sandy stretches of al-ʿAqīq.

verses.h1: When my eye overflows with tears for it, my companion says:
verses.h2: “For a man like you, this is a trial and torment.”

notes.note: Shāriʿ appears to be a place name; I cannot securely identify its location.
Several places bear the name al-ʿAqīq; the particular location intended here is uncertain.
The construction بمثلك هذا فتنة وغرام is somewhat ambiguous. The translation takes هذا as referring to the speaker’s longing; غرام can mean consuming passion as well as persistent torment.

verses.h1: وقفنا فلا الأطلال ردت إجابة
verses.h2: ولا العذل أجدى في المشوق المخاطب

verses.h1: وما انفك رسم الدار حتى تهللت
verses.h2: دموعي، وحتى أكثر اللوم صاحبي

verses.h1: تمادت عقابيل الهوى وتطاولت
verses.h2: لجاجة معتوب عليه وعاتب

verses.h1: We stopped, but the ruins returned no answer,
verses.h2: nor did reproach avail with the lovelorn man addressing them.

verses.h1: The dwelling’s traces held me until there flowed
verses.h2: my tears, and until my companion reproached me again and again.

verses.h1: Love’s lingering torments persisted, and long endured
verses.h2: the obstinacy of the reproached and the reproacher.

notes.note: The construction وما انفك رسم الدار is unclear as transmitted: انفك appears to lack a complement. It may be elliptical or corrupt. “The dwelling’s traces held me” is a contextual interpretation.

verses.h1: أمن آل سلمى عرفت الطلولا
verses.h2: بذي حرض ماثلات مثولا

verses.h1: بلين وتحسب آياتهم
verses.h2: عن فرط حولين رقا محيلا

verses.h1: Was it the ruins of Salmā’s people that you recognized,
verses.h2: at Dhū Ḥaraḍ, still plainly standing?

verses.h1: They have weathered away; you would think their traces,
verses.h2: after two years have passed, a faded parchment.

notes.note: The place ذي حرض is provisionally transliterated Dhū Ḥaraḍ; its precise location and vocalization are uncertain.
عن فرط حولين is understood as ‘after two years have passed’; the exact force of فرط here is uncertain.

verses.h1: أأطلال هند ساء ما اعتضت من هند
verses.h2: أقايضت حور العين بالعين والربد

verses.h1: فلا دمع ما لم يجر في إثره دم
verses.h2: ولا وجد ما لم تعي عن صفة الوجد

verses.h1: O ruins of Hind, wretched is what you have taken in Hind’s stead!
verses.h2: Have you bartered lovely-eyed women for wide-eyed wild cattle and gray ostriches?

verses.h1: There are no tears unless blood flows in their wake,
verses.h2: And no longing unless you are powerless to describe longing.

notes.note: The unvocalized verbs اعتضت and قايضت can be first-person (‘I’) or second-person (‘you’). I read them as addressing the ruins; alternatively, the speaker may be lamenting his own exchange.

verses.h1: قف بالطلول الدارسات علاثا
verses.h2: أضحى حبال قطينهن رثاثا

verses.h1: فتأبدت من كل مخطفة الحشا
verses.h2: غيداء تكسى يارقا ورعاثا

verses.h1: Stop at the effaced ruins, O ʿUlāth;
verses.h2: the ropes of those who dwelt there have grown threadbare.

verses.h1: They have become deserted, bereft of every slender-waisted maiden,
verses.h2: graceful, adorned with bracelets and earrings.

notes.note: علاثا is uncertain. It is provisionally read as an address to ʿUlāth, possibly a shortened form of the name ʿUlātha; the person is unidentified, and textual corruption cannot be ruled out.
حبال is translated literally as ‘ropes,’ presumably tent ropes; figurative ‘bonds’ with the former inhabitants may also be intended.

verses.h1: لمن طلل عافى المحل دفين
verses.h2: عفا آيه إلا خوالد جون

verses.h1: كما اقترنت عند المساء حمائم
verses.h2: غريبات ممسى ما لهن وكون

verses.h1: ديار التي أما جنى رشفاتها
verses.h2: فيحلوا، وأما مسها فيلين

verses.h1: Whose are these buried ruins, their site effaced,
verses.h2: their traces vanished save for enduring dark stones?

verses.h1: Like doves gathered together at dusk,
verses.h2: far from home at nightfall, with no nests.

verses.h1: The abodes of her—the fruit of her kisses
verses.h2: is sweet, and her touch is soft.

notes.note: عافى appears to represent عافي, meaning effaced or obliterated here. خوالد جون literally means ‘enduring dark ones’; I understand this as the blackened hearthstones left at the campsite, though stones are not explicitly named.
غريبات ممسى is compressed and somewhat ambiguous: it may describe doves far from home at evening or doves whose evening resting place is unfamiliar.
فيحلوا appears to be a spelling or transcription error for فيحلو, ‘it is sweet.’

poems.intro: وقال كثير بن عبد الرحمن الخزاعي:

verses.h1: متى أسل عن سعدى يهجني لذكرها
verses.h2: حمائم أو أطلال دار مواثل

verses.h1: أضر بها الأنواء والريح والندى
verses.h2: وغير مغناها الضحى والأصائل

verses.h1: Whenever I forget Suʿdā, I am stirred to remember her
verses.h2: by doves or the still-standing ruins of a dwelling.

verses.h1: Seasonal rains, wind, and dew have ravaged it,
verses.h2: and mornings and evenings have altered the dwelling-place.

prose_translation.intro: And Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khuzāʿī said:

verses.h1: عزة أطلال أبت أن تكلما
verses.h2: تهيج مغانيها الطروب المتيما

verses.h1: كأن الرياح الذاريات عشية
verses.h2: بأطلالها ينسجن ريطا مسهما

verses.h1: أبت وأبى وجدي بعزة إذ نأت
verses.h2: على عدواء الدار أن يتصرما

verses.h1: ʿAzza’s ruins refuse to speak;
verses.h2: her dwelling-places stir the yearning, love-stricken man.

verses.h1: It is as though the dust-scattering winds at evening
verses.h2: weave fine, arrow-patterned cloth across her ruins.

verses.h1: They would not speak; nor would my longing for ʿAzza, when she went far away,
verses.h2: despite the remoteness of her dwelling, come to an end.

notes.note: The opening عزة أطلال appears to lack an initial ل in لعزة أطلال, ‘ʿAzza has ruins.’ The translation assumes this reading.

verses.h1: أهاجك من سعدى الغداة طلول
verses.h2: بذي الطلح عامي ومحيل

verses.h1: وما هاجه من منزل لعبت به
verses.h2: لهوجاء مرقال العشي ذيول

verses.h1: بما قد ترى سعدى به وكأنها
verses.h2: طلا راشح للبارحات خذول

verses.h1: Have Saʿdā’s ruined dwellings stirred you this morning,
verses.h2: at Dhū al-Ṭalḥ, [effaced] and weathered?

verses.h1: How it stirred him—a dwelling where there played
verses.h2: the trailing skirts of a wild wind racing at dusk!

verses.h1: There you once would see Saʿdā, as though she were
verses.h2: a fawn just learning to walk, hanging back from the departing herd.

notes.note: عامي is unclear and may be corrupt. The bracketed ‘effaced’ tentatively assumes عافي, a word commonly used of vanished dwelling traces; the wording of this hemistich remains uncertain.
The construction وما هاجه من منزل is ambiguous; it is rendered here as an exclamation. The Arabic shifts from addressing ‘you’ in line 1 to speaking of ‘him’ here.

راشح describes a young animal beginning to walk with its mother. للبارحات خذول is less certain: خذول suggests remaining behind or apart from the herd, while البارحات may mean departing animals or, more specifically, game crossing from right to left, traditionally an ill omen.

verses.h1: ألم تربع فتخبرك الطلول
verses.h2: ببينة رسمها عاف محيل

verses.h1: تحمل أهلها وجرى عليها
verses.h2: رياح الصيف والسرب الهطول

verses.h1: تحن بها الدبور إذا أربت
verses.h2: كما حنت مولهة ثكول

verses.h1: Did you not halt, so the ruins might tell you—
verses.h2: at Bayna, their traces faded and changed?

verses.h1: Their people departed, and over them swept
verses.h2: the summer winds and pouring rain.

verses.h1: The west wind moans there when it lingers,
verses.h2: as a distraught, bereaved mother moans.

notes.note: ببينة is tentatively read as ‘at Bayna,’ a place name whose identification and vocalization are uncertain. It could instead mean ‘with clear proof.’
السرب الهطول is unusual. السرب can denote flowing water; ‘pouring rain’ is a contextual rendering. السرب may also be a textual error for السحب, ‘clouds.’

poems.intro: وقال الحادرة، واسمه قطبة بن أوس:

verses.h1: لعمرة بين الأخشبين طلول
verses.h2: تقادم منها مشهر ومحيل

verses.h1: Between al-Akhshabayn lie the traces of ʿAmra’s dwellings;
verses.h2: some have weathered a month, others a year.

notes.note: I take mushhir (مشهر) and muḥīl (محيل) to describe traces over which a month and a year, respectively, have passed; the exact temporal sense is uncertain.
Al-Akhshabayn means “the two rugged mountains”; whether the familiar pair near Mecca is intended here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Ḥādira, whose name was Quṭba ibn Aws, said:

poems.intro: وقفت بها حتى تعالى بي الضحى ... لأخبر عنها إنني لسؤول وقال أبو نصر الخيشي:

verses.h1: أطيل وقوفي في الطلول كأنما
verses.h2: تخلف خلفي صاحب أتأناه

verses.h1: ومن شيم العشاق في مذهب الهوى
verses.h2: وقوفهم في الربع أقفر مغناه

verses.h1: I linger long among the ruins, as though
verses.h2: a companion had fallen behind me and I were waiting for him.

verses.h1: Among lovers’ customs in the way of love
verses.h2: is to stand at an encampment whose dwellings lie deserted.

prose_translation.intro: “I stood there until the morning was far advanced ... seeking news of it—for I am much given to asking.” And Abū Naṣr al-Khayshī said:

verses.h1: هل تعرف الدار والأطلال والدمنا
verses.h2: زدن الفؤاد على علاته حزنا

verses.h1: دار لأسماء إذ كنا نحل بها
verses.h2: وأنت إذ ذاك قد كانت لكم وطنا

verses.h1: Do you recognize the dwelling, the ruins, and the darkened traces?
verses.h2: They have added grief to a heart already afflicted.

verses.h1: A dwelling of Asmāʾ, where we once stayed;
verses.h2: and you—in those days it had been your home.

notes.note: The opening وأنت (“and you,” singular) in the second hemistich is syntactically awkward and shifts to plural “you” in لكم. The text may be corrupt; the translation preserves its abrupt construction.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو الوليد عبد الملك بن عبد الرحيم الحارثي
poems.intro: وقال أبو الوليد عبد الملك بن عبد الرحيم الحارثي:

poet.from_text: أبو الوليد عبد الملك بن عبد الرحيم الحارثي

verses.h1: بأطلال دار من عميرة عرج
verses.h2: كوشي اليماني برده غير منهج

verses.h1: أقامت على الأنواء يسحقن تربها
verses.h2: وتنسجها الأرواح من كل منسج

verses.h1: أراني على شيب القذال متى أقف
verses.h2: بأطلال دار من عميرة أنشج

verses.h1: Turn aside at the ruins of ʿUmayra’s dwelling,
verses.h2: like a Yemeni’s embroidery on an unworn cloak.

verses.h1: They have endured the seasonal rains that wear away their soil,
verses.h2: while winds weave over them from every quarter.

verses.h1: I find that, despite my graying nape, whenever I stop
verses.h2: at the ruins of ʿUmayra’s dwelling, I sob.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Walīd ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-Ḥārithī said:

verses.h1: أأطلال سعدى باللوى تتعهد
verses.h2: أقامت على الإقواء أم تتجدد

verses.h1: وبين التراقي واللهاة حرارة
verses.h2: مكان الشجى ما تستقر فتبرد

verses.h1: وقلت لماء العين: أمعن لعله
verses.h2: بما لا يرى من غائب الوجد يشهد

verses.h1: ولم أر مثل العين ضنت بمائها
verses.h2: علي، ولا مثلي على الدمع يحسد

verses.h1: Do you revisit Saʿdā’s ruins at al-Liwā?
verses.h2: Have they remained desolate, or are they renewed?

verses.h1: Between my collarbones and uvula is a burning,
verses.h2: where the choking lump lodges; it will not subside and cool.

verses.h1: I said to my tears, “Flow freely,” so that perhaps
