verses.h2: they might bear witness to the hidden passion none can see.

verses.h1: I have never seen the like of my eye, withholding its water
verses.h2: from me, nor anyone like me, begrudged his tears.

notes.note: I read يحسد as passive, “is envied” or “is begrudged,” taking the eye to begrudge the speaker his tears. The unvocalized text also permits an active reading: “envies [others] for their tears.”

prose_translation.intro: And Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said:

verses.h1: خليلي عوجا عوجة ناقتيكما
verses.h2: على طلل بين القلات وسارع

verses.h1: وقفنا فقلنا: إيه عن أم سالم
verses.h2: وما بال تكليم الديار البلاقع

verses.h1: فما كلمتنا دارها غير أنها
verses.h2: ثنت هاجسات من خبال مراجع

verses.h1: خلت غير آجال الصريم وقد ترى
verses.h2: بها وضح اللبات حور المدامع

verses.h1: My two companions, turn your she-camels aside
verses.h2: toward a ruined campsite between al-Qilāt and Sāriʿ.

verses.h1: We stopped and said, “Tell us more of Umm Sālim!”
verses.h2: Yet what use is speaking to deserted dwellings?

verses.h1: Her dwelling said nothing to us, except that it
verses.h2: brought back passing thoughts born of recurring madness.

verses.h1: It lies empty save for the wild herds of al-Ṣarīm, though once you could see
verses.h2: there women with gleaming throats and dark eyes.

notes.note: I have not identified al-Qilāt or Sāriʿ; the vocalization of القلات is uncertain.
The phrase ثنت هاجسات من خبال مراجع is obscure. I take ثنت as “brought back,” هاجسات as passing inward thoughts, and مراجع as “recurring,” qualifying خبال, “madness” or mental confusion.

الصريم may be a place-name, rendered here as al-Ṣarīm, or a common noun meaning a detached stretch of sand. حور المدامع describes eyes with a pronounced contrast between their dark centers and whites.

poems.intro: قيل: دخل بشار بن برد على عقبة بن سلم، فأنشده بعض مدائحه فيه، وعنده عقبة بن رؤبة بن العجاج، فأنشده عقبة بن رؤبة رجزا يمدحه به، فشيعه بشار، وجعل يستحسن ما قال، إلى أن فرغ، ثم أقبل على بشار، فقال: هذا طراز لا تحسنه أنت يا أبا معاذ، فقال بشار: ألى يقال مثل هذا؟ والله لأنا أرجز منك ومن أبيك ومن جدك، فقال له عقبة: أنا - والله - وأبي وجدي فتحنا للناس باب الغريب وباب الرجز، وإني لخليق أن أسده عليهم، فقال له بشار: ارحمهم رحمك الله، فقال عقبة، أتستخف بي يا أبا معاذ وأنا شاعر ابن شاعر ابن شاعر؟ فقال له بشار: فأنت إذن من الذين أذهب الله عنهم الرجس، وطهرهم تطهيرا. ثم خرج [من عنده] عقبة مغضبا، فلما كان من غد غدا بشار على عقبة بن سلم، وعنده عقبة ابن رؤبة فأنشده أرجوزته - التي مدحه فيها -:

verses.h1: يا طلل الحي بذات الصمد
verses.h2: بالله خبر كيف كنت بعدي؟

verses.h1: أحسست من دعد وترب دعد
verses.h2: سقيا لأسماء ابنة الأشد

verses.h1: قامت تراءي إذ رأتني وحدي
verses.h2: كالشمس بين الزبرج المنقد

verses.h1: صدت بخد وجلت عن خد
verses.h2: ثم انثنت كالنفس المرتد

verses.h1: عهدا لها سقيا له من عهد
verses.h2: تخلف وعدا أو تفى بوعد

verses.h1: فنحن من جهد الهوى في جهد
وافق حظا من سعى بجد
verses.h2: ما ضر أهل النوك ضعف الكد

verses.h1: الحر يلحي والعصا للعبد
verses.h2: وليس للملحف مثل الرد

verses.h1: والنصف يكفيك من التعدي
verses.h2: وصاحب كالدمل الممد

verses.h1: حملته في رقعة من جلدي
verses.h2: أرقب منه مثل حمى الورد

verses.h1: حتى مضى غير فقيد الفقد
verses.h2: وما درى ما رغبتي من زهدي

verses.h1: واسلم وحييت أبا الملد
verses.h2: مفتاح باب الحدب المنسد

verses.h1: مشترك النبل ورى الزند
verses.h2: أغر لباسا ثياب المجد

poems.after: والأرجوزة طويلة، فطرب عقبة بن سلم وأجزل صلته، وقام عقبة بن رؤبة فخرج عن المجلس بخزي، وهرب من تحت ليلته [فلم يعد إليه] .

verses.h1: O remnant of the tribe’s camp at Dhāt al-Ṣamad,
verses.h2: by God, tell me: how have you been since I left?

verses.h1: Have you sensed any trace of Daʿd and her companion?
verses.h2: May rain bless Asmāʾ, daughter of al-Ashadd!

verses.h1: She stood displaying herself when she saw me alone,
verses.h2: like the sun amid parted clouds.

verses.h1: She turned one cheek away and revealed the other,
verses.h2: then turned back like a returning breath.

verses.h1: A bond with her—may that bond be blessed!—
verses.h2: she breaks a promise or keeps one.

verses.h1: So love’s affliction keeps us in distress.
Whoever strives with luck on his side meets good fortune;
verses.h2: scant effort does the foolish no harm.

verses.h1: A free man is reproached; the rod is for the slave.
verses.h2: Nothing answers an importunate petitioner like refusal.

verses.h1: Fair dealing suffices to ward off aggression.
verses.h2: And a companion, like a festering boil,

verses.h1: I bore in a patch of my own skin,
verses.h2: expecting from him the likes of a recurring fever,

verses.h1: until he went away, unmissed when gone;
verses.h2: he never knew my liking from my aversion.

verses.h1: May you be safe and long-lived, Abū al-Mukhallad,
verses.h2: key to compassion’s bolted door,

verses.h1: whose bounty all may share, whose fire-stick readily sparks,
verses.h2: illustrious, ever wearing the robes of glory.

notes.note: Dhāt al-Ṣamad is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain.
Daʿd, her unnamed companion, and Asmāʾ daughter of al-Ashadd are unidentified. The vocalization al-Ashadd is tentative. ترب denotes a companion of the same age.
The construction عهدا لها is unclear. عهد may mean a bond or pledge, as translated, or a former time of acquaintance with her.
بجد can mean either ‘with good fortune’ (bi-jadd) or ‘with diligence’ (bi-jidd). The following statement about fools prospering despite scant effort favors the former.
حمى الورد appears to designate a recurrent fever; the precise periodicity intended is uncertain.
The source reads أبا الملد, an unclear name or epithet. The translation tentatively restores أبا المخلد, Abū al-Mukhallad, with a possibly omitted خ; this restoration is uncertain.

The source has مشترك النبل, whose sense is uncertain. ‘Whose bounty all may share’ tentatively reads النيل (‘bounty’) for النبل, a possible dotting or OCR error. If النبل is retained, it may refer to nobility or generosity.

prose_translation.intro: It is related: Bashshār ibn Burd came into the presence of ʿUqba ibn Salm and recited to him some of his poems in his praise. ʿUqba ibn Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj was with him, and ʿUqba ibn Ruʾba recited some rajaz verse praising him. Bashshār encouraged him, expressing admiration for what he said until he finished. Then he turned to Bashshār and said, “This is a style you have no skill in, Abū Muʿādh.” Bashshār replied, “Is such a thing to be said to me? By God, I am a better rajaz poet than you, your father, or your grandfather!” ʿUqba said to him, “By God, my father, my grandfather, and I opened for people the door to rare vocabulary and the door to rajaz, and I am well able to shut it against them.” Bashshār said to him, “Spare them, may God have mercy on you!” ʿUqba said, “Do you belittle me, Abū Muʿādh, when I am a poet, the son of a poet, the son of a poet?” Bashshār replied, “Then you are among those from whom God ‘has removed defilement and whom He has purified thoroughly.’” Then ʿUqba left [his presence] in anger. The following morning, Bashshār went to ʿUqba ibn Salm, with whom ʿUqba ibn Ruʾba was sitting, and recited to him his rajaz poem in his praise:
interludes: … And in it he says:
And he spoke in praise, saying:
prose_translation.after: The rajaz poem is long. ʿUqba ibn Salm was delighted and rewarded him generously. ʿUqba ibn Ruʾba rose and left the gathering in disgrace, then fled that very night [and never returned to him].

verses.h1: قد لعمري بت ليلى
verses.h2: كأخي الداء الوجيع

verses.h1: ونجي الهم مني
verses.h2: بات أدنى من ضجيعي

verses.h1: كلما أبصرت ربعا
verses.h2: خاليا فاضت دموعي

verses.h1: By my life, I spent my night
verses.h2: like one afflicted with painful illness.

verses.h1: Grief, my intimate companion,
verses.h2: lay nearer to me than my bedmate.

verses.h1: Whenever I saw an encampment
verses.h2: lying empty, my tears overflowed.

notes.note: Read ليلى as ليلي, ‘my night’; the final letter appears to be a spelling or digitization error, rather than the name Laylā.
The construction نجي الهم is ambiguous: literally ‘grief’s confidant,’ it is understood here as grief personified as an intimate companion.

verses.h1: أقشيب ربعهم أراك دريسا
verses.h2: وقرى ضيوفك لوعة ورسيسا

verses.h1: ولئن حبست على البلى لقد اغتدى
verses.h2: دمعي عليك إلى الممات حبيسا

verses.h1: وأرى ربوعك موحشات بعد ما
verses.h2: قد كنت مألوف المحل أنيسا

verses.h1: O once-fresh abode of theirs, I see you worn away,
verses.h2: and your guests’ fare is anguish and lingering pain.

verses.h1: Though you are held captive to decay, now
verses.h2: my tears are held captive to you until death.

verses.h1: I see your dwelling places desolate, although
verses.h2: you were once a familiar abode, full of company.

notes.note: رسيس can mean a lingering trace or an abiding feeling, especially of love or pain. Its precise sense here is uncertain; it is rendered as “lingering pain.”

verses.h1: أجل أيها الربع الذي خف آهله
verses.h2: لقد أردكت فيك النوى ما تحاوله

verses.h1: أسائلكم: ما باله حكم البلى
verses.h2: عليه!، وإلا فاتركوني أسائله

verses.h1: وقفنا على جمر الوداع عشية
verses.h2: ولا قلب إلا وهو تغلي مراجله

verses.h1: Yes, O dwelling whose people have departed,
verses.h2: separation has indeed achieved in you what it sought.

verses.h1: I ask you: why has decay passed judgment
verses.h2: upon it? Otherwise, leave me to question it.

verses.h1: We stood on the embers of farewell one evening,
verses.h2: and there was no heart whose cauldrons were not boiling.

notes.note: أردكت appears to be a transposition error for أدركت (‘achieved’), the reading translated here.

verses.h1: سلم على الربع من سلمى بذي سلم
verses.h2: عليه وسم من الأيام والقدم

verses.h1: ما دام عيش لبسناه بساكنه
verses.h2: لدنا، ولو أن عيشا دام لم يدم

verses.h1: يا منزلا أعنقت فيه الجنوب على
verses.h2: رسم محيل، وشعب غير ملتئم

verses.h1: هرمت بعدي والربع الذي أفلت
verses.h2: منه بدورك معذور على الهرم

verses.h1: Greet Salmā’s dwelling at Dhū Salam;
verses.h2: it bears the mark of passing days and age.

verses.h1: The life we wore with its dweller did not remain
verses.h2: fresh; even if any life could last, that life would not.

verses.h1: O dwelling, where the south wind sped over
verses.h2: a weathered trace and a rift unhealed.

verses.h1: You have aged since I left; and a dwelling forsaken
verses.h2: by your full moons may be forgiven for growing old.

notes.note: The subject of the final «لم يدم» is implicit. I take it to mean that their former life together would not endure, even if some other life could. «لدناً», literally ‘supple’ or ‘tender’, describes that life as fresh and pleasant.

verses.h1: يا موسم اللذات غالتك النوى
verses.h2: بعدي فربعك للصبابة موسم

verses.h1: ولقد أراك من الكواعب كاسيا
verses.h2: فاليوم أنت من الكواعب معدم

verses.h1: لحظت بشاشتك الحوادث لحظة
verses.h2: ما زلت أعلم أنها لا تسلم

verses.h1: O gathering place of delights, separation has ravaged you
verses.h2: since I left; your grounds are now a gathering place for longing.

verses.h1: I once saw you clothed in youthful maidens;
verses.h2: today you are bereft of maidens.

verses.h1: Calamities cast a glance at your radiance—
verses.h2: I always knew it would not escape unscathed.

poems.intro: قيل: خرج يحيى بن خالد بن برمك يوما من داره يريد الرشيد، فمر ببعض أفنية قصره، فرأى على بعض حيطانه مكتوبا:

verses.h1: أنعموا آل برمك
verses.h2: وارقبوها متى هيه

verses.h1: وارقبوا الدهر أن يدو
verses.h2: ر عليكم بداهيه

verses.h1: Enjoy your ease, house of Barmak,
verses.h2: and watch for it—when will it come?

verses.h1: And watch for Time to turn
verses.h2: upon you with a calamity.

notes.note: The wording «وارقبوها متى هيه» is elliptical. The feminine pronoun apparently anticipates the calamity named in line 2; «هيه» is read as «هي» with a pause-ending h.

prose_translation.intro: It is said: One day Yaḥyā ibn Khālid ibn Barmak left his house to go to al-Rashīd. As he passed through one of the courtyards of his palace, he saw written on one of its walls:

poems.intro: فوجم وجزع لذلك، ثم دخل - في ذلك اليوم - عليه أبو نواس، فأنشده:

verses.h1: أربع البلى إن الخشوع لباد
verses.h2: عليك وإني لم أخنك ودادي

verses.h1: فمعذرة مني إليك بأن ترى
verses.h2: رهينة أرواح وصوب غواد

verses.h1: ولا أدرأ الضراء عنك بحيلة
verses.h2: فما أنا فيها قائل لسعاد

verses.h1: وإن كنت قد بدلت بؤسي بنعمة
verses.h2: لقد بدلت عيني قذى برقاد

verses.h1: سلام على الدنيا إذا ما فقدتم
verses.h2: بني برمك من رائحين وغاد

verses.h1: O dwelling worn by decay, abasement is plain
verses.h2: upon you; I have not betrayed you in my love.

verses.h1: Forgive me, then, that you should lie
verses.h2: captive to winds and the downpour of morning clouds,

verses.h1: while I have no means to ward harm off from you;
verses.h2: for here I am not addressing Suʿād.

verses.h1: Though once you exchanged my misery for comfort,
verses.h2: you have now given my eye grit instead of sleep.

verses.h1: Farewell to the world when you are gone,
verses.h2: sons of Barmak, going forth at evening or at dawn.

notes.note: The reference to Suʿād is uncertain, possibly contrasting this lament with conventional love poetry. The second hemistich could also be read as a question: ‘What, then, am I to say to Suʿād about it?’

I take the verbs as addressing the dwelling: it formerly relieved the poet’s misery but now causes sleepless grief. The unvocalized كنت and بدلت also permit first-person readings; the direction of exchange in the second hemistich is not entirely certain.

prose_translation.intro: He was struck silent and distressed by this. Then, that same day, Abū Nuwās came in to him and recited:
interludes: Until he reached the words:

poems.intro: فتطير، فنكب في تلك الليلة. كان محمد بن واسع - رحمه الله - يمر برباع إخوانه بعد موتهم، فيناديهم: أي فلان، أي فلان، ثم يرجع إلى نفسه فيقول: ماتوا والله، وإن نعلا فقدت أختها لسريعة اللحاق بصاحبتها. وقال الفند الزماني، واسمه شهل بن شيبان بن ربيعة بن زمان:

verses.h1: أشجاك الربع أقوى والديار
verses.h2: وبكاء المرء للربع خسار

verses.h1: أي لب لامرئ في قدره
verses.h2: عائذ بالحزن إذ تشجيه دار

verses.h1: إنما يبكي الألى كانوا بها
verses.h2: فانتأوه بعد ما شط المزار

verses.h1: يخرب الدهر ويبني جاهدا
verses.h2: وخراب الدهر للدار عمار

verses.h1: أيها الباكي على ما فاته
verses.h2: أقصرن عنك، فبعض القول عار

verses.h1: ليس يغني جزع القوم إذا
verses.h2: وقع الأمر بهم إلا الغيار

verses.h1: فاجزعوا للأمر، أو لا تجزعوا
verses.h2: قد تداعى السقف وأنهار الجدار

interludes.text: (يقول: ليس يغني عنهم أن يجزعوا، ولكن أن يغيروا) .

verses.h1: Has the deserted campsite saddened you, and the dwellings?
verses.h2: A man’s weeping for a campsite is a loss.

verses.h1: What sense has a man faced with his fate,
verses.h2: who seeks refuge in grief when a dwelling saddens him?

verses.h1: He weeps only for those who dwelt there,
verses.h2: then withdrew far from him, once their abode lay distant.

verses.h1: Time destroys and builds tirelessly,
verses.h2: and Time’s destruction of a dwelling is its rebuilding.

verses.h1: You who weep for what has passed you by,
verses.h2: desist, for some words bring shame.

verses.h1: The people’s anguish avails nothing when
verses.h2: calamity befalls them, save a change.

verses.h1: Grieve over what has happened, or do not grieve:
verses.h2: the roof has fallen in and the wall has collapsed.

notes.note: في قدره is ambiguous. I have provisionally understood قدر as ‘fate’; it could instead concern the man’s standing or worth. Its grammatical connection to the rest of the line is uncertain.

فانتأوه is an unusual form with an attached object pronoun. I have provisionally understood it as ‘withdrew far from him,’ referring to the grieving man, but the construction and the pronoun’s referent are uncertain.
The second hemistich literally identifies Time’s destruction of a dwelling with its flourishing or rebuilding. The intended sense of this apparent reversal is unclear; the translation preserves it.
الغيار can denote change, but its precise meaning here, and the logic of ‘save a change’ after ‘avails nothing,’ are unclear. The text may be defective.
أنهار appears to be a spelling or transcription error for انهار, ‘collapsed,’ which is the reading translated.

prose_translation.intro: He took it as an ill omen, and that very night misfortune befell him. Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ—may God have mercy on him—used to pass by the dwellings of his brethren after their deaths and call out to them: “O so-and-so! O so-and-so!” Then he would turn to himself and say: “They have died, by God! A sandal that has lost its mate will surely soon follow its companion.” al-Find al-Zimmānī, whose name was Shahl ibn Shaybān ibn Rabīʿa ibn Zimmān, said:
interludes: (This is an inversion; he means that its being built up is its ruin):
(He is saying: it does them no good to grieve, but rather to bring about change.)

poems.intro: وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة المخزومي:

verses.h1: سائلا الربع بالبلى وقولا
verses.h2: هجت شوقا لنا الغداة طويلا

verses.h1: أين حي حلوك إذ أنت محفو
verses.h2: ف بهم آهلا أراك جميلا

verses.h1: قال: ساروا بأجمع فاستقلوا
verses.h2: وبكرهي لو استطعت سبيلا

verses.h1: Question the dwelling in its decay, you two, and say:
verses.h2: “You have stirred a long yearning in us this morning.

verses.h1: Where are the people who dwelt in you, when you were surrounded
verses.h2: by them, and I saw you peopled and beautiful?”

verses.h1: It said: “They all set out and departed,
verses.h2: against my will—if only I had had some way to prevent it!”

notes.note: بالبلى is uncertain: rendered here as “in its decay,” but it may conceal a place-name or a textual error.
لو استطعت سبيلا (“if I could find a way”) is elliptical; “to prevent it” supplies the understood wish to prevent their departure.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī said:

verses.h1: يا ربع أين انتجع الحاضر
verses.h2: جادك نوء الجبهة الماطر

verses.h1: مالي أرى مغناك قفرا كأن
verses.h2: لم يله في ساحته سامر

verses.h1: أصبح قد ردى ثوب البلى
verses.h2: فالآي منه مخلق دائر

verses.h1: وقد أراه قبل صرف النوى
verses.h2: يعدب من بهجته الناظر

verses.h1: O campsite, where have your people gone in search of pasture?
verses.h2: May the rains of al-Jabhah water you.

verses.h1: Why do I see your dwelling-place deserted, as though
verses.h2: no one had ever made merry in its courtyard by night?

verses.h1: It has now been clothed in the robe of decay;
verses.h2: its traces are worn and effaced.

verses.h1: Yet once I would see it, before the ravages of separation,
verses.h2: delighting the beholder with its beauty.

notes.note: يعدب appears to be a misprint for يعجب, ‘delights’ or ‘pleases,’ which is the reading translated here.

verses.h1: قفا عند مما تعرفان ربوعي
verses.h2: وإن سبقت فرط العزاء دموعي

verses.h1: نحيي على طول البلى رسم دمنة
verses.h2: كأن لم تكن من آلفين جميع

verses.h1: وماذا نحيي من رسوم كأنها
verses.h2: بأسفل سلمانين سحق صديع

verses.h1: كأن حمامات ثلاثا بربعها
verses.h2: وقعن فما يسأمن طول وقوع

verses.h1: وإني لصب ما علمت وإنني
verses.h2: لبعض هوى نفسي لغير مطيع

verses.h1: Stop, you two, at what you recognize of my dwellings,
verses.h2: even if my tears have outrun my utmost fortitude.

verses.h1: Let us greet, despite long decay, the trace of a campsite,
verses.h2: as though no band of companions had ever been there.

verses.h1: And what do we greet of traces that seem,
verses.h2: at the foot of Salmānayn, like a worn and tattered cloth?

verses.h1: As though three doves at the campsite
verses.h2: had alighted, never wearying of their long stay.

verses.h1: I am indeed lovesick, as you know; yet I
verses.h2: resist some of my soul’s desires.

notes.note: The wording عند مما تعرفان ربوعي is syntactically irregular and may contain a copying or OCR error. The translation provisionally takes it to mean ‘at what you recognize of my dwellings.’
Salmānayn appears to be a place-name; its precise location is uncertain.
The three motionless ‘doves’ may represent the three hearthstones left at the campsite, though the stones are not explicitly named.
The unvocalized ما علمت is taken as ‘as you know’; it could also be read as ‘as far as I know.’

verses.h1: يا ربوع الديار إني على ما
verses.h2: قد أراه منكن غير جلدي

verses.h1: أخلق الدهر عهدكن وللده
verses.h2: ر صروف يبلين كل جديد

verses.h1: فرقت شملنا النوى بعد ما ك
verses.h2: نا جميعا في ظل عيش حميد

verses.h1: O dwelling grounds, faced with what
verses.h2: I see of you, I have no strength to endure.

verses.h1: Time has worn away the memory of you; and time
verses.h2: has vicissitudes that wear out all that is new.

verses.h1: Separation scattered our company, after we had been
verses.h2: together in the shade of a pleasant life.

notes.note: The transmitted غير جلدي is unclear and likely contains a transposition for غير جليد, meaning ‘not steadfast’ or ‘unable to endure.’ The translation follows that reading.

verses.h1: لأحسن من بطن الرصافة منظرا
verses.h2: وميدانها فالرخ فالدور فالجسر

verses.h1: ربائع لا يلبسن والريح ريدة
verses.h2: قتاما ولا يلثقن للوابل الهمر

verses.h1: إذا ما كساهن الربيع رياطه
verses.h2: تأرجن مسكا أو تضاحكن عن در

verses.h1: Fairer indeed to behold than the lowlands of al-Ruṣāfa
verses.h2: and its parade ground, al-Rukh, al-Dūr, and the bridge,

verses.h1: are meadows that never clothe themselves, when the breeze is gentle,
verses.h2: in dust, nor turn muddy beneath torrential rain.

verses.h1: When spring clothes them in its robes,
verses.h2: they breathe musk or smile to reveal pearls.

notes.note: الرخ, provisionally transliterated al-Rukh, is an unidentified place-name here; it may be a misprint for الكرخ (Al-Karkh). The particular locality intended by al-Dūr is also uncertain.
ربائع is taken as a plural meaning meadows or spring pastures; its precise sense here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Qabīṣa ibn ʿAmr al-Muhallabī said:

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: قفا صاحبي اليوم أسأل حاجة
verses.h2: ولا ترجعا سمعي بغير بيان

verses.h1: هل الربع بعد الظاعنين كعهده
verses.h2: وهل راجع فيه علي زماني؟

verses.h1: Stop, my two companions: today I ask a favor;
verses.h2: do not leave my ears without a clear reply.

verses.h1: Is the campsite, since its people left, still as it was?
verses.h2: And will my former days return to me there?

prose_translation.intro: Al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبد الله أحمد بن محمد بن علي بن صدقة الخياط الدمشقي
poems.intro: وقال أبو عبد الله أحمد بن محمد بن علي بن صدقة الخياط الدمشقي:

poet.from_text: أبو عبد الله أحمد بن محمد بن علي بن صدقة الخياط الدمشقي

verses.h1: أحب ثرى الوادي الذي بان أهله
verses.h2: وأصبوا إلى الربع الذي مح مغناه

verses.h1: وبالجزع حي كلما عن ذكرهم
verses.h2: أمات الهوى مني فؤادا وأحياه

verses.h1: فمنيتهم بالرقمتين، ودارهم
verses.h2: بوادي الغضا يا بعد ما أتمناه

verses.h1: وما شغفي بالريح إلا لأنها
verses.h2: تمر بحي دون رامة مثواه

verses.h1: I love the soil of the valley whose people have departed,
verses.h2: and yearn for the campsite whose traces have worn away.

verses.h1: At the valley bend dwell people whose memory, whenever it comes to mind,
verses.h2: makes love kill the heart within me and revive it.

verses.h1: I dream of them at al-Raqmatayn, while their home
verses.h2: is in Wādī al-Ghaḍā—how far away is what I long for!

verses.h1: My passion for the wind is only because
verses.h2: it passes a tribe dwelling on this side of Rāma.

notes.note: The unvocalized مح is uncertain; I have understood it as indicating that the campsite has become worn or effaced.
فمنيتهم is unclear as printed and may be corrupt. “I dream of them” is a tentative contextual rendering, taking it to express a wish concerning their whereabouts.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū ʿAbd Allah Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Ṣadaqa al-Khayyāṭ al-Dimashqī said:

verses.h1: أللربع ظلت يعنك الماء تهمل
verses.h2: رشاشا كما استن الجمان المفصل؟

verses.h1: لعرفان أطلال كأن رسومها
verses.h2: بوهبين وشيء أو رداء مسلسل

verses.h1: نبت نبوة عيني بها ثم بينت
verses.h2: يحاميم سود أنها الدار مثل

verses.h1: عهدت بها الحي الحلول بسلوة
verses.h2: جميعا، وآيات الهوى ما تزيل

verses.h1: Is it for the campsite that your eye has kept shedding tears
verses.h2: in sprays, as strung pearls stream down?

verses.h1: At the recognition of ruins whose outlines seemed
verses.h2: at Wahbayn like embroidery or a chain-patterned cloak?

verses.h1: At first my eye failed to recognize it; then it was made plain
verses.h2: by black stones standing upright that this was the dwelling.

verses.h1: I remember the tribe settled there in carefree ease,
verses.h2: all together, with the signs of love still undiminished.

notes.note: يعنك appears to be a typographical error for عينك, ‘your eye.’ المفصل likely describes pearls separated by intervening beads or other ornaments; the precise arrangement is uncertain.

وشيء appears to be an error for وشي, ‘embroidery’ or ‘figured fabric.’ وهبين is treated as the place name Wahbayn, but its vocalization and location are uncertain. مسلسل is understood as describing a chainlike pattern on the cloak.
يحاميم سود is understood as black stones, probably blackened hearthstones marking the abandoned dwelling. The precise objects intended are uncertain; مثل is read as مُثَّل, ‘standing upright.’

بسلوة is taken to mean ‘in carefree ease,’ though a place name, Salwa, is also possible. ما تزيل is understood as ‘do not disappear’; the transmitted verb form is unusual in this sense and may be corrupt.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: حييت يا ربع الهوى من مربع
verses.h2: وسقيت أندية الغيوث الهمع

verses.h1: فلقد عهدتك والزمان مسالم
verses.h2: فيك المنى وشفاء داء الموجع

verses.h1: أيام إن يدع الهوى بي اتبع
verses.h2: وإذا دعيت إلى النهى لم أتبع

verses.h1: سقيا له زمنا نعمت بظله
verses.h2: لكنه لما مضى لم يرجع

verses.h1: Hail to you, abode of love—what a dwelling-place!
verses.h2: May you be watered by the moisture of pouring rains.

verses.h1: For I knew you when time was kind:
verses.h2: in you lay my hopes and a cure for the sufferer’s pain.

verses.h1: Days when, if passion called me, I would follow,
verses.h2: but when called to reason, I would not follow.

verses.h1: May rain bless that time whose shade I enjoyed,
verses.h2: though once it passed, it never returned.

notes.note: The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, while the Arabic introduction names al-Sharīf al-Raḍī.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: عوجا نحي الربع فيه لنا الهوى
verses.h2: فلربما نفع المحب سلامه

verses.h1: واستعبرا عني به إن خانني
verses.h2: جفني، ولم يمطر على غمامه

verses.h1: دمن رضعت بهن أخلاف الصبي
verses.h2: لو لم يكن بعد الرضاع فطامه

verses.h1: Turn aside, you two: let us greet the campsite where our love abides;
verses.h2: for often a lover’s greeting has done him good.

verses.h1: Weep there on my behalf, you two, if I am betrayed
verses.h2: by my eyelid, and its cloud sheds no rain upon me.

verses.h1: Ruins where I suckled at the teats of youth—
verses.h2: if only that suckling had not been followed by weaning!

notes.note: The phrase على غمامه is unclear as printed. The translation reads على as عليّ, ‘upon me,’ with غمامه (‘its cloud’) referring to the eyelid’s tears.
الصبي (‘the boy’) appears to be a misprint for الصبا (‘youth’), which is the reading translated here.

verses.h1: وقفنا على ربع الأحبة وقفة
verses.h2: فلم نر إلا رمددا وأثافيا

verses.h1: وأشعث منقد السراة مهمشا
verses.h2: أضر به ضرب الوليدة باليا

verses.h1: فما زال رسم الدار حتى أعادني
verses.h2: وكنت جليد القوم في القوم باكيا

verses.h1: وقفت به صحبي صحيحا فلم تكن
verses.h2: سوى نظرة حتى رجعت بدائيا

verses.h1: We paused at the encampment of our loved ones,
verses.h2: but saw only ashes and hearthstones.

verses.h1: And a rough tent peg, split along its back and scarred,
verses.h2: worn out, damaged by the serving girl’s blows.

verses.h1: The dwelling’s traces would not relent until they left me—
verses.h2: once the staunchest of my companions—weeping in their midst.

verses.h1: I halted my companions there, myself in sound health; it took
verses.h2: only a glance before I returned sick.

notes.note: The object described is not named; I take it to be an old tent peg, battered by hammering. منقد السراة appears to mean ‘split along its back,’ and مهمشا ‘scratched’ or ‘scarred.’
I take the unusual بدائيا to represent بِدائي with a final alif lengthening the rhyme: ‘with my ailment.’

poems.poet_from_text: القاضي المهذب أبو محمد حسن بن علي بن الزبير
poems.intro: وقال القاضي المهذب أبو محمد حسن بن علي بن الزبير - رحمه الله -:

poet.from_text: القاضي المهذب أبو محمد حسن بن علي بن الزبير

verses.h1: ربع الفؤاد خلال تلك الأربع
verses.h2: فكأنها أولى به من أضلعي

verses.h1: وأقام فيه فالجوانح بلقع
verses.h2: منه، وما البيد القفار ببلقع

verses.h1: وأرى الصبا تمري السحاب وإنما
verses.h2: تمري صبابته سحاب الأدمع

verses.h1: My heart’s abode lies amid those encampments,
verses.h2: as though they had more claim to it than my ribs.

verses.h1: It has settled there, and my breast is desolate
verses.h2: without it, while the empty deserts are not desolate.

verses.h1: I see the east wind milking the clouds, but in truth
verses.h2: it is the heart’s longing that milks the clouds of tears.

notes.note: The unvocalized opening ربع الفؤاد can also be read verbally: “My heart settled.” I have read ربع as “abode,” which provides an antecedent for “in it” (فيه) in line 2.

prose_translation.intro: And the judge al-Muhadhdhab Abū Muḥammad Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Zubayr—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: أمر بربع كنت فيه كأنما
verses.h2: أمر من الإجلال بالحجر والركن

verses.h1: وإجلال مغناك اجتهاد مقصر
verses.h2: إذا السيف أودي فالعفاء على الجفن

verses.h1: I pass a dwelling where you once lived, as though
verses.h2: in reverence I were passing the Stone and the Corner.

verses.h1: Revering your dwelling is the striving of one who falls short:
verses.h2: when the sword has perished, let oblivion take the sheath.

notes.note: The unvocalized كنت can mean either ‘I was’ or ‘you were’; ‘you’ is adopted here in light of ‘your dwelling’ in line 2.
أودي appears to stand for أودى, ‘perished,’ with a possible typing or OCR error in the final letter.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: على مثلها من أربع وملاعب
verses.h2: أذيلت مصونات الدموع السواكب

verses.h1: أقول لقرحان من البين لم يضف
verses.h2: رسيس الهوى بين الحشا والترائب

verses.h1: أعني على تفريق دمعي فإنني
verses.h2: أرى الشمل منهم ليس بالمتقارب

verses.h1: أميدان لهوى من أتاح لك البلى
verses.h2: وأصبحت ميدان الصبا والجنائب؟

verses.h1: أصابتك أبكار الخطوب فشتتت
verses.h2: نواك بأبكار الظباء الكواعب

verses.h1: Over dwelling sites and playgrounds like these
verses.h2: once-guarded tears were freely shed in streams.

verses.h1: I say to one unscathed by parting, who has never lodged
verses.h2: love’s lingering ache between his vitals and his breastbones:

verses.h1: Help me scatter my tears, for I
verses.h2: see that their company is not drawing together.

verses.h1: O playground of my pleasures, who brought decay upon you,
verses.h2: so that you became a playground for the east and south winds?

verses.h1: The first assaults of calamity struck you and scattered
verses.h2: your people, those maiden gazelles with budding breasts.

notes.note: The wording نواك بأبكار is unclear. نواك ordinarily suggests your destination, intended journey, or separation, rather than your inhabitants. The translation provisionally understands the phrase as referring to the dispersal of the women who occupied the site; the text may be corrupt.

verses.h1: أمسح الربع بخدي
verses.h2: أن مشى فيه الخليل

verses.h1: وعلى مثلك يبكى
verses.h2: أيها الربع المحيل

verses.h1: I brush the campsite with my cheek,
verses.h2: for the beloved walked there.

verses.h1: It is for the likes of you that one weeps,
verses.h2: O timeworn campsite.

verses.h1: يا ربع مالك لا تجيب متيما
verses.h2: قد عاج نحوك زائرا ومسلما

verses.h1: جادتك كل سحابة هطالة
verses.h2: حتى ترى عن زهره متبسما

verses.h1: لو كنت تدري من دعاك أجبته
verses.h2: وبكيت من حرق عليه إذا دما

verses.h1: O dwelling, why do you not answer a lovesick man
verses.h2: who has turned toward you to visit and offer greetings?

verses.h1: May every cloud pour abundant rain upon you,
verses.h2: until you are seen smiling with flowers.

verses.h1: If you knew who called to you, you would answer him,
verses.h2: and then weep blood over him from burning grief.

notes.note: The masculine suffix in زهره (‘its flowers’) has no clear antecedent: سحابة (‘cloud’) is feminine, while the dwelling is addressed in the second person. The translation leaves this possessive unresolved.
I take إذا دما as إذًا دمًا, ‘then [weep] blood’; the unvocalized wording permits uncertainty.

verses.h1: إن يمس حبلك بعد طول تواصل
verses.h2: خلقا، ويصبح ربعنا مهجورا

verses.h1: فلقد أراني
verses.h2: والجديد إلى بلى دهرا بوصلك ناعما مسرورا

verses.h1: كنت الهوى وأعز من وطىء الحصا
verses.h2: عندي، وكنت بذاك منك جديرا

verses.h1: If the bond with you grows threadbare after long communion,
verses.h2: and our dwelling stands deserted,

verses.h1: I well remember myself—
verses.h2: and all that is new must decay—long happy and joyful in union with you.

verses.h1: You were my love, the dearest of all who trod the pebbles
verses.h2: to me; and I deserved the same from you.

notes.note: The hemistich division appears misplaced: والجديد إلى بلى likely belongs at the end of the first hemistich, with the second beginning دهرا. The supplied division is preserved. The phrase about decay is read as a parenthesis.

poems.intro: وقال جبيهاء الأشجعي، واسمه يزيد بن عبيد:

verses.h1: أمن الجميع بذي النعاج ربوع
verses.h2: هاجت فؤادك والربوع ربوع

verses.h1: من بعد ما نكرت وغير آيها
verses.h2: قطر ومسبلة الذيول خريع؟

verses.h1: Did the tribe’s encampments at Dhū al-Niʿāj
verses.h2: stir your heart—though encampments are only encampments—

verses.h1: after they had grown unrecognizable, their traces altered
verses.h2: by rain and a wind with trailing skirts?

notes.note: Dhū al-Niʿāj is a place-name whose location I could not identify.
خريع is understood here as an epithet of the wind, but its precise descriptive sense is uncertain and is not separately rendered.

prose_translation.intro: And Jubayhāʾ al-Ashjaʿī, whose name was Yazīd ibn ʿUbayd, said:

verses.h1: وقفت على ربع لسعدى وعبرتي
verses.h2: ترقرق في العينين ثم تسيل

verses.h1: أسائل ربعا قد تعفت رسومه
verses.h2: عليه لأصناف الرياح ذيول

verses.h1: I stood at a campsite of Saʿdā, while my tears
verses.h2: welled in my eyes, then flowed.

verses.h1: I question a campsite whose traces have been effaced;
verses.h2: across it, winds of every kind trail their skirts.

verses.h1: قد نابت الجزع من أروية النوب
verses.h2: واستحقبت جدة من ربعها الحقب

verses.h1: ألوى بصبرك إخلاق اللوى وهفا
verses.h2: بلبك الشوق لما أقفر اللبب

verses.h1: خفت دموعك في إثر الخليط لدن
verses.h2: خفت من الكثب القضبان والكثب

verses.h1: Misfortunes have visited al-Jizʿ of Urwiyya;
verses.h2: the ages have carried off the freshness of her dwelling.

verses.h1: The decay of al-Liwā has swept away your patience;
verses.h2: longing carried off your wits when al-Labab lay deserted.

verses.h1: Your tears flowed swiftly in the company’s wake, ever since
verses.h2: the branches and dunes departed from the dunes.

notes.note: Urwiyya (أروية) is unidentified; both its vocalization and whether it names a woman or a locality are uncertain. Al-Jizʿ may instead be descriptive: ‘the valley-bend.’
Al-Liwā and al-Labab are treated as place-names, though they can also describe sandy terrain: a bend in the sands and a sandy slope, respectively.

The ‘branches and dunes’ apparently represent the departing women, suggesting slender figures and rounded hips. Both occurrences of الكثب are read as al-kuthub, ‘dunes’; the unvocalized text leaves some uncertainty.

verses.h1: ألا حي ربعا باللديد المقابل
verses.h2: يهيج الهوى من بين تلك المنازل

verses.h1: يهيج الذي قد كان من سالف الصبى
verses.h2: على مستهام قلبه غير ذاهل

verses.h1: يهيم بذكر الغانيات، وهمه
verses.h2: طلاب الصبى في غيه المتمايل

verses.h1: فما ظبية الغر التي هاجت الهوى
verses.h2: ولكنما شبهتها أم واصل

verses.h1: من البيض مكسالا كأن حديثها
verses.h2: جنى النحل هيفاء صموت الخلاخل

verses.h1: Come, greet a dwelling on the opposite valley-side,
verses.h2: which, among those abodes, stirs longing.

verses.h1: It stirs the passions of youth long past
verses.h2: in a love-stricken man whose heart has not forgotten.

verses.h1: He is lost in memories of lovely women; his concern
verses.h2: is to pursue youthful passion in his wavering folly.

verses.h1: It was not the gazelle of al-Gharr that stirred desire,
verses.h2: but her likeness, Umm Wāṣil.

verses.h1: A languid, fair-skinned woman, whose speech is like
verses.h2: the bees’ harvest—slender-waisted, her anklets silent.

notes.note: اللديد can mean the side of a valley, as translated here; it may instead be a place name, al-Ladīd.
The expression في غيه المتمايل, rendered closely as “in his wavering folly,” is unusual; the precise force of المتمايل is uncertain.

الغَرّ is provisionally treated as a place name, al-Gharr; its vocalization and identification are uncertain. The unvocalized شبهتها is also ambiguous: “her likeness” is a tentative nominal reading, though the letters can also represent a verb meaning “I likened her.”

verses.h1: وقفنا على ربع البخيلة فانبرت
verses.h2: وسابق قد كانت بها العين تبخل

verses.h1: فلم يدر ربع الدار كيف يجيبنا
verses.h2: ولا نحن من فرط الأسى كيف نسأل

verses.h1: We stopped at the campsite of the withholding beloved, and forth rushed
verses.h2: tears the eye had once begrudged.

verses.h1: The deserted dwelling did not know how to answer us,
verses.h2: nor did we, in our overwhelming grief, know how to ask.

notes.note: وسابق appears to be a misprint for سوابق, meaning things that race ahead—here, rushing tears. The translation follows this conjectural reading.

verses.h1: أشجاك الربع م قدمه
verses.h2: أم رماد دارس حممه

verses.h1: حابسي رسم وقفت به
verses.h2: لو أطيع النفس لم أرمه

verses.h1: Has the campsite saddened you, or its age,
verses.h2: or ashes whose charred remnants have worn away?

verses.h1: A trace where I stopped holds me captive;
verses.h2: if I obeyed my heart, I would not leave it.

notes.note: The isolated م in the first hemistich appears defective. I have read it as أم (‘or’); من (‘because of’), giving ‘Has the campsite saddened you because of its age?’, is also possible.

verses.h1: أتصرم هذا الربع أم أنت زائره
verses.h2: وكيف يزار الربع قد بان عامره

verses.h1: وقد كان ممن يسكن الربع مرة
verses.h2: جميل المحيا، قاصر الطرف فاتره

verses.h1: سقى الله بيتا لست أقرب أهله
verses.h2: ولا أنت إلا أن تعنف زائره

verses.h1: رأيتك تأبى البيت تبغض أهله
verses.h2: وقلبك في البيت الذي أنت هاجره

verses.h1: Will you forsake this dwelling, or will you visit it?
verses.h2: How can the dwelling be visited when its inhabitant has departed?

verses.h1: Once among those who lived in the dwelling was
verses.h2: one fair of face, with a modest, languid gaze.

verses.h1: May God send rain upon a house whose people I do not approach,
verses.h2: and which you visit only when reproached.

verses.h1: I have seen you shun the house and hate its people,
verses.h2: though your heart is in the house you forsake.

notes.note: The syntax and vocalization are uncertain. I read لست أقرب as lastu aqrabu (‘I do not approach’) and تعنف as passive tuʿannaf (‘you are reproached’), with زائره as the delayed predicate of أنت (‘you are its visitor’). The resulting shift from ‘I’ to ‘you’ and the precise sense of the condition remain uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Jamīl ibn Maʿmar al-ʿUdhrī said:

poems.intro: وقال كثير بن عبد الرحمن الخزاعي:

verses.h1: خليلي هذا ربع عزة فاعقلا
verses.h2: فلوصيكما ثم ابكيا حيث حلت

verses.h1: وما كنت أدرى قبل عزة ما البكا
verses.h2: ولا موجعات القلب حتى تولت

verses.h1: فيا عجبا للقلب كيف اعترافه
verses.h2: وللنفس لما وطنت كيف ذلت

verses.h1: وإني وتهيامي بعزة بعد ما
verses.h2: تخليت عما بيننا، وتخلت

verses.h1: لكالمرتجى ظل الغمامة كلما تبوأ منها للمقيل اضمحلت
كأني وإياها سحابة ممحل
verses.h2: رجاها، فلما جاوزته استهلت

verses.h1: My two friends, this is ʿAzza’s campsite: hobble
verses.h2: your two young she-camels, then weep where she once dwelt.

verses.h1: Before ʿAzza, I did not know what weeping was,
verses.h2: nor the things that wound the heart, until she turned away.

verses.h1: How strange the heart—how it confesses!
verses.h2: And the soul—once reconciled, how it submits!

verses.h1: And I, with my infatuation with ʿAzza, after
verses.h2: I had forsaken what lay between us, and she had too,

verses.h1: am like one hoping for a cloud’s shade: whenever he settles beneath it for his midday rest, it dissolves.
She and I are like a cloud sought by a drought-stricken man:
verses.h2: he hoped for its rain, but only after passing him did it pour.

notes.note: فلوصيكما appears to be a misprint for قلوصيكما, ‘your two young she-camels,’ which is the reading translated.

اعترافه means ‘its acknowledgment/confession,’ but what the heart acknowledges is unstated. وطنت is also ambiguous without vocalization; ‘once reconciled’ takes it as the soul becoming accustomed or resigned to its situation.

prose_translation.intro: And Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khuzāʿī said:

verses.h1: خليلي عوجا عوجة ثم سلما
verses.h2: عسى الربع بالجرعاء أن يتكلما

verses.h1: تعرفته لما وقفت بربعه
verses.h2: كأن بقاياه تماثيل أعجما

verses.h1: ديار لمى قد تعفت رسومها
verses.h2: تخال نواحيها كتابا معجما

verses.h1: My two friends, turn aside a moment, then offer greetings;
verses.h2: perhaps the campsite at al-Jarʿāʾ will speak.

verses.h1: I recognized it when I stood within its bounds,
verses.h2: its remnants like a foreigner’s drawings.

verses.h1: Dwellings of Mayy, whose traces have been effaced—
verses.h2: you would take their expanses for writing marked with dots.

notes.note: Al-Jarʿāʾ may be a place name or simply a description of sandy ground; its specific location is uncertain.
تماثيل أعجما is interpreted as ‘a foreigner’s drawings.’ أعجم can also mean someone unable to speak intelligibly, so the precise force of the comparison is uncertain.
لمى is read as لِمَيّ, ‘of Mayy.’ معجما is understood as describing writing supplied with distinguishing dots, though an association with foreign or unintelligible writing is also possible.

verses.h1: وقفت على ربع لمية ناقتي
verses.h2: فما زلت أبكي عنده وأخاطبه

verses.h1: وأسقيه حتى كاد مما سقيته
verses.h2: تكلمني أحجاره وملاعبه

verses.h1: أسقيه: أدعو له بالسقيا
ألا لا أرى مثل الهوى داء مسلم
verses.h2: كريم، ولا مثل الهوى ليم صاحبه

verses.h1: متى يعصه تبرح معاصاته به
verses.h2: وإن يتبع أسبابه فهو عائبه

verses.h1: I halted my she-camel at a campsite of Mayya,
verses.h2: and kept weeping beside it and addressing it.

verses.h1: And I prayed for rain upon it, until, through all my prayers,
verses.h2: its stones and playing grounds almost spoke to me.

verses.h1: “I water it”: I pray that it receive rain.
Ah, I see no disease like love for bringing to ruin
verses.h2: a noble man, nor any like love whose sufferer is blamed.

verses.h1: Whenever he resists it, his resistance torments him;
verses.h2: and if he follows its paths, it brings him disgrace.

notes.note: This appears to be an explanatory prose gloss on أسقيه in line 2, rather than a verse.
I take مسلم as musْlim, meaning ‘giving over to ruin,’ with كريم as its object, and ليم as līma, ‘was blamed.’ The unvocalized wording leaves some uncertainty about the construction.

verses.h1: عهدي بربعك مأنوسا ملاعبه
verses.h2: مثال آرامه حسنا كواعبه

verses.h1: يشبن للصب في صفو الهوى كدرا
verses.h2: إن وخط شيب أعيرته ذوائبه

verses.h1: I remember your dwelling, its pleasure grounds peopled,
verses.h2: its full-breasted maidens matching its gazelles in beauty.

verses.h1: They cloud the purity of love for the lovesick man
verses.h2: if his locks are lent a sprinkling of gray.

verses.h1: إذا شئت أجرت أدمعي من شؤونها
verses.h2: ربوع لها بالأبرقين وأرسم

verses.h1: وقفت بها والركب شتى سبيلهم
verses.h2: يفيضون، منهم عاذرون ولوم

verses.h1: هي الدار إلا أنها لا تكلم
verses.h2: عفا معلم منها وأقفر معلم

verses.h1: تقيض لي
verses.h2: من حيث لا أعلم النوى ويسري إلي الشوق من حيث أعلم

verses.h1: Whenever I wish, my tears are drawn from their ducts
verses.h2: by her campsites and traces at al-Abraqayn.

verses.h1: I stood there while the riders differed in their views,
verses.h2: speaking freely—some excusing me, others reproaching.

verses.h1: It is the dwelling, except that it cannot speak;
verses.h2: one landmark is effaced, another stands deserted.

verses.h1: There is ordained for me
verses.h2: from where I do not know, separation; and longing steals upon me from where I know.

notes.note: I take يفيضون to mean speaking freely, and شتى سبيلهم to describe differing views. The wording could instead describe the riders streaming away along different paths.
The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the first hemistich would naturally end after النوى, with the second beginning ويسري. The translation preserves the supplied division.

verses.h1: هو ذاك ربع العامرية فاربع
verses.h2: واسأل مصيفا عافيا عن مربعي

verses.h1: واستسق للدمن الخوالي بالحمى
verses.h2: غر السحائب واعتذر عن أدمعي

verses.h1: فلقد فنين أمام دان هاجر
verses.h2: في قربه، ووراء ناء مزمع

verses.h1: That is al-ʿĀmiriyya’s dwelling: halt there,
verses.h2: and ask an effaced summer camp about my spring abode.

verses.h1: And seek rain for the deserted traces in the protected grounds
verses.h2: from the bright clouds, and make excuses for my tears.

verses.h1: For they were spent before one near who shunned me
verses.h2: despite his nearness, and in the wake of one distant, resolved to depart.

notes.note: The object of مُزْمِع (‘resolved, intent’) is unstated; ‘resolved to depart’ is the likely sense. ناء can mean either ‘distant’ or ‘departing.’

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Fityān ibn Ḥayyūs said:

verses.h1: خليلي عوجا
verses.h2: ويكما ساعة معي على الربع نقضي حاجة ونودع

verses.h1: ولا تعجلاني أن ألم بدمنة
verses.h2: لعزة لاحت لي ببيداء بلقع

verses.h1: وقولا لقلب قد سلا راجع الهوى
verses.h2: وللعين أذرى من دموعك أودعي

verses.h1: فلا عيش إلا مثل عيش مضى لنا
verses.h2: مصيفا، أقمنا فيه من بعد مربع

verses.h1: My two friends, turn aside—
verses.h2: come now, you two—for a while with me at the campsite, that we may fulfill a need and bid farewell.

verses.h1: Do not hurry me; let me visit the ruined campsite
verses.h2: of ʿAzza, which appeared to me in a barren waste.

verses.h1: And say to a heart that has forgotten love: “Return to love,”
verses.h2: and to the eye: “Shed your tears, or leave off.”

verses.h1: There is no life like the life we once knew,
verses.h2: at a summer abode where we stayed after a spring encampment.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the expected division is after معي. The translation preserves the supplied division.
I read أذرى as the feminine imperative أذري, “shed,” addressed to the eye, and أودعي as أو دعي, “or leave off.”
مصيف and مربع can denote summer and spring seasons or the places occupied during them. The translation takes them as seasonal abodes, though a temporal reading is also possible.

verses.h1: كيف أرضى عن الزمان وما أر
verses.h2: ضى كريما قبلي الزمان فأرضى

verses.h1: عرصات أصبحن وهي سماء
verses.h2: ثم أمسين بالحوادث أرضا

verses.h1: ورباع كانت عرين أسود
verses.h2: أصبحت للضباع مأوى ومفضى

verses.h1: وثرى ينبت النعيم إذا أن
verses.h2: بت ترب البلاد عشبا وحمضا

verses.h1: ولقد مضنى هجومي على الدا
verses.h2: ر بلا آذن على الباب مضا

verses.h1: How can I be content with Time,
verses.h2: when Time has pleased no noble man before me, that I should be content?

verses.h1: Courtyards that at dawn were heaven,
verses.h2: then by evening, through calamities, were earth.

verses.h1: And dwellings that were lions’ dens
verses.h2: have become a shelter and resort for hyenas.

verses.h1: And soil that brings forth luxuriant ease
verses.h2: when the soil of other lands brings forth grass and saltwort.

verses.h1: Indeed, it pained me to enter the dwelling
verses.h2: with no one at the door to grant leave—it pained me sorely.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي
poems.intro: وقال أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي:

poet.from_text: أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي

verses.h1: أيدري الربع أي دم أراقا
verses.h2: وأي قلوب هذا الركب شاقا

verses.h1: لنا ولأهله أبدا قلوب
verses.h2: تلاقي في جسوم ما تلاقى

verses.h1: فليت هوى الأحبة كان عدلا
verses.h2: فحمل كل قلب ما أطاقا

verses.h1: Does the dwelling know what blood it has shed,
verses.h2: and what hearts in this caravan it has stirred to longing?

verses.h1: We and its people have hearts that forever
verses.h2: meet within bodies that never meet.

verses.h1: If only love for our beloveds were just,
verses.h2: and burdened each heart only with what it could bear.

notes.note: I take the dwelling as the subject of both verbs, and ‘this caravan’ as qualifying ‘hearts.’ The unvocalized second hemistich could also mean ‘and what hearts this caravan has stirred to longing.’

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Mutanabbī said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي

poet.from_text: أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي

verses.h1: فديناك من ربع وإن زدتنا كربا
verses.h2: فإنك كنت الشرق للشمس والغربا

verses.h1: وكيف عرفنا رسم من لم يدع لنا
verses.h2: فؤادا لعرفان الرسوم ولا لبا

verses.h1: نزلنا عن الأكوار نمشي كرامة
verses.h2: لمن بان عنه أن نلم به ركبا

verses.h1: نذم السحاب الغر في فعلها به
verses.h2: ونعرض عنها كلما طلعت عتبا

verses.h1: ذكرت به وصلا كأن لم أفز به
verses.h2: وعيشا كأني كنت أقطعه وثبا

verses.h1: May we be your ransom, dwelling, though you deepen our grief,
verses.h2: for you were the sun’s place of rising and setting.

verses.h1: How did we recognize the traces of one who had left us
verses.h2: no heart to recognize such traces, nor any mind?

verses.h1: We dismounted from our camel-saddles to walk, out of respect
verses.h2: for the one who had left it, rather than approach it mounted.

verses.h1: We blame the white clouds for what they have done to it,
verses.h2: and turn away from them in reproach whenever they appear.

verses.h1: There I recalled a union as though I had never attained it,
verses.h2: and a life I seemed to have passed through in leaps.

verses.h1: تحية كسرى في السناء وتبع
verses.h2: لربعك، لا أرضى تحية أربع

verses.h1: أمير المغاني لم تزالي أميرة
verses.h2: به للغواني في مصيف ومربع

verses.h1: لقد نصحتني في المقام بأرضكم رجال، ولكن رب نصح مضيع
فلا كان سيرى عنكم رأى ملحد
verses.h2: يقول بيأس من معاد ومرجع

verses.h1: A greeting fit in splendor for Kisrā and Tubbaʿ
verses.h2: to your dwelling—I will not settle for a greeting for mere camps.

verses.h1: The prince of dwellings—you have always been a princess
verses.h2: there over lovely women, in summer and spring.

verses.h1: Men counseled me to remain in your land, but much good counsel goes unheeded.
May my departure from you not follow an unbeliever’s view,
verses.h2: who declares there is no hope of resurrection or return.

notes.note: مصيف ومربع may mean summer and spring quarters rather than the seasons themselves.

verses.h1: ملث الغيث أعطشها ربوعا
verses.h2: وإلا فاسقها السم النقيعا

verses.h1: أسائلها عن المتديريها
verses.h2: فما تدري ولا تذري دموعا

verses.h1: لحاها الله إلا ماضييها
verses.h2: زمان اللهو والخود الشموعا

verses.h1: O lingering rain, leave those dwellings parched,
verses.h2: or else water them with deadly poison.

verses.h1: I question them about those who dwelt there,
verses.h2: but they know nothing and shed no tears.

verses.h1: May God curse them, save the two they once held:
verses.h2: the season of pleasure and the playful maiden.

verses.h1: دمع جرى فقضى في الربع ما وجبا
verses.h2: لأهله وشفى أنى ولا كربا

verses.h1: عجنا فأذهب ما أبقى الفراق لنا
verses.h2: من العقول، وما رد الذي ذهبا

verses.h1: سقيته عبرات ظنها مطرا
verses.h2: سوائلا من جفون ظنها سحبا

verses.h1: Tears flowed, paying at the campsite the debt owed
verses.h2: to its people, but eased no anguish—how could they?

verses.h1: We turned aside, and it took away what parting had left us
verses.h2: of our reason, yet restored nothing of what was gone.

verses.h1: I watered it with tears it took for rain,
verses.h2: streaming from eyelids it took for clouds.

notes.note: The syntax of «وشفى أنى ولا كربا» is abrupt and uncertain. I take «أنى» as an incredulous question (‘how could they?’), interrupting and retracting the claim that the tears brought relief.

verses.h1: بكيت يا ربع حتى كدت أبكيكا
verses.h2: وجدت بي وبدمعي في مغانيكا

verses.h1: فعم صابحا لقد هيجت لي شجنا
verses.h2: واردد تحيتنا إنا محيوكا

verses.h1: بأي حكم زمان صرت متخذا
verses.h2: ريم الفلا بدلا من ريم أهليكا؟

verses.h1: أيام فيك شموس ما انبعثن لنا
verses.h2: إلا التعثن دما بالحظ مسفوكا

verses.h1: I wept, O dwelling, until I almost made you weep,
verses.h2: and lavished myself and my tears upon your haunts.

verses.h1: Good morning to you! You have stirred sorrow in me;
verses.h2: return our greeting, for we greet you.

verses.h1: By what decree of time have you come to take
verses.h2: the desert gazelle in place of the gazelle among your people?

verses.h1: In those days, suns dwelt in you that never rose before us
verses.h2: without wrapping themselves in blood shed by their glances.

notes.note: التعثن is obscure; I tentatively understand it as ‘wrapped themselves.’ بالحظ (‘by fortune’) appears to be a misprint for باللحظ (‘by a glance’), which the translation follows.

verses.h1: علي لربع العامرية وقفة
verses.h2: يمل علي الشوق والدمع كاتب

verses.h1: فلا وأبي العشاق ما أنا عاشق
verses.h2: إذا أنا لم تلعب بصبري الملاعب

verses.h1: ومن مذهبي حب الديار لأهلها
verses.h2: وللناس فيما يعشقون مذاهب

verses.h1: I owe the dwelling of al-ʿĀmiriyya a pause;
verses.h2: longing dictates to me, and tears are the scribe.

verses.h1: No, by the father of lovers, I am no lover
verses.h2: if the haunts of play do not toy with my patience.

verses.h1: My way is to love dwellings for their people;
verses.h2: and people have their ways in what they love.

notes.note: Al-ʿĀmiriyya apparently designates a woman of the tribe of ʿĀmir; her identity is uncertain.
It is unclear whether the oath ‘by the father of lovers’ refers to a particular figure.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Firās ibn Ḥamdān said:

verses.h1: أتهجر هذا الربع أم أنت زائره
verses.h2: وكيف يزار الربع قد بان عامره؟

verses.h1: فذ العرش قد أجرمت في أن هجرتها
verses.h2: وما يك من ذنب فإنك غافره

verses.h1: Will you forsake this dwelling, or will you visit it?
verses.h2: And how can the dwelling be visited when its inhabitant has departed?

verses.h1: O Lord of the Throne, I have sinned in forsaking her;
verses.h2: whatever sin there may be, You are its forgiver.

notes.note: The opening فذ العرش appears defective, perhaps through loss of an alif in an invocation such as فذا العرش. The translation provisionally takes it as an address to God, ‘O Lord of the Throne.’
The feminine pronoun in هجرتها (‘forsaking her’) has no explicit antecedent; it may refer to an unnamed beloved.

poems.intro: قد تقدمت هذه الأبيات - بزيادة فيها - منسوبة إلى جميل بن معمر العذري. وقال أبو تمام:

verses.h1: يا ربع لو ربعوا على ابن هموم
verses.h2: مستسلم لجوى الفراق سليم؟

verses.h1: قد كنت معهودا بأحسن ساكن
verses.h2: منا، وأحسن دمنة ورسوم

verses.h1: أيام للأيام فيك غضارة
verses.h2: والدهر في وفيك غير مليم

verses.h1: O dwelling, if only they had been gentle with a man beset by cares,
verses.h2: stricken, surrendered to the burning grief of separation!

verses.h1: You were once known for the fairest inhabitant
verses.h2: among us, and the fairest dwelling-site and traces.

verses.h1: In those days, life within you had its freshness,
verses.h2: and time was blameless in its dealings with me and you.

notes.note: ربعوا على can mean either ‘treated gently’ or ‘waited for’; the former is adopted here. سليم, literally ‘sound,’ also denotes someone bitten or stung, and is taken here as ‘stricken’ by love or grief.

prose_translation.intro: These verses have already appeared—with additional lines—attributed to Jamīl ibn Maʿmar al-ʿUdhrī. Abū Tammām said:

verses.h1: ولو أن ربعا راجع القول قبله
verses.h2: لرد السلام ربع سعدى وسلما

verses.h1: ولكنه هاج الهوى لمكلف
verses.h2: لسعدى وأمسى دارس العلم أعجما

verses.h1: Had any encampment before it ever answered speech,
verses.h2: Saʿdā’s encampment would have returned my greeting and greeted me.

verses.h1: But it stirred longing in a man enamored
verses.h2: of Saʿdā, and has become mute, its landmarks effaced.

poems.intro: وقال الرماح بن ميادة - وميادة أمه، وهي سنديه، وأبوه الأبرد بن ثوبان بن سراقة بن سلمى بن ظالم - من قصيدة يمدح بها يزيد بن عبد الملك بن مروان:

verses.h1: هل ينطق الربع بالعلياء غيره
verses.h2: سافي الرياح ومستن له طنب

verses.h1: جرت به ذات أذيال مزعزعة
verses.h2: لها تقى، وذيل عارم حصب

verses.h1: تكسو معارفه حبرا تجدده
verses.h2: من التراب، وأخرى بعد تستلب

verses.h1: دار لبيضاء مسود مسائحها
verses.h2: كأنها ظبية ترعى وتنصب

verses.h1: جاورتها رجبا أيام ذي سلم
verses.h2: ثم استمرت ولاقى دونها رجب

verses.h1: Does the campsite at al-ʿAlyāʾ speak, altered as it is
verses.h2: by windblown sand and a racing cloud with trailing fringes?

verses.h1: A blustering wind with trailing skirts swept over it,
verses.h2: with [unclear] and a fierce, gravel-scattering train.

verses.h1: It clothes the site’s landmarks in patterned robes it renews
verses.h2: from dust; another wind later strips them away.

verses.h1: The dwelling of a fair woman whose tresses are black,
verses.h2: like a gazelle that grazes and lifts its head.

verses.h1: I dwelt beside her through Rajab, in the days at Dhū Salam;
verses.h2: then she went away, and Rajab stood between us.

notes.note: Al-ʿAlyāʾ may be a place name or simply mean ‘the high ground.’ I take مستن له طنب to describe a racing cloud with extended fringes, though the referent is not explicit.
I cannot make satisfactory sense of لها تقى in this description of a wind or storm. تقى may be a transcription error; its place is marked ‘[unclear]’ in the translation.
I take أخرى to mean another wind. It could instead imply ‘at another time,’ with the same wind stripping away what it previously deposited.

The second occurrence of رجب and the construction لاقى دونها are unclear. The translation provisionally treats Rajab as something intervening between the speaker and the woman; I cannot establish whether it denotes the month again, a person, or a place.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rammāḥ ibn Mayyāda—Mayyāda was his mother, a woman from Sind, and his father was al-Abrad ibn Thawbān ibn Surāqa ibn Salmā ibn Ẓālim—said, in a poem praising Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān:

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: مثلت ربعك والمراحل دونه
verses.h2: نصب الضمير فكنت في مغناك

verses.h1: ورأيت ظبيا واقفا بفنائكم
verses.h2: يرنو إلي كما رنت عيناك

verses.h1: فبكيت من أسف عليك وإنما
verses.h2: أجرى مدامع مقلتي ذكراك

verses.h1: قالت: أكنت نسيتنا فذكرتنا
verses.h2: للظبي نشكر، لا للدمع الباكي

verses.h1: I pictured your campsite, though stages of travel lay between us,
verses.h2: before my inward eye, and found myself in your abode.

verses.h1: I saw a gazelle standing in your courtyard,
verses.h2: gazing at me as your eyes once gazed.

verses.h1: I wept from longing for you, but it was only
verses.h2: the memory of you that made my eyes shed tears.

verses.h1: She said: “Had you forgotten us, then remembered us?
verses.h2: It is the gazelle we thank, not the weeping tears.”

notes.note: الدمع الباكي literally means “the weeping tears,” an unusual expression retained here. It may be personification or a textual error; الباكي also departs from the preceding rhyme endings.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: سقيا لربعك من ربع بذي سلم
verses.h2: وللزمان به إذ ذاك من زمن

verses.h1: إذ أنت فينا لمن ينهاك عاصية
verses.h2: وإذ أجر إليكم سادرا رسنى

verses.h1: May rain bless your dwelling at Dhū Salam,
verses.h2: and the days we knew there then.

verses.h1: When you were among us, defying those who would restrain you,
verses.h2: and I would trail my reins toward you, carefree.

verses.h1: استنجد الريح من سليمى
verses.h2: مرا على ربعها المحيل

verses.h1: ولم أخل قبلها شفائي
verses.h2: عند نسيم الصبا العليل

verses.h1: وأقتضى أذرع المطايا
verses.h2: ما استصحبت من ثرى الطلول

verses.h1: I seek the wind’s aid against Sulaymā,
verses.h2: as it passes over her desolate dwelling.

verses.h1: Before this, I had not thought my cure
verses.h2: lay in the languid breath of the east wind.

verses.h1: And I claim from the mounts’ forelegs
verses.h2: whatever dust of the ruins they have carried away.

notes.note: I read استنجد as أستنجد, “I seek aid.” The syntax of مرا is uncertain; the translation takes it as describing the wind’s passage, though it could describe the speaker’s passage or be a dual imperative, “pass, you two.”
The pronoun in قبلها, rendered “before this,” has an uncertain antecedent: it may refer to Sulaymā or to the wind and the experience described in line 1.

verses.h1: أربع سلامة بالمنحنى
verses.h2: بخيف سلع جادك الهاطل

verses.h1: إن تمس وحشا فبما قد ترى
verses.h2: وأنت معمور بهم آهل

verses.h1: O dwellings of Sallāmah at the bend,
verses.h2: at Khayf Salʿ, may pouring rain water you!

verses.h1: If you now lie deserted, how often you were seen
verses.h2: inhabited by them and full of people.

notes.note: The meter supports reading سلامة as Sallāmah rather than Salāmah; the person is unidentified. المنحنى may be a place-name, al-Munḥanā, rather than simply ‘the bend.’
The compressed phrase فبما قد ترى is understood as contrasting present desolation with former habitation: ‘how often you were seen.’

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد
poems.intro: وقال أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد - رحمه الله -:

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد

verses.h1: أربع بتلك الأربع
verses.h2: بين اللوى فالأجرع

verses.h1: وقف ولو رجع الصدى
verses.h2: وقفة صب موجع

verses.h1: وسل صباها إن سرت
verses.h2: عن الغزال الألمع

verses.h1: إن كن قد أتهم لما
verses.h2: أنجد الوجد معي

verses.h1: كم لي إليه أنة
verses.h2: تقيم عوج أضلعي

verses.h1: أودعته قلبي قلم
verses.h2: يرع حقوق المودع

verses.h1: وإن يكن خان ولم
verses.h2: يرع حقوقي فرعي

verses.h1: فيا زماني والصبا
verses.h2: هل فيكما من مطمع؟

verses.h1: وهل لأيام التصا
verses.h2: بي والحمى من مرجع؟

verses.h1: ويا غراب البين طر
verses.h2: بعد الفراق أو قع

verses.h1: فما أبالي بعدهم
verses.h2: كيف أتاني مصرعي

verses.h1: Linger at those dwelling places
verses.h2: between al-Liwā and al-Ajraʿ.

verses.h1: Pause, if only for an echo’s return,
verses.h2: as a lovesick, suffering man would pause.

verses.h1: Ask their east wind, if it blows,
verses.h2: about the gleaming gazelle.

verses.h1: If he went down to Tihāma when
verses.h2: longing climbed to Najd with me—

verses.h1: how many a groan I utter for him
verses.h2: that straightens my curving ribs!

verses.h1: I entrusted him with my heart, but he did not
verses.h2: honor the rights of the one who entrusted it.

verses.h1: Though he has betrayed me and has not
verses.h2: honored my rights, may he be kept safe.

verses.h1: O days of mine, O youth,
verses.h2: is there any hope in you?

verses.h1: And is there, for the days of youthful
verses.h2: play and al-Ḥimā, any return?

verses.h1: O raven of separation, fly
verses.h2: after our parting, or alight.

verses.h1: After their departure, I do not care
verses.h2: how my death comes to me.

notes.note: Al-Liwā and al-Ajraʿ are treated as place names, but may instead describe a bend of sand and an open sandy tract.
The precise sense of الألمع, translated as “gleaming,” is uncertain; applied to a gazelle, it may refer to contrasting patches in its coat.

كن appears defective, probably for كان. The translation assumes إن كان قد أتهم. أتهم and أنجد mean to enter Tihāma and Najd respectively, also contrasting descent to the lowlands with ascent to the uplands.
قلم appears to be a misprint for فلم, “but he did not.”
فرعي is unclear. It is tentatively read as a passive blessing, فَرُعِيَ, “may he be cared for,” despite his betrayal; the wording or vocalization may be defective.
Al-Ḥimā is unidentified here; الحمى may simply mean the protected pastureland rather than a particular named place.

prose_translation.intro: And my brother, ʿIzz al-Dawla Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Murshid—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.intro: قال رقيع بن عبيد بن صيفي:

verses.h1: ألم تلمم على الدمن البوالي
verses.h2: ديار الحي في الحجج الخوالي

verses.h1: عفتها كل معصرة، ومر
verses.h2: من الأيام بعدك والليالي

verses.h1: فأبقى من معارفها قليلا
verses.h2: عيبا حين يسأل بالسؤال

verses.h1: بها عمروا، وكل نعيم عيش
verses.h2: من الدنيا يصير إلى زوال

verses.h1: هم كانوا الحماة وكان فيهم
verses.h2: ذوو الأفضال والأيدي الطوال

verses.h1: Have you not stopped at the timeworn campsite traces,
verses.h2: the tribe’s dwellings in the years gone by?

verses.h1: Every rain-laden cloud has effaced them, and the passing
verses.h2: of days and nights since you left.

verses.h1: It left only a few of their recognizable traces,
verses.h2: speechless when questioned.

verses.h1: There they dwelt; and every pleasure of life
verses.h2: in this world must pass away.

verses.h1: They were the defenders, and among them were
verses.h2: men of bounty and far-reaching power.

notes.note: The printed عيبا does not yield a clear sense here. The translation tentatively reads عييا, meaning unable to speak or answer, describing the surviving traces.
الأيدي الطوال, literally “long hands,” may signify great generosity rather than the extensive power adopted here.

prose_translation.intro: Ruqayʿ ibn ʿUbayd ibn Ṣayfī said:

verses.h1: ألفوا الفراق كأنه وطن لهم
verses.h2: لا يقربون إليه حتى يبعدوا

verses.h1: في كل يوم دمنة من حيهم
verses.h2: تقوى، وربع منهم يتأبد

verses.h1: أسند صدور اليعملات بوقفة
verses.h2: في الماثلات كأنهن المسند

verses.h1: دمن تقاضاهن إعلان البلى
verses.h2: هوج الرياح الباديات العود

verses.h1: حتى فنين، وما البقاء لواقف
verses.h2: والدهر في أطرافه يتردد

verses.h1: They have grown familiar with parting, as though it were their homeland,
verses.h2: which they approach only by going far away.

verses.h1: Each day, a campsite left by their tribe
verses.h2: grows desolate, and a dwelling of theirs turns to wilderness.

verses.h1: Steady the breasts of the sturdy she-camels for a halt
verses.h2: among the standing remnants, as though they were Musnad writing.

verses.h1: Ruins forced to proclaim their decay
verses.h2: by the raging winds, coming and coming again,

verses.h1: until they vanished. How can what stands endure,
verses.h2: while time ranges round its edges?

notes.note: The unvocalized أسند can be read as an imperative, ‘steady,’ or as a first-person present, ‘I steady.’ The imperative is adopted here. المسند is understood as Musnad, the ancient South Arabian script to which the remnants are compared.

verses.h1: بين السقيفة فاللوى فالأجرع
verses.h2: دمن حبسن على الرياح الأربع

verses.h1: فكأنما ضمنت معالمها الذي
verses.h2: ضمنته أحشاء المحب الموجع

verses.h1: ولو أن أنواء الربيع تطيعني
verses.h2: لشفى الربيع غليل تلك الأربع

verses.h1: ما أحسن الأيام إلا أنها
verses.h2: تمضي بنا، وإذا مضت لم ترجع

verses.h1: Between al-Saqīfa, al-Liwā, and al-Ajraʿ
verses.h2: lie traces of dwellings, left to the four winds.

verses.h1: It is as though their landmarks held within them
verses.h2: what the tormented lover’s breast contains.

verses.h1: If spring’s rains would obey me,
verses.h2: spring would quench the thirst of those dwellings.

verses.h1: How lovely the days are, except that
verses.h2: they pass us by, and once gone, never return.

notes.note: Al-Saqīfa, al-Liwā, and al-Ajraʿ are treated as place names; their precise locations are uncertain. The latter two can also denote terrain: curving sands and a sandy tract.

verses.h1: ما جو خبت وإن نأت ظعنه
verses.h2: تاركنا أو تشوقنا دمنه

verses.h1: إذا استجدت دارا تعلقها
verses.h2: بالإلف حتى كأنها وطنه

verses.h1: تالله ما إن يني يدلهنا
verses.h2: سرور هذا الزمان أو حزنه

verses.h1: The valley of Khabt, though its caravans have gone far away,
verses.h2: will not leave us without its ruins stirring our longing.

verses.h1: Whenever a new dwelling is taken, one grows attached to it
verses.h2: through familiarity, until it seems one’s homeland.

verses.h1: By God, it never ceases to bewilder us—
verses.h2: this age’s joy or its sorrow.

notes.note: I take جو خبت as ‘the valley of Khabt’; the precise location is uncertain. The construction أو تشوقنا is unusual here; I understand it as ‘without its ruins stirring our longing,’ though ‘until its ruins stir our longing’ is also possible.

The subjects and pronouns are unclear. Unvocalized استجدت permits several readings, including ‘I/you took a new dwelling,’ whereas تعلقها and وطنه appear to refer to an unidentified third-person subject (‘he grows attached to it’; ‘his homeland’). The impersonal translation is provisional; the text may be faulty.

verses.h1: دمن ألم بها فقال سلام
verses.h2: كم حل عقدة صبره الإلمام

verses.h1: نحرت ركاب الركب حتى يغبروا
verses.h2: رجلى، لقد عنفوا علي ولاموا

verses.h1: وقفوا على اللوم حتى خيلوا
verses.h2: أن الوقوف على الديار حرام

verses.h1: لا مر يوم واحد إلا وفي
verses.h2: أحشائه لمحلتيك غمام

verses.h1: ولقد أراك فهل أراك بغرة
verses.h2: والعيش غض والزمان غلام

verses.h1: أعوام وصل كان ينسى طولها
verses.h2: ذكر النوى فكأنها أيام

verses.h1: ثم انبرت أيام هجر أردفت
verses.h2: بجوى أسى فكأنها أعوام

verses.h1: ثم انقضت تلك السنون وأهلها
verses.h2: فكأنهم وكأنها أحلام

verses.h1: Ruins—he visited them and said, “Peace!”
verses.h2: How often a visit has undone the knot of his patience!

verses.h1: I faced the caravan’s mounts until they covered
verses.h2: my feet with dust; they treated me harshly and blamed me.

verses.h1: They persisted in reproaching me until they made it seem
verses.h2: that stopping at the dwellings was forbidden.

verses.h1: May not a single day pass without
verses.h2: a rain cloud in its breast for your two dwelling places.

verses.h1: I once beheld you; shall I behold you in your early splendor,
verses.h2: with life still fresh and time a youth?

verses.h1: Years of union whose long span made one forget
verses.h2: the thought of parting—as though they were mere days.

verses.h1: Then days of estrangement came upon us, followed
verses.h2: by searing grief—as though they were years.

verses.h1: Then those years and their people passed away;
verses.h2: both they and those years were as dreams.

notes.note: The wording نحرت ركاب الركب حتى يغبروا رجلى is obscure and may be corrupted. The translation tentatively takes نحرت as “faced” and يغبروا رجلى as “covered my feet with dust,” but the connection between these actions remains unclear.
The sense of بغرة is uncertain: it may refer to early splendor or freshness, as translated, or to an unguarded moment.
The unvocalized ينسى is taken as يُنسي, “makes one forget,” with طولها (“their long span”) as its subject.

verses.h1: دمن كمسحبة الأزم
verses.h2: ة مسحلا إمرارها

verses.h1: ماتت حقائها وخل
verses.h2: د زورها ومعارها

verses.h1: وامتد ليل السافيا
verses.h2: ت بجوها، ونهارها

verses.h1: عندي لها إن أجدبت
verses.h2: وكافة تمتارها

verses.h1: أنست بإسبال الدمو
verses.h2: ع، كأنها أشفارها

verses.h1: Ruins, like the track of trailing reins,
verses.h2: their tight strands unravelled.

verses.h1: Their realities have died,
verses.h2: but their false semblance and borrowed guise endure.

verses.h1: Long has grown the night of the sand-driving winds
verses.h2: across their open ground—and their day.

verses.h1: For them, if they grow barren, I have
verses.h2: a streaming eye from which they may draw sustenance.

verses.h1: They have grown accustomed to streaming tears,
verses.h2: as though the ruins were the tears’ own lashes.

notes.note: The wording كمسحبة الأزمة مسحلا إمرارها is difficult and may be corrupt. The translation provisionally takes مسحبة الأزمة as the track of dragged reins, and مسحلا إمرارها as tightly twisted strands being loosened or unravelled.
حقائها appears corrupt. The translation conjectures حقائقها, ‘their realities,’ in contrast with زورها ومعارها, ‘their false semblance and borrowed guise.’
The pronouns in كأنها أشفارها are ambiguous. The translation takes the ruins as resembling eyelashes over which the speaker’s tears flow.

poems.intro: قال زهير بن أبي سلمى، واسمه ربيعة بن رزاح المزني:

opening.actual: أمن أم أوفى دمنة لم تكلم

verses.h1: أمن أم أوفى دمنة لم تكلم
verses.h2: بحومانة الدراج فالمتثلم

verses.h1: ديار لها بالرقمتين كأنها
verses.h2: مراجع وشم في نواشر معصم

verses.h1: بها العين والآرام يمشين خلفة
verses.h2: وأطلاؤها ينهضن من كل مجثم

verses.h1: وقفت بها من بعد عشرين حجة
verses.h2: فلايا عرفت الدار بعد توهم

verses.h1: فلما عرفت الدار قلت لربعها:
verses.h2: ألا انعم صباحا أيها الربع واسلم

verses.h1: Is this a silent remnant of Umm Awfā’s camp,
verses.h2: at Ḥawmānat al-Darrāj and al-Mutathallam?

verses.h1: Her dwellings at al-Raqmatayn are like
verses.h2: retraced tattoo marks upon the sinews of a wrist.

verses.h1: Wide-eyed wild cattle and white gazelles walk there, one after another,
verses.h2: and their young rise from every resting-place.

verses.h1: I stood there after twenty years;
verses.h2: only with difficulty, after pondering, did I recognize the dwelling.

verses.h1: When I recognized the dwelling, I said to its deserted ground:
verses.h2: “Good morning to you, dwelling-place, and may you remain unharmed!”

prose_translation.intro: Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā, whose name was Rabīʿa ibn Razāḥ al-Muzanī, said:
interludes: [Al-nawāshir]: the sinews of the forearm.

verses.h1: عوجوا فحيوا لنعم دمنة الدار
verses.h2: ماذا تحيون من نؤى وأحجار

verses.h1: أقوى وأقفر من نعم وغيرها
verses.h2: هوج الرياح بهابي الترب موار

verses.h1: وقفت فيها سراة اليوم أسألها
verses.h2: عن آل نعم أمونا عبر أسفار

verses.h1: فاستعجمت دار نعم ما تكلمنا
verses.h2: والدار لو كلمتنا ذات أخبار

verses.h1: Turn aside and greet the traces of Nuʿm’s dwelling;
verses.h2: what do you greet but a ditch and stones?

verses.h1: It lies deserted, empty of Nuʿm, and has been altered
verses.h2: by raging winds bearing billowing, swirling dust.

verses.h1: I stopped there at midday, asking the dwelling
verses.h2: about Nuʿm’s folk, on a trusty she-camel hardened by journeys.

verses.h1: But Nuʿm’s dwelling remained mute; it did not speak to us,
verses.h2: though, had it spoken to us, it had much to tell.

notes.note: «أمونًا عبر أسفار» appears to describe a dependable she-camel, strong or seasoned in travel. The exact construction and the sense of «عبر أسفار» are uncertain; «أمونًا» may be the delayed object of «وقفت», meaning that the speaker halted his camel.

poems.intro: وقال كثير بن عبد الرحمن الخزاعي:

verses.h1: أهاجك مغنى دمنة ومساكن
verses.h2: خلت وعفاها المعصرات السوافن

verses.h1: ديار ابنة السعدي إذ عقد حبلها
verses.h2: متين، وإذ معروفها لك عاهن

verses.h1: وما زلت في ليلى لدن طرشاربي
verses.h2: إلى اليوم أطفئ إحنة وأداجن

verses.h1: وأحمل في ليلى لقوم ضغينة
verses.h2: وتحمل في ليلى على الضغائن

verses.h1: Has the site of a ruined camp stirred you, and dwellings
verses.h2: left empty, effaced by the scouring rain clouds?

verses.h1: The dwellings of al-Saʿdī’s daughter, when the knot of her bond
verses.h2: was firm, and her kindness was yours to find.

verses.h1: Ever since my mustache first sprouted, on Laylā’s account
verses.h2: I have kept quelling rancor and making peace, down to this day.

verses.h1: On Laylā’s account I bear a grudge against some people,
verses.h2: and on Laylā’s account grudges are borne against me.

notes.note: المعصرات السوافن is taken as rain clouds that scour away the traces. المعصرات can also denote rain-bringing winds, and السوافن suggests scraping or sweeping away.
على appears to be a typing or OCR error for عليّ, ‘against me.’ The translation also reads تحمل as passive تُحمل, ‘are borne.’

prose_translation.intro: And Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khuzāʿī said:
interludes: [Al-sawāfin]: he means al-sawāfī, those that sweep away.
[ʿĀhin]: present, at hand.

verses.h1: تحن إلى مي كما حن نازع
verses.h2: دعاه الهوى فارتد في قيده قسرا

verses.h1: فقلت: أربعا يا صاحبي بدمنة
verses.h2: بذي الرمث قد أقوت منازلها عصرا

verses.h1: أرشت بها عيناك حتى كأنما
verses.h2: يحلان من سفح الدموع بها نذرا

verses.h1: ولا مي إلا أن تزور بمشرف
verses.h2: أو الزرق من أطلالها دمنا قفرا

verses.h1: You yearn for Mayy as one yearns for home,
verses.h2: called by longing, then forced back by his fetters.

verses.h1: I said: “Halt, my two companions, at the campsite’s traces
verses.h2: at Dhū al-Ramth, whose dwellings have long lain deserted.”

verses.h1: Your eyes have shed tears there, until it is as though
verses.h2: by pouring out tears there, they were fulfilling a vow.

verses.h1: There is no Mayy—only a visit at Mushrif
verses.h2: or al-Zurq to the desolate traces of her encampments.

notes.note: نازع denotes one longing for home; the fetters may suggest a tethered camel, but the referent is not explicit.
Dhū al-Ramth is a place name; its location is unidentified.

Mushrif and al-Zurq appear to be place names; their locations and vocalizations are uncertain. The elliptical ولا مي إلا أن تزور is understood as denying Mayy’s presence and leaving only a visit to her deserted campsites.

verses.h1: أمن دمنة بين القلات وشارع
verses.h2: تصابيت حتى ظلت العين تدمع

verses.h1: أجل عبرة ظلت إذا ما وزعتها
verses.h2: بحلمي أبت منها عوارض تسرع

verses.h1: وما يرجع الوجد الزمان الذي مضى
verses.h2: وما للفتى في دمنة الدار مجزع

verses.h1: عشية مالي حيلة غير أنني
verses.h2: بلقط الحصى والخط في الدار مولع

verses.h1: أخط وأمحو الخط ثم أعيده
verses.h2: بكفي والغربان في الدار وقع

verses.h1: كأن سنانا فارسيا أصابني
verses.h2: على كبدي، بل لوعة الحب أوجع

verses.h1: ألا ليت أيام القلات وشارع
verses.h2: رجعن لنا، ثم انقضى العيش أجمع

verses.h1: Was it a campsite’s traces between al-Qilāt and Shāriʿ
verses.h2: that made you yearn like a youth, until your eye kept shedding tears?

verses.h1: Yes—tears that kept flowing: whenever I checked them
verses.h2: with my self-command, fresh surges refused restraint and rushed forth.

verses.h1: Longing does not bring back the time that has passed,
verses.h2: nor is a dwelling’s ruin a place for a man to despair.

verses.h1: That evening I had no recourse, save that I was
verses.h2: absorbed in picking up pebbles and tracing lines at the dwelling.

verses.h1: I draw a line and erase it, then draw it again
verses.h2: with my palm, while crows perch at the dwelling.

verses.h1: It is as though a Persian spearhead had struck me
verses.h2: in the liver—no, love’s burning anguish hurts still more.

verses.h1: Ah, if only the days of al-Qilāt and Shāriʿ
verses.h2: would return to us, and then all life come to an end!

notes.note: Al-Qilāt and Shāriʿ are unidentified place names, repeated in line 7. The vocalization al-Qilāt is tentative.
I take عوارض to mean recurrent or sudden surges of tears; the compressed phrasing أبت منها عوارض تسرع leaves the precise construction uncertain.
I take مجزع as a place or occasion for despair; its precise force here is uncertain.

verses.h1: أمن دمنة بالجو جو جلاجل
verses.h2: زميلك منهل الدموع جزوع؟

verses.h1: عصيت الهوى يوم القلات وإنني لداعي الهوى يوم النقا لسميع
أربت به هوجاء تستدرج الصبا
verses.h2: مفرقة تذرى التراب جموع

verses.h1: أراجعة يا مي أيامنا الألى
verses.h2: بذي الرمث، أم لا مالهن رجوع؟
