It has also been related from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī—may God have mercy on him—that Banū Salima complained to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, of the distance of their homes from the mosque. Then God—glorified be He—revealed: “Indeed, We give life to the dead, and We record what they have sent ahead and the traces they leave behind.” They said: “Keep to your homes, for your footsteps are indeed recorded.”

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may God be pleased with him—said: “If God Most High were to overlook anything, He would overlook these traces that the winds efface.” He meant His words—mighty and majestic is He: “Indeed, We give life to the dead, and We record what they have sent ahead and the traces they leave behind.” al-Aḥwaṣ said:

verses.h1: تصفو الحياة لجاهل أو غافل
verses.h2: عما مضى فيها، وما يتوقع

verses.h1: ولمن يغالط في الحقائق نفسه
verses.h2: ويسومها طلب المحال فتقنع

verses.h1: أين الذي الهرمان من بنيانه؟
verses.h2: ما قومه؟ ما يومه؟ ما المصرع؟

verses.h1: تتخلف الآثار عن أربابها
verses.h2: حينا، ويدركها الفناء فتتبع

verses.h1: Life is untroubled for one ignorant or heedless
verses.h2: of what has passed in it and what is yet expected.

verses.h1: And for one who deceives himself about the truth
verses.h2: and bids his soul seek the impossible, and it is content.

verses.h1: Where is he whose buildings include the two pyramids?
verses.h2: Who were his people? When was his final day? Where did he fall?

verses.h1: Remains outlast their masters
verses.h2: for a while; then destruction overtakes them, and they follow.

notes.note: “His day” (يومه) is taken here as the day of his death, though it could refer to his time more broadly. “His fall” (المصرع) may refer to the place or manner of his death.

poems.intro: وللبيد بن ربيعة السبق إلى هذا المعنى الذي قصده الأحوص بقوله:

verses.h1: فعفا آخر الزمان عليهم
verses.h2: فعلى آخر الزمان الدمار

verses.h1: وكذاك الزمان يذهب بالنا
verses.h2: س وتبقى الرسوم والآثار

verses.h1: Time’s latter days effaced them;
verses.h2: so may destruction fall upon time’s latter days!

verses.h1: Thus time carries people away,
verses.h2: while the traces and remains endure.

prose_translation.intro: Labīd ibn Rabīʿa was the first to express this idea, which al-Aḥwaṣ intended in his words:

verses.h1: سلام على الأطلال والمنزل القفر
verses.h2: وإن كان لا يعنيه وصلي ولا هجري

verses.h1: ولكن آثار الأحبة بينها
verses.h2: بلين، وما تبلى البلابل في صدري

verses.h1: Peace upon the ruins and the deserted dwelling,
verses.h2: though neither my visits nor my absence matter to it.

verses.h1: But the traces of loved ones amid those ruins
verses.h2: have faded, while the sorrows in my breast do not fade.

prose_translation.intro: And Salm ibn ʿAmr al-Khāsir said:

verses.h1: لا تأمرني بالعزاء، وقد ترى
verses.h2: أثر الخليط، ولات حين عزاء

verses.h1: زدني اشتياقا بالمدام وغنني
verses.h2: أعزز علي بفرقة القرناء

verses.h1: فلعلني ألقى الردى فيريحني
verses.h2: عما قليل من جوى البرحاء

verses.h1: Do not bid me take comfort, when you can see
verses.h2: the traces of my companions—this is no time for comfort.

verses.h1: Heighten my longing with wine, and sing to me:
verses.h2: “How grievous to me is parting from companions!”

verses.h1: Perhaps I shall meet death, and it will relieve me
verses.h2: before long of this consuming anguish.

notes.note: The second hemistich appears to quote words to be sung; I could not identify a source for the possible quotation.

verses.h1: لمن أسائل لا رسم ولا أثر
verses.h2: رحلتم وأقام الدمع والسهر

verses.h1: كنتم لعيني صباحا لا مساء له
verses.h2: فعاضها البين ليلا ماله سحر

verses.h1: وما أعاب بشيء بعد فرقتكم
verses.h2: غير البقاء فإني منه أعتذر

verses.h1: Whom can I ask? There is neither vestige nor trace.
verses.h2: You departed, while tears and sleeplessness remained.

verses.h1: To my eyes you were a morning without evening;
verses.h2: Separation gave them instead a night without dawn.

verses.h1: I cannot be reproached for anything since your departure
verses.h2: Except remaining alive—for that I beg forgiveness.

notes.note: The opening لمن أسائل is syntactically unusual: the preposition in لمن does not fit the straightforward sense ‘Whom can I ask?’ adopted here. The intended construction is uncertain.

poems.poet: علي بن أحمد بن أبي أمية
poems.poet_from_text: علي بن أحمد بن أبي أمية الكاتب
poems.intro: وقال علي بن أحمد بن أبي أمية الكاتب:

poet.expected: علي بن أحمد بن أبي أمية
poet.from_text: علي بن أحمد بن أبي أمية الكاتب

verses.h1: يا ريح ما تصنعين بالدمن
verses.h2: كم لك من محو منظر حسن

verses.h1: محوت آثارنا وأحدثت آثا
verses.h2: را بربع الحبيب لم تكن

verses.h1: إن تك يا ربع قد بليت من الر
verses.h2: يح فإني بال من الحزن

verses.h1: O wind, what are you doing to the campsite’s remains?
verses.h2: How many a lovely scene you have effaced!

verses.h1: You effaced our traces and made new marks
verses.h2: in the beloved’s dwelling that were not there before.

verses.h1: If, O dwelling, you have been worn away
verses.h2: by the wind, I am worn away by grief.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Umayya, the secretary, said:

poems.intro: قد أوردت هذه الأبيات بتمامها وخبرها في فصل المغاني. وقلت:

verses.h1: أعاضني الدهر من رؤياكم نظري
verses.h2: آثاركم، وبرغمي ذلك العوض

verses.h1: ثم استقال فقد أضحت موانعه
verses.h2: دون التداني من الآثار تعترض

verses.h1: فقل لمن يمنع الحل المباح غدا
verses.h2: توفى وحقك ما أصبحت تقترض

verses.h1: In place of seeing you, Time has granted me the sight
verses.h2: of your traces—an exchange against my will.

verses.h1: Then it sought release from the bargain: its obstacles now
verses.h2: bar the way to drawing near those traces.

verses.h1: Tell him who forbids what is lawful and permitted: tomorrow
verses.h2: you will, by your honor, be paid in full what you now borrow.

notes.note: الحل المباح is uncertain: it may mean simply ‘what is lawful and permitted,’ or refer more specifically to permitted lodging or access to the site.
I read توفى as تُوَفَّى, ‘you will be paid in full.’ The debt metaphor is awkward with تقترض, ‘you borrow’; the intended sense may instead be that the addressee will have to repay his present debt.

prose_translation.intro: I have already quoted these verses in full, along with their story, in the chapter on dwelling places. And I said:

verses.h1: عمي صباحا بعدنا وانعمي
verses.h2: يا دار صفراء على الأنعم

verses.h1: دعاء من أقنعه البين بع
verses.h2: د العين بالآثار والمعلم

verses.h1: بكى النوى أمس، فلم يدخر
verses.h2: دمعا يفيض اليوم في الأرسم

verses.h1: خان بكاء العين أجفانه
verses.h2: فناح، والنوح بكاء الفم

verses.h1: May your mornings be fair after our departure, and may you flourish,
verses.h2: O dwelling of Ṣafrāʾ at al-Anʿam.

verses.h1: The prayer of one whom separation has made content
verses.h2: with traces and a landmark in place of direct sight.

verses.h1: Yesterday he wept over separation, leaving no
verses.h2: tears to pour today upon the remnants.

verses.h1: His eyes’ weeping failed his eyelids,
verses.h2: so he lamented—and lamentation is the mouth’s weeping.

notes.note: Ṣafrāʾ is taken as a woman’s name and al-Anʿam as a place-name; their identities are uncertain.
بعد العين literally means ‘after direct sight’ or ‘after the thing itself.’ It is unclear whether the lost sight or presence is that of the beloved or her dwelling.

poems.intro: روى أن الأخطل سأل بكر بن وائل، فلما انتهى إلى بني غبر، فنزل بهم أبطئوا عليه، فقال:

verses.h1: تنزو الدجاج عليها وهي باركة
verses.h2: ترجو عطاء سويد من بني غبرا

verses.h1: قبيلة كشراك النعل دارجة
verses.h2: إن يهبطوا عفو أرض لا ترى أثرا

verses.h1: Chickens leap upon her while she kneels,
verses.h2: hoping for a gift from Suwayd of Banū Ghubar.

verses.h1: A tribe like a sandal strap, passing along:
verses.h2: if they alight on untouched ground, you see no trace.

notes.note: The feminine pronouns apparently refer to the poet’s she-camel, though she is not explicitly named in these verses.
دارجة is ambiguous: translated here as ‘passing along,’ it can also mean ‘passing away’ or ‘dying out.’

prose_translation.intro: It is related that al-Akhṭal sought gifts from Bakr ibn Wāʾil. When he reached Banū Ghubar and lodged among them, they kept him waiting, so he said:
interludes: [ʿalayhā]: “upon her,” meaning his she-camel.

verses.h1: أرى آثاركم فأذوب شوقا
verses.h2: وأسفح في منازلكم دموعي

verses.h1: وأسأل من بفرقتكم بلاني
verses.h2: يمن علي منكم بالرجوع

verses.h1: I see your traces and melt with longing,
verses.h2: and pour out my tears in your dwellings.

verses.h1: I ask Him who afflicted me with separation from you
verses.h2: to bless me with your return.

prose_translation.intro: (He disparages them for their small numbers and weakness.) Another poet said:

poems.intro: وقال القاضي أبو المجد بن سليمان - رحمه الله -:

verses.h1: مررت بالدار وقد غيرت
verses.h2: معالم منها وآثار

verses.h1: فقلت
verses.h2: والقلب به لوعة تحرقه، والدمع مدرار

verses.h1: أين زمان فيك خلفته
verses.h2: وأين سكانك يا دار؟

verses.h1: أجابت الدار على عيها:
verses.h2: إن سكوتي عنك إقرار

verses.h1: أما تراني اليوم من بعدهم
verses.h2: مقفرة ما في ديار؟

verses.h1: I passed by the dwelling; now altered were
verses.h2: its landmarks and traces.

verses.h1: I said—
verses.h2: with anguish burning in my heart and tears streaming—

verses.h1: “Where is the time I left behind in you?
verses.h2: And where are your inhabitants, O dwelling?”

verses.h1: Despite its speechlessness, the dwelling answered:
verses.h2: “My silence toward you is an admission.

verses.h1: Do you not see me now, after they are gone,
verses.h2: desolate, with not a soul within me?”

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced. The likely division is «فقلت والقلب به لوعة / تحرقه والدمع مدرار». The translation retains the supplied division.

prose_translation.intro: And the judge Abū al-Majd ibn Sulaymān—may God have mercy on him—said:

opening.actual: أعاد الدجى في الصبح من بعد

verses.h1: أعاد الدجى في الصبح من بعد فقدهم
verses.h2: أم الحزن غطى ناظر العين بالدمع

verses.h1: وقفت على آثارهم فقريتها
verses.h2: دموع اشتياق مثل منهمر الرجع

verses.h1: دموعا جرت جريا تحلل عقده
verses.h2: غداة ربعنا بالهموم على الربع

verses.h1: سلام على قلبي فقد بان إثرهم
verses.h2: وقد صم إلا عن حديثهم سمعي

verses.h1: Has darkness returned at dawn since I lost them,
verses.h2: or has grief veiled the pupil of my eye with tears?

verses.h1: I stood over their traces and offered them hospitality:
verses.h2: tears of longing, like rain pouring down.

verses.h1: Tears that streamed, their string come undone,
verses.h2: the morning we lingered with our sorrows at the dwelling.

verses.h1: Peace upon my heart—it has departed in their wake;
verses.h2: my hearing has grown deaf to all but talk of them.

notes.note: The construction جرياً تحلل عقده is uncertain: literally, ‘a flowing whose knot/string came undone.’ I understand an image of tears streaming like beads from an unfastened string, but the pronoun’s reference is unclear.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان
poems.intro: كتب أرسطاطاليس إلى الإسكندر كتابا يوصيه فيه بمصالح ملكه، ثم قال له فيه: "اعلم أن الأيام تأتي على كل شيء، فتخلق الأفعال، وتمحو الآثار، وتميت الذكر، إلا ما رسخ في القلوب بمحبة تتوارثها الأعقاب، فاجهد أن تظفر بالذكر الذي لا يموت، بأن تودع الناس محبة يبقى بها ذكر مناقبك". وقال أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان:

poet.from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان

verses.h1: اتبع طريقا للهدى لاحبا
verses.h2: وخل آثارا بملحوب

verses.h1: أف لديناي، فإني بها
verses.h2: لم أخل من هم وتعذيب

verses.h1: قلت لها: امضي غير مصحوبة
verses.h2: فقالت: اذهب غير مصحوب

verses.h1: Follow a well-marked path to right guidance,
verses.h2: and leave the ruins at Malḥūb.

verses.h1: Fie on this world of mine! In it I have
verses.h2: never been free of care and torment.

verses.h1: I said to her, “Go, with none to accompany you”;
verses.h2: she replied, “Go, with none to accompany you.”

notes.note: The printed لديناي appears to be a transposition error for لدنياي, “on this world of mine,” which is the reading translated.

prose_translation.intro: Arisṭāṭālīs wrote al-Iskandar a letter advising him on the welfare of his kingdom, and then said to him in it: “Know that time overtakes everything: it wears deeds away, effaces traces, and puts remembrance to death, except what is firmly rooted in hearts through a love inherited by succeeding generations. Strive, then, to attain a remembrance that does not die, by instilling in people a love through which the memory of your virtues will endure.” And Abū [Al-ʿAlāʾ Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: جمعوا فما أكلوا الذي جمعوا
verses.h2: وبنوا مساكنهم فما سكنوا

verses.h1: وكأنهم كانوا بها ظعنا
verses.h2: لما استراحوا ساعة ظعنوا

verses.h1: They hoarded, but did not eat what they hoarded;
verses.h2: they built their dwellings, but did not dwell in them.

verses.h1: It was as though they were a caravan there:
verses.h2: once they had rested a little while, they departed.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: روى عن أبي الدرداء - رضي الله عنه - أنه أشرف على أهل حمص فقال: "ألا تستحيون؟ تبنون ما لا تسكنون، وتأملون ما لا تدركون، وتجمعون ما لا تأكلون! أين الذين بنوا قبلكم تشييدا، وجمعوا كثيرا، وأملوا بعيدا،؟ أصبحت مساكنهم قبورا، وآمالهم غرورا، وجمعهم بورا". وقال أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

poet.from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: سكنتك يا دنيا برغمي مكرها
verses.h2: وما كان لي في ذاك صنع ولا أمر

verses.h1: وجربت حتى قد قتلتك خبرة
verses.h2: فأنت وعاء حشوه الهم والوزر

verses.h1: فإن أرتحل يوما أدعك ذميمة
verses.h2: وما فيك من عودي غراس ولا بذر

verses.h1: I dwelt in you, O world, unwilling and compelled,
verses.h2: and I had neither hand nor say in that.

verses.h1: I tried you until I knew you through and through:
verses.h2: you are a vessel filled with sorrow and sin.

verses.h1: If one day I depart, I shall leave you despised,
verses.h2: with neither sapling nor seed of my stock left in you.

prose_translation.intro: It is related of Abū al-Dardāʾ—may God be pleased with him—that he looked out upon the people of Ḥimṣ and said: “Have you no shame? You build what you will not inhabit, hope for what you will not attain, and amass what you will not eat! Where are those before you who built lofty buildings, amassed great wealth, and cherished far-reaching hopes? Their dwellings have become graves, their hopes delusions, and their accumulated wealth a ruin.” And Abū [al-ʿAlāʾ Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

poems.intro: عن حاتم الأصم - رحمه الله - أنه قال: ما من صباح إلا والشيطان يقول لي: ما تأكل؟ وما تلبس؟ وأين تسكن؟ فأقول؛ آكل الموت، وألبس الكفن، وأسكن القبر. وقال النابغة الذبياني:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: لليلى بشرقي النجاد مساكن
verses.h2: قفار تعفتها شمال وداجن

verses.h1: توهمت منها معهدا، فعرفته
verses.h2: لسبعة أعوام وذا العام ثامن

verses.h1: أقامت على ريب الزمان وأعجت
verses.h2: بليلى نوى عن دار أهلك شاطن

verses.h1: Laylā has dwellings to the east of al-Nijād,
verses.h2: desolate, effaced by the north wind and persistent rain.

verses.h1: I faintly discerned a familiar spot among them, then recognized it,
verses.h2: after seven years—and this year is the eighth.

verses.h1: They endured time’s vicissitudes, but [separation carried]
verses.h2: Laylā far away from your people’s home.

notes.note: النجاد may be a place name, rendered here as al-Nijād, or simply the plural of najd, meaning uplands.

The form أعجت is unclear and may be corrupt. The bracketed rendering is conjectural, based on the following phrase بليلى نوى عن دار أهلك شاطن, which describes a departure or separation taking Laylā far from the addressee’s people.

prose_translation.intro: It is related of Ḥātim al-Aṣamm—may God have mercy on him—that he said: “Not a morning passes without Satan saying to me, ‘What will you eat? What will you wear? And where will you dwell?’ I reply, ‘I shall eat death, wear a shroud, and dwell in the grave.’” al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: غشيت لليلى بالبرود مساكنا
verses.h2: تقادمن واستنت عليها الأعاصر

verses.h1: وأوحشن بعد الحي إلا مساكنا
verses.h2: يرين حديثات وهن دوائر

verses.h1: وكانت إذ أخلت وأمرع ربعها
verses.h2: يكون عليها من صديقك حاضر

verses.h1: فقد خف منها الحي بعد إقامة
verses.h2: فما إن بها إلا الرياح العوائر

verses.h1: I visited Laylā’s dwellings at al-Burūd,
verses.h2: grown old, with the ages sweeping over them.

verses.h1: They lay desolate after their people left, save for dwellings
verses.h2: that look newly made, though they are falling into ruin.

verses.h1: When they grew grassy and their dwelling-ground flourished,
verses.h2: a company of your beloved’s people would be staying there.

verses.h1: Now the tribe has departed after dwelling there,
verses.h2: and nothing is there but the wandering winds.

notes.note: The precise identification and vocalization of البرود, rendered al-Burūd, are uncertain.
The exception إلا مساكنا, ‘save for dwellings,’ is awkward because the preceding subject is itself the dwellings. The wording may be defective; it is translated as transmitted.

أخلت is taken here to mean ‘grew grassy,’ from الخلى, fresh herbage, rather than ‘became empty.’ The phrase من صديقك حاضر is also ambiguous: صديقك may mean ‘your friend’ or ‘your beloved,’ and حاضر may denote either a settled company or someone present.

prose_translation.intro: And Kuthayyir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: لعمري لئن أبكتك كل محلة
verses.h2: لشماء أو طيف متى تمس يطرق

verses.h1: لتلتمسن عينا سوى عينك التي
verses.h2: ذهبت بجاري دمعها المترقرق

verses.h1: By my life, if every dwelling makes you weep—
verses.h2: of Shammāʾ, or a phantom that visits you whenever evening falls—

verses.h1: you will surely seek an eye other than your own, which
verses.h2: has wasted away with its flowing, shimmering tears.

notes.note: Shammāʾ appears to be a woman’s name; her identity is unclear.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أسقى محلتك الغمام، ولا يزال
verses.h2: نوء بها خضل، ونور جاسد

verses.h1: فلقد عهدت العيش في أفيائها
verses.h2: فينان يحمد مجتناه الرائد

verses.h1: May the clouds water your dwelling, and may there always be
verses.h2: abundant rain there, and deep-red blossoms.

verses.h1: For I once knew life beneath its shade,
verses.h2: luxuriant, its harvest praised by the scout.

notes.note: جاسد is an uncommon epithet for blossoms; translated as “deep-red,” though the precise color intended is uncertain. That is Astra’s reading. The edition glosses it as yābis (NM)
الرائد ordinarily means a scout seeking pasture and water. Here it appears within the image of life as luxuriant growth yielding a harvest.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: قل للسحاب إذا حداه الشمأل
verses.h2: وسرى بليل ركبه المتحمل

verses.h1: عرج على حلب فسق محلة
verses.h2: مأنوسة، فيها لعلوة منزل

verses.h1: لغريرة أدنو وتبعد في الهوى
verses.h2: وأجود بالود المصون وتبخل

verses.h1: أحنو عليك وفي فؤادي لوعة
verses.h2: وأصد عنك ووجه ودي مقبل

verses.h1: وأعز ثم أذل ذلة عاشق
verses.h2: والحب فيه تعزز وتذلل

verses.h1: وإذا هممت بوصل غيرك ردني
verses.h2: وله عليك وشافع لك أول

verses.h1: Say to the clouds, when the north wind drives them onward
verses.h2: and their departing caravan travels by night:

verses.h1: Turn aside to Ḥalab and water a quarter
verses.h2: inhabited and welcoming, where ʿAlwa has a home.

verses.h1: A guileless girl’s home—I draw near in love, while she draws away;
verses.h2: I lavish my treasured affection, while she withholds hers.

verses.h1: I incline tenderly toward you, with anguish in my heart;
verses.h2: I turn away from you, yet the face of my love turns toward you.

verses.h1: I stand proud, then abase myself with a lover’s abasement;
verses.h2: for love holds both pride and humility.

verses.h1: Whenever I think of union with another, I am held back
verses.h2: by yearning for you, and an earlier advocate pleading for you.

notes.note: The referent of “an earlier advocate” (شافع لك أول) is unspecified; it may mean the speaker’s prior love for her, which argues against a new attachment.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أمحلتي سلمى بكاظمة اسلما
verses.h2: وتعلما أن الهوى ما هجتما

verses.h1: هل ترويان من الأحبة حائما
verses.h2: أو تسعدان على الصبابة مغرما

verses.h1: أبكيكما دمعا، ولو أني على
verses.h2: قدر الهوى أبكى بكيتكما دما

verses.h1: طللا أكفكف فيه دمعا معربا
verses.h2: بجوى، وأقرأ فيه خطا أعجما

verses.h1: تأبى رباه أن تجيب، ولم يكن
verses.h2: مستخبر ليجيب حتى تفهما

verses.h1: O two abodes of Salmā at Kāẓima, may you remain unharmed;
verses.h2: and know that love is what you have stirred.

verses.h1: Can you slake the thirst of one seeking his loved ones,
verses.h2: or help a love-stricken man bear his longing?

verses.h1: I weep tears for you both; were I to weep
verses.h2: in proportion to my love, I would weep blood for you.

verses.h1: A ruin where I hold back tears eloquent
verses.h2: with burning grief, and read a script that cannot speak.

verses.h1: Its hillocks refuse to answer; yet no one questioned
verses.h2: could answer before he understood.

notes.note: طللا appears to be the accusative singular ṭalalan, “a ruin,” but its grammatical connection to the preceding address to two abodes is unclear.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان
poems.intro: وقال أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

poet.from_text: أبو [العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان

verses.h1: محل بأرض الشام يطرد أهله
verses.h2: ولكنهم عما يقول نيام

verses.h1: وقد تنطق الأشياء وهي صوامت
verses.h2: وما كل نطق المخبرين كلام

verses.h1: An abode in the land of al-Shām drives out its people,
verses.h2: yet they are asleep to what it says.

verses.h1: Things may speak even while silent,
verses.h2: and not every message conveyed takes the form of words.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū [Al-ʿAlāʾ Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: سقيت محلا، وأحيت ربا
verses.h2: ك، مدامع كل فتى تهمل

verses.h1: May you be watered, O dwelling, and your hills revived
verses.h2: by the streaming tears of every young man.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: يا محلا أبلته هوج الليالي
verses.h2: وغرامي بساكنيه قشيب

verses.h1: ما اطمأنت بك المحاسن حتى
verses.h2: شردتها عني وعنك الخطوب

verses.h1: ساء عهدي لقاطنيك متى آ
verses.h2: ويت دمعا في مقلة لا يصوب

verses.h1: لست فردا فيما دهته الليالي
verses.h2: كل شيء بكرهن سليب

verses.h1: O dwelling worn away by the raging nights,
verses.h2: my passion for your inhabitants is still fresh.

verses.h1: No sooner had beauties settled in you
verses.h2: than calamities drove them away from you and me.

verses.h1: I would be false to your inhabitants if ever
verses.h2: I harbored in my eye a tear that did not fall.

verses.h1: You are not alone among what the nights have ravaged:
verses.h2: everything is stripped bare by their repeated assaults.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: محل من القاطول أخلق عامره
verses.h2: وعادت صروف الدهر جيشا يغاوره

verses.h1: كأن الصبا توفى نذورا إذا سرت
verses.h2: تراوحه أذياله وتباكره

verses.h1: ورب زمان ناعم ثم عهده
verses.h2: ترق حواشيه ويورق ناضره

verses.h1: تغير حسن الجعفري وأنسه
verses.h2: وقوض بادي الجعفري وحاضره

verses.h1: تحمل عنه ساكنوه فجاءة
verses.h2: فعادت سواء دوره ومقابره

verses.h1: إذا نحن زرناه أجد لنا الأسى
verses.h2: وقد كان قبل اليوم يبهج زائره

verses.h1: ولم أنس وحش القصر إذ ريع سربه
verses.h2: وإذ ذعرت أطلاؤه وجآذره

verses.h1: وإذ صيح فيه بالرحيل فهتكت
verses.h2: على عجل استاره وستائره

verses.h1: ووحشته حتى كأن لم يكن به
verses.h2: أنيس، ولم تحسن لعين مناظره

verses.h1: A dwelling at al-Qāṭūl, whose once-inhabited quarters have decayed,
verses.h2: and time’s vicissitudes have become an army raiding it.

verses.h1: As though the east wind fulfills vows when it journeys by night,
verses.h2: its trailing skirts visit the place at evening and at dawn.

verses.h1: Many a season there was gentle in its course,
verses.h2: its edges soft, its verdure bursting into leaf.

verses.h1: Al-Jaʿfarī’s beauty and convivial life have changed;
verses.h2: its desert folk and townspeople have struck camp.

verses.h1: Its inhabitants departed suddenly,
verses.h2: and its houses and graves became alike.

verses.h1: Whenever we visit it, it renews our grief,
verses.h2: though before this day it used to delight its visitor.

verses.h1: I have not forgotten the palace’s wild creatures when their herd was startled,
verses.h2: when its fawns and wild-cow calves were terrified.

verses.h1: And when the call to depart rang out within it, and they tore away
verses.h2: in haste its curtains and hangings.

verses.h1: And its desolation—as though it had never held
verses.h2: a friendly soul, nor its vistas ever pleased the eye.

notes.note: The masculine pronoun in أذياله (‘its trailing skirts’) is unexpected with الصبا (‘the east wind’), normally feminine. The translation takes the skirts to belong to the wind.
The palace’s ‘wild creatures,’ ‘fawns,’ and ‘wild-cow calves’ apparently stand metaphorically for its women or young inhabitants; the precise referents are not explicit.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: قفوا جددوا من عهدكم بالمعاهد
verses.h2: وإن هي لم تسمع لنشدان ناشد

verses.h1: لقد أطرق الربع المحيل لفقدهم
verses.h2: وبينهم إطراق ثكلان فاقد

verses.h1: سقته ذعافا عادة الدهر فيهم
verses.h2: وسم الليالي فوق سم الأساود

verses.h1: به غلة للبين صماء لم تصخ
verses.h2: لبرء، ولم توجب عيادة عائد

verses.h1: Stop, and renew your acquaintance with the familiar haunts,
verses.h2: though they do not heed a seeker’s inquiry.

verses.h1: The desolate dwelling has bowed its head at their loss
verses.h2: and their departure, like one bereaved, mourning the dead.

verses.h1: Time’s way with them has given it deadly poison to drink;
verses.h2: the venom of nights surpasses the venom of black serpents.

verses.h1: Within it burns an anguish of parting, deaf and unresponsive
verses.h2: to healing, yet calling forth no visitor to tend it.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: سقيت معاهدك اللواتي شقنني
verses.h2: ومحل منزلك الذي أبكاني

verses.h1: إما أقمت فإن لبى ظاعن
verses.h2: أو سرت منطلقا فقلبي عان

verses.h1: May rain water your old haunts, which made me yearn,
verses.h2: and the site of your dwelling, which made me weep.

verses.h1: If I stay, my mind is journeying;
verses.h2: or if I travel freely, my heart is captive.

notes.note: The unvocalized أقمت and سرت could refer either to the speaker (‘I stay/travel’) or to the addressee (‘you stay/travel’); I have taken both as referring to the speaker.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أمعاهد الأحباب هل عود إلى
verses.h2: مغدى يبل به الجوى ومراح

verses.h1: يكفيك من أنفاسنا ودموعنا
verses.h2: أن تمطري من بعدنا وتراحي

verses.h1: فسقى اللوى صوب الغمام ودره
verses.h2: وسقى النوازل فيه صوب الراح

verses.h1: فلرب عيش رق فيه نسيمه
verses.h2: كالماء رق على جنوب بطاح

verses.h1: O haunts of loved ones, is there a return to
verses.h2: a morning haunt where longing is cooled, and an evening resting-place?

verses.h1: Our sighs and tears suffice you
verses.h2: for rain and breezes after we are gone.

verses.h1: May the clouds’ pouring rain and copious flow water al-Liwā,
verses.h2: and may a downpour of wine refresh those dwelling there.

verses.h1: How often life there had a gentle breeze,
verses.h2: like water lying thin along the sides of broad valleys.

notes.note: The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names al-Sharīf al-Raḍī, while the introduction names al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā.
I take the uncommon form «تراحي» to mean being swept by breezes, pairing the lovers’ breaths with wind and their tears with rain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أنا لائمي إن كنت وقت اللوائم
verses.h2: علمت بما بي بين تلك المعالم

verses.h1: ولكنني مما ذهلت متيم
verses.h2: كسال، وقلبي بائح مثل كاتم

verses.h1: وقفنا كأنا كل وجد قلوبنا
verses.h2: تمكن من أذوادنا في القوائم

verses.h1: ودسنا بأخفاف المطي ترابها
verses.h2: فلا زلت استشفى بلثم المناسم

verses.h1: Let me blame myself if, at the time of reproach,
verses.h2: I knew what ailed me among those landmarks.

verses.h1: But in my bewilderment I am a lovesick man
verses.h2: like one cured of love; my heart reveals its love as though concealing it.

verses.h1: We halted, as though all the longing in our hearts
verses.h2: had taken hold in our camels’ legs.

verses.h1: We trod their soil with our camels’ feet;
verses.h2: may I never cease seeking healing by kissing their footpads.

poems.intro: وقال الرئيس أبو علي أبزون العماني:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: تحل عقود الصبر مني المعالم
verses.h2: وتبدي دموع العين ما أنا كاتم

verses.h1: وتطمس آثار العزاء إذا بدت
verses.h2: رسوم ديار الحي وهي طواسم

verses.h1: خلت من طباء الإنس ثم تبدلت
verses.h2: ظباء، وقلبي بالمبدل هائم

verses.h1: يديروني عن سالم وأديره
verses.h2: وجلدة بين العين والأنف سالم

verses.h1: The landmarks undo the knots of my endurance,
verses.h2: and my eyes’ tears reveal what I conceal.

verses.h1: And they blot out all trace of solace when they appear—
verses.h2: the remnants of the tribe’s dwellings, themselves effaced.

verses.h1: They were emptied of human gazelles, then took in their place
verses.h2: gazelles, while my heart remains lovesick for those replaced.

verses.h1: They try to turn me away from Sālim, and I turn them back;
verses.h2: yet Sālim is the skin between my eye and nose.

notes.note: طباء appears to be a misprint for ظباء, ‘gazelles,’ here used of beautiful people. المبدل is understood as those replaced, rather than their replacements.

The first hemistich appears textually defective. The translation tentatively reads يديرونني for يديروني and وأديرهم (‘and I turn them’) for وأديره (‘and I turn him’). Sālim’s identity and the precise allusion are uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: The chief Abū ʿAlī Abzūn al-ʿUmānī said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أهاجتك المعالم والطلول
verses.h2: عفون وخف منهن الحلول

verses.h1: نعم وذكرت دنيا قد تولت
verses.h2: وأي نعيم دنيا لا يزول؟

verses.h1: أسائل دار بثنة أين حلت
verses.h2: كأن الدار تفهم ما أقول!

verses.h1: Have the landmarks and ruins stirred your longing,
verses.h2: now faded, their dwellers gone?

verses.h1: Yes, and I remembered a life now past—
verses.h2: and what earthly bliss does not pass away?

verses.h1: I ask Buthna’s dwelling where she has settled,
verses.h2: as though the dwelling understood what I say!

prose_translation.intro: (Incorporating borrowed verse): And Jamīl ibn Maʿmar al-ʿUdhrī said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: ألا تلكما أعلام بثنة قد بدت
verses.h2: كأن ذراها عممت بسبيب

verses.h1: طوامس فيمادونهن عداوة
verses.h2: لنا، ووراء الطامسات حبيب

verses.h1: بعيد على من ليس يطلب حاجة
verses.h2: وأما على ذي حاجة قفريب

verses.h1: Look, you two: Buthna’s landmarks have come into view,
verses.h2: as though their summits were turbaned with horsehair.

verses.h1: Fading landmarks; on this side of them lies enmity
verses.h2: toward us, and beyond those fading landmarks is a beloved.

verses.h1: Far away for one who seeks nothing,
verses.h2: but near for one who has something to seek.

notes.note: Sabīb (سبيب), rendered as “horsehair,” can also mean a strip of cloth. The precise image intended by the turbaned summits is uncertain.
قفريب appears to be a typographical or OCR error for فقريب, “then/but near,” which is followed here.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: خليلي لا والله ما أملك البكا
verses.h2: إذا علم من أرض ليلى بداليا

verses.h1: خليلي إلا تبكيا لي أستعن
verses.h2: خليلا إذا أذريت دمعا بكى ليا

verses.h1: كأن لم يكن بين إذا كان بعده
verses.h2: تلاق، ولكن لا إخال تلاقيا

verses.h1: My two friends, no, by God, I cannot hold back my tears
verses.h2: when a landmark in Laylā’s land appears before me.

verses.h1: My two friends, if you will not weep for me, I shall seek help from
verses.h2: a friend who, when I shed tears, weeps for me.

verses.h1: Parting is as though it never was, if after it comes
verses.h2: reunion—but I expect no reunion.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: أفي كل يوم أنت من غبر الهوى
verses.h2: إلى الشم من أعلام ميلاء ناظر؟

verses.h1: بعمشاء من طول البكاء كأنما
verses.h2: بها خزر، أو طرفها متخازر

verses.h1: تمنى المنى، حتى إذا نالت المنى
verses.h2: بدا واكف من دمعها متبادر

verses.h1: كما أرفض هلكي
verses.h2: بعد ما ضم ضمة بحبل الفتيل اللؤلؤ المتناثر

verses.h1: Is it every day, from lingering love,
verses.h2: that you gaze toward the lofty peaks of Maylāʾ?

verses.h1: With an eye bleared by long weeping, as though
verses.h2: it had a squint, or were feigning one.

verses.h1: It wishes and wishes; then, when its wishes are granted,
verses.h2: a stream of its tears comes rushing forth.

verses.h1: As [unclear] scattered,
verses.h2: after a twisted cord had clasped them tightly—the strewn pearls.

notes.note: Maylāʾ appears to be a place name, but I could not identify its location or confirm its vocalization.

هلكي is unintelligible in this context and appears corrupt. The hemistich division also seems misplaced. The translation is provisional: the recognizable wording apparently compares the tears to pearls scattering after a twisted cord had held them together.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد
poems.intro: وقال أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

poet.from_text: أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد

verses.h1: ألا إنها الأعلام من هضباتها
verses.h2: فكيف تكف العين عن عبراتها

verses.h1: ذراني وإذراء الدموع لعلها
verses.h2: تسكن ما قد هاج من ذكراتها

verses.h1: 'هدت بها أصنام حسن عهدتني
verses.h2: هوى عبد عزاها، وعبد مناتها

verses.h1: أهل بأشواقي إليها وأتقي
verses.h2: شرائعها في الحب حق تقاتها

verses.h1: Ah, those are the landmarks among her hills;
verses.h2: how can the eye hold back its tears?

verses.h1: Leave me, you two, to shed tears; perhaps they
verses.h2: will calm what memories of her have stirred.

verses.h1: There I knew idols of beauty that knew me
verses.h2: in my passion, as a worshipper of their ʿUzzā and their Manāt.

verses.h1: I cry aloud my longings for her, and revere
verses.h2: her laws in love with the reverence they are due.

notes.note: The opening «'هدت» appears corrupted; I provisionally read عهدت, “I knew.” The grammatical role of هوى in the second hemistich is uncertain; “in my passion” is tentative.

The feminine pronouns are not explicitly anchored: they may refer to the beloved, her dwelling, or, in the later lines, the “idols of beauty.” The translation uses “her” except where “their” refers directly to those idols.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān, known as Ibn al-Ḥaddād, said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: ما للمعالم والطلول، أما كفى
verses.h2: بالعاشقين معالما وطلولا؟

verses.h1: فكأننا شمل الدموع تفرقا
verses.h2: وكأننا سر الوداع نحولا

verses.h1: سأروع من ضمنت حجالكم ولو
verses.h2: غدت الأسنة دون ذلك غيلا

verses.h1: أعصى رماح الخط دونك شرعا
verses.h2: وأطيع فيك صبابة وغليلا

verses.h1: Why these landmarks and ruins? Is it not enough
verses.h2: to have lovers as landmarks and ruins?

verses.h1: We are like a gathering of tears in our dispersal,
verses.h2: like the secret of farewell in our wasting away.

verses.h1: I shall startle whoever your curtained chambers hold, even if
verses.h2: the spearheads become a thicket barring the way.

verses.h1: I defy the spears of al-Khaṭṭ leveled to keep me from you,
verses.h2: and obey, for your sake, yearning and burning desire.

notes.note: سر الوداع literally means ‘the secret of farewell.’ The precise image linking this to نحولا (‘wasting away’ or ‘emaciation’) is unclear.

prose_translation.intro: And Muḥammad ibn Hāniʾ al-Maghribī said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: سقى العلم الفرد الذي في ظلاله
verses.h2: غزالان مكحولان مؤتلفان

verses.h1: أرغتهما صيدا فلم أستطعهما
verses.h2: ورميا ففاتاني وقد قتلاني

verses.h1: May the solitary hill be watered, in whose shade
verses.h2: two kohl-eyed gazelles keep each other company.

verses.h1: I sought to catch them as prey, but could not;
verses.h2: and to shoot them, but they eluded me, though they had slain me.

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: لا مزار منكم يدني سوى
verses.h2: أن أرى أعلام هضب ونجاد

verses.h1: قد عقلنا العيس في أوطانها
verses.h2: وهي ما بين ذميل ووخاد

verses.h1: أسلوا عنكم أهجركم
verses.h2: قلما يسلو عن الماء الصوادي

verses.h1: فعلى الأيام من بعدكم
verses.h2: ما على الظلماء من ثوب الحداد

verses.h1: No place to visit brings me near you, save
verses.h2: the sight of landmarks on rocky hills and uplands.

verses.h1: We have hobbled the pale camels in their home grounds,
verses.h2: yet they move between a gentle trot and a long-striding pace.

verses.h1: Shall I forget you? Shall I forsake you?
verses.h2: Rarely do the thirsty forget water.

verses.h1: So the days since your departure wear
verses.h2: the same robe of mourning as the dark night.

notes.note: The camels are described as hobbled, yet also as moving at two different gaits. The intended relation between these descriptions is unclear; ‘yet’ makes the apparent contrast explicit.
أسلوا appears to be an irregular spelling or transcription of أسلو, ‘I forget’ or ‘I cease to long.’ It is translated here as a rhetorical question, parallel to أهجركم, ‘Shall I forsake you?’

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: ما هاج شوقك من معارف عرصة
verses.h2: البرق بين أصالف وفدافد

verses.h1: ولقد رددت بها السؤال صبابة
verses.h2: والدار قبلي ما تبين لناشد

verses.h1: ولقد نظرت فما رأيت لناظر
verses.h2: غير الصفيح وغير أس بائد

verses.h1: What stirred your longing among the familiar traces of the campsite
verses.h2: of al-Barq, amid stony ground and barren uplands?

verses.h1: There I asked my questions again and again, out of longing,
verses.h2: though before me the dwelling had answered no inquirer.

verses.h1: I looked, but saw nothing for an eye to see
verses.h2: save flat stones and a ruined foundation.

notes.note: I take البرق as a place name, provisionally vocalized al-Barq; its identification and vocalization are uncertain. أصالف and فدافد are taken as terrain terms, ‘stony ground’ and ‘barren uplands,’ rather than place names.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:
poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: عرصات أصبحن وهي سماء
verses.h2: ثم أمسين بالحوادث أرضا

verses.h1: وثرى ينبت النعيم إذا أن
verses.h2: بت ترب البلاد عشبا وحمضا

verses.h1: Courtyards that at dawn were heaven,
verses.h2: then by evening, through calamities, were earth.

verses.h1: And soil that brings forth bliss, while
verses.h2: the soil of other lands brings forth grass and saltwort.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: عرصات كأنهن ليال
verses.h2: فارقتها عند الكمال البدور

verses.h1: تخبر الغافلين كيف يحول الده
verses.h2: ر عن حاله وكيف يجور

verses.h1: Deserted courtyards, like nights
verses.h2: forsaken by their moons at the height of fullness.

verses.h1: They tell the heedless how Time turns
verses.h2: from its former state, and how it deals unjustly.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Muḥammad ibn Sinān said:

poems.chapter: 9- فصل في ذكر المساكن و المحال و المعاهد والأعلام والمعالم والعرصات

verses.h1: ألستم عائجين لنا لعنا
verses.h2: نرى العرصات أو اثر الخيام؟

verses.h1: فقالوا: إن عرضت فأغن عنا
verses.h2: دموعا غير راقئة السجام

verses.h1: Will you not turn aside for us, that we may
verses.h2: see the deserted grounds or the traces of the tents?

verses.h1: They said, “If you turn aside, then weep enough for us—
verses.h2: tears whose streaming never ceases.”

notes.note: لعنا is understood as a dialectal form of لعلنا, ‘that perhaps we may.’

عرضت is uncertain in this context; it may be a misprint for عرجت, ‘you turn aside,’ which is the sense adopted here. فأغن عنا is understood as asking the speaker to do enough weeping on the others’ behalf.

verses.h1: وعاذلة تغدو علي تلومني
verses.h2: على الشوق لم تمح الصبابة من قلبي

verses.h1: فما لي إن أحببت أرض عشيرتي
verses.h2: وأبغضت طرفاء القصيبة من ذنب

verses.h1: ولو أن ريحا بلغت وحي مرسل
verses.h2: حفي لناجيت الجنوب على النقب

verses.h1: وقلت لها: أدى إليهم رسالتي
verses.h2: ولا تخلطيها طال سعدك بالترب

verses.h1: A woman comes each morning to reproach me
verses.h2: for my longing; she has not erased yearning from my heart.

verses.h1: What fault is mine if I love my people’s land
verses.h2: and hate the tamarisks of al-Quṣayba?

verses.h1: If a wind could convey the words of a sender
verses.h2: full of affection, I would confide in the south wind at al-Naqb.

verses.h1: And I would say to her: “Carry my message to them,
verses.h2: and do not mingle it—may your good fortune endure—with dust.”

notes.note: The place القصيبة, provisionally vocalized al-Quṣayba, has not been securely identified.
I read مرسل حفي as ‘a sender full of affection’; the unvocalized مرسل could alternatively mean ‘messenger.’
النقب is treated here as the place name al-Naqb, but it could instead mean ‘the mountain pass.’

verses.h1: ومغترب بالمرج يبكي لشجوه
verses.h2: وقد بان عنه المسعدون على الحب

verses.h1: إذا ما أتاه الركب من نحو أرضه
verses.h2: تنفس يستشفى برائحة القرب

verses.h1: An exile at al-Marj weeps in his grief,
verses.h2: for those who comforted him in love have departed.

verses.h1: Whenever a caravan comes to him from the direction of his homeland,
verses.h2: he draws breath, seeking healing in the scent of nearness.

notes.note: Al-Marj literally means “the meadow.” It appears to be a place name here, but the specific location is uncertain.

verses.h1: ما أحببت أرضكم ولكن
verses.h2: أقبل أثر من وطئ الترابا

verses.h1: لقد لافيت من كلفي بلبني
verses.h2: بلاء لا أسيغ له شرابا

verses.h1: إذا نادى المنادي باسم لبنى
verses.h2: عييت، فما أرد له جوابا

verses.h1: It is not your land that I have loved, but
verses.h2: I kiss the footprints of the one who trod its dust.

verses.h1: Through my passion for Lubnā, I have indeed encountered
verses.h2: an affliction that leaves me unable to swallow any drink.

verses.h1: When a caller calls out Lubnā’s name,
verses.h2: I am struck speechless and give him no reply.

notes.note: لافيت appears to be a misprint for لاقيت (“encountered”). بلبني is read as بلبنى, referring to Lubnā.

verses.h1: سقى الله أرضا لو ظفرت بتربها
verses.h2: كحلت بها من شدة الشوق أجفاني

verses.h1: فهل بعد هذا للمحبين غاية
verses.h2: وهل أحد أشجانه مثل أشجاني؟

verses.h1: May God water a land whose dust, if I could obtain it,
verses.h2: I would apply as kohl to my eyelids, so intense is my longing.

verses.h1: Is there any further limit for lovers beyond this?
verses.h2: And does anyone have sorrows like mine?

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: ألا يا نسيم الريح من أرض بابل
verses.h2: تحمل إلى أهل الخيام سلامي

verses.h1: وقل لحبيب فيك بعض نسيمه:
verses.h2: أما آن أن تسطيع رجع كلامي؟

verses.h1: وإني لأهوى أن أكون بأرضكم
verses.h2: على أنني منها استفدت سقامي

verses.h1: O breeze from the land of Bābil,
verses.h2: carry my greetings to the people of the tents.

verses.h1: And say to a beloved whose breath you partly bear:
verses.h2: “Is it not time you could answer my words?”

verses.h1: Indeed, I long to be in your land,
verses.h2: though it was there that I acquired my sickness.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: أرى كل أرض دمنتها وإن مضت
verses.h2: لها حجج يزداد طيبا ترابها

verses.h1: ألم تعلمن يا رب، أن رب دعوة
verses.h2: دعوتك فيها مخلصا لو أجابها

verses.h1: فأقسم لو أني أرى نسبا لها
verses.h2: ذئاب الفلا حبت إلى ذئابها

verses.h1: لعمر أبي ليلى لئن هي أصبحت
verses.h2: بوادي القرى ما ضر غيري اغترابها

verses.h1: I see that every land she has dwelt in—even as
verses.h2: years pass over it—has ever more fragrant soil.

verses.h1: Do You not know, O Lord, how many a prayer
verses.h2: I have offered You sincerely—if only He had answered it!

verses.h1: I swear, if I could regard as kin to her
verses.h2: the wolves of the wild, those wolves would be dear to me.

verses.h1: By the life of Laylā’s father, if she now dwells
verses.h2: in Wādī al-Qurā, her absence has harmed no one but me.

notes.note: The unvowelled دمنتها permits several readings, including ‘I dwelt in it,’ ‘you dwelt in it,’ and ‘she dwelt in it.’ I have chosen the last in light of the subsequent references to the beloved.

The wording is uncertain: لو أجابها literally means ‘if he had answered it,’ shifting from addressing God to the third person and supplying no explicit consequence. I have provisionally read it as a wish, ‘if only He had answered it’; the text may be defective.

I read حبت إلى as حَبَّت إليَّ, ‘would be dear to me’; the printed إلى (‘to’) appears erroneous. The construction نسباً لها ذئاب الفلا is unusual; I understand it to mean regarding the wolves as kin to the beloved.

verses.h1: قد كنت أقصرت عن نجد فهيجني
verses.h2: على تذكرها الخفان والحضن

verses.h1: لما وردت بلادا لست أعرفها
verses.h2: وشاقني ذكر أخرى هاج لي حزن

verses.h1: فقلت: قد حان من أرض ولدت بها
verses.h2: أوب، وقد حان من صرف النوى قرن

verses.h1: عل النوى بك يوما أن تريع، فقد
verses.h2: تدنو الغريبة حتى يدنو الوطن

verses.h1: I had ceased to yearn for Najd, but I was stirred
verses.h2: to remember it by al-Khaffān and al-Ḥuḍan.

verses.h1: When I came to a land I did not know,
verses.h2: and the memory of another stirred my longing, sorrow rose within me.

verses.h1: I said: “It is time, from the land where I was born,
verses.h2: to return; and time for separation’s vicissitudes to yield reunion.

verses.h1: Perhaps your wanderings will one day bring you back; for
verses.h2: a foreign land draws near, until home draws near.”

notes.note: The vocalization and identification of الخفان, rendered al-Khaffān, are uncertain.

The text says من أرض ولدت بها, “from the land where I was born,” although the context seems to require a return to that land. The wording may be corrupt. The second hemistich is also difficult: قرن is provisionally understood as “joining, reunion,” and صرف النوى as the vicissitudes of separation.
The referent of الغريبة is not explicit; “a foreign land” assumes an omitted أرض. The precise sense of its drawing near before the homeland does remains uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Qaʿnab ibn Umm Ṣāḥib said:

poems.intro: وقال أبو نصر بن النحاس الحلبي:

verses.h1: سقى الله أرضا لبسنا الشبا
verses.h2: بأرجائها وخلعنا الوقارا

verses.h1: ديارا شكت فرقة الظاعن
verses.h2: ين بألوانها فتحلت بهارا

verses.h1: زمان صحبناه مستعذبا
verses.h2: فبان، ولم يبق إلا ادكارا

verses.h1: May God water a land where we clothed ourselves in youth
verses.h2: throughout its reaches, and cast off solemnity.

verses.h1: Dwellings that lamented the parting of those who journeyed away
verses.h2: through their colors, and adorned themselves with yellow flowers.

verses.h1: A time whose company we found sweet—
verses.h2: it passed, leaving nothing but remembrance.

notes.note: The word الشباب appears to be divided across the hemistichs, but a ب is apparently missing at the join. The translation assumes الشباب بأرجائها, “youth throughout its reaches.”
بهار denotes a flowering plant, often identified as a yellow oxeye or a kind of narcissus; the precise botanical identification is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Naṣr ibn al-Naḥḥās al-Ḥalabī said:

verses.h1: تعوضت من دودان حملا وأرضها
verses.h2: فما طاب لي شربي ولا راق مشربي

verses.h1: فإن تلتبس حلى بدودان لا أرم
verses.h2: لئن كنت ذا ذنب، وإن غير مذنب

verses.h1: ألا إن قوم المرء خير تفية
verses.h2: من الأبعد الأقصى، وإن لم تقرب

verses.h1: I exchanged Dūdān for Ḥamal and its land,
verses.h2: but neither my drink nor my drinking place pleased me.

verses.h1: If my fortunes were bound to Dūdān, I would not be assailed,
verses.h2: whether I were guilty or innocent.

verses.h1: Surely a man’s own people are better protection
verses.h2: than the farthest stranger, even if they are not near.

notes.note: The identities of دودان and حمل are uncertain; Dūdān and Ḥamal are provisional vocalizations. Dūdān may designate a tribe rather than a place.

حلى is unclear and may be corrupt. ‘My fortunes’ provisionally assumes حالي (‘my condition’). لا أرم is read as لا أُرْمَ (‘I would not be assailed’); another possible reading is لا أَرِمْ (‘I would not depart’). The construction لئن كنت ... وإن غير مذنب is also awkward as transmitted; the translation takes it to mean ‘whether guilty or innocent.’

تفية is unclear, probably a misprint for تقية (‘protection’), adopted in the translation. The subject and vocalization of تقرب are uncertain: ‘even if they are not near’ is provisional; ‘even if you are not welcomed’ is another possible interpretation.

poems.poet_from_text: مروان بن أبي حفصة من قصيدة في معن بن زائدة الشيباني
poems.intro: وقال مروان بن أبي حفصة من قصيدة في معن بن زائدة الشيباني:

poet.from_text: مروان بن أبي حفصة من قصيدة في معن بن زائدة الشيباني

verses.h1: إني إلى كل أرض أنت ساكنها
verses.h2: صب، وإن كنت عنها نازح الوطن

verses.h1: قلدتني منك حبلا فاعتصمت به
verses.h2: أسبابه غير رثات ولا وهن

verses.h1: تضيق أعطان قوم إن هم سئلوا
verses.h2: وأنت بالخير سهل واسع العطن

verses.h1: لو لم تكن للندى جارا فتطلقه
verses.h2: ما انفك والبخل مجموعين في قرن

verses.h1: For every land in which you dwell
verses.h2: I yearn, though my home lies far from it.

verses.h1: You placed a cord from you about my neck, and I held fast to it;
verses.h2: its strands are neither frayed nor weak.

verses.h1: Others’ quarters grow cramped when they are asked for gifts,
verses.h2: but you give freely, and your quarters are spacious.

verses.h1: Had you not been generosity’s protector, setting it free,
verses.h2: it would have remained bound to avarice by a single rope.

prose_translation.intro: Marwān ibn Abī Ḥafṣa said, in a poem in praise of Maʿn ibn Zāʾida al-Shaybānī:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو الفتيان محمد بن سلطان بن حيوس الغنوي
poems.intro: وقال أبو الفتيان محمد بن سلطان بن حيوس الغنوي، من قصيدة يرثى بها محمود بن نصر بن صالح، ويعزى ولده نصر بن محمود، ويمدحه:

poet.from_text: أبو الفتيان محمد بن سلطان بن حيوس الغنوي

verses.h1: فلله ملك زين الأرض ملكه
verses.h2: وجاد الحيا ملكا تضمنه القبر

verses.h1: وكنا نظن الأرض تظلم بعده
verses.h2: فقمت مقام البدر إذ أفل البدر

verses.h1: وكاد شعار الخوف ينبث في الورى
verses.h2: فنادى شعار الأمن يا نصر يا نصر

verses.h1: What a king, whose rule adorned the earth!
verses.h2: May rain water the king whom the grave encloses.

verses.h1: We thought the earth would grow dark after him,
verses.h2: but you took the full moon’s place when the full moon set.

verses.h1: The watchword of fear almost spread among mankind,
verses.h2: but the watchword of safety called out: “O Naṣr, O Naṣr!”

prose_translation.intro: Abū al-Fityān Muḥammad ibn Sulṭān ibn Ḥayyūs al-Ghanawī said, in a poem mourning Maḥmūd ibn Naṣr ibn Ṣāliḥ, consoling his son Naṣr ibn Maḥmūd, and praising him:

verses.h1: سقى الله أرضا يعلم الضب أنها
verses.h2: بعيد من الأدواء طيبة البقل

verses.h1: بنى بيته في رأس نشز وكدية
verses.h2: وكل امرئ في حرفة العيش ذو عقل

verses.h1: May God water a land that the spiny-tailed lizard knows
verses.h2: is far from disease and wholesome in its herbage.

verses.h1: It built its home atop a rise and a rocky knoll;
verses.h2: every man has sense in the craft of making a living.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان
poems.intro: قال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان

verses.h1: تحمل عن الأرض المريضة غاديا
verses.h2: ولا ترض للداء العياء سوى الحسم

verses.h1: وما فتئت روح الفتى في نوائب
verses.h2: تمارسها حتى استقلت عن الجسم

verses.h1: إذا ما تفرقنا خلصنا من الأذى
verses.h2: ولم يحتج الراعي المسيم إلى الوشم

verses.h1: Depart in the morning from the ailing land,
verses.h2: and accept no treatment for an intractable disease but excision.

verses.h1: A man’s spirit is ever beset by calamities,
verses.h2: grappling with them until it breaks free of the body.

verses.h1: When we part, we are rid of harm,
verses.h2: and the shepherd pasturing his flock has no need to mark them.

notes.note: الحسم can mean cutting off or decisive termination, and can also refer to cauterization. ‘Excision’ preserves the force of cutting away, though the precise treatment intended is uncertain.

الوشم ordinarily means tattooing. Here it apparently means marking livestock for identification, though الوسم would be the more usual word for branding animals. The precise connection between this pastoral image and ‘when we part’ is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān said:

verses.h1: وفي الأرض منأى للكريم عن الأذى
verses.h2: وفيها لمن رام القلى متحول

verses.h1: لعمرك ما بالأرض ضيق على امرئ
verses.h2: سرى راغبا أو راهبا وهو يعقل

verses.h1: أديم مطال الجرع حتى أمله
verses.h2: وأضرب عنه الذكر صفحا فأذهل

verses.h1: واستف ترب الأرض كيلا يرى له
verses.h2: على من الطول امرؤ متطول

verses.h1: ولولا اجتناب الذام لم يلف مشرب
verses.h2: يعاش به إلا لدى ومأكل

verses.h1: ولكن نفسا مرة لا تقيم بي
verses.h2: على الضيم إلا ريثما أتحول

verses.h1: On earth the noble have a refuge from harm,
verses.h2: and those who seek estrangement have somewhere else to go.

verses.h1: By your life, the earth is not too narrow for a man
verses.h2: who travels by night, in hope or fear, with his wits about him.

verses.h1: I keep putting hunger off until I weary it,
verses.h2: and turn my thoughts away from it until I forget.

verses.h1: I swallow the earth’s dust, lest he think he has
verses.h2: a claim of favor over me—some bestower of favors.

verses.h1: But for my avoidance of reproach, no drink would be found
verses.h2: to sustain life, nor food, except in my possession.

verses.h1: But an unyielding soul will not let me remain
verses.h2: under oppression longer than it takes me to depart.

notes.note: الجرع (‘swallowing’) appears to be a misprint for الجوع (‘hunger’), which is translated here. أمله is read as ‘I weary it’; without vocalization, it could also mean ‘I grow weary of it.’
على appears to be a misprint for عليّ (‘over me’), the reading used here.
لدى is understood as لديّ (‘in my possession’ or ‘with me’).

poems.intro: عن عبد الرحمن بن عبد الله بن عمر بن حفص بن عاصم بن عمر بن الخطاب - رضي الله عنه - أن رجلا من بني كلاب يكنى أبا حبال نزل على عبد الله بن عمر بن حفص، ومعه ابنه حبال، فمرض ابنه ثم مات، قال عبد الله: فأمر أبي بكفنه، فكفناه، فلما فرغنا منه استأذن أبوه أبي أن يدخل عليه، فيسلم عليه ويودعه، فأذن له، فدخل، فأكب عليه، فسمعناه يقول:

verses.h1: ولولا حبال لم تنخ بي مطيتي
verses.h2: بأرض بها الحمى بورد وصالب

verses.h1: وقائلة أرداك والله حبه
verses.h2: بنفسي حبال من خليل وصاحب

verses.h1: Were it not for Ḥibāl, my mount would never have knelt with me
verses.h2: in a land of fevers, recurring and fierce.

verses.h1: A woman said, “By God, your love for him has ruined you!”
verses.h2: My life for Ḥibāl—what a dear friend and companion!

notes.note: The name حبال is unvocalized; its rendering as Ḥibāl is uncertain.
ورد and صالب appear to designate types of fever. They are rendered as “recurring” and “fierce,” though the precise medical distinction is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: On the authority of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ ibn ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—may God be pleased with him—that a man of Banū Kilāb, known by the kunyah Abū Ḥibāl, stayed with ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ, accompanied by his son Ḥibāl. His son fell ill and then died. ʿAbd Allah said: “My father ordered that he be shrouded, so we shrouded him. When we had finished, his father asked my father’s permission to go in to him, greet him, and bid him farewell. He gave him permission, and he went in and bent over him. We heard him say:”

poems.intro: فجعل يكرر ذلك، ثم فقدنا صوته، فقال لنا أبي: أظنه والله قد مات، فدخلنا فوجدناه ميتا، فجهزناهما، وحملناهما فقبرناهما. وقال آخر - وتروى لحاتم -:

verses.h1: إن كنت تزعم أن الأض واسعة
verses.h2: فيها لغيرك مرتاد ومرتحل

verses.h1: فارحل فإن بلاد الله ما خلقت
verses.h2: إلا ليسكن منها السهل والجبل

verses.h1: وابغ المكاسب من أرض مطالبها
verses.h2: من حيث يجمل حتى ينفد الأجل

verses.h1: If you claim that the earth is spacious,
verses.h2: with places where others may seek their living and travel,

verses.h1: then depart, for God’s lands were created
verses.h2: only that their plains and mountains might be inhabited.

verses.h1: Seek your earnings in lands where they may be found,
verses.h2: where seeking them is honorable, until your allotted span runs out.

notes.note: الأض appears to be a misprint for الأرض, “the earth.”
The construction من أرض مطالبها / من حيث يجمل is compressed and somewhat unclear. I take it to mean seeking earnings where they are obtainable and where doing so is fitting or honorable.

prose_translation.intro: He kept repeating that; then we could no longer hear his voice. My father said to us, “By God, I think he has died.” We went in and found him dead, so we prepared the two of them for burial, carried them out, and buried them. Another poet said—the verses are also attributed to Ḥātim:

verses.h1: كيف المقام بأرض لا أشد بها
verses.h2: نضوى إذا ما اعترتني سورة الغضب؟

verses.h1: How can I stay in a land where I cannot saddle
verses.h2: my travel-worn mount when a surge of anger seizes me?

notes.note: أشدّ نضوي is taken here as saddling or making ready a travel-worn mount; the verb literally means to bind or fasten, so the precise action intended is uncertain.

verses.h1: وا سوأتا لامرئ شبيبته
verses.h2: في عنفوان، وماؤه خضل

verses.h1: وهو مقيم بأرض مضيعة
verses.h2: يمنعه من طلابه الكسل

verses.h1: إلى متى تخدم الرجال ولا
verses.h2: تخدم يوما، لأمك الهبل؟

verses.h1: Shame on a man whose youth
verses.h2: is in its prime, whose sap is still fresh,

verses.h1: yet he stays in a land where he goes to waste,
verses.h2: laziness keeping him from pursuing his aims.

verses.h1: How long will you serve other men, and never
verses.h2: be served a single day? May your mother be bereaved of you!

verses.h1: ما أشغل الحي في الدنيا بحاجته
verses.h2: والميت بالموت مشغول عن الحي

verses.h1: هون عليك فأرض الله واسعة
verses.h2: والشيء يغنيك في الدنيا عن الشيء

verses.h1: How engrossed the living are in their needs in this world,
verses.h2: while the dead are too occupied with death to heed the living.

verses.h1: Ease your mind, for God’s earth is vast,
verses.h2: and one thing in this world can suffice in place of another.

verses.h1: الأرض أوسع من دار ألظ بها
verses.h2: والناس أكثر من خل أجاذبه

verses.h1: أعاتب الخل فيما ساء واحدة
verses.h2: ثم السلام علين، لا أعاتبه

verses.h1: The earth is wider than one dwelling I cling to,
verses.h2: and people are more numerous than one friend I wrangle with.

verses.h1: I reproach a friend just once for what displeases me;
verses.h2: then farewell to him—I reproach him no more.

notes.note: علين appears to be a textual or OCR error for عليه, giving ثم السلام عليه, translated here as a farewell: “then farewell to him.”

verses.h1: إنني ما حللت بالأرض إلا
verses.h2: كنت في أهلها المجل المفدى

verses.h1: وإذا القوم لم يراحوا لقرى
verses.h2: كان لي عنهم مراح ومغدى

verses.h1: Never did I settle in a land
verses.h2: but I was honored and cherished among its people.

verses.h1: And if its people took no pleasure in hospitality,
verses.h2: I had somewhere else to go, at evening and at dawn.

verses.h1: فلا تسألن عن مضجعي ونبوه
verses.h2: بأرضي وعن نومي بها وامتناعه

verses.h1: أراني مشتاقا وأهلي حضر
verses.h2: على رأي عيني ناظر واستماعه

verses.h1: ومغترب المثوى وسرجي سارب
verses.h2: بأودية الساجور أو بتلاعه

verses.h1: لفرقة من خليت دنياي غضة
verses.h2: لديه، وعزى معصما في يفاعه

verses.h1: وما غلبتني نية الدار عنده
verses.h2: على رفده في ساحتي واصطناعه

verses.h1: Do not ask about my bed and its discomfort
verses.h2: in my homeland, or about my sleep there and its refusal to come.

verses.h1: I find myself yearning, though my people are present,
verses.h2: in a beholder’s plain sight and within his hearing.

verses.h1: And a stranger where I dwell, though my saddle roams
verses.h2: through the valleys of al-Sājūr or its ravines.

verses.h1: For I am parted from one—I left my life flourishing
verses.h2: beside him, and my honor finding refuge on his heights.

verses.h1: Nor did the remoteness of my dwelling deprive me, with him,
verses.h2: of his gifts reaching my courtyard and his favor.

notes.note: The syntax of على رأي عيني ناظر واستماعه is unusual. I take عيني ناظر as ‘a beholder’s two eyes’ and the phrase as indicating that the speaker’s people are within sight and hearing.

I read خليت as khallaytu, ‘I left,’ and معصما as muʿṣiman, ‘seeking or finding refuge.’ The wording is compressed, and the precise relationship between leaving the person and leaving one’s flourishing life with him is uncertain.

نية الدار is interpreted as the distance or separation of the dwelling. The construction with غلبتني ... على is compressed; I understand it to mean that distance did not prevent the patron’s gifts and favor from reaching the speaker.

verses.h1: في سعة الأرض وفي عرضها مستبدل بالخل والجار
فمن دنا منك فأهلا به
verses.h2: ومن تناءى فإلى النار

verses.h1: In the earth’s vastness and breadth, there are replacements for friend and neighbor.
Whoever draws near you, welcome him;
verses.h2: whoever keeps his distance—to the fire with him.

verses.h1: إذا المرء لم يحببك إلا تكرها
verses.h2: فدعه، ولا يعجزك عنه التحول

verses.h1: وفي الأرض أكفاء وفيها مراغم
verses.h2: عريض لمن خاف الهوان ومرحل

verses.h1: If a man loves you only reluctantly,
verses.h2: leave him; do not let turning away from him prove beyond you.

verses.h1: The earth holds others your equal, and a refuge
verses.h2: ample for whoever fears humiliation, and somewhere to move on to.

verses.h1: طلبت المستقر بكل أرض
verses.h2: فلم أر لي بأرض مستقرا

verses.h1: أطعت مطامعي فاستعبدتني
verses.h2: ولو أني قنعت لعشت حرا

verses.h1: I sought a settled home in every land,
verses.h2: but found no settled home for me in any land.

verses.h1: I obeyed my desires, and they enslaved me;
verses.h2: had I been content, I would have lived free.

verses.h1: فما ولدتني حاضن ربعية
verses.h2: لئن أنا مالأت الهوى لا تباعها

verses.h1: أم تر أن الأرض رحب فسيحة
verses.h2: فهل تعجزني بقعة من بقاعها؟

verses.h1: Then no chaste woman of Rabīʿa bore me
verses.h2: if I side with desire in following her.

verses.h1: Have you not seen that the earth is broad and spacious?
verses.h2: Can any one of its regions thwart me?

notes.note: The wording لا تباعها is unclear and may be misprinted. The translation tentatively reads it as لاتّباعها, ‘in following her’; the feminine pronoun’s referent is uncertain.
أم تر appears to be a misprint for ألم تر, ‘Have you not seen,’ which is the reading translated here.

prose_translation.intro: And Iyās ibn Qabīṣa al-Ṭāʾī said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان [المعري]
poems.intro: قال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان [المعري] :

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان [المعري]

verses.h1: أقول لصاحبي إذ هام وجدا
verses.h2: ببرق ليس يثبته نزوحا

verses.h1: متى نصبح وقد فتنا الرزايا
verses.h2: نقم حتى تقول الشمس روحا

verses.h1: بأرض للحمامة أن تغني
verses.h2: بها ولمن تأسف أن ينوحا

verses.h1: I say to my companion, as he wanders distraught with longing
verses.h2: for a distant flash of lightning he cannot clearly make out:

verses.h1: “When morning finds us having escaped calamities,
verses.h2: let us stay until the sun says, ‘Set out, you two,’

verses.h1: in a land where the dove is free to sing
verses.h2: and whoever grieves is free to lament.”

notes.note: The construction ليس يثبته نزوحا is uncertain. I take يثبته to mean ‘make out distinctly’ and نزوحا (‘far distant’) to describe the lightning.

prose_translation.intro: Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān [Al-Maʿarrī] said:

poems.poet: أحمد بن محمد ابن الفضل بن الخازن
poems.poet_from_text: أحمد بن محمد بن الفضل الخازن
poems.intro: وقال أحمد بن محمد بن الفضل الخازن:

poet.expected: أحمد بن محمد ابن الفضل بن الخازن
poet.from_text: أحمد بن محمد بن الفضل الخازن

verses.h1: سقيت لمعنى حل فيك أوده
verses.h2: ولولاه لم أسمح لتربك بالقطر

verses.h1: فإنك أرض ما وجدت بها رضى
verses.h2: وحرة سوء ما تضيع سوى الحر

verses.h1: قد اعتل فيها كل شيء سوى الصبا
verses.h2: ورق سوى الأخلاق والماء والخمر

verses.h1: May rain water you, for the sake of something dear to me that dwells in you;
verses.h2: were it not for that, I would not grant your soil any rain.

verses.h1: For you are a land where I have found no contentment,
verses.h2: a wretched tract that brings none but the freeborn to ruin.

verses.h1: Everything there has fallen ill except the east wind,
verses.h2: and grown soft—except manners, water, and wine.

notes.note: معنى, literally “meaning” or “something,” appears to be a veiled reference to a beloved person or presence dwelling in the land.
حرة can mean a stony lava tract (Ḥarra) or a freeborn woman (Ḥurra). The wording likely plays on these senses alongside الحر, “the freeborn man”; the translation follows the geographical sense.
رقّ can mean “grew thin,” “delicate,” or “soft.” Its precise force here is uncertain; the exceptions may suggest coarse manners, hard water, and harsh wine.

prose_translation.intro: And Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl al-Khāzin said:

verses.h1: ودع أخا العزم مصرا، لا لميس، وخفض
verses.h2: بالسابحات غمار المهمه البيد

verses.h1: وسر عن الأرض تنبو بالكرام فقد
verses.h2: طال انتظار الجنى من يابس العود

verses.h1: Bid farewell, man of resolve, to Miṣr—not Lamīs—and plunge
verses.h2: on swift steeds into the depths of the desert wastes.

verses.h1: Depart the land that spurns the noble, for
verses.h2: the wait for fruit from a withered bough has lasted too long.

notes.note: The printed وخفض appears corrupt. Translated as وخض, ‘and plunge,’ which fits the following غمار, ‘depths.’
لميس is understood as the woman’s name Lamīs; her identity or the specific allusion is unclear.

prose_translation.intro: And I said, while I was in Miṣr:

verses.h1: تطامن إذا أنكرت دهرك إنما
verses.h2: يفوز بخفض العيش من عاش في خفض

verses.h1: وكن كالذباب إن رأى الريح عاصفا
verses.h2: تلاصق من خوف الأذية بالأرض

verses.h1: Keep low when you find your times hostile; only
verses.h2: those who live humbly win a life of ease.

verses.h1: Be like the fly: when it sees the wind raging,
verses.h2: it hugs the ground for fear of harm.

verses.h1: إن ترمك الغربة في معشر
verses.h2: توافقوا فيك على بغضهم

verses.h1: فدارهم ما دمت في دارهم
verses.h2: وأرضهم ما دمت في أرضهم

verses.h1: If exile casts you among a people
verses.h2: united in their hatred of you,

verses.h1: humor them as long as you dwell in their home,
verses.h2: and please them as long as you remain in their land.

poems.intro: قال إبراهيم بن أدهم - رضي الله عنه: "ما قاسيت فيما تركت من الدنيا أشد علي من مفارقة الأوطان". قال الرياشي: أنشدني أعرابي:

verses.h1: سلم على قطن إن كنت تألفه
verses.h2: سلام من كان يهوى مرة قطنا

verses.h1: أحبه والذي أرسى قواعده
verses.h2: حبا إذا ظهرت آياته بطنا

verses.h1: يا ليته لا نريم الدهر ساحته
verses.h2: وليته حيث سرنا غربة معنا

verses.h1: ما من غريب وإن أبدى تجلده
verses.h2: إلا سيذكر بعد الغربة الوطنا

verses.h1: Greet Qaṭan, if you know it well,
verses.h2: with the greeting of one who once loved Qaṭan.

verses.h1: I love it—by Him who set its foundations firm—
verses.h2: with a love that lies hidden when its signs appear.

verses.h1: Would that we might never leave its grounds,
verses.h2: and would that it were with us wherever we journeyed far from home.

verses.h1: No stranger, however much he shows himself steadfast,
verses.h2: will fail to remember his homeland after living away.

notes.note: Qaṭan is probably the mountain of that name in Najd, though the identification is uncertain.
The wording «إذا ظهرت آياته بطنا» is puzzling: literally, the love becomes hidden when its signs appear. It may mean that its full depth remains concealed despite its outward signs.

prose_translation.intro: Ibrāhīm ibn Adham—may God be pleased with him—said: “Of all I endured in giving up the things of this world, nothing was harder for me than parting from my homeland.” al-Riyāshī said: A Bedouin recited to me:
interludes: [Qaṭan]: a mountain.

poems.poet: عبد الوهاب بن علي بن نصر
poems.poet_from_text: القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب بن علي بن نصر
poems.intro: وقال القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب بن علي بن نصر:

poet.expected: عبد الوهاب بن علي بن نصر
poet.from_text: القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب بن علي بن نصر

verses.h1: أهيم بذكر الشرق والغرب دائما
verses.h2: وما لي لا شرق البلاد ولا الغرب

verses.h1: ولكن أوطانا نأت وأحبة
verses.h2: فقدت، متى أذكر عهودهم أصب

verses.h1: وما أنس من ودعت بالشط سحرة
verses.h2: وقد غرد الحادون واستعجل الركب

verses.h1: أليفان: هذا سائر نحو غربة
verses.h2: وهذا مقيم سار عن جسمه القلب

verses.h1: I pine, forever recalling East and West,
verses.h2: yet neither the land’s east nor its west is mine.

verses.h1: Rather, I long for homelands far away, and loved ones
verses.h2: I have lost; whenever I recall our days together, I yearn.

verses.h1: I do not forget the one I bade farewell to by the riverbank at dawn,
verses.h2: when the camel-drivers sang out and the caravan hastened.

verses.h1: Two close companions: one setting out into exile,
verses.h2: the other remaining, his heart departed from his body.

notes.note: The unvocalized أصب is taken as a form of صبا, ‘to yearn’; a passive reading, ‘I am stricken,’ is also possible.

أنس appears where the negative construction would normally require أنسى, ‘I forget.’ The final letter may have been dropped in transcription; the translation follows the apparent sense, ‘I do not forget.’

prose_translation.intro: And the judge Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAlī ibn Naṣr said:

verses.h1: لا تنهرن غريبا طال غربته
verses.h2: فالدهر يضربه بالذل والمحن

verses.h1: حسب الغريب من الدنيا ندامته
verses.h2: عض الأنامل من شوق إلى الوطن

verses.h1: Do not rebuke a stranger whose exile has been long;
verses.h2: for fate strikes him with humiliation and trials.

verses.h1: The stranger’s regret in this world is burden enough—
verses.h2: biting his fingertips in longing for his homeland.

verses.h1: استودع الله في أرض الحجاز رشا
verses.h2: في روضة القلب مأواه ومرتعه

verses.h1: بالله يا شوق رفقا بالفؤاد فما
verses.h2: أطيق أكثر مما أنت تصنعه

verses.h1: وأنت يا وصل عج في ربع فرقتنا
verses.h2: عساك تجمع شملا عز مجمعه

verses.h1: وسقه من حيا التقريب سارية
verses.h2: فإنه دائر قد مح موضعه

verses.h1: عسى الليالي بأوطاني التي سلفت
verses.h2: ترجعن فيه رجوعا لا نودعه

verses.h1: I entrust to God a young gazelle in the land of al-Ḥijāz,
verses.h2: whose shelter and pasture lie in the garden of my heart.

verses.h1: By God, O Longing, be gentle with my heart, for
verses.h2: I cannot bear more than what you are doing to it.

verses.h1: And you, O Reunion, turn aside at the dwelling of our parting;
verses.h2: perhaps you can bring together those so hard to reunite.

verses.h1: Water it with a night cloud bearing the rain of nearness,
verses.h2: for it lies ruined, its very site effaced.

verses.h1: May the bygone nights in my homeland
verses.h2: return there, with no farewell to follow.

notes.note: The wording دائر قد مح موضعه is uncertain. I take it as describing an effaced or ruined dwelling, reading مح as مُحَّ, ‘was worn away or effaced.’

poems.intro: عن ابن الكلبي قال: كان رجل من طيء يقال له: زامل بن عفير، نازلا في أخواله من كلب في الدهر الأول، وذلك قبل حرب الفجار، فأغار عليهم منسر من بني القين، فاستخفوا إبله، فاستنصر أخواله، فأبطئوا عليه، فعمد إلى جمل سائب، فاكتفله وتوجه نحو الشام، فقيل له: أتركب الحرام؟ قال: "يركب الحرام من لا حلال له" فلما قرب من الشام مر بروضة غناء وغدران، فقيد بعيره، وأكل من نبات تلك الروضة، واضطجع، فبينا هو كذلك، إذ أقبل فارس إلى الروضة، فنزل عن فرسه، وحط سرجه، وقيد فرسه، وقعد قريبا من مضطجع الطائي فاستيقظ الطائي بحرسه، فاستوى قاعدا، فقال له الفارس: من الرجل؟ فانتسب له، وسأله عن شأنه، فقص عليه قصته، فقال له الفارس: يا هذا. هل عندك طعام فإني طاو منذ أمس؟ فقال له: أتطلب الطعام وهذا اللحم معرض؟ ثم وثب إلى سيفه، فعقر بعيره، ثم اجتب سنامه، وبقر عن كبده، وذلك بعين الفارس، ثم أوقد نارا عظيمة، ثم اشتوى، وأقبل يلقى إلى الفارس، حتى انتهى، فما لبث أن ثار العجاج، فإذا الخيل مقبلة، تتوقص بفرسانها، حتى انتهوا إلى الفارس فحيوه بتحية الملك، فركب، وقال: دونكم الرجل، فأردفه بعضهم حتى أتى دار ملكه، فإذا هو الحارث الأكبر الغساني، فأمر بعض غلمانه بإنزال الطائي، وخاف زامل أن يكون قد نسيه الملك، فقال للغلام: هل لك أن توليني عارفة، وتبلغ الملك ما أقول؟ قال: أفعل، فأنشده:

verses.h1: أبلغ الحارث المردد في المج
verses.h2: د وفي المكرمات جدا فجد

verses.h1: وابن أرباب واطئ السب
verses.h2: ب الأرحب والمالكين غورا ونجدا

verses.h1: إنني ناظر إليك ودوني
verses.h2: عائقات غادرن قربي بعدا

verses.h1: إن أكن نازلا بمثوى كريم
verses.h2: ناعم البال في مراح ومغدى

verses.h1: غير أن الأوطان يجتذب المر
verses.h2: ء إليها الهوى وإن عاش كدا

verses.h1: وتأنى بالشآم مفيدي
verses.h2: حسرات يقددن قلبي قدا

verses.h1: ليس يستعذب الغريب مقاما
verses.h2: في سوى أرضه وإن نال جدا

verses.h1: Tell al-Ḥārith, rooted in glory
verses.h2: and noble deeds, forefather after forefather,

verses.h1: and son of lords who trod
verses.h2: the broad way and ruled Ghawr and Najd:

verses.h1: I look toward you, but between us
verses.h2: stand obstacles that have turned my nearness into distance.

verses.h1: Though I lodge in a noble abode,
verses.h2: at ease in my evening and morning pursuits,

verses.h1: yet a man is drawn to his homeland
verses.h2: by longing, even if he lives there in hardship.

verses.h1: My lingering in al-Shām brings me
verses.h2: sorrows that tear my heart to shreds.

verses.h1: A stranger finds no dwelling pleasant
verses.h2: outside his own land, even if he finds good fortune.

notes.note: المردد appears to describe glory repeatedly inherited through the ancestry. جدا فجد is understood as ‘forefather after forefather’; the final word may be missing an alif.

واطئ is singular as printed, although the surrounding construction seems to require plural واطئي, ‘those who tread.’ السبب الأرحب is tentatively rendered ‘the broad way’; its precise reference is unclear.
وتأنى is unclear. The translation provisionally reads it as وتأنّي, ‘and my lingering,’ but it may be corrupted from وتنائي, ‘and my being far away.’

prose_translation.intro:
From Ibn al-Kalbī, who said: There was a man of Ṭayyiʾ called Zāmil ibn ʿUfair, who was staying among his maternal kinsmen of Kalb in former times, before the War of al-Fijār. A raiding party of Banū al-Qayn attacked them and drove off his camels. He appealed to his maternal kinsmen for help, but they were slow to respond. So he took a camel that had been set free as a sacred offering, mounted it bareback, and set out toward al-Shām. Someone said to him, “Will you ride what is forbidden?” He replied, “He who has nothing lawful rides what is forbidden.”

As he drew near al-Shām, he passed a luxuriant meadow with pools of water. He hobbled his camel, ate some of the plants in that meadow, and lay down. While he lay there, a horseman approached the meadow, dismounted, removed his saddle, hobbled his horse, and sat down near where the man of Ṭayyiʾ was lying. The sound of his movements woke the man of Ṭayyiʾ, who sat upright. The horseman asked him, “Who are you?” He gave his lineage, and the horseman asked about his circumstances. He told him his story, and the horseman said, “My good man, have you any food? I have eaten nothing since yesterday.” He replied, “Do you ask for food when this meat is here before us?” Then he sprang to his sword and slaughtered his camel, cut off its hump, and opened its belly to take out its liver, all before the horseman’s eyes. He then lit a great fire, roasted the meat, and kept passing pieces to the horseman until he had finished.

Before long, a cloud of dust rose, and there were horses approaching, jolting their riders as they came. When they reached the horseman, they greeted him with the salutation due to a king. He mounted and said, “Take charge of this man.” One of them took him up behind him, and they brought him to the royal residence. The horseman proved to be al-Ḥārith al-Akbar al-Ghassānī. He ordered one of his servants to provide lodging for the man of Ṭayyiʾ. Zāmil feared that the king had forgotten him, so he said to the servant, “Would you do me a kindness and convey to the king what I have to say?” He replied, “I will.” Then Zāmil recited to him:

poems.intro: فتسبب الغلام إلى أن أنشد الملك الأبيات، فقال الملك: وا سوأتاه، كرم ولؤمنا، إيذن له يا غلام، فلما دخل قال: والله لا يرحض عارها عني إلا عطاؤها حتى ترضى، ثم أمر له بجائزة سنية، وقال له: يا زامل. إن الأوطان جواذب، كما ذكرت، فهل لك في المقام في جملتنا يفيء عليك ظلنا، وتسيل عليك صلتنا؟ فقال: أيها الملك. ما كنت لأوثر وطني عليك، ثم أقام بالشام في جواره. وقال ابن الرومي:

verses.h1: ولي وطن آليت ألا أبيعه
verses.h2: وألا أرى غيري له الدهر مالكا

verses.h1: فقد ألفته النفس حتى كأنه
verses.h2: لها جسد إن بان غودرت هالكا

verses.h1: وحبب أوطان الرجال إليهم
verses.h2: مآرب قضاها الرجال هنالكا

verses.h1: إذا ذكروا أوطانهم ذكرتهم
verses.h2: عهود الصبى فيها فحنوا لذلكا

verses.h1: I have a homeland I have sworn never to sell,
verses.h2: nor ever to see another own it.

verses.h1: My soul has grown so attached to it that it seems
verses.h2: a body for my soul: were it to depart, I would be left to perish.

verses.h1: What endears men’s homelands to them
verses.h2: are the desires they fulfilled there.

verses.h1: When they recall their homelands, these remind them
verses.h2: of their youthful days there, and for that they yearn.

prose_translation.intro: The servant contrived to recite the verses to the king, who said, “Shame on me! He was generous, while we were base! Admit him, lad.” When he entered, the king said, “By God, nothing will wash away the shame of this from me except giving until you are satisfied.” Then he ordered a handsome reward for him and said to him, “Zāmil, homelands exert a pull, as you have said.
