Would you care to remain among us, sheltered by our shade, with our bounty flowing upon you?” He replied, “O king, I would never prefer my homeland to you.” He then remained in al-Shām under his protection. Ibn al-Rūmī said:

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: لا يذكر الرمل إلا حن مغترب
verses.h2: له بذي الرمل أوطار وأوطان

verses.h1: يهفو إلى البان من قلبي نوازعه
verses.h2: وما بي البان، بل من دارهالبان

verses.h1: أسد سمعي إذا غنى الحمام بها
verses.h2: كيلا يبين سر الوجد إعلان

verses.h1: ورب دار أوليها مجانبة
verses.h2: ولي إلى الدار أطراب وأشجان

verses.h1: إذا تلفت في أطلالها ابتدرت
verses.h2: للقلب والعين أمواه ونيران

verses.h1: The sands are never mentioned but an exile yearns,
verses.h2: whose heart’s desires and homes lie in Dhū al-Raml.

verses.h1: My heart’s longings flutter toward the bān trees;
verses.h2: it is not the bān trees that move me, but the one whose home is there.

verses.h1: I stop my ears when the doves sing there,
verses.h2: lest an outcry betray the secret of my longing.

verses.h1: Many a dwelling I keep my distance from,
verses.h2: though that dwelling stirs raptures and sorrows in me.

verses.h1: When I turn to gaze among its ruins, there rush forth
verses.h2: waters and fires for my heart and eye.

notes.note: Dhū al-Raml is treated as a place name, but its location is unidentified; the expression could also describe a sandy tract.
The joined text «دارهالبان» is read as «داره البان», ‘whose home is the bān trees.’ bān denotes the moringa tree, though al-Bān could here be a place name.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العرب مصعب بن محمد بن الفرات
poems.intro: قيل لبعض الحكماء: ما اللذة؟ قال: الكفاية مع لزوم الأوطان، ومحادثة الإخوان، وقيل: فما الذلة؟ قال: النزوح عن الأوطان، والتنقل في البلدان. وقال أبو العرب مصعب بن محمد بن الفرات:

poet.from_text: أبو العرب مصعب بن محمد بن الفرات

verses.h1: أهم ولى عزمان: عزم مشرق
verses.h2: وآخر يغري همتي بالمغارب

verses.h1: ولا بد لي أن أسأل العيس حاجة
verses.h2: تشق على أخفافها والغوارب

verses.h1: علي لآمالي اضطراب مؤمل
verses.h2: ولكن على الأقدار نجح المطالب

verses.h1: فيا نفس لا تستصحبي الهون إنه
verses.h2: وإن خدعت أسبابه

verses.h1: شر صاحب
ويا وطني إن بنت عني فإنني
verses.h2: سأوطن أكوار العتاق النجائب

verses.h1: إذا كان أصلي من تراب فكلها
verses.h2: بلادي، وكل العالمين أقاربي

verses.h1: I ponder my course, with two resolves: one points east,
verses.h2: while the other urges my ambition westward.

verses.h1: I must ask the camels to fulfill a need
verses.h2: that will tax their hooves and withers.

verses.h1: It falls to me to strive hopefully toward my aspirations,
verses.h2: but the fulfillment of desires rests with fate.

verses.h1: O my soul, do not take abasement as your companion: it is—
verses.h2: though its inducements may deceive—

verses.h1: the worst companion.
O my homeland, if you part from me, I
verses.h2: shall make my home on the saddles of noble, fleet camels.

verses.h1: If my origin is dust, then all the earth is
verses.h2: my homeland, and all the world’s people are my kin.

notes.note: The unvocalized أهم is taken as ‘I ponder [my course]’; it could also convey being troubled or preoccupied.
This fragment evidently completes the second hemistich of line 4, rather than forming a separate verse. The supplied line division has been retained.

prose_translation.intro: One of the sages was asked, “What is pleasure?” He replied, “Having enough while remaining in one’s homeland and conversing with friends.” He was then asked, “What is humiliation?” He replied, “Being far from one’s homeland and wandering from land to land.” Abū al-ʿArab Muṣʿab ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt said:

verses.h1: يا بعيد الدار من وطنه
verses.h2: مفردا يبكي على سكنه

verses.h1: كلما جد النجاء به
verses.h2: جدت الأسقام في بدنه

verses.h1: ولقد زاد الفؤاد شجي
verses.h2: صوت قمري على فننه

verses.h1: شفه ما شفني فبكى
verses.h2: كل من يبكي على شجنه

verses.h1: O you who dwell far from your homeland,
verses.h2: alone, weeping for your home!

verses.h1: Whenever his journey pressed him onward,
verses.h2: the ailments in his body grew more severe.

verses.h1: The heart’s sorrow was deepened
verses.h2: by a turtledove’s voice upon its branch.

verses.h1: What wasted me wasted him, and he wept—
verses.h2: each weeping over his own sorrow.

notes.note: سكن can mean a dwelling or someone in whom one finds comfort, especially a beloved; ‘home’ is chosen here.
النجاء denotes swift travel or flight; the verse does not specify whether he is fleeing.
شجي is read as شجى, ‘sorrow,’ with an apparent spelling or transcription irregularity.

كل من يبكي على شجنه literally reads ‘everyone who weeps over his sorrow.’ Its syntax here is awkward and may reflect a textual error; the translation takes the intended sense to be that the speaker and dove each weep over their own sorrow.

verses.h1: لابد للمشتاق من ذكر الوطن
verses.h2: واليأس والسلوة من بعد الحزن

verses.h1: For one who yearns, remembrance of home is inevitable,
verses.h2: as are despair and solace after sorrow.

poems.poet_from_text: عبد السلام بن رغبان المعروف بديك الجن
poems.intro: وقال عبد السلام بن رغبان المعروف بديك الجن:

poet.from_text: عبد السلام بن رغبان المعروف بديك الجن

verses.h1: أما آن للطيف أن يأتيا
verses.h2: وأن يطرق الوطن الدانيا؟

verses.h1: وإني لأحسب ريب الزما
verses.h2: ن يتركني جسدا باليا

verses.h1: سأنشر ذكرك لا ناسيا
verses.h2: جميل الصفاء ولا قاليا

verses.h1: وقد كنت أنشره ضاحكا
verses.h2: فقد صرت أنشره باكيا

verses.h1: Is it not time for your dream-phantom to come
verses.h2: and visit this nearby home by night?

verses.h1: Indeed, I think the ravages of time
verses.h2: will leave me a wasted body.

verses.h1: I shall keep speaking of you, neither forgetting
verses.h2: the beauty of our affection nor bearing you ill will.

verses.h1: Once I spoke of you laughing;
verses.h2: now I speak of you weeping.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Raghbān, known as Dīk al-Jinn, said:

poems.intro: وقال الشريف المرتضى - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: هل لليالي بالمنقى رجوع
verses.h2: مثلما كن لي ونحن جميع

verses.h1: زمن راعني تذكره الثا
verses.h2: وي وإن كان ماضيا لا يريع

verses.h1: وطن طاب جوه وثراه
verses.h2: فكأن المصيف فيه ربيع

verses.h1: حيث لا تهتدي الخطوب لا يخ
verses.h2: فق من خشية الحوادث روع

verses.h1: Can the nights at al-Munaqqā return,
verses.h2: as they were for me when we were all together?

verses.h1: A time whose lingering memory shakes me,
verses.h2: though it is past and does not return.

verses.h1: A homeland whose air and soil were sweet,
verses.h2: so that summer there seemed spring.

verses.h1: Where misfortunes cannot find their way,
verses.h2: no heart trembles for fear of calamities.

notes.note: The place المنقى is unidentified here; its vocalization as al-Munaqqā is tentative.
الثاوي (‘abiding’ or ‘lingering’), divided between the hemistichs, is taken as modifying ‘memory’; its grammatical attachment is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: وماء بلادي كان أنجع مشربا
verses.h2: ولو أن ماء الكرخ صهباء جريال

verses.h1: فيا وطني إن فاتني بك سابق
verses.h2: من الدهر، فلينعم لساكنك البال

verses.h1: وإن استطع في الحشر آتك زائرا
verses.h2: وهيهات، لي يوم القيامة أشغال

verses.h1: The water of my homeland was more wholesome to drink,
verses.h2: even if the water of al-Karkh were deep-red wine.

verses.h1: O my homeland, if my former days with you are lost to me,
verses.h2: may those who dwell in you enjoy peace of mind.

verses.h1: If I can, I shall come to visit you at the Gathering—
verses.h2: but what a distant hope! On Resurrection Day I shall have much to occupy me.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: بما التعلل؟ لا أهل ولا وطن
verses.h2: ولا نديم ولا كأس ولا سكن

verses.h1: أريد من زمني ذا أن يبلغني
verses.h2: ما ليس يبلغه في نفسه الزمن

verses.h1: لا تلق دهرك إلا غير مكترث
verses.h2: ما دام يصحب فيه روحك البدن

verses.h1: فما يدوم سرور ما سررت به
verses.h2: ولا يرد عليك الفائت الحزن

verses.h1: What is there to console me? No family, no homeland,
verses.h2: no boon companion, no cup, no beloved.

verses.h1: I ask this age of mine to grant me
verses.h2: what time itself cannot attain.

verses.h1: Face time with unconcern,
verses.h2: so long as your body keeps your soul company.

verses.h1: The joy of whatever delights you does not endure,
verses.h2: nor does grief bring back what you have lost.

poems.intro: عن رجل من أهل خراسان قال: رأيت علي بن الجهم بعد أن أطلق من محبسه جالسا في المقابر، فقلت: ما يجلسك هنا؟ فقال:

verses.h1: يشتاق كل غريب عند غربته
verses.h2: ويذكر الأهل والجيران والسكنا

verses.h1: وليس لي وطن أمسيت أذكره
verses.h2: إلا المقابر إذ كانت لهم وطنا

verses.h1: Every stranger yearns while far from home,
verses.h2: remembering family, neighbors, and dwelling.

verses.h1: I have no homeland now to remember
verses.h2: except the graveyards, for they have become their home.

prose_translation.intro: From a man of Khurāsān, who said: I saw ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm sitting among the graves after he had been released from prison. I asked, “What brings you to sit here?” He replied:

poems.intro: قلت: لي أبيات تنظر إلى هذا المعنى، وهي:

verses.h1: أشتاق أهلي وأوطاني وقد ملكت
verses.h2: دوني وأفنى الردى أهلي وأحبابي

verses.h1: فأستريح إلى رؤيا القبور، ففي
verses.h2: أمثالها حل إخواني وأترابي

verses.h1: ولست أحيا حياة استلذ بها
verses.h2: من بعدهم ولحاق القوم أولى بي

verses.h1: I long for my kin and my homelands, now taken
verses.h2: from me; death has swept away my kin and loved ones.

verses.h1: So I find solace in the sight of graves, for in
verses.h2: graves like these my brothers and companions of my age have settled.

verses.h1: I live no life in which I find delight
verses.h2: now they are gone; it would be better for me to join them.

notes.note: رؤيا usually means a dream or vision. Here it is rendered as the sight of graves, but dreaming of graves is also a possible reading.

prose_translation.intro: I say: I have some verses that touch on this theme. They are as follows:

poems.intro: وقال أبو بكر، المعروف بابن اللبانة، في نكبة آل عباد أرباب الأندلس - وكان تغلب عليهم يوسف بن تاشفين، وملك بلادهم، وكانوا محسنين إلى أجل العلم وإلى هذا الشاعر، وله فيهم أشعار كثيرة يبكيهم ويتأسف على أيامهم:

verses.h1: بكى آل عباد ولا كمحمد
verses.h2: بأبياته صوب السحاب إذا همى

verses.h1: حبيب إلى قلبي حبيب لقوله:
verses.h2: عسى وطن يدنو بهم، ولعلما

verses.h1: قصور خلت من ساكنيها فما بها
verses.h2: سوى الأدم تمشى حول واقفة الدمى

verses.h1: يجيب بها البوم الصدى، ولطالما
verses.h2: أجاب القيان الطائر المترنما

verses.h1: كأن لم يكن فيها أنيس ولا التقى
verses.h2: بها الوفد جمعا والخميس عرمرما

verses.h1: مصاب هوى بالنيرات من العلى
verses.h2: ولم يبق في أرض المكارم معلما

verses.h1: حكيت وقد فارقت ملكك مالكا
verses.h2: ومن ولهى أحكى عليك متمما

verses.h1: بكيتك حتى لم يخل لي الأسى
verses.h2: دموعا بها أبكى عليك ولا دما

verses.h1: وإني على رسمي مقيم، فإن أمت
verses.h2: سأترك للباكين رسمي موسما

verses.h1: For Āl ʿAbbād it wept—but not as Muḥammad did
verses.h2: in his verses—the rain pouring from the clouds.

verses.h1: Ḥabīb is dear to my heart for saying:
verses.h2: “Perhaps a homeland will bring them near—perhaps.”

verses.h1: Palaces emptied of their inhabitants: nothing remains in them
verses.h2: but pale antelopes walking around the standing statues.

verses.h1: There the owls answer the echo, where so often
verses.h2: the singing girls answered the warbling bird.

verses.h1: As though no companion had ever dwelt there, nor gathered
verses.h2: there the envoys in throngs and the army in mighty numbers.

verses.h1: A calamity that cast the luminaries down from the heights
verses.h2: and left no landmark in the land of noble deeds.

verses.h1: Having parted with your kingdom, you resembled Mālik;
verses.h2: in my anguish over you, I resemble Mutammim.

verses.h1: I wept for you until sorrow left me
verses.h2: neither tears with which to mourn you nor blood.

verses.h1: I remain steadfast in my wont; and if I die,
verses.h2: I shall leave my traces as a gathering-place for mourners.

notes.note: The syntax is compressed: I take “the clouds’ downpour” as the delayed subject of “wept,” and “in his verses” as referring to Muḥammad. Muḥammad may be Ibn al-Labbāna himself, whose given name was Muḥammad, or the poet-king al-Muʿtamid Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād. بأبياته could alternatively mean “at his dwellings,” yielding a different construction.
Ḥabīb probably refers to Abū Tammām, Ḥabīb ibn Aws. I have not securely identified the quoted verse; its concluding ولعلما is an elliptical expression of hope, rendered “perhaps.”

رسم can mean an established practice or a remaining trace. The line appears to shift between these senses; the final “traces” may specifically suggest the poet’s grave. موسما is understood as a place where mourners gather or return.

prose_translation.intro: Abū Bakr, known as Ibn al-Labbāna, said of the calamity that befell Āl ʿAbbād, the rulers of al-Andalus—Yūsuf ibn Tāshfīn had overcome them and taken possession of their lands, and they had been generous to men of learning and to this poet, who composed many poems about them, lamenting them and grieving for their days:
interludes: He says in this poem:

verses.h1: حنت قلوصي في عدان إلى نجد
verses.h2: ولم ينسها أوطانها قدم العهد

verses.h1: إذا شئت لاقيت القلوص ولا أرى
verses.h2: لقومي أشباها فيألفهم ودى

verses.h1: My young she-camel yearned in ʿAdān for Najd;
verses.h2: the long passage of time had not made her forget her homeland.

verses.h1: Whenever I wish, I can find the young she-camel, yet I see
verses.h2: none like my people, to whom my heart might warm.

notes.note: عدان is treated as a place name, provisionally transliterated ʿAdān; its vocalization and precise location are uncertain.
The phrase لاقيت القلوص literally means ‘I meet the young she-camel.’ Its connection with the following contrast is unclear; the wording may be corrupt, but it has been translated as supplied.

prose_translation.intro: And a man of Tamīm said:

verses.h1: حن إلى أوطانهم معشر
verses.h2: لهم غرام ولي اثنان

verses.h1: إذا تشكوا شجنا واحدا
verses.h2: تكاثرت ععدة أشجاني

verses.h1: A people yearned for their homelands;
verses.h2: they have one longing, while I have two.

verses.h1: When they lament a single sorrow,
verses.h2: my sorrows multiply in number.

notes.note: ععدة appears to be a typographical or OCR error for عدة, meaning ‘number’ or ‘count’; translated accordingly.

verses.h1: لئن سلمني الله
verses.h2: وبالحفظ تولاني

verses.h1: وأعطاني أعطاني
verses.h2: وأوطاني أوطاني

verses.h1: وأخلى ذرعي الآ
verses.h2: ن، وخلاني خلاني

verses.h1: فلا عدت إلى الغر
verses.h2: بة ماكر الجديدان

verses.h1: فإن عدت لها يوما
verses.h2: فسجاني سجاني

verses.h1: If God keeps me safe
verses.h2: and takes me into His protection,

verses.h1: and grants me my dwelling places,
verses.h2: and sets me in my homelands,

verses.h1: and gives me freedom now,
verses.h2: and my friends let me go,

verses.h1: then may I never return to exile
verses.h2: as long as night and day recur.

verses.h1: And if I return to it one day,
verses.h2: may my jailer shroud me.

notes.note: The repeated forms appear to be wordplay: أعطاني أعطاني, ‘grants me my dwelling places,’ with the second word understood as أعطانِي (literally, my camels’ resting places beside water). أوطاني أوطاني apparently means ‘sets me in my homelands’; the first form may represent أوطأني with the hamza omitted.
أخلى ذرعي is uncertain; ‘gives me freedom’ is tentative. خلاني خلاني is read as خَلّاني خِلّاني, ‘my friends let me go,’ though the intended sense is not entirely clear.

فسجاني سجاني is read as فَسَجّاني سَجّاني: ‘may my jailer shroud me,’ taking the first word from سجّى, ‘cover or shroud,’ and the second as سجّان, ‘jailer.’ The unvocalized wordplay leaves some uncertainty.

poems.intro: قال الجهم بن المغيرة: كنا عند حيوس بن ثمال القرمطي بضرية، فمرت بنا جارية صفراء مولدة، فقال لي حيوس: استفتح كلامها فإنها ظريفة، فقلت: يا جارية أين نشأت؟ فقالت: بقرقري، قلت: فأين شعبعب؟ فضحكت، ثم قالت: بين الحوض والعطن، قلت: فمن الذي يقول:

verses.h1: يا صاحبي فدت نفسي نفوسكما
verses.h2: عوجا على صدور الأبغل السنن

verses.h1: ثم ارفعا الصوت ننظر صبح خامسة
verses.h2: بقرقري، ما عناء النفس بالوطن

verses.h1: هل أجعلن يدي للخد مرفقة
verses.h2: على شعبعب بين الحوض والعطن؟

verses.h1: My two companions, may my life ransom yours!
verses.h2: Turn the mules’ breasts toward the open road.

verses.h1: Then raise your voices; on the fifth morning let us see,
verses.h2: at Qarqarā, what anguish the soul feels for its homeland.

verses.h1: Shall I ever make my hand a cushion for my cheek
verses.h2: at Shaʿbaʿb, between al-Ḥawḍ and al-ʿAṭan?

notes.note: The syntax of «عوجا على صدور الأبغل السنن» is unclear and may be corrupt. The translation is provisional, taking «الأبغل» as ‘mules’ and «السنن» as ‘the open or direct road’; the wording does not straightforwardly support the resulting construction.
«ما عناء النفس بالوطن» is ambiguous: it may express anguish over the homeland, as translated, or ask rhetorically what hardship the soul could feel when at home.
The vocalization of Shaʿbaʿb is uncertain. Al-Ḥawḍ and al-ʿAṭan are treated as place names, but they could mean ‘the watering trough’ and ‘the camels’ resting place by the water.’

prose_translation.intro: Al-Jahm ibn al-Mughīra said: We were with Ḥayūs ibn Thimāl al-Qarmaṭī at Ḍariyya when a light-skinned slave girl of mixed parentage passed by us. Ḥayūs said to me, “Strike up a conversation with her, for she is witty.” I said, “Girl, where did you grow up?” She replied, “At Qarqarā.” I asked, “Then where is Shaʿbaʿb?” She laughed, then said, “Between al-Ḥawḍ and al-ʿAṭan.” I asked, “Who is it who says:”

poems.intro: فالتفتت إلى حيوس، فقالت: خبره بقائلها، فقال: ما أعرفه، فقالت: بلى هذا يقوله شاعرنا وظريف بلادنا وغزلها، قال: ويحك: ومن ذاك؟ فقالت: أشهد إن كنت لا تعرفه وأنت من أهل الوادي إنها لسوأة، ذاك يحيى بن طالب الحنفي، وأقسم بالله ما منعك من معرفته إلا غلظ الطبع، وجفاء الخلق، فجعل حيوس يضحك من قولها. ويحيى بن طالب الحنفي من أهل اليمامة، وكان أديبا كريما، فابتاع من عامل السلطان غلة ضيعة مما تحت يده يريد بها الربح، فأصاب الناس باليمامة قحط ومسغبة، ففرق يحيى تلك الغلة وأطعمهم إياها، وآن محل الوفاء، ولم يكن له شيء، فهرب إلى الري، وبها توفي. وقد روى عن إسحاق بن إبراهيم الموصلي، قال: غنيت بين يدي الرشيد:

opening.actual: ألا هل إلى شم الخزامى ونظرة

verses.h1: ألا هل إلى شم الخزامى ونظرة
verses.h2: إلى قرقري قبل الممات سبيل؟

verses.h1: فأشرب من ماء الحجيلاء شربة
verses.h2: يداوى بها قبل الممات عليل

verses.h1: فيا أثلات القاع من بطن توضح
verses.h2: حنيني إلى إظلالكن طويل

verses.h1: ويا أثلات القاع قلبي موكل
verses.h2: بكن وجدوى نيلكن قليل

verses.h1: ويا أثلات القاع قدمل صحبتي
verses.h2: مقامي، فهل في ظلكن مقيل

verses.h1: أحدث عنك النفس أن لست راجعا
verses.h2: إليك فهمي في الفؤاد دخيل

verses.h1: أريد رجوعا نحوكم فيصدني
verses.h2: إذا رمته دين على ثقيل

verses.h1: Is there any way to smell the lavender and look
verses.h2: upon Qarqarā before death?

verses.h1: Then I might drink a draught of al-Ḥujaylāʾ’s water,
verses.h2: with which an ailing man might be healed before death.

verses.h1: O tamarisks of the plain in the valley of Tūḍiḥ,
verses.h2: long has been my yearning for your shade.

verses.h1: O tamarisks of the plain, my heart is bound
verses.h2: to you, but there is little hope of reaching you.

verses.h1: O tamarisks of the plain, my companions have grown weary
verses.h2: of my staying; is there a place for a midday rest in your shade?

verses.h1: I tell myself of you that I shall not return
verses.h2: to you, and my sorrow is lodged deep within my heart.

verses.h1: I wish to return to you, but I am held back,
verses.h2: whenever I attempt it, by a heavy debt upon me.

notes.note: The expression «جدوى نيلكن قليل» is compressed and uncertain: literally something like “the benefit of attaining you is little.” It is rendered here as little hope of reaching the trees again.
The printed «قدمل» is read as «قد ملّ». «صحبتي» is understood as “my companions,” the subject, and «مقامي» as “my staying,” the object.
The printed «على» is read as «عليّ» (“upon me”), modifying the debt.

prose_translation.intro:
She turned to Ḥayyūs and said, “Tell him who composed them.” He replied, “I do not know him.” She said, “Yes, you do! These are the words of our poet, the wit of our land and its poet of love.” He said, “Confound you! Who is that?” She replied, “I declare, if you do not know him, though you are one of the people of the valley, that is a disgrace! That is Yaḥyā ibn Ṭālib al-Ḥanafī. By God, nothing has kept you from knowing him but your dull nature and coarse character.” Ḥayyūs began laughing at what she said.

Yaḥyā ibn Ṭālib al-Ḥanafī was from al-Yamāma, and he was a cultivated and generous man. He bought from the ruler’s official the produce of an estate under his administration, intending to make a profit from it. Then drought and famine struck the people of al-Yamāma, so Yaḥyā distributed that produce and fed them with it. When payment fell due, he had nothing, so he fled to al-Rayy, where he died. It is also related from Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī, who said: “I sang before al-Rashīd:”

poems.intro: فطرب الرشيد، وسأل عن قائل هذا الشعر: من هو؟ فقلت: هو يحيى بن طالب الحنفي، شاعر من أهل اليمامة، وإنه لحي، وهرب إلى الري من دين غلبه، وقد ذكر ذلك في شعره هذا، فقال:

verses.h1: أريد رجوعا نحوكم فيصدني
verses.h2: إذا رمته دين على ثقيل

verses.h1: I wish to return to you, but I am held back,
verses.h2: whenever I try, by a heavy debt I bear.

notes.note: Read على as عليّ (“upon me”), apparently a typing or OCR error.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rashīd was delighted and asked, “Who composed this poetry?” I said, “He is Yaḥyā ibn Ṭālib al-Ḥanafī, a poet from al-Yamāma. He is still alive, and he fled to al-Rayy because of a debt that overwhelmed him. He mentioned this in these verses of his, saying:”

poems.intro: فأمر الرشيد أن يكتب إلى عامل الري بقضاء دينه، وإعطائه نفقة، وإنفاذه على البريد، فوصل الكتاب إلى الري يوم مات يحيى بن طالبن وقيل: مات قبل وصوله بشهر. وقلت:

verses.h1: أين السلو من المروع بالنوى
verses.h2: أبدا، فلا وطن ولا خلان

verses.h1: عيد البرية موسم لعويله
verses.h2: وسرورهم فيه له أحزان

verses.h1: وإذا رأى الشمل الجميع تزاحمت
verses.h2: في قلبه الأمواه والنيران

verses.h1: Where is solace for one stricken by separation
verses.h2: forever, with neither homeland nor friends?

verses.h1: The people’s festival is a season for his wailing;
verses.h2: their joy that day is sorrow to him.

verses.h1: When he sees everyone united, there crowd together
verses.h2: within his heart the waters and the fires.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rashīd ordered that a letter be sent to the governor of al-Rayy instructing him to pay off his debt, give him money for his expenses, and send him on by the postal service. The letter reached al-Rayy on the day Yaḥyā ibn Ṭālib died; it is also said that he died a month before it arrived. And I said:

verses.h1: ها قد تبدلت أوطانا بأوطان
verses.h2: عمدا، وفارقت إخوانا لإخوان

verses.h1: فليبلغ الشوق بي أقصى مراتبه
verses.h2: إلى بدور على قضبان كثبان

verses.h1: See, I have exchanged homelands for other homelands,
verses.h2: Deliberately, and parted with friends for other friends.

verses.h1: So let longing carry me to its furthest reaches—
verses.h2: Longing for full moons atop boughs upon sand dunes.

poems.intro: وكتب إلي القاضي المهذب أبو محمد حسن بن علي بن الزبير قصيدة أنفذها من أسوان، وانا بمصر، منها:

verses.h1: أأحبابنا مالي إذا ما ذكرتكم
verses.h2: وما أنا ناس غال صبري غول؟

verses.h1: وإن شام برق الشام طرفي وشمرت
verses.h2: على البعد عنه للظلام ذيول

verses.h1: تدارك قلبي أن يطير صبابة
verses.h2: بنان كأنبوب اليراع نحيل

verses.h1: وخيل لي أن السيوف بجوه
verses.h2: سللن، وأني بينهن قتيل

verses.h1: لئن أقفرت منا الديار ومنكم
verses.h2: وأمست مغانيهن وهي طلول

verses.h1: فإن لنا في آل منقذ أسوة
verses.h2: يهون لديها الخطب وهو جليل

verses.h1: نبت بهم أوطانهم فترحلوا
verses.h2: وللمجد في ذاك الرحيل رحيل

verses.h1: بلاد بها من عزهم وعطائهم
verses.h2: وعور لمن ينتباها وسهول

verses.h1: وللدهر من أيمانهم ووجدوههم
verses.h2: بها غرر ما تنقضي وحجول

verses.h1: خلت، فالربيع الغض محل لفقدهم
verses.h2: بها والصباح المستنير أصيل

verses.h1: وساروا على رغم العدا، ودليلهم ثناء لهم في الخافقين جميل
وما كنت أدرى قبل أن يترحلوا
verses.h2: بأن الجبال الراسيات تزول

verses.h1: أذلوا خطوب الدهر قهرا فبينهم
verses.h2: قديما وبين الحادثات ذحول

verses.h1: O our beloved ones, why, whenever I remember you—
verses.h2: though I do not forget—does a demon devour my patience?

verses.h1: Whenever my eye glimpses the lightning of al-Shām, and
verses.h2: the skirts of darkness are drawn back from it in the distance,

verses.h1: My heart is checked before it flies away with longing
verses.h2: by fingers slender as the shaft of a reed.

verses.h1: And I fancy that swords in that sky
verses.h2: have been drawn, and that I lie slain among them.

verses.h1: Though the dwellings stand deserted by us and you,
verses.h2: and their once-inhabited grounds have become ruins,

verses.h1: We have in the house of Munqidh an example
verses.h2: beside which our plight grows light, though it is grievous.

verses.h1: Their homelands cast them out, and they departed;
verses.h2: and with that departure glory too departed.

verses.h1: A land where, through their might and their bounty,
verses.h2: those who visited found rugged ground and smooth.

verses.h1: From their right hands and their faces, Time has
verses.h2: there blazes and white stockings that never fade.

verses.h1: The land lies empty: without them, lush spring is drought
verses.h2: there, and radiant morning is dusk.

verses.h1: They departed to their enemies’ chagrin, their guide the fair praise of them in East and West.
I had not known, before they departed,
verses.h2: that firmly rooted mountains could move away.

verses.h1: They humbled time’s ordeals by force; between them
verses.h2: and calamities there are ancient blood-feuds.

notes.note: I read شمرت as passive, ‘were drawn back.’ The placement and relation of على البعد عنه are compressed; I understand the distant lightning as parting the darkness.
I take بنان, ‘fingers,’ as the subject of تدارك, checking the heart before it flies away. Whose fingers these are is not explicitly stated.
وجدوههم appears to be a typographical or OCR error for وجوههم, ‘their faces,’ which is the reading translated.

prose_translation.intro: The judge al-Muhadhdhab Abū Muḥammad Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Zubayr wrote me a poem, which he sent from Aswan while I was in Miṣr. Among its verses were the following:

verses.h1: قد طال بي أقطع البيداء منفردا
verses.h2: وليس يسفر عن وجه المنى سفر

verses.h1: كأنما الأرض عني غير راضية
verses.h2: فليس لي وطن فيها ولا وطر

verses.h1: Long have I wandered, crossing the desert alone,
verses.h2: yet no journey unveils the face of my desire.

verses.h1: It is as though the earth were displeased with me:
verses.h2: I have neither a homeland upon it nor a wish fulfilled.

notes.note: Waṭar can mean a need, aim, or object of desire. Its sense here is uncertain; ‘a wish fulfilled’ takes it to mean the attainment of what one desires.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Bakr ibn al-Labbāna said:

poems.intro: قلت: لي أبيات تشابه هذا المعنى، وهي:

verses.h1: وقد أفردتني الحادثات فليس لي
verses.h2: أنيس، ولا في طارق الخطب أعوان

verses.h1: كأني من غير التراب نبت بي الب
verses.h2: لاد، فما لي في البسيطة أوطان

verses.h1: أجول، كما جالت قذاة بمقلة
verses.h2: وأسرى، وسارى النجم في الأفق حيران

verses.h1: إذا قلت: هذا حين ألقى عصا السرى
verses.h2: دعاني إلى الترحال ظلم وعدوان

verses.h1: Calamities have left me alone: I have
verses.h2: no companion, nor helpers when misfortune strikes.

verses.h1: As though I were made of something other than dust, the lands reject me;
verses.h2: I have no homeland anywhere on earth.

verses.h1: I wander as a speck of dust wanders in an eye,
verses.h2: and journey by night, while the night-roaming star is bewildered on the horizon.

verses.h1: Whenever I say, “Now is the time to lay down my staff of night travel,”
verses.h2: injustice and aggression summon me to depart.

notes.note: I read أسرى and سارى as أسري (“I journey by night”) and ساري (“night-roaming”), respectively, understanding ساري النجم as a star traveling through the night sky.

prose_translation.intro: I say: I have some verses expressing a similar meaning. They are:

verses.h1: وللحمية لا عن زلة حكمت
verses.h2: بالبعد فارقت إخوانا وأوطانا

verses.h1: تخيفني بلدة حتى أميل إلى
verses.h2: أخرى، كأني عمران بن حطانا

verses.h1: Out of pride, not for an offense that sentenced me
verses.h2: to exile, I left brothers and homelands behind.

verses.h1: One town frightens me until I turn toward
verses.h2: another, as though I were ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Fityān ibn Ḥayyūs said:

poems.intro: قلت: ربما وقف على هذين البيتين من يتطلع إلى معنى قول أبي الفتيان: "كأني عمران بن حطان" فرأيت أن اذكر شيئا من أخباره، وإن لم يقتض التأليف ذلك. عن الهيثم بن عدي قال: طلب الحجاج عمران بن حطان السدوسي، وكان من الخوارج، وكتب فيه إلى عماله، وإلى عبد الملك بن مروان، فهرب، فلم يزل يتنقل في أحياء العرب، وقال في ذلك:

verses.h1: حللنا في بني كعب بن عمرو
verses.h2: وفي عك وعامر عوثبان

verses.h1: وفي جرم، وفي عمرو بن مر
verses.h2: وفي زيد، وحي بن العدان

verses.h1: We settled among Banū Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr,
verses.h2: and among ʿAkk and ʿĀmir of ʿAwthabān.

verses.h1: And among Jurm, and among ʿAmr ibn Murr,
verses.h2: and among Zayd and Ḥayy ibn al-ʿAdān.

notes.note: The wording عامر عوثبان is uncertain. “ʿĀmir of ʿAwthabān” provisionally treats it as a genealogical designation, but the relationship between the names is unclear; the text may be defective. The vocalization of عوثبان is also uncertain.
I could not identify حي بن العدان. It is provisionally rendered as the name Ḥayy ibn al-ʿAdān, with uncertain vocalization; حي might instead mean “clan,” and the wording may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro: I say: Someone reading these two verses may wish to know the meaning of Abū al-Fityān’s words, “As though I were ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān,” so I thought I would mention something of his story, even though the plan of this book does not call for it. On the authority of al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī, who said: Al-Ḥajjāj sought ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān al-Sadūsī, who was one of the Kharijites, and wrote concerning him to his governors and to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He fled and kept moving among the tribes of the Arabs. Of this he said:

poems.intro: ثم لحق بالشام، فنزل بروح بن زنباع الجذامي، فقال له روح: من أنت؟ فقال: من الأزد أزد السراة، وكان روح يسمر عند عبد الملك بن مروان، فقال لعبد الملك: إن في أضيافنا رجلا ما سمعت منك حديثا إلا حدثني به، وزادني ما لم يكن عندي، فقال: ممن هو؟ قال: من الأزد، قال: إني لأسمعك تصف عمران بن حطان، أسمعك تصف وتذكر لغة نزارية، قال روح: وما أنا وعمران بن حطان، ثم أنشد عبد الملك:

verses.h1: يا ضربة من تقى ما أراد بها
verses.h2: إلا ليبلغ من ذي العرش رضوانا

verses.h1: O blow dealt by a pious man, who sought by it
verses.h2: only to gain the favor of the Lord of the Throne!

prose_translation.intro: Then he made his way to al-Shām and stayed with Rawḥ ibn Zinbāʿ al-Judhāmī. Rawḥ asked him, “Who are you?” He replied, “I am of al-Azd, the Azd of al-Sarāt.” Rawḥ used to spend the evening conversing with ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, and he said to him, “Among our guests is a man who has related to me every account I have heard from you, and has added things I did not know.” He asked, “What tribe is he from?” Rawḥ replied, “From al-Azd.” He said, “It sounds to me as though you are describing ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān. I hear you describing and mentioning a manner of speech belonging to Nizār.” Rawḥ said, “What have I to do with ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān?” Then ʿAbd al-Malik recited:

poems.intro: قاتل علي بن أبي طالب رضوان الله عليه، فراح روح فأخبر عبد الملك، فقال: من أخبرك؟ قال: ضيفي، قال: أظنه والله عمران بن حطان، فأعلمه أني قد أمرتك أن تأتيني به، فقال: أفعل، فراح روح إلى أضيافه، فأقبل على عمران، فقال له: إني ذكرتك لعبد الملك، فأمرني أن آتيه بك، فقال: قد كنت أحب ذاك، وما منعني من ذكره إلى الحياء، وأنا متبعك، فدخل روح على عبد الملك، فقال له: أين صاحبنك؟ قال: قال لي: أنا متبعك فانطلق، فقال عبد الملك: أظنك والله سترجع فلا تجده، فلما رجع روح إلى منزله، فإذا عمران قد مضى، وإذا هو قد خلف رقعة في كوة عند رأسه، وإذا فيها:
poems.index_hemistich: يا روح كم من أخي مثوى

opening.expected: يا روح كم من أخي مثوى
opening.actual: يا روح كم من أخي مثوى نزلت

verses.h1: يا روح كم من أخي مثوى نزلت به
verses.h2: قد ظن ظنك من لخم وغسان

verses.h1: حتى إذا خفته زايلت منزله
verses.h2: من بعد ما قيل: عمران بن حطان

verses.h1: قد كنت ضيفك حولا لا يروعني
verses.h2: فيه طوارق من إنس ومن جان

verses.h1: حتى أردت بي العظمى فأوحشني
verses.h2: ما أوحش الناس من خوف ابن مروان

verses.h1: فاعذر أخاك ابن زنباع فإن له
verses.h2: في الحادثات هنات ذات ألوان

verses.h1: يوما يمان إذا لاقيت ذا يمن
verses.h2: وإن لقيت معديا فعدناني

verses.h1: لو كنت مستغفرا يوما لطاغية
verses.h2: كنت المقدم في سري وإعلاني

verses.h1: لكن أبت لي آيات مطهرة
verses.h2: عند التلاوة من طه وعمران

verses.h1: O Rūḥ, how many a host with whom I lodged
verses.h2: among Lakhm and Ghassān has thought as you did!

verses.h1: Then, when I feared him, I left his dwelling,
verses.h2: after someone had said, “ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān.”

verses.h1: For a year I was your guest, untroubled
verses.h2: by night intruders, whether human or jinn.

verses.h1: Then you intended the worst for me, and I was frightened
verses.h2: by what frightens others: fear of Ibn Marwān.

verses.h1: So excuse your brother, Ibn Zinbāʿ, for he has,
verses.h2: in times of adversity, evasions of many kinds.

verses.h1: One day I am a Yamānī, when I meet a man of Yaman;
verses.h2: if I meet a Maʿaddī, I am an ʿAdnānī.

verses.h1: If ever I were to seek forgiveness for a tyrant,
verses.h2: you would come first, in private and in public.

verses.h1: But pure verses forbade me that—
verses.h2: verses recited from Ṭā Hā and ʿImrān.

notes.note: The precise force of هنات is uncertain: it can mean minor matters, faults, or peculiarities. “Evasions” follows the next line’s description of changing his claimed ancestry.

prose_translation.intro: the killer of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him. Rūḥ went and informed ʿAbd al-Malik, who asked, “Who told you?” He replied, “My guest.” He said, “By God, I think he is ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān. Tell him that I have ordered you to bring him to me.” He replied, “I shall.” Rūḥ went back to his guests, turned to ʿImrān, and said, “I mentioned you to ʿAbd al-Malik, and he ordered me to bring you to him.” He replied, “I had wished for that; nothing but shyness kept me from mentioning it. I shall follow you.” Rūḥ went in to ʿAbd al-Malik, who asked him, “Where is your companion?” He replied, “He told me, ‘I shall follow you,’ so I set off.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “By God, I think you will return and not find him.” When Rūḥ returned home, ʿImrān had indeed gone. He had left a note in a niche by his head, and in it was written:

poems.intro: قال: ثم أتى عمران بن حطان الجزيرة، فنزل بزفر بن الحارث الكلابي بقرقيسيا فجعل شباب بني عامر يتعجبون من طول صلاته، وانتسب لزفر أوزاعيا، فقدم على زفر رجل من أهل الشام، وكان قد رأى عمران بن حطان عند روح بن زنباع، فصافحه وسلم عليه، فقال: زفر للرجل الشامي: أتعرفه؟ قال: نعم، هذا الشيخ من الأزد، فقال زفر: أزدي مرة، وأوزاعي مرة؟ إن كنت خائفا أمناك، وإن كنت عائلا أغنيناك، فقال: إن الله هو المغني، وخرج من عنده وهو يقول:

verses.h1: إن التي أصبحت يعيا بها زفر
verses.h2: أعيا عياها على روح بن زنباع

verses.h1: أمسى يسائلني حولا لأخبره
verses.h2: والناس من بين مخدوع وخداع

verses.h1: حتى إذا انجذمت مني حبائله
verses.h2: كف السؤال، ولم يولع بإهلاعي

verses.h1: فاكفف كما كف روح إنني رجل
verses.h2: إما صويح وإما فقعة القاع

verses.h1: أما الصلاة فإني غير تاركها
verses.h2: كل امرئ بالذي يعنى له ساع

verses.h1: فاكفف شبابك عن هزلي ومسألتي
verses.h2: ماذا تريد إلى شيخ لأوزاع؟

verses.h1: أكرم بروح بن زنباع وأسرته
verses.h2: قوم دعا أوليهم للعلى داع

verses.h1: جاورتهم زمنا فيما دعوت به
verses.h2: عرضي صحيح ونومي غير تهجاع

verses.h1: فاعمل فإنك منعي بحادثة
verses.h2: حسب اللبيب بهذا الشيب من ناع

verses.h1: The matter that now leaves Zufar baffled
verses.h2: had already proved too perplexing for Rawḥ ibn Zinbāʿ.

verses.h1: For a year he kept questioning me, seeking an answer,
verses.h2: while people are either deceived or deceivers.

verses.h1: Until, when his snares broke loose from me,
verses.h2: he stopped questioning and did not persist in frightening me.

verses.h1: So desist as Rawḥ desisted: I am a man
verses.h2: either of pure lineage or a puffball of the plain.

verses.h1: As for prayer, I do not abandon it;
verses.h2: every man strives for what concerns him.

verses.h1: Keep your young men from mocking and questioning me:
verses.h2: what do you want with an old man of Awzāʿ?

verses.h1: How noble are Rawḥ ibn Zinbāʿ and his family—
verses.h2: a people whose forebears were summoned to greatness!

verses.h1: I lived among them for a time under the affiliation I claimed,
verses.h2: my honor intact, my sleep more than fitful dozing.

verses.h1: Act, then, for some calamity will bring tidings of your death;
verses.h2: for a discerning man, these gray hairs suffice as a herald of death.

notes.note: The supplied صويح is unclear. I tentatively read صريح, ‘of pure lineage,’ in contrast to فقعة القاع, a puffball growing on open ground, suggesting someone without recognized ancestry.
The phrase فيما دعوت به is compressed and ambiguous. I take it to refer to the tribal affiliation the speaker claimed, in keeping with the introductory account of his assumed identities.

prose_translation.intro: He said: Then ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān came to al-Jazīra and stayed with Zufar ibn al-Ḥārith al-Kilābī at Qarqīsiyā. The young men of Banū ʿĀmir began to marvel at the length of his prayers, and he claimed to Zufar that he belonged to Awzāʿ. Then a man from al-Shām came to Zufar. He had previously seen ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān with Rawḥ ibn Zinbāʿ, so he shook his hand and greeted him. Zufar said to the man from al-Shām, “Do you know him?” He replied, “Yes, this old man is from al-Azd.” Zufar said, “An Azdī one time, and an Awzāʿī another? If you are afraid, we will give you safety; if you are needy, we will make you prosperous.” He replied, “It is God who grants prosperity,” and left him, saying:

poems.intro: ثم خرج فنزل بعمان بقوم يكثرون ذكر أبي بلال، ويبكون عليه، ويذكرون مقتله فأظهر أمره عندهم، فبلغ الحجاج مكانه، فطلبه، فهرب، فنزل فيروذستان "طسوجا من طساسيج السواد، إلى جانب الكوفة" فلم يزل به حتى مات، وفي ذلك يقول:

verses.h1: نزلت بحمد الله في خير أسرة
verses.h2: أسر بما فيهم من الخير والخفر

verses.h1: نزلت بقوم يجمع الله شملهم
verses.h2: وليس لهم عود سوى المجد يعتصر

verses.h1: من الأزد، إن الأزد أكرم أسرة
verses.h2: يمانية تربو إذا انتسب البشر

verses.h1: فأصبحت فيهم آمنا، لا كمعشر
verses.h2: أتوني فقالوا: من ربيعة أو مضر؟

verses.h1: أو الحي قحطان، فتلكم سفاهة
verses.h2: كما قال لي روح وصاحبه زفر

verses.h1: وما فيهم إلا يسر بنسبة
verses.h2: تقربني منه، وإن كان ذا نفر

verses.h1: فنحن بنو الإسلام والله واحد
verses.h2: وأولي عباد الله بالله من شكر

verses.h1: I lodged, praise be to God, among the finest clan;
verses.h2: I rejoice in their goodness and modesty.

verses.h1: I lodged among a people—may God keep them united—
verses.h2: who have no stock to press but glory.

verses.h1: Of al-Azd—for al-Azd are the noblest clan,
verses.h2: of Yaman, preeminent when people recount their ancestry.

verses.h1: So I came to live safely among them—not as with those
verses.h2: who came to me and asked, “Are you of Rabīʿah or Muḍar?

verses.h1: Or of the tribe of Qaḥṭān?” Such questioning is folly;
verses.h2: so Rawḥ and his companion Zufar said to me.

verses.h1: Not one of them but rejoices in a kinship
verses.h2: that brings me close to him, even though he has kinsmen of his own.

verses.h1: We are the sons of Islam, and God is one;
verses.h2: the servant of God closest to God is he who gives thanks.

notes.note: الخفر is read as khafar, “modesty.” Without vowel marks it could also be khafr, “protection,” which would suit the context of taking refuge.

The image in عود سوى المجد يعتصر is unusual: literally, “no stem/wood except glory that is pressed.” The translation preserves the apparent metaphor of extracting glory from their stock, but its precise force is uncertain.
“So Rawḥ and his companion Zufar said” is taken to refer back to the questions about tribal ancestry, rather than to the judgment that such questioning is folly.

prose_translation.intro: Then he departed and stayed in ʿUmān among people who frequently spoke of Abū Bilāl, wept for him, and recounted his killing. He made his cause known among them, and news of his whereabouts reached al-Ḥajjāj, who sought him out. He fled and settled in Fīrūdhistān, “one of the districts of al-Sawād, near al-Kūfa,” where he remained until he died. Concerning this he says:

poems.intro: هذا الذي أشار إليه أبو الفتيان بن حيوس. قلت - وقد نزلت بصور في دار ابن أبي عقيل، وكتبتها على بعض الرخام -:

verses.h1: دار سكنت بها كرها وما سكنت
verses.h2: نفسي إلى سكن فيها ولا شجن

verses.h1: والقبر أرفق لي منها وأجمل بي
verses.h2: إن صدني الدهر عن عود إلى وطني

verses.h1: A house I dwelt in unwillingly; never did
verses.h2: my soul find comfort in any companion there, or any attachment.

verses.h1: The grave would be kinder to me than it, and more fitting for me,
verses.h2: if fate bars me from returning to my homeland.

notes.note: The pairing سكن ولا شجن is uncertain. سكن can mean a companion or someone who affords comfort; شجن usually means sorrow or concern, but may also denote a desire or attachment, the sense adopted here.

prose_translation.intro: This is what Abū al-Fityān ibn Ḥayyūs alluded to. I said the following—while lodging in Sur, in the house of Ibn Abī ʿAqīl—and inscribed these verses on a piece of marble:

verses.h1: إذا نلت في أرض معاشا وإن نأت
verses.h2: فلا تكثرن فيها نزاعا إلى الوطن

verses.h1: فما هي إلا بلدة مثل بلدة
verses.h2: وخيرهما ما كان عونا على الزمن

verses.h1: If you find a livelihood in a land, however distant,
verses.h2: do not pine too much there for your homeland.

verses.h1: For it is only one land like another,
verses.h2: and the better is whichever helps you withstand the times.

verses.h1: كم مشرق لي قد نقلت نواله
verses.h2: فجعلته لي عدة للمغرب

verses.h1: وأحب أوطان البلاد إلى الفتى
verses.h2: أرض ينال بها كريم المكسب

verses.h1: From many an eastern land I have carried away its bounty,
verses.h2: and made it my provision for the West.

verses.h1: The dearest homeland to a man
verses.h2: is a land where he earns an honorable livelihood.

verses.h1: لا يصرفنك عن عزم تهم به
verses.h2: نزوع نفس إلى أهل وأوطان

verses.h1: تلقى بكل بلاد أنت ساكنها
verses.h2: أرضا بأرض وإخوانا بإخوان

verses.h1: Do not be turned from a purpose you mean to pursue
verses.h2: by your soul’s longing for family and homeland.

verses.h1: In every country you settle in, you will find
verses.h2: land in place of land, and friends in place of friends.

verses.h1: قلقل ركابك في الفلا
verses.h2: ودع الغواني في القصور

verses.h1: فمحالفو أوطانهم
verses.h2: كشبيه سكان القبور

verses.h1: لولا التغرب ما ارتقى
verses.h2: در البحور إلى النحور

verses.h1: Urge your mounts across the wilderness,
verses.h2: and leave the beauties in their palaces.

verses.h1: For those who cleave to their homelands
verses.h2: are like the dwellers in graves.

verses.h1: Were it not for travel abroad, never would rise
verses.h2: the pearls of the seas to necks.

verses.h1: لأرحلن المطايا رحلة عجبا
verses.h2: يكون أدنى مداها الصين أو عدن

verses.h1: فكل خل إذا صافيته سكن
verses.h2: وكل أرض إذا أحمدتها وطن

verses.h1: I shall surely saddle my mounts for a wondrous journey,
verses.h2: whose nearest destination will be al-Ṣīn or ʿAdan.

verses.h1: Every friend, if you offer him sincere affection, is a solace,
verses.h2: and every land, if you find it good, is a homeland.

verses.h1: وملوح الخدين تحمله
verses.h2: أبدا على أعناقها السبل

verses.h1: ناب عن الأوطان فهو متى
verses.h2: ظفرت به الأوطان يرتحل

verses.h1: ترك البلاد لمن أقام بها
verses.h2: وتقطعت عن عيسه العقل

verses.h1: يسعى إلى العلياء يحرزها
verses.h2: سعيا تحامى وقعة الزلل

verses.h1: وإذا الفتى كتب النجاء له
verses.h2: فالكلم يعفو والأذى جلل

verses.h1: And a man with sun-scorched cheeks, whom
verses.h2: the roads forever carry upon their necks.

verses.h1: He shuns his native lands; whenever
verses.h2: those lands gain hold of him, he journeys on.

verses.h1: He has left the lands to those who dwell in them,
verses.h2: and the hobbles have snapped off his pale camels.

verses.h1: He strives for eminence and wins it,
verses.h2: with a striving that avoids a stumbling fall.

verses.h1: When deliverance is decreed for a young man,
verses.h2: the wound heals, and hurt is a small thing.

notes.note: النجاء can mean deliverance or swift travel; I have understood it as deliverance here.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, may God have mercy on him, said:

poems.poet_from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: يا لهف نفسي على أني رجعت إلى
verses.h2: أرض الشآم ولم أهلك ببغداذا

verses.h1: إذا رأيت أمورا لا توافقني
verses.h2: قلت: الإياب إلى الأوطان أدى ذا

verses.h1: Alas for me, that I returned to
verses.h2: the land of al-Shām and did not die in Baghdad!

verses.h1: Whenever I see things that do not suit me,
verses.h2: I say, “Returning to my homeland brought this about.”

prose_translation.intro: And Shaykh Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

poems.intro: وقال جدي الأمير سديد الملك ذو المناقب أبو الحسن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ رحمه الله:

verses.h1: ولست بمحيار العزيمة إن جرت
verses.h2: عليه رياح الخطب وهي زعازع

verses.h1: يكر إلى الأوطان طرفا موزعا
verses.h2: يلين لها طورا وطورا يمانع

verses.h1: إذا ساف من تلقائها الريح لم يزل
verses.h2: له نفس في إثرها متتابع

verses.h1: أبى ذاك نفس لا يداني عقالها
verses.h2: ثواء، ولا تقضي عليها المطامع

verses.h1: I am not a man whose resolve falters when
verses.h2: the winds of calamity sweep over him in violent gusts—

verses.h1: one who turns a distracted gaze toward his homeland,
verses.h2: now yielding to its pull, now resisting;

verses.h1: when he scents the breeze coming from its direction,
verses.h2: his sighs follow it without cease.

verses.h1: My soul rejects that: it cannot be bound
verses.h2: by staying put, nor can desires rule it.

notes.note: I take the third-person verbs in lines 2–3 as continuing the description of the wavering man whom the speaker denies resembling, rather than describing the speaker himself.

The compressed expression «لا يداني عقالها ثواء», literally something like ‘settled residence does not approach its tether,’ is uncertain. I understand it to mean that remaining in one place cannot bind the speaker’s soul.

prose_translation.intro: And my grandfather, the emir Sadīd al-Mulk Dhū al-Manāqib Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Muqallad ibn Naṣr ibn Munqidh—may God have mercy on him—said:

verses.h1: لله ما طيف ألم بفتية
verses.h2: تحنو رؤوسهم على الأكوار

verses.h1: يطوى بهم عرض الفلاة مسربل
verses.h2: حلل الثناء ممزق الأطمار

verses.h1: لا تلفت الأوطان عزمته ولا
verses.h2: يهدي الحنين إلى رسوم الدار

verses.h1: How wondrous the phantom that visited a band of youths,
verses.h2: their heads bent over the camel-saddles!

verses.h1: A man bears them across the wilderness’s breadth, clothed
verses.h2: in robes of praise, his ragged garments torn.

verses.h1: Homelands do not turn him from his purpose, nor
verses.h2: does longing guide him to the dwelling’s traces.

notes.note: The wording لله ما طيف is unusual; it is taken here as an exclamation of wonder at the visiting phantom.

يطوى is read as يطوي, ‘he traverses’ or ‘bears across,’ with مسربل, ‘one clothed,’ as its subject. The person described is not explicitly identified; the transmitted spelling also permits a passive reading, which leaves the syntax less clear.

يهدي الحنين is taken as ‘longing guides [him],’ with the object understood. It could alternatively be read يُهدي الحنينَ, ‘he offers his longing,’ yielding ‘nor does he offer his longing to the dwelling’s traces.’

verses.h1: وقارعتني صروف الدهر فانكشف
verses.h2: طخياؤها عن كريم الأصل والغصن

verses.h1: عن ابن ليل كنجم الليل همته
verses.h2: مشيع القلب لا يلوي على وطن

verses.h1: وأي حر إلى الأوطان ملتفت
verses.h2: إذا ألح عليه الدهر بالمحن

verses.h1: أينفع الظامئ الملهوف موقفه
verses.h2: وقد فنى الماء بين الحوض والعطن؟

verses.h1: مسدد العزم إن نابته نائبة
verses.h2: فما يقيم على ربع ولا سكن

verses.h1: Time’s vicissitudes assailed me; then lifted
verses.h2: their darkness from one noble in root and branch.

verses.h1: From a night-roamer whose ambition is like the night’s star,
verses.h2: stouthearted, casting no backward glance toward any homeland.

verses.h1: What noble man turns his gaze toward his homeland
verses.h2: when time relentlessly besets him with afflictions?

verses.h1: Does standing still avail the desperate, thirsty man
verses.h2: when the water has run out between the trough and the camels’ resting place?

verses.h1: Firm in resolve when a calamity befalls him,
verses.h2: he will not remain at any dwelling or abode.

notes.note: ابن ليل, literally “son of night,” is taken here as a night-roamer or night-traveler; the epithet’s precise implication is uncertain.

verses.h1: قوض خيامك عن أرض تهان بها
verses.h2: وجانب الذل إن الذل يجتنب

verses.h1: وارحل إذا كانت الأوطان نابية
verses.h2: فالمندل الرطب في أوطانه حطب

verses.h1: Strike your tents and leave a land where you are humiliated;
verses.h2: shun abasement, for abasement is to be shunned.

verses.h1: Depart when your homeland turns hostile;
verses.h2: for even fresh aloeswood is firewood in its native land.

notes.note: Al-mandal denotes a fragrant Indian wood, variously identified as aloeswood or sandalwood; the precise identification is uncertain.

verses.h1: يا مصر ما درت في وهمي ولا خلدي
verses.h2: ولا أجالتك خلواتي بأفكاري

verses.h1: ما أنت أول أرض مس تربتها
verses.h2: جلدي ولا فيك أوطاني وأوطاري

verses.h1: لكن إذا حمت الأقدار كان لها
verses.h2: قوى تؤلف بين الماء والنار

verses.h1: O Miṣr, you never crossed my fancy or my mind,
verses.h2: nor did my hours of solitude bring you into my thoughts.

verses.h1: You are not the first land whose soil has touched
verses.h2: my skin, nor are my native homes or my heart’s desires in you.

verses.h1: Yet when fate’s decrees are sealed, they have
verses.h2: the power to bring water and fire together.

prose_translation.intro: And I said, while I was in Miṣr:

verses.h1: ترى الذي اتخذ الدنيا له وطنا
verses.h2: لم يدر أن المنايا عنه تزعجه

verses.h1: من كان يعلم أن الموت مدرجه
verses.h2: والقبر منزله، والبعث مخرجه

verses.h1: وأنه بين جنات ستبهجه
verses.h2: يوم القيامة، أو نار ستنضجه

verses.h1: فكل شيء سوى التقوى به سمج
verses.h2: وما أقام عليه فهو أسمجه

verses.h1: You see one who has made this world his home,
verses.h2: not knowing that death will drive him from it.

verses.h1: Whoever knows that death is his path,
verses.h2: the grave his dwelling, and resurrection his departure,

verses.h1: and that he faces either gardens that will delight him
verses.h2: on the Day of Resurrection, or a fire that will roast him—

verses.h1: then everything but piety ill becomes him,
verses.h2: and whatever else he persists in is ugliest of all.

notes.note: The final hemistich is compressed and ambiguous, particularly the pronoun in أسمجه. I take ما أقام عليه to mean whatever conduct other than piety he persists in, with persistence making it especially unseemly.

verses.h1: من الخراب من الأوطان أوطاني
verses.h2: وقد مضى لي في العمران عمران

verses.h1: قد لمت أول من يثني عناني عن
verses.h2: سبل الهوى وزجرت الثاني الثاني

verses.h1: في مجلس تبهج الرائين رؤيته
verses.h2: ولي قرينان من حلوان حلوان

verses.h1: لا يحضران امرءا عندي بمنقصة
verses.h2: ولا إذا جادت الكفان كفاني

verses.h1: لكن يكدر عيشي بعد ذي هيف
verses.h2: إدمانه الخطر بالأردان أرداني

verses.h1: تقول ألحاظه: أنظر، فقد ضمنت
verses.h2: أشباه ما ضمت الأجفان أجفاني

verses.h1: جفا، وما كان يجفوني وغادرني
verses.h2: ميتا، ولو شاء في الأحيان أحياني

verses.h1: والحين أبعد عن مأواي مسكنه
verses.h2: ولو تقاربت الداران داراني

verses.h1: وحاسد غره بعدي فأسخطني
verses.h2: ولو تجاورت الأرضان أرضاني

verses.h1: كم قد وري من حسود ما يعاين من
verses.h2: فضلي، وكم قد شجى من شأني شاني

verses.h1: My homes are among the homelands laid waste;
verses.h2: two lifetimes of mine have passed among thriving dwellings.

verses.h1: I blamed the first to turn my reins away from
verses.h2: the paths of passion, and rebuked the second who turned me back.

verses.h1: In a gathering whose sight delights those who behold it,
verses.h2: I have two sweet companions from Ḥulwān.

verses.h1: They speak of no one’s shortcomings in my presence,
verses.h2: nor, when my hands give generously, do they restrain me.

verses.h1: But separation from a slender-waisted one clouds my life;
verses.h2: his ceaseless swagger, sleeves swinging, has undone me.

verses.h1: His glances say: “Look! Held within
verses.h2: my eyelids are the likes of what scabbards hold.”

verses.h1: He shunned me, though he never used to, and left me
verses.h2: dead; yet, if he wished, he could sometimes bring me back to life.

verses.h1: Cruel fate has set his dwelling far from my abode;
verses.h2: had our two homes been close, he would have treated me kindly.

verses.h1: An envious man, emboldened by my distance, has angered me;
verses.h2: had our lands adjoined, he would have sought to please me.

verses.h1: How many an envious man has been consumed by what he sees of
verses.h2: my merit; how many a hater has choked with grief at my fortunes!

notes.note: I read عمران as the dual of عُمر, “two lifetimes,” in wordplay with العمران, “inhabited or flourishing places”; the intended force of the dual is uncertain.
Ḥulwān is a place-name borne by several localities; which one is intended is uncertain.
لا يحضران امرءا عندي بمنقصة literally suggests bringing someone before the speaker with a fault attributed to him. I take it to mean that the companions do not disparage others in his presence.
وري appears to be وَرِيَ, referring to an internal consuming disease or ulceration, here caused figuratively by envy. “Has been consumed” reflects this reading.

poems.intro: عن سهل بن عبد الله - رحمه الله - أنه كان ينفق ماله في طاعة الله تعالى، فجاءت أمه وإخوته إلى عبد الله بن المبارك - رضي الله عنه - يشكونه، فقالوا: هذا لا يمسك شيئا، ونخشى عليه الفقر، فأراد عبد الله أن يعينهم عليه، فقال له سهل: يا عبد الله أرأيت لو أن رجلا من أهل المدينة اشترى ضيعة برستاق، وهو يريد أن يتحول عن المدينة إليها، أكان يخلف بالمدينة شيئا وهو يسكن الرستاق؟ فقال عبد الله - رحمه الله -: خصمكم، يعني أنه إذا أراد أن يتحول إلى الرستاق لا يترك بالمدينة شيئا، فالذي يريد أن يتحول إلى الآخرة كيف يترك في الدنيا شيئا؟ قال أبو نواس:

verses.h1: أين من كان قبلنا
verses.h2: من ذويب البأس والخطر

verses.h1: سائلوا عنهم المدا
verses.h2: ئن واستخبروا الخمر

verses.h1: سبقونا إلى الرحي_ل، وإنا لبالأثر
من مضى عبرة لنا
verses.h2: وغدا نحن معتبر

verses.h1: Where are those who lived before us,
verses.h2: men of might and high standing?

verses.h1: Ask the cities about them,
verses.h2: and seek tidings from the thickets.

verses.h1: They departed before us, and we follow in their tracks.
Those who have passed are a lesson to us,
verses.h2: and tomorrow we shall be a lesson.

notes.note: ذويب appears to be a typographical error for ذوي, giving ذوي البأس والخطر, ‘men of might and high standing.’
الخمر is uncertain. I read it as al-khamar, ‘thickets’ or ‘coverts,’ which fits the rhyme in -ar, rather than al-khamr, ‘wine.’
الرحي_ل contains an intrusive underscore and has been read as الرحيل, ‘departure.’

prose_translation.intro: It is related of Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah—may God have mercy on him—that he used to spend his wealth in obedience to God Most High. His mother and brothers came to ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubārak—may God be pleased with him—to complain about him. They said, “He keeps nothing, and we fear he will fall into poverty.” ʿAbd Allah wished to take their side against him, but Sahl said to him, “O ʿAbd Allah, tell me: if a man from the city bought an estate in a rural district, intending to move there from the city, would he leave anything behind in the city when he was going to live in the countryside?” ʿAbd Allah—may God have mercy on him—said, “He has bested you in argument!” He meant that if someone intends to move to the countryside, he leaves nothing in the city; how, then, could someone who intends to move to the Hereafter leave anything in this world?! Abū Nuwās said:

verses.h1: قد قلت للزباء لما أصبحت
verses.h2: في حد ناب للزمان ومخلب

verses.h1: لمدينة عجماء قد أمسى البلى
verses.h2: فيها خطيبا باللسان المعرب

verses.h1: فكأنما سكن الفناء فناءها
verses.h2: أوصال فيها الدهر صولة مغضب

verses.h1: I said to al-Zabbāʾ, when it had come
verses.h2: within reach of Time’s fang and claw—

verses.h1: to a speechless city, where decay had become
verses.h2: a preacher speaking in an eloquent tongue:

verses.h1: It was as though destruction had settled in its courtyard,
verses.h2: or Time had assailed it with an angry man’s onslaught.

notes.note: Al-Zabbāʾ is described here as a city; its precise identification is uncertain.
Read «أوصال» as «أو صال» (“or [Time] assailed”); the words appear to have been joined through a spacing error.

verses.h1: سل المدائن عمن كان يملكها
verses.h2: هل آنست منهم من بعدهم خبرا

verses.h1: فلو أجابتك قالت
verses.h2: وهي عالمة بسيرة الذاهب الماضي ومن غبرا

verses.h1: أرتهم العبر الدنيا، فما اعتبروا
verses.h2: فصيرتهم لقوم بعدهم عبرا

verses.h1: Ask the cities about those who once ruled them:
verses.h2: “Have you heard any tidings of them since they departed?”

verses.h1: Had they answered you, they would have said—
verses.h2: knowing the ways of those who have passed away and those who remain—

verses.h1: “The world showed them lessons, but they took no heed;
verses.h2: so it made them lessons for a people coming after them.”

notes.note: غبر can mean either ‘remained’ or ‘passed away.’ ‘Those who remain’ is adopted here, but ‘those who passed away’ is also possible.
The hemistich division appears misplaced: metrically, وهي عالمة likely belongs at the end of h1. The supplied division has been retained.

poems.intro: عن سليمان بن عياش قال: قالت أنيسة زوجة جبهاء الأشجعي لجبهاء: لو هاجرت إلى المدينة، وبعت إبلك، وافترضت في العضاء، كان خيرا لك، قال: أفعل، فأقبل غاديا بإبله، حتى إذا كان بحرة واقم من شرقي المدينة شرعها بحوض واقم يسقيها، فحنت ناقة منها، ثم نزعت، وتبعتها الإبل ففاتته، فقال جبهاء لزوجته: هذه الإبل لا تعقل تحن إلى أوطانها، ونحن أولى بالحنين منها، أنت طالق إن لم ترجعي [فقالت] : فعل الله بك وفعل، فردها، وقال:

verses.h1: قالت أنيسة: دع بلادك والتمس
verses.h2: دارا بطيبة ربة الآطام

verses.h1: تكتب عيالك في العطاء، وتفترض
verses.h2: وكذاك يفعل حازم الأقوام

verses.h1: فهممت ثم ذكرت ليل لقاحنا
verses.h2: بلوى عنيزة أو بقف بسام

verses.h1: إذ هن عن حسبي مذاود كلما
verses.h2: نزل الظلام بعصبة أعيام

verses.h1: إن المدينة لا مدينة فالزمي
verses.h2: حقف السناد، وقنة الاجام

verses.h1: وتجاوري النفر الذين بنبلهم
verses.h2: أرمى العدو إذا تهضم رام

verses.h1: الباذلين
verses.h2: إذا طلبت تلادهم

verses.h1: والمانعي ظهري من العرام
Unaysah said: “Leave your country and seek
verses.h2: a home in Ṭaybah, the city of strongholds.

verses.h1: You can register your dependents for stipends and claim an allowance yourself;
verses.h2: that is what prudent men do.”

verses.h1: I nearly agreed, then remembered our milch-camels at night
verses.h2: at Liwā ʿUnayzah or Quff Bassām,

verses.h1: when they defended my honor whenever
verses.h2: darkness fell upon a band of men craving milk.

verses.h1: “Al-Madīnah is no city for us; keep, then, to
verses.h2: the sand-ridge of al-Sinād and the peak of al-Ājām,

verses.h1: and dwell beside those men with whose arrows
verses.h2: I shoot the enemy when an archer wrongs me:

verses.h1: those who freely give,
verses.h2: when you ask, their inherited wealth,

verses.h1: and shield my back from aggression.”

notes.note: Liwā ʿUnayzah and Quff Bassām are unidentified here; the vocalization of Bassām is uncertain. The phrase ليل لقاحنا, literally “the night of our milch-camels,” is compressed and somewhat obscure.
أعيام is understood as describing men craving milk, from the root عيم. The implied defense of the speaker’s honor appears to be the camels’ provision of milk for guests.
The places al-Sinād and al-Ājām are unidentified, and their vocalization is uncertain. “For us” is supplied in interpreting the elliptical إن المدينة لا مدينة, literally “al-Madīnah is no city.”
The wording إذا تهضم رام is ambiguous. The translation takes رام as “an archer” and تهضم as “acts unjustly toward”; the object “me” is inferred.
The supplied lines 7–8 appear to divide one bayt irregularly: الباذلين إذا طلبت تلادهم / والمانعي ظهري من العرام. The supplied divisions have been preserved.

prose_translation.intro: From Sulaymān ibn ʿAyyāsh, who said: Unaysah, the wife of Jabhāʾ al-Ashjaʿī, said to Jabhāʾ, “If you were to move to al-Madīnah, sell your camels, and have yourself enrolled for a stipend, it would be better for you.” He said, “I shall.” So he set out early in the morning with his camels. When he reached Ḥarrat Wāqim, east of al-Madīnah, he brought them to Wāqim’s watering trough to give them water. One she-camel among them let out a yearning cry, then broke away, and the other camels followed her and escaped him. Jabhāʾ said to his wife, “These camels, though they have no understanding, yearn for their homeland, and we have more reason to yearn than they do. You are divorced if you do not return.” [She said,] “May God do this and that to you!” So he took her back, and said:

verses.h1: ذهب الرجال فلا أحس رجالا
verses.h2: وأرى الإقامة بالعراق ضلالا

verses.h1: وأرى المرجى للعراق وأهله
verses.h2: ظمآن هاجرة يؤمل آلا

verses.h1: وطربت أن ذكر المدينة ذاكر
verses.h2: يوم الخميس فهاج لي بلبالا

verses.h1: وجعلت أنظر في السماء كأنني
verses.h2: أبغي بناحية السماء هلالا

verses.h1: طربا إلى أهل الحجاز وتارة
verses.h2: أبكي بدمع مسبل إسبالا

verses.h1: The men are gone; I find no men remaining,
verses.h2: and I see staying in al-ʿIrāq as folly.

verses.h1: I see one who pins his hopes on al-ʿIrāq and its people
verses.h2: as a man thirsty in the midday heat, hoping for a mirage.

verses.h1: I was stirred with longing when someone mentioned al-Madīnah
verses.h2: on Thursday, rousing anguish within me.

verses.h1: I began to gaze into the sky, as though I
verses.h2: were seeking a crescent in some quarter of the heavens,

verses.h1: in longing for the people of al-Ḥijāz; and at times
verses.h2: I weep with tears streaming freely.

notes.note: I read المرجى as المرجِّي, “one who hopes.” The printed spelling could suggest a passive form, “one hoped for,” which is difficult to construe here.

poems.intro: عن عبد الله بن مسعود - رضي الله عنه - قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "ما من بلدة تاب فيها تائب إلا رحم الله تعالى أهل تلك البلدة، ورفع عنهم العذاب". وقال ابن مسعود - رضي الله عنه - قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "أيما رجل جلب طعاما إلى بلد من بلاد المسلمين، فباعه بسعر يومه محتسبا، كان عند الله بمنزلة الشهيد، ثم تلا: (وآخرون يضربون في الأرض يبتغون من فضل الله) . قال أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليه - "من سعادة الرجل خمس: أن تكون زوجته موافقة، وأولاده أبرارا، وإخوانه أتقياء، وجيرانه صالحين، ورزقه في بلده". عن الأصمعي قال: سمعت أعرابيا يقول: شر المال ما لا ينفق، وشر الإخوان الخاذل في الشدائد، وشر السلاطين من يخافه البريء، وشر البلاد ما ليس فيه خصب ولا أمن. وقال أبو زياد الطائي:

verses.h1: أحقا عباد الله أن لست ناسيا
verses.h2: بلادي ولا قومي ولا ساكنا نجدا؟

verses.h1: ولا ناظرا نحو الحمى اليوم نظرة
verses.h2: أسلى بها قلبي، ولا محدثا عهدا

verses.h1: بلاد بها نيطت على تمائمي
verses.h2: وكان بها عصر الصبي نضرا رغدا

verses.h1: بلاد بها قومي، وارض أحبها
verses.h2: وإن لم أجد من طول هجرتها بدا

verses.h1: Is it true, servants of God, that I shall not forget
verses.h2: my homeland or my people, nor dwell in Najd?

verses.h1: Nor cast a glance today toward the protected pasture
verses.h2: to soothe my heart, nor renew my acquaintance with it?

verses.h1: A land where my amulets were hung upon me,
verses.h2: where childhood’s days were fresh and full of ease.

verses.h1: A land where my people live, a land I love,
verses.h2: though I have found no escape from long absence from it.

notes.note: The wording ‘نيطت على تمائمي’ appears to require ‘نيطت عليّ تمائمي’: ‘my amulets were hung upon me.’ Also, ‘عصر الصبي’ may be a misprint for ‘عصر الصبا’, ‘the days of childhood’; the translation follows that sense.

prose_translation.intro: From ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿūd—may God be pleased with him—who said: The Messenger of God—may God bless him and grant him peace—said: “There is no town in which someone repents but that God Most High has mercy on the people of that town and lifts punishment from them.” Ibn Masʿūd—may God be pleased with him—also said: The Messenger of God—may God bless him and grant him peace—said: “Any man who brings food to a town among the towns of the Muslims and sells it at that day’s price, seeking God’s reward, has with God the standing of a martyr.” Then he recited: “And others travel through the land, seeking of God’s bounty.” The Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God’s good pleasure be upon him—said: “Five things contribute to a man’s happiness: that his wife be agreeable, his children dutiful, his brothers pious, his neighbors righteous, and his livelihood in his own town.” From al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: I heard a Bedouin say: “The worst wealth is that which is not spent; the worst brother is one who abandons you in adversity; the worst ruler is one whom the innocent fear; and the worst land is one with neither abundance nor security.” Abū Ziyād al-Ṭāʾī said:

verses.h1: ألا ليت شعري هل أسير ناقتي
verses.h2: ببيضاء نجد حيث كان مسيرها

verses.h1: بلاد بها أنضيت راحلة الصبي
verses.h2: ولانت لنا أيامها وشهورها

verses.h1: فقدنا بها الهم المضل وشربه
verses.h2: ودار علينا بالنعيم سرورها

verses.h1: Ah, would that I knew: shall I drive my she-camel
verses.h2: through Bayḍāʾ Najd, where she used to travel?

verses.h1: A land where I wore out the mount of youth,
verses.h2: and its days and months were gentle with us.

verses.h1: There we were free of bewildering care and its draught,
verses.h2: and its joy brought bliss round to us.

notes.note: بيضاء نجد may be a place name, Bayḍāʾ Najd, or simply mean ‘the white plain of Najd’; the locality is uncertain.
الصبي is read as الصِّبا, ‘youth,’ in the metaphor ‘the mount of youth.’ The printed spelling may be an error; read literally, it could mean ‘the boy.’
وشربه is unclear. ‘And its draught’ is tentative; شربه could also refer to drinking companions. The intended expression, or the integrity of the text, is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Ṣadaqa ibn Nāfiʿ al-Ghanawī said:

poems.intro: حكي عن كاتب لأمير الحاج أنه قال: نزلنا مرة بظاهر الكوفة، ونحن متوجهون إلى الحج، فكنت كل يوم أغدو إلى الكوفة لحوائجي، ويقابلني رجل زمن يزحف. فكنت أظنه يقصد الحاج للسؤال، فاتفق أن تبعته يوما، حتى كان بموضع يشرف منه على أخبية الحاج، فسمعته يقول:

verses.h1: أعلمت كيف تصبري
verses.h2: عن رؤية البلد الحرام

verses.h1: والمشعرين ومسجد
verses.h2: بالخيف يشهد كل عام

verses.h1: وعن التزام المشعري
verses.h2: ن وعن صلاة بالمقام

verses.h1: وعن الزيارة للنب
verses.h2: ي المصطفى خير الأنام

verses.h1: كتصبر المدفوع بال
verses.h2: أسقام عن طيب المنام

verses.h1: Do you know how I bear being kept
verses.h2: from the sight of the Sacred City,

verses.h1: And the two sacred sites, and a mosque
verses.h2: at al-Khayf, frequented every year,

verses.h1: And from clinging to the two sacred sites,
verses.h2: and from prayer at the Maqām,

verses.h1: And from visiting the Prophet,
verses.h2: the Chosen One, the best of humankind?

verses.h1: Like the endurance of one driven
verses.h2: by sickness from sweet sleep.

notes.note: The precise places intended by al-mashʿarayn, “the two sacred sites,” are uncertain.
Iltizām means embracing or clinging to; its application here to “the two sacred sites” is unusual, and the intended ritual action is unclear.

prose_translation.intro: It is related that a secretary to the commander of the pilgrimage said: Once, while on our way to perform the pilgrimage, we camped outside al-Kūfa. Every morning I would go into al-Kūfa on my errands, and I would encounter a crippled man crawling along. I thought he was making his way toward the pilgrims to beg. One day I happened to follow him until he reached a spot overlooking the pilgrims’ tents, and I heard him say:

poems.intro: قال: ثم ظعنا عن الكوفة ليالي وأياما، ثم إني سمرت عند الأمير ليلة، فحدثته الحديث، فأحضر نجابا، وثلاثة نجب، وقال لي: اذهب مع هذا النجاب فأتيني به، فقلت: إن ذلك يشق علي، وأنا أدل الرسول عليه، فقال: قد علمت أنك تدل الرسول، ولكني أردت عقوبتك؛ لتأخيرك إخباري عنه، فمضيت فأتيت به. وقال أشجع السلمي:

verses.h1: ومغترب ينقضي ليله
verses.h2: فنونا ومقلته تدمع

verses.h1: يؤرقه نأيه في البلا
verses.h2: د، فما يستقر به مضجع

verses.h1: إذا الليل ألبسه ثوبه
verses.h2: تقلب فيه فتى موجع

verses.h1: And an exile whose night passes
verses.h2: in varied woes, while his eye sheds tears.

verses.h1: His remoteness in distant lands keeps him awake,
verses.h2: and no bed gives him rest.

verses.h1: When night clothes him in its robe,
verses.h2: he tosses within it, a young man in pain.

notes.note: فنونا literally means ‘in various kinds or forms’; what varies is unstated. ‘In varied woes’ takes it as referring to changing forms of distress.

prose_translation.intro: He said: Then we journeyed away from al-Kūfa for nights and days. One night I stayed up conversing with the emir and told him the story. He summoned a camel courier and three swift riding camels, and said to me, “Go with this courier and bring him to me.” I said, “That would be a hardship for me, but I can direct the messenger to him.” He replied, “I know you can direct the messenger, but I wished to punish you for delaying your report about him.” So I went and brought him. And Ashjaʿ al-Sulamī said:

verses.h1: ألا هل إلى نص النواعج بالضحى
verses.h2: وشم الخزامى بالغوير سبيل؟

verses.h1: بلاد بها أهل الهوى غير أنني
verses.h2: أميل مع الأقدار حيث تميل

verses.h1: Ah, is there a way to urge the swift she-camels on at midmorning
verses.h2: and breathe the scent of lavender at al-Ghuwayr?

verses.h1: A land where those I love dwell; yet I
verses.h2: turn with fate wherever it turns.

notes.note: Al-Ghuwayr is a place name, but its precise location is uncertain.
أهل الهوى could mean ‘lovers’ generally rather than ‘those I love.’

poems.poet_from_text: أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد الأندلسي يرثي صديقا له
poems.intro: وقال أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد الأندلسي يرثي صديقا له:

poet.from_text: أبو عبد الله محمد بن عثمان المعروف بابن الحداد الأندلسي يرثي صديقا له

verses.h1: تيقن أن الله أكرم جيرة
verses.h2: فأزمع عن دار الفناء رحيلا

verses.h1: فإن أقفرت منه العيون فإنه
verses.h2: تعوض منها بالقلوب بديلا

verses.h1: ولم أر أنسا بعده صار وحشة
verses.h2: وبردا على الأكباد صار غليلا

verses.h1: ومن كن أيام السرور قصيرة
verses.h2: به كان ليل الحزن فيه طويلا

verses.h1: He knew for certain that God was the most generous of neighbors,
verses.h2: so he resolved to depart from the abode of mortality.

verses.h1: Though eyes are bereft of him,
verses.h2: he has taken hearts in their stead.

verses.h1: Never have I seen such companionship turn, after him, to desolation,
verses.h2: or such coolness upon the heart turn to burning thirst.

verses.h1: For one whose presence made the days of joy seem short,
verses.h2: the night of grief for him was long.

notes.note: The negative construction ولم أر is awkward in context. I have understood it as an expression of astonishment, supplying an implied comparison (‘such’); read strictly literally, it would deny having seen companionship turn to desolation.

prose_translation.intro: Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān, known as Ibn al-Ḥaddād al-Andalusī, said, elegizing a friend of his:

poems.poet: عُيَيْنة بن الحباب بن المنذر بن الجموح
poems.poet_from_text: عيينة بن الحباب بن المنذر بن الجموح الأنصاري
poems.intro: وقال عيينة بن الحباب بن المنذر بن الجموح الأنصاري:

poet.expected: عُيَيْنة بن الحباب بن المنذر بن الجموح
poet.from_text: عيينة بن الحباب بن المنذر بن الجموح الأنصاري

verses.h1: أراكم بقلبي من بلاد بعيدة
verses.h2: تراكم تروني بالقلوب على بعدي؟

verses.h1: فؤادي وطرفي يأسفان عليكم
verses.h2: وعندكم روحي، وذكركم عندي

verses.h1: ولست ألذ العيش حتى أراكم
verses.h2: ولو كنت في الفردوس أو جنة الخلد

verses.h1: I see you in my heart from a distant land;
verses.h2: I wonder, do you see me in your hearts, though I am far away?

verses.h1: My heart and my eyes grieve for you;
verses.h2: my soul is with you, and your memory is with me.

verses.h1: I find no pleasure in life until I see you,
verses.h2: even were I in al-Firdaws or the Garden of Eternity.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUyayna ibn al-Ḥubāb ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jamūḥ al-Anṣārī said:

poems.intro: وقالت امرأة من العرب زوجها عمها رجلا شاميا، فنقلها إلى الشام، فاشتاقت بلادها:

verses.h1: ألا يا خليلي اللذين أراهما
verses.h2: ذوي ثقتي من دون من كان حافيا

verses.h1: سقى الله
verses.h2: والسقيا إليه بلادنا بحزم قناوين الذهاب الغواديا

verses.h1: بلاد جميع، والعظيم أحبهم
verses.h2: وإن كنت قد أيقنت ألا تلاقيا

verses.h1: ألا ليت لي عما بعمى، وليت لي
verses.h2: مكان بنيه من معد مواليا

verses.h1: أناسا إذا خافوا على ظلامة
verses.h2: وضيما أحاطوا بالقنا من ورائيا

verses.h1: فلا بارك الرحمن في وجه حرة
verses.h2: يمانية بعدي تحب شآميا

verses.h1: O my two friends, whom I regard
verses.h2: as my trusted confidants above all who show me care,

verses.h1: May God water
verses.h2: —for watering is His to grant—our lands at Ḥazm Qanāwayn with gentle morning rains:

verses.h1: The lands of my people—by the Almighty, I love them—
verses.h2: though I have become certain we shall not meet.

verses.h1: Would that I had another uncle in place of mine, and would that I had,
verses.h2: in place of his sons, allies from Maʿadd:

verses.h1: People who, if they feared injustice against me
verses.h2: or oppression, would surround me with spears, standing at my back.

verses.h1: May the Merciful never bless the face of any freeborn
verses.h2: Yemeni woman who, after me, loves a Syrian.

notes.note: حافيا is uncertain here. I have tentatively understood it as someone showing care or solicitude; its more familiar meaning, “barefoot,” does not readily fit the context.
Ḥazm Qanāwayn is an unidentified place; the vocalization of قناوين is uncertain. The supplied hemistich division is unusual, but has been preserved.
بلاد جميع is ambiguous. I have taken جميع as a company of people, understood here as her own people, but it might instead be a proper name, Jamīʿ. والعظيم is read as an oath, “by the Almighty.”

prose_translation.intro: An Arab woman whose paternal uncle had married her to a man from al-Shām, who then took her to al-Shām, said when she longed for her homeland:

verses.h1: وجدنا أبانا كان حل ببلدة
verses.h2: سوى بين قيس قيس عيلان والفزر

verses.h1: فلما نأت عنا العشيرة كلها
verses.h2: أنخنا فحالفنا السيوف على الدهر

verses.h1: فما أسلمتنا عند يوم كريهة
verses.h2: ولا نحن أغضينا الجفون على وتر

interludes.text: (الفزر: لقب لسعد بن زيد مناة بن تميم، وكان أنهب معزاه بعكاظ، ويقال لجماعة المعزى: الفزر، فسمي بذلك) :

verses.h1: We found that our father had settled in a land
verses.h2: midway between Qays—Qays ʿAylān—and al-Fizr.

verses.h1: When the whole clan had moved far away from us,
verses.h2: we made camp and bound ourselves to swords forever.

verses.h1: They never forsook us on a day of battle,
verses.h2: nor did we close our eyes to an unavenged wrong.

notes.note: سوى بين is understood as ‘midway between,’ though the construction is uncertain. Al-Fizr may designate Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt of Tamīm and, by extension, his descendants; the identification is uncertain.

interludes: (Al-Fizr: a sobriquet of Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. He had let his goats be plundered at ʿUkāẓ. A herd of goats is called al-fizr, and so he was given this name.)

verses.h1: أقول وقد جاوزت نقمي وناقتي
verses.h2: تحن إلى جنبي فليج مع الفجر

verses.h1: سقى الله يا ناق البلاد التي بها
verses.h2: هواك وإن عنا نأت سبل القطر

verses.h1: فما عن قلى منا لها خفت النوى
verses.h2: بنا عن مراعيها وكثبانها العفر

verses.h1: ولكن صرف الدهر فرق بيننا
verses.h2: وبين الأداني والفتى غرض الدهر

verses.h1: فسقيا لصحراء الإهالة مربعا
verses.h2: وللوقبي من منزل دمث مثرى

verses.h1: وسقيا ورعيا حيث حلت لمازن
verses.h2: وأيامها الغر المحجلة الزهر

verses.h1: I speak, having passed Naqamā, while my she-camel
verses.h2: yearns at dawn for the two banks of Fulayj.

verses.h1: May God water, O she-camel, the lands where
verses.h2: your heart lies, though the roads to that region lie far from us.

verses.h1: It was not through any aversion to them that separation swept
verses.h2: us away from their pastures and pale dunes.

verses.h1: But the turns of time parted us
verses.h2: from those nearest to us; a man is time’s target.

verses.h1: May rain water Ṣaḥrāʾ al-Ihāla, a spring encampment,
verses.h2: and al-Waqbā—what a soft-soiled, fertile dwelling!

verses.h1: And rain and protection for Māzin wherever it has settled,
verses.h2: and for its radiant days, white-blazed and white-footed.

notes.note: The vocalization of نقمي, rendered Naqamā, is uncertain. I take جنبي فليج as the two banks or sides of the place Fulayj; its precise geographical reference is unclear.
I read القطر as quṭr, ‘region,’ and understand سبل القطر as the roads to that region. The unvocalized word can also mean ‘rain’ (Qaṭr), but the phrase would then be unclear.
I could not securely identify Ṣaḥrāʾ al-Ihāla or al-Waqbā. The latter is printed الوقبي; its rendering assumes الوقبى.

prose_translation.intro: And Hilāl ibn al-Asʿar al-Māzinī said:

verses.h1: وارحمنا للغريب في البلد النا
verses.h2: زح ماذا بنفسه صنعا؟

verses.h1: فارق أحبابه، فما انتفعوا
verses.h2: بالعيش من بعده ولا انتفعا

verses.h1: Ah, pity the stranger in a distant land—
verses.h2: what has he done to himself?

verses.h1: He parted from his loved ones, and they took no pleasure
verses.h2: in life after his departure, nor did he.

notes.note: The opening وارحمنا appears corrupt, probably for وارحمتا, an exclamation of pity; the translation follows that reading.

poems.poet: بشر أو عبد العزيز ابن مروان
poems.intro: وقال آخر: "قيل قائلها بشر بن مروان، وقيل: عبد العزيز بن مروان":

poet.expected: بشر أو عبد العزيز ابن مروان

verses.h1: كأني وعمرا لم نسر في مجاهل
verses.h2: ولم نزجر الوجناء في البلد القفر

verses.h1: لحى الله دنيا تدخل النار أهلها
verses.h2: وتهتك ما بين الأقارب من ستر

verses.h1: As though ʿAmr and I had never journeyed through trackless wastes,
verses.h2: nor urged the sturdy she-camel onward through the barren land.

verses.h1: May God curse a world that sends its people into the Fire
verses.h2: and rends the veil between kinsfolk.

prose_translation.intro: Another poet said (the author is said to have been Bishr ibn Marwān, or, according to another account, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān):

poems.intro: هذان البيتان في عمر بن سعيد بن العاص المعروف بالأشدق حين قتله عبد الملك بن مروان. عن يحيى بن سعيد الأموي قال: كسا عبد الله بن الزبير - رحمه الله - قومه بني أسد جبابا، فقال أبو العباس الأعمى:

verses.h1: كست أسد إخوانها ولو أنني
verses.h2: ببلدة إخواني إذن لكسيت

verses.h1: فلم أر مثل الحي حيا تحملوا
