verses.h1: A man’s life is only a moment,
verses.h2: with none of it before that moment or after.

verses.h1: How spacious the world is for its people,
verses.h2: if only its end were not the grave!

notes.note: The unvocalized أفرطت permits either ‘I have indulged too much’ or ‘you have indulged too much’; the second-person reading is adopted in light of the letter’s address.
The compressed wording لا قبلها منها ولا بعد is grammatically ambiguous; it is taken here to mean that life consists only of the present moment.

prose_translation.intro: From Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUbayd Allah al-Kūfī—may God have mercy on him—who said: Dāwūd al-Fārisī—may God have mercy on him, a learned and devout man—wrote to me in these words: “My brother, this world is an abode of stumbling and passing away, of change from one condition to another.” Then, at the end of his letter, he wrote these verses:

verses.h1: وللموت تغذو الوالدات سخالها
verses.h2: كما لخراب الدور تبنى المساكن

verses.h1: عجبت من الدنيا وذمي نعيمها
verses.h2: وحبي لها في مضمر القلب باطن

verses.h1: وقولي: أعذني رب من كل فتنة
verses.h2: وأكلف منها بالذي هو فاتن

verses.h1: It is for death that mothers nourish their young,
verses.h2: just as dwellings are built to fall to ruin.

verses.h1: I marvel at the world and at my condemning its pleasures,
verses.h2: while love for it lies concealed deep in my heart;

verses.h1: And at my saying, “Lord, protect me from every temptation,”
verses.h2: while I am enamored of what is alluring in it.

verses.h1: أرسوم دار أم سطور كتاب
verses.h2: درست بشاشتها مع الأحقاب؟

verses.h1: يجتاز زائرها بغير لبانة
verses.h2: ويرد سائلها بغير جواب

verses.h1: ولربما كان الزمان محببا
verses.h2: فينا بمن فيها من الأحباب

verses.h1: Are these the traces of a dwelling, or lines in a book,
verses.h2: whose brightness has faded with the ages?

verses.h1: Its visitor passes by with his longing unfulfilled,
verses.h2: and its questioner is sent back without an answer.

verses.h1: How often the days were dear
verses.h2: to us, because of the loved ones who dwelt there.

verses.h1: مالي في الدار بعد ساكنها
verses.h2: وإن تذكرت أهلها أرب

verses.h1: لا الدار ردت جواب سائلها
verses.h2: ولا بكت أهلها إذ اغتربوا

verses.h1: I have no desire for the dwelling now its inhabitants are gone,
verses.h2: though I remember its people.

verses.h1: The dwelling gave no answer to the one who questioned it,
verses.h2: nor did it weep for its people when they went far away.

verses.h1: لمن الدار كأنضاء الكتاب
verses.h2: هاجت الشوق وعيت بالجواب

verses.h1: لم تزدك الدار إلا طربا
verses.h2: والصبي غير شبيه بالتصابي

verses.h1: وبما قد كان فيها ساكن
verses.h2: أهل أنعام وخيل وقباب

verses.h1: Whose is the abode, like the worn remnants of a manuscript?
verses.h2: It stirred longing but could give no answer.

verses.h1: The abode only heightened your yearning;
verses.h2: youth is not the same as feigning youth.

verses.h1: Once there were people dwelling in it,
verses.h2: owners of herds, horses, and domed tents.

notes.note: الصبي normally means “the boy.” The contrast with التصابي (“acting young”) suggests that الصبا or الصبى (“youth”) is intended, and the translation follows that reading.
The construction وبما قد is uncertain; it is taken here as introducing a recollection of the abode’s former inhabitants.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿAdī ibn al-Riqāʿ al-ʿĀmilī said:

poems.intro: وقال أبو داوود الإيادي (واسمه جارية بن الحجاج) :

verses.h1: وقد عرفت الدار قفرا لم تحل
verses.h2: بين أجياد خفاف فالرحل

verses.h1: ظعن الحي الألى كانوا بها
verses.h2: وعفا رسم وأضحى كالخلل

verses.h1: هيج الشوق الذي كان صحا
verses.h2: حبسك اليوم على ذاك الطلل

verses.h1: I recognized the dwelling, deserted yet unchanged,
verses.h2: between Ajyād Khifāf and al-Raḥl.

verses.h1: The people who once lived there have departed;
verses.h2: its outline has faded and become like sheath-linings.

verses.h1: It stirred the longing that had subsided—
verses.h2: your lingering today over that ruined campsite.

notes.note: I take لم تحل to mean ‘unchanged,’ though the unvocalized wording also permits a reading connected with habitation. The places are unidentified; the vocalization and grouping of أجياد خفاف فالرحل are uncertain.
The comparison كالخلل is uncertain. ‘Sheath-linings’ provisionally takes الخلل as khilal, the plural of a word for the lining of a sword sheath.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Dāwūd al-Iyādī (whose name was Jāriya ibn al-Ḥajjāj) said:

verses.h1: أدار الجميع الصالحين بذي السدر
verses.h2: أبيني لنا إن التحية عن عفر

verses.h1: لقد طرفت في الدار عيني دمنة
verses.h2: تعاورها الأزمان بالريح والقطر

verses.h1: فقلت لأدنى صاحبي وإنني
verses.h2: لأكتم وجدا في الجوانح كالجمر

verses.h1: بعمركما لا تعجلاني موقفا
verses.h2: على الدار فيه القتل أو راحة الدهر

verses.h1: O dwelling of the goodly company at Dhū al-Sidr,
verses.h2: answer us: this greeting comes after long absence.

verses.h1: A darkened trace in the dwelling has struck my eye,
verses.h2: visited in turn by the seasons with wind and rain.

verses.h1: I said to the nearer of my two companions, while I
verses.h2: concealed within my ribs a longing like burning coals:

verses.h1: “By your lives, do not hurry me away from a halt
verses.h2: at the dwelling, where there is death or lasting relief.”

notes.note: Ṭarafat … ʿaynī literally suggests striking or pricking the eye. The ruined trace may be described as painfully affecting the poet’s sight, rather than merely catching his eye.

verses.h1: ألا حي رهبي ثم حي المطالي
verses.h2: فقد كان مأنوسا فأصبح خاليا

verses.h1: فلا عهد إلا أن تذكر أو ترى
verses.h2: ثماما حوالي نصب الخيم باليا

verses.h1: فيا ليت أن الحي لم يتفرقوا
verses.h2: وأمسوا جميعا جيرة متدانيا

verses.h1: فقد خفت ألا تجمع الدار بيننا
verses.h2: ولا الدهر إلا أن نجد الأمانيا

verses.h1: Ah, greet Rahbā, then greet al-Maṭālī:
verses.h2: once a place of company, it now lies empty.

verses.h1: No trace remains, save what you recall or see:
verses.h2: withered thumām grass around the places where the tents stood.

verses.h1: If only the people had not scattered,
verses.h2: but had remained together, neighbors close to one another.

verses.h1: For I have feared that no abode would bring us together,
verses.h2: nor time itself—save in the wishes we renew.

notes.note: I read رهبي as the place name Rahbā (رهبى), and المطالي as al-Maṭālī. Their precise locations are uncertain.
نصب الخيم is ambiguous: it may refer to the pitching sites of the tents or to their upright supports. The translation follows the former reading.

I provisionally read نجد as nujiddu, ‘we renew,’ from أجَدّ. The unvocalized wording and the relation of the final exception to the preceding statement are uncertain; the translation takes it to mean that reunion survives only in renewed wishes.

verses.h1: يا دار غيرها التقادم والبلى
verses.h2: بين السليل ومأمي أكباد

verses.h1: لا زلت في خفض عليك تهافتت
verses.h2: ديم عليك طويلة الإرعاد

verses.h1: وأنار واديك الربيع، فربما
verses.h2: نغني به ونراه أبهج واد

verses.h1: وأرى به الأنس الذين تحبهم
verses.h2: عيني، ويألف من تحب فؤادي

verses.h1: O dwelling, changed by passing time and decay,
verses.h2: between al-Salīl and Maʾmī Akbād!

verses.h1: May you ever know ease; may there pour upon you
verses.h2: steady rains, long thundering over you.

verses.h1: May spring brighten your valley, for often
verses.h2: we dwelt there and saw it as the loveliest of valleys.

verses.h1: And there I would see the companions whom
verses.h2: my eye loved; my heart cherished those my eye loved.

notes.note: The locations are unidentified. مأمي أكباد, provisionally transliterated Maʾmī Akbād, is unclear and may be corrupted; it could represent مآمي أكباد, ‘the wastes of Akbād.’
نغني is understood as نغنى, ‘we dwelt,’ rather than ‘we sing,’ in keeping with the context.

verses.h1: يا دار أقوت من بعد حاضرها
verses.h2: لم يبق فيها سوى أواصرها

verses.h1: ألقت عليها الرياح أردية
verses.h2: تنشرها من كسى أعاصرها

verses.h1: حييت من دمنة بما خلفت عين عطوف على جآذرها
يا ربما راقني بساحتها
verses.h2: طيب هواها، ولهو سامرها

verses.h1: أيام لا خوف من شتات نوى
verses.h2: تخشى، ولا روع من تطايرها

verses.h1: كنا بها حقبة فأزعجنا
verses.h2: خطب نفى الخفض عن مجاورها

verses.h1: شتت بين الخليط فارتحلوا
verses.h2: عنها وأبدى خراب عامرها

verses.h1: فالدار لو زرتها رأيت بها
verses.h2: آيا تهيج الأسى لزائرها

verses.h1: تلك المغاني فإن مررت بها
verses.h2: يوما فسلم على دواثرها

verses.h1: وانظر إليها؛ ألم تصر دمنا
verses.h2: تهفو السوافي على دعاثرها؟

verses.h1: O dwelling, deserted since its people left,
verses.h2: nothing remains within it but its fastenings.

verses.h1: The winds have cast cloaks over it,
verses.h2: spreading them from the garments of its whirlwinds.

verses.h1: Hail, ruined campsite, for what the wide-eyed cows, tender toward their calves, have left in you.
How often, in its courtyard, I delighted
verses.h2: in its pleasant air and the merriment of its evening company.

verses.h1: Days when no scattering through separation
verses.h2: was feared, nor any terror of dispersal.

verses.h1: We lived there for a time, then were driven out
verses.h2: by a calamity that banished ease from those dwelling there.

verses.h1: It scattered the gathered company, and they departed
verses.h2: from it; it laid bare the ruin of what had flourished there.

verses.h1: Were you to visit the dwelling, you would see there
verses.h2: traces that stir sorrow in its visitor.

verses.h1: Those are the former abodes; if you pass them
verses.h2: one day, greet their crumbling remains.

verses.h1: And look at them: have they not become ruined campsites,
verses.h2: with windblown dust sweeping over their fallen remains?

notes.note: أواصر usually means bonds or ties. Its physical referent here is uncertain; “fastenings” provisionally takes it as the cords or attachments of the former encampment.

The construction بما خلفت عين is unclear. The translation provisionally reads خلفت as “left behind” and عين as “wide-eyed wild cows,” whose young are جآذر. It may instead describe wild cattle replacing the former inhabitants, but the wording does not make that reading secure.

verses.h1: وسكان دار لا تواصل بينهم
verses.h2: على قرب بعض في التجاور من بعض

verses.h1: كأن خواتيما من الطين فوقهم
verses.h2: فليس لها حتى القيامة من فض

verses.h1: And dwellers in an abode, with no contact between them,
verses.h2: though they are close neighbors to one another.

verses.h1: It is as though seals of clay lie over them,
verses.h2: not to be broken until the Resurrection.

verses.h1: ألا يا نفس ما أرجو بدار
verses.h2: أرى من حلها قلق القرار؟

verses.h1: بدار إنما الشهوات فيها
verses.h2: معلقة بأيام قصار

verses.h1: نرى الأموال أربابا علينا
verses.h2: وما هي بيننا إلا عواري

verses.h1: ونذكر أن ندب لها وننسى
verses.h2: دبيب الليل فينا والنهار

verses.h1: O soul, what can I hope for in an abode
verses.h2: where I see every dweller restless in his stay?

verses.h1: An abode where pleasures are only
verses.h2: bound to a few short days.

verses.h1: We see riches as masters over us,
verses.h2: though among us they are only things on loan.

verses.h1: We remember to pursue them, yet forget
verses.h2: how night and day creep through us.

poems.intro: وقال آخر: (هذه الأبيات من قصيدة تنسب إلى أكثم بن صيفي) :

verses.h1: أيسأل رسم الدار، والدار قلبه
verses.h2: وأنى لها ما قد حواه من الوجد؟

verses.h1: ويسخط أفعال السحاب بتربها
verses.h2: إذا معهد منها تغير من عهد؟

verses.h1: وما متعة الأحباب إلا تعلة
verses.h2: تلم لتشتيت وتقرب عن بعد

verses.h1: Does he question the dwelling’s traces, when the dwelling is his heart?
verses.h2: How could it contain the longing his heart holds?

verses.h1: And does he resent what the clouds have done to its soil,
verses.h2: when a familiar spot there has changed from what he remembers?

verses.h1: The enjoyment of loved ones is only a passing solace:
verses.h2: it gathers only to scatter, and brings near from afar.

notes.note: The pronoun references are somewhat ambiguous. I take لها to refer to the dwelling and the subject of حواه to be his heart.
The unvocalized تلم can mean either “gathers together” or “visits briefly”; I have chosen the former. عن بعد may mean “from afar” or “after separation.”

prose_translation.intro: Another poet said (these verses are from a poem attributed to Aktham ibn Ṣayfī):

poems.intro: روى أن قوما تشاجروا بين يدي أمير المؤمنين عمر بن الخطاب - رضي الله عنه - في أشعر الناس، فقال عمر: سأرسل إلى سيد الناس فأسأله، فقال الناس: قد تشاجرنا في سيد الشعراء فنريد الآن أن ننظر إلى سيد الناس، فأرسل إلى عبد الله بن العباس - رضوان الله عليهما - فجاءه، فقال له: يا أبا العباس أنشدنا ما تستحسن من الشعر، فقال: سأنشدكم لسيد الشعراء، فأنشدهم لزهير بن أبي سلمى:

verses.h1: هل في تذكر أيام الصبى فند
verses.h2: أم هل لما فات من أيامه ردد؟

verses.h1: أم هل يلامن باك هاج عبرته
verses.h2: بالحجر إذ شفه الوجد الذي يجد؟

verses.h1: أوفى على شرف نشز فأزعجه
verses.h2: قلب إلى آل سلمى تائق كمد

verses.h1: متى أرى دار حي عهدنا بهم
verses.h2: حيث التقى الغور من نعمان والنجد؟

verses.h1: لهم هوى من هوانا ما يقربنا
verses.h2: ماتت على قربه الأحشاء والكبد

verses.h1: إني لما استودعتني يوم ذي عذم
verses.h2: راع إذا طال بالمستودع الأمد

verses.h1: إن تمس دارهم منا مباعدة
verses.h2: فما الأحبة إلا هم وإن بعدوا

verses.h1: Is there folly in recalling the days of youth?
verses.h2: Or can its vanished days ever return?

verses.h1: Or can a weeping man be blamed, his tears stirred
verses.h2: at al-Ḥijr, when the longing he feels has wasted him?

verses.h1: He climbed a lofty ridge, and was driven on
verses.h2: by a grief-stricken heart yearning for Salmā’s people.

verses.h1: When shall I see the dwelling of a people we once knew,
verses.h2: where the lowlands of Naʿmān and the uplands meet?

verses.h1: They have a love akin to ours that draws us near;
verses.h2: my heart and liver have wasted away yearning for that nearness.

verses.h1: Of what you entrusted to me on the day at Dhū ʿAdham,
verses.h2: I am a keeper, though the years grow long for the one entrusted.

verses.h1: Though their dwelling may lie far from us,
verses.h2: they alone are our loved ones, however distant they may be.

notes.note: The place الحجر is provisionally read as al-Ḥijr; its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

The syntax of لهم هوى من هوانا ما يقربنا and the reference of قربه are unclear. The translation tentatively understands a shared love that brings the lovers near, and yearning for that nearness. The transmitted wording may be defective.

ذي عذم appears to be a place name, provisionally rendered Dhū ʿAdham; its vocalization and location are uncertain. المستودع can mean either the person entrusted or the thing entrusted; the translation takes it as the person.

prose_translation.intro: It is related that some people disputed before the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—may God be pleased with him—over who was the greatest poet. ʿUmar said, “I shall send for the foremost of men and ask him.” The people said, “We have been disputing over the foremost of poets, and now we wish to see the foremost of men.” So he sent for ʿAbd Allah ibn al-ʿAbbās—may God be pleased with them both—and he came to him. He said to him, “Abū al-ʿAbbās, recite to us some poetry that you admire.” He replied, “I shall recite to you some verses by the foremost of poets.” Then he recited to them these verses by Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā:

verses.h1: على الدار التي لبست بلاها
verses.h2: قفا يا صاحبي فسائلاها

verses.h1: وما يبكيك من عرصات دار
verses.h2: تقادم عهدها وبدا بلاها؟

verses.h1: At the dwelling clothed in its own decay,
verses.h2: halt, my two companions, and question it.

verses.h1: What makes you weep over the courts of a dwelling
verses.h2: whose days are long past and whose decay is plain?

poems.intro: عن محمد بن يزداد، قال: دخلت على المأمون يوما فرأيته وبيده رقعة، فقال لي: يا محمد، قرأت ما فيها؟ قلت: هي في يد أمير المؤمنين، فرمى بها إلي، فإذا فيها مكتوب:

verses.h1: إنك في دار لها مدة
verses.h2: يقبل فيها عمل العامل

verses.h1: أما ترى الموت محيطا بنا
verses.h2: يقطع فيها أمل الآمل

verses.h1: تعجل الذنب لما تشتهي
verses.h2: وتأمل التوبة من قابل

verses.h1: والموت يأتي بعد ذا بغتة
verses.h2: ماذا بفعل الحازم العاقل

verses.h1: You are in an abode whose term is fixed,
verses.h2: where the deeds of those who act are accepted.

verses.h1: Do you not see death surrounding us,
verses.h2: cutting short the hopes of those who hope within it?

verses.h1: You hasten to sin for what you desire,
verses.h2: and hope to repent next year.

verses.h1: Then death comes suddenly—
verses.h2: what is a prudent, sensible man to do?

notes.note: The text reads بفعل, which appears to be a misprint for يفعل, ‘does’ or ‘will do’; the translation follows that correction.

prose_translation.intro: From Muḥammad ibn Yazdād, who said: I went in to see al-Maʾmūn one day and found him holding a slip of paper. He said to me, “Muḥammad, have you read what is on it?” I replied, “It is in the hand of the Commander of the Faithful.” He tossed it to me, and there I found written:

poems.poet_from_text: المساور بن هند بن قيس بن زهير العبسي
poems.intro: قلما قرأتها قال لي المأمون: هذا من أحكم شعر قرأته وقال المساور بن هند بن قيس بن زهير العبسي:

poet.from_text: المساور بن هند بن قيس بن زهير العبسي

verses.h1: ودار حفاظ قد حللتم مهانة
verses.h2: بها نبيكم، والضيف غير مهان

verses.h1: إذا سئلوا ما ليس بالحق فيهم
verses.h2: أبى كل مجني عليه وجان

verses.h1: And an abode of honor, where you have sanctioned the humiliation
verses.h2: of your prophet, though the guest is not dishonored.

verses.h1: When an unjust demand is made of them,
verses.h2: all refuse, the wronged and the wrongdoer alike.

notes.note: The wording is uncertain and may be corrupt. The translation tentatively reads حللتم as ḥallaltum, ‘you sanctioned,’ and مهانة ... نبيكم as ‘the humiliation of your prophet.’ حللتم could instead mean ‘you took up residence,’ but the remaining wording then does not yield a clear construction. The prophet intended is unidentified.

prose_translation.intro: When I read it, al-Maʾmūn said to me, “This is among the most finely crafted poetry I have read.” And al-Musāwir ibn Hind ibn Qays ibn Zuhayr al-ʿAbsī said:

verses.h1: وقفت فأبكنني بدار عشيرتي
verses.h2: على رزئهن الباكيات الحواسر

verses.h1: غدوا كسيوف الهند وراد حومة
verses.h2: من الموت أعيا وردهن المصادر

verses.h1: فوارس حاموا عن حريمي وحافظوا
verses.h2: بدار المنايا، والقنا متشاجر

verses.h1: ولو أن سلمى نالها مثل رزئنا
verses.h2: لهدت، ولكن تحمل الرزء عامر

verses.h1: I stood at my clan’s dwelling, and they made me weep—
verses.h2: the bareheaded women mourning their loss.

verses.h1: They went forth like Indian swords, entering the thick
verses.h2: of death; their entry into it allowed no return.

verses.h1: Horsemen who defended my household and held their ground
verses.h2: in the abode of death, as spears interlocked.

verses.h1: Had Salmā suffered a loss like ours,
verses.h2: it would have crumbled; yet ʿĀmir bears the loss.

notes.note: The compressed phrase أعيا وردهن المصادر uses the imagery of approaching and leaving a watering place. I understand it to mean that entering the fray left no possibility of return. The feminine pronoun in وردهن apparently refers to the swords to which the warriors are compared, but the construction is uncertain.
Salmā probably denotes the mountain associated with Ṭayyiʾ, rather than a woman. ʿĀmir presumably denotes the tribe Banū ʿĀmir; neither identification is explicit in the verse.

verses.h1: يا دار لازالت رباك مجردة
verses.h2: من كل سارية تعل وتنهل

verses.h1: أذكرتنا دول الزمان وصرفه
verses.h2: وأريتنا كيف الخطوب النزل

verses.h1: أصبابة برسوم رامة بعدما
verses.h2: عرفت معارفها الصبا والشمأل

verses.h1: وسألت من لا يستجيب فكنت في استخ
verses.h2: باره كمجيب من لا يسأل

verses.h1: O dwelling, may your heights remain forever deprived
verses.h2: of every night-cloud that drenches and drenches again.

verses.h1: You reminded us of time’s changing fortunes and reversals,
verses.h2: and showed us how calamities descend.

verses.h1: Is this longing for the traces of Rāma, after
verses.h2: the east and north winds have come to know its landmarks?

verses.h1: You questioned one who does not answer; in seeking
verses.h2: word from him, you were like one answering someone who does not ask.

notes.note: The unvocalized النزل is understood here as describing calamities that descend or befall; its precise vocalization and sense are uncertain.

عرفت معارفها is translated literally as “have come to know its landmarks,” with the winds as subject. The expression is unusual and may contain a textual error, possibly concealing a verb meaning that the winds effaced the landmarks.

verses.h1: هب الدار ردت رجع ما أنا قائله
verses.h2: وأبدى الجواب الربع عما تسائله

verses.h1: أفي ذاك برء من جوى ألهب الحشى
verses.h2: توقده، واستغزر الدمع جائله

verses.h1: هو الدمع موقوفا على كل دمنة
verses.h2: نعرج فيها أو خليط نزايله

verses.h1: ترادفهم خفض الزمان ولينه
verses.h2: وجادهم طل الربيع ووابله

verses.h1: Suppose the dwelling echoed back what I say,
verses.h2: and the campsite gave an answer to what you ask it.

verses.h1: Would that cure a heartache that has set my innards aflame
verses.h2: with its burning, and drawn abundant tears with its restless stirrings?

verses.h1: These are tears, held in store for every ruined campsite
verses.h2: where we turn aside, or companions from whom we part.

verses.h1: May time’s ease and gentleness come to them in succession,
verses.h2: and spring’s light rain and downpour water them generously.

notes.note: The expression جائله is compressed and somewhat ambiguous. It is taken here as the heartache’s restless movement or stirring, which draws abundant tears.

verses.h1: يا دار أضحت خلاء لا أنيس بها
verses.h2: إلا الظباء، وإلا الناشط الفرد

verses.h1: أين الذين إذا ما زرتهم جذلوا
verses.h2: فطار عن قلبي التشواق والكمد؟

verses.h1: O dwelling, now deserted, with no companion within
verses.h2: save gazelles and a solitary, wandering wild bull.

verses.h1: Where are those who rejoiced whenever I visited them,
verses.h2: so that longing and grief flew from my heart?

verses.h1: لمن الدار أقفرت بمعان
verses.h2: بين شط اليرموك فالصمان

verses.h1: فالقريات من بلاس فداريا
verses.h2: فسكا إلى الرسوم الدواني

verses.h1: فقفا جاسم، فأودية الصف
verses.h2: ر مغى قبائل وهجان

verses.h1: ذاك مغنى لآل جفنة في الده
verses.h2: ر وحقا تصرف الأزمان

verses.h1: نكلت أمهم
verses.h2: وقد ثكلتهم يوم حلوا بحارث الجولان

verses.h1: Whose is the dwelling, deserted at Maʿān,
verses.h2: between the bank of the Yarmūk and al-Ṣammān?

verses.h1: Then al-Qurayyāt by Balās, then Dārayyā,
verses.h2: then Sakkā, as far as the nearby traces.

verses.h1: Then the land behind Jāsim, then the valleys of al-Ṣufr,
verses.h2: the dwelling of tribes and white camels.

verses.h1: That was the home of the house of Jafna through the ages;
verses.h2: and truly, time brings change.

verses.h1: May their mother be bereaved of them—
verses.h2: and bereaved she was, the day they settled at Ḥārith al-Jawlān.

notes.note: مغى appears to be a misprint for مغنى, “dwelling.” هجان is taken here as white, thoroughbred camels, though the word can also denote purity of lineage. The reading of this hemistich is uncertain.
The identification and vocalization of الصفر, provisionally transliterated al-Ṣufr, are uncertain. The name is split across the source hemistichs.
نكلت أمهم is unclear as printed. The translation assumes ثكلت أمهم, “May their mother be bereaved of them,” supported by وقد ثكلتهم, “and she was indeed bereaved of them,” immediately afterward.
Ḥārith al-Jawlān is treated as a place-name; its precise identification is uncertain.

verses.h1: عجبا لي ولاغتراري بدار
verses.h2: لست أبقى لها ولا تبقى لي

verses.h1: ما تصافي قوم على غير ذات الله
verses.h2: إلا تفرقوا عن تقالي

verses.h1: How strange of me to be beguiled by an abode
verses.h2: when neither I shall last for it, nor it for me.

verses.h1: No people form bonds of friendship for any sake but God’s
verses.h2: without parting in mutual hatred.

verses.h1: يا مشيد الحصن يبغي نفعه
verses.h2: قلما تغني من الموت الحصون

verses.h1: تطلب التخليد في دار الفنا
verses.h2: خاب من يطلب شيئا لا يكون

verses.h1: سائل الأيام عن أملاكها
verses.h2: أي در قطعت عنها اللبون

verses.h1: كم بها من راكض أيامه
verses.h2: وله من ركضها يوم حرون

verses.h1: O builder of the fortress, hoping it will help you,
verses.h2: rarely do fortresses avail against death.

verses.h1: You seek immortality in the abode of decay;
verses.h2: whoever seeks what cannot be is disappointed.

verses.h1: Ask the days about their kings:
verses.h2: what milk the milch camel has withheld from them!

verses.h1: How many a man within it races through his days,
verses.h2: yet amid their galloping comes a day that balks.

notes.note: أملاكها is read as ‘their kings,’ though it can also mean ‘their possessions.’ The syntax of the second hemistich is uncertain, particularly the antecedent of عنها (‘from them/it’). The translation tentatively takes the milch camel’s withholding of milk as an image of bounty withdrawn from the kings.

verses.h1: نعمر الدنيا وما الدن
verses.h2: يا لنا دار إقامه

verses.h1: إنما الغبطة والحس
verses.h2: رة في يوم القيامة

verses.h1: We build up this world, yet this world
verses.h2: is no lasting home for us.

verses.h1: Happiness and regret
verses.h2: are only on the Day of Resurrection.

poems.intro: روى أن فاطمة بنت الحسن - رضوان الله عليه - نظرت إلى دار زوجها الحسن بن الحسين - رضي الله عنهما - فغطت وجهها وقالت:

verses.h1: وكانوا رجاء ثم صاروا رزية
verses.h2: لقد عظمت تلك الرزايا وجلت

verses.h1: They were once a source of hope, then became a grievous loss;
verses.h2: great indeed were those calamities, and grave.

prose_translation.intro: It is related that Fāṭima bint al-Ḥasan—may God be pleased with him—looked at the house of her husband, al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥusayn—may God be pleased with them both—then covered her face and said:

poems.intro: ثم ضربت على قربه فسطاطا أقامت فيه سنة، فلما استكملتها أمرت بالفسطاط فقلع، ودخلت المدينة، فسمعت قائلا يقول - من جانب البقيع -: هل وجدوا ما فقدوا؟ وقائلا من الجانب الآخر يقول: بل يئسوا فانقلبوا. قال وهب بن منبه - رحمه الله -: نحن بنو آدم من نسل الجنة، سبانا إبليس إلى الدنيا بخطية أبينا، فليس لنا إلا البكاء حتى نعود إلى الدار التي سبانا منها. روى أن عبد الله بن عبيد الله بن عتبة بن عبد الله بن مسعود - رحمه الله - باع درا بثمانين ألف درهم، فقيل له: لو اتخذت لولدك من هذا المال ذخرا فقال: أنا أجعل هذا المال ذخرا لي عند الله تعالى، وأجعل الله سبحانه ذخرا لولدي، ثم تصدق بالمال. كتب رجل إلى صالح بن عبد القدوس:

verses.h1: الموت باب وكل الناس داخله
verses.h2: فليست شعري بعد الباب ما الدار؟

verses.h1: Death is a gate that everyone must enter;
verses.h2: would that I knew: what dwelling lies beyond the gate?

notes.note: فليست شعري appears to be a misprint for فليت شعري, “would that I knew,” which is the reading translated here.

prose_translation.intro:
Then she pitched a tent beside his grave and stayed in it for a year. When the year was complete, she ordered the tent to be taken down and entered al-Madina. She heard a voice from one side of al-Baqīʿ saying, “Have they found what they lost?” and another voice from the other side saying, “No, they have despaired and gone away.”

Wahb ibn Munabbih—may God have mercy on him—said: “We, the children of Adam, are descended from Paradise. Iblis carried us captive into this world through our father’s sin, and we can do nothing but weep until we return to the abode from which he carried us captive.”

It is related that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿūd—may God have mercy on him—sold a house for eighty thousand dirhams. Someone said to him, “If only you would set aside some of this money as a reserve for your children!” He replied, “I shall make this money a treasure stored up for me with God Most High, and I shall make God—glory be to Him—a provision for my children.” Then he gave the money away in charity.

A man wrote to Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Quddūs:

verses.h1: الدار جنة عدن إن عملت بما
verses.h2: يرضي الإله وإن فرطت فالنار

verses.h1: هما محلان ما للناس غيرهما
verses.h2: فانظر لنفسك ماذا أنت مختار

verses.h1: The abode is the Garden of Eden if you do what
verses.h2: pleases God; but if you fall short, it is the Fire.

verses.h1: These are two dwellings; people have no others.
verses.h2: So consider for yourself which you will choose.

verses.h1: درج الليل والنهار على فه
verses.h2: م بن عمرو فأصبحوا كالصريم

verses.h1: وخلت دارهم فأضحت يبابا
verses.h2: بعد عز وثروة ونعيم

verses.h1: وكذاك الزمان يذهب بالناس، وتبقى ديارهم كالرسوم
Night and day passed over Fahm
verses.h2: ibn ʿAmr, till they became like a field cut bare.

verses.h1: Their dwelling stood empty and became a wasteland
verses.h2: after glory, wealth, and ease.

verses.h1: So time carries people away, while their dwellings remain like faded traces.

notes.note: Fahm ibn ʿAmr appears to designate a clan collectively, accounting for the plural ‘they’; its precise identification is uncertain.
Al-ṣarīm is ambiguous: it can mean a harvested or devastated field, but also the darkness of night. The translation adopts the image of a field stripped bare.

verses.h1: ما رأيت العيش يصفو لأحد
verses.h2: دون كد وعناء ونكد

verses.h1: نحن في دار فناء وبلى
verses.h2: تنقل الناس إلى دار الأبد

verses.h1: كن لما قدمته مغتنما
verses.h2: لا تؤخر عمل اليوم لغد

verses.h1: I have never seen life run clear for anyone,
verses.h2: free of toil, hardship, and distress.

verses.h1: We dwell in an abode of extinction and decay
verses.h2: that carries people to the abode of eternity.

verses.h1: Count as gain the deeds you have sent ahead;
verses.h2: do not put off today’s work until tomorrow.

verses.h1: ما إن هذا موقف
verses.h2: الجازع أقوى، وسؤر الزمن الفاجع

verses.h1: دار سقاها بعد سكانها
verses.h2: صرف النوى من سمه الناقع

verses.h1: فلا تلومن ذا الهوى إنها
verses.h2: ليست ببدع حنة النازع

verses.h1: This is no stopping-place for
verses.h2: the grief-stricken; it stands deserted, a remnant of devastating time.

verses.h1: An abode that, after its inhabitants departed,
verses.h2: the havoc of separation watered with its deadly poison.

verses.h1: So do not blame the lover, for it is
verses.h2: nothing new—the homesick one’s yearning cry.

notes.note: The text appears metrically disturbed, and the supplied hemistich break splits موقف الجازع (‘the stopping-place of the grief-stricken’). The connection of أقوى وسؤر is uncertain; I take أقوى as ‘stands deserted’ and سؤر as ‘remnant.’

verses.h1: قرى دارهم مني الدموع السوافك
verses.h2: وإن عاد صبحي بعدهم وهو حالك

verses.h1: سقت ربعهم، لا، بل سقت منتواهم
verses.h2: من الأرض أخلاف السحاب الحواشك

verses.h1: وألبسهم عصب الربيع ووشيه
verses.h2: ويمنته نبت الندى المتلاحك

verses.h1: My offering to their dwelling is my streaming tears,
verses.h2: though since their departure my dawn has turned dark.

verses.h1: May their campsite—no, rather, the place they have sought—be watered,
verses.h2: there on earth, by the swollen udders of the clouds.

verses.h1: And may they be clothed in spring’s striped cloth and embroidery,
verses.h2: and its Yemeni mantle, by dew-fed plants growing thick together.

verses.h1: يا دار ما فعلت بك الأيام
verses.h2: لم تبق فيك بشاشة تستام

verses.h1: عرم الزمان على الذين عهدتهم
verses.h2: بك قاطنين وللزمان عرام

verses.h1: أيام لا أغشى لأهلك منزلا
verses.h2: إلا مراقبة، على ظلام

verses.h1: ولقد نهزت مع الغواة بدلوهم
verses.h2: وأسمت سرح اللهو حيث أساموا

verses.h1: وبلغت ما بلغ امرؤ بشبابه
verses.h2: فإذا غضارة كل ذاك أثام

verses.h1: O dwelling, what have the days done to you?
verses.h2: They have left no cheer in you worth seeking.

verses.h1: Time dealt savagely with those I once knew
verses.h2: dwelling in you—and Time has its savagery.

verses.h1: In those days I never approached a dwelling of your people
verses.h2: except warily, under cover of darkness.

verses.h1: With the wayward I dipped their bucket,
verses.h2: and pastured the herd of pleasure wherever they pastured theirs.

verses.h1: I attained all that a man can attain in his youth;
verses.h2: yet the bloom of all that proved to be sin.

notes.note: تستام is understood as ‘sought after,’ though it may retain the commercial sense of being valued or priced.
The construction إلا مراقبة، على ظلام is somewhat uncertain: مراقبة may mean keeping watch rather than proceeding warily; على ظلام is taken as ‘under cover of darkness.’
أثام is translated as ‘sin’; it can also mean the penalty or requital for sin.

poems.poet_from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: الشيخ أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: هل تسمع القول دار غير ناطقة
verses.h2: وفقدها السمع مقرون إلى الخرس؟

verses.h1: لأنسينك إن طال الزمان بنا
verses.h2: كم من حبيب تمادى عهده فنسى؟

verses.h1: Can a speechless dwelling hear what is said,
verses.h2: when its deafness is coupled with muteness?

verses.h1: I shall surely forget you, if the years stretch on for us;
verses.h2: how many a loved one has been forgotten after long separation!

prose_translation.intro: And Shaykh Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

poems.intro: وقال النابغة الجعدي، وهو قيس بن عبد الله:

verses.h1: وهاجت لك الأحزان دار كأنها
verses.h2: بذي بقر أو بالعنابة مذهب

verses.h1: أواري خيل قد عفت ومنازل
verses.h2: أراح بها حي كرام وأعزبوا

verses.h1: تحمل منها أهلها فتفرقوا
verses.h2: فريقين منهم مصعد ومصوب

verses.h1: A dwelling stirred your sorrows, as though it were—
verses.h2: at Dhū Baqar or al-ʿUnābah—a gilded cloth.

verses.h1: Horse-tethering stakes, now effaced, and campsites
verses.h2: where a noble clan rested at evening, then went far away.

verses.h1: Its people departed from it and scattered
verses.h2: in two bands, one heading upland, the other down.

notes.note: The precise object meant by مُذْهَب is uncertain: a gilded or gold-decorated article, provisionally rendered as ‘gilded cloth.’ The identification and vocalization of the place name العنابة are also uncertain.
أراح بها and أعزبوا may refer specifically to livestock: bringing the herds back there at evening and subsequently driving them to distant pasture, rather than simply resting and departing.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī, who is Qays ibn ʿAbd Allah, said:

verses.h1: دور عفت بقرى الخابور غيرها
verses.h2: بعد الأنيس سوا في الريح والمطر

verses.h1: إن تمس دارك ممن كان يسكنها
verses.h2: وحشا فذلك صرف الدهر والقدر

verses.h1: وقد تحل بها بيض ترائبها
verses.h2: كأنها بين كثبان النقا البقر

verses.h1: Dwellings lie effaced in the villages of al-Khābūr, altered
verses.h2: after their people left, by dust-laden winds and rain.

verses.h1: If your dwelling stands empty of those who once inhabited it,
verses.h2: desolate, that is the turning of time and fate.

verses.h1: Once women with fair breasts dwelt there,
verses.h2: like wild cows among the sand dunes.

notes.note: The text’s «سوا في» appears to be an erroneous splitting of «سوافي», understood here as dust-laden or dust-driving winds.
«النقا» is taken here as a common noun referring to sandhills; it could instead be a place-name, al-Naqā.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Rabīʿ ibn Abī al-Ḥuqayq said:

poems.intro: وقال ابن المولى، وهو محمد بن عبد الله بن مسلم بن المولى، مولى الأنصار - رضي الله عنهم - من بني عمرو بن عوف:

verses.h1: سلا دار ليلى هل تبين فتنطق
verses.h2: وكيف ترد القول بيداء سملق؟

verses.h1: وأنى يرد القول دار كأنها
verses.h2: لطول بلاها والتقادم مهرق

verses.h1: فلا تجزعن للبين، كل جماعة
verses.h2: وجدك مكتوب عليها التفرق

verses.h1: وخذ بالتعزي؛ كل ما أنت لابس
verses.h2: جديدا على الأيام يبلى ويخلق

verses.h1: فصبر الفتى عما تولى ففاته
verses.h2: من الأمر أولى بالسداد وأوفق

verses.h1: وإنك بالإشفاق لا تدفع الردى
verses.h2: ولا الخير مجلوب فما لك تشفق

verses.h1: كأن لم يرعك الدهر، أو أنت آمن
verses.h2: لأحداثه فيما يغادي ويطرق

verses.h1: وقال خليلي
verses.h2: والبكالي غالب أقاض على هذا الأسى والتشوق؟

verses.h1: وقد طال توقا في أكفكف عبرة
verses.h2: على دمنة كادت بها النفس تزهق

verses.h1: وإنسان عيني في دوائر لجة
verses.h2: من الماء يبدو تارة ثم يغرق

verses.h1: Ask Laylā’s dwelling, you two: can it make itself clear and speak?
verses.h2: But how can a bare, level waste return an answer?

verses.h1: How can a dwelling answer, when it resembles—
verses.h2: through long decay and age—a sheet of parchment?

verses.h1: Do not despair at parting: every gathering,
verses.h2: by your fortune, is destined to disperse.

verses.h1: Seek consolation: everything you put on
verses.h2: when new will, with the passing days, wear thin and fray.

verses.h1: A man’s patience over what has passed and escaped him
verses.h2: in life’s affairs is wiser and more fitting.

verses.h1: Through apprehension you cannot ward off death,
verses.h2: nor is good fortune brought by it—why, then, are you afraid?

verses.h1: As though time had never frightened you, or you were safe
verses.h2: from its calamities, whatever it brings by morning or by night.

verses.h1: My friend said—
verses.h2: while weeping overcame me—“Will this grief and longing prove fatal?”

verses.h1: My lingering had grown long as I held back a tear
verses.h2: over a ruined campsite where my soul had nearly fled.

verses.h1: The pupil of my eye, in the swirling depths
verses.h2: of water, appears a moment, then drowns.

notes.note: البكالي appears to represent البكا لي, “weeping … over me.” The wording أقاض على is uncertain: it may represent أقاضٍ عليَّ, “will … finish me off?” The translation leaves the affected person unspecified because the pronoun and the boundaries of the friend’s speech are unclear.
توقا في appears to be a mistaken division of توقافي, understood as “my lingering” or “my prolonged standing.”

prose_translation.intro: And Ibn al-Mawlā—who was Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn al-Mawlā, a client of the Ansar (may God be pleased with them), of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: الزم ذراك إذا لقيت خصاصة
verses.h2: فالليث يستر حاله الإخدار

verses.h1: هذي الجسوم من التراب كوائن
verses.h2: والمرء لولا أن يحس جدار

verses.h1: ويقول: داري من يقول، وأعبدي
verses.h2: مه، فالعبيد لربنا والدار

verses.h1: أتروم من زمن وفاء مرضيا؟
verses.h2: إن الزمان كأهله غدار

verses.h1: يقفون والفلك المسخر دائر
verses.h2: ويقدرون فيضحك المقدار

verses.h1: Keep to your shelter when poverty befalls you;
verses.h2: for staying in its lair conceals the lion’s plight.

verses.h1: These bodies are formed from dust;
verses.h2: a man, were he not able to feel, would be a wall.

verses.h1: Some say, “My house! My slaves!”
verses.h2: Enough! The slaves and the house belong to our Lord.

verses.h1: Do you seek satisfying faithfulness from time?
verses.h2: Time, like its people, is treacherous.

verses.h1: They stand still while the celestial sphere, under command, revolves;
verses.h2: they make their plans, and destiny laughs.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

poems.intro: مر رجل من مراد بأويس القرني - رحمه الله - فقال: كيف أصبحت يا أويس؟ قال: أصحبت أحمد الله - قال: كيف الزمان عليك؟ قال: يا أخا مراد. إن الموت وذكره لم يدع في الأرض لمومن فرحا، وإن علمه بكتاب الله لن يدع في ماله فضة ولا ذهبا، وإن قيامه بالحق لم يدع له صديقا، قال: حدثني بحديث سمعته من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: يا أخا مراد ما شهدت رسول صلى الله عليه وسلم فأحدثك عنه، ولكن افعلوا كما قال لكم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، حاسبوا نفوسكم قبل أن تحاسبوا، فهو أيسر لحسابكم غدا، وزنوا أعمالكم قبل أن توزن، فهو أثقل لوزنكم، ولا تخربوا دوركم من الآخرة بعمران دوركم في الدنيا؛ فإن الله تبارك وتعالى جعل الدنيا قنطرة للآخرة فاعبروها". وقال مهيار:

verses.h1: يا دار ليس اليوم عهدك أمس لي
verses.h2: ظهرت مفارقة وبان خلاف

verses.h1: وتغيرت فيك الصباعن خلقها
verses.h2: وليانها، فنسيمها إعصاف

verses.h1: O dwelling, today you are not as I knew you yesterday;
verses.h2: estrangement has appeared, and change is plain.

verses.h1: Within you, the east wind has departed from its nature
verses.h2: and its gentleness: its breeze is now a gale.

notes.note: The source’s الصباعن appears to omit a space; read as الصبا عن, “the east wind … from.”

prose_translation.intro: A man of Murād passed by Uways al-Qaranī—may God have mercy on him—and said, “How are you this morning, Uways?” He replied, “I greet the morning praising God.” The man asked, “How is time treating you?” He replied, “Brother of Murād, death and the remembrance of it have left no joy on earth for a believer. His knowledge of the Book of God will leave neither silver nor gold among his possessions, and his upholding the truth has left him no friend.” The man said, “Tell me a saying you heard from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.” He replied, “Brother of Murād, I was never in the presence of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, so that I might relate anything from him to you. But do as the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, told you: call yourselves to account before you are called to account, for that will make your reckoning tomorrow easier; weigh your deeds before they are weighed, for that will make your weight heavier; and do not ruin your dwellings in the hereafter by building up your dwellings in this world. For God, blessed and exalted, has made this world a bridge to the hereafter, so cross it.” And Mihyār said:

verses.h1: لن يقنع النفس إذ كانت مصرفة
verses.h2: إلا التنقل من حال إلى حال

verses.h1: لأظعنن إلى دار خلقت لها
verses.h2: وخير زادي فيها خير أعمالي

verses.h1: The soul, subject as it is to change, will never be satisfied
verses.h2: except by passing from one state to another.

verses.h1: I shall surely depart for an abode for which I was created;
verses.h2: my best provision there is the best of my deeds.

verses.h1: انصرف الناس إلى دورهم
verses.h2: وغودر الميت في رمسه

verses.h1: مرتهن النفس بأعماله
verses.h2: لا يرتجى الإطلاق من حبسه

verses.h1: لنفسه صالح أعماله
verses.h2: وما سواه فعلى نفسه

verses.h1: The people returned to their homes,
verses.h2: and the dead man was left in his grave.

verses.h1: His soul is held in pledge for his deeds;
verses.h2: there is no hope of release from his prison.

verses.h1: His righteous deeds are to his own benefit;
verses.h2: all else counts against his own soul.

verses.h1: طوى الموت ما بيني وبين محمد
verses.h2: وليس لما تطوى المنية ناشر

verses.h1: وكنت عليه أحذر الموت وحده
verses.h2: فلم يبق لي شيء عليه أحاذر

verses.h1: لئن عمرت دور بمن لا أحبه
verses.h2: لقد عمرت ممن أحب المقابر

verses.h1: Death has folded away what bound me to Muḥammad,
verses.h2: and none can unfold what death folds away.

verses.h1: Death alone was what I feared for him;
verses.h2: now nothing remains for me to fear for him.

verses.h1: Though houses are peopled with those I do not love,
verses.h2: the graves are indeed peopled with those I love.

notes.note: Muḥammad’s identity is not established by the excerpt.

verses.h1: قالوا نراك بلا سقم، فقلت لهم:
verses.h2: السقم في القلب ليس السقم في البدن

verses.h1: يا عاذلي خل عن قلب تملكه
verses.h2: من قبل عذلك طول الهم والحزن

verses.h1: لا يعرف الدار إلا قام يندبها
verses.h2: ولا يسائلها إلا عن السكن

verses.h1: They said, “We see no sickness in you.” I told them:
verses.h2: “The sickness is in the heart, not in the body.”

verses.h1: You who reproach me, leave alone a heart possessed,
verses.h2: even before your reproach, by prolonged care and sorrow.

verses.h1: Whenever it recognizes the dwelling, it rises to lament it;
verses.h2: and it questions it only about those who dwelt there.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Murtaḍā—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.intro: عن الأصمعي قال: دخلت على الرشيد وهو يقرأ كتابا ودموعه تتحدر، فلما أبصرني قال: أرأيت ما كان مني؟ قلت: نعم يا أمير المؤمنين، فقال: أما إنه لو كان لأمر الدنيا ما رأيت هذا، ورمى بالقرطاس، فإذا فيه شعر لأبي العتاهية:

verses.h1: هل أنت معتبر بمن خربت
verses.h2: منه غداة مضى دساكره

verses.h1: وبمن أذل الدهر مصرعه
verses.h2: وتبرأت منه عساكره

verses.h1: وبمن خلت منه أسرته
verses.h2: وبمن خلت منه منابره

verses.h1: أين الملوك؟ وأين عزهم؟
verses.h2: صاروا مصيرا أنت صائره

verses.h1: يا مؤثر الدنيا للذته
verses.h2: والمستعد لمن يفاخره

verses.h1: نل ما بدا لك أن تنال من الد
verses.h2: نيا فإن الموت آخره

verses.h1: Will you take warning from him whose estates fell to ruin
verses.h2: the morning he passed away?

verses.h1: And from him whom Time brought low in death,
verses.h2: and whose armies disowned him?

verses.h1: And from him whose thrones stand empty,
verses.h2: and from him whose pulpits stand empty?

verses.h1: Where are the kings? Where is their might?
verses.h2: They have met a fate that you will meet.

verses.h1: O you who prefer this world for your pleasure,
verses.h2: and stand ready for anyone who rivals you in boasting:

verses.h1: Gain whatever you wish to gain from this
verses.h2: world, for death is its end.

notes.note: The grammar of أذل الدهر مصرعه is uncertain without vowel marks. The translation takes Time as the agent of humiliation at death; another possible reading is ‘whose downfall humbled Time.’

prose_translation.intro: Al-Aṣmaʿī related: I entered the presence of al-Rashīd while he was reading a document, with tears streaming down his face. When he saw me, he said, “Did you see what happened to me?” I said, “Yes, Commander of the Faithful.” He said, “Had it been over some worldly matter, you would not have seen this.” He tossed aside the sheet, and there on it were verses by Abū al-ʿAtāhiya:

poems.intro: فقال الرشيد: والله لكأني أخاطب بهذا دون سائر الناس، فلم يلبث بعد ذلك إلا قليلا حتى مات. وقال الشاعر:

opening.actual: إلى متى أنا في حل وترحال

verses.h1: إلى متى أنا في حل وترحال
verses.h2: وهم عيش بإدبار وإقبال

verses.h1: ونازح الدار لا أنفك مغتربا
verses.h2: ناء عن الأهل لا يدرون ما حالي

verses.h1: بمشرق الأرض طورا ثم مغربها
verses.h2: لا يخطر الموت من همي على بال

verses.h1: ولو قعدت أتاني الرزق في دعة
verses.h2: إن القنوع الغنى لا كثرة المال

verses.h1: How long shall I keep halting and journeying,
verses.h2: and fretting over a livelihood, through its ebb and flow?

verses.h1: Far from home, I remain a stranger,
verses.h2: distant from my family, who do not know how I fare.

verses.h1: Now in the east of the earth, then in its west,
verses.h2: so consumed by worry that death never crosses my mind.

verses.h1: Yet if I stayed put, sustenance would come to me at ease;
verses.h2: contentment is wealth, not an abundance of money.

notes.note: بإدبار وإقبال may refer to the ebb and flow of his livelihood, as translated, or to his own coming and going.

prose_translation.intro: Then al-Rashīd said, “By God, it is as though these words are addressed to me alone, rather than to anyone else.” He lived only a short while after that before he died. And the poet said:

poems.intro: عن الأصمعي - رحمه الله - قال: جاءني رسول الرشيد - رضي الله عنه - ليلة، وقد ذهب من الليل شطر، فقال: أجب أمير المؤمنين، ففزعت من ذلك، وقلت: حدث أمر يكره، فمضيت معه، فإذا هو قاعد في أقصى مجلسه، وبين يديه دواة وقرطاس، وهو يبكي، فقلت: السلام عليك يا أمير المؤمنين. فقال: وعليك السلام يا ابن قريب، اجلس، فجلست، فقال: أبكاني هذا البيت وأسهر ليلتي، فقلت: لا أبكى الله عينك يا أمير المؤمنين، وأي بيت هو؟ قال: بيت ابن ذي سلم عند موته:

verses.h1: لم تحتقب غير أثواب يمزقها
verses.h2: ريب الزمان وطول العهد والقدم

verses.h1: You have carried away nothing but garments, to be torn by
verses.h2: the ravages of time, the passing years, and age.

prose_translation.intro: On the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī—may God have mercy on him—who said: A messenger of al-Rashīd—may God be pleased with him—came to me one night, when half the night had passed, and said, “Answer the summons of the Commander of the Faithful.” I was alarmed by this and thought, “Something unwelcome has happened.” I went with him, and there was al-Rashīd, seated at the far end of his reception room, with an inkwell and a sheet of paper before him, weeping. I said, “Peace be upon you, Commander of the Faithful.” He said, “And upon you be peace, Ibn Qurayb. Sit down.” So I sat down, and he said, “This verse has made me weep and kept me awake tonight.” I said, “May God never make your eyes weep, Commander of the Faithful. Which verse is it?” He said, “The verse of Ibn Dhī Salam at the time of his death:”

poems.intro: فقلت: والله يا أمير المؤمنين لقد صدق، وهذه سبيل الناس جميعا، فطوبى للمتقين، فقال: ويحك يا أصمعي ذهب. جلساء الخير، ومجالس الفضل، أين من كان إذا جالسهم المسرفون على أنفسهم وعظتهم صورته، وذكرتهم هيئته، وبلغت بهم كل المبالغ مقالته؟ فقلت: يا أمير المؤمنين. لقد أسعد الله دولتك بجماعة من أهل الفضل، ثم قلت: إن أمرت أن أحدثك بحديث وعشر قرئ على بعض القبور، فقال: هاته، فقلت: حدثني من أثق به قال: غزونا في البحر، فمالت بنا السفينة إلى جزيرة، فإذا نحن بقصر شاهق، وإلى جانبه قبر، وعلى القصر بابان، وبين القصر والقبر فسيل نخل لم أر شيئا أحسن منه، فإذا على القصر مكتوب:

verses.h1: يؤمل دنيا لتبقى له
verses.h2: فمات المؤمل قبل الأمل

verses.h1: وبات يروي أصول الفس
verses.h2: يل فعاش الفسيل ومات الرجل

verses.h1: He hoped the world would remain his,
verses.h2: but the hopeful man died before his hope was fulfilled.

verses.h1: He spent the night watering the young palms’ roots;
verses.h2: the young palms lived, and the man died.

prose_translation.intro: I said, “By God, Commander of the Faithful, he spoke truly. This is the path of all mankind, so blessed are the God-fearing.” He said, “Alas, Aṣmaʿī! Gone are the good companions and the gatherings of virtue. Where are those whose very appearance admonished people who had sinned against themselves when they sat with them, whose bearing reminded them, and whose words moved them to the utmost?” I said, “Commander of the Faithful, God has indeed blessed your reign with a company of virtuous men.” Then I said, “If you command, I will tell you a story and recite some verses that were read on certain graves.” He said, “Let us hear it.” I said, “Someone I trust told me: We went on a campaign by sea, and our ship veered toward an island. There we found a lofty palace with a grave beside it. The palace had two doors, and between the palace and the grave were young date palms, more beautiful than anything I had ever seen. On the palace was written:

verses.h1: وفتى كأن جبينه بدر الدجى
verses.h2: قامت عليه نوائح وروامس

verses.h1: غرس الفسيل مؤملا لبقائه
verses.h2: فحيا الفسيل ومات عنه الفارس

verses.h1: A youth whose brow was like the full moon in the dark of night—
verses.h2: over him rose mourners and dust-bearing winds.

verses.h1: He planted palm-shoots, hoping for a long life;
verses.h2: the palm-shoots lived, but the horseman died and left them.

notes.note: روامس is understood here as winds that cover or efface traces with dust; it could also mean those who bury or cover the dead.
لبقائه is taken to refer to the planter’s hoped-for survival, though the pronoun could instead refer to the survival of the palm-shoots.

prose_translation.intro: And on the façade of the palace was written:

verses.h1: تلك المدائن في الآفاق خاوية
verses.h2: أمست خلاء وذاق الموت بانيها

verses.h1: Those cities across the lands lie empty;
verses.h2: they have become deserted, and their builder has tasted death.

prose_translation.intro: On one of the palace’s two gates is written:

verses.h1: أين القرون التي عن حظها غفلت
verses.h2: حتى سقاها بكأس الموت ساقيها

verses.h1: Where are the generations that neglected their own good,
verses.h2: until their cupbearer gave them drink from the cup of death?

notes.note: Ḥaẓẓ (حظ), rendered as “their own good,” can also mean one’s share or lot; its precise sense here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And on the other door was written:

poems.intro: قال الرجل: فبقيت متعجبا أنظر إلى الشعر والقصر، والفسيل والقبر، ثم تمثلت:

verses.h1: ناد رب الدار والحصن الذي
verses.h2: جمع الدنيا بحرص ما فعل؟

verses.h1: كان في دار سواها داره
verses.h2: عللته بالمنى، ثم انتقل

verses.h1: Call out to the master of the house and fortress, who
verses.h2: greedily amassed the world: what has become of him?

verses.h1: He lived in an abode, though his true home lay elsewhere;
verses.h2: it beguiled him with hopes, then he departed.

notes.note: The compressed phrase «سواها داره» is read here as “his home was elsewhere,” apparently contrasting his earthly dwelling with the grave.

prose_translation.intro: The man said: I stood there in amazement, looking at the verse and the palace, the young palms and the grave; then I recited these lines:

poems.intro: قال: فلم يزل الرشيد يبكي ويصرخ حتى أصبح، فلما أصبح أمر أن يخرج مال جليل فيتصدق به على الفقراء والمساكين، وأن يدفع إلي منه عشرة آلاف درهم. وقال أبو العتاهية:

verses.h1: هي الدار، دار الأذى والقذى
verses.h2: ودار الفناء، ودار الغير

verses.h1: فلو نلتها بحذافيرها
verses.h2: لمت ولم تقض منها الوطر

verses.h1: It is the abode—an abode of harm and vexation,
verses.h2: an abode of passing away, an abode of changing fortunes.

verses.h1: Even if you gained it in its entirety,
verses.h2: you would die without having had your fill of it.

prose_translation.intro: He said: Al-Rashīd went on weeping and crying out until morning. When morning came, he ordered that a great sum of money be brought out and distributed as alms to the poor and needy, and that ten thousand dirhams of it be given to me. Abū al-ʿAtāhiya said:

poems.poet: الراضي يزيد بن محمد بن عباد
poems.poet_from_text: الراضي يزيد بن محمد بن عباد
poems.intro: وقال الراضي يزيد بن محمد بن عباد، من ملوك الأندلس:

poet.expected: الراضي يزيد بن محمد بن عباد
poet.from_text: الراضي يزيد بن محمد بن عباد

verses.h1: هي الدار غادرة بالرجال
verses.h2: وقاطعة لحبال الوصال

verses.h1: نفجع فيها بغير اللذي
verses.h2: ذ ونشرق منها بغير الزلال

verses.h1: ونزداد مع ذاك عشقا لها
verses.h2: ألا إنما سعينا في ضلال

verses.h1: لمعشوقة ودها لا يدو
verses.h2: م، وعاشقها أبدا غير سال

verses.h1: This abode is treacherous to men,
verses.h2: severing the cords of affection.

verses.h1: In it we are stricken by what is not sweet,
verses.h2: and choke on what it gives us—not clear water.

verses.h1: Yet despite this, we grow more enamored of it.
verses.h2: Indeed, our striving is nothing but error.

verses.h1: Truly, it is a beloved whose affection does not last,
verses.h2: while its lover never ceases to yearn.

notes.note: The wording نفجع فيها بغير اللذيذ is unusual. I understand it literally as being afflicted by something that is not sweet; the precise force of نفجع here is uncertain.
I take the initial lām in لمعشوقة as emphatic. It could instead mean ‘for a beloved,’ linking this line to ‘our striving’ in the preceding line.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rāḍī Yazīd ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād, one of the kings of al-Andalus, said:

verses.h1: هل هيجتك مغاني الحي والدور
verses.h2: فاشتقت إن البعيد الدار معذور

verses.h1: وقد يحل بها إذ عيشنا أنق
verses.h2: بيض أوانس أمثال الدمى حور

verses.h1: Have the tribe’s old haunts and dwellings stirred you,
verses.h2: so that you yearned? One far from home may be forgiven.

verses.h1: There dwelt in them, when our life was sweet,
verses.h2: fair, gentle women, like statues, with wide, dark eyes.

verses.h1: سائل الدار إن سألت خبيرا
verses.h2: واستجر بالدموع تدع مجيرا

verses.h1: أفهمتني على نحول رباها
verses.h2: فكأني قرأت منها سطورا

verses.h1: Question the dwelling, if you would question one who knows;
verses.h2: seek refuge in tears, and you will call upon a protector.

verses.h1: It made its meaning clear to me, despite its wasted knolls,
verses.h2: as though I had read lines of writing in it.

notes.note: بالدموع may mean seeking refuge in tears themselves or using tears to appeal for protection.

poems.intro: يقال: شحطت الدار، إذا بعدت، ونزحت، وشسعت. ودار شطون، وبين شطون، وإلية شطون: فيه عوج. ودار غربة قذف، أي بعيدة. ويقال: أسقبت الدار، إذا قربت وأسعفت. والولي - بتخفيف اللام -: القرب. قال ساعدة بن جوية:

verses.h1: هجرت جنوب وحب من يتجنب
verses.h2: وعدت عواد دون وليك تشعب

verses.h1: Janūb has forsaken me—yet how dear is she who shuns me!
verses.h2: Adversities have barred my way to your nearness, driving us apart.

notes.note: I take حب as an exclamation of affection, “how dear”; its precise grammatical construction is uncertain in the unvowelled text.

prose_translation.intro: One says shaḥaṭat al-dār when the dwelling is far away, as also nazaḥat and shasaʿat. Dār shaṭūn means a distant dwelling, and bayn shaṭūn a far separation; an ilyah shaṭūn is an oath containing something crooked. Dār ghurbah qadhaf means a far-distant abode of exile. One says asqabat al-dār when the dwelling is near and within reach. Waly—with the lām un doubled—means nearness. Sāʿidah ibn Juʾayyah said:

poems.intro: والكثب: القرب، يقال: رماه من كثب، أي من قرب. قال يحيى بن معاذ - رضي الله عنه -: الدنيا دار خراب، وأخرب منها قلب من يشتهي عمارتها، والآخرة دار عمران، وأعمر منها قلب من يطلبها. وقال مهيار:

verses.h1: ما أنت بعد البين من أوطاني
verses.h2: دار الهوى، والدار بالجيران

verses.h1: كنت المنى من قبل طارقة النوى
verses.h2: والشمل شملي والزمان زماني

verses.h1: ولئن خلوت فليس أول حادث
verses.h2: خلت الكناس له من الغزلان

verses.h1: طرب الحمام بطبعهن وإنما اس
verses.h2: تملين فيك النوح من أحزاني

verses.h1: After parting, you are no longer a home of mine,
verses.h2: O dwelling of love—a dwelling is made by its neighbors.

verses.h1: You were all I wished for before separation struck,
verses.h2: when the company was my own and the times were mine.

verses.h1: Though you stand empty, this is not the first calamity
verses.h2: that has left the covert empty of gazelles.

verses.h1: Doves rejoice by nature; they only
verses.h2: learned their lament in you from my sorrows.

notes.note: الكناس is understood as the gazelles’ covert, but its agreement with the feminine verb خلت is unclear as printed.

prose_translation.intro: [Kathab]: nearness. One says, “He shot at him min kathab,” meaning “from close by.” Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh—may God be pleased with him—said: “This world is an abode of ruin, and more ruined still is the heart of one who longs to build it up. The Hereafter is an abode of flourishing, and more flourishing still is the heart of one who seeks it.” Mihyār said:

poems.poet_from_text: جدي سديد الملك ذو المناقب أبو الحسن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ
poems.intro: قال جدي سديد الملك ذو المناقب أبو الحسن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ - رضي الله -
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

poet.from_text: جدي سديد الملك ذو المناقب أبو الحسن علي بن مقلد بن نصر بن منقذ

verses.h1: لله ما طيف ألم بفتية
verses.h2: تحنو رؤوسهم على الأكوار

verses.h1: كيف اهتديت لراحلين ترودوا
verses.h2: ما شاء قومك من دجى ونهار

verses.h1: لفظتهم دار الإقامة فيكم
verses.h2: فنضوا عقال مطية الأسفار

verses.h1: ورنوا إلى الحي المقيم بأعين
verses.h2: ينهلن من ماء الدموع الجاري

verses.h1: By God, what a phantom visited those young men,
verses.h2: their heads drooping over their camel saddles!

verses.h1: How did you find travelers who had journeyed
verses.h2: through as much darkness and daylight as your people wished?

verses.h1: Their dwelling among you cast them out,
verses.h2: so they slipped the hobble from the mount of travel.

verses.h1: They gazed toward the tribe that stayed behind, with eyes
verses.h2: drinking their fill of flowing tears.

notes.note: ترودوا is uncertain here. I have understood it as تروّدوا, ‘wandered’ or ‘journeyed.’ It may instead be a misprint for تزودوا, ‘took provisions,’ which would make darkness and daylight their figurative provisions.
ينهلن can suggest drinking one’s fill or, when said of eyes, shedding tears. I have retained the drinking image suggested by من ماء الدموع, ‘from the water of tears.’

prose_translation.intro: My grandfather, Sadīd al-Mulk Dhū al-Manāqib Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Muqallad ibn Naṣr ibn Munqidh—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.intro: وقال عمي عز الدولة أبو المرهف، نصر بن علي - رحمه الله -:
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: لهفي لدار عفاها كل منهمر
verses.h2: جون ملث عليها رائح ساري

verses.h1: وما عفا ذكر أحبابي الذين لهم
verses.h2: حزني مقيم ودمعي إثرهم جاري

verses.h1: Alas for a dwelling effaced by every pouring rain cloud,
verses.h2: dark, lingering over it, coming at evening and roaming by night.

verses.h1: Yet the memory of my loved ones has not faded; for them
verses.h2: my grief abides, and my tears flow in their wake.

prose_translation.intro: And my paternal uncle, ʿIzz al-Dawla Abū al-Murhaf, Naṣr ibn ʿAlī—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: والدي مجد الدين أبو سلامة مرشد بن علي بن مقلد
poems.intro: وقال والدي مجد الدين أبو سلامة مرشد بن علي بن مقلد - رحمه الله -:
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

poet.from_text: والدي مجد الدين أبو سلامة مرشد بن علي بن مقلد

verses.h1: أيا دار التصابي والتصافي
verses.h2: وخصب العيش في السنة الجماد

verses.h1: لقد جارت عليك صروف دهر
verses.h2: رمتك بكل داهية ناد

verses.h1: فكم لي فيك من إخوان صدق
verses.h2: تملك صفو ودهم قيادي

verses.h1: قضت بفراقهم نوب الليالي
verses.h2: فميعاد التلاقي في المعاد

verses.h1: O abode of youthful dalliance and mutual affection,
verses.h2: of plentiful living in a barren year!

verses.h1: Time’s vicissitudes have indeed wronged you,
verses.h2: assailing you with every grievous calamity.

verses.h1: How many true brothers I had within you,
verses.h2: whose pure affection held my reins!

verses.h1: The turns of the nights decreed our parting,
verses.h2: so our appointed reunion is in the world to come.

notes.note: ناد is obscure as printed; I take it as نآد, ‘grievous’ or ‘overwhelming,’ qualifying ‘calamity.’

prose_translation.intro: And my father, Majd al-Dīn Abū Salama Murshid ibn ʿAlī ibn Muqallad—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي
poems.intro: وقال أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي - رحمه الله -:
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي

verses.h1: أصبحت دور آل مرشد قفرا
verses.h2: بعد عز وهيبة وجلال

verses.h1: عظة للعيون فيها اعتبار
verses.h2: ونذير من حادثات الليالي

verses.h1: تخبر الغافلين أن اقتناء الخ
verses.h2: لق فان معرض للزوال

verses.h1: فعليها السلام بعد بلاها
verses.h2: من حزين ما حزنه الدهر بال

verses.h1: The dwellings of Āl Murshid have become desolate
verses.h2: after glory, awe, and grandeur.

verses.h1: An admonition to the eyes, a lesson to be learned,
verses.h2: and a warning of the calamities time brings.

verses.h1: They tell the heedless that what people acquire
verses.h2: is perishable, subject to passing away.

verses.h1: So peace be upon them after their decay,
verses.h2: from a sorrowful man whose grief will never fade.

prose_translation.intro: And my brother, ʿIzz al-Dawla Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Murshid ibn ʿAlī—may God have mercy on him—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي

verses.h1: يا حيرة النفس أنى وجهة سلكوا
verses.h2: ومن هم في سواد القلب حلال

verses.h1: لا أوحش الله دارا كنت أعهدها
verses.h2: مغنى بكم، وهي بعد البين أطلال

verses.h1: O bewilderment of the soul! Which way have they gone—
verses.h2: those who dwell in the depths of my heart?

verses.h1: May God not leave desolate a house I once knew
verses.h2: as your dwelling—now, since our parting, only ruins.

notes.note: The wording ومن هم at the start of the second hemistich is syntactically awkward. I take it as referring back to those who departed: ‘those who dwell in the depths of my heart.’

poems.poet_from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي
poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

poet.from_text: أخي عز الدولة أبو الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي

verses.h1: كفى حسرة في النفس بعد أحبة
verses.h2: وقرب أعاد يشتهون حمامي

verses.h1: لعمرك ما دار الفتى حين لا يرى
verses.h2: أحبته فيها بدار مقام

verses.h1: Sorrow enough for the soul is the distance of loved ones,
verses.h2: and the nearness of enemies who wish for my death.

verses.h1: By your life, a man’s home, when he does not see
verses.h2: his loved ones there, is no place to remain.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يا دار غيرك البلى وتحكمت
verses.h2: فيك الخطوب ومحت الآثار

verses.h1: أصبحت تعرفك القلوب توهما
verses.h2: ويصد عنك الأعين الإنكار

verses.h1: لم يبق منك الدهر رسما ماثلا
verses.h2: ينبي بأن هناك كانت دار

verses.h1: لهفي على الزمن القصير قطعته
verses.h2: بك، إن أيام السرور قصار

verses.h1: لم يبقى منه سوى جوى متسعر
verses.h2: في القلب يذكى ناره التذكار

verses.h1: O dwelling, decay has changed you, and calamities have held sway
verses.h2: over you and effaced your traces.

verses.h1: Hearts now recognize you only by surmise,
verses.h2: while failure to recognize you turns the eyes away.

verses.h1: Time has left no trace of you standing
verses.h2: to tell that a dwelling once stood there.

verses.h1: How I grieve for the brief time I spent
verses.h2: within you! Indeed, the days of joy are short.

verses.h1: Nothing remains of it but blazing anguish
verses.h2: in the heart, whose fire remembrance feeds.

notes.note: لم يبقى appears to be a spelling or transcription error for لم يبق, the expected form after لم.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: سقى دارهم هامي الغمام وهامله
verses.h2: ونور ذاوى الروض فيها وذابله

verses.h1: وعاد بها طيب الليالي التي خلت
verses.h2: وغبطة عيش قد تقضت غياطله

verses.h1: منى يتمناها على بعد نيلها
verses.h2: كذوب الأماني ذاهب القلب ذاهله

verses.h1: وبعض الأماني ضلة، وإذا انقضت
verses.h2: أواخر دهر، كيف تثنى أوائله؟

verses.h1: ديار بها صاحبت شرخ شبيبتي
verses.h2: أجادده طورا، وطورا أهازله

verses.h1: أروح إلى لهو الصبي ونعيمه
verses.h2: وأغدو على ليث كمي أنازله

verses.h1: عهدت بها عين ألمها دون حجبها
verses.h2: أسود الشرى يلقى الردى من تصاوله

verses.h1: وسرب ظباء تحجب الشمس دونه
verses.h2: وتحجب عن طيف الخيال عقائله

verses.h1: وكل أخي بأس كريم تخاله
verses.h2: إذا ما انتضى سيفا جلته صياقله

verses.h1: فلم يبق مما كان إلا إدكاره
verses.h2: وحسرة قلب لا تقر بلابله

verses.h1: وكنت أرى ما سرني غير زائل
verses.h2: ويخطى نهج الحزم من هو جاهله

verses.h1: فما كان إلا الطيف يحسب في الكرى
verses.h2: يقينا، فإن بان الكرى بان باطله

verses.h1: May streaming, pouring clouds water their abode,
verses.h2: and may its shriveled, withered garden bloom.

verses.h1: May the sweetness of nights gone by return there,
verses.h2: and the bliss of a life whose lush abundance has passed away.

verses.h1: Wishes longed for, though far beyond attainment,
verses.h2: by one whose hopes deceive him, his heart lost and bewildered.

verses.h1: Some hopes are folly; and once there have passed
verses.h2: the last days of an age, how can its first days return?

verses.h1: Abodes where I kept company with the prime of my youth,
verses.h2: at times treating it earnestly, at times jesting with it.

verses.h1: I would go at evening to the play and pleasures of boyhood,
verses.h2: and set forth at dawn to face an armored lion in combat.

verses.h1: I knew there wide-eyed oryx, before whose veils
verses.h2: stood lions of al-Sharā: whoever fought them met death.

verses.h1: And a herd of gazelles, with the sun kept from them,
verses.h2: their noble does screened even from an apparition in a dream.

verses.h1: And every noble man of valor whom you would think—
verses.h2: whenever he drew his blade—a sword burnished by its polishers.

verses.h1: Nothing remains of what once was except its remembrance
verses.h2: and the grief of a heart whose turmoil never rests.

verses.h1: I thought that what delighted me would never pass away;
verses.h2: one ignorant of the path of prudence misses it.

verses.h1: It was nothing but a dream-image, taken in sleep
verses.h2: for truth; when sleep departs, its falsehood becomes plain.

notes.note: The rare word غياطله appears to evoke luxuriant or tangled growth; its figurative sense here is rendered as ‘lush abundance.’
عين ألمها appears to be a typing or OCR error for عين المها, ‘wide-eyed oryx.’ al-Sharā is apparently the place traditionally associated with lions; its precise location is uncertain.
تحجب الشمس دونه is somewhat ambiguous. I take it to mean that the sun is kept from reaching the gazelles, rather than that their beauty eclipses it.

I take سيفاً as the delayed complement of تخاله (‘you would think him a sword’), with إذا ما انتضى parenthetical (‘whenever he drew his blade’). The unvocalized syntax also permits taking سيفاً as the object of انتضى, but that leaves the comparison less explicit.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يقول صحابي: قد أطلت وقوفنا
verses.h2: على الدار مسلوب الأسى والتماسك

verses.h1: أفي كل دار قد عفت أنت واقف
verses.h2: تروي ثراها بالدموع السوافك

verses.h1: كأنك في رسم الديار "متمم
verses.h2: وفيما عفا من ربعها "قبر مالك

verses.h1: فقلت: نعم هذي ديار عهدتها
verses.h2: بها معشري مثل النجوم الشوابك

verses.h1: أصابهم ريب الزمان فأصبحت
verses.h2: قفارا، وهم ما بين ناء وهالك

verses.h1: My companions say: “You have kept us standing long
verses.h2: at the dwelling, bereft of solace and self-command.

verses.h1: Do you stand at every dwelling whose traces have faded,
verses.h2: watering its soil with streaming tears?

verses.h1: As though, among the dwellings’ traces, you were Mutammim,
verses.h2: and in their vanished encampment lay Mālik’s grave.”

verses.h1: I said: “Yes, these are dwellings I once knew,
verses.h2: with my people there like clustered stars.

verses.h1: Time’s calamities struck them, and the dwellings became
verses.h2: desolate; my people are either far away or dead.”

notes.note: الأسى is taken here as al-usā, ‘solace’ or ‘consolation.’ The more usual reading al-asā means ‘grief,’ which would be awkward after مسلوب, ‘bereft of’; the intended reading is uncertain.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يقولون: قد أعولت في الدار ما كفا
verses.h2: وليس على ربع عفا بمعول

verses.h1: وكم قدر ما تبقى الدموع إذا جرت
verses.h2: على كل ربع، أو على كل منزل؟

verses.h1: فقلت: نعم. هذي ديار عهدتها
verses.h2: عرين أسودي في الخطوب ومعقلي

verses.h1: فقد أصبحت قفرا، وفرق شملهم
verses.h2: حوادث دهر بالفراق موكل

verses.h1: سأبكيهم أو يمزج الدم أدمعي
verses.h2: فينهل سمطا كالجمان المفصل

verses.h1: They say, “You have wailed enough over the dwelling;
verses.h2: there is no help in lamenting an effaced encampment.

verses.h1: How long can tears last if they flow
verses.h2: over every encampment, or over every dwelling?”

verses.h1: I said, “Yes—these are dwellings I knew
verses.h2: as my lions’ den in adversity, and my stronghold.

verses.h1: Now they lie deserted, and their company has been scattered
verses.h2: by the blows of an age charged with bringing separation.

verses.h1: I shall weep for them until blood mingles with my tears
verses.h2: and streams down in a strand, like pearls interspersed with beads.”

notes.note: معول can denote lamentation or something relied upon. The translation takes the phrase to mean that lamenting an effaced encampment offers no help.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يا دار أنت التي كانت الجميع بها
verses.h2: وكان في ربعك الولدان والحشم

verses.h1: وكنت للضيف والعافين مرتبعا
verses.h2: يقتادهم نحوك الإكرام والكرم

verses.h1: أصبحت قفرا، وأضحى أهلك افترقوا
verses.h2: أيدي سبا، وانثنت عن قصدك الهمم

verses.h1: ما أعجب الدهر! عيش الناس أجمعهم
verses.h2: إن سرهم صرفه أو ساءهم

verses.h1: حلم
O dwelling, you are the one where everyone once gathered,
verses.h2: and within your grounds were boys and retainers.

verses.h1: You were a spring pasture for guests and seekers of bounty,
verses.h2: drawn toward you by hospitality and generosity.

verses.h1: You have become deserted, and your people have scattered,
verses.h2: like the people of Sabaʾ; no one now feels the urge to seek you out.

verses.h1: How strange is time! The life of all mankind,
verses.h2: whether its turns delight or grieve them, is

verses.h1: a dream.

notes.note: The wording كانت الجميع بها has unexpected feminine agreement in كانت with الجميع. It may contain a textual error; the translation follows the apparent sense, ‘where everyone once gathered.’
حلم (‘a dream’) evidently completes the sentence and verse in line 4, rather than forming a separate verse. The supplied division is preserved.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: دار على قلل الجبال تفجرت
verses.h2: فيها بحار فضائل ومكارم

verses.h1: فيها الندى والجود حقا لا الذي
verses.h2: كنا نحدث عن سماحة حاتم

verses.h1: وفوارس جمعوا المكارم والعلى
verses.h2: لين التواضع في قلوب ضراغم

verses.h1: أفناهم ريب المنون فلم يدع
verses.h2: منهم سوى ذكر لحلم الحالم

verses.h1: A dwelling on the mountain peaks: there burst forth
verses.h2: within it seas of virtue and noble deeds.

verses.h1: There are bounty and generosity in truth—not what
verses.h2: we used to recount of Ḥātim’s openhandedness.

verses.h1: And horsemen who combined noble deeds and high renown:
verses.h2: the gentleness of humility in the hearts of lions.

verses.h1: The blows of fate destroyed them, leaving
verses.h2: nothing of them but the memory of a dreamer’s dream.

notes.note: The phrase «ذكر لحلم الحالم» is uncertain. Translated literally here as a memory of a dreamer’s dream, it may contain a misprint for «ذكر كحلم الحالم», ‘a memory like a dreamer’s dream.’ Alternatively, حلم الحالم could mean ‘the forbearing man’s forbearance.’

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يا دار لو روت محولك أدمعي
verses.h2: لسفحتها بك، أو يمازجها الدم

verses.h1: لكن دمع الحزن يحسب قطره
verses.h2: ماء برودا، وهو جمر مضرم

verses.h1: وإذا رأيتك قفرة من معشري
verses.h2: وبني أبي، وهم لعمرك ما هم؟

verses.h1: فكأنني عاينت حفرة مالك
verses.h2: وكأنني وجدا عليه متمم

verses.h1: O dwelling, if my tears could water your parched ground,
verses.h2: I would pour them out upon you until blood mingled with them.

verses.h1: But sorrow’s tears—their drops are thought
verses.h2: to be cool water, though they are blazing coals.

verses.h1: And when I see you empty of my people
verses.h2: and my father’s sons—by your life, what men they were!—

verses.h1: it is as though I beheld Mālik’s grave,
verses.h2: and as though, grieving for him, I were Mutammim.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: وا وحشتي في الدار لما أصبحت موشحة من الظباء العين
كانت عرينا، وكناسا فاغتدت
verses.h2: مقفرة الكناس والعرين

verses.h1: تقارن الأسد بها عين المها
verses.h2: والدهر قطاع قوى القرين

verses.h1: فأصبحت كما ترى ليس بها
verses.h2: إلا دواعي الوجد والحنين

verses.h1: Ah, my loneliness in the abode, now bereft of wide-eyed gazelles!
It was a lion’s den and a gazelle’s covert; then it became
verses.h2: Desolate in covert and den alike.

verses.h1: Lions there would consort with wide-eyed oryx,
verses.h2: But time keeps severing the bonds between companions.

verses.h1: Now, as you see, nothing remains there
verses.h2: But what awakens grief and longing.

notes.note: The text reads موشحة (‘adorned’ or ‘girdled’), which is difficult to reconcile with من الظباء and the ensuing description of abandonment. The translation tentatively reads موحشة (‘desolate’), taking the phrase to mean deserted by the wide-eyed gazelles.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: نظرت إلى دار الأحبة قفرة
verses.h2: وقد كان فيها العز والكرم المحض

verses.h1: فلما رأى صحبي عليها تلددي
verses.h2: ودمعي بكى بعض وعنفني بعض

verses.h1: وقالوا: أفق، للأرض تبكي؟ فقلت: لا
verses.h2: ولكنني أبكي لمن وارث الأرض

verses.h1: I gazed upon the loved ones’ dwelling, desolate,
verses.h2: where once were glory and generosity unalloyed.

verses.h1: When my companions saw my restless turning there
verses.h2: and my tears, some wept and some rebuked me.

verses.h1: They said, “Come to your senses! Do you weep for the earth?” I said, “No,
verses.h2: but I weep for those whom the earth has buried.”

notes.note: The source reads وارث الأرض, which appears corrupt. The translation assumes وارت الأرض, ‘the earth has covered/buried,’ with لمن referring to those buried.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

verses.h1: يا دار إن بخلت على
verses.h2: مغناك سارية العهاد

verses.h1: فلأمطرنك من دمو
verses.h2: عي ما ينوب عن الغوادي

verses.h1: حتى تعود رباك حا
verses.h2: لية مفوفة الوهاد

verses.h1: كم حل ربعك من غض
verses.h2: يض الطرف ممنوع الوداد

verses.h1: يستوقف الأبصار فه
verses.h2: ي عليه حائمة صوادي

verses.h1: فرمت جموعهم اللي
verses.h2: الي بالتشتت والبعاد

verses.h1: وصروف هذا الدهر تط
verses.h2: رق بالحوادث أو تغادي

verses.h1: عاداتها رد الأمو
verses.h2: ر من الصلاح إلى الفساد

verses.h1: يحسن لا عمدا ويأ
verses.h2: تين الإساءة باعتماد

verses.h1: O dwelling, if your grounds are denied
verses.h2: the night-cloud’s returning showers,

verses.h1: I shall surely rain upon you with my tears
verses.h2: enough to replace the morning rains,

verses.h1: until your hills are adorned once more,
verses.h2: and your hollows clothed in many colors.

verses.h1: How many dwelt within your precincts,
verses.h2: with downcast eyes and love beyond reach!

verses.h1: They arrest all eyes, which then
verses.h2: hover thirstily about them.

verses.h1: Then the nights struck their gathered company
verses.h2: with dispersal and separation.

verses.h1: And the vicissitudes of this age come by night
verses.h2: with calamities, or arrive in the morning.

verses.h1: Their habit is to turn affairs
verses.h2: from soundness to decay.

verses.h1: They do good without intending it,
verses.h2: but inflict harm deliberately.

poems.subchapter: أبيات في هذا المعنى من شعر جدي، ووالدي، وعمي، وأخي - رضي الله عنهم - وشعري

opening.actual: ما أنت أول من تناءت داره

verses.h1: ما أنت أول من تناءت داره
verses.h2: فعلام قلبك ليس تخبو ناره؟

verses.h1: إما السلو أو الحمام، وما سوى
verses.h2: هذين قسم ثالث تختاره

verses.h1: ما بعد يومك من لقاء يرتجى
verses.h2: أو يلتقي جنح الدجى ونهاره

verses.h1: هذا وقوفك للوداع وهذه أظعان من تهوى وتلك دياره
فاستبق دمعك فهو أول خاذل
verses.h2: بعد الفراق، وإن طما تياره

verses.h1: مدد الدموع يقل عن أمد النوى
verses.h2: إن لم تكن من لجة تمتاره

verses.h1: You are not the first whose home has grown distant;
verses.h2: why, then, will your heart’s fire not die down?

verses.h1: Either forgetfulness or death; beyond
verses.h2: these two there is no third course for you to choose.

verses.h1: After this day, no meeting can be hoped for,
verses.h2: unless the darkness of night and its daylight meet.

verses.h1: Here you stand to say farewell; here is the departing caravan of those you love, and there are their dwellings.
Save your tears, for they are the first to fail you
verses.h2: after parting, though their flood runs high.

verses.h1: The supply of tears falls short of separation’s span,
verses.h2: unless you draw that supply from a deep sea.

notes.note: The force of أو before يلتقي is uncertain: it can introduce an ‘until’ or ‘unless’ condition. Here it is taken as ‘unless,’ apparently making reunion depend on night and day meeting.

poems.intro: وقلت - وكتبت بها إلى أخي عز الدولة أبي الحسن علي بن مرشد بن علي بن مقلد - رحمه الله - وأنا بالعسكر الأتابكي بإربل:
