(ولمن دخل بيتي مؤمنا) قيل: صديقي الداخل إلى منزلي، وقيل: من دخل مسجدي وقيل: من دخل في ديني. وقال الله تبارك وتعالى: (ليس [على الأعمى حرج ولا على الأعرج حرج، ولا على المريض حرج، ولا على أنفسكم] أن تأكلوا من بيوتكم، أو بيوت آبائكم، أو بيوت أمهاتكم، أو بيوت إخوانكم، أو بيوت أخواتكم، أو بيوت أعمامكم، أو بيوت عماتكم، أو بيوت أخوالكم، أو بيوت خالاتكم) . أباح سبحانه الأكل في بيوت هؤلاء لمكان النسب من غير استئذانهم في الأكل إذا كان الطعام مبذولا، فإن كان محرزا دونهم لم يكن لهم هتك حرزه، ولا يجوز أن يتجاوز الأكل إلى الادخار، [أو] إلى ما ليس بمأكول، وإن كان غير محرز عنهم إلا بإذن منهم. وقال الله تبارك وتعالى: (وأوحينا إلى موسى وأخيه أن تبوآ لقومكما بمصر بيوتا) أي مساكن يسكنونها، وقيل: [في] قوله "مصر" إنها الإسكندرية، وقيل: بل هي مصر، وقيل: اتخذوا قصورا، وقيل: مساجد (واجعلوا بيوتكم قبلة) ، قيل: مقابل بعضها بعضا، وقيل: اجعلوا مساجدكم قبل الكعبة. وقال الله تبارك وتعالى: (وأوحى ربك إلى النخل أن اتخذي من الجبال بيوتا، ومن الشجر ومما يعرشون) . في (أوحى) ثلاثة أقوال: أحدها: ألهمها. والآخر: سخرها. والثالث: أنه سبحانه جعل ذلك في غرائزها مما يخفى مثله على غيرها. (أن اتخذي من الجبال بيوتا) ذكر الله تعالى بيوتها لما ألهمها وأودعه غرائزها من صحة القسمة، وحسن الصنعة. وقال الله تبارك وتعالى: (مثل الذين اتخذوا من دون الله أولياء، كمثل العنكبوت اتخذت بيتا، وإن أوهن البيوت لبيت العنكبوت لو كانوا يعلمون) . يعني سبحانه آلهة من أصنام وأوثان عبدوها، (كمثل العنكبوت اتخذت بيتا) يعني أنهم عبدوا ما لا يغني عنهم شيئا، كبيت العنكبوت لا يستر الأبصار، ولا يدفع الأيدي. وعن عطاء عن ابن عباس - رضي الله عنه - ذكر آلهة المشركين فقال سبحانه: (وإن يسلبهم الذباب شيئا لا يستنقذوه منه) وذكر كيد الآلهة، فجعله كبيت العنكبوت، فقالوا: - حيث ذكر الله الذباب والعنكبوت فما أنزل على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم: أي شيء يصنع بهذا؟ فأنزل الله - عز وجل -: (إن الله لا يستحي أن يضرب مثلا ما بعوضة فما فوقها ... ) الآية. قال القاضي الماوردي - رحمه الله -: البعوضة من صغار البق، سميت بذلك لأنها كبعض البقة في صغرها. وقيل: نسجت العنكبوت مرتين: مرة على داوود عليه السلام، ومرة على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، وجمع عنكبوت عناكب، وتصغيره عنيكب. وقد ذكر علي - رضوان الله عليه - العنكبوت في كلام له، روى أن رجلا أتى عليا - رضوان الله عليه - فقال: يا أمير المؤمنين إنه قضيت علي قضية ذهب فيها مالي وأهلين فخرج إلى الرحبة، فاجتمع عليه الناس، فقال - رضوان الله عليه -: ذمتي بما أقول رهينة، وأنا به زعيم، إن من صرحت له العبر عما بين يديه من المثلات حجزه التقوى عن تقحم الشبهات، وإن أشقى الناس رجل قمش علما في أوباش الناس بغير علم ولا دليل، فاستكثر مما قل منه خير، فأكثر، حتى إذا ارتوى من آجن آسن غير طائل جلس للناس مفتيا؛ ليخلص ما التبس على غيره، فهو في قطع من الشبهات، في مثل نسج العنكبوت، لا يدري أصاب أم أخطأ، خباط عشوات، ركاب جهالات، لم يعض على العلم بضرس قاطع فيغنم، ولم يسكت فيسلم، تصرخ منه الدماء، وتبكي منه المواريث، وتستحل بقضائه الفرج الحرام، أولئك الذين حلت عليهم النياحة في أيام حياتهم. -أوجب إيراد هذا الحديث ما فيه من ذكر العنكبوت) . عن أنس بن مالك - رحمه الله - قال: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: ما من بيت إلا وملك الموت يقف على بابه في كل يوم خمس مرات، فإذا وجد إنسانا قد نفذ أجله، وانقطع عمله، ألقى عليه غم الموت، فغشيته كرباته، وغمرته غمراته، وجهرت الباكية بشجوها، والصارخة بويلها، فيقول ملك الموت - عليه السلام -: ويلكم، وفيم الفزع؟ وفيم الجزع؟ ما أذهبت لواحد منكم رزقا، ولا قربت له أجلا، ولا أتيته حتى أمرت، ولا قبضت روحه حتى استأمرت، وغن لي فيكم عودة، ثم عودة، ثم عودة، حتى لا أبقى منكم أحدا. قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: فوالذي نفسي بيده، لو يرون مكانه، أو يسمعون كلامه، لذهلوا عن ميتهم، ولبكوا على أنفسهم، حتى إذا حمل الميت على نعشه، رفرفت الروح فوق النعش، فهو ينادي: يا أهلي، ويا ولدي. لا تلعبن بكم الدنيا، كما لعبت بي، جمعت المال من حله ومن غير حله، ثم خلفته لغيري، فالهناءة له، والتبعة علي، فاحذروا ما حل بي. عن أبي موسى الأشعري - رحمه الله - قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "مثل بيت يذكر الله تعلى فيه، وبيت لا يذكر الله فيه، مثل الحي والميت". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "نوروا بيوتكم بتلاوة القرآن يفر منها الشيطان". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "نزول الضيف في البيت بركة". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "لا تدخل الخيانة بيتا إلا خرب". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "لا تدخل السرقة بيتا إلا أورثتهم الذل". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "ما من أحد يخرج من بيته يطلب العلم إلا وضعت له الملائكة أجنحتها رضى بما يصنع". وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "ما من أحد يخرج من بيته مجاهدا في سبيل الله تعالى إلا لم تزل الملائكة تستغفر له حتى يرجع". وقال الوزير الكامل أبو القاسم بن المغربي، وقد حج:

poet.from_text: الوزير الكامل أبو القاسم بن المغربي

verses.h1: أستار بيتك أمن الخوف منك وقد
verses.h2: علقتها مستجيرا منك يا باري

verses.h1: وما أظنك لما أن علقت بها
verses.h2: خوفا من النار تدنيني من النار

verses.h1: وها أنا جار بيت أنت قلت لنا: حجوا إليه، وقد أوصيت بالجار
The curtains of Your House are safety from fear of You; I have
verses.h2: clung to them, seeking refuge from You, O my Creator.

verses.h1: I do not think that, once I have clung to them
verses.h2: for fear of the Fire, You will bring me near the Fire.

verses.h1: Here I am, a neighbor of a House of which You told us, “Make pilgrimage to it”—and You have enjoined care for the neighbor.

prose_translation.intro:
God, blessed and exalted, said: “And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a place of safety …”—the verse. By mathaba, it is meant that they are rewarded for making pilgrimage to it. It is also said to mean a gathering place, because people gather there for the hajj and the ʿumra; and it is said to mean a place of return, from their expression thabat al-ʿilla, when an illness returns.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “And take the Station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer.” There are two accounts of why he stood upon the stone. The first is that, when the structure of the House grew high and Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, could no longer lift the stones, he stood upon this stone; thus it is the Station of Ibrāhīm. The second is that it was a stone which the wife of Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him, placed beneath Ibrāhīm’s foot when she washed his head. He placed his foot upon it, and his foot sank into it.

I shall relate the circumstances in which Ibrāhīm, God’s blessings be upon him, had his head washed, abridging what the writers of prophetic history have related on the subject. When Hājar gave birth to Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him, God, glorified be He, commanded Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, to settle the two of them in Makka. He took them there, and when he wished to return, Hājar said to him, “Ibrāhīm, who commanded you to leave me in a land with neither crops nor milk-giving livestock, neither companion nor water nor provisions?” He said, “My Lord commanded me.” She said, “Then He will not abandon us.” When Ibrāhīm departed, he said, “Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we reveal,” meaning their sorrow.

When Ismāʿīl grew thirsty, he began scraping the ground with his heels. Hājar went and climbed al-Ṣafā. The valley was deep at that time. She looked out, but saw nothing, so she descended into the valley and ran through it until she emerged. Then she came to al-Marwa, climbed it, and looked out, but saw nothing. She did this seven times. Then she returned from al-Marwa to Ismāʿīl, who was scraping the ground with his heel, and the spring—Zamzam—had begun to gush. She began digging at the earth around the water with her hand. Whenever some water collected, she scooped it up with her cup and poured it into her waterskin. The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “May God have mercy on her! Had she left it alone, it would have been a flowing spring, running until the Day of Resurrection.”

Jurhum were then in a valley near Makka. When the birds saw the water, they stayed in the valley. Seeing that the birds had stayed there, Jurhum said, “They would not stay there unless there were water in it.” They came to Hājar and said, “If you wish, we will stay with you and keep you company, while the water remains yours.” She said, “Yes.” They stayed with her until Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him, grew to manhood and Hājar died. He married a woman of Jurhum.

Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, asked Sāra’s permission to visit Hājar. She permitted him, on condition that he not dismount. Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, arrived after Hājar had died. He went to Ismāʿīl’s house and said to his wife, “Where is your husband?” She said, “He has gone hunting.” He said, “Have you anything with which to entertain a guest?” She said, “I have neither food nor drink.” Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, said, “When your husband returns, convey my greetings to him and tell him to change the threshold of his house.”

Ibrāhīm left, and Ismāʿīl returned and detected his father’s scent. He said to his wife, “Did anyone come to you?” She said, “An old man came to me, looking such-and-such,” speaking as though she thought little of him. He said, “What did he say to you?” She said, “He told me, ‘Convey my greetings to your husband and tell him to change the threshold of his door.’” So he divorced her and married another woman.

Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, remained away for as long as God willed. Then he asked Sāra’s permission to visit Ismāʿīl. She permitted him, on condition that he not dismount. Ibrāhīm came to Ismāʿīl’s door, peace be upon them both, and said to his wife, “Where is your husband?” She said, “He has gone hunting and will return presently, God willing. Dismount, may God have mercy on you.” He said, “Have you anything with which to entertain a guest?” She said, “Yes.” He said, “Have you bread, wheat, barley, or dates?” She brought milk and meat, and he prayed for a blessing upon them. Had she brought bread, wheat, barley, or dates that day, Makka would have been the most abundant of God’s lands in wheat, barley, and dates.

Then, seeing that his hair was disheveled, she said to him, “Dismount, may God have mercy on you, so that I may wash your head.” He did not dismount, but excused himself. She brought him the stone of the Station and placed it beneath his right side. He put his foot upon it, and the impression of his foot remained on it. Then she washed the right side of his head. She moved the stone of the Station to the left side of his head and washed it, just as she had done on the right. He said to her, “When your husband comes, convey my greetings to him and tell him, ‘The threshold of your door is now sound.’”

When Ismāʿīl returned, he detected his father’s scent, peace be upon them both, and said to his wife, “Did anyone come to you?” She said, “Yes, an old man, the most handsome and fragrant of men. He said such-and-such to me, and I said such-and-such to him. I washed his head, and this is the impression of his foot. He told me, ‘Tell your husband when he comes: The threshold of your door is now sound.’” He said, “That was my father Ibrāhīm, the intimate friend of the All-Merciful, mighty and majestic.”

I have related this account in abridged form only so that someone who encounters the mention of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, having his head washed, without knowing how it happened, will not be left longing to know.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “And We charged Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl: Purify My House …” There are five interpretations of this: first, of idols; second, of unbelievers; third, of impurities; fourth, of afflictions and doubts; and fifth, that it is for those who make pilgrimage to it and circumambulate it. If it is asked, “But in Ibrāhīm’s time, peace be upon him, before the House was built, was there a house to be purified?” there are two answers. The first is: “Build My House in a state of purity.” The second is: “Purify the site of My House for those who circumambulate it.”

He, blessed and exalted, said: “Whoever leaves his home, emigrating to God and His Messenger, and is then overtaken by death, his reward is incumbent upon God …”—the verse. There are two interpretations. The first is that whoever leaves Makka to emigrate and dies on the road before reaching al-Madina has earned the reward for his deed and the recompense for his emigration. The second concerns someone who sets out on a military expedition and dies before the battle: he receives the reward for his striving.

There is disagreement over the person concerning whom this verse was revealed. It is said that it was revealed concerning Abū Umayya Ḍamra ibn Jundab al-Khuzāʿī, who left Makka as an emigrant and died in the mountain pass. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Khālid ibn Ḥizām, the brother of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām, who set out as an emigrant and died on the road.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him, said, in the account transmitted by ʿAṭāʾ: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, may God be pleased with him, used to inform the people of Makka of whatever was revealed of the Quran. He wrote to them with the words of God, mighty and majestic: “Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves—the angels say, ‘In what condition were you?’ They say, ‘We were oppressed in the land.’ They say, ‘Was God’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate within it?’ Those—their abode is Hell, and evil is that destination.”

When Ḥabīb ibn Ḍamra al-Laythī read this, being a very old man, he said, “Carry me, for I am not one of the oppressed, and I can certainly find the road.” They carried him on a bed toward al-Madina. When he reached al-Tanʿīm, he was close to death. He struck his right hand against his left and said, “O God, this is for You, and this is for Your Messenger. I pledge allegiance to You upon the terms on which I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace.” Then he died. News of him reached the Companions of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and they said, “Had he reached al-Madina, his reward would have been more complete.” Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed: “Whoever leaves his home, emigrating to God and His Messenger, and is then overtaken by death, his reward is incumbent upon God …”—the verse.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “God desires only to remove defilement from you, people of the Household, and to purify you completely.” ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, may God have mercy on him, said: Someone who heard Umm Salama, may God be pleased with her, told me that she related: The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, was in her house when Fāṭima, peace be upon her, brought him a pot containing khazira, a meat-and-flour porridge. She brought it in to him, and he said, “Call your husband and your two sons for me.” She said: ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn, may God be pleased with them, came in to him and sat eating that porridge. He was on a bed of his upon a raised platform, with a Khaybarī cloak beneath him. She said: I was praying in the chamber when God, mighty and majestic, revealed: “God desires only to remove defilement from you, people of the Household, and to purify you completely.” The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, took the loose portion of the cloak and covered them with it. Then he raised his hands toward heaven and said, “O God, these are the people of my household and my closest kin. Remove defilement from them, the people of the Household, and purify them completely.” She said: I put my head into the room and said, “Am I with you, Messenger of God?” He said, “You are assured of good; you are assured of good.”

God, blessed and exalted, said: “O you who believe, do not enter the Prophet’s houses unless you are given permission for a meal, without waiting for it to be ready. But when you are invited, enter; and when you have eaten, disperse …”—the verse. Most commentators say: When the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, consummated his marriage to Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, may God be pleased with her, he held a wedding feast with dates and parched-grain meal, and slaughtered a sheep. Anas ibn Mālik, may God have mercy on him, said: My mother, Umm Sulaym, sent him hays, a mixture of dates, clarified butter, and dried curds, in a stone bowl. The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, commanded me to invite his Companions, may God be pleased with them, to the meal. People kept coming, eating, and leaving. I said, “Messenger of God, I have invited people until I can find no one else to invite.” He said, “Take away your food.” They took it away, and the people departed, but three men remained talking in the house. They lingered a long time, and the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, was troubled by them, but he was exceedingly shy. Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse.

His words, mighty and majestic, relating the words of Ibrāhīm, God bless him and grant him peace: “My Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley beside Your Sacred House.” His offspring means Ismāʿīl, together with his mother Hājar. “In an uncultivated valley” means Makka. He settled her in its gravelly valley bed, where no one lived, trusting in God Most High and relying upon Him. “Beside Your Sacred House”: He ascribed the House to Himself, glorified be He, because no one else owns it. It is called sacred because things are forbidden there which are lawful elsewhere, such as intercourse and treating it without reverence.

His words, mighty and majestic, “By the frequented House,” have four interpretations. The first is what Qatāda transmitted from Anas ibn Mālik, may God have mercy on him, who said: The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “I was taken to the seventh heaven, and the frequented House was displayed to us. It was directly opposite the Kaʿba: if it fell, it would fall upon it. Seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and when they leave it, they never return to it.”

The second is that the frequented House is a house among the six heavens below the seventh, called al-Ḍurāḥ. Every day seventy thousand angels of the tribe of Iblis pray in it, never returning to it again. It stands opposite the Ancient House.

The third is what al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: The frequented House was on earth, on the site of the Kaʿba, in the time of Adam, peace be upon him, and remained until the time of Nūḥ, peace be upon him. Nūḥ commanded his people to make pilgrimage to it, but they refused and disobeyed him. When the water rose, it was lifted up and placed directly opposite its former site in the lowest heaven. Every day seventy thousand angels pass through it, and they do not return until the trumpet is blown. He said: God Most High then assigned to Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, the site of the Kaʿba, the Sacred House, as He, glorified be He, says: “And when We assigned to Ibrāhīm the site of the House …”—the verse.

The fourth is what al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him, said: The frequented House is the Sacred House. As for “frequented,” it is said to mean that it is kept in use by people journeying to it, and it is said to mean by their remaining there.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “In houses which God has permitted to be raised and His name to be remembered therein.” It is said that these are mosques, and it is said that they are houses generally. “God has permitted to be raised” means to be built, as in His words, exalted be He: “And when Ibrāhīm raised the foundations of the House,” meaning built them. It is also said to mean that requests are raised in them to God, mighty and majestic.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have made yourselves known and greeted their inhabitants …”—the verse. It is related from ʿAdī ibn Thābit that he said: A woman of the Ansar came and said, “Messenger of God, I am sometimes in my house in a condition in which I would not like anyone to see me, neither parent nor child. My father comes and enters, and men of my family keep coming in while I am in that condition. What should I do?” Then God Most High revealed this verse. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, said, “Messenger of God, what of the inns and lodgings on the roads of al-Shām which have no inhabitants?” Then God Most High revealed: “There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses …”—the verse.

There are three interpretations of His words, exalted be He: “O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have made yourselves known and greeted their inhabitants.” It is said to mean: until you have asked permission. It is said to mean: until you have made your presence known to the inhabitants by clearing your throat, so that they know you are coming in. And it is said that “until you have made yourselves known” means: until you ascertain whether there is someone inside whose permission you may ask, and then greet him. Similar is His saying, exalted be He, “If you perceive sound judgment in them,” meaning if you know it to be present.

Permission may be given in words or by a gesture. From Abū Hurayra, may God have mercy on him, who said: The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “A man’s messenger is his permission.” If someone asks permission three times and is not admitted, he should turn away and not renew his request. It is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, from al-Ashʿarī, that he asked permission to enter the presence of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, three times. He was not admitted, so he went back. ʿUmar sent for him and said, “What made you turn back?” He said, “The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Whoever asks permission three times and is not admitted should turn back.’” ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said, “You must bring me evidence, or I shall make an example of you.” He went to Ṭalḥa, may God have mercy on him, who testified for him.

Al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him, said: The first request is a request for admission; the second allows consultation; the third is decisive: if they wish, they admit him, and if they wish, they turn him away. One should not ask permission while facing the doorway if the door is open. If the first of a group is admitted, permission extends to the last of them. One should not sit at the door after being turned away, for people have matters to attend to.

Then He, exalted be He, said: “And greet their inhabitants.” Greeting is recommended, while asking permission is obligatory. There are two opinions concerning the greeting. The first is that it is prescribed after permission has been given, as the verse indicates by placing permission before it, and because greeting is a salutation upon meeting, and meeting takes place after permission. The second is that it is prescribed before asking permission: although it comes later in the recitation, it comes first in practice. The sense of the words is thus: “Until you greet them and ask permission.” This is based on what Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, may God have mercy on him, related: A man asked permission to enter the presence of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, saying, “May I enter?” The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said to a man who was with him, “Go and teach him how to ask permission, for he has not done it properly.” The man heard him, so he gave the greeting and asked permission.

It has also been said that, if their eyes meet before permission is asked, it is preferable to greet before asking permission; but if their eyes do not meet before permission, it is preferable to ask permission before greeting.

As for asking permission to enter the homes of relatives: if they are not within the degrees of kinship that prohibit marriage, one must ask their permission, just as with strangers. If they are within those degrees and the dwelling is shared, with both him and them living there, he must warn them before entering, either through his footsteps or by clearing his throat in a way that makes his presence known. The exception is one’s wife: this is not required with her, because there is no restriction upon their seeing one another’s nakedness. If the dwelling is not shared, there are two opinions about asking their permission. The first is that it is done by clearing the throat and making a sound of movement. The second is that it is done verbally, as with strangers.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, may God have mercy on him, related that a man said to the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, “Should I ask permission to enter my mother’s presence?” He said, “Yes.” The man said, “But I attend to her needs.” He said, “Ask her permission.” The man repeated his question three times, and he, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “Would you like to see her naked?” He said, “No.” He said, “Then ask her permission.”

“If you find no one therein”—meaning anyone to give you permission—“then do not enter them until permission is given to you.” It is not permissible to peer into a dwelling to see who is inside and ask his permission, if the door is closed, because the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “Asking permission was instituted only on account of sight.” If the door is open, however, someone outside it may look in, because by opening it the owner has allowed people to look.

“If you are told, ‘Go back,’ then go back; that is purer for you.” If this occurs after someone has entered with permission, he must depart, and remaining is forbidden. If it occurs before entry, it is a refusal of permission and a prohibition against entering; he need only leave the place where he is standing.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses.” These are said to be shared inns containing occupied rooms; or merchants’ shops; or lodgings for travelers and places where loads are set down, used by wayfarers on their journeys; or deserted ruins; or the houses of Makka. “In which there is some benefit for you”: it is not necessary to ask permission to enter these places.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth.” It is said to mean: Just as your Lord brought you out of Makka to al-Madina in truth, despite the reluctance of a group of the believers, so He will fulfill His promise to you by granting you victory over your enemies. It is also said that there are two interpretations of His words, exalted be He, “in truth.” The first is that you went out with the truth accompanying you. The second is that He brought you out in accordance with the obligation incumbent upon you.

He, blessed and exalted, said, relating the words of the polytheists: “And they said, ‘We will not believe you until you make a spring gush forth for us from the earth; or you have a garden of palms and vines and make rivers gush abundantly through it; or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you have claimed; or you bring God and the angels before us; or you have a house of ornament.’” [Zukhruf]: it is said to mean decoration, and it is said to mean gold. Mujāhid said, “I did not know what zukhruf meant until we heard, in the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, ‘a house of zukhruf.’” Its root is zakhrafa, which means making an appearance beautiful. From this come the words of God, mighty and majestic: “Until, when the earth has taken on its adornment and become beautiful.”

Those who addressed these words to the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, were a group of Quraysh. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him, said: They were ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, Shayba ibn Rabīʿa, Abū Sufyān, al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Asad, Zamʿa ibn al-Aswad, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abī Umayya, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Nabīh and Munabbih, the two sons of al-Ḥajjāj.

He, blessed and exalted, said: “Even if you had remained in your houses, those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone forth to their resting places.” There are two interpretations. The first is: Had you stayed behind, those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone forth, and their remaining at home would not have saved them. The second is: Had you stayed behind, the believers among you would have gone out and would not have stayed behind because you did. In that case the meaning of the words of God, mighty and majestic, “those for whom killing had been decreed” is those upon whom fighting had been imposed. He expressed it as killing because fighting leads to it, whether through victory or martyrdom.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “A group of them ask the Prophet’s permission, saying, ‘Our houses are exposed.’” al-Suddī said: Those among them who asked his permission, God bless him and grant him peace, were two men of the Ansar: Abū ʿArāba ibn Aws and Aws ibn Qayẓī. Eighty men went back without permission. “Saying, ‘Our houses are exposed’” means: far from al-Madina, so that we fear that the unprotected women and children may be taken captive. It is also said to mean: empty, with no one in them except the vulnerable women. It is also said to mean: their walls are exposed, so that theft and attack are feared. The Arabs say aʿwara manziluka when a dwelling has lost its screening or its wall has fallen. Anything whose exposure they dislike is called ʿawra.

“Had it been entered against them from its outskirts”—meaning had the hypocrites been attacked from the outskirts and surrounding districts of al-Madina—“and they had then been asked to cause discord, they would have done so.” It is said to mean: Had they been asked to fight out of tribal partisanship, they would have hastened to it. It is also said: Had they been asked to embrace polytheism, they would have responded swiftly. “And they would have delayed”—in responding to the call to discord—“only a little.” It is also said to mean that they would have remained in al-Madina only a short time before being punished.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “They destroy their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers.” It is said: with their own hands through breaking the truce, and the hands of the Muslims through fighting. It is said: with their own hands by abandoning them, and the hands of the believers by expelling them from them. It is said: with their own hands by destroying their interiors and what was inside them, so that the Muslims would not take it, and the hands of the believers by destroying their exteriors in order to reach them. It is said that their dwellings were ornamented, and they begrudged the Muslims living in them, so they destroyed them from within while the Muslims destroyed them from without. It is said that, whenever the Muslims demolished part of their fortifications, they pulled down portions of their houses to rebuild what had been destroyed of their fortifications. It is also said that their destruction of their houses consisted in this: when a settlement was reached allowing them to carry away whatever their camels could bear, they began dismantling whatever pleased them in their houses, even the pegs, to load it onto their camels.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “God has made for you in your houses a place of rest.” Mujāhid said: a place in which you dwell. “And He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, houses”—these are tents—“which you find light on the day of your departure and the day of your encampment.” Thus God reminded them of His favor in providing them with the fixed houses of their homelands and the movable houses of their travels, so that His favor encompasses them both at home and on their journeys.

God, blessed and exalted, said, relating the words of Nūḥ, peace be upon him: “My Lord, forgive me, my parents, and whoever enters my house as a believer.” It is said that he meant his father Lamka and his mother Mankhīl, both of whom were believers. It is also said that he meant his father and his grandfather. “And whoever enters my house as a believer”: it is said to mean my friend who enters my dwelling; or whoever enters my mosque; or whoever enters my religion.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “There is no blame upon the blind, nor blame upon the lame, nor blame upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, if you eat in your own houses, or your fathers’ houses, or your mothers’ houses, or your brothers’ houses, or your sisters’ houses, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts.” He, glorified be He, permitted eating in the houses of these people because of the bond of kinship, without asking their permission to eat, provided the food is freely available. If it is secured against them, however, they may not break into its place of safekeeping. Nor may they go beyond eating to storing food away, or to taking anything that is not food, even if it is not secured against them, except with their permission.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “And We revealed to Mūsā and his brother: Establish houses for your people in Miṣr”—that is, dwellings for them to live in. As for His word “Miṣr,” it is said that it means al-Iskandariyya, and it is said that it means Miṣr itself. It is said to mean: take palaces; and it is said: mosques. “And make your houses a direction of prayer”: it is said to mean facing one another; and it is said: make your mosques face the Kaʿba.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “And your Lord revealed to the bees: Take houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they build.” There are three interpretations of “revealed.” The first is: He inspired them. The second is: He directed them. The third is that He, glorified be He, placed this in their instincts, something the like of which is hidden from other creatures. “Take houses in the mountains”: God Most High mentioned their houses because of the exactness of division and beauty of construction which He inspired in them and placed in their instincts.

God, blessed and exalted, said: “The likeness of those who take protectors other than God is that of the spider, which takes a house for itself; and surely the frailest of houses is the spider’s house, if only they knew.” He, glorified be He, means the gods they worshiped, idols and images. “Like the spider, which takes a house for itself” means that they worshiped what could avail them nothing, like the spider’s house, which neither screens one from sight nor keeps hands away.

From ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him: He, glorified be He, mentioned the gods of the polytheists and said, “If a fly takes anything away from them, they cannot recover it from it.” He mentioned the power of the gods to contrive and likened it to the spider’s house. When God mentioned flies and spiders among what was revealed to Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace, they said, “What is He doing with this?” Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed: “God is not ashamed to set forth a parable, whether of a gnat or anything beyond it …”—the verse.

The judge al-Māwardī, may God have mercy on him, said: [Baʿūḍa]: one of the smallest kinds of biting insects. It is so called because, in its smallness, it is like only a part, baʿḍ, of such an insect. It is said that the spider spun its web twice: once over Dāwūd, peace be upon him, and once over the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace. The plural of ʿankabūt is ʿanākib, and its diminutive is ʿunaykib.

ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, mentioned the spider in a speech of his. It is related that a man came to ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, and said, “Commander of the Faithful, a judgment has been passed against me through which I have lost my property and my family.” He went out to al-Raḥba, and the people gathered around him. He, may God be pleased with him, said:

“My honor is pledged for what I say, and I stand surety for it. Whoever is shown clearly by the lessons of the past the exemplary punishments before him will be restrained by piety from plunging into doubtful matters. The most wretched of people is a man who has scraped together learning among the rabble, without knowledge or proof. He amassed much of that of which a little would be better, and went on amassing it, until, when he had drunk his fill of stagnant, fetid water of no benefit, he sat among the people issuing legal opinions, to unravel what had confused others. Yet he is caught among fragments of uncertainties, as though in a spider’s web, not knowing whether he has been right or wrong: stumbling through darkness, riding headlong into ignorance. He has not bitten firmly into knowledge with a cutting tooth, and so gained; nor has he kept silent, and so remained safe. Blood cries out because of him, inheritances weep because of him, and through his judgment unlawful sexual relations are made lawful. Those are the ones over whom lamentation has become due while they are still alive.”

What prompted the inclusion of this report was its mention of the spider.

From Anas ibn Mālik, may God have mercy on him, who said: The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: “There is no house at whose door the Angel of Death does not stand five times every day. If he finds a person whose allotted term has run out and whose deeds have come to an end, he casts upon him the anguish of death. Its agonies overcome him and its overwhelming pangs engulf him. The weeping woman raises her voice in sorrow, and the wailing woman cries out in grief. Then the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, says, ‘Woe to you! Why this terror? Why this anguish? I have taken away none of your provisions, nor brought anyone’s appointed term nearer. I did not come to him until I was commanded, nor take his soul until I had sought permission. I shall return among you, and return again, and return again, until I leave none of you remaining.’”

The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: “By Him in whose hand is my soul, if they could see where he stands or hear his words, they would forget their dead and weep for themselves. Then, when the dead person is carried upon his bier, the soul flutters above the bier, calling out, ‘My family! My children! Do not let this world play with you as it played with me. I amassed wealth by lawful and unlawful means, then left it behind for someone else. Its enjoyment is his, while the liability is mine. Beware of what has befallen me.’”

From Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, may God have mercy on him, who said: The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “The likeness of a house in which God Most High is remembered and a house in which God is not remembered is that of the living and the dead.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “Illuminate your houses with the recitation of the Quran, and Satan will flee from them.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “A guest’s lodging in a house is a blessing.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “Betrayal never enters a house without ruining it.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “Theft never enters a house without bringing humiliation upon its inhabitants.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “No one leaves his house seeking knowledge without the angels lowering their wings for him in approval of what he does.”

He, God bless him and grant him peace, said, “No one leaves his house striving in the path of God Most High without the angels continuing to ask forgiveness for him until he returns.”

The accomplished vizier Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Maghribī said, having performed the pilgrimage:

poems.intro: قرئ على حائط قصر بأعلى الحجاز، قد خرب، وباد أهله:

verses.h1: بالله ربك كم بيت مررت به
verses.h2: قد كان يعمر باللذات والطرب

verses.h1: طارت عقاب المنايا في سقائفه
verses.h2: فصار من بعدهم للويل والحرب

verses.h1: By God, your Lord, how many a house have you passed
verses.h2: that once was filled with pleasures and merriment!

verses.h1: The eagle of death flew through its roofed halls,
verses.h2: and after its people were gone, it became a place of woe and ruin.

notes.note: الحرب is read here as al-ḥarab, meaning despoilment or devastation, hence ‘ruin’; the unvocalized text also permits al-ḥarb, ‘war.’

prose_translation.intro: The following was read on the wall of a palace in upper al-Ḥijāz, which had fallen into ruin and whose inhabitants had perished:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: (هذان البيتان لإبراهيم بن المهدي) . وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: كل بيت للهدم، ما تبتنى الور
verses.h2: قاء، والسيد الرفيع العماد

verses.h1: واللبيب اللبيب من ليس يغت
verses.h2: ر بكون مصيره لفساد

verses.h1: Every dwelling is destined for ruin, whether built by
verses.h2: the gray dove or the lord of lofty tent-poles.

verses.h1: The truly wise man is he who is not deceived
verses.h2: by an existence whose end is decay.

prose_translation.intro: (These two verses are by Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī.) Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: عش ما بدا لك قصرك الموت
verses.h2: لا معقل منه ولا فوت

verses.h1: بينا غنى بيت وساكنه
verses.h2: زال الغنى، وتقوض البيت

verses.h1: Live as long as you please; your end is death.
verses.h2: There is no refuge from it, nor escape.

verses.h1: Even as a house and its dweller prospered,
verses.h2: Prosperity vanished, and the house fell apart.

verses.h1: قد آن أن يسمعك الصوت
verses.h2: أنائم قلبك أم ميت؟

verses.h1: يا باني البيت على غرة
verses.h2: أمامك المنزل والبيت

verses.h1: وإنما الدنيا على طولها
verses.h2: ثنية مطلعها الموت

verses.h1: It is time you heard the voice:
verses.h2: is your heart asleep, or dead?

verses.h1: O you who build a house in heedlessness,
verses.h2: ahead of you lie the dwelling and the house.

verses.h1: This world, for all its length, is only
verses.h2: a mountain pass whose ascent is death.

notes.note: مطلعها is rendered literally as “whose ascent.” The image may instead place death at the crest of the pass; the precise spatial sense is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Another poet—I think it was Abū al-ʿAtāhiya—said:

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان من قصيدة يرثي بها والده
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان من قصيدة يرثي بها والده:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان من قصيدة يرثي بها والده

verses.h1: هنيئا لك البيت الجديد موسدا
verses.h2: يمينك فيه بالسعادة واليمن

verses.h1: مجاور سكن من ديار بعيدة
verses.h2: من الحي سقيا للديار وللسكن

verses.h1: أمر بربع كنت فيه كأنما
verses.h2: أمر من الإجلال بالحجر والركن

verses.h1: وإجلال مغناك اجتهاد مقصر
verses.h2: إذا النصل أودى فالعفاء على الجفن

verses.h1: May you find joy in your new home, pillowed
verses.h2: on your right hand there, in happiness and good fortune.

verses.h1: Neighbor to dwellers whose abodes are far
verses.h2: from the living—may rain bless those abodes and their dwellers!

verses.h1: I pass a dwelling where you once lived, as though
verses.h2: in reverence I were passing the Black Stone and the Corner.

verses.h1: Revering your dwelling is an effort that falls short:
verses.h2: when the blade is gone, let dust cover the sheath.

notes.note: The construction من ديار بعيدة من الحي is ambiguous. I take it to describe the dead as dwelling far from the living; الحي could also mean ‘the tribe,’ and من ديار literally means ‘from abodes.’

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān said, in a poem elegizing his father:

verses.h1: أسعداني بعبرة أسراب
verses.h2: من دموع كثيرة التسكاب

verses.h1: إن أهل الحصاب قد تركوني
verses.h2: موزعا مولعا بأهل الحصاب

verses.h1: أهل بيت تتابعوا للمنايا
verses.h2: ما على الدهر بعدهم من عتاب

verses.h1: فارقوني، وقد علمت يقينا
verses.h2: ما لمن ذاق ميتة من إياب

verses.h1: كم بذاك الحجون من [حي صدق]
verses.h2: وكهول أعفة وشباب

verses.h1: فلى الويل بعدهم وعليهم
verses.h2: صرت فردا، وملني أصحابي

verses.h1: Help me weep, you two, with streaming tears,
verses.h2: With tears poured forth in abundance.

verses.h1: The people of al-Ḥaṣāb have left me
verses.h2: Consumed with longing, devoted to the people of al-Ḥaṣāb.

verses.h1: People of one household, they followed one another to their deaths;
verses.h2: After them, I have no reproach left for Time.

verses.h1: They parted from me, and I knew for certain
verses.h2: That whoever tastes death will never return.

verses.h1: How many a noble clan lies there at al-Ḥajūn,
verses.h2: And virtuous elders and young men!

verses.h1: Woe is mine, bereft of them and mourning them;
verses.h2: I am left alone, and my companions have wearied of me.

notes.note: The unusual expression «عبرة أسراب» is understood as streaming tears; the precise form and vocalization of «أسراب» are uncertain.
The precise identification and vocalization of «الحصاب», provisionally transliterated al-Ḥaṣāb, are uncertain.

The source brackets «حي صدق», apparently indicating an editorial restoration. It is rendered as “a noble clan,” though «حي» may instead refer here to a living person or group of people remembered among the dead.

poems.intro: عن حماد الراوية قال: حدثنا ابن أخت لنا من مراد قال: وليت صدقات قوم من العرب، فبينا أنا أقسمها في أهلها، إذ قال لي رجل منهم: ألا أريك عجبا؟ قلت: بلى، فأدخلني في شعب من جبل، فإذا أنا بسهم من سهام عاد بن قنا قد نشب في ذروة من الجبل مكتوب عليه:

verses.h1: ألا هل إلى أبيات شمخ إلى اللوى
verses.h2: لوى الرمل يوما للنفوس معاد؟

verses.h1: بلاد بها كنا، وكنا من أهلها
verses.h2: إذ الناس ناس، والبلاد بلاد

verses.h1: Ah, to the lofty dwellings by al-Liwā—
verses.h2: Liwā al-Raml—will souls ever return?

verses.h1: A land where we once lived, and were among its people,
verses.h2: when people were truly people, and lands were truly lands.

notes.note: The unvocalized شمخ is uncertain: translated here as “lofty,” it could instead be a proper name, Shamkh, giving “the dwellings of Shamkh.”

prose_translation.intro: From Ḥammād al-Rāwiya, who said: A son of a sister of ours, from Murād, told us: “I was put in charge of the alms of a group of Arabs. While I was distributing them among those entitled to them, one of their men said to me, ‘Shall I show you something wondrous?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ He led me into a mountain ravine, and there I found an arrow, one of the arrows of ʿĀd ibn Qanā, embedded in a mountain peak, with the following inscribed upon it:

poems.intro: ثم أخرجني إلى ساحل البحر، فإذا أنا بحجر يعلوه الماء طورا، يظهر طورا، عليه مكتوب: يا ابن آدم، يا عبد ربه، اتق الله، ولا تعجل في أمرك؛ فإنك لن تسبق رزقك، ولا ترزق ما ليس لك. ومن البصرة إلى دبيل ستمائة فرسخن فمن لم يصدق، فليمش على الطريق على الساحل حتى يتحققه، فمن لم يقدر على ذلك فلينطح برأسه هذا الحجر" وقال أبو بكر محمد بن عيسى الداني - من شعراء الأندلس - يندب المعتمد على الله أبا القاسم محمد بن المعتضد بالله أبي عمرو عباد بن محمد بن عباد، حين تغلب على بلاده يوسف بن تاشفين المثلم، وانتزعه من ملكه، وكان أدبيا جوادا محسنا إلى أهل الأدب:

verses.h1: يا ضيف أقفر بيت المكرمات فخذ
verses.h2: في ضم رحلك واجمع فضلة الزاد

verses.h1: ويا مؤمل واديهم ليسكنه
verses.h2: خف القطين، وجف الزرع بالوادي

verses.h1: ضللت سبل الندى يا ابن السبيل فسر
verses.h2: بغير قصد، فما يهديك من هاد

verses.h1: إن يخلعوا فبنو العباس قد خلعوا
verses.h2: وقد خلت قبل حمص أرض بغداد

verses.h1: سارت سفائنهم والنوح يتبعها
verses.h2: كأنها إبل يحدو بها حاد

verses.h1: تبكي السماء بدمع رائح غاد
verses.h2: على البهاليل من أبناء عباد

verses.h1: عريسة دخلتها الحادثات على
verses.h2: أساود منهم فيها وآساد

verses.h1: وكعبة كانت الآمال تعمرها
verses.h2: فاليوم لا عاكف فيها ولا باد

verses.h1: كم من درارى سعود قد هوت وزهت
verses.h2: منهم، ومن درر للمجد أفراد

verses.h1: O guest, the house of noble deeds is deserted; begin
verses.h2: packing your baggage, and gather what provisions remain.

verses.h1: O you who hoped to settle in their valley,
verses.h2: the dwellers have departed, and the valley’s crops have withered.

verses.h1: You have lost the paths of generosity, O wayfarer; travel on
verses.h2: without a destination, for no guide will lead you.

verses.h1: If they are deposed, the Banū al-ʿAbbās were deposed before;
verses.h2: before Ḥimṣ, the land of Baghdad stood empty.

verses.h1: Their ships sailed away, with lamentation following them,
verses.h2: as though they were camels urged onward by a driver’s chant.

verses.h1: The sky weeps tears, evening and morning,
verses.h2: over the noble men of the sons of ʿAbbād.

verses.h1: A lion’s lair that calamities entered to assail
verses.h2: the black serpents and lions of their house within.

verses.h1: A Kaʿba that hopes once thronged,
verses.h2: where today neither resident nor visitor remains.

verses.h1: How many radiant stars of good fortune have fallen and shone
verses.h2: among them—and how many peerless pearls of glory!

notes.note: Ḥimṣ here is an Arabic name used for Seville. The precise earlier deposition of the Abbasids and emptying of Baghdad intended by the comparison are uncertain.

The text reads «هوت وزهت», translated literally as “have fallen and shone.” «زهت» normally suggests shining, flourishing, or being splendid; its coordination with “fallen” is puzzling in this context and may reflect a textual error.

prose_translation.intro:
Then he took me out to the seashore, where I saw a stone that was sometimes covered by the water and sometimes exposed. On it was written: “O son of Adam, O servant of your Lord, fear God and do not be hasty in your affairs, for you will never outstrip your allotted provision, nor will you be granted what is not yours. From al-Basra to Dabīl is six hundred farsakhs. Whoever does not believe this, let him walk along the coastal road until he verifies it; whoever cannot do that, let him butt his head against this stone.”

Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Dānī—one of the poets of al-Andalus—said the following, lamenting al-Muʿtamid ʿalā Allah, Abū al-Qāsim Muḥammad ibn al-Muʿtaḍid bi-Allah, Abū ʿAmr ʿAbbād ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād, when Yūsuf ibn Tāshfīn al-Muthallam overran his lands and stripped him of his kingdom. Al-Muʿtamid was a man of letters, generous and benevolent toward men of letters:
interludes: The beginning of this poem is:

poems.poet_from_text: الشمردل بن شريك المنقري يرثي أخاه وائلا
poems.intro: (وبعده الشعر المقدم) . وقال الشمردل بن شريك المنقري يرثي أخاه وائلا:

poet.from_text: الشمردل بن شريك المنقري يرثي أخاه وائلا

verses.h1: لعمرك إن الموت منا لمولع
verses.h2: بمن كان يرجى نفعه وفواضله

verses.h1: وما البعد إلا أننا بعد صحة
verses.h2: كأن لم نبايت وائلا ونقايله

verses.h1: فأصبح بيت الهجر قد حال دونه
verses.h2: وغال أمرأ ما كان تخشى غوائله

verses.h1: سقى الصفرات الغيث ما دام ثاويا
verses.h2: بهن، وجادت أهل شول مخايله

verses.h1: وما بي حب الأرض إلا جوارها
verses.h2: صداه، وقول ظن أني قائله

verses.h1: By your life, death among us is bent
verses.h2: on those whose help and bounty we hoped for.

verses.h1: Separation is nothing but this: after sound health, we are
verses.h2: as though we had never spent nights with Wāʾil or rested beside him at noon.

verses.h1: Now the house of separation has come between us and him,
verses.h2: and claimed a man from whom no harm was feared.

verses.h1: May rain water al-Ṣafarāt as long as he lies
verses.h2: there, and may its promising clouds drench the people of Shawl.

verses.h1: It is not love of the land that moves me, but its nearness
verses.h2: to his remains, and words he thought I would utter.

notes.note: بعد صحة literally means ‘after health.’ Its connection to the rest of the sentence is awkward; the wording may be defective.
Al-Ṣafarāt and Shawl are provisionally treated as place names; their identification and vocalization are uncertain. أهل شول could alternatively mean ‘owners of dry she-camels.’

صداه is interpreted as ‘his remains’; صدى can also denote the dead person’s spirit or its imagined owl-form. The reference and grammatical connection of ‘and words he thought I would utter’ are unclear.

prose_translation.intro: (After it comes the verse cited above.) al-Shamardal ibn Sharīk al-Minqarī said, elegizing his brother Wāʾil:

poems.poet: مسعود بن عبد الله ابن عوف
poems.intro: عن عمير الرماح قال: رأيت مهنأة بنت الذيال اليشكرية، وقد أفسدت الدموع خديها، لكثرة بكائها، فقلت لها: إلى كم هذه العبرة، وشرق الحسرة؟ قالت: إلى أن يضمني ما ضم مسعود، تعني القبر، ومسعود بن عبد الله بن عوف زوجها، قتله بنو جعفر من كلاب يوم الحاصة، فقالت لناعيه: هل قال شيئا، وهو يجود بنفسه؟ قال: نعم قال:

poet.expected: مسعود بن عبد الله ابن عوف

verses.h1: أترى التي خلفتها في بيتها
verses.h2: وضممت ساعدها إلى نحري

verses.h1: ثبتت على العهد الذي عاهدتها
verses.h2: أم أخلفته وأغفلت أمري

verses.h1: Do you think the woman I left in her home,
verses.h2: whose arm I clasped against my breast,

verses.h1: has stayed true to the pledge we made,
verses.h2: or broken it and ceased to think of me?

prose_translation.intro: From ʿUmayr al-Rammāḥ, who said: I saw Muhannaʾa bint al-Dhayyāl al-Yashkuriyya, whose cheeks had been marred by tears from her constant weeping. I said to her, “How long will these tears and this choking grief continue?” She replied, “Until that which enfolded Masʿūd enfolds me,” meaning the grave. Masʿūd ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAwf was her husband; Banū Jaʿfar of Kilāb killed him on the day of al-Ḥāṣṣa. She asked the man who brought news of his death, “Did he say anything as he lay dying?” He replied, “Yes. He said:”

poems.intro: فصاحت وقالت: يا مسعود إن أغفلته فأغفلني الله من رحمته. وقال آخر:

verses.h1: لله أبيات إذا أوطنتها
verses.h2: غنى الفقير بها، وعز الجاني

verses.h1: قوم إذا نزل الغريب بدارهم
verses.h2: منحوه سلوته عن الأوطان

verses.h1: How splendid those dwellings! When you settle there,
verses.h2: the poor grow rich, and the offender finds protection.

verses.h1: A people who, when a stranger lodges in their home,
verses.h2: grant him relief from longing for his homeland.

notes.note: غنى appears to represent غني, ‘grew rich.’ عز الجاني could mean that the offender gains honor or enjoys protection; the latter sense is adopted here.

prose_translation.intro: Then she cried out, saying, “O Masʿūd, if you neglect him, may God leave me out of His mercy!” Another poet said:

poems.intro: عن ابن جريح قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إن الله تعالى ليحب البيت الخصيب" يعني الكثير الخير. حضرت جليلة بنت مرة بن ذهل بن شيبان أخت جساس بن مرة - قاتل كليب، وهي امرأة كليب بن ربيعة - مأتم زوجها كليب، فأخرجتها أخته، وقالت لها: اخرجي يا هذه عن مأتمنا، فأنت أخت واترنا، وشقيقته، فلما خرجت لقيها أبوها مرة، فقال: ما وراءك يا جليلة؟ قالت: ثكل الأبد، وقلة العدد، وفقد حليل، وقتل أخ عن قليل، وبين ذين غرس الأحقاد، وتفتت الأكباد. فقال لها: أويكف ذلك كرم الصفح، وإغلاء الديات؟ فقالت: أمنية مخدوع ورب الكعبة، أبالبدن تدع لك تغلب دم ربها؟ ثم قالت جليلة في ذلك:

verses.h1: يا ابنة الأقوام إن شئت فلا
verses.h2: تعجلي باللوم حتى تسألي

verses.h1: فإذا أنت تبينت الذي
verses.h2: يوجب اللوم فلومي واعذلي

verses.h1: إن تكن أخت امرئ ليمت على
verses.h2: شفق منها عليه فافعلي

verses.h1: جل عندي فعل جساس فيا
verses.h2: حسرتا عما انجلت أو تنجلي

verses.h1: يا قتيلا قوض الدهر به
verses.h2: سقف بيتي جميعا من عل

verses.h1: هدم البيت الذي استحدثته
verses.h2: وانثنى في هدم بيتي الأول

verses.h1: خصني يوم كليب بلظى
verses.h2: من ورائي، ولظى مستقبلي

verses.h1: ليس من يبكي ليوميه كمن
verses.h2: إنما يبكي ليوم قد خلى

verses.h1: يشتفي المدرك بالثأر وفي
verses.h2: دركي ثأري ثكل مثكلي

verses.h1: إنني قاتلة مقتولة
verses.h2: فلعل الله أن يرتاح لي

verses.h1: Daughter of the clans, if you will, do not
verses.h2: hasten to blame me before you ask.

verses.h1: Once you have clearly understood what
verses.h2: warrants blame, then blame me and reproach me.

verses.h1: If a man’s sister has ever been blamed for
verses.h2: her tender concern for him, then blame me.

verses.h1: Grievous to me is what Jassās has done—oh,
verses.h2: my anguish over what has unfolded, or has yet to unfold!

verses.h1: O slain man, through whose death Time tore down
verses.h2: the roof of both my homes from on high!

verses.h1: It destroyed the home I had newly built,
verses.h2: then turned to destroy my first home.

verses.h1: The day of Kulayb singled me out for a blaze
verses.h2: behind me, and a blaze ahead of me.

verses.h1: One who weeps for both his days of sorrow is not like one
verses.h2: who weeps only for a day gone by.

verses.h1: Whoever gains vengeance finds relief, but in
verses.h2: my gaining vengeance lies the loss of him who bereaved me.

verses.h1: I am both slayer and slain;
verses.h2: perhaps God will have compassion on me.

notes.note: The wording عما انجلت أو تنجلي is syntactically unclear: the feminine verbs have no explicit subject. The translation takes it to refer to the calamity and what has unfolded or will unfold.

ثكل مثكلي could grammatically mean either losing the person who bereaved her or that person’s own bereavement. The translation adopts the former: vengeance for her husband would mean losing her brother Jassās.

prose_translation.intro:
On the authority of Ibn Jurayḥ, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “God Most High surely loves a plentiful household,” meaning one abounding in good things.

Jalīla bint Murra ibn Dhuhl ibn Shaybān, the sister of Jassās ibn Murra—the slayer of Kulayb—and the wife of Kulayb ibn Rabīʿa, attended the mourning gathering for her husband Kulayb. His sister expelled her, saying, “Leave our mourning gathering, woman! You are the sister of the man who has shed our blood—his own full sister.” When she went out, her father Murra met her and said, “What news do you bring, Jalīla?” She said, “Bereavement forever, dwindling numbers, the loss of a husband, and, before long, the slaying of a brother; and between the two, the sowing of rancor and the breaking of hearts.” He said to her, “Will generous forgiveness and lavish blood money avert that?” She replied, “The wish of a deluded man, by the Lord of the Kaʿba! Will Taghlib forgo its lord’s blood for your sake in exchange for camels?!” Then Jalīla said these verses about it:

poems.intro: عن إسماعيل بن محمد بن أبي محمد، قال: قلت لأبي العتاهية: يا أبا إسحاق. كل شعرك حسن عجيب، وقد مرت بي منذ أيام لك أبيات استحسنتها جدا، وقال: إنها معادة من أنصاف أوائلها على أواخرها، كأنها رسالة، لو كتبها إنسان إلى صديق له كان حسنا. فدع ما يكون من شعر، فقال: وما هي؟ فأنشدته:

verses.h1: المرء في مآخير مدته
verses.h2: كالثوب يخلق بعد جدته

verses.h1: وحياته نفس يعد له
verses.h2: ووفاته استكمال عدته

verses.h1: ومصيره من بعد أنسته
verses.h2: بالناس، ظلمة بيت وحدته

verses.h1: من مات مال ذوو مودته
verses.h2: عنه، وحالوا عن مودته

verses.h1: عجبا لمحتجب يضيع ما
verses.h2: يحتاج فيه ليوم رقدته

verses.h1: أزف الرحيل ونحن في لعب
verses.h2: لا نستعد له بعدته

verses.h1: ولقلما تبقي الخطوب على
verses.h2: أشر الشباب وحر وقدته

verses.h1: A man, in the latter part of his allotted span,
verses.h2: is like a garment that wears out after being new.

verses.h1: His life is breaths counted out for him,
verses.h2: and his death comes when their number is complete.

verses.h1: His destination, after his companionship
verses.h2: with people, is the darkness of his solitary dwelling.

verses.h1: When a man dies, those who loved him turn
verses.h2: away from him and abandon their affection.

verses.h1: How strange that one who secludes himself should neglect what
verses.h2: he needs for the day of his repose.

verses.h1: Departure draws near while we are at play,
verses.h2: not making due provision for it.

verses.h1: Rarely do life’s calamities spare
verses.h2: youth’s exuberance and the heat of its blaze.

notes.note: محتجب literally means someone who veils or secludes himself; its intended significance here is uncertain. The reference and grammatical role of فيه in يحتاج فيه ليوم رقدته are also unclear; the translation gives the apparent general sense.

prose_translation.intro: From Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad, who said: I said to Abū al-ʿAtāhiya, “Abū Isḥāq, all your poetry is beautiful and remarkable. A few days ago I came across some verses of yours that I admired greatly.” He continued: “They run on from their opening half-lines into their closing ones, like a letter. If someone wrote them to a friend, they would be beautiful—even apart from their being poetry.” He asked, “Which verses?” So I recited to him:

poems.intro: عن هشام بن عروة قال: قال ابن عمر بن الخطاب لعمر رضي الله عنهما: اخطب على ابنة نعيم النحام - رحمه الله - فقال: ليس بفاعل؛ إن له ابن أخ يتيم في حجره، وإنه لن يعدوه بها، فقال ابن عمر لأبيه: إيذن لي في ذلك، فأنا أكلمه، قال: فخرج حتى كلمه، فقال: يا ابن أخي والله لأبوك خير من أبيها، وأنت خير منها، ولكن لي ابن أخ يتيم في حجري قد زوجته إياها، وأصدقتها عنه من مالي عشرة آلاف درهم، ولست بالذي أنفض لحوم الناس وأترك لحمي تربا، ثم تمثل بشعر قاله خالد بن واثلة الليثي:

verses.h1: ولست ببان لامرئ سمك بيته
verses.h2: وأترك بيتي خاليا بخمالي

verses.h1: جعلت بناتي في موالي قصرة
verses.h2: وما راعني ذو سورة وجمال

verses.h1: رأيت الألى يأتون للنصر دعوتي
verses.h2: موالي والأقصين غير موال

verses.h1: I am not one to raise the roof of another man’s house
verses.h2: while leaving my own house empty at Khumāl.

verses.h1: I married my daughters exclusively to my own kin;
verses.h2: no man of high standing and beauty impressed me.

verses.h1: I found that those who answer my call for help
verses.h2: are my kin, while distant men are no allies.

notes.note: بخمالي is unclear; tentatively read as ‘at Khumāl,’ a place-name whose identification and vocalization are uncertain.
قصرة is tentatively understood as ‘exclusively,’ restricting the daughters’ marriages to the speaker’s kin; its precise force here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: On the authority of Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, who said: Ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said to ʿUmar—may God be pleased with them both—“Ask for the hand of Nuʿaym al-Naḥḥām’s daughter on my behalf—may God have mercy on him.” He replied, “He will not agree. He has an orphaned nephew in his care, and he will not pass him over to give her to anyone else.” Ibn ʿUmar said to his father, “Give me permission to do that, and I will speak to him myself.” He said: So he went out and spoke to him. Nuʿaym replied, “My nephew, by God, your father is better than her father, and you are better than she is. But I have an orphaned nephew in my care, and I have married her to him and paid her a dowry of ten thousand dirhams on his behalf out of my own wealth. I am not one to shake the dust from other people’s flesh while leaving my own flesh dust-covered.” Then he quoted verses by Khālid ibn Wāthila al-Laythī:

poems.intro: مما ينسب إلى المجنون قيس بن الملوح:

verses.h1: ألا أيها البيت الذي لا أزوره
verses.h2: وهجرانه منى إليه ذنوب

verses.h1: هجرتك إشفاقا، وزرتك خائفا
verses.h2: وفيك على الدهر منك رقيب

verses.h1: أرى أهلك الأدنين صاروا لنا عدى
verses.h2: وأنت لنا سلم وفيك حبيب

verses.h1: سأستعتب الأيام فيك لعلها
verses.h2: بيوم سرور في الزمان تئوب

verses.h1: فكم من بعيد الدار ساعفه الهوى
verses.h2: ومنقطع الأسباب وهو قريب!

verses.h1: O house that I do not visit,
verses.h2: to forsake it is to sin against it.

verses.h1: I shunned you out of apprehension, and visited you in fear;
verses.h2: within you, always, stands a watcher of your own.

verses.h1: I see that your nearest folk have become our enemies,
verses.h2: yet you are at peace with us, and within you is a beloved.

verses.h1: I shall ask the days to make amends concerning you; perhaps they
verses.h2: will return, in time, with a day of joy.

verses.h1: How many a man whose dwelling is distant has love favored,
verses.h2: and how many have had all ties severed, though they are near!

notes.note: The phrase منك رقيب, literally “a watcher from you,” is somewhat obscure. It is rendered as a watcher belonging to the house, perhaps one of its inhabitants.

prose_translation.intro: Among the verses attributed to al-Majnūn, Qays ibn al-Mulawwaḥ:

verses.h1: لعمرك إن البيت بالظاهر الذي
verses.h2: مررت فلم ألمم به لي شائق

verses.h1: وإن مروري لا أكلم أهله
verses.h2: أشد من الموت الذي أنا ذائق

verses.h1: وبالجرع من أعلى الجنينة منزل
verses.h2: فسيح شحا صدري به متضايق

verses.h1: وماذا عسى الواشون أن يتحدثوا
verses.h2: سوى أن يقولوا: إنني لك عاشق

verses.h1: أجل صدق الواشون أنت حبيبة
verses.h2: إلي، وإن لم تصف منك الخلائق

verses.h1: كأن على أنيابها الخمر شابها
verses.h2: بماء الندى من آخر الليل غابق

verses.h1: وما ذقته إلا بعيني تفرسا
verses.h2: كما شيم من أعلى السحابة بارق

verses.h1: By your life, that house at al-Ẓāhir—
verses.h2: I passed without stopping there—fills me with longing.

verses.h1: And passing without speaking to its people
verses.h2: is harder than the death I am to taste.

verses.h1: At al-Jarʿ, in upper al-Junayna, stands a dwelling,
verses.h2: wide in expanse, yet there my breast is constricted.

verses.h1: What could the talebearers possibly say
verses.h2: except that I am in love with you?

verses.h1: Yes, the talebearers spoke truly: you are beloved
verses.h2: to me, though your character is not without blemish.

verses.h1: It is as though upon her teeth were wine, mixed
verses.h2: with dew from the end of night by an evening drinker.

verses.h1: I have tasted it only with my eyes, gazing intently,
verses.h2: as one watches lightning flash from the heights of a cloud.

notes.note: Al-Ẓāhir is taken as a place-name; its location is uncertain.
Al-Junayna is not securely identified. Al-Jarʿ may be a place-name or a description meaning sandy ground.
The unvocalized شحا is taken to refer to breadth or extent, giving ‘wide in expanse’; its precise form and reading are uncertain.
وإن لم تصف منك الخلائق may refer specifically to her unkind or troubled dealings with the speaker, rather than to flaws in her character generally.
غابق is associated with an evening draught. ‘Evening drinker’ is tentative; someone serving that draught may instead be intended.

prose_translation.intro: Among the verses also attributed to him are the following:

verses.h1: ألا أيها البيتان بالأجرع الذي
verses.h2: بأسفل مفضاه غضى وكثيب

verses.h1: هجرتكما هجر البغيض، وفيكما
verses.h2: من الناس إنسان إلى حبيب

verses.h1: O you two tents at al-Ajraʿ, whose
verses.h2: lower open ground holds ghaḍā shrubs and a sand dune!

verses.h1: I shunned you as one shuns the hated, though within you
verses.h2: is one person, among all people, dear to me.

notes.note: Al-Ajraʿ may be a place name or simply a description of sandy ground; its location is unidentified.
The printed إلى حبيب appears to stand for إليّ حبيب, ‘dear to me,’ which is the reading translated here.

verses.h1: وإني على هجران بيتك كالذي
verses.h2: رأى نهلا ريا وليس بناهل

verses.h1: رأى برد ماء ذيد عنه وروضة
verses.h2: برود الضحى فينانة بالأصائل

verses.h1: In staying away from your house, I am like one
verses.h2: who sees a thirst-quenching draught, yet does not drink.

verses.h1: He sees cool water he is barred from, and a meadow
verses.h2: cool in the forenoon, thick with shade in the late afternoon.

notes.note: The precise reading of «نهلا ريا» is uncertain; I understand it as a draught sufficient to quench thirst.

verses.h1: أرى بيت لبنى أصبح اليوم يهجر
verses.h2: وهجران لبنى يا لك الخير منكر

verses.h1: فإن تكن الدنيا بلبنى تقلبت
verses.h2: فللدهر والدنيا بطون وأظهر

verses.h1: أتبكي على لبنى وأنت تركتها
verses.h2: وأنت عليها بالملا كنت تقدر

verses.h1: I see Lubnā’s house now standing deserted;
verses.h2: and forsaking Lubnā—may good be yours—is a shameful thing.

verses.h1: If the world has brought a reversal upon Lubnā,
verses.h2: then time and the world have their inward and outward sides.

verses.h1: Do you weep for Lubnā, when you yourself left her,
verses.h2: though at al-Malā you had the power to keep her?

notes.note: بالملا is uncertain. It is provisionally treated as the place-name al-Malā, whose location here is unidentified; it might instead represent بالملأ, ‘before the assembly’ or ‘in public.’ ‘Had the power to keep her’ interprets the more literal ‘had power over her.’

verses.h1: ما بال ذا البيت الذي كنت آلفا
verses.h2: أنارك فيه بعد إلفك نائر؟

verses.h1: تزور بيوتا حوله ما تحبها
verses.h2: وتهجره؟ سقيا لمن أنت هاجر

verses.h1: What ails this house you used to frequent?
verses.h2: Has someone turned you against it, after your former fondness?

verses.h1: You visit houses around it that you do not love,
verses.h2: yet forsake it? May rain bless the one you forsake!

notes.note: The expression أنارك ... نائر is obscure; provisionally understood as someone alienating or driving the addressee away. إلفك is taken as ‘your fondness/familiarity,’ though it can also mean ‘your familiar companion’ or ‘your beloved.’

poems.intro: قال بعضهم: خرجت [أنا] والأحوص بن محمد الأنصاري مع عبد الله بن الحسن إلى الحج، فقلنا لعبد الله: لو أرسلت إلى سليمان بن أبي دباكل، فأنشدنا من شعره؟ فأرسل إليه، فأتانا، فاستنشدناه، فأنشدنا قصيدته التي أولها:

verses.h1: يا بيت خنساء الذي أتجنب
verses.h2: ذهب الشباب وحبها لا يذهب

verses.h1: أصبحت أمنحك الصدود وإنني
verses.h2: قسما إليك مع الصدود لأجنب

verses.h1: مالي أحن إذا جمالك قربت
verses.h2: وأصد عنك وأنت مني أقرب؟

verses.h1: وأرى البعيد يحبكم فأحبه
verses.h2: إن كان ينسب منك أو يتنسب

verses.h1: لله درك؟ هل لديك معول
verses.h2: لمتيم، أم هل لودك مطلب

verses.h1: تبكي الحمامة شجوها فتهيجني
verses.h2: ويروح عازب همي المتأوب

verses.h1: وتهب جارية الرياح من أرضكم
verses.h2: فأرى البلاد لها تطل وتخصب

verses.h1: وأرى السمية باسمكم فيزيدني
verses.h2: شوقا إليك سميك المتنسب

verses.h1: وأخالق الواشين منك تجملا
verses.h2: وهم على ذوو ضغائن درب

verses.h1: ثم اتخذتهم على وليجة حتى غضبت، ومثل ذلك يغضب
O house of Khansāʾ, which I avoid,
verses.h2: youth has gone, but love for her does not depart.

verses.h1: I now offer you only avoidance, though I,
verses.h2: I swear, for all my avoidance, am drawn toward you.

verses.h1: Why do I yearn when your camels draw near,
verses.h2: yet turn away from you when you are nearer to me?

verses.h1: I see a stranger who loves you, and I love him,
verses.h2: whether he is your kin or merely claims kinship.

verses.h1: God bless you! Is there refuge with you
verses.h2: for one enslaved by love, or any way to win your affection?

verses.h1: The dove cries out her sorrow and stirs me,
verses.h2: and my grief, long absent, returns again at evening.

verses.h1: The coursing wind blows from your land,
verses.h2: and I see the countryside bedewed by it and growing fertile.

verses.h1: I see a woman bearing your name, and she increases
verses.h2: my longing for you—your namesake, claiming kinship.

verses.h1: I deal graciously with the tale-bearers concerning you, to keep up appearances,
verses.h2: though they harbor grudges against me and are practiced in spite.

verses.h1: Then you took them as confidants against me, until I grew angry—and such conduct does provoke anger.

notes.note: لأجنب is obscure here; “am drawn toward you” is a tentative rendering.
The text shifts from feminine السمية to masculine سميك المتنسب. I take both expressions to refer to the woman sharing the beloved’s name.
على appears to stand for عليّ, “against me.” The unvocalized درب is taken to mean “practiced” or “experienced”; “in spite” is supplied from the context.
على is again read as عليّ, “against me.” The unvocalized verbs are understood as “you took them” and “I grew angry.”

prose_translation.intro: Someone said: “Al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Muḥammad al-Anṣārī and I set out on pilgrimage with ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥasan. We said to ʿAbd Allah, ‘Why not send for Sulaymān ibn Abī Dabākil, so that he might recite some of his poetry to us?’ So he sent for him, and he came to us. We asked him to recite, and he recited his ode, which begins:

poems.intro: قال: فلما كان من قابل حج أبو بكر بن عبد العزيز بن مروان، فقدم المدينة، فدخل عليه الأحوص، فاستصحبه، أي طلب منه أن يصحبه إلى دمشق، فوعده أبو بكر بذلك، فلما خرج الأحوص قال له بعض جلسائه: تقدم بالأحوص الشام، وفيه من يناسبك من بني أبيك، وهو من السفه على ما قد علمت؟، فلما أراد أبو بكر الرجوع من الحج، دخل عليه الأحوص مستنجزا لما وعده من الصحابة، فدعا له بمائة دينار، وأثواب، وقال: يا خال إني نظرت فيما سألتني فكرهت أن أهجم بك على أمير المؤمنين من غير إذن، فيحجبك، فيشمت بي عدوي من أهل بيتي، ولكن خذ هذه الدنانير والثياب، وأنا استأذن لك أمير المؤمنين، فإذا أذن لك كتبت إليكفقدمت، قال: لا، ولكني قد سبعت عندك، ولا حاجة لي بعطيتك، ثم خرج من عنده، وبلغ ذلك أخاه عمر بن عبد العزيز - رضي الله عنه - وهو يومئذ أمير المدينة فأرسل إلى الأحوص، فأتاه، فلما دخل عليه أعطاه مائة دينار، وكساه ثيابا فأخذ ذلك منه، ثم قال له: يا خال هب لي عرض أخي أبي بكر، قال: هو لك، ثم خرج الأحوص، فقال في عراض قصيدة سليمان بن أبي دباكل قصيدة مدح بها عمر بن عبد العزيز، أولها:

verses.h1: يا بيت عائكة التي أتعزل
verses.h2: حذر العدى، وبه الفؤاد موكل

verses.h1: إني لأمنحك الصدود وإنني
verses.h2: قسما إيك مع الصدود لأميل

verses.h1: هل عيشنا بك في زمانك راجع
verses.h2: فلقد تفاحش بعدك المتعلل

verses.h1: وتجنبي بيت الحبيب أوده
verses.h2: أرضى البغيض به حديث معضل

verses.h1: ولئن صددت لأنت
verses.h2: لولا رقبتي أهوى من اللائي أزور وأدخل

verses.h1: أين الشباب وعيشنا اللذ الذي
verses.h2: كنا به زمنا نسر ونجذل

verses.h1: ذهبت بشاشته وأصبح ذكره
verses.h2: حزنا يعل به الفؤاد وينهل

verses.h1: إلا تذكر ما مضى وصبابة
verses.h2: منيت لقلب متيم لا يذهل

verses.h1: أودي الشباب وأخلفت أيامه
verses.h2: وأنا الحزين على الشباب المعول

verses.h1: وأراك تفعل ما تقول، وبعضهم
verses.h2: مذق اللسان يقول ما لا يفعل

verses.h1: وأرى المدينة حين صرت أميرها
verses.h2: أمن البريء بها، ونام الأعزل

interludes.text: والقصيدة طويلة، ثم خرج فيها إلى مدح عمر بن عبد العزيز - رضي الله عنه - وشكره، ثم ختمها بقوله:

verses.h1: O house of ʿĀtika, which I shun
verses.h2: for fear of enemies, while my heart remains bound to it.

verses.h1: I turn away from you, yet I
verses.h2: swear that, despite my turning away, I incline toward you.

verses.h1: Will the life we lived within you in those days return?
verses.h2: For since leaving you, the search for solace has grown unbearable.

verses.h1: My avoiding the beloved’s house, though I love him,
verses.h2: to please someone I loathe—a perplexing affair!

verses.h1: Though I turn away, you are—
verses.h2: but for my fear of watchers—dearer than the houses I visit and enter.

verses.h1: Where is youth, and that sweet life of ours
verses.h2: in which, for a time, we rejoiced and were glad?

verses.h1: Its brightness has departed, and its memory has become
verses.h2: a grief the heart drinks, draught upon draught.

verses.h1: Nothing but remembrance of the past, and a yearning
verses.h2: allotted to a love-enslaved heart that cannot forget.

verses.h1: Youth has perished, and its days have broken their promise;
verses.h2: I am the sorrowing one who wails for youth.

verses.h1: I see you do what you say, while some men,
verses.h2: false of tongue, say what they do not do.

verses.h1: And I see that in al-Madina, since you became its governor,
verses.h2: the innocent are safe, and the unarmed sleep.

notes.note: The source reads عائكة, apparently a misprint for عاتكة (ʿĀtika), adopted here. The feminine relative التي is also unexpected if it refers to بيت; الذي would fit the apparent sense.
إيك appears to be a misprint for إليك, ‘toward you,’ adopted in the translation.

The expression تفاحش بعدك المتعلل is difficult. المتعلل can denote a means of consolation or diversion; the translation tentatively takes the phrase to mean that seeking consolation after separation has become intolerable.

The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: h1 is unusually short and h2 unusually long. It is preserved here. رقبتي is also uncertain; it may concern the speaker’s vigilance or those watching him. ‘Houses’ is supplied as the apparent referent of اللائي.
The construction beginning إلا is elliptical, rendered as ‘Nothing but.’ The unvocalized منيت is tentatively understood as مُنِيَتْ, ‘was allotted or destined.’

prose_translation.intro: He said: The following year, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān went on pilgrimage and came to al-Madina. Al-Aḥwaṣ visited him and asked to accompany him—that is, he asked him to take him along to Dimashq. Abū Bakr promised him this. When al-Aḥwaṣ had left, one of his companions said to him, “Will you bring al-Aḥwaṣ to al-Shām, where there are kinsmen of yours from your paternal clan, knowing as you do how foolish he is?” When Abū Bakr was about to return from the pilgrimage, al-Aḥwaṣ visited him to ask him to fulfill his promise of taking him along. Abū Bakr ordered that a hundred dinars and some garments be brought for him, and said, “Uncle, I have considered what you asked of me, and I am reluctant to bring you unannounced before the Commander of the Faithful without permission, lest he refuse to admit you and my enemies among my own family gloat over me. But take these dinars and garments, and I shall ask the Commander of the Faithful’s permission for you. When he grants it, I shall write to you, and you can come.” He replied, “No! Rather, I have been slandered to you, and I have no need of your gift.” Then he left him. News of this reached his brother ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may God be pleased with him—who was then governor of al-Madina. He sent for al-Aḥwaṣ, who came to him. When he entered, ʿUmar gave him a hundred dinars and clothed him in garments, which he accepted. Then ʿUmar said to him, “Uncle, for my sake, spare the honor of my brother Abū Bakr.” He replied, “It is yours.” al-Aḥwaṣ then left and composed, on the model of the ode of Sulaymān ibn Abī Dabākil, an ode praising ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. It begins:
interludes: The ode is long. He then turned in it to praising and thanking ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may God be pleased with him—and concluded it with these words:

poems.intro: فلما أنشدها قال عمر - رضي الله عنه -: ما أراك أعفيتني مما استعفيك منه؛ ذلك أنه مدح عمر، وعرض بأخيه أبي بكر. وقال الأحوص، وهو عبد الله بن محمد بن عبد الله بن عاصم بن ثابت بن أبي الأقلح:

opening.actual: أدور، ولولا أن أرى أم جعفر

verses.h1: أدور، ولولا أن أرى أم جعفر
verses.h2: بأبياتكم ما درت حيث أدور

verses.h1: وما كنت زوارا، ولكن ذا الهوى
verses.h2: إذا لم يزر لا بد أن سيزور

verses.h1: أزور على أن ليس ينفك
verses.h2: كلما أتيت عدو بالبنان يشير

verses.h1: فقد أنكرت بعد اعتراف زيارتي
verses.h2: وقد وغرت فيها على صدور

verses.h1: I wander about; were it not that I see Umm Jaʿfar
verses.h2: among your dwellings, I would not wander where I do.

verses.h1: I was never much of a visitor, but one in love,
verses.h2: even if he does not visit, must eventually come.

verses.h1: I visit, though invariably,
verses.h2: whenever I come, an enemy points a finger.

verses.h1: My visits, once accepted, are now disapproved of,
verses.h2: and hearts have grown bitter against me because of them.

notes.note: I read على as عليّ (‘against me’), probably a typing or OCR error. The unvocalized أنكرت is taken as passive (‘are disapproved of’); it could also mean ‘she disapproved of my visits.’

prose_translation.intro: When he recited it, ʿUmar—may God be pleased with him—said, “I do not see that you have spared me what I asked you to spare me”; for he had praised ʿUmar while making a veiled attack on his brother Abū Bakr. Al-Aḥwaṣ, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Thābit ibn Abī al-Aqlaḥ, said:

verses.h1: وإني لآتي البيت ما إن أحبه
verses.h2: وأكثر هجر البيت وهو حبيب

verses.h1: وأغضى على أشياء منك تسوءني
verses.h2: وأدعي إلى ما سركم فأجيب

verses.h1: I do indeed visit a house I do not love,
verses.h2: and often stay away from a house that is dear to me.

verses.h1: I overlook things you do that distress me,
verses.h2: and when summoned to what pleases you, I answer.

notes.note: I read «وأغضى» as «وأُغضي» (‘I overlook’) and «وأدعي» as «وأُدعى» (‘I am summoned’); the final ي and ى appear to have been interchanged.

poems.intro: وقال عمر بن أبي ربيعة المخزومي:

verses.h1: ولهن بالبيت العتيق لبانة
verses.h2: والركن يعرفهن لو يتكلم

verses.h1: لو كان حيا قبلهن ظعائنا
verses.h2: حيا الحطيم وجوههن وزمزم

verses.h1: لبثوا ثلاث مني بأنعم عيشة
verses.h2: وهم على سفر لعمرك ما هم

verses.h1: متجاورين بغير دار إقامة
verses.h2: ول قد أجد رحيلهم لم يندموا

verses.h1: وكأنهن وقد حسرن لواغبا
verses.h2: بيض بأكناف الحطيم مركم

verses.h1: They have a longing to fulfill at the Ancient House;
verses.h2: the Corner knows them, could it but speak.

verses.h1: Were it alive, it would kiss them, women in their litters;
verses.h2: al-Ḥaṭīm and Zamzam would greet their faces.
