verses.h1: They stayed the three days of Minā in the sweetest ease,
verses.h2: though on a journey—by your life, they seemed not to be.

verses.h1: Dwelling as neighbors, though not in a lasting home;
verses.h2: their departure had indeed become pressing, yet they felt no regret.

verses.h1: And, weary, with their faces unveiled, they seemed
verses.h2: like eggs heaped around al-Ḥaṭīm.

notes.note: The abrupt phrase «لعمرك ما هم» is ambiguous. The translation tentatively takes it as denying that their comfortable stay felt like travel, with the predicate left unstated.

«ول قد» appears corrupted or incorrectly spaced. The translation provisionally reads «ولقد أجد رحيلهم», ‘their departure had indeed become pressing’; the intended wording and connection remain uncertain.
«حسرن» can mean that they uncovered themselves, here understood as unveiling their faces, but it can also mean that they became exhausted. «لواغبا» explicitly describes them as weary.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī said:

verses.h1: ألا أيها البيت الذي أنا هاجره
verses.h2: وإني بتلماح من الطرف ناظره

verses.h1: لهنك من بيت إلى لمونق
verses.h2: وآنق في عيني من البيت عامره

verses.h1: أصد حياء أن يلج بي الهوى
verses.h2: وأنت المنى لولا عدو أحاذره

verses.h1: وفيك حبيب النفس لو نستطيعه
verses.h2: لمات الهوى والشوق حين نجاوره

verses.h1: فإن يكن الأعداء أحموا كلامه
verses.h2: علينا، فلما تحم عنا مناظره

verses.h1: أتهجر بيتا بالحجاز تلعبت
verses.h2: به الحرب، والأعداء، أم أنت زائره

verses.h1: فإن آته لا أنج إلا بظنة
verses.h2: وإن يأته غيري تنط بي جرائره

verses.h1: ومستخبر عنها؛ ليعلم ما الذي
verses.h2: لها في فؤادي، ود أني أحاوره

verses.h1: تركت على عمياء ظن ولم أكن
verses.h2: إذا ما وشى واش بليلي أناظره

verses.h1: O house that I am leaving,
verses.h2: even as I watch you with sidelong glances!

verses.h1: What a delightful house you are to me!
verses.h2: Yet lovelier in my eyes than the house is its inhabitant.

verses.h1: I turn away in modesty, lest passion carry me too far;
verses.h2: you are my heart’s desire, were it not for an enemy I fear.

verses.h1: Within you is my soul’s beloved; could we but reach him,
verses.h2: love and longing would die when we dwelt beside him.

verses.h1: If enemies have forbidden conversation with him
verses.h2: to us, they have not yet barred us from seeing him.

verses.h1: Will you forsake a house in al-Ḥijāz that has been ravaged
verses.h2: by war and enemies, or will you visit it?

verses.h1: If I visit it, I escape only under suspicion;
verses.h2: if someone else visits it, his offenses are laid upon me.

verses.h1: Many an inquirer about her, seeking to learn
verses.h2: her place in my heart, wished I would converse with him.

verses.h1: I left him to blind conjecture; I was not one
verses.h2: to debate with a slanderer when he spoke against Laylā.

notes.note: Read إلى as إليّ, “to me,” and لمونق as لمؤنق, “indeed delightful.” The transmitted spelling appears defective.
Read بليلي as بليلى, “about Laylā.” The spelling as given is uncertain. The object of تركت, “I left,” is understood as the inquirer mentioned in line 8.

verses.h1: أمر مجنبا عن بيت ليلى
verses.h2: ولم ألمم به وبي الغليل

verses.h1: أمر مجنبا وهواي فيه
verses.h2: وطرفي عنه منكسر كليل

verses.h1: وقلبي فيه مرتهن فهل لي
verses.h2: إلى قلبي ومالكه سبيل؟

verses.h1: فآمل أن أعل بشرب ليلى ولم أنهل فكيف لي العلول؟
I pass by, keeping clear of Laylā’s house,
verses.h2: and do not visit it, though longing burns within me.

verses.h1: I pass by, keeping clear, though my love is there,
verses.h2: my gaze turned away from it, downcast and weary.

verses.h1: My heart is held captive there—is there
verses.h2: a way for me to reach my heart and its possessor?

verses.h1: I hope for a second draught of Laylā’s drink, though I have not had a first—how, then, can I have a second?

notes.note: The phrase بشرب ليلى is ambiguous: it may refer to Laylā’s drink or to drinking with her.

verses.h1: وإني وإن لم آت أبيات بحدل
verses.h2: إلى أم يحيى من مدى العين ناظر

verses.h1: بنفسي مجرى الطوق منها وحبذا
verses.h2: إلينا غشاشا طرفها المتشازر

verses.h1: Though I have not come to the tents of Baḥdal,
verses.h2: I gaze toward Umm Yaḥyā from as far as sight can reach.

verses.h1: I would ransom with my life the place her necklace rests; how dear
verses.h2: to us is her fleeting, sidelong glance.

notes.note: The identities of Baḥdal and Umm Yaḥyā are uncertain.

poems.intro: وقال أبو ذؤيب الهذلي، واسمه خويلد بن [خالد بن] محرث:

verses.h1: لعمري لأنت البيت أكرم أهله
verses.h2: وأقعد في أفيائه بالأصائل

verses.h1: وإن حديثا منك لو تبدلينه
verses.h2: جنى النحل في ألبان عوذ مطافل

verses.h1: فتلك التي لا يذهب الدهر حبها
verses.h2: ولا ذكرها ما أرزمت أم حائل

verses.h1: ولو أن ما عند ابن بجرة عندها
verses.h2: من الخمر لم تبلل لهاتي بناطل

verses.h1: By my life, you are the house whose people I honor,
verses.h2: and in whose shade I sit in the late afternoons.

verses.h1: A word from you—if you would offer it—
verses.h2: is the bees’ honey in the milk of newly calved she-camels nursing their young.

verses.h1: She is the one whose love time cannot efface,
verses.h2: nor her memory, as long as a she-calf’s mother lows.

verses.h1: Even if she had what Ibn Bajra possesses
verses.h2: of wine, she would not moisten my palate with a single measure.

notes.note: The text has تبدلينه, normally meaning ‘you exchange/change it.’ I have provisionally read تبذلينه, ‘you offer it,’ which fits the context; the printed form may be a transcription error.
Ibn Bajra is apparently associated with a supply of wine, but his identity and the vocalization of his name are uncertain.
ناطل denotes a measure or small quantity of wine; its precise quantity here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī, whose name was Khuwaylid ibn [Khālid ibn] Muḥarrith, said:

verses.h1: ألا يا بيت بالعلياء بيت
verses.h2: ولولا حب أهلك ما أتيت

verses.h1: ألا يا بيت أهلك أوعدوني
verses.h2: كأني كل ذنبهم جنيت

verses.h1: O house upon the heights, O house!
verses.h2: But for my love of your people, I would not have come.

verses.h1: O house, your people have threatened me,
verses.h2: As though I had committed all their sins.

notes.note: The final بيت is syntactically unclear; it is rendered as a repeated address, though the text may be corrupt. العلياء may mean ‘the heights’ or be the place-name al-ʿAlyāʾ.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: أيا جارة البيت الممنع جاره
verses.h2: رحلت ومن لي عندكم بمقيل

verses.h1: نسيت مكان العقد من دهش النوى
verses.h2: وعلقته في وجنة ومسيل

verses.h1: وأرسلت طيفا خان لما بعثته
verses.h2: فلا تثقي من بعده برسول

verses.h1: أسرت أخانا بالخداع وإنه
verses.h2: يعد إذا اشتد الوغى بقبيل

verses.h1: فإن تطلقيه ترتجى شكر قومه
verses.h2: وإن تقتليه تؤخذي بقتيل

verses.h1: وإن عاش لاقى ذلة، واختياره
verses.h2: وفاة عزيز، لا حياة ذليل

verses.h1: O neighbor of the house whose neighbor is protected,
verses.h2: you have departed—who will grant me a noonday resting-place among you?

verses.h1: Bewildered by parting, you forgot where the necklace belongs
verses.h2: and hung it on your cheek and the track of your tears.

verses.h1: You sent a phantom that proved faithless when you dispatched it;
verses.h2: after it, trust no messenger.

verses.h1: You captured our brother by guile, though he,
verses.h2: when battle rages, counts as a whole tribe.

verses.h1: If you release him, you may hope for his people’s thanks;
verses.h2: if you kill him, you will answer for a slain man.

verses.h1: If he lives, he will meet with humiliation; his choice is
verses.h2: an honorable man’s death, not a humiliated man’s life.

notes.note: The unvocalized رحلت can mean either “you departed” or “I departed.” I have taken it as addressing the woman, as in the later lines.

نسيت and علقته likewise permit either first-person or second-person readings. The necklace apparently represents tears strung like pearls; مسيل literally means a watercourse or channel, here understood as the tears’ track down the cheek.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: أجارة بيتينا أبوك غيور
verses.h2: وميسور ما يرجى لديك عسير

verses.h1: فإن كنت لا خلما ولا أنت زوجة
verses.h2: فلا برحت دوني عليك ستور

verses.h1: وجاورت قوما لا تجاور بينهم
verses.h2: ولا وصل إلا أن يكون نشور

verses.h1: O neighbor of our two houses, your father is jealous,
verses.h2: and even the easiest favor hoped for from you is hard to obtain.

verses.h1: If you are neither lover nor wife,
verses.h2: may veils forever screen you from me.

verses.h1: And may you dwell among folk with no neighborly contact between them,
verses.h2: and no reunion unless the dead rise again.

notes.note: The wording لا تجاور بينهم is unusual; translated here as ‘no neighborly contact between them.’ تجاور may be a misprint for تزاور, ‘mutual visiting.’
جاورت is read as continuing the preceding wish (‘may you dwell’), though its unvocalized form could also mean ‘you dwelt’ or ‘I dwelt.’

verses.h1: تقول التي من بيتها خف مركبي
verses.h2: عزيز علينا أن نراك تسير

verses.h1: أما دون مصر للغنى متطلب؟
verses.h2: بلى إن أسباب الغنى لكثير

verses.h1: فقلت لها
verses.h2: واستعجلتها بوادر

verses.h1: جرت فجرى في جريهن عبير
ذريني أكثر حاسديك برحلة
verses.h2: إلى بلد فيه الخصيب أمير

verses.h1: إذا لم تزر أرض الخصيب ركابنا
verses.h2: فأي فتى بعد الخصيب تزور؟

verses.h1: فتى يشترى حسن الثناء بماله
verses.h2: ويعلم أن الدائرات تدور

verses.h1: She from whose house my mount set off says:
verses.h2: “It grieves us to see you leave.

verses.h1: Is there nowhere short of Miṣr to seek wealth?
verses.h2: Surely the ways to wealth are many.”

verses.h1: I said to her—
verses.h2: as sudden tears overtook her,

verses.h1: flowing, and carrying perfume in their flow—
“Let me make more people envy you by journeying
verses.h2: to a land where al-Khaṣīb is governor.

verses.h1: If our mounts do not visit al-Khaṣīb’s land,
verses.h2: what noble man after al-Khaṣīb will they visit?

verses.h1: A man who buys fine praise with his wealth
verses.h2: and knows that fortune’s reversals come around.”

notes.note: The source appears to divide a single bayt across entries 3–4: «فقلت لها واستعجلتها بوادر» forms its first hemistich, and «جرت فجرى في جريهن عبير» its second. The supplied divisions are preserved.

poems.intro: روى الفرزدق قال: أبق غلامان لرجل منا، فخرج في طلبهما، فلما صار في ماء لبني حنيفة ارتفعت له حلة، قال: فعدلت إلى بعض ديارهم، وسألت القرى، فأجابوا، فدخلت الدار، وأنخت الناقة، وجلست تحت ظلة لهم من جريد النخل، وفي الدار جارية سوداء، إذ دخلت جارية، كأنها سبيكة فضة، فقالت للسوداء: لمن هذه الناقة؟ قالت: لضيفكم، فعدلت إلي، فسلمت، فرددت السلام، وقالت: من الرجل؟ قلت: رجل من بني حنظلة، قالت: من أيهم؟ قلت: من بني نهشل، فتبسمت، ثم قالت: أنت إذن ممن عناه الفرزدق بقوله:

verses.h1: إن الذي رفع السماء بنى لنا
verses.h2: بيتا دعائمه أعز وأطول

verses.h1: بيتا زرارة محتب بفنائه
verses.h2: ومجاشع، وأبو الفوارس نهشل

verses.h1: He who raised the heavens built for us
verses.h2: a house whose pillars are mightier and taller.

verses.h1: A house in whose courtyard Zurārah sits clasping his knees,
verses.h2: and Mujāshiʿ, and Abū al-Fawāris Nahshal.

notes.note: The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyyah, while the introduction attributes these verses to al-Farazdaq.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Farazdaq related: “Two slaves belonging to a man of our people ran away, and he went out in search of them. When he reached a watering place belonging to Banū Ḥanīfah, an encampment came into view.” The man said: “I turned aside toward one of their dwellings and asked for hospitality. They welcomed me, so I entered the house, made my she-camel kneel, and sat beneath a shelter of palm fronds they had. There was a black slave girl in the house. Then a young woman entered, looking like an ingot of silver, and said to the black girl, ‘Whose she-camel is this?’ She replied, ‘Your guest’s.’ The young woman turned toward me and greeted me, and I returned her greeting. She asked, ‘Who are you?’ I said, ‘A man of Banū Ḥanẓalah.’ She asked, ‘From which of them?’ I said, ‘From Banū Nahshal.’ She smiled, then said, ‘Then you are one of those al-Farazdaq meant when he said:’”

poems.intro: فضحكت، فقالت: فإن ابن المراغة قد نقض عليكم بيتكم هذا حيث يقول:

verses.h1: أخزى الذي رفع السماء مجاشعا
verses.h2: وبنى بناءك بالحضيض الأسفل

verses.h1: بيتا يتمم قينكم بفنائه
verses.h2: دنس مقاعده خبيث المأكل

verses.h1: He who raised the sky has disgraced Mujāshiʿ
verses.h2: and built your dwelling in the lowest depths:

verses.h1: a house in whose courtyard your smith finishes his work,
verses.h2: its seats filthy, its fare foul.

notes.note: The reading يتمم is uncertain. Read literally as ‘completes,’ it lacks an explicit object; ‘his work’ is supplied tentatively. The text may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro: I laughed, and she said: “But Ibn al-Marāgha has countered this verse of yours, saying:”

poems.intro: قال: فوجمت، فلما رأت ذلك في وجهي قالت: لا عليك، فإن الناس يقولون ويقال لهم، ثم قالت: أين تؤم؟ قلت: اليمامة فتنفست الصعداء، ثم قالت:

verses.h1: تذكرني بلادا خير أهلي
verses.h2: بها أهل المروءة والكرامة

verses.h1: ألا فسقى الإله أجش صوب
verses.h2: يسح بدره بلد اليمامة

verses.h1: وحيا بالسلام أبا نجيد
verses.h2: وقل له التحية والسلامة

verses.h1: You remind me of a land: the best of my kin
verses.h2: dwell there, people of noble character and honor.

verses.h1: Oh, may God send a thunder-voiced raincloud
verses.h2: to pour its abundant rain upon the land of al-Yamāma.

verses.h1: And may He greet Abū Nujayd with peace;
verses.h2: and tell him: greetings and well-being.

notes.note: حيا is read here as a past-tense verb expressing a wish, continuing the prayer to God. The following قل, however, addresses the traveler directly; حيا may instead be a textual error for the imperative حيّ, ‘greet.’ Abū Nujayd has not been securely identified.

prose_translation.intro: He said: I fell silent in dismay. When she saw this in my face, she said, “Do not let it trouble you, for people speak of others and are spoken of themselves.” Then she asked, “Where are you bound?” I said, “Al-Yamāma.” She heaved a deep sigh, then said:

poems.intro: قال: فأنست بها، وقلت: أخالية أم ذات بعل؟ فقالت:

verses.h1: إذا رقد النيام فإن عمرا
verses.h2: تؤرقه الهموم إلى الصباح

verses.h1: تقطع قلبه الذكرى وقلبي
verses.h2: فلا هو بالخلي ولا بصاح

verses.h1: سقى الله اليمامة دار قوم
verses.h2: بها عمرو يحن إلى الرواح

verses.h1: When sleepers lie down, ʿAmr
verses.h2: is kept awake by cares until morning.

verses.h1: Remembrance tears his heart and mine;
verses.h2: he is neither carefree nor clear-headed.

verses.h1: May God send rain upon al-Yamāma, the abode of a people,
verses.h2: where ʿAmr longs to be on his way.

notes.note: بصاح can mean ‘sober’ or ‘awake’; ‘clear-headed’ takes it as describing someone overcome by longing, though the intended sense is uncertain.
الرواح can denote setting out, especially in the evening, or returning. The verse does not specify whether ʿAmr longs to depart or to return.

prose_translation.intro: He said: I felt at ease with her and asked, “Are you unmarried, or do you have a husband?” She replied:

poems.intro: فقلت لها: ومن عمرو؟ فأنشأت تقول:

verses.h1: سألت، ولو علمت بحال عمرو
verses.h2: ومن لك بالجواب سوى الخبير؟

verses.h1: فإن تك ما علمت، فإن عمرا
verses.h2: لكالقمر المضيء المستنير

verses.h1: وما لي بالتبعل مستراح
verses.h2: ولو رد التبعل لي أسيري

verses.h1: تخيل لي هيا عمرو بن كعب
verses.h2: كأنك قد حملت على السرير

verses.h1: فإن تك هكذا يا عمرو إني
verses.h2: مبكرة عليك إلى القبور

interludes.text: ثم سكتت سكتة، كأنها تسمع إلى كلام، ثم تهافتت، وقالت:

verses.h1: You ask—if only you knew ʿAmr’s plight!
verses.h2: Who can give you an answer but one who knows?

verses.h1: If you did not know, then ʿAmr
verses.h2: is like the radiant, shining moon.

verses.h1: Marriage offers me no solace,
verses.h2: even if marriage were to restore my captive to me.

verses.h1: I seem to see you, O ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb,
verses.h2: as though you had been borne upon a bier.

verses.h1: If that is so, O ʿAmr, then I
verses.h2: shall go early to the graves to visit you.

notes.note: The clause ولو علمت بحال عمرو has no explicit conclusion. It is rendered as a wish, ‘if only you knew,’ though an unfinished conditional, ‘had you known,’ is also possible.
The unvocalized تخيل لي is taken as ‘it appears to me’; it could also be read as an imperative, ‘appear to me.’

prose_translation.intro: I said to her, “And who is ʿAmr?” She began to recite:
interludes: Then she fell silent for a moment, as though listening to someone speaking; then she broke down and said:

poems.intro: ثم شهقت شهقة فخرت ميتة، فقلت: من هذه؟ قالوا: هذه عقيلة بنت الضحاك بن عمرو بن محرق بن النعمان بن المنذر بن ماء السماء: فقلت لهم: ومن عمرو هذا؟ قالوا: ابن عمها، عمرو بن كعب [بن عمرو] بن محرق، قال: فارتحلت من عندهم، فلما دخلت اليمامة، سألت عن عمرو، فإذا هو قد دفن في ذلك الوقت الذي قالت فيه ما قالت. قال مهيار:

verses.h1: استودع الله في أبياتكم قمرا
verses.h2: تراه بالشوق عيني، وهو محجوب

verses.h1: أرضاه أسخط أو أرضى تلونه
verses.h2: وكل ما يفعل المحبوب محبوب

verses.h1: I entrust to God a moon within your dwellings;
verses.h2: my eye sees him through longing, though he is veiled.

verses.h1: I am content with him, whether his fickleness angers or pleases me;
verses.h2: and whatever the beloved does is beloved.

prose_translation.intro: Then she gave a gasp and fell down dead. I said, “Who is this?” They said, “This is ʿAqīla bint al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn ʿAmr ibn Muḥarriq ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ.” I said to them, “And who is this ʿAmr?” They said, “Her paternal cousin, ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb [ibn ʿAmr] ibn Muḥarriq.” He said: “I departed from them, and when I entered al-Yamāma, I asked about ʿAmr. It turned out that he had been buried at the very time when she had said what she said.” Mihyār said:

verses.h1: مقام الفتى في الحي حيا مسلما
verses.h2: معافى مقام ذلة بالفتى يزري

verses.h1: متى ما تنم في ظل بيتك عاجزا
verses.h2: تصبك خطوب الدهر بالناب والظفر

verses.h1: A young man’s remaining among his people, alive and safe,
verses.h2: in good health, is a state of abasement that demeans him.

verses.h1: Whenever you sleep helpless in the shade of your house,
verses.h2: time’s calamities will strike you with fang and claw.

notes.note: The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names Mihyār, while the introduction names al-Buḥturī.
I read مسلما as musallaman, meaning ‘safe’ or ‘unharmed’; the unvocalized spelling is ambiguous.

poems.poet_from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري
poems.intro: وقال أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري:

poet.from_text: أبو العلاء [أحمد بن عبد الله] بن سليمان المعري

verses.h1: لزمت بيتا بناه الجد من مدر
verses.h2: كأنه بيت شعر ليس يتزن

verses.h1: إذا شتوت فمن توكافه عنتي
verses.h2: وبالحرور إذا ما صفت يقترن

verses.h1: عدم فحسبي، وعين غير مبصرة
verses.h2: وشقوة وحليف الشقوة اليفن

verses.h1: لولا القناعة جاءتني بمملكة
verses.h2: لهتكت دوني الأستار والجنن

verses.h1: I have kept to a house my grandfather built of clay,
verses.h2: like a line of poetry that will not scan.

verses.h1: When I winter there, its dripping brings me hardship;
verses.h2: when I summer there, it is joined with scorching heat.

verses.h1: Poverty—enough for me!—and an eye that cannot see,
verses.h2: and misery, and a decrepit old man, misery’s companion.

verses.h1: Had contentment not brought me a kingdom,
verses.h2: the veils and shields protecting me would have been torn away.

notes.note: Al-yafan means a very old or decrepit man. Its grammatical connection to the preceding list is unclear; the phrase probably describes the poet himself as misery’s aged companion.
The unvocalized لهتكت is read here as passive, ‘would have been torn away.’ An active reading, ‘I would have torn away,’ is also grammatically possible.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAlāʾ [Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah] ibn Sulaymān al-Maʿarrī said:

verses.h1: وليلة واكف لا نوم فيها
verses.h2: سهرت بها إلى الصبح الفتيق

verses.h1: ترق قلوب جيرتنا علينا
verses.h2: إذا نظروا إلى الغيم الرقيق

verses.h1: حماني النوم فيه سقف بيت
verses.h2: كأن سماءه عين المشوق

verses.h1: تواصلت السحائب وهو بيت
verses.h2: وصدت وهو قارعة الطريق

verses.h1: A night of dripping rain, with no sleep in it—
verses.h2: I lay awake through it until the breaking dawn.

verses.h1: Our neighbors’ hearts grow tender toward us
verses.h2: when they look at the thin clouds.

verses.h1: The roof of a house kept sleep from me there,
verses.h2: as though its ceiling were a yearning lover’s eye.

verses.h1: The clouds came one after another, and it was a house;
verses.h2: they turned away, and it was the middle of the road.

notes.note: واكف can describe falling rain or a dripping roof; the phrase may refer specifically to a night beneath a leaking roof.

I read وصدت as wa-ṣaddat, ‘and they turned away,’ referring to the clouds. The contrast between the house and the middle of the road is obscure; it may suggest that the rain left the dwelling exposed or destroyed.

verses.h1: وبيت تساوى والغمام وإنه
verses.h2: لآغزر منها دمعة حين تذرف

verses.h1: إذا السحب عنه أقلعت فلو كفه
verses.h2: سحاب هتون ماؤها ليس ينزف

verses.h1: فثؤبي من توكاف أسود سقفه
verses.h2: وتربته الحمراء برد مفوف

verses.h1: فدعه، ونم تحت السحاب فإنه
verses.h2: سحاب ولكن صيب الجو أنظف

verses.h1: A house that rivals the clouds—indeed,
verses.h2: its tears, when shed, are more abundant than theirs.

verses.h1: When the clouds withdraw from it, its leaks are fed by
verses.h2: a pouring cloud whose water never runs dry.

verses.h1: My robe—from the dripping of its black roof
verses.h2: and its red earth—is a striped mantle.

verses.h1: Leave it, and sleep beneath the clouds, for it
verses.h2: is a cloud too, but rain from the sky is cleaner.

notes.note: لآغزر appears to be a misprint for لأغزر, ‘more abundant.’
The spaced wording فلو كفه is read as فَلِوَكْفِهِ, literally ‘for its dripping there is…’; ‘its leaks are fed by’ renders this somewhat unusual construction.
فثؤبي appears to be a misprint for فثوبي, ‘so my robe.’

verses.h1: بيتي ستور العنكبوت ستوره
verses.h2: ومطارح الغبراء فيه مطارحي

verses.h1: وإذا أصابته السماء بطلها
verses.h2: فسماؤه تهمي بوكف سافح

verses.h1: وكأنني من ضيقه وظلامه
verses.h2: ميت دفين في ثرى وصفائح

verses.h1: My house has spiders’ webs for curtains,
verses.h2: and where the dust settles, there I lie.

verses.h1: When the sky touches it with drizzle,
verses.h2: its own roof pours down a streaming rain.

verses.h1: In its narrowness and darkness, I seem
verses.h2: a dead man buried in earth beneath stone slabs.

verses.h1: العنكبوت بنت بيتا على وهو
verses.h2: تأوى إليه ومالي مثلها وطن

verses.h1: والخنفساء لها من حشها سكن
verses.h2: وليس لي مثلها إلف ولا سكن

verses.h1: The spider has built a house, frail though it is,
verses.h2: where it takes shelter; yet I have no home as it does.

verses.h1: The beetle has a dung heap for its dwelling,
verses.h2: yet I have neither companion nor dwelling as it does.

notes.note: على وهو appears corrupt, probably for على وهن, referring to the weakness of the spider’s house; the translation follows that reading.
حشها is understood here as a dung heap or privy, though حش can also mean a garden. The precise sense is uncertain.

verses.h1: إذا نحن جئنا للسلام ورفعت
verses.h2: ستورك، فانظر ما به أنا خارج

verses.h1: فسيان بيت العنكبوت وجوسق
verses.h2: على الشط ما لم تقض فيه الحوائج

verses.h1: When we come to pay our respects and your curtains are raised,
verses.h2: consider what I am leaving with.

verses.h1: For a spider’s house is no different from a palace
verses.h2: on the riverbank, unless needs are met within it.

poems.intro: وقال أبو القاسم أسعد بن إبراهيم، وتروى لابن الشقاق:

verses.h1: رأيت ليوسف في بيته
verses.h2: فخربه الله بين البيوت

verses.h1: حصير صلاة علاه الغبا
verses.h2: ر، وقد نسجت فوقه العنكبوت

verses.h1: فقلت له: كم لهذا الحص
verses.h2: ير، وكم لك لم تقر فيه القنوت؟

verses.h1: فقال: هنالك ألفيته
verses.h2: وثم يدوم إلى أن أموت

verses.h1: I saw in Yūsuf’s house—
verses.h2: may God lay it waste among the houses!—

verses.h1: a prayer mat covered in dust,
verses.h2: over which a spider had woven its web.

verses.h1: I asked him, “How long has this mat been here,
verses.h2: and how long have you gone without reciting the supplication upon it?”

verses.h1: He said, “I found it there,
verses.h2: and there it will remain until I die.”

notes.note: The form تقر appears to stand for تقرأ, “recite,” perhaps through poetic shortening or a textual error. القنوت is understood here as the supplication recited during prayer.

prose_translation.intro: Abū al-Qāsim Asʿad ibn Ibrāhīm said (these verses are also attributed to Ibn al-Shaqqāq):

verses.h1: لما رأيت الزمان نكسا
verses.h2: وليس في أهله انتفاع

verses.h1: لزمت بيتي وصنت نفسا
verses.h2: لها عن الذلة امتناع

verses.h1: أشرب مما اقتنيت راحا
verses.h2: لها على راحتي شعاع

verses.h1: لي من قواريرها ندامى
verses.h2: ومن قواقيزها سماع

verses.h1: وأجتني من ثمار قوم
verses.h2: قد أوحشت منهم الرباع

verses.h1: When I saw that the age had turned base,
verses.h2: and no benefit could be had from its people,

verses.h1: I kept to my house and guarded a soul
verses.h2: that refuses humiliation.

verses.h1: I drink wine from what I have laid by,
verses.h2: its radiance shining upon my palm.

verses.h1: Its bottles are my drinking companions,
verses.h2: and its goblets furnish my music.

verses.h1: I gather the fruits of people
verses.h2: whose dwellings have grown desolate without them.

notes.note: The ‘fruits’ may be literal produce or, figuratively, works left by people now gone; the intended sense is uncertain.

poems.intro: قال الأحنف بن قيس: جزية المسلم كرى بيته، وذلك رقبته، وعذاب الرجل سوء خلق امرأته. وقال آخر:

verses.h1: وبيت خلا من كل خير علمته
verses.h2: وضاق علينا وهو رحب المساكن

verses.h1: كأنا مع الجدران في جنباته
verses.h2: دمى، في انقطاع الرزق لا في المحاسن

verses.h1: A house devoid of every good I know,
verses.h2: cramped us, though its rooms were spacious.

verses.h1: Within its confines, we and the walls are like
verses.h2: statues—in being deprived of sustenance, not in beauty.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays said: “A Muslim’s poll tax is the rent of his house, and therein lies his bondage; a man’s torment is his wife’s ill temper.” Another poet said:

verses.h1: نزلت في آل مكحول، وضيفهم
verses.h2: كنازل بين سمع الأرض والبصر

verses.h1: لا تستضيء بضوء في بيوتهم
verses.h2: إن لم يكن لك تطفيل على القمر

verses.h1: I lodged with the clan of Makhul; their guest
verses.h2: is like one encamped beyond all human sight and hearing.

verses.h1: You have no light to see by in their houses,
verses.h2: unless you can cadge it from the moon.

notes.note: The clan of Makhul is unidentified.

prose_translation.intro: And Ibn al-Marʿazī the Christian said:

verses.h1: يريد إهال النحض، والنحض معوز
verses.h2: وليس لنا ناب يكب ولا بكر

verses.h1: ولا ضأن يغنينا، ولا ماعز لنا
verses.h2: ويقبح أن يشكى إلى جارنا الفقر

verses.h1: ونحن أناس منفضون بمعزل
verses.h2: عن الخير، لا بر لدينا، ولا تمر

verses.h1: ولو كان في الأرض العريضة نابت
verses.h2: رعينا، ولكن لا نبات ولا قطر

verses.h1: فدنونك هذا البيت فاستتري به
verses.h2: وأستر منه إن رضيت به القبر

verses.h1: He wants the fat of meat, but meat is not to be had;
verses.h2: we have no old she-camel to slaughter, nor a young male camel.

verses.h1: We have no sheep to sustain us, nor any goats;
verses.h2: and it is shameful to complain of poverty to our neighbor.

verses.h1: We are people whose provisions are spent, cut off
verses.h2: from prosperity: we have neither wheat nor dates.

verses.h1: If anything grew upon the broad earth,
verses.h2: we would graze; but there is neither vegetation nor rain.

verses.h1: So take this house and conceal yourself within it;
verses.h2: the grave conceals still better, if you will accept it.

notes.note: إهال is unusual; I take it as related to إهالة, melted fat or grease. النحض means flesh or lean meat. يكب is understood here as referring to felling a camel for slaughter.
فدنونك appears to be a typing or OCR error for فدونك, ‘so take’ or ‘here is … for you.’

poems.intro: روى أن رجلا تعاهد هو وامرأته: أيهما مات لا يتزوج الآخر بعده، فمات الرجل، فلما أوفت الامرأة العدة، خطبت، فامتنعت، فما زلن بها النساء يسهلن عليها الأمر، ويشرن عليها بالزوج، حتى أجابت، وحمل إليها الصداق، فرأت قبل دخلوها بليلة كأن زوجها قد وقف ببابها، ومد يديه فأخذ عضادتي الباب، وقال:

verses.h1: حييت ساكن هذا البيت كلهم
verses.h2: إلا الرباب، فإني لا أحييها

verses.h1: استبدلت بدلا مني، فقد علمت
verses.h2: أن القبور توارى من ثوى فيها

verses.h1: I greet all who dwell in this house,
verses.h2: except al-Rabāb: her I do not greet.

verses.h1: She has taken another in my place, knowing well
verses.h2: that graves conceal those who lie within them.

notes.note: ساكن (‘dweller’) is singular, whereas كلهم (‘all of them’) is plural. It is translated collectively here; the intended reading may be سكان (‘dwellers’).
توارى appears to stand for تواري (‘conceal’), the reading followed here.

prose_translation.intro: It is related that a man and his wife made a pact: whichever of them died, the other would not marry again. The man died, and when the woman had completed her waiting period, she received a proposal of marriage but refused. The women kept pressing her, making the matter seem easy and urging her to marry, until she agreed, and the bridal gift was brought to her. On the night before the marriage was to be consummated, she saw in a dream her husband standing at her door. He stretched out his hands, took hold of the two doorposts, and said:

poems.intro: فاستيقظت مرعوبة، وقد حفظت الأبيات، فردت ما قدم لها، وقالت: والله لا ضمني وبعلا بيت أبدا. وقال مهيار:

verses.h1: نعم سقى الله بيوتا بالحمى
verses.h2: مسدلة على الدمى أستارها

verses.h1: وأوجها يشف من أثوابها
verses.h2: عنصرها الكريم [أ] ونجارها

verses.h1: Yes, may God send rain upon homes in al-Ḥimā,
verses.h2: their curtains drawn over beauties;

verses.h1: And faces through whose garments shines
verses.h2: their noble nature—or their lineage.

notes.note: Al-Ḥimā means ‘the protected pasture’; its geographical reference here is uncertain.
The printed ‘[أ] ونجارها’ appears to supply an alif to form أو نجارها (‘or their lineage’). Without that addition, it reads ‘and their lineage.’

prose_translation.intro: She awoke terrified, having memorized the verses. She returned what had been offered to her and said, “By God, no house shall ever shelter me and a husband together.” Mihyār said:

verses.h1: عزفت بأعشاش وما كدت تعزف
verses.h2: وأنكرت من حدراء ما كنت تعرف

verses.h1: ولج بك الهجران حتى كأنما
verses.h2: ترى الموت في البيت الذي كنت تيلف

verses.h1: You grew indifferent at Aʿshāsh, though you could scarcely do so,
verses.h2: and no longer recognized in Ḥadrāʾ what you once knew.

verses.h1: Estrangement has taken such hold of you that it is as though
verses.h2: you see death in the house you once frequented.

notes.note: Aʿshāsh is taken as a place-name; its location is uncertain.
تيلف is understood as تألف, meaning to be familiar with or frequent a place. It may represent a dialectal pronunciation or a textual error.

verses.h1: ثلاثة أبيات: فبيت أحبه
verses.h2: وبيتان ليسا من هواي ولا شكلي

verses.h1: ألا أيها البيت الذي حيل دونه
verses.h2: بنا أنت من بيت، وأهلك من أهل

verses.h1: بنا أنت من بيت دخولك لذة
verses.h2: وظلك لو يسطاع بالبارد السهل

verses.h1: Three houses: one house I love,
verses.h2: and two are neither to my liking nor my kind.

verses.h1: O house to which access has been barred,
verses.h2: we would give ourselves for you, house, and for your people.

verses.h1: We would give ourselves for you, house: entering you is a delight,
verses.h2: and your shade, could it be reached, is cool and pleasant.

notes.note: The prefixed bāʾ in بالبارد السهل is grammatically unexpected here; the phrase is taken as describing the shade as ‘cool and pleasant.’

prose_translation.intro: And Jamīl ibn Maʿmar al-ʿUdhrī said:

verses.h1: ألا هل إلى الأبيات بالحبل ذي الغضى
verses.h2: ذراهن أو أظلالهن سبيل

verses.h1: بنفسي من قد حيل دون لقائه
verses.h2: ومن حبه حب على ثقيل

verses.h1: Ah, to the dwellings by the sand ridge of ghaḍā trees—
verses.h2: to their rooftops or their shade—is there a way?

verses.h1: I would give my life for the one I am barred from meeting,
verses.h2: for him whose love weighs heavily upon me.

notes.note: الحبل ذي الغضى is translated descriptively as ‘the sand ridge of ghaḍā trees’; it may instead designate a particular place, Ḥabl Dhī al-Ghaḍā.
ذراهن is read as dhurāhunna, ‘their upper parts’ or ‘their rooftops’; the unvocalized text may alternatively refer to their shelter.
على is read as عليّ, ‘upon me,’ likely a typing or OCR error. The second hemistich is understood literally as ‘and him, love of whom is a love heavy upon me.’

poems.intro: وقال إبراهيم بن خفاجة - في الحمام -:

verses.h1: أهلا ببيت النار من منزل
verses.h2: شيد لأبرار وفجار

verses.h1: نقصده ملتمسي لذة
verses.h2: فندخل الجنة في النار

verses.h1: Welcome to the house of fire, a dwelling
verses.h2: built for the righteous and the wicked.

verses.h1: We seek it out in search of pleasure,
verses.h2: and enter paradise amid the fire.

prose_translation.intro: And Ibrāhīm ibn Khafāja said, concerning the bathhouse:

poems.intro: نزل حماد عجرد على محمد بن طلحة، فأبطأ عليه بالطعام، واشتد جوع حماد، فقال:

verses.h1: زرنا امرأ في بيته مرة
verses.h2: له حياء وله خير

verses.h1: يكره أن يتخم أضيافه
verses.h2: إن أذى التخمة محذور

verses.h1: ويشتهي أن يؤجروا عنده
verses.h2: بالصوم، والصائم مأجور

verses.h1: We once visited a man in his house,
verses.h2: a man of modesty and goodness.

verses.h1: He dislikes his guests overeating,
verses.h2: for the harm of overindulgence must be avoided.

verses.h1: He wishes them to earn reward in his house
verses.h2: by fasting—for those who fast are rewarded.

prose_translation.intro: Ḥammād ʿAjrad stayed as a guest with Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa, who was slow to bring him food. Ḥammād grew very hungry and said:

poems.intro: فقال هل محمد: عليك لعنة الله، ما حملك على هذا؟ قال: الجوع وحياتك، وإن زدت في الإبطاء زدت في القول، فبادر بإحضار المائدة. وقال صخر بن الجعد:

verses.h1: مررت على أبيات كاس فأسبلت
verses.h2: مدامع عيني، والرياح تميلها

verses.h1: وفي دارهم قوم سواهم فأسبلت
verses.h2: دموع من الأجفان باق مثيلها

verses.h1: كذاك الليالي، ليس فيها بسالم
verses.h2: صديق، ولا يبقى عليها خليلها

verses.h1: I passed by the tents of Kās, and down streamed
verses.h2: the tears of my eyes, while the winds swayed them.

verses.h1: Others now dwelt in their home, and down streamed
verses.h2: tears from my eyelids, with more like them still remaining.

verses.h1: Such are the nights: they leave unharmed
verses.h2: no friend, nor does a dear companion survive their passing.

notes.note: Kās (كاس) appears to be a personal or place name, but I cannot identify it or confirm its vocalization.
The pronoun in تميلها, ‘swayed them,’ could refer to the tents or to the tears.
باق مثيلها literally means ‘their like remaining.’ I understand this to mean that more tears remain to be shed, but the expression is unusual and its precise sense uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Muḥammad said to him, “God’s curse be upon you! What drove you to this?” He replied, “Hunger, by your life! If you delay any longer, I shall say still more.” So he hastened to have the meal brought in. Ṣakhr ibn al-Jaʿd said:

poems.intro: قلت: هذا الفصل كان موضعه صدر الكتاب؛ إذ كانت المنازل والديار إنما تبكي لسكانها من الأهل والإخوان والأحباب، لكني أخرته؛ لأختم به الكتاب. روى عن أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليه - أنه كان كثيرا ما يتمثل بهذا الشعر:

verses.h1: ألا قد أرى والله أن لست منكم
verses.h2: ولا أنتم مني، وإن كنتم أهلي

verses.h1: وإني ثوى قد أحم انطلاقه
verses.h2: يحييه من حياه وهو على رجل

verses.h1: ومنطلق منكم بغير صحابة
verses.h2: وتابع إخواني الذين مضوا قبلي

verses.h1: ألم أك قد صاحبت عمرا ومالكا
verses.h2: وأدهم يغدو في فوارس أو رجل؟

verses.h1: وصاحبت شيبانا وصاحبت ضابئا
verses.h2: وصاحبني الشم الطوال بنو شبل

verses.h1: أولئك إخواني مضوا لسبيلهم
verses.h2: يكاد ينسيني تذكرهم عقلي

verses.h1: يقول أناس أخلياء: تناسهم
verses.h2: وليس بناس مثلهم أبدا مثلي

verses.h1: أولاك أخلائي إذا ما ذكرتهم
verses.h2: بكيت بعين ماء عبرتها كحلي

verses.h1: وكانوا إذا ما القر هبت رياحه
verses.h2: وضم سواد الليل رحلا إلى رحل

verses.h1: يدرون بالسيف الوريدين والنسا
verses.h2: إذا لم يقم راعي أناس إلى رسل

verses.h1: إذا ما لقوا أقرانهم قتلوهم
verses.h2: وإن قتلوا لم يقشعروا من القتل

verses.h1: فكم من أسير قد فككتم قيوده
verses.h2: وسجل دم أهرقتموه على سجل

verses.h1: Indeed, by God, I see that I am not of you,
verses.h2: nor you of me, though you are my kin.

verses.h1: I am a sojourner whose departure is at hand;
verses.h2: whoever greets him greets him as he stands ready to leave.

verses.h1: I am leaving you without companions,
verses.h2: following my brothers who went before me.

verses.h1: Did I not keep company with ʿAmr and Mālik,
verses.h2: and Adham, who went forth among horsemen or men on foot?

verses.h1: I kept company with Shaybān and with Ḍābiʾ,
verses.h2: and the proud, tall Banū Shibl were my companions.

verses.h1: Those were my brothers; they have gone their way.
verses.h2: Remembering them nearly makes me lose my reason.

verses.h1: People untouched by grief say, “Put them out of mind”;
verses.h2: but one like me will never forget men like them.

verses.h1: Those are my dear friends; whenever I remember them,
verses.h2: I weep from an eye whose tears are my kohl.

verses.h1: And when the cold winds blew,
verses.h2: and night’s blackness drew one household close to another,

verses.h1: they would make the two jugular veins and the sciatic vein flow with the sword,
verses.h2: when no people’s herdsman went out for milk.

verses.h1: When they met their peers in battle, they killed them;
verses.h2: and if they themselves faced death, they did not shudder at being killed.

verses.h1: How many a captive’s bonds you have undone,
verses.h2: and bucket after bucket of blood you have spilled!

notes.note: I read ثوى as ثَوِيّ, ‘guest’ or ‘sojourner.’ The expression على رجل appears to describe someone poised to depart, though its precise sense here is uncertain.
ʿAmr, Mālik, and Adham cannot be securely identified from this passage. رجل is read as a collective meaning ‘men on foot,’ contrasted with horsemen.
Shaybān, Ḍābiʾ, and the Banū Shibl cannot be securely identified from this passage.
رحل can mean a saddle or, by extension, a dwelling or household. I take the image to be households drawing close together at night.

The bleeding vessels apparently belong to livestock slaughtered to feed others when milk was scarce, but the animals are not explicitly named. النسا is the vessel traditionally called the ‘sciatic vein.’

prose_translation.intro: I say: This chapter belonged at the beginning of the book, since abodes and dwellings are wept over only for the family, brethren, and loved ones who inhabited them. But I deferred it so as to close the book with it. It is related of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with him—that he would often quote these verses:

poems.intro: وقال يزيد بن ضبة بن مقسم:

verses.h1: لم ينس سلمى فؤادك السدك
verses.h2: وكيف تصبو وأنت محتنك؟

verses.h1: لو كان ما واحدا هواك لقد
verses.h2: أقصرت، لكن هواك مشترك

verses.h1: تقول سلمى
verses.h2: واستنكرت

verses.h1: Your clinging heart has not forgotten Salmā;
verses.h2: how can you yield to youthful passion when you are seasoned?

verses.h1: Had your love been for one alone, you would have
verses.h2: desisted; but your love is divided.

verses.h1: Salmā says—
verses.h2: and she found it strange—

notes.note: The contrast between واحداً and مشترك is ambiguous: it may mean love directed toward one person versus several, as translated, or one-sided versus mutual love. The particle ما appears to be pleonastic.

The line is incomplete. استنكرت can mean finding something strange or expressing disapproval; its object is missing. Without vowels or further context, its subject is also uncertain; the translation takes it as Salmā.

prose_translation.intro: And Yazīd ibn Ḍabba ibn Miqsam said:

verses.h1: ما بال أشياء منك تنتهك
فقلت: من ترحة، ومن أسف
verses.h2: أبناء عوف ومالك هلكوا

verses.h1: خلوا فجاجا علي فانخرقت
verses.h2: لم يستطع سدهن من تركوا

verses.h1: Why are parts of you being ravaged?
I said: From grief and sorrow—
verses.h2: the sons of ʿAwf and Mālik have perished.

verses.h1: They left wide breaches around me, which gaped open;
verses.h2: those they left behind could not close them.

notes.note: The expression «أشياء منك تنتهك», literally “things of/from you are violated,” is unclear. “Parts of you being ravaged” is tentative; the reference might instead be to things belonging to the addressee being violated.

verses.h1: ألم ترني بعد الذين تتابعوا
verses.h2: وكانوا الألى أعطي بهم وأمانع

verses.h1: كذي وقرات كدن يكسرن عظمه
verses.h2: ولن تلبث العظم الصحيح القوارع

verses.h1: فإني وتأميلي الحياة، وقد مضوا
verses.h2: كمحتبس عن مطلع، وهو طالع

verses.h1: Have you not seen me after those who departed one after another—
verses.h2: those with whose support I gave and stood my ground?

verses.h1: I am like one with cracks that nearly shatter his bone;
verses.h2: blows will not spare even sound bone for long.

verses.h1: For I, in hoping to live when they have gone,
verses.h2: am like one held back from an ascent, yet bound to climb it.

notes.note: وقرات is understood provisionally as cracks or notches in bone; its precise sense here is uncertain.

The image in محتَبِس عن مطلع وهو طالع is uncertain. I take مطلع as an ascent and وهو طالع as expressing the inevitability of climbing it, apparently an image of unavoidable death; the latter phrase could also mean ‘while he is climbing.’

poems.intro: وقال مقاس بن شريك بن عمرو، حليف لبني شيبان:

verses.h1: بكيت شريكا في الغوار، وأسودا
verses.h2: وذو العلق حتى ما بعيني من بلل

verses.h1: رجالا له ربعية المجد لم يخف
verses.h2: مجاورهم ريب الحوادث والزلل

verses.h1: وكنا بهم نرعى الجميع، ونأكل الر
verses.h2: بيع، ونكفي حامل الغرم ما حمل

verses.h1: I wept for Sharīk in al-Ghawār, and for Aswad,
verses.h2: and Dhū al-ʿAlaq, until no moisture remained in my eyes.

verses.h1: Men who held the first fruits of glory; there was no fear
verses.h2: for their neighbor of the blows of fate or reversals.

verses.h1: Through them we tended the whole community and fed on
verses.h2: spring pasture, and relieved the debtor of the burden he bore.

notes.note: Al-Ghawār is provisionally treated as a place name; I cannot identify it securely, and الغوار may instead refer to raiding. ذو العلق appears to be a personal epithet, but its expected accusative form here would be ذا العلق.
The phrase له ربعية المجد is unclear and may be corrupt. The translation provisionally reads له as لهم, referring to the men, and takes ربعية المجد as an image of glory’s early or first yield.
نرعى الجميع is ambiguous: it may mean looking after the whole company or pasturing together. The translation adopts the former.

prose_translation.intro: And Muqās ibn Sharīk ibn ʿAmr, an ally of the Banū Shaybān, said:

verses.h1: لله أقوام فقدتهم
verses.h2: سكنوا بطون الأرض والحفرا

verses.h1: God bless those whom I have lost—
verses.h2: They dwell in the earth’s depths and in graves.

poems.intro: وقال نهار بن توسعة، يرثي أخاه عتبان:

verses.h1: عتبان قد كنت امرأ لي جانب
verses.h2: حتى رزئتك، والجدود تضعضع

verses.h1: قد كنت أشوس في المقادة سادرا
verses.h2: فنظرت قصدي واستقام الأخدع

verses.h1: وفقدت إخواني الذين بعيشهم
verses.h2: قد كنت أعطي ما أشاء وأمنع

verses.h1: فلمن أقول، إذا تلم ملمة
verses.h2: أرني برأيك، أو إلى من أفزع؟

verses.h1: ʿItbān, I was a man of strength,
verses.h2: until I was bereft of you—and fortunes crumble.

verses.h1: I was defiant of restraint, heedless;
verses.h2: then I looked straight ahead, and my neck straightened.

verses.h1: And I lost my brothers, in whose lifetime
verses.h2: I could give what I wished and withhold.

verses.h1: To whom can I say, when a calamity strikes,
verses.h2: ‘Guide me with your counsel’? To whom can I turn?

notes.note: فنظرت قصدي is elliptical; I take it to mean ‘I looked straight ahead.’ الأخدع literally denotes a neck vein, apparently standing here for the neck. The precise force of this image is uncertain, but it seems to contrast humbled obedience with former defiance.

prose_translation.intro: Nahār ibn Tawsiʿa said, elegizing his brother ʿItbān:

verses.h1: أبعد بني أمي الذين تتابعوا
verses.h2: أرجى حياة، أو من الموت أجزع؟

verses.h1: ثمانية كانوا ذؤابة قومهم
verses.h2: بهم كنت أعطي ما أشاء وأمنع

verses.h1: وكانوا كنبل المرتمى في كنانة
verses.h2: فأضحت وما فهيا من النبل أهزع

verses.h1: After my mother’s sons, who followed one another in death,
verses.h2: am I to hope for life, or dread death?

verses.h1: Eight they were, the foremost of their people;
verses.h2: through them I could give or withhold whatever I wished.

verses.h1: They were like an archer’s arrows in a quiver;
verses.h2: then it was left without a single arrow.

notes.note: فهيا appears to be a typo for فيها, ‘in it.’ I take المرتمى to mean ‘archer,’ normally written المرتمي.

verses.h1: ولرب من طأطأته في حفرة
verses.h2: من كل مقتبل الشباب محبر

verses.h1: ثم انثنيت، فلا أبثك حيبتي
verses.h2: رعش القيام أميس ميس الأصور

verses.h1: Many a man have I lowered into a grave,
verses.h2: each in the first bloom of youth, well favored.

verses.h1: Then I turned away—I will not pour out my despair to you—
verses.h2: trembling on my feet, swaying like a man with a bent neck.

notes.note: محبر can suggest someone adorned, handsome, or living in comfort; its precise nuance here is uncertain.

verses.h1: أصبحت بعد مضرس ومغلس
verses.h2: غرضا بصردحة لمن راماني

verses.h1: فلأرمينهم
verses.h2: برغم أنوفهم أبدا على عدم من الفتيان

verses.h1: Since Muḍarris and Mughallis are gone, I have become
verses.h2: a target on open ground for whoever would shoot at me.

verses.h1: So I shall surely shoot back at them,
verses.h2: in defiance of them, forever, though bereft of young warriors.

notes.note: Muḍarris and Mughallis appear to be personal names, but their identities and exact vocalization are uncertain.
The hemistich division appears misplaced: برغم أنوفهم likely belongs with the first hemistich. The translation preserves the supplied division.

opening.actual: أخ لا أخا لي غيره، غير

verses.h1: أخ لا أخا لي غيره، غير أنني كراعي الخيال يستطيف بلا فكر
فإن حراما أن أرى الدهر باكيا
verses.h2: على إلفه إلا بكيت على عمرو

verses.h1: A brother—I have no brother but him—yet I am like one watching a phantom, wandering without thought.
For never may I see someone weeping
verses.h2: for his companion without weeping for ʿAmr.

notes.note: The phrase كراعي الخيال يستطيف بلا فكر is obscure and may be corrupt. The rendering ‘like one watching a phantom, wandering without thought’ is tentative: the precise sense of يستطيف and whether its subject is the watcher or the phantom are uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Abū Zayd recited on the authority of al-Mufaḍḍal:

poems.intro: وقال هذيلة بن سماعة بن أشول:

verses.h1: وعاذلة باتت بليل تلومني
verses.h2: فبت كأن الهم قرن أجاذبه

verses.h1: ذكرت بني سهل وبيني وبينهم
verses.h2: شراج الحمى أركانه ومناكبه

verses.h1: أجدى لن ألقى زيادا، ولا أرى
verses.h2: قنانا يقود الخيل شعثا ذوائبه

verses.h1: ولا مثل فتيان تولوا بمنعج
verses.h2: عجالي إذا ما الخوف أوضع راكبه

verses.h1: رجالا لو أن الصم من جانبي قنا
verses.h2: هوت مثلهم منه لزلت جوانبه

verses.h1: A reproaching woman spent the night blaming me,
verses.h2: while I lay as though grief were an adversary I wrestled.

verses.h1: I remembered Banū Sahl, with between me and them
verses.h2: the ravines of al-Ḥimā, its corners and its slopes.

verses.h1: Is it true that I shall never meet Ziyād, nor see
verses.h2: Qinān leading the cavalry, his locks disheveled?

verses.h1: Nor see the like of those young men who passed away at Manʿij,
verses.h2: swift when fear sends its rider galloping.

verses.h1: Men—had the solid rocks on either flank of Qanā
verses.h2: fallen from it as they fell, its sides would have collapsed.

notes.note: شراج is understood as ravines or watercourses. الحمى may designate a particular place, provisionally rendered al-Ḥimā, or simply mean protected pastureland.

أجدى appears to represent أجِدّي, an interrogative expression meaning approximately ‘Is it really true?’ The transmitted spelling is uncertain. The unvocalized personal name قنان is provisionally read Qinān.

prose_translation.intro: And Hudhayla ibn Samāʿa ibn Ashwal said:

poems.intro: وقال الفرزدق، همام بن غالب، يرثي همام بن ناشرة، أحد بني عامر:

verses.h1: وقفت فأبكتني بدار عشيرتي
verses.h2: على رزئهن الباكيات الحواسر

verses.h1: غدوا كسيوف الهند وراد حومة
verses.h2: من الموت أعيا وردهن المصادر

verses.h1: محامين حاموا عن حريم، وحافظا
verses.h2: بدار المنايا، والقنا متشاجر

verses.h1: كأنهم تحت الخوافق إذ غدوا
verses.h2: إلى الموت أسد الغابتين الهواصر

verses.h1: ولو أن سلمى نالها مثل رزئنا
verses.h2: لهدت، ولكن تحمل الرزء عامر

verses.h1: I stopped at my clan’s dwelling and was moved to tears
verses.h2: by the bareheaded women mourning their loss.

verses.h1: They went forth like Indian swords, entering a maelstrom
verses.h2: of death—an entry that allowed no return.

verses.h1: Defenders who protected their sacred charges and kept watch
verses.h2: in the abode of death, with spears entangled.

verses.h1: They seemed, beneath the fluttering banners, as they went
verses.h2: toward death, like lions of the two thickets, crushing their prey.

verses.h1: Had Salmā suffered a loss like ours,
verses.h2: it would have crumbled; yet ʿĀmir bears the loss.

notes.note: The wording أعيا وردهن المصادر is difficult. The translation takes المصادر as departures or returns, contrasting with ورود, entry or arrival. The feminine plural pronoun in وردهن may refer back to the swords, but its reference is uncertain.
وحافظا is grammatically unclear after the plural حاموا and may be corrupted. It is translated provisionally as though وحافظوا (‘and kept watch’ or ‘and guarded’) were intended.
الغابتين literally means ‘the two thickets/forests’; it is unclear whether a particular locality is intended.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Farazdaq, Hammām ibn Ghālib, said, elegizing Hammām ibn Nāshira, one of the Banū ʿĀmir:

poems.intro: عن الشعبي قال: كنت عند عبد الله بن جعفر بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليهما - فأنشدته قول حارثة بن بدر الغداني:

verses.h1: وكان لنا نبع تقينا فروعه
verses.h2: فقد بلغت إلا قليلا عروقها

verses.h1: وشيب رأسي واستخف حلومنا
verses.h2: رعود المنايا حولنا وبروقها

verses.h1: وإنا لتستحلي المنايا نفوسنا
verses.h2: وتترك أخرى مرة ما تذوقها

verses.h1: رأيت المنايا باديات وعودا
verses.h2: إلى دارنا، سهلا إلينا طريقها

verses.h1: وقد قسمت نفسي فريقين: منهما
verses.h2: فريق مع الموتى، وعندي فريقها

verses.h1: We once had a nabʿ tree whose branches sheltered us;
verses.h2: now death has reached all but a few of its roots.

verses.h1: My head has been grayed and our judgment shaken
verses.h2: by death’s thunder and lightning all around us.

verses.h1: Death indeed finds our souls sweet,
verses.h2: and leaves others bitter, never tasting them.

verses.h1: I have seen death come, and come again,
verses.h2: to our house, its path to us easy.

verses.h1: My soul has been divided into two parts:
verses.h2: one part is with the dead, and the other remains with me.

notes.note: The syntax of فقد بلغت إلا قليلا عروقها is uncertain. I understand it as saying that nearly all the tree’s roots have been reached, supplying death as the agent from the following verses.

prose_translation.intro: From al-Shaʿbī, who said: I was with ʿAbd Allah ibn Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with them both—and recited to him these verses by Ḥāritha ibn Badr al-Ghudānī:

poems.intro: فقال لي ابن جعفر - رضي الله عنهما: نحن كنا أحق بهذا الشعر، وجاءه غلام بدراهم في منديل، فقال: هذه غلة أرضك بمكان كذا وكذا، فقال: ألقها في حجر الشعبي، فرمى بها إلي وقال أبو دواد الإيادي:

verses.h1: لا أعد الإقتار عدما ولكن
verses.h2: فقد من قد رزئته الإعدام

verses.h1: من رجال من الأقارب فادوا
verses.h2: من خذام، هم الرؤوس العظام

verses.h1: من رجال أبوهم وأبو عمرو وكع
verses.h2: ب بيض الوجوه وسام

verses.h1: وشباب كأنهم أسد غيل
verses.h2: حالفت فرط حدها الأحلام

verses.h1: (حالفت
verses.h2: إلخ) يريد خالط حدتهم حلم.

verses.h1: وكهول بني لهم أولوهم
verses.h2: مأثرات يهابها الأقوام

verses.h1: فيهم للملاينين أناة
verses.h2: وعرام إذا يراد العرام

verses.h1: وسماح لدى السنين إذا ما
verses.h2: قحط القر، واستقل الغمام

verses.h1: I do not count poverty as destitution, but
verses.h2: the loss of those I have been bereaved of is destitution:

verses.h1: men among my kinsfolk who have died,
verses.h2: men of Khidhām, the great leaders.

verses.h1: Men—their father and Abū ʿAmr, and
verses.h2: Kaʿb—fair-faced and handsome.

verses.h1: And young men like lions of the thicket,
verses.h2: whose utmost fierceness was allied with forbearance.

verses.h1: (“Was allied”
verses.h2: etc.): he means that forbearance mingled with their fierceness.

verses.h1: And older men, for whom their forebears built
verses.h2: a legacy of glorious deeds that peoples hold in awe.

verses.h1: They show patience toward those who deal gently,
verses.h2: and fierceness when fierceness is called for.

verses.h1: And generosity in years of dearth, when
verses.h2: the cold season brings drought and the clouds depart.

notes.note: خذام appears to name a kinship group; its identification and vocalization are uncertain. Khidhām is provisional.

The wording من رجال أبوهم is syntactically unclear and may be corrupt. أبوهم is translated literally as ‘their father,’ but its referent is uncertain. The source divides كعب (Kaʿb) between the two hemistichs; the complete name is placed in h2.
This is an explanatory prose gloss on line 4, not a verse. It has been translated in the supplied two-part division.

القر is read as al-qurr, ‘cold,’ here understood as the cold season. The phrase قحط القر is unusual. استقل الغمام is also uncertain: it may describe clouds rising or departing, or clouds becoming scarce.

prose_translation.intro: Then Ibn Jaʿfar—may God be pleased with them both—said to me, “We had a greater claim to these verses.” A servant boy came to him with some dirhams in a cloth and said, “This is the revenue from your land at such-and-such a place.” He said, “Put it in al-Shaʿbī’s lap,” and the boy tossed it to me. And Abū Duʾād al-Iyādī said:
interludes: [Fādū]: he means, “they died.” [Khidhām]: a tribe.

verses.h1: سلط الموت والمنون عليهم
verses.h2: فلهم في صدى المقابر هام

verses.h1: وكذاكم يصير كل أناس
verses.h2: سوف حقا تبليهم الأيام

verses.h1: فعلى إثرهم تساقط نفسي
verses.h2: حسرات، وذكرهم لي سقام

verses.h1: Death and doom were given power over them;
verses.h2: their skulls lie amid the echoes of the graves.

verses.h1: So shall every people end:
verses.h2: the days will surely wear them away.

verses.h1: In their wake my soul wastes away
verses.h2: in sorrow upon sorrow; remembering them makes me ill.

notes.note: The phrase «في صدى المقابر هام» is uncertain. I have rendered صدى as “echoes” and هام as “skulls,” but both words can also designate owls associated in ancient Arab belief with the dead; that imagery may be intended.

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: بني أبي، قد رمى فيكم بشكته
verses.h2: ونال ما شاء هذا الأزلم الجذع

verses.h1: كنتم نجوما لدى الدهناء زاهرة
verses.h2: تضيء منها الدياجي السود والدرع

verses.h1: إن تخب أنواركم من بعد ما صدعت
verses.h2: ثوب الدجى، فلضوء الصبح منقطع

verses.h1: أرسى النسيم بناديكم، ولا برحت
verses.h2: حوامل المزن في أجداثكم تضع

verses.h1: My father’s sons, he has struck at you with all his weapons
verses.h2: and gained all he wished—this ever-youthful Fate.

verses.h1: You were stars shining beside al-Dahnāʾ,
verses.h2: lighting nights wholly black and nights dark before moonrise.

verses.h1: If your lights go out after they have rent
verses.h2: the robe of darkness—even dawn’s light has an end.

verses.h1: May the breeze settle at your gathering place, and may
verses.h2: pregnant rainclouds never cease to give birth upon your graves.

notes.note: الأزلم الجذع is understood as the traditional epithet of Time or Fate. الجذع suggests enduring youth; the precise literal force of الأزلم in this epithet is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

poems.intro: وقال زبان بن منظور بن سيار:

verses.h1: لئن فجعت بالقرناء يوما
verses.h2: لقد متعت بالأمل البعيد

verses.h1: وما تجد المنية فوق نفسي
verses.h2: ولا نفس الأحبة من مزيد

verses.h1: ألسنا أنفسا، وبني نفوس
verses.h2: ولسنا بالسلام ولا الحديد

verses.h1: Though one day I was bereaved of my companions,
verses.h2: I have indeed enjoyed far-reaching hopes.

verses.h1: Death can find nothing more beyond my own life
verses.h2: and the lives of those I love.

verses.h1: Are we not living souls, the offspring of living souls,
verses.h2: and neither stone nor iron?

prose_translation.intro: And Zabbān ibn Manẓūr ibn Sayyār said:

poems.intro: قال الأصمعي: أنشدني المذحجي لأم معدان الأنصارية:

verses.h1: لا يبعد الله فتيانا رزئتهم
verses.h2: بانوا لوقت مناياهم فقد بعدوا

verses.h1: أضحت قبورهم شتى، وتجمعهم
verses.h2: زو المنون، ولم يجمعهم بلد

verses.h1: الزو: الهلاك واختلاف المنية
ميت بمصر، وميت بالعراق ومي
verses.h2: ت بالحجاز، منايا بينهم بدد

verses.h1: رعوا من المجد أكنافا إلى أجل
verses.h2: حتى إذا بلغت أظماؤهم وردوا

verses.h1: كانت لهم همم فرقن بينهم
verses.h2: إذا القعاديد عن أمثالها قعدوا

verses.h1: فعل الجميل، وتفريج الجليل
verses.h2: وإعطاء الجزيل إذا لم يعطه أحد

verses.h1: May God not banish the young men of whom I was bereft;
verses.h2: they departed at their appointed deaths, and now are far away.

verses.h1: Their graves now lie scattered, yet what unites them
verses.h2: is death’s havoc; no single land gathered them together.

verses.h1: Al-zaw: destruction and the varying forms of death.
One dead in Miṣr, one dead in al-ʿIrāq, and one dead
verses.h2: in al-Ḥijāz—the deaths that took them were far apart.

verses.h1: They grazed the broad tracts of glory for an appointed span;
verses.h2: then, when their intervals of thirst were complete, they came to water.

verses.h1: They had ambitions that scattered them apart,
verses.h2: when the stay-at-homes held back from ambitions like theirs:

verses.h1: doing good, relieving grave distress,
verses.h2: and giving lavishly when no one else would give.

notes.note: The uncommon expression زو المنون is rendered as “death’s havoc,” following the gloss supplied in line 3; its precise force is uncertain.
This appears to be an explanatory prose gloss incorporated into the verse list. اختلاف المنية may mean the varying forms or circumstances of death.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Aṣmaʿī said: Al-Madhḥijī recited to me these verses by Umm Maʿdān al-Anṣāriyya:

poems.intro: قلت: لي أبيات تشبه معنى هذه الأبيات، وهي شرح حال صحيحة، لا على مذاهب الشعراء وذلك أنني مر بي قول رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "من زار قبر أبويه، أو أحدهما في كل جمعة غفر له، وكتب برا" فآسفني ما حرمته من زيارتهما، وشتات شملنا أحياء وأمواتا، فقلت:

verses.h1: نافستني صروف دهري في الفو
verses.h2: ز ببر الآباء في الرجم

verses.h1: لو كنت أسطيع أن أزورهما
verses.h2: مشيا على الرأس لا على القدم

verses.h1: لكن بمصر قبر، وفي شي
verses.h2: زر قبر وداري بمنتأى العجم

verses.h1: والظلم في الأرض ما نعي كل
verses.h2: ل ما أبغيه حتى زيارة الرمم

verses.h1: وما ظننت الذي لقيت من الد
verses.h2: نيا تراه عيناي في الحلم

verses.h1: The turns of my fate have begrudged me the blessing
verses.h2: of honoring my parents in their graves.

verses.h1: If only I could visit them both,
verses.h2: walking on my head, not on my feet!

verses.h1: But one grave is in Miṣr, and in Shayzar
verses.h2: another grave, while my home lies far away in the lands of the ʿAjam.

verses.h1: And injustice on earth denies me
verses.h2: everything I seek—even visiting their mortal remains.

verses.h1: I never thought that what I have suffered from this world
verses.h2: my eyes would ever see even in a dream.

notes.note: الرجم is unusual here; I understand it as referring to graves marked or covered with stones.
Miṣr can mean Egypt or its capital. The ʿAjam are non-Arabs, often specifically Persians; the precise region intended by منتأى العجم is uncertain.
I read ما نعي as مانعي, ‘denying me.’ The division كل / ل appears to represent the doubled l of كلّ across the hemistich boundary.

prose_translation.intro: I say: I have some verses resembling these in meaning. They are a truthful account of my circumstances, not composed in the manner of poets. I came across the saying of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: “Whoever visits the grave of his parents, or of either one of them, every Friday will be forgiven and recorded as dutiful to his parents.” It grieved me that I had been denied the chance to visit them, and that we were scattered, in life and in death. So I said:

verses.h1: وكانوا
verses.h2: بني كن كثرا فأصبحوا بني الأرض، قد وارتهم غير واحد

verses.h1: وقد خط للباقي المخلف أنه
verses.h2: لما وردوا من حومة الموت وارد

verses.h1: They were
verses.h2: sons of a shelter, many in number; now they are sons of the earth, which has buried all but one.

verses.h1: And it is written for the survivor left behind
verses.h2: that he too shall enter the depths of death they entered.

notes.note: بني كن is obscure. I have provisionally read كن as kinn, ‘shelter’; the text may instead contain a corrupted word or name. The division between hemistichs also appears misplaced, but has been preserved as supplied.

poems.intro: وقال أبو ذؤيب الهذلي، واسمه خويلد بن خالد، وهلك له بنون خمسة في عام واحد أصابهم الطاعون، وكانوا توجهوا إلى مصر:

verses.h1: أمن المنون وريبها تتوجع
verses.h2: والدهر ليس بمعتب من يجزع؟

verses.h1: قالت أميمة: ما لجسمك شاحبا
verses.h2: منذ ابتدلت ومثل مالك ينفع

verses.h1: أم مالجنبك لا يلائم مضجعا
verses.h2: إلا أقض عليك ذاك المضجع

verses.h1: فأجبتها أن مالجسمي أنه
verses.h2: أودى بني من البلاد فودعوا

verses.h1: أودى بني وأعقبوني حسرة
verses.h2: بعد الرقاد، وعبرة ما تقلع

verses.h1: سبقوا هوى، وأعنقوا لهواهم
verses.h2: ففقدتهم، ولكل جنب مصرع

verses.h1: ولبثت بعدهم بعيش ناصب
verses.h2: وإخال أني لاحق مستتبع

verses.h1: ولقد حرصت بأن أدافع عنهم
verses.h2: وإذا المنية أقبلت لا تدفع

verses.h1: وإذا المنية أنشبت أظفارها
verses.h2: ألفيت كل تميمة لا تنفع

verses.h1: فالعين بعدهم كأن حداقها
verses.h2: كحلت بشوك فهي عور تدمع

verses.h1: حتى كأني للحوادث مروة
verses.h2: بصفا المشقر كل يوم تقرع

verses.h1: وتجلدي للشامتين أريهم
verses.h2: أني لريب الدهر لا أتضعضع

verses.h1: Is it death and its calamities that make you grieve?
verses.h2: Time will not appease those who lament.

verses.h1: Umayma said: “Why has your body grown so pale
verses.h2: since you began neglecting yourself, when wealth like yours can help?

verses.h1: And why does your side find no resting place
verses.h2: without that bed becoming a torment to you?”

verses.h1: I answered her: “What ails my body is this:
verses.h2: my sons have perished from the land and taken their leave.

verses.h1: My sons have perished, leaving me anguish
verses.h2: after sleep, and tears that never cease.

verses.h1: They went ahead against my wish and hastened toward their own;
verses.h2: I lost them—and every side has a place where it must fall.

verses.h1: I lingered after them in a life of suffering,
verses.h2: and I think I shall follow, drawn along after them.

verses.h1: How earnestly I strove to defend them!
verses.h2: But when death approaches, it cannot be driven back.

verses.h1: When death sinks in its claws,
verses.h2: you find that no amulet avails.

verses.h1: After them, it is as though my eyes’ pupils
verses.h2: were kohled with thorns: wounded eyes, streaming tears.

verses.h1: Until I seem, beneath calamities, a flint
verses.h2: among the rocks of al-Mushaqqar, struck day after day.

verses.h1: I hold firm before those who gloat, showing them
verses.h2: that I do not crumble beneath time’s calamities.”

notes.note: The source has ابتدلت, probably a misprint for ابتذلت, the familiar reading of this verse. The translation takes this as neglecting one’s appearance or treating oneself roughly; the precise implication is uncertain.

هوى appears to represent هواي, ‘my wish.’ The contrast with لهواهم, ‘toward their own desire,’ is difficult: the first phrase likely means that the sons died before their father wished, but what their own desire refers to is not explicit.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī, whose name was Khuwaylid ibn Khālid, said the following after five sons of his died in a single year, stricken by the plague; they had set out for Miṣr:

verses.h1: فإنك
verses.h2: حقا أي نظرة ناظر نظرت، و"وقف" دونها و"قبر"

verses.h1: ديار التي قالت
verses.h2: غداة لقيتها صبوت أبا ذيب وأنت كبير

verses.h1: تغيرت بعدي أو أصابك حادث
verses.h2: من الدهر، أم مرت عليك مرور

verses.h1: فراق كنغض السن، فالصبر، إنه
verses.h2: لكل أناس عثرة وجبور

verses.h1: فأصبحت أمشي في ديار كأنها
verses.h2: خلاف ديار الكاهلية عور

verses.h1: يقال: خلف أعور، إذا كان فاسدا، يقول: هذا الدار خلف أعور من هاتيك
أنادي إذا أوفى من الدهر مربئا
verses.h2: لأي سميع، لو أجاب بصير

interludes.text: فقلت لها: فقد الأحبة، إنني حديث بأرزاء الكرام جدير
"نغض السن: تحريكها، قال الله تعالى (فسينغضون إليك رؤوسهم) أي يحركونها، ويروي "كقيض السن" وقيضها: انشقاقها.

verses.h1: For you—
verses.h2: truly, what a watcher’s gaze you cast, with Waqf and Qabr between you and her!

verses.h1: The dwellings of her who said—
verses.h2: on the morning I met her, “You have fallen in love, Abū Dhīb, though you are old.

verses.h1: Have you changed since I left, or has some calamity befallen you
verses.h2: from time, or have bitter trials passed over you?”

verses.h1: Parting is like a loosening tooth; so have patience, for
verses.h2: every people has its stumbling and its recovery.

verses.h1: Now I walk among dwellings that seem
verses.h2: a defective substitute for the dwellings of al-Kāhiliyya.

verses.h1: One says “a defective substitute” when it is unsound. He means: “This dwelling is a defective substitute for those.”
I call out whenever [he] mounts a lookout in the course of time—
verses.h2: to what listener, if anyone with sight would answer?

notes.note: The opening syntax and hemistich division appear disrupted: h1 contains only فإنك. Waqf and Qabr are treated as place names because the source marks them as such, but their identification and vocalization are uncertain. The referent of the feminine pronoun in دونها is also unclear.
The source has أبا ذيب, rendered Abū Dhīb, rather than the poet’s usual name Abū Dhuʾayb (أبو ذؤيب). This may reflect textual corruption.
مرور is obscure here. “Bitter trials” is a tentative interpretation; the word may be corrupt.

The unusual phrase خلاف ديار الكاهلية عور is interpreted with the help of the prose gloss supplied as line 6. Al-Kāhiliyya apparently designates a woman associated with Kāhil, but her identity is uncertain.
This source item is an explanatory prose gloss, not a verse. It has been translated in its supplied position. هذا الدار also shows irregular gender agreement.

The syntax is uncertain, particularly the subject of أوفى and the construction من الدهر مربئا. The translation provisionally takes مربئا as a lookout or elevated vantage point. The relationship between سميع (“one who hears”) and بصير (“one who sees”) in the second hemistich is also unclear.

interludes: I said to her: “The loss of loved ones! I am newly stricken by the calamities of the noble, and worthy of them.”

[Naghḍ al-sinn]: the movement of a tooth. God Most High said, “They will wag their heads at you,” meaning that they will move them. Another reading is “like the splitting of a tooth” [ka-qayd al-sinn]; its qayd is its splitting.

verses.h1: تفانوا، ولم يبقوا، وكل قبيلة
verses.h2: سريع إلى ورد الفناء كرامها

verses.h1: وكيف وقد صاروا عظاما وأقبرا
verses.h2: يصيح صداها بالعشي وهامها؟

verses.h1: They have all perished; none remain. And every tribe—
verses.h2: its noble men hasten to the watering-place of death.

verses.h1: And how, when they have become bones and graves,
verses.h2: whose owls and death-birds cry out at dusk?

notes.note: “And how” leaves the question incomplete: what is being questioned is not explicit in this excerpt.

Ṣadā and hām, rendered “owls” and “death-birds,” can denote owl-like birds associated with the dead, including birds imagined to emerge from their heads. Ṣadā can also mean “echo”; the precise distinction between the two terms here is uncertain.

verses.h1: وكم من صاحب قد ناء عني
verses.h2: رميت بفقده وهو الحبيب

verses.h1: فلم أبد الذي تخفى ضلوعي
verses.h2: عليه وإنني لأنا الكئيب

verses.h1: مخافة أن يراني مستكينا
verses.h2: عدو، أو يساء به قريب

verses.h1: فيشمت كاشح، ويظن أني
verses.h2: جزوع عند نائبة تنوب

verses.h1: فبعدك مدت الأعداء طرفا
verses.h2: إلى ورابني دهر مريب

verses.h1: وأنكرت الزمان، وكل أهلي
verses.h2: وهرتني لغيبتك الكليب

verses.h1: وكنت تقطع الأبصار دوني
verses.h2: وإن وغرت من الغيظ القلوب

verses.h1: ويمنعني من الأعداء أني
verses.h2: وإن رغموا لمخشى مهيب

verses.h1: فلم أر مثل يومك كان يوما
verses.h2: بدت فيه النجوم، فما تغيب

verses.h1: وليل ما أنام به، طويل
verses.h2: كأني للنجوم به رقيب

verses.h1: وما يك جائيا لا بد منه
verses.h2: إليك فسوف تجلبه الجلوب

verses.h1: How many a companion has gone far from me—
verses.h2: I was stricken by his loss, and he was dear to me.

verses.h1: Yet I did not reveal what my ribs concealed,
verses.h2: though I was indeed grief-stricken,

verses.h1: for fear that I might be seen humbled
verses.h2: by an enemy, or that a kinsman might be distressed,

verses.h1: and a spiteful foe might gloat and think me
verses.h2: unable to bear a calamity when it strikes.

verses.h1: After you were gone, enemies turned their gaze
verses.h2: toward me, and treacherous times filled me with misgiving.

verses.h1: The times and all my kin seemed strangers to me,
verses.h2: and in your absence the dogs growled at me.

verses.h1: You used to keep their eyes from reaching me,
verses.h2: even when their hearts seethed with rage.

verses.h1: What protects me from enemies is that I,
verses.h2: despite their spite, am feared and held in awe.

verses.h1: I have never seen a day like the day of your loss:
verses.h2: the stars appeared in it and never set.

verses.h1: And many a long night I pass without sleep,
verses.h2: as though I were keeping watch over the stars.

verses.h1: Whatever must come, with no escaping it,
verses.h2: the bringer will in time bring to you.

notes.note: The printed إلى appears to stand for إليّ, ‘toward me,’ which the syntax requires.
The precise significance of stars appearing during the day and never setting is unclear; the image is translated literally. ‘Your day’ is understood as the day of the addressee’s loss.
الجلوب means ‘the bringer’ or ‘that which brings,’ but its referent is unclear here, possibly fate or death.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAyṣ ibn Ḥizām said:

poems.poet: كثير بن عبد الله ، ابن الغريرة
poems.intro: وقال كتير بن عبد الله، وهو ابن الغريرة، وهي أمه:

poet.expected: كثير بن عبد الله ، ابن الغريرة

verses.h1: ألا من لشوق آخر الليل شائق
verses.h2: وقلب كمكسور الجناحين خافق

verses.h1: وصب حزين كلما جن ليله
verses.h2: تذكر ذكرى من حبيب مفارق

verses.h1: فلا تعذليني يا ابنة الخير إنما
verses.h2: تخرمت الأيام مني أصادقي

verses.h1: فأصبحت رهنا بعدهم في ديارهم
verses.h2: كمستوثق منه، وليس بآبق

verses.h1: Ah, who can ease a longing that stirs late at night,
verses.h2: and a heart fluttering like a bird with broken wings,

verses.h1: and a sorrowful lover who, whenever night closes in,
verses.h2: recalls a beloved from whom he is parted?

verses.h1: Do not reproach me, noble lady: it is only that
verses.h2: the days have carried off my friends.

verses.h1: I have become a captive in their dwellings after they are gone,
verses.h2: like one bound fast, though he is no runaway.

prose_translation.intro: Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah, known as Ibn al-Gharīra—Al-Gharīra being his mother—said:

verses.h1: فإن تكن الحوادث غيرتني
verses.h2: فلم أر هالكا كابني زياد

verses.h1: هما رمحان خطيان كانا
verses.h2: من السمر المثقفة الجلاد

verses.h1: تهال الأرض أن يطآ عليها
verses.h2: بمثلهما تسالم أو تعادي

verses.h1: If calamities have changed me,
verses.h2: I have seen none among the fallen like Ziyād’s two sons.

verses.h1: They were two spears of al-Khaṭṭ,
verses.h2: of the dark, straightened, sturdy kind.

verses.h1: The earth dreads their treading upon it;
verses.h2: with men like them you make peace or wage war.

notes.note: The identity of Ziyād’s two sons is uncertain.
تسالم أو تعادي can address an unspecified ‘you’ or have ‘the earth’ as its grammatical subject; the translation takes it as the former.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf al-Jushamī said:

poems.poet_from_text: تميم بن أبي بن مقبل العجلاني
poems.intro: وقال تميم بن أبي بن مقبل العجلاني:

poet.from_text: تميم بن أبي بن مقبل العجلاني

verses.h1: تذكرت إخواني الذين عهدتهم
verses.h2: كأن لم يكن شكلي لهم مرة شكلا

verses.h1: هجرتهم من غير بغض ولا قلى
verses.h2: ولكن مر الدهر كان لهم شغلا

verses.h1: I remembered my companions whom I once knew,
verses.h2: as though I had never once been one of their kind.

verses.h1: I parted from them without hatred or aversion,
verses.h2: but the passage of time had kept them occupied.

notes.note: The unvocalized مر الدهر may mean either ‘the passage of time’ or ‘the bitterness of fate.’ The former reading is adopted here; the precise implication of time keeping them occupied is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Tamīm ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil al-ʿAjlānī said:

poems.poet_from_text: محمد بن خالد بن الوليد بن عقبة
poems.intro: وقال محمد بن خالد بن الوليد بن عقبة:

poet.from_text: محمد بن خالد بن الوليد بن عقبة

verses.h1: هل في الخلود إلى القيامة مطمع
verses.h2: أم للمنون عن ابن آدم مدفع؟

verses.h1: هيهات ما للنفس من متأخر
verses.h2: عن وقتها، لو أن علمك ينفع

verses.h1: أين الملوك، وعيشهم فيما مضى
verses.h2: وزمانهم فيهم وما قد جمعوا؟

verses.h1: ذهبوا، ونحن على طريقة من مضى
verses.h2: منهم، فمفجوع به، ومفجع

verses.h1: عثر الزمان بنا، فأوهى عظمنا
verses.h2: إن الزمان بما كرهت لمولع

verses.h1: Is there any hope of living on until the Resurrection,
verses.h2: or any way to ward off death from Adam’s son?

verses.h1: Far from it! No soul can linger
verses.h2: beyond its appointed hour—if only your knowledge could help.

verses.h1: Where are the kings, and the life they once lived,
verses.h2: and the age that was theirs, and all they amassed?

verses.h1: They have gone, and we follow the way of those who died
verses.h2: among them: one mourned, another stricken with grief.

verses.h1: Time has brought us down and weakened our bones;
verses.h2: time is indeed bent on what you hate.

notes.note: The phrase وزمانهم فيهم, literally something like “and their time among them,” is awkward and may be corrupt. “The age that was theirs” is a tentative rendering.
The unvocalized مفجع is read here as مُفَجَّع, “stricken with grief,” in contrast to مفجوع به, the person whose loss is mourned.

prose_translation.intro: And Muḥammad ibn Khālid ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba said:

verses.h1: تعز فإن الصبر بالحر أجمل
verses.h2: وليس على ريب الزمان معول

verses.h1: فلو كان يغني أن يرى المرء جازعا
verses.h2: لحادثة أو كان يغني التذلل

verses.h1: لكان التعزي عند كل مصيبة
verses.h2: ونائبة بالحر أولى وأجمل

verses.h1: فكيف، وكل ليس يعدو حمامه
verses.h2: وما لامرئ عما قضى الله مزحل

verses.h1: فإن تكن الأيام فينا تبدلت
verses.h2: ببؤسي ونعمي والحوادث تفعل

verses.h1: فما لينت منا قناة صليبة
verses.h2: ولا ذللتنا للتي ليس تجمل

verses.h1: ولكن رحلناها نفوسا أبية
verses.h2: تحمل ما لا تستطيع فتحمل

verses.h1: Take comfort, for patience better befits a noble man;
verses.h2: lamenting the blows of time is of no avail.

verses.h1: For even if it helped a man to be seen distraught
verses.h2: at a calamity, or if abasing himself could help,

verses.h1: composing himself at every affliction
verses.h2: and misfortune would still be fitter and finer for a noble man.

verses.h1: How much more so, when no one escapes his appointed death,
verses.h2: and no man can evade what God has decreed.

verses.h1: Though the days have brought us changes,
verses.h2: with hardship and ease—as events will do—

verses.h1: they have not bent our sturdy spear-shaft,
verses.h2: nor humbled us to anything unbecoming.

verses.h1: Rather, we have journeyed through them with unyielding souls,
verses.h2: laden with what they cannot bear, yet bearing it.

notes.note: معول can denote lamentation or something to rely upon. The translation takes it here as lamentation that offers no relief.

رحلناها is unclear in this construction. ‘Journeyed through them’ tentatively takes the pronoun as referring to the days. The text may be corrupt, possibly for حملناها, suggesting that proud souls were made to bear these hardships.
The unvocalized تحمل ... فتحمل is read here as تُحَمَّل ... فتَحْمِل: ‘are laden ... yet bear.’ Other vocalizations are possible.

poems.intro: وقال أبو الحسن علي بن محمد بن جعفر بن محمد بن زيد بن علي بن الحسين بن علي بن أبي طالب - رضي الله عنهم -:

verses.h1: هبني بقيت على الأيام والأبد
verses.h2: ونلت ما شئت من مال ومن ولد

verses.h1: من لي برؤية من قد كنت آلفهم
verses.h2: وبالزمان الذي ولى فلم يعد؟

verses.h1: لا فارق الحزن قلبي بعدهم أبدا
verses.h2: حتى يفرق بين الروح والجسد

verses.h1: Suppose I lived on through the days, forever,
verses.h2: and gained all I wished for in wealth and children—

verses.h1: Who could restore to me the sight of those whose company I once enjoyed,
verses.h2: and the time that passed and never returned?

verses.h1: May sorrow never leave my heart after their departure,
verses.h2: until soul and body are parted.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad ibn Zayd ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with them—said:

verses.h1: صبرت ابتغاء الأجر بعد خويلد
verses.h2: وبعد رزام والنفوس توالف

verses.h1: وبعد الفتى فجر وليث تتابعا
verses.h2: فلم يبقى بعد الإلف إلا المعارف

verses.h1: فقد جعلت نفسي تلذ إتباعهم
verses.h2: كما لذ برد الماء حران صائف

verses.h1: I bore patiently, seeking reward, the loss of Khuwaylid
verses.h2: and of Rizam—for souls grow attached to one another.

verses.h1: And of the young man Fajr and Layth, who followed one another in death;
verses.h2: after the beloved companion, only acquaintances remained.

verses.h1: My soul has come to relish following them,
verses.h2: as a parched man in summer relishes cool water.

notes.note: Khuwaylid and Rizam have not been identified; the vocalization of رزام as Rizam is uncertain.
فجر is taken as the personal name Fajr, but this reading is uncertain. Neither Fajr nor Layth has been identified.
فلم يبقى appears to contain a textual or grammatical error for فلم يبقَ, ‘so none remained.’ الإلف can mean a beloved companion or companionship; the former is adopted here.

poems.intro: غاب شبيب بن البرصاء عن أهله غيبة، ثم عاد بعد مدة، وقد مات جماعة من أهله، وبنى عمه، فقال:

verses.h1: تخرم الدهر إخواني وغادرني
verses.h2: كما يغادر ثور الطارد الفرد

verses.h1: إني لباق قليلا ثم لاحقهم
verses.h2: ووارد منهل الحوض الذي وردوا

verses.h1: Time has taken my brothers one by one and left me
verses.h2: as a hunter leaves a solitary wild bull.

verses.h1: I shall remain but a little while, then join them,
verses.h2: and come to the watering pool to which they came.

notes.note: The unvocalized phrase «ثور الطارد الفرد» is syntactically ambiguous. I read «الطارد» as the subject, ‘the hunter,’ and «ثور … الفرد» as the object, ‘a solitary wild bull.’
