prose_translation.intro: Shabīb ibn al-Barṣāʾ was away from his family for a time. When he returned after a while, a number of his family members and paternal cousins had died, so he said:

verses.h1: ينام المسعدون ومن يلوم
verses.h2: وتوقظني وأوقظها الهموم

verses.h1: صحيح بالنهار لمن يراني
verses.h2: وليلى لا ينام ولا ينيم

verses.h1: كأن الليل محبوس دجاه
verses.h2: وأوله وآخره مقيم

verses.h1: لمهلك فتية تركوا أباهم
verses.h2: وأصغر ما به منهم عظيم

verses.h1: يذكرنيهم ما كنت فيه
verses.h2: فسيان المساءة والنعيم

verses.h1: وبالخدين من دمعي ندوب
verses.h2: وبالأحشاء من وجدي كلوم

verses.h1: فإن يهلك بني فليس شيء
verses.h2: من الدنيا على أحد مقيم

verses.h1: Those who share my grief sleep, as do those who blame me;
verses.h2: cares keep me awake, and I keep them awake.

verses.h1: By day I seem healthy to anyone who sees me,
verses.h2: but my night neither sleeps nor lets me sleep.

verses.h1: As though night’s darkness were held captive,
verses.h2: its beginning and its end standing still.

verses.h1: Because of the death of young men who left their father—
verses.h2: the least of what he suffers for them is immense.

verses.h1: Whatever my condition, it reminds me of them;
verses.h2: so misery and happiness are alike.

verses.h1: On my cheeks are scars from my tears,
verses.h2: and within me are wounds from my grief.

verses.h1: If my sons have perished, nothing
verses.h2: in this world remains with anyone.

notes.note: The unvocalized المسعدون could mean either those who assist or console the mourner, or those blessed with happiness. The translation adopts the former reading.
وليلى is understood as وليلي, ‘and my night,’ with final ي written as ى.
ما كنت فيه may refer to the speaker’s former circumstances (‘what I once enjoyed’) rather than, as translated here, whatever condition he finds himself in.

verses.h1: من رأى العير لابن أروى على ظه
verses.h2: ر المروري حداتهن عجال

verses.h1: مصعدات، والبيت بيت أبي وه
verses.h2: ب خلاء تهب فيه الشمال

verses.h1: يعرف الجاهل المضلل أن الد
verses.h2: هر فيه النكراء والزلزال

verses.h1: ليت شعري! كذاكم العهد أم كا
verses.h2: نوا أناسا كمن يزول فزالوا

verses.h1: بعد ما تعلمين يا أم زيد
verses.h2: كان فيهم عز لنا وجمال

verses.h1: من وجوه بودنا مشرقات
verses.h2: ونوال إذا أريد النوال

verses.h1: Who has seen Ibn Arwā’s caravan on the expanse
verses.h2: of the desert, its camel-drivers hurrying?

verses.h1: Heading upland, while the house—the house of Abū Wahb—
verses.h2: stands empty, the north wind blowing through it.

verses.h1: Even the ignorant and misguided know that time
verses.h2: holds calamity and upheaval.

verses.h1: Would that I knew! Was this what we once knew, or were they
verses.h2: people like others who pass away, and so passed away?

verses.h1: After all that you know, O Umm Zayd—
verses.h2: among them we once had honor and splendor:

verses.h1: Faces radiant with affection for us,
verses.h2: and bounty whenever bounty was sought.

notes.note: I take المروري as a spelling of المَرَوْرَى, meaning open deserts or wilderness, rather than a place name. Ibn Arwā may be ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, whose mother was Arwā, but the identification is uncertain.
Abū Wahb may be al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba, an associate of the poet, but this identification is not certain.
كذاكم العهد is ambiguous. I understand العهد as the formerly familiar state of things; it could instead mean a pledge or bond of loyalty.
Umm Zayd is unidentified. The syntax of بعد ما تعلمين is compressed; I take it as referring back to their passing after the former circumstances known to her.

opening.actual: ما إن أبو زيد برث سلاحه

verses.h1: ما إن أبو زيد برث سلاحه
verses.h2: جبان وما إن وجهه بدميم

verses.h1: وكنت إذا الأيام أحدثن نكبة
verses.h2: أقول: شوى، ما لم يصبن صميمي

verses.h1: أصبن أبا زيد، ولا حي مثله
verses.h2: وكان أبو زيد أخي وحميمي

verses.h1: فأصبحن لا أدعو من الناس واحدا
verses.h2: سوى ولدة في الدار غير حكيم

verses.h1: كأن عجوزي لم تلد غير واحد
verses.h2: وماتت بذات الشرى غير عقيم

interludes.text: يقال: رمى فأصمي، إذا أصاب مقتلا، ورمى فأشوى، إذا لم يصب مقتلا.

verses.h1: Abū Zayd was no poorly armed
verses.h2: coward, nor was his face ugly.

verses.h1: Whenever the days brought some calamity,
verses.h2: I would say, “A slight wound, so long as they do not strike my heart.”

verses.h1: They struck Abū Zayd, and no living man is his equal;
verses.h2: Abū Zayd was my brother and my dearest friend.

verses.h1: Now I call on no one among men
verses.h2: save children in the house, lacking sound judgment.

verses.h1: As though my old mother had borne only one son,
verses.h2: though she died at Dhāt al-Sharā no barren woman.

notes.note: I take ولدة to mean “children,” but its construction with the singular غير حكيم (“not wise”) is uncertain.
Dhāt al-Sharā (ذات الشرى) is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain.

interludes: One says ramā fa-aṣmā, “he shot and struck a vital spot,” when he hits a vital spot; and ramā fa-ashwā, “he shot but struck no vital spot,” when he does not hit a vital spot.
(He means: death has spared only the children.)

poems.intro: (الشرى: الحنظل، [وذات الشرى] : موضع) . يقول: كانت كثيرة الولد، فماتوا، ويقيت أنا وحدي؛ فكأنها لم تلد غيري. وقال وضاح اليمن، واسمه عبد الرحمن بن إسماعيل بن عبد كلال:

verses.h1: كأني إذ أكفكف دمع عيني
verses.h2: وأنهاها، أقول لها: هريقي

verses.h1: سأصبر للقضاء، فكل حي
verses.h2: سيلقى سكرة الموت المذوق

verses.h1: فما الدنيا بقائمة وفيها
verses.h2: من الأحياء من عين رموق

verses.h1: فأغناهم كأعدمهم إذا ما
verses.h2: تقضت مدة العيش الرقيق

verses.h1: كذلك يبعثون وهم فرادى
verses.h2: ليوم فيه توفية الحقوق

verses.h1: It is as though, when I wipe the tears from my eye
verses.h2: and bid it stop, I am telling it, “Pour forth!”

verses.h1: I shall bear fate patiently, for every living being
verses.h2: will meet the stupor of death, which must be tasted.

verses.h1: This world will not endure, nor will there remain in it
verses.h2: a single watchful eye among the living.

verses.h1: Their richest is like their poorest once
verses.h2: the span of life’s comforts has run its course.

verses.h1: Thus they will be raised, each alone,
verses.h2: for a day when every due is paid in full.

notes.note: The scope of the negation in «فما الدنيا بقائمة وفيها…» is ambiguous. The translation takes it to deny permanence both to the world and to any living inhabitant.
«العيش الرقيق» literally means ‘tender/delicate living’; it is rendered here as ‘life’s comforts,’ though the intended nuance is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: (Al-sharā: colocynth; Dhāt al-Sharā: a place.) He says: “She had many children, but they died, and I alone remained; it is as though she had borne no one but me.” And Waḍḍāḥ al-Yaman, whose name was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Kulāl, said:

verses.h1: أثر الدهر في رجالي فقلوا
verses.h2: بعد جمع، فراح عظمي مهيضا

verses.h1: ما تذكرتهم فتملك عيني
verses.h2: فيض دمعي، وحق لي أن تفيضا

verses.h1: Time has taken its toll on my men, and they are few
verses.h2: after being many; my bones are left broken.

verses.h1: Whenever I remember them, my eye cannot restrain
verses.h2: the flood of my tears—and rightly does it overflow.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū Saʿīd, the client of Qāʾid, said:

verses.h1: أولئك قومي بعد عز وثروة
verses.h2: تفانوا، فإلاتذرف العين أكمد

verses.h1: أرى أسرتي في كل يوم وليلة
verses.h2: يروح بهم ريب المنون ويغتدي

verses.h1: كأنهم لا ناس للموت غيرهم
verses.h2: وإن كان فيهم منصف غير معتقد

verses.h1: Those were my people: after power and prosperity,
verses.h2: they perished one and all; if my eyes shed no tears, I waste away with grief.

verses.h1: I see my family, every day and night:
verses.h2: the ravages of death bear them off at evening and at dawn.

verses.h1: It is as though death had no people other than them,
verses.h2: though in dealing with them it is impartial, with no special attachment.

notes.note: The second hemistich is uncertain, especially غير معتقد. I have taken death as the implicit subject of كان and tentatively understood غير معتقد as denying any special attachment or partiality. The wording may be corrupt.

poems.intro: وقال نصيب، يرثي عبد العزيز بن مروان:

verses.h1: عرفت، وجربت الأمور فما أرى
verses.h2: كماض تلاه الغابر المتأخر

verses.h1: ولكن أهل الفضل، من أهل نعمتي
verses.h2: يمرون أرسالا أمامي وأغبر

verses.h1: فإن أبكهم أعذر، وإن أغلب الأسى
verses.h2: بصبر فمثلي عندما اشتد يصبر

verses.h1: I have known and tested life’s affairs, and I do not see
verses.h2: in the one who comes after the equal of the departed whom he follows.

verses.h1: Yet the men of worth, those who have shown me favor,
verses.h2: pass on before me, company after company, while I remain.

verses.h1: If I weep for them, I am excused; and if I overcome sorrow
verses.h2: with patience, one such as I is patient when hardship grows.

notes.note: The syntax is ambiguous without case endings. I take الغابر المتأخر (‘the one who remains behind’) as the delayed object of أرى, compared unfavorably with his departed predecessor; تلاه then means ‘whom he follows.’

prose_translation.intro: And Nuṣayb said, elegizing ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān:

poems.intro: دخل نصيب على عبد الملك بن مروان، فاستنشده ما قال في أخيه عبد العزيز، فلما أنشده هذه الأبيات، قال: أنا كنت أولى منك بهذا القول. وقال عصيمة التيمي -[من] تيم الله بن ثعلبة -:

verses.h1: ولو أن قومي مثل قوم عباعب
verses.h2: وإخوتهم ما استيق ظلما ركائبي

verses.h1: ولكن أصابتهم خطوب، وأخطأت
verses.h2: رجالا أروني بالنهار كواكبي

verses.h1: Had my people been like the people of ʿAbāʿib
verses.h2: and their brothers, my riding camels would not have been driven off unjustly.

verses.h1: But calamities struck them, while sparing
verses.h2: men who made me see stars in broad daylight.

notes.note: ʿAbāʿib (عباعب) is unidentified; the vocalization of the name is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Nuṣayb came before ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, who asked him to recite what he had composed about his brother ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. When he recited these verses, ʿAbd al-Malik said, “I had more right than you to say this.” And ʿUṣayma al-Taymī—[of] Taym Allah ibn Thaʿlaba—said:

poems.intro: وقال أبو عبد الله القزاز، وهو محمد بن جعفر النحوي من أبيات:

verses.h1: واحسرتا، مات إخواني وأقراني
verses.h2: وشتت الدهر خلاني وأعواني

verses.h1: وغيرت غير الأيام خالصتي
verses.h2: والمصطفى الحر من أهلي وجيراني

verses.h1: وصار من كنت في السراء أذكره
verses.h2: بل لست أنساه في الضراء ينساني

verses.h1: Alas for me! My brothers and peers have died,
verses.h2: and time has scattered my friends and helpers.

verses.h1: The reversals of fortune have changed my closest friends,
verses.h2: and the choicest, noblest among my kin and neighbors.

verses.h1: Now the man I used to remember in prosperity
verses.h2: —indeed, whom I never forget—forgets me in adversity.

notes.note: The phrase في الضراء (‘in adversity’) could alternatively qualify ‘I never forget him,’ giving: ‘—indeed, whom I never forget in adversity—now forgets me.’

prose_translation.intro: Abū ʿAbd Allah al-Qazzāz, who is Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar the grammarian, said in some verses:

poems.poet_from_text: الفقيه أبو طاهر إبراهيم بن خفاجة المغربي
poems.intro: وقال الفقيه أبو طاهر إبراهيم بن خفاجة المغربي:

poet.from_text: الفقيه أبو طاهر إبراهيم بن خفاجة المغربي

verses.h1: أإخواني، ولا إخوان صدق
verses.h2: أصافي بعدكم إلا الصفاح

verses.h1: لحسن الصبر دونكم حران
verses.h2: وللعبرات بعدكم جماح

verses.h1: فديتكم بنفسي من كرام
verses.h2: يهز بهم معاطفه السماح

verses.h1: أرى بهم النجوم ولا ظلام
verses.h2: وأوضاح النهار ولا صباح

verses.h1: لهم همم كما شمخت جبال
verses.h2: وأخلاق كما دمثت بطاح

verses.h1: O my brothers! There are no true brothers
verses.h2: I can befriend after you, save the stone slabs.

verses.h1: Goodly patience balks in your absence,
verses.h2: and tears run wild after you.

verses.h1: I would ransom you with my life, noble men
verses.h2: who make generosity sway its shoulders with pride.

verses.h1: In them I see the stars, though there is no darkness,
verses.h2: and the brightness of day, though it is not morning.

verses.h1: Their aspirations tower as mountains tower,
verses.h2: and their characters are gentle as the plains are soft.

notes.note: الصفاح can mean broad, flat stones or broad sword blades. I have taken it as stone slabs, perhaps those of graves, but the intended sense is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And the jurist Abū Ṭāhir Ibrāhīm ibn Khafāja al-Maghribī said:

poems.intro: قيل إن الرشيد أحضر بعض جواري البرامكة - بعد نكبتهم - وقال لها: غنى، فغنت:

verses.h1: أبكى فراقهم عيني وأرقها
verses.h2: إن التفرق للأحباب بكاء

verses.h1: ما زال يعدو عليهم ريب دهرهم
verses.h2: حتى تفانوا، وريب الدهر عداء

verses.h1: فظلت أبكيهم طورا وأندبهم
verses.h2: حتى أنثنيت، وما في مقلتي ماء

verses.h1: Parting from them made my eye weep and kept it sleepless;
verses.h2: indeed, separation from loved ones brings tears.

verses.h1: Time’s misfortunes kept assailing them
verses.h2: until they all perished—and time’s misfortunes are relentless assailants.

verses.h1: So I went on weeping for them a while, and lamenting them,
verses.h2: until I turned away, with no tears left in my eye.

prose_translation.intro: It is said that al-Rashīd summoned one of the slave girls of the Barmakids—after their downfall—and said to her, “Sing.” So she sang:

verses.h1: مضوا بددا عني وحلق بعدهم
verses.h2: بما سرني في العيش قادمتا نسر

verses.h1: فما أغمض الأجفان إلا على قذى
verses.h2: ولا أقلب الجنبين إلا على جمر

verses.h1: وأصبحت أعفو عن ذنوب كثيرة
verses.h2: وأحمل زلات الصديق على الدهر

verses.h1: واعذر قوما لو أحاكم بعضهم
verses.h2: إلى نفسه أغضى حياء من العذر

verses.h1: They scattered far from me, and after them flew off
verses.h2: a vulture’s two pinions, bearing all that gladdened me in life.

verses.h1: I never close my eyelids except on grit,
verses.h2: nor turn from side to side except on embers.

verses.h1: I have come to pardon many offenses
verses.h2: and lay a friend’s lapses at time’s door.

verses.h1: I excuse people who, were I to summon any of them
verses.h2: before his own conscience, would lower his eyes, too ashamed to offer an excuse.

notes.note: The phrase «حياء من العذر» is ambiguous: it may mean being too ashamed to offer an excuse, as translated, or feeling ashamed at the excuse or pardon offered on his behalf.

verses.h1: نقبوا في البلاد من حذر المو
verses.h2: ت، وجالوا في الأرض كل مجال

verses.h1: ثم صاروا إلى التي خلقوا من
verses.h2: ها، وكل مصيره لزوال

verses.h1: They scoured the lands in fear of death,
verses.h2: and roamed the earth in every direction.

verses.h1: Then they returned to the earth from which they were created,
verses.h2: and everyone is destined to pass away.

verses.h1: ثوى بين الحريش وتل محرى
verses.h2: فوارس من نمارة غير ميل

verses.h1: فلا فرحين إن نعماء واتت
verses.h2: ولا جزعين للخطب الجليل

verses.h1: Between al-Ḥarīsh and Tall Maḥrā lie buried
verses.h2: horsemen of Nimārah, never wavering.

verses.h1: They did not exult when good fortune came their way,
verses.h2: nor lose heart at grievous calamity.

notes.note: The precise identification and vocalization of al-Ḥarīsh and Tall Maḥrā are uncertain. Nimārah appears to be a tribal name, but its identification here is uncertain.
Mīl (ميل), translated as ‘wavering,’ can describe riders unsteady in the saddle or, by extension, cowardly men.

verses.h1: قد كنت أبكى على من مات من سلفي
verses.h2: وأهل ودي جميع غير أشتات

verses.h1: فالقيوم
verses.h2: إذ فرقت بيني وبينهم نوى بكيت على أهل المودات

verses.h1: وما حياة امرئ أضحت مدامعه
verses.h2: مقسومة بين أحياء وأموات؟

verses.h1: I used to weep for those of my forebears who had died,
verses.h2: while my loved ones were all together, not scattered.

verses.h1: But today,
verses.h2: since distance has parted me from them, I weep for those I love.

verses.h1: What sort of life has a man whose tears are now
verses.h2: divided between the living and the dead?

notes.note: فالقيوم appears to be a misprint for فاليوم (‘but today’), which is the reading translated here. The hemistich division also appears misplaced; the translation preserves the supplied division.

verses.h1: نفسي على حسراتها موقوفة
verses.h2: فوددت لو خلصت من الحسرات

verses.h1: لو في يدي حساب أيامي إذن
verses.h2: خطرفتهن تعجلا لوفاتي

verses.h1: لا خير بعدك في الحياة وإنما
verses.h2: أبكي مخافة أن تطول حياتي

verses.h1: My soul is held captive to its sorrows;
verses.h2: I wish I could be freed from sorrow.

verses.h1: If the reckoning of my days were in my hands,
verses.h2: I would hurry them by, hastening my death.

verses.h1: There is no good in life after you; I only
verses.h2: weep for fear that my life will be long.

notes.note: خطرفتهن is an unusual verb with ‘days’ as its object. I take it as ‘I would hurry them by,’ from a root associated with rapid movement, but the precise sense is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And ʿInān, the slave girl of al-Naṭṭāf, said:

verses.h1: تخون الدهر منا إذ تخونهم
verses.h2: ما لا يعود علينا آخر الأبد

verses.h1: يا ليت شعري إذا ما برمك درجت
verses.h2: وأصبح الفرح المسرور ذا كمد

verses.h1: هل يستقل كيحيى بعده بشر
verses.h2: أم هل يجود كجود الفضل من أحد؟

verses.h1: Time took from us, when it took them away,
verses.h2: what will never return to us for all eternity.

verses.h1: Would that I knew, now that Barmak’s house has passed away
verses.h2: and the joyous, happy man has become grief-stricken:

verses.h1: Can any man after Yaḥyā shoulder responsibilities as he did,
verses.h2: or can anyone give as generously as al-Faḍl?

notes.note: The feminine verb درجت appears to treat برمك as a collective referring to Barmak’s family, the Barmakids; hence “Barmak’s house.”
يستقل has no expressed object. “Shoulder responsibilities” takes it to mean bearing the burdens of leadership, though the precise sense is uncertain.

verses.h1: ذكرت أبا أروى فبت كأنني
verses.h2: برد الأمور الماضيات وكيل

verses.h1: وإن افتقادي واحدا بعد واحد
verses.h2: دليل على أن لا يدوم خليل

verses.h1: لكل اجتماع من خليلين فرقة
verses.h2: وكل الذي دون الفراق قليل

verses.h1: I remembered Abū Arwā and spent the night as though I
verses.h2: were charged with bringing back what has passed.

verses.h1: My losing them, one after another,
verses.h2: is proof that no friend endures.

verses.h1: Every meeting of two friends must end in parting,
verses.h2: and everything short of parting is slight.

interludes: Another reading is: “Abā Awfā.”

verses.h1: كم من أخ لي لا يرى
verses.h2: متصرفا فيمن تراه

verses.h1: أمسى قريب الدار في ال
verses.h2: أجداث قد شحطت نواه

verses.h1: قد كان مغترا بيو
verses.h2: م وفاته حتى أتاه

verses.h1: الناس في غفلاتهم
verses.h2: والموت دائرة رحاه

verses.h1: فالحمد لله الذي يبقى ويهلك من سواه
How many a brother of mine is no longer seen
verses.h2: going about among those you see.

verses.h1: He now dwells close by, in
verses.h2: the graves, yet he is far removed.

verses.h1: He had thought himself safe from the day
verses.h2: of his death, until it came to him.

verses.h1: People remain in their heedlessness,
verses.h2: while death’s millstone turns.

verses.h1: Praise be to God, who endures while all besides Him perish.

opening.actual: أخلاي من أهل القبور: عليكم الس

verses.h1: أخلاي من أهل القبور: عليكم الس
verses.h2: لام، أما من دعوة تسمعونها؟

verses.h1: ولا من كلام ترجعون جوابه
verses.h2: إلينا، ولا من حاجة تلطبونها

verses.h1: سكنتم ظهور الأرض في الدهر برهة
verses.h2: فلم تلبثوا حتى سكنتم بطونها

verses.h1: وقد كان في الدنيا قرون كثيرة
verses.h2: ولكن ريب الدهر أفنى قرونها

verses.h1: My friends among the dwellers in graves: peace be upon you—
verses.h2: is there no call that you can hear?

verses.h1: And no words to which you send an answer
verses.h2: back to us, nor any request you would make?

verses.h1: You dwelt upon the earth’s surface for a while,
verses.h2: then before long you came to dwell within it.

verses.h1: There have been many generations in this world,
verses.h2: but the calamities of time have destroyed its generations.

notes.note: تلطبونها appears to be a typographical error for تطلبونها, “you seek” or “you ask for,” which is the reading translated here.

poems.intro: وقال أصرم بن حميد - وقيل: هي لمفضل العمى:

verses.h1: عادات قومي من بني أسد
verses.h2: ري القنا، وخضاب كل حسام

verses.h1: لهفي على قتلى النباج فإنهم
verses.h2: كانوا الذرى ورواسي الأعلام

verses.h1: كانوا على الأعداء جمرا محرقا
verses.h2: ولقومهم حرما من الأحرام

verses.h1: لا تهلكي أسفا، فإني واثق
verses.h2: برماحنا وعواقب الأيام

verses.h1: The ways of my people of Banū Asad
verses.h2: are to slake the spears and dye every sword.

verses.h1: Alas for those slain at al-Nibāj! They
verses.h2: were the summits and the firmly rooted mountains.

verses.h1: To their enemies they were burning embers,
verses.h2: but to their people, a sacred refuge.

verses.h1: Do not perish of grief, for I have faith
verses.h2: in our spears and what the days will bring.

notes.note: I could not identify the particular battle or killings at al-Nibāj to which this refers.

prose_translation.intro: Aṣram ibn Ḥumayd said—and it is also said that these verses are by Mufaḍḍal al-ʿAmmī:

poems.intro: وصف أعرابي قومه فقال: كانوا والله ليوث حرب، وغيوث جدب، إن قاتلوا أبلوا، وإن أعطوا أغنوا، ثم عجل لهم الدهر ما أخر لغيرهم. قال أمير المؤمنين عمر بن الخطاب - رضوان الله عليه - لعمرو بن معد يكرب الزبيدي: صف لي قومك، فقال: نعم القوم عند السيف المسلول، والخير المسؤول، والطعام المأكول. وقال آخر:

verses.h1: أبعد بني بكر أؤمل مقبلا
verses.h2: من الدهر أو آسى على فقد مدبر؟

verses.h1: وليس وراء الفوت شيء يرده
verses.h2: عليك إذا ولى سوى الصبر، فاصبر

verses.h1: After the Banū Bakr, shall I hope for anything yet to come
verses.h2: from time, or grieve over the loss of what has passed?

verses.h1: Once something is lost, nothing can bring it back
verses.h2: to you when it is gone; only patience remains—so be patient.

notes.note: The excerpt does not establish which group called Banū Bakr is intended.

prose_translation.intro: A Bedouin described his people, saying: “By God, they were lions in war and rain in drought. When they fought, they acquitted themselves valiantly; when they gave, they enriched. Then time hastened upon them what it deferred for others.” The Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—may God be pleased with him—said to ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Zubaydī: “Describe your people to me.” He replied: “An excellent people when swords are drawn, bounty is sought, and food is eaten.” Another said:

verses.h1: أشكو إلى الله أحداثا من الزمن
verses.h2: برينني مثل بري القدح بالسفن

verses.h1: لم يبق في العيش لي إلا مرارته
verses.h2: إذا تذوقته، والحلو منه فني

verses.h1: يا نفس صبرا، وإلا فاهلكي جزعا
verses.h2: إن الزمان على ما تكرهين بني

verses.h1: I complain to God of the calamities of time:
verses.h2: they have whittled me down as an arrow shaft is shaved with a rasp.

verses.h1: Nothing of life remains for me but its bitterness
verses.h2: when I taste it; its sweetness is gone.

verses.h1: O soul, be patient—or perish of anguish:
verses.h2: for time is built upon what you detest.

verses.h1: أثبت بالحظ لو ناديت مستعما
verses.h2: والحظ عني بالجهال في شغل

verses.h1: تقدمتني رجال كان شوطهم
verses.h2: وراء ظهري لو أمشى على مهل

verses.h1: هذا جزاء امرئ أقرانه درجوا
verses.h2: من قبله فتمنى فسحة الأجل

verses.h1: فإن علاني من دوني فلا عجب
verses.h2: لي أسوة بانحطاط الشمس عن زحل

verses.h1: وقال بيهس
verses.h2: ويلقب نعامة

verses.h1: I called out to fortune—if only I had called to one who listened—
verses.h2: but fortune is too busy with fools to attend to me.

verses.h1: Men have overtaken me whose best pace
verses.h2: would leave them behind me even if I walked at leisure.

verses.h1: This is the reward of a man whose peers passed away
verses.h2: before him, and who then wished for a longer life.

verses.h1: If someone beneath me rises above me, it is no wonder:
verses.h2: I have a precedent in the sun’s being lower than Zuḥal (Saturn).

verses.h1: And Bayhas said—
verses.h2: he was nicknamed Naʿāmah.

notes.note: The first hemistich appears corrupted: أثبت بالحظ is likely أهبت بالحظ, ‘I called out to fortune,’ and مستعما is likely مستمعا, ‘one who listens.’ The translation follows these readings.
This appears to be an editorial attribution introducing another poet, rather than a verse by al-Ṭughrāʾī. It has been translated in the supplied divisions.

prose_translation.intro: And the master Abū Ismāʿīl al-Ṭughrāʾī said:

verses.h1: أرقادا أردت أم تهويما
verses.h2: أم عرتك الهموم، فانف الهموما

verses.h1: لا، بل الحادث الجليل من الخط
verses.h2: ب أتاني، فبت أرعى النجوما

verses.h1: عين فابكي الحماة للمجد، وابكي
verses.h2: من يجير الجاني ويحمي الحريما

verses.h1: Was it sleep you sought, or a light doze?
verses.h2: Or have cares beset you? Then banish your cares.

verses.h1: No—the grievous blow of misfortune
verses.h2: befell me, and I spent the night watching the stars.

verses.h1: O eye, weep for the defenders of glory, and weep
verses.h2: for those who shelter the offender and protect the womenfolk.

notes.note: Ḥarīm, translated as ‘womenfolk,’ can also mean more broadly those things or persons held inviolable and entitled to protection.

verses.h1: أسد الوغى وبدور أن
verses.h2: دية، وفرسان المنابر

verses.h1: خاضوا غدير الموت من
verses.h2: جردا من الأقذاء حاسر

verses.h1: فمضوا وأبقوا آجنا
verses.h2: مرا تقسمه الحناجر

verses.h1: Lions of battle, full moons of
verses.h2: gatherings, knights of pulpits.

verses.h1: They waded into death’s pool—
verses.h2: clear of debris, laid bare.

verses.h1: They passed away, leaving stagnant water,
verses.h2: bitter, shared out among throats.

notes.note: I read من / جردا across the hemistich boundary as منجرداً, ‘stripped, clear,’ describing the pool. The syntax of حاسر (‘bare, uncovered’) is uncertain; if it also describes the pool, حاسراً would normally be expected.

verses.h1: لا يهنأ الدهر الخئ
verses.h2: ون، ولا أساغ، فكم أكل

verses.h1: فتك الزمان بمثله
verses.h2: بطل أتيح له بطل

verses.h1: من للمحامد، لا أقو
verses.h2: ل عسى يكون، ولا لعل!

verses.h1: May treacherous Time find no pleasure in its food,
verses.h2: nor swallow with ease—how much it has devoured!

verses.h1: Time struck down its equal:
verses.h2: a champion matched against a champion.

verses.h1: Who is left for noble deeds? I will not say
verses.h2: “Perhaps someone will come,” or “Maybe!”

notes.note: The spelling الخئ / ون appears to represent الخؤون, “treacherous,” with the word divided between hemistichs. “In its food” is implicit in the wish expressed by لا يهنأ and the following imagery of swallowing and devouring.
I take بمثله to mean that Time slew someone equal to itself, making Time and the deceased the two champions. The compressed wording leaves this comparison somewhat ambiguous.

poems.intro: أنشد ابن دريد عن أبي حاتم:

verses.h1: ألا في سبيل الله ماذا تضمنت
verses.h2: بطون الثرى، واستودع البلد القفر

verses.h1: بدور، إذا الدنيا دجت أشرقت بهم
verses.h2: وإن أجدبت يوما فأيديهم القطر

verses.h1: فيا شامتا بالموت، لا تشمتن بهم
verses.h2: حياتهم فخر، وموتهم ذكر

verses.h1: حياتهم كانت لأعدائهم عمى
verses.h2: وموتهم للفاخرين بهم فخر

verses.h1: Ah, for God’s sake, what lies enfolded
verses.h2: in the depths of the earth, entrusted to the barren land!

verses.h1: Full moons—when the world grew dark, it shone through them;
verses.h2: and if it grew barren one day, their hands were rain.

verses.h1: You who gloat over death, do not gloat over them:
verses.h2: their life is glory, and their death remembrance.

verses.h1: Their life brought blindness to their enemies;
verses.h2: their death brings pride to those who boast of them.

prose_translation.intro: Ibn Durayd recited, on the authority of Abū Ḥātim:

poems.poet: منقذ بن عبد عبد الرحمن الهلالي
poems.intro: وقال منقذ بن عبد الرحمن الهلالي:

poet.expected: منقذ بن عبد عبد الرحمن الهلالي

verses.h1: الدهر لاءم بين ألفتنا
verses.h2: زمنا، وفرق بيننا الدهر

verses.h1: وكذاك يفعل في تصرفه والدهر ليس يناله وتر
كنت الضنين بمن فجعت به
verses.h2: وسلوت حين تفاقم الأمر

verses.h1: ولخير حظك في الرزية أن
verses.h2: يلقاك عند نزولها الصبر

verses.h1: Time bound us together in affection
verses.h2: for a while, then Time parted us.

verses.h1: Such is its way in its changing turns, and no vengeance can touch Time.
I had clung dearly to the one whose loss afflicted me,
verses.h2: yet I found solace when the calamity grew overwhelming.

verses.h1: Surely your best fortune in calamity is that
verses.h2: patience should meet you when it strikes.

prose_translation.intro: And Munqidh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Hilālī said:

verses.h1: أبعد أبي حصن حصين، ومالك وعبدة، أبكى الهالكين وأجزع
أولئك إخوان الصفاء رزئتهم
verses.h2: وما الكف إلا إصبع ثم إصبع

verses.h1: After Abū Ḥiṣn, Ḥuṣayn, and Mālik and ʿAbda, shall I weep for the dead and grieve?
Those were my true brothers, of whom I was bereft;
verses.h2: a hand is but one finger, then another.

notes.note: I take Ḥuṣayn as an appositive identifying Abū Ḥiṣn. The individuals mentioned are not securely identified, and the unvocalized name عبدة is provisionally rendered ʿAbda.
The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field gives السد بن سرك, while the introduction gives السيد بن برك الأسدي. At least one form appears corrupted.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sayyid ibn Bark al-Asadī said:

poems.intro: كان الشمردل بن شريك المنقري خرج هو وإخوته: حكم، ووائل، وقدامة في جيش مع وكيع بن أبي سود، فبعث كل واحد منهم في جيش، فأتاه الشمردل، فقال: أيها الأمير، إن رأيت أن تبعثنا معا في وجه واحد؛ فإنا إذا اجتمعنا تعاونا، وتواسينا، وتناصرنا، فأبى عليه، وبعث كل واحد منهم في جيش، فقتل إخوته، وأتاه نعيهم، فرثاهم، قال:

verses.h1: أعاذل كم من روعة قد شهدتها
verses.h2: وغصة حزن من فراق أخ جزل

verses.h1: إذا وقعت بين الحيازيم أسدفت
verses.h2: على الضحى حتى يوسيني أهلي

verses.h1: أقول
verses.h2: إذا آسيت نفسي بإخوة مضوا لا ضعاف في الحياة ولا عزل

verses.h1: أبى الموت إلا أن كل بني أب
verses.h2: سيمسون شتى غير مجتمعي الشمل

verses.h1: سأبكي أخلائي الذي تبرضوا
verses.h2: دموعي، حتى أسرع الحزن في عقلي

verses.h1: كأنك لم نعش يوما، ونحن بغبطة
verses.h2: جميعا، وينزل عند رحلهم رحلي

verses.h1: O you who reproach me, how many terrors I have witnessed,
verses.h2: and choking grief at parting from a noble brother.

verses.h1: When it settles within my ribs, it casts darkness
verses.h2: over the morning light, until my family console me.

verses.h1: I say—
verses.h2: when I console myself for brothers departed, neither weak in life nor unarmed—

verses.h1: Death insists that all sons of one father
verses.h2: shall come to be scattered, no longer united.

verses.h1: I shall weep for my dear companions, who drew forth
verses.h2: my tears drop by drop, until grief swiftly ravaged my mind.

verses.h1: As though we had never lived a day in happiness,
verses.h2: all together, with my camp pitched beside theirs.

notes.note: يوسيني is understood as يواسيني, ‘console me’; the spelling may be defective. The construction أسدفت على الضحى is also unusual; على may represent عليّ, giving ‘it darkened the morning light for me.’
The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: h1 contains only أقول, while h2 contains the rest of the verse. The supplied division has been retained.
الذي does not agree with the plural أخلائي and تبرضوا; الذين appears to be intended.
كأنك لم نعش mixes ‘you’ with ‘we’ and appears corrupt. The translation follows the probable sense, ‘as though we had not lived,’ possibly intended as كأنّا لم نعش.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Shamardal ibn Sharīk al-Minqarī set out with his brothers, Ḥakam, Wāʾil, and Qudāma, in an army under Wakīʿ‘ ibn Abī Sūd. Wakīʿ‘ sent each of them off with a separate force. Al-Shamardal came to him and said, “Commander, if you see fit, send us together in one direction, for when we are together we help one another, share what we have, and come to one another’s aid.” But he refused his request and sent each of them off with a separate force. His brothers were killed, and when news of their deaths reached him, he lamented them, saying:

poems.intro: كان متمم بن نويرة لا ينفك يبكي أخاه مالكا، فخاف قومه عليه أن يذهب بصره من البكاء، فزوجوه أم خالد، لعله يسلو، ويكف عن البكاء، فبينا هو وضاع رأسه على فخذها، إذ بكى، فقالت: لا إله إلا الله، ألا تنسى أخاك في حال؟ فقال:

verses.h1: أقول لها
verses.h2: لما نهتني عن البكا

verses.h1: فإن كان إخواني أصيبوا وأخطأت
verses.h2: بني أمك أسباب الحتوف الرواصد

verses.h1: فكل بني أم سيمسون ليلة
verses.h2: ولم يبق من أعيانهم غير واحد

verses.h1: ذريني، فإن لا أبك لم أنس ذكره
verses.h2: وإن أمرتني بالعزاء عوائدي

verses.h1: ذريني، فكم من صالح قد رزئته
verses.h2: أخ لي كصدر الهندواني ماجد

verses.h1: بودي لو أني تمليت عمره
verses.h2: بمالي من مال طريف وتالد

verses.h1: وبالكف من يمنى يدي حياته
verses.h2: ففارقني منها بناني وساعدي

verses.h1: فعشنا لنا أيد ثلاث وإنما
verses.h2: تصافي الحياة بذلها بالتحامد

verses.h1: I say to her,
verses.h2: when she forbids me to weep:

verses.h1: If my brothers have been struck down, while the snares
verses.h2: of lurking death have missed your mother’s sons,

verses.h1: every band of brothers will come to a night
verses.h2: when only one of their number remains.

verses.h1: Leave me be: even if I do not weep, I will not forget him,
verses.h2: though the women who visit me bid me bear it patiently.

verses.h1: Leave me be: how many a worthy man have I lost—
verses.h2: a noble brother to me, like the blade of an Indian sword.

verses.h1: Would that I could have enjoyed his company for a lifetime,
verses.h2: at the price of all my wealth, newly acquired and inherited,

verses.h1: and bought his life with my right hand,
verses.h2: though my fingers and forearm were severed from me.

verses.h1: Then we would have lived with three hands between us;
verses.h2: true amity in life means giving it with mutual gratitude.

notes.note: This is much shorter than a complete bayt in the stated meter and appears to be a fragment or an irregularly divided line.

The phrase تمليت عمره is unusual: literally it suggests enjoying his lifetime. I take it to mean enjoying his continued companionship, with the following phrases imagining his life redeemed by wealth and a hand.
The grammatical connection of حياته (‘his life’) to the preceding line is unclear. ‘Bought’ is supplied from the apparent sense of exchanging wealth and a hand for his life.
The wording تصافي الحياة بذلها بالتحامد is obscure. The translation tentatively takes it to describe amity expressed through giving one’s life, accompanied by reciprocal gratitude or praise.

prose_translation.intro: Mutammim ibn Nuwayra never ceased weeping for his brother Mālik. His people feared that he would lose his sight from weeping, so they married him to Umm Khālid, hoping that he might find solace and cease weeping. Once, while he was resting his head on her thigh, he began to weep. She said, “There is no god but God! Can you not forget your brother for even a moment?!” He replied:
interludes: “Is it for Mālik that you reproach me, Umm Khālid?!”

verses.h1: لعمري، وما دهري بتأبين هالك
verses.h2: ولا جزعا، والدهر يعثر بالفتى

verses.h1: لئن مالك خلي على مكانه
verses.h2: لفي أسوة إن كان ينفعني الأسى

verses.h1: كهول ومرد من بني عم مالك
verses.h2: وأيسار صدق لو تمليتهم رضى

verses.h1: سقوا بالعقار الصرف حتى تتابعوا
verses.h2: كدأب ثمود إذ رغا بكرهم ضحى

verses.h1: وهون وجي بعد ما كدت أنتحى
verses.h2: على السيف حتى يبلغ الجوف والشحى

verses.h1: رجال أراهم من ملوك وسوقة
verses.h2: خبوا بعد ما نالوا السلامة والغنى

verses.h1: على مثل أصحاب البعوضة فاخمشي
verses.h2: لك الويل حر الوجه، وليبك من بكى

verses.h1: على يسر منهم يسير، وفارس
verses.h2: إذا ارتدف الشيء الحوارك والذرى

verses.h1: إذا القوم قالوا من فتى؟ يوم نجدة
verses.h2: فما كلهم يعنى، ولكنه الفتى

verses.h1: By my life, it is not my way to lament the dead
verses.h2: or give way to grief, though time makes a man stumble.

verses.h1: Though Mālik was left where he lay,
verses.h2: there are examples to console me, if such consolation can help:

verses.h1: men in their prime and beardless youths among Mālik’s kinsmen,
verses.h2: and trusty, generous gamesters—worthy companions, had you long enjoyed their company.

verses.h1: They were given unmixed wine to drink until they fell one after another,
verses.h2: as happened to Thamūd when their camel-calf bellowed at midmorning.

verses.h1: My pain was eased, after I had nearly flung myself
verses.h2: upon the sword until it reached my belly and jaws,

verses.h1: by men I see, kings and commoners,
verses.h2: whose light went out after they had attained safety and wealth.

verses.h1: For men like those of al-Baʿūḍa, scratch
verses.h2: your cheeks—woe to you!—and let whoever would weep, weep.

verses.h1: For a generous gamester among them who played the stakes, and a horseman,
verses.h2: when calamity rode upon withers and humps.

verses.h1: When the people asked, “Who is our champion?” on a day calling for valor,
verses.h2: not all of them were meant: he alone was the champion.

notes.note: خلي على مكانه is ambiguous without vocalization. I have provisionally read it as “was left where he lay”; an active reading, possibly with عليّ rather than على, could mean that Mālik left his place vacant for the speaker. The syntax of لفي أسوة with the following line is also uncertain. الأسى is taken here as أُسَى, “consoling examples,” rather than أَسَى, “grief.”
The construction لو تمليتهم رضى is compressed. تمليتهم may address “you” or refer to “I”; رضى is understood as describing men worthy of approval.
الشحى is an obscure anatomical term here, tentatively rendered “jaws.”
يسر is understood as a participant in the arrow-game associated with distributing slaughtered camel meat. The following يسير is unclear; “who played the stakes” is conjectural.
الشيء literally means “the thing.” Its reference is unclear, and the text may be corrupt. “Calamity” is a tentative interpretation of the image of something mounting the animals’ withers and humps.

poems.poet: عبد الله بن عمرو العبلي، أو غيره

poet.expected: عبد الله بن عمرو العبلي، أو غيره

verses.h1: تقول أمامة لما رأت
verses.h2: نشوزي عن المضجع الأنفس

verses.h1: وقلة نومي على مضجعي
verses.h2: لدى هجعة الأعين النعس:

verses.h1: أبي ما عراك؟ فقلت: الهمو
verses.h2: م عرون أباك، فلا تبأسي

verses.h1: لفقد الأحبة إذ نالها
verses.h2: سهام من الحدث المؤيس

verses.h1: رمتها المنون بلا نصل
verses.h2: ولا طائشات ولا نكس

verses.h1: بأسهمها المتلفات النفو
verses.h2: متى ما تصب مهجة تخلس

verses.h1: فصرعنهم بنواحي البلا
verses.h2: ملقى بأرض ولم يرمس

verses.h1: فذاك الذي غالني فأعلمي
verses.h2: ولا تسأللي بامرئ مؤتس

verses.h1: أولئك قومي أناخت بهم
verses.h2: نوائب من زمن متعس

verses.h1: Umāma says, when she sees
verses.h2: me rising from the finest bed,

verses.h1: and how little I sleep upon my bed
verses.h2: when drowsy eyes are slumbering:

verses.h1: “Father, what has befallen you?” I said, “Sorrows
verses.h2: have beset your father; do not despair—

verses.h1: for the loss of loved ones, struck
verses.h2: by arrows of despair-bringing calamity.

verses.h1: Death shot them with arrows without heads,
verses.h2: neither straying nor defective,

verses.h1: with its soul-destroying arrows:
verses.h2: whenever they strike a life, they snatch it away.

verses.h1: They struck them down in the reaches of desolation,
verses.h2: left lying upon the earth, unburied.

verses.h1: That is what has undone me—know this,
verses.h2: and ask not about a man who takes consolation.

verses.h1: Those were my people; upon them settled
verses.h2: the calamities of an age of misery.”

notes.note: نكس apparently describes defective arrows, possibly broken arrows reversed and refitted with heads. The precise technical sense here is uncertain.
النفو appears to be missing the final س of النفوس, ‘souls.’ Unlike the divided word in line 3, the missing letter does not appear at the beginning of the second hemistich.
البلا may represent البلاء, ‘affliction,’ or البلى, ‘decay’; ‘desolation’ is provisional. The second hemistich has singular ملقى and يرمس after plural ‘them,’ which may indicate textual damage.

تسأللي appears to be a misprint for تسألي. The construction بامرئ مؤتس is unclear: مؤتس probably means someone who takes consolation, but its relationship to the prohibition against asking is uncertain. The second hemistich is translated provisionally.

poems.poet: عبد الله بن عمرو العبلي، أو غيره
poems.intro: قال: فرأيت دموع عبد الله بن حسن بن حسن - رضي الله عنهم - تتحدر على خده. ويروى أن هذا الشعر لأبي سعيد مولى فايد مولى عمر بن عثمان بن عفان - رضوان الله عليه - يرثي قتلى بني أمية الذين قتلهم عبد الله وداود ابنا علي بن عبد الله بن العباس - رضي الله عنهم - وكان الرشيد لما حج أحضرأبا سعيد، وقال له: أنشدني قصيدتك:

poet.expected: عبد الله بن عمرو العبلي، أو غيره

verses.h1: تقول أمامة لما رأت
Umāma said, when she saw—

prose_translation.intro: He said: I saw tears streaming down the cheek of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan—may God be pleased with them. It is also related that these verses are by Abū Saʿīd, the client of Fāyid, who was the client of ʿUmar ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān—may God be pleased with him—lamenting those of the Banū Umayya who were killed by ʿAbd Allah and Dāwūd, the two sons of ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-ʿAbbās—may God be pleased with them. When al-Rashīd performed the pilgrimage, he summoned Abū Saʿīd and said to him: “Recite your ode to me:”

poems.intro: فأنشده، وقال: يا أمير المؤمنين، كان القوم موالي، وأنعموا على، فرثيتهم ولم أهج أحدا، فتركه. وقال الأشهب بن رميلة:

verses.h1: إن الألى حانت بفلج دماؤهم
verses.h2: هم القوم كل القوم يا أم خالد

verses.h1: هم ساعد الدهر الذي يتقى به
verses.h2: وما خير كف لا تنوء بساعد

verses.h1: Those whose blood was shed at Falj—
verses.h2: they are men, men in every sense, O Umm Khālid.

verses.h1: They are the arm with which one shields oneself against Time;
verses.h2: what good is a hand with no arm to raise it?

prose_translation.intro: So he recited it to him and said, “O Commander of the Faithful, those people were my patrons and had bestowed favors upon me, so I elegized them; I did not satirize anyone.” He then let him go. And al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said:

poems.intro: أنشد النجيرمي لمنظور بن مرثد الراجز، يرثي مقاتلا، وحبيشا ابني جزء:

verses.h1: أما تريني اليوم يا أم صالح
verses.h2: طويلا قيامي للأسى وقعودي

verses.h1: فإن مصيبات أصبن مقاتلا
verses.h2: وأصحابه استجهلن كل جلدي

verses.h1: وكانوا جمالي في الحياة وعدتي
verses.h2: وحرزي إذا ما قلت أي أسودي

verses.h1: Do you not see me today, Umm Ṣāliḥ,
verses.h2: how long I stand and sit in sorrow?

verses.h1: For calamities that struck Muqātil
verses.h2: and his companions have shattered all my fortitude.

verses.h1: They were my pride in life and my strength,
verses.h2: and my refuge whenever I cried, ‘O my lions!’

notes.note: I read أي as the vocative particle ay (‘O’), making أي أسودي an appeal to ‘my lions’; the unvocalized wording is somewhat uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Najīramī recited verses by Manẓūr ibn Marthad, the rajaz poet, lamenting Muqātil and Ḥubaysh, the two sons of Juzʾ:

verses.h1: كانت خزاعة ملء الأرض ما اتسعت
verses.h2: فقص مر الليالي من حواشيها

verses.h1: هذا أبو القاسم الثاوي ببلقعة
verses.h2: تسفي الرياح عليه من سوافيها

verses.h1: هبت، وقد علمت أن لا هبوب به
verses.h2: وقد تكون حسيرا إذ يباريها

verses.h1: أضحى قرى للمنايا إذ نزلن به
verses.h2: وكان في سالف الأيام يقريها

verses.h1: Khuzāʿa once filled the earth, for all its breadth;
verses.h2: then the passing nights trimmed away its fringes.

verses.h1: Here is Abū al-Qāsim, lying in a barren waste;
verses.h2: the winds scatter their drifting dust over him.

verses.h1: They blew, knowing that he could stir no more,
verses.h2: though once they would grow weary when he raced them.

verses.h1: He became a feast for deadly fates when they lodged with him,
verses.h2: though in days gone by he used to feed them.

notes.note: I could not establish the identity of Abū al-Qāsim.

prose_translation.intro: And Diʿbil ibn ʿAlī al-Khuzāʿī said:

verses.h1: من للخصوم إذا جد الخصام بهم
verses.h2: بعد ابن سعد، ومن للضمر القود

verses.h1: وموقف قد كفيت الناطقين به
verses.h2: في مجمع من نواصي الناس مشهود

verses.h1: فرجته بلسان غير ملتبس
verses.h2: عند الحفاظ وقلب غير مزؤود

verses.h1: Who will deal with disputants when their quarrel grows fierce
verses.h2: after Ibn Saʿd—and who will care for the lean, long-necked steeds?

verses.h1: Many a difficult occasion you handled on the spokesmen’s behalf,
verses.h2: in an assembly attended by the foremost men.

verses.h1: You resolved it with a clear-speaking tongue,
verses.h2: when honor was at stake, and an undaunted heart.

notes.note: Ibn Saʿd cannot be securely identified from this extract. The phrase asking who will be there for the steeds leaves his precise role unstated; “care for” is interpretive.

poems.intro: فقال الرشيد: أعد، فأعاد، فقال له: ويحك، كأن قائل هذا الشعر يصف يحيى بن خالد، وجعفر بن يحيى، وبكى حتى جرت دموعه، ووصل الزبير بصلة سنية. وقال أبو خراش الهذلي، يرثي إخوته:

verses.h1: فقدت بني لبنى فلما فقدتهم
verses.h2: صبرت، ولم أقطع عليهم أناملي

verses.h1: رماح من الخطي، زرق نصالها
verses.h2: حداد أعاليها، شداد الأسافل

verses.h1: فلهفي على ميت بنعمان للفتى
verses.h2: ولهفي على ميت بقوس المعاقل

verses.h1: حسان الوجوه طيب حجزاتهم
verses.h2: كريم نثاهم غير لف معازل

verses.h1: I lost the sons of Lubnā, and when I lost them,
verses.h2: I bore it patiently and did not cut off my fingertips in grief for them.

verses.h1: They were spears from al-Khaṭṭ, their blades blue,
verses.h2: their points sharp, their lower shafts strong.

verses.h1: Oh, my grief for one dead at Naʿmān—for the young man!
verses.h2: And my grief for one dead at Qaws al-Maʿāqil!

verses.h1: Handsome of face, chaste in conduct,
verses.h2: honorable in reputation, neither inept nor aloof from battle.

notes.note: The phrase للفتى, literally “for the young man,” is syntactically awkward here and may reflect a textual error. It has been retained rather than silently emended.
Naʿmān is probably the valley near Mecca. I cannot securely identify قوس المعاقل; it is provisionally treated as the place-name Qaws al-Maʿāqil, though المعاقل may instead describe its strongholds.
The precise force of لف معازل is uncertain. لف may denote tongue-tied or ineffectual men; معازل may denote men who remain apart from battle or go unarmed.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Rashīd said, “Repeat it,” and he repeated it. Then he said to him, “Woe to you! It is as though the author of these verses were describing Yaḥyā ibn Khālid and Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā.” He wept until his tears flowed, and bestowed a lavish gift upon al-Zubayr. Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī said, lamenting his brothers:

verses.h1: أجدك ما تعفوا كلوم مصيبة
verses.h2: على صاحب إلا فجعت بصاحب؟

verses.h1: تقطع أحشائي إذا ما ذكرتهم
verses.h2: وتنهل عيني بالدموع السواكب

verses.h1: وكن امرأ جلدا على ما ينوبني
verses.h2: ومعترفا بالصبر عند النوائب

verses.h1: فهد أبو سفيان ركني، ولم أكن
verses.h2: جزوعا ولا مستنكرا للنوائب

verses.h1: غنينا معا بضعا وخمسين حجة
verses.h2: خليلي صفاء، ودنا غير كاذب

verses.h1: فأصبحت لما حالت الأرض دونه
verses.h2: على قربه مني كمن لم أصاحب

verses.h1: Tell me: scarcely do the wounds of grief heal
verses.h2: for one friend before I am bereaved of another?

verses.h1: My very insides are torn whenever I remember them,
verses.h2: and my eye pours forth streaming tears.

verses.h1: I was a man steadfast in whatever befell me,
verses.h2: and accepting the need for patience in calamity.

verses.h1: But Abū Sufyān shattered my strength, though I had never been
verses.h2: distraught or bewildered by calamities.

verses.h1: We lived together for fifty-odd years,
verses.h2: two friends in pure affection, our love unfeigned.

verses.h1: Now that the earth has shut him away,
verses.h2: despite his nearness, I am as though I had never been his companion.

notes.note: تعفوا appears to stand for تعفو (‘heal’ or ‘fade’), with an extra final alif.
وكن appears to be a misprint for وكنت (‘and I was’), which fits the first-person context. The translation follows that reading.
Abū Sufyān’s identity is uncertain. The context indicates that his death is what shattered the speaker’s strength.

The construction كمن لم أصاحب is awkward: literally, ‘like someone I never accompanied.’ It is understood here as expressing that burial has separated the friends as though their companionship had never existed.

poems.intro: وقال أعشى بني أسد، وهو خيثمة بن معروف، أخو الكميت بن معروف:

verses.h1: نام الخلي، وبت الليل مرتفقا
verses.h2: كما تزاور يخشى دفه النكب

verses.h1: إذا رجعت إلى نفسي أحدثها
verses.h2: عمن تضمن من أصحابي القلب

verses.h1: ازددت وجدا على وجد أكابده
verses.h2: حتى تكاد بنات الصدر تلتهب

verses.h1: فقد علمت وإن مليت بعدهم
verses.h2: أني سأنهل بالشرب الذي شربوا

verses.h1: The carefree man slept, while I spent the night propped on my elbow,
verses.h2: like one who turns aside, fearing blows to his flank.

verses.h1: Whenever I turn inward and speak to myself
verses.h2: of those companions of mine whom the pits have enclosed,

verses.h1: grief upon grief is added to what I endure,
verses.h2: until the cares within my breast almost burst into flame.

verses.h1: For I know, even if I am granted long life after them,
verses.h2: that I shall drink the draught they drank.

notes.note: The second hemistich is unclear and may be corrupted. The rendering is tentative: تزاور suggests turning or leaning aside, and دفه may mean ‘his flank,’ but I cannot confidently resolve النكب or the clause’s syntax.
I read القلب as القُلُب, the plural of قليب (‘well’ or ‘pit’), as supported by the meter. These appear to be burial pits, though literal wells may be intended.

prose_translation.intro: And Aʿshā Banī Asad—Kh aythama ibn Maʿrūf, the brother of al-Kumayt ibn Maʿrūf—said:

poems.intro: وقال أبو العباس الأعمى، وهو السائب بن فروخ:

verses.h1: آمت نساء بني أمية بعدهم
verses.h2: وبناتهم بمضيعة أيتام

verses.h1: نامت جدودهم وأسقط نجمهم
verses.h2: والنجم يسقط والجدود تنام

verses.h1: خلت المنابر والأسرة منهم
verses.h2: فعليهم حتى الممات سلام

verses.h1: The women of Banū Umayya were widowed after them,
verses.h2: and their daughters are orphans, left uncared for.

verses.h1: Their fortunes slept, and their star was cast down—
verses.h2: stars fall, and fortunes sleep.

verses.h1: The pulpits and thrones stood empty of them;
verses.h2: so peace be upon them until death.

prose_translation.intro: And Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aʿmā, who is al-Sāʾib ibn Farrūkh, said:

verses.h1: ليت شعري من أين رائحة المس
verses.h2: ك وما إن إخال بالخيف إنسي؟

verses.h1: حين غابت بنو أمية عنها
verses.h2: والبهاليل من بني عبد شمس

verses.h1: خطباء على المنابر فرسا
verses.h2: ن، عليها، وقالة غير خرس

verses.h1: لا يعابون صامتين، وإن قا
verses.h2: لوا أصابوا، ولم يقولوا بلبس

verses.h1: بحلوم، إذا الحلوم استخفت
verses.h2: ووجوه مثل الدنانير ملس

verses.h1: If only I knew whence comes the scent of musk,
verses.h2: when I think there is not a soul at al-Khayf!

verses.h1: Now that the Banū Umayya have departed from it,
verses.h2: and the noble lords of the Banū ʿAbd Shams.

verses.h1: Orators upon the pulpits,
verses.h2: knights upon them, eloquent speakers, never tongue-tied.

verses.h1: Beyond reproach when silent; and when they spoke,
verses.h2: they hit the mark and spoke without obscurity.

verses.h1: With composure when others’ composure failed,
verses.h2: and faces smooth as dinars.

notes.note: The feminine pronoun in ʿanhā (‘from it’) has no explicit feminine antecedent in the excerpt; it presumably refers to the place mentioned as al-Khayf.
ʿalayhā (‘upon them’) appears to refer to the pulpits, making ‘knights upon them’ a metaphor for mastery in public speaking.

poems.intro: عن خداش بن فراس النميري، قال: أغارت علينا بنو جشم بن بكر بظهر البشر، فأصابوا منا أخوين فارسين سيدين، يقال لأحدهما: مسعود، وللآخر حاتم، ابنا شيظم، وكانت لهما أخت سيدة برزة، يقال لها: رائطة بنت شيظم، فبكتهما، ورثتهما طويلا، وكانت أحر ما تكون أسى وأسفا، وأطول ما تكون حزنا ولهفا، إذا صاح صائحنا، وذعر سارحنا، وركب فارسنا، ولقد رأيتها على مثل تلك الحال في بعض الأيام، وساس ثائرون والأصوات متواترة، والخيل متبادرة، والصارخ هاتف، وهي تندبهما، وتقول:

verses.h1: لهفي على الأخوين كالأ
verses.h2: سدين مسعود وحاتم

verses.h1: السيدين المانعين الذ
verses.h2: ائدين عن المحارم

verses.h1: الفاتقين الراتقين السابقين إلى المكارم
الضاربين جماجم ال
verses.h2: أبطال بالبيض الصوارم

verses.h1: والطاعنين بكل ما
verses.h2: رنة وقاصمة وقاصم

verses.h1: حدق الفوارس بالأس
verses.h2: نة والقلوب لدى الغلاصم

verses.h1: كانا يدي فشلتا
verses.h2: بالساعدين وبالمعاصم

verses.h1: فبقيت كالطير المقص
verses.h2: ض ريشه واهي القوادم

verses.h1: لا أستطيع، ولا أطي
verses.h2: ق أرد عني كف ظالم

verses.h1: مع كل رنة مأتم
verses.h2: لي مأتم، وعلى ماتم

verses.h1: فاليوم أخضع للذلي
verses.h2: ل وللمجارب والمسالم

verses.h1: My grief for the two brothers, like
verses.h2: two lions—Masʿūd and Ḥātim!

verses.h1: The two lords, the protectors,
verses.h2: the defenders of all held sacred;

verses.h1: Who tore apart and mended, who led the way to noble deeds;
Who struck the skulls
verses.h2: of heroes with bright, keen-edged swords;

verses.h1: Who thrust with every
verses.h2: supple spear, every shattering shaft and blade,

verses.h1: At horsemen’s eyes with spearheads,
verses.h2: and at hearts lodged in their throats.

verses.h1: They were my two hands, now paralyzed
verses.h2: at forearms and wrists.

verses.h1: I am left like a bird
verses.h2: with clipped plumage and feeble flight feathers.

verses.h1: I cannot, I have no strength
verses.h2: to ward off a tyrant’s hand.

verses.h1: With every wail of mourning,
verses.h2: I have mourning of my own, and mourning weighs upon me.

verses.h1: Today I bow even to the lowly,
verses.h2: to the hostile and the peaceable alike.

notes.note: مارنة is understood as a supple spear. قاصمة وقاصم are feminine and masculine forms meaning something that breaks or shatters; their precise weapon referents are uncertain. ‘Shaft and blade’ is tentative.
المقصض appears corrupt, probably for المقصص, ‘clipped,’ describing the bird’s plumage.
وعلى ماتم appears to stand for وعليّ مأتم, ‘and upon me is mourning.’ The translation follows this reading, though the wording is uncertain.
المجارب may be a misprint for المحارب, ‘the hostile one’ or ‘one who wages war,’ contrasting with المسالم, ‘the peaceable one.’ The translation follows that conjecture.

prose_translation.intro: From Khidāsh ibn Firās al-Numayrī, who said: “Banū Jusham ibn Bakr raided us on the uplands of al-Bishr and killed two brothers of ours, both horsemen and chiefs. One was called Masʿūd and the other Ḥātim, the sons of Shayẓam. They had a sister, a noblewoman who appeared freely in public, called Rāʾiṭa bint Shayẓam. She wept for them and mourned them long. Her sorrow and anguish burned most fiercely, and her grief and lamentation lasted longest, whenever our alarm-raiser cried out, our grazing herds were startled, and our horsemen mounted. Indeed, I saw her in just such a state one day, when people were rushing about, cries followed one another, horses raced forward, and the alarm-raiser was shouting. She was lamenting them, saying:”

poems.intro: وقال فاطمة بنت الأجحم بن دندنة الخزاعية، ترثي أباها. (والجحم: حمرة العين) .

verses.h1: قد كنت ذات حمية ما عشت لي
verses.h2: أمشي البراح، وكنت أنت جناحي

verses.h1: قد كنت لي جبلا ألوذ بظله
verses.h2: فتركتني أمشي بأجرد ضاح

verses.h1: فالآن أخشع للذليل وأتقى
verses.h2: منه، وأدفع ظالمي بالراح

verses.h1: وإذا دعت قمرية شجنا لها
verses.h2: يوما على فنن دعوت صباحي

verses.h1: I was proud of spirit as long as you lived for me;
verses.h2: I walked the open ground, and you were my wing.

verses.h1: You were a mountain in whose shade I sought refuge;
verses.h2: you left me walking on bare ground beneath the sun.

verses.h1: Now I bow to the lowliest man and guard myself
verses.h2: against him, and fend off my oppressor with my palms.

verses.h1: And when a turtledove voices her sorrow
verses.h2: one day upon a branch, I raise my own cry of grief.

notes.note: The expression دعوت صباحي is uncertain. It is rendered as raising a cry of grief, possibly referring to the traditional cry of alarm or distress wā-ṣabāḥāh.

prose_translation.intro: Fāṭima bint al-Ajḥam ibn Dandana al-Khuzāʿiyya said, elegizing her father. (Al-jaḥam: redness of the eye.)

poems.intro: وقع الطاعون بالكوفة، فأفنى بني غاضرة، ومات فيه بنو زر بن حبيش صاحب أمير المؤمنين علي رضوان الله عليه، فقال ابن ميادة يرثيهم:

verses.h1: أبعد بني زر وبعد ابن جندل
verses.h2: وعمرو، أرجى لذة العيش في خفض

verses.h1: مضوا وبقينا نأمل العيش بعدهم
verses.h2: ألا إن من يبقى على إثر من يمضي

verses.h1: After Zirr’s sons and after Ibn Jandal,
verses.h2: and ʿAmr, can I hope to enjoy life at ease?

verses.h1: They have passed on, while we remain, hoping to live after them;
verses.h2: surely whoever remains follows on the heels of whoever departs.

notes.note: أرجى is understood as “I hope for,” probably representing أُرَجِّي; the printed spelling leaves the reading uncertain.
Ibn Jandal and ʿAmr could not be identified; the vocalization of Jandal is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: The plague struck al-Kūfa and wiped out Banū Ghāḍira. Among those who died in it were the sons of Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, the companion of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him. Ibn Mayyāda said, elegizing them:

poems.intro: وقال الخنساء بنت عمرو بن الشريد:

verses.h1: تعرقني الدهر نهسا وحزا
verses.h2: وأوجعني الدهر قرعا وغمزا

verses.h1: وأفنى رجالي، فبادروا معا
verses.h2: فأصبح قلبي لهم مستفزا

verses.h1: وكانوا سراة بني مالك
verses.h2: وزين المقامة فخرا وعزا

verses.h1: كأن لم يكونوا حمى يتقى
verses.h2: إذ الناس في ذاك من عز بزا

verses.h1: Time has gnawed me to the bone, biting and cutting,
verses.h2: and Time has hurt me with blows and jabs.

verses.h1: It destroyed my men, and they hastened away together;
verses.h2: my heart is left distraught for them.

verses.h1: They were the chieftains of Banū Mālik,
verses.h2: the pride and glory adorning the assembly.

verses.h1: As though they had never been a sanctuary none dared assail,
verses.h2: when the rule among men was: whoever prevailed took the spoil.

notes.note: فبادروا معا literally means ‘they hastened together,’ apparently implying departure in death. It may be a misprint for فبادوا معا, ‘they perished together,’ which would also fit the meter better.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Khansāʾ bint ʿAmr ibn al-Sharīd said:

poems.poet_from_text: البحتري يرثي المتوكل والفتح بن خاقان من قصيدة
poems.intro: وقال البحتري يرثي المتوكل والفتح بن خاقان من قصيدة:

poet.from_text: البحتري يرثي المتوكل والفتح بن خاقان من قصيدة

verses.h1: مضى جعفر والفتح بين مزمل
verses.h2: وبين صبيغ بالدماء مضرج

verses.h1: أأطلب أنصارا على الدهر بعدما
verses.h2: ثوى منهما في الترب أوسي وخزرجي؟

verses.h1: أولئك ساداتي الذين بفضلهم
verses.h2: حلبت أفاويق الربيع المثجج

verses.h1: Jaʿfar and al-Fatḥ have passed away, one shrouded,
verses.h2: the other stained and drenched in blood.

verses.h1: Shall I seek helpers against Time, now that
verses.h2: those two—my Awsī and my Khazrajī—lie in the dust?

verses.h1: Those are my masters, through whose bounty
verses.h2: I milked the successive yields of rain-pouring spring.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Buḥturī said, elegizing al-Mutawakkil and al-Fatḥ ibn Khāqān, in an excerpt from a poem:

verses.h1: وسائلة عن توبة بن مصرس
verses.h2: وهان عليها ما أصاب به الدهر

verses.h1: وسائلة أخرى حفي سؤالها
verses.h2: إذا ذكرته فاض من دمعها غزر

verses.h1: رأت إخوتي بعد ائتلاف تفرقوا
verses.h2: فلم يبق إلا واحدا منهم شفر

verses.h1: فلا وأبيك الخير، ما كان إخوتي
verses.h2: معازيل أبراما إذا جارد القطر

verses.h1: أرب بهم ريب المنون كأنما
verses.h2: على الدهر فيهم أن يفرقهم نذر

verses.h1: One woman asks about Tawba ibn Muḍarris,
verses.h2: caring little for what Time has inflicted on him.

verses.h1: Another asks, solicitous in her questioning;
verses.h2: whenever she remembers him, her tears flow abundantly.

verses.h1: She saw my brothers scattered after being united;
verses.h2: not a soul of them remained except one.

verses.h1: No, by your worthy father, my brothers were not
verses.h2: men who held aloof, misers when the rain failed.

verses.h1: The calamities of death beset them, as though
verses.h2: Time were bound by a vow to scatter them.

notes.note: The verse gives the father’s name as مصرس, apparently a misprint for مضرس (Muḍarris), the name supplied in the attribution.

جارد القطر is unclear as printed and may be corrupt; ‘when the rain failed’ is a conjectural rendering. معازيل can describe men who keep apart from others or who hold back from fighting; its precise sense here is uncertain.

verses.h1: وقائلة لما رأت شيب لمتى
verses.h2: لها ويلها! ما بال شعر أبي الجعد؟

verses.h1: برأسي خطوب
verses.h2: لو علمت كثيرة أصبت بها ظلما، وأطلبها وحدي

verses.h1: تعرى المصيبات الفتى وهو عاجز
verses.h2: ويلعب ريب الدهر بالجازم الجلد

verses.h1: وإني امرؤ لا ينقض العجز مرتي
verses.h2: إذا ما انطوى مني الفؤاد على الحقد

verses.h1: ولست بمختار الحياة بسبة
verses.h2: تثنى بها حيا على بنو سعد

verses.h1: A woman said, when she saw my graying locks—
verses.h2: woe to her!—“What has happened to Abū al-Jaʿd’s hair?”

verses.h1: Upon my head are calamities—
verses.h2: many, if you only knew—that I have suffered unjustly, and for which I seek redress alone.

verses.h1: Calamities assail a man while he is powerless,
verses.h2: and the vicissitudes of time toy with the resolute and steadfast.

verses.h1: I am a man whose resolve helplessness cannot undo
verses.h2: once my heart has closed upon a grudge.

verses.h1: I would not choose life at the cost of disgrace
verses.h2: that Banū Saʿd would hold against me while I lived.

notes.note: The supplied hemistich division appears misplaced: the likely division is after كثيرة, with أصبت beginning the second hemistich. The translation preserves the supplied division. وأطلبها is understood as seeking redress or vengeance for the wrongs suffered.
تعرى appears to be a misprint for تعرو, ‘assail’ or ‘befall,’ which is the reading followed here.

The wording تثنى بها حيا على is uncertain. I tentatively read تثنى as تُثني and على as عليّ, taking the phrase to mean that Banū Saʿd would speak reproachfully of him for this disgrace during his lifetime.

poems.intro: وقال دريد بن الصمة، يرثي إخوته:

verses.h1: تقول: ألا تبكي أخاك وقد أرى
verses.h2: مكان البكا لكن بنيت على الصبر

verses.h1: فقلت: أعبد الله أبكي، أم الذي
verses.h2: على الشرف الأعلى، قتيل أبي بكر؟

verses.h1: وعبد يغوث أم نديمي مالكا
verses.h2: وعز المصاب حثو قبر على قبر

verses.h1: أبى القتل إلا آل صمة إنهم
verses.h2: أبوا غيره، والقدر يجري على القدر

verses.h1: She says, “Will you not weep for your brother?” I do indeed see
verses.h2: cause for weeping, but I was fashioned for endurance.

verses.h1: I said, “Should I weep for ʿAbd Allah, or for the one
verses.h2: on al-Sharaf al-Aʿlā, slain by Abū Bakr?

verses.h1: And ʿAbd Yaghūth—or my companion Mālik?
verses.h2: Grievous is the loss: heaping grave upon grave.

verses.h1: Death in battle would have none but the house of Ṣimma; they
verses.h2: would have no other end, and fate follows what is decreed.”

notes.note: Al-Sharaf al-Aʿlā may be a place-name or simply mean “the highest ridge.” Abū Bakr is not securely identified here; the name may designate a clan rather than an individual.
Mālik, described as the poet’s companion, is not securely identified.

prose_translation.intro: And Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma said, elegizing his brothers:

poems.intro: قال أبو الفرج الأصبهاني: ذكر عند النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قس بن ساعدة الإيادي، فقال رجل: يا رسول الله، لقد رأيت من قس عجبا، فقال: وما رأيت؟ قال: بينا أنا بجبل يقال له: سمعنا، في يوم شديد الحر، إذا بقس بن ساعدة تحت ظل شجرة عند عين ماء، وعنده سباع، كلما زأر منها سبع على صاحبه ضربه بيده، وقال: كف حتى يشرب الذي ورد قبلك، قال: فرقت، فقال: لا تخف، وإذا بقبرين بينهما مسجد، فقلت: ما هذان القبران اللذان أراهما؟ قال: هما قبرا أخوين كانا لي، فماتا، فاتخذت بينهما مسجدا أعبد الله فيه حتى ألحق بهما، ثم ذكر أيامهما، فبكى، وأنشأ يقول:

verses.h1: خليلي هبا، طال ما قد رقدتما
verses.h2: أجدكما ما تقضيان كراكما؟

verses.h1: ألم تعلما أني بسمعان مفرد
verses.h2: ومالي فيه من حبيب سواكما؟

verses.h1: أقيم على قبريكما لست بارحا
verses.h2: طوال الليالي أو يجيب صداكما

verses.h1: كأنكما، والموت أقرب غاية
verses.h2: بجسمي في قبريكما قد أتاكما

verses.h1: My two friends, awake! Long have you slept.
verses.h2: Will you truly never finish your sleep?

verses.h1: Do you not know that I am alone at Samʿān,
verses.h2: with no loved one there but you two?

verses.h1: I remain beside your graves and will not leave,
verses.h2: through the long nights, until your echo answers.

verses.h1: It is as though death—the nearest destination—
verses.h2: has already brought my body to you in your graves.

notes.note: The location سمعان, provisionally transliterated Samʿān, is unidentified; its vocalization is uncertain.
صداكما is rendered as “your echo,” but ṣadā can also denote the owl associated in pre-Islamic belief with the dead person’s spirit. That sense may be intended here.

The syntax is difficult, particularly كأنكما (“as though you two”) and its connection to قد أتاكما (“has come to you two”). The translation tentatively takes death as the subject of أتاكما and بجسمي as “bringing my body.”

prose_translation.intro: Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī said: Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. A man said, “O Messenger of God, I saw something remarkable about Quss.” He asked, “What did you see?” The man said, “While I was on a mountain called Samʿna on a fiercely hot day, there was Quss ibn Sāʿida beneath the shade of a tree beside a spring, with wild beasts around him. Whenever one beast roared at another, he struck it with his hand and said, ‘Hold back until the one that came before you has drunk.’ I was frightened, but he said, ‘Do not be afraid.’ There were two graves, with a place of worship between them. I asked, ‘What are these two graves I see?’ He said, ‘They are the graves of two brothers of mine who died. I made a place of worship between them, where I worship God until I join them.’ Then he recalled their days together, wept, and began to recite:”

poems.intro: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "يرحم الله قسا". وروى أن هذا الشعر لعيسى بن قدامة الأسدي وكان له نديما، فماتا براوند فكان يجيء فيجلس بين القبرين بموضع يقال له حزاق، فيشرب، ويصب على القبرين، حتى يقضي وطره، وينصرف، وينشد وهو منصرف:

verses.h1: خليلي هبا طال ما قد رقدتما
verses.h2: أجدكما ما تقضيان كراكما؟

verses.h1: أم تعلما مالي براوند من أخ
verses.h2: ولا بجزاق من نديم سواكما

verses.h1: مقيما على قبريكما، لست بارحا
verses.h2: طوال الليالي أو يجيب صداكما

verses.h1: جرى النوم مجرى اللحم والدم منكما
verses.h2: كأن الذي يسقي العقار سقاكما

verses.h1: تحمل من يهوى القفول، وغادروا
verses.h2: أخا لكما أشجاه ما قد شجاكما

verses.h1: فأي أخ يجفو أخا بعد موته
verses.h2: فلست الذي من بعد موت جفاكما

verses.h1: أصبت على قبريكما من مدامة
verses.h2: فإلا تذوقاها ترو ثراكما

verses.h1: أناديكما كيما تجيبا وتنطقا
verses.h2: وليس مجابا صوته من دعاكما

verses.h1: أمن طول نوم لم تجيبا وتنطقا؟
verses.h2: خليلي ما هذا الذي قد دهاكما؟

verses.h1: قضيت بأني لا محالة هالك
verses.h2: وأني سيعروني الذي قد عراكما

verses.h1: سأبكيكما طول الحياة وما الذي
verses.h2: يرد على ذي لوعة إن بكاكما؟

verses.h1: My two friends, awake! Long have you slept.
verses.h2: Truly, will you never have your fill of sleep?

verses.h1: Do you not know that I have no brother in Rāwand,
verses.h2: nor any drinking companion in Jazāq besides you two?

verses.h1: I remain beside your graves and will not leave
verses.h2: through the long nights, until your echoes answer.

verses.h1: Sleep has permeated you like flesh and blood,
verses.h2: as though the wine-pourer had given you both to drink.

verses.h1: Those eager to return home departed, leaving behind
verses.h2: a brother of yours, deeply grieved by what has afflicted you.

verses.h1: What brother would forsake a brother after his death?
verses.h2: I am not one who has forsaken you after death.

verses.h1: I poured some wine upon your graves;
verses.h2: if you do not taste it, it will moisten your earth.

verses.h1: I call to you so that you might answer and speak,
verses.h2: but whoever calls you receives no answer to his voice.

verses.h1: Is it from sleeping so long that you do not answer or speak?
verses.h2: My two friends, what is this that has befallen you?

verses.h1: I have concluded that I must inevitably perish,
verses.h2: and that what befell you will befall me.

verses.h1: I will weep for you all my life; yet what
verses.h2: does one in anguish gain by weeping for you?

notes.note: أم تعلما appears defective; the translation assumes ألم تعلما, ‘Do you not know?’

The verse names جزاق (provisionally vocalized Jazāq), while the introduction gives حزاق (Ḥazāq). The correct spelling and identification are uncertain; the verse’s spelling is retained. Rāwand’s precise location is also uncertain.
صداكما is rendered ‘your echoes.’ Ṣadā can also denote an owl associated in pre-Islamic belief with the dead; that sense may be intended here.
أصبت is probably a misprint for أصببت, ‘I poured,’ which is the reading adopted here.

prose_translation.intro: Then the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “May God have mercy on Quss.” It is also related that this poetry was by ʿĪsā ibn Qudāma al-Asadī, who had two drinking companions. They died at Rāwand, and he would come and sit between their graves at a place called Hazaq, drinking and pouring wine over the two graves until he had satisfied his desire. Then he would depart, reciting as he went:

poems.intro: وذكر العتبي أن الشعر للحارث بن الحارث، أحد بني عامر بن صعصعة، وكان له نديمان: أحدهما من بني أسد، والآخر من بني حنيفة، فمات أحدهما، فكانا يشربان ويصبان على قبره، ويقول أحدهما:

verses.h1: لا تصرد هامة عن شربها
verses.h2: واسقه الراح وإن كان قبر

verses.h1: كان حرا فهوى فيمن هوى
verses.h2: كل عود ذي شعوب ينكسر

verses.h1: Do not deny a dead man’s spirit its drink;
verses.h2: give him wine to drink, though he is buried.

verses.h1: He was noble, then fell among the fallen;
verses.h2: every cracked branch must break.

notes.note: Hāmah can mean a skull or the bird believed to embody a dead person’s spirit; I have taken it in the latter sense. Tuṣarrid may mean to stint someone’s drink rather than withhold it entirely.
The sense of shuʿūb in «كل عود ذي شعوب» is uncertain. I have understood it as cracks or splits in a piece of wood; it might instead refer to branching.

prose_translation.intro: Al-ʿUtbī mentioned that the verse was by al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith, one of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa. He had two drinking companions, one from the Banū Asad and the other from the Banū Ḥanīfa. When one of them died, the two survivors would drink and pour wine upon his grave, and one of them would say:

poems.intro: ثم مات الآخر، فكان الثالث يشرب عند قبريهما، وينشد:

verses.h1: خليلي هبا طال ما قد رقدتما
verses.h2: أجدكما ما تقضيان كراكما؟

verses.h1: My two friends, wake! Long have you slept.
verses.h2: Will you truly never finish your slumber?

prose_translation.intro: Then the other one died, and the third would drink beside their two graves and recite:

verses.h1: ألا يا دهر أفرش عن شريدي
verses.h2: فقد أدركت مني ما تريد

verses.h1: ذهبت بسالم، وأبي سنان
verses.h2: فما للرزء بعدهما مزيد

verses.h1: تصيب أقاربي، وتحيد عني
verses.h2: ومن حولي التخوف والوعيد

verses.h1: ومن تكن المنية غيبته
verses.h2: فسوف على تفيئته تعود

verses.h1: O Time, spare my surviving kinsman:
verses.h2: you have had from me what you desire.

verses.h1: You have taken Sālim and Abū Sinān;
verses.h2: after those two, no greater loss remains.

verses.h1: You strike my kin and turn aside from me,
verses.h2: with fear and menace all around me.

verses.h1: Whoever death has hidden from sight,
verses.h2: it will return in his wake.

notes.note: شريدي literally means ‘my fugitive’ or ‘my straggler’; it is understood here as a surviving kinsman whom the speaker begs Time to spare. The person’s identity is unclear.
The uncommon expression على تفيئته is understood as ‘in his wake’ or ‘following after him’: apparently death will return for those the deceased has left behind.

prose_translation.intro: The verses. And a Bedouin said:
interludes: [Afrish]: desist.

poems.intro: [تفيئته] : هكذا رأيتها بخط الوزير أبي القاسم بن المغربي، وكنت أظنها "بقيته". كان محمد بن صالح بن عبد الله بن موسى بن عبد الله بن حسن بن حسن بن علي بن أبي طالب - رضوان الله عليهم - لما من عليه المتوكل، وأخرجه من الحبس سلمه إلى الفتح بن خاقان، وضمنه إياه ألا يفارق "سر من رأى" فكان مقيما بها يلتمس الرجوع إلى الحجاز، فلا يقدر، وكان مألفا لسراة الناس، ووجوه أهل البلد، وكان كثير الأنس بسعيد بن حميد، لا يكاد يفارقه، وفي سعيد يقول محمد بن صالح:

verses.h1: أصاحب من صاحبت ثمت أنثني
verses.h2: إليك أبا عثمان عطشان صاديا

verses.h1: أبى القلب لم ينقع بهم وهو حائم
verses.h2: إليك، وإن كانوا الفروع العواليا

verses.h1: وإنا إذا جئناك لم نبغ مشرا
verses.h2: سواك، وروينا العظام البواليا

verses.h1: فتوفى محمد بن صالح
verses.h2: رحمه الله

verses.h1: I keep company with whomever I will, then turn back
verses.h2: to you, Abū ʿUthmān, thirsty and parched.

verses.h1: My heart refused: they did not quench its thirst, and it still thirsts
verses.h2: for you, though they are the loftiest branches.

verses.h1: When we come to you, we seek no watering place
verses.h2: but you, and we slake the thirst of our wasted bones.

verses.h1: Then Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ died—
verses.h2: may God have mercy on him.

notes.note: The printed مشرا appears defective, probably for مشربا, ‘a drinking place’ or ‘source of drink,’ which is the reading translated here.
This appears to be the compiler’s prose reporting the poet’s death, not a verse of the poem. It has been translated in the supplied divisions.

prose_translation.intro: [Tafīʾatuhu]: This is how I saw it in the handwriting of the vizier Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Maghribī; I had thought it was “baqiyyatuhu.” When al-Mutawakkil granted clemency to Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Mūsā ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with them—and released him from prison, he entrusted him to al-Fatḥ ibn Khāqān, making him responsible for ensuring that Muḥammad did not leave Surr Man Raʾā. He remained there, seeking permission to return to al-Ḥijāz but unable to obtain it. He was a close associate of the leading men and notables of the city, and was particularly fond of the company of Saʿīd ibn Ḥumayd, whom he scarcely ever left. It was of Saʿīd that Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ said:

poems.intro: بسر من رأى، فجزع عليه سيعد، وقال يرثيه:

verses.h1: بأي يد أسطو على الدهر بعدما
verses.h2: أبان يدي عضب الذبابين قاضب

verses.h1: وهاض جناحي حادث جل خطبه
verses.h2: فسدت على الصبر الجميل المذاهب

verses.h1: ومن عادة الأيام أن صروفها
verses.h2: إذا سر منها جانب ساء جانب

verses.h1: لعمري لقد غال التجلد أننا
verses.h2: فقدناك فقد الغيث، والعام جادب

verses.h1: وما أعرف الأيام إلا ذميمة
verses.h2: ولا الدهر إلا وهو بالثأر طالب

verses.h1: لعمري لئن كان الردى بك فاتني
verses.h2: فكل امرئ يوما إلى الله ذاهب

verses.h1: لقد أخذت مني النوائب حقها
verses.h2: فما تركت حقا على النوائب

verses.h1: ولا تركتني أرهب الدهر بعد
verses.h2: لقد كل عني بابه والمخالف

verses.h1: سقى جدثا أمسى الكريم ابن صالح
verses.h2: يحل به دان من المزن ساكب

verses.h1: With what hand can I assail Time, now that
verses.h2: a keen, two-edged blade has severed my hand?

verses.h1: A calamity of terrible moment has broken my wing,
verses.h2: and every path to graceful patience has been barred.

verses.h1: It is the way of days that their shifting fortunes,
verses.h2: when they gladden on one side, bring sorrow on another.

verses.h1: By my life, what destroyed our fortitude was that we
verses.h2: lost you as one misses rain in a year of drought.

verses.h1: I have known the days only as blameworthy,
verses.h2: and Time only as a seeker of vengeance.

verses.h1: By my life, though death has carried you beyond my reach,
verses.h2: every man will one day go to God.

verses.h1: Calamities have taken their due from me,
verses.h2: and left no further claim against me.

verses.h1: Nor have they left me fearing Time any longer:
verses.h2: its fang and claws have grown blunt against me.

verses.h1: May the grave in which noble Ibn Ṣāliḥ now
verses.h2: dwells be watered by a low-hanging cloud pouring rain.

notes.note: على appears to be a misprint for عليّ (‘against me’). The translation takes النوائب (‘calamities’) as the delayed subject of تركت.

The second hemistich appears corrupt. بابه (‘its door’) and المخالف (‘the opponent’) are provisionally read as نابه (‘its fang’) and المخالب (‘claws’); the latter also restores the rhyme. بعد at the end of the first hemistich may be incomplete.
The identity of Ibn Ṣāliḥ cannot be established from the supplied excerpt.

prose_translation.intro: At Surra Man Raʾā, Saʿīd grieved deeply for him and said, elegizing him:

poems.poet_from_text: عمرو بن الحصين العنبري يرثي عبد الله بن يحيى
poems.intro: لما ظهر عبد الله بن يحيى الكندي الإباضي، الملقب بطالب الحق، واستولى على صنعاء، وكثير من بلاد اليمن، جهز أبا حمزة في جيش من الإباضية فيهم أبرهة بن الصباح، وبلج بن عقبة، فاستولى على المدينة ومكة، فجهز إليه مروان بن محمد عبد الله بن عطية، فلقيه أبو حمزة بوادي العفرة، فقتل أبا حمزة من معه، واستولى عبد الله بن عطية على عسكرهم، وحاز غنائمهم، وبلغ ذلك عبد الله بن يحيى الملقب بطالب الحق، وهو بصنعاء، فسار يريد عبد الله بن عطية وبلغ مسيره ابن عطية، فسار إليه، فالتقى العسكران فظفر به عبد الله بن عطية وقتل عبد الله بن يحيى الكندي، ومعظم جمعه، وتفرق من سلم منهم من القتل في البلاد، وبعث برأسه إلى مروان بن محمد، فقال عمرو بن الحصين العنبري يرثي عبد الله بن يحيى، وأبا حمزة، وأبرهة، وبلجا، وغيرهم ممن قتل من الإباضية:

poet.from_text: عمرو بن الحصين العنبري يرثي عبد الله بن يحيى

verses.h1: هبت قبيل تبلج الفجر
verses.h2: هند تقول ودمعها يجري

verses.h1: إذ أبصرت عيني وأدمعها
verses.h2: ينهل واكفها على نحري:

verses.h1: أنى عراك، وكنت عهدي لا
verses.h2: سرب الدموع، وكنت ذا صبر

verses.h1: أقذى بعينك ما يفارقها
verses.h2: أم عائر، أم مالها تذري؟

verses.h1: أم ذكر إخوان فجعت بهم
verses.h2: سلكوا سبيلهم على خبر

verses.h1: فأجبتها: من ذكر مصرعهم
verses.h2: لا غيره، عبراتها تجري

verses.h1: في فتية صبروا نفوسهم
verses.h2: للمشرفية والقنا السمر

verses.h1: تالله ألقى الدهر مثلهم
verses.h2: حتى أكون رهينة القبر

verses.h1: أوفى بذمتهم إذا عقدوا وأعف عند العسر واليسر
متأهلون لكل صالحة
verses.h2: ناهون من لاموا عن النكر

verses.h1: صمت إذا احتضروا مجالسهم
verses.h2: أذن لقول جليسهم، وقر

verses.h1: متأوهون كأن جمر غضى
verses.h2: للخوف بين ضلوعهم يسري

verses.h1: لم تلقهم إلا كأنهم
verses.h2: صدروا لخوفهم عن الحشر

verses.h1: كم من أخ لك قد فجعت به
verses.h2: قوام ليلته إلى الفجر

verses.h1: صوام وقدة كل هاجرة
verses.h2: تراك لذته على قدر

verses.h1: تراك ما تهوى النفوس إذا
verses.h2: رغب النفوس دعت إلى النزر

verses.h1: خواض غمرة كل متلفة
verses.h2: في الله تحت العثير الكدر

verses.h1: في فتية صبر رزئتهم
verses.h2: كانوا يدي، وهم أولو نصري

verses.h1: Just before dawn broke,
verses.h2: Hind rose and spoke, her tears flowing,

verses.h1: when she saw my eye and its tears
verses.h2: streaming down upon my breast:

verses.h1: “How has this overtaken you? I knew you never
verses.h2: to shed tears freely; you were steadfast.

verses.h1: Is there grit in your eye that will not leave it,
verses.h2: or an inflammation—or why does it shed tears?

verses.h1: Or is it remembering brothers whose loss afflicted you,
verses.h2: who went their way with full knowledge?”

verses.h1: I answered her: “It is remembering how they fell—
verses.h2: nothing else—that makes its tears flow,

verses.h1: for young men who held themselves firm
verses.h2: before Mashrafī swords and dark spear-shafts.

verses.h1: By God, I shall never meet their like
verses.h2: until I am held captive by the grave:

verses.h1: More faithful to their covenant when they pledged it, more self-restrained in hardship and ease;
ready for every righteous deed,
verses.h2: forbidding wrongdoing to those they rebuked;

verses.h1: silent when they attended their gatherings,
