verses.h2: attentive to their companion’s words, dignified;

verses.h1: sighing, as though embers of ghaḍā wood
verses.h2: ran between their ribs from fear.

verses.h1: Whenever you met them, they seemed,
verses.h2: in their fear, to have returned from the Last Gathering.

verses.h1: How many a brother have you lost—
verses.h2: one who stood through his night in prayer until dawn,

verses.h1: fasting through the blaze of every midday,
verses.h2: forsaking his pleasure though able to enjoy it;

verses.h1: forsaking what souls desire, when
verses.h2: their cravings called them to paltry gain;

verses.h1: plunging into the depths of every mortal peril
verses.h2: for God’s sake, beneath the murky dust,

verses.h1: among steadfast young men whose loss I suffered—
verses.h2: they were my hand, the men who gave me aid.”

notes.note: ʿĀʾir (عائر) can denote an eye affliction or an irritating particle in the eye; “inflammation” is tentative.
The supplied text has no explicit negative before ألقى. I understand the oath as implying an omitted لا: “I shall never meet their like.”
The unvocalized فجعت here and رزئتهم in line 18 permit either first- or second-person readings. I take this line as an address and line 18 as first-person, following its explicit “my hand.”
على قدر is taken to mean “despite having the ability [to enjoy it].” The terse expression is uncertain.
النزر ordinarily means something scant or paltry. “Paltry gain” interprets it as meager worldly advantage, but its intended sense here is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: When ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaḥyā al-Kindī, the Ibāḍī known as Ṭālib al-Ḥaqq, rose up and took possession of Ṣanʿāʾ and much of the land of al-Yaman, he dispatched Abū Hamza with an army of Ibāḍīs, among them Abraha ibn al-Ṣabbāḥ and Balj ibn ʿUqba. Abū Hamza took possession of al-Madina and Makka, whereupon Marwān ibn Muḥammad sent ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAṭiyya against him. Abū Hamza met him at Wādī al-ʿAfra, and Abū Hamza and those with him were killed. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAṭiyya seized their camp and took their spoils. News of this reached ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaḥyā, known as Ṭālib al-Ḥaqq, while he was in Ṣanʿāʾ, and he marched out against ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAṭiyya. When Ibn ʿAṭiyya heard of his advance, he marched to meet him. The two armies met, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAṭiyya defeated him, killing ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaḥyā al-Kindī and most of his forces. Those who escaped death scattered throughout the land. He sent his head to Marwān ibn Muḥammad. ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥuṣayn al-ʿAnbarī then said, lamenting ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaḥyā, Abū Hamza, Abraha, Balj, and the other Ibāḍīs who had been killed:

poems.intro: (القصيدة طويلة: اقتصرت منها على ما أثبته) . روى أن رجلين قدما الموسم أيام الحج، فسألا رجلا يعرف بابن أبي دباكل أن يقفهما على قبر ابن سريج، فلما وقفا حسر أحدهما عمامته فإذ هو عبد الله بن سعيد بن عبد الملك بن مروان، فنزل فعقر ناقته، وأنشد عند قبر ابن سريج:

verses.h1: وقفنا على قبر بدسم فهاجنا
verses.h2: وذكرنا بالعيش إذ هو مصحب

verses.h1: فجالت بأرجاء الجفون سوافح
verses.h2: من الدمع تستتلي الذي يتعقب

verses.h1: إذا أبطأت عن ساحة الخد ساقها
verses.h2: دم بعد دمع إثره يتصبب

verses.h1: فإن تسعدا نندب عهدا بعبرة
verses.h2: وقل له منا البكا والتنحب

verses.h1: We stood at a grave in Dasm, and it stirred our grief
verses.h2: and reminded us of life when it was kind to us.

verses.h1: Then streams coursed along the rims of our eyelids—
verses.h2: tears calling forth still more to follow.

verses.h1: Whenever they are slow to reach the expanse of the cheek, they are driven on
verses.h2: by blood pouring down after tears, in their wake.

verses.h1: If you two join in my grief, we shall mourn bygone days with tears;
verses.h2: yet our weeping and sobbing are little enough to offer him.

notes.note: دسم is treated as a place name and provisionally vocalized Dasm; its precise vocalization and location are uncertain.
عهدا can mean a former time or a bond; it is rendered here as ‘bygone days.’ The pronoun in له (‘for him’) appears to refer to the deceased rather than to عهد.

prose_translation.intro: (The poem is long; I have confined myself to the lines recorded here.) It is related that two men came for the pilgrimage season and asked a man known as Ibn Abī Dabākil to lead them to the grave of Ibn Surayj. When they stood there, one of them removed his turban, revealing himself to be ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He dismounted, hamstrung his she-camel, and recited at Ibn Surayj’s grave:

poems.intro: ثم نزل صاحبه، فعقر ناقته، فقال له القرشي: خذ في صوت أبي يحيى، فاندفع يغني:

verses.h1: أسعداني بعبرة أسراب
verses.h2: من دموع كثيرة التسكاب

verses.h1: إن أهل الحصاب قد تركوني
verses.h2: موزعا مولعا بأهل الحصاب

verses.h1: أهل بيت تتابعوا للمنايا
verses.h2: ما على الدهر بعدهم من عتاب

verses.h1: فارقوني، وقد علمت يقينا
verses.h2: ما لمن ذاق ميتة من إياب

verses.h1: كم بذاك الحجون من حي صدق
verses.h2: وكهول أعفة، وشباب

verses.h1: فلي الويل بعدهم، وعليهم
verses.h2: صرت فردا وملني أصحابي

verses.h1: You two, join me in streaming grief,
verses.h2: with tears poured out in abundance.

verses.h1: The people of al-Ḥiṣāb have left me
verses.h2: consumed with longing, enthralled by the people of al-Ḥiṣāb.

verses.h1: A household whose members met death one after another—
verses.h2: after them, there is no more reproaching Time.

verses.h1: They have parted from me, and I know for certain
verses.h2: that whoever tastes death never returns.

verses.h1: How many a worthy clan lies in that al-Ḥajūn,
verses.h2: and upright men of mature years, and youths!

verses.h1: Woe to me after them, and woe for their loss!
verses.h2: I am left alone, and my companions have wearied of me.

notes.note: The form أسراب is unclear in this construction. It is tentatively understood as describing streaming or freely flowing tears.
الحصاب is treated as the place-name al-Ḥiṣāb, apparently associated with the Meccan pilgrimage grounds; its precise identification and vocalization are uncertain.
حي صدق is taken as ‘a worthy clan’; حي can denote a tribal community, though the reference here may be more broadly to worthy people buried at al-Ḥajūn.

prose_translation.intro: Then his companion dismounted and hamstrung his she-camel. Al-Qurashī said to him, “Begin Abū Yaḥyā’s song,” and he launched into singing:

poems.intro: قال: ثم وهبا لي عشرين دينارا، وسارا، فعدت إلى الناقتين فبعتهما ورحليهما بثلاثين دينارا. وقال الفرزدق يرثي بنيه:

verses.h1: إذا ذكرت عيني الذين هم لها
verses.h2: قذى هيج منها للبكاء انسكابها

verses.h1: بنى الأرض قد كانوا بنى فعزني
verses.h2: عليهم لآجال المنايا كتابها

verses.h1: ولولا الذي للأرض ما ذهبت بهم
verses.h2: ولما يفلل بالسيوف جذابها

verses.h1: إذا ذكرت أسماؤهم، أودعوا بها
verses.h2: تكاد حيازيمي تفرى صلابها

verses.h1: When my eye recalls those who are to it
verses.h2: a mote, it is stirred to pour out tears.

verses.h1: Sons of the earth—they once were my sons; but I was overcome
verses.h2: in my claim to them by the decree fixing death’s appointed times.

verses.h1: Had it not been for what is owed to the earth, it would not have taken them
verses.h2: without its grasp first being broken by swords.

verses.h1: Whenever their names are mentioned, or they are called by them,
verses.h2: the stout bones of my breast almost split apart.

notes.note: The exact sense of جذابها is uncertain. Rendered provisionally as “its grasp,” it may refer to the earth’s pulling or to those who seize on its behalf; the reading may be corrupt.
I read أودعوا بها as أو دُعوا بها, “or they are called by them,” with a missing space, rather than أُودعوا بها, “they were deposited in it.”

prose_translation.intro: He said: “Then the two of them gave me twenty dinars and departed. I returned to the two she-camels and sold them, together with their saddles, for thirty dinars.” al-Farazdaq said, elegizing his sons:

poems.intro: وقال شتيم بن خويلد، يرثي بني خالدة:

verses.h1: لا يبعد الله رب العباد وال
verses.h2: ملح ما ولدت خالدة

verses.h1: هم المطعمون سديف العشا
verses.h2: ر واللحم في الليلة الباردة

verses.h1: وهم يكسرون صدور الرما
verses.h2: ح في الخيل تطرد أو طارده

verses.h1: يذكرني حسن آلائهم
verses.h2: تأوه معولة فاقدة

verses.h1: فإن يكن الموت أفناهم
verses.h2: فللموت ما تلد الوالدة

verses.h1: وإن التي بقيت بعدهم
verses.h2: على إثر موردهم وارده

verses.h1: May God, Lord of humankind, never cast far away—
verses.h2: by the bond of salt!—those whom Khālida bore.

verses.h1: They are the ones who feed others the hump-fat of pregnant she-camels
verses.h2: and meat on a cold night.

verses.h1: They are the ones who shatter the heads of lances
verses.h2: against cavalry, whether pursued or pursuing.

verses.h1: I am reminded of their gracious favors
verses.h2: by the moaning of a bereaved woman lamenting.

verses.h1: If death has destroyed them,
verses.h2: whatever a mother bears belongs to death.

verses.h1: And the soul that has remained after them
verses.h2: will follow in their wake to the watering place they reached.

notes.note: والملح, literally ‘and/by salt,’ is obscure here. I tentatively take it as an oath invoking a bond of kinship or mutual obligation, figuratively expressed by salt.
The feminine phrase التي بقيت (‘she/that which has remained’) has no explicit antecedent. ‘The soul’ is supplied tentatively; it may refer to the speaker’s surviving soul or to the bereaved woman.

prose_translation.intro: And Shutaym ibn Khuwaylid said, elegizing the Banū Khālida:

poems.intro: بنو خالدة الذين رثاهم شتيم بن خويلد خمسة، منهم: كردم، وهو الذي طعن دريد بن الصمة يوم قتل أخوه عبد الله، الذي يقول فيه دريد:

verses.h1: تنادوا، فقالا: أردت الخيل فارسا
verses.h2: فقلت: أعبد الله ذلكم الردى؟

verses.h1: They called to one another and said, “The horsemen have felled a rider!”
verses.h2: I said, “Is that fallen man ʿAbd Allah?”

notes.note: فقالا (“the two said”) appears to be a misprint for فقالوا (“they said”), matching تنادوا (“they called to one another”).
الردى is understood here as الردي (Al-radī), “the slain man,” with an undotted final yāʾ, rather than al-radā, “death.”

prose_translation.intro: The men of Banū Khālida whom Shutaym ibn Khuwaylid mourned were five in number. Among them was Kardam, who stabbed Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma on the day Durayd’s brother ʿAbd Allah was killed—the brother of whom Durayd says:

poems.intro: فوقع دريد بين القتلى، فأقبل رجل من بني عبس، فرآه، فقال: إني لأظنه حيا، فأهوى له ليطعنه، فقال كردم بالسيف دونه، وقال: لا يدن من قتيلي أحد، ثم إن دريدا تحامل في الليل، ومضى إلى قومه، وبرأ، وحج كردم بعد زمان في أصحاب له، فلم يشعروا حتى هجموا على بيت دريد بن الصمة، فأقبل دريد، حتى انتهى إليهم، فسلم عليهم، ورحب بهم، وقال من القوم؟ وهو لا يعرفهم فغالطوه عن نسبهم، وكان دريد عالما بالنسب، فلم يزل حتى عرفهم، فلما رأى ذلك كردم كشف عن وجهه، فعرفه دريد، فسلم عليه، وحياه، وقال: مرحبا بكم وبمن معكم، وأمر بقبة، فضربت على كردم، وبعث إليه بحلة وجزور، فقال كردم: أما الجزور فقد قبلتها، وأما الحلة فتكون عندك حتى أرجع إليك، فأقام ما أقام، ثم ارتحل، فكان آخر العهد به. ورأيت هذه الأبيات بخط الوزير الكامل أبي القاسم الحسين بن علي بن الحسين المغربي، منسوبة إلى الحارث بن عمرو الفزاري، يرثي بني خالدة، كردم واخوته، وهم بنو سعد بن حرام، والبيت السادس من الأبيات ما أورده الوزير. وقال آخر:

verses.h1: أميم، هيهات الصبي، ذهب الصبي
verses.h2: وأطار عني الحلم جهل غرابي

verses.h1: أبكي الألى بالأمس كانوا جيرة
verses.h2: أمسوا دفين جنادل وتراب

verses.h1: ماتوا، ولو أني قدرت بحيلة
verses.h2: لأحدت صرف الموت عن أحبابي

verses.h1: ما حيلتي إلا البكاء عليهم
verses.h2: إن البكاء سلاح كل مصاب

verses.h1: O Umaym, youth is far away; youth has gone,
verses.h2: and good sense has driven my youthful folly from me.

verses.h1: I weep for those who only yesterday were neighbors;
verses.h2: now they lie buried beneath stones and earth.

verses.h1: They died; had I found some way,
verses.h2: I would have turned death’s onslaught from my loved ones.

verses.h1: What can I do but weep for them?
verses.h2: Weeping is the weapon of everyone afflicted.

notes.note: I understand الصبي here as الصبا, ‘youth.’ The phrase جهل غرابي literally means ‘my raven’s folly’; I take the raven as an image of youth, possibly through its association with black hair, but the precise expression is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro:
Durayd fell among the slain. A man of Banū ʿAbs came up, saw him, and said, “I think he is still alive.” He bent down to stab him, but Kardam interposed with his sword and said, “Let no one come near the man I have slain.” Then, during the night, Durayd dragged himself away and made his way to his people, and he recovered.

Some time later, Kardam went on pilgrimage with a party of his companions. Before they knew it, they had come upon the dwelling of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma. Durayd approached them, greeted them, welcomed them, and asked, “Who are you?” He did not recognize them, and they tried to mislead him about their lineage. But Durayd was well versed in genealogy, and he persisted until he identified them. When Kardam saw this, he uncovered his face, and Durayd recognized him. He greeted him, saluted him, and said, “Welcome to you and those with you!” He ordered a tent to be pitched for Kardam and sent him a suit of clothes and a camel for slaughter. Kardam said, “As for the camel, I accept it; but let the clothes remain with you until I return to you.” He stayed for a time and then departed, and that was the last that was seen of him.

I saw these verses in the handwriting of the accomplished vizier Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Maghribī, attributed to al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr al-Fazārī, lamenting the sons of Khālida—Kardam and his brothers—who were of Banū Saʿd ibn Ḥarām. The vizier did not include the sixth of these verses. Another poet said:

poems.intro: وقال النابغة الجعدي، يرثي أهله، من قصيدة أولها: ألم تسأل الدار الغداة متى هيا
poems.index_hemistich: ألم تسأل الدار الغداة متى هيا

opening.expected: ألم تسأل الدار الغداة متى هيا

verses.h1: عهدت بها حيا كراما، كأنهم
verses.h2: عظام الملوك عزة وتباهيا

verses.h1: لهم مجلس غلب الرقاب مرازب
verses.h2: بدار الحفاظ أو يعدن الأعاديا

verses.h1: وفتيان صدق غير وخش أشابة
verses.h2: مكاسب للمال الطريف معاطيا

verses.h1: غدا فتيا دهر، وراحا عليهم
verses.h2: نهار وليل يلحقان التواليا

verses.h1: فلم يبق من تلك الديار وأهلها
verses.h2: سرى الليل والأيام إلا مغانيا

verses.h1: مغاني من غالت شعوب فأصبحت
verses.h2: حلولهم تبكي، وتبكي البواكيا

verses.h1: إذا أتيا حيا كراما بغبطة
verses.h2: أناخا بهم حتى يلاقوا الدواهيا

verses.h1: I once knew a noble clan there, who seemed
verses.h2: like mighty kings in their power and pride.

verses.h1: They had an assembly of stout-necked chiefs,
verses.h2: swift to defend their honor or assail their foes.

verses.h1: And true young men, no base, motley rabble,
verses.h2: earners of new wealth, generous in giving.

verses.h1: Time’s two youths came upon them morning and evening:
verses.h2: day and night, overtaking each successive generation.

verses.h1: Of those abodes and their people, nothing was left
verses.h2: by the passage of night and days but deserted dwelling-sites—

verses.h1: The dwelling-sites of those whom Shaʿūb—Death—destroyed; now
verses.h2: their encampments weep and make the mourners weep.

verses.h1: Whenever those two came upon a noble clan living in prosperity,
verses.h2: they encamped among them until calamities befell them.

notes.note: The second hemistich is uncertain. بدار is tentatively understood as بُدّار, ‘quick to act.’ أو يعدن الأعاديا is unclear as transmitted; ‘assail their foes’ is conjectural and may require reading يعدون for يعدن.

يلحقان التواليا may mean ‘overtaking those who follow’ or, with a causative reading, ‘making those who follow join their predecessors.’ The translation takes التوالي to refer to successive generations.
حلولهم is rendered ‘their encampments,’ but it can also denote encamped groups or inhabitants; the intended sense is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: Al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī said, lamenting his family, in a poem beginning: “Did you not ask the dwelling this morning when it was inhabited?”
interludes: [Wakhsh]: base or inferior; [Ashāba]: a motley mixture.

verses.h1: لمن الدار كأنضاء الخلل
verses.h2: عهدها من حقب الدهر الأول

verses.h1: دار قومي قبل أن يدركهم
verses.h2: عنت الدهر، وعيش ذو خبل

verses.h1: إذ هم من خير حي سوقة
verses.h2: وطيء الأرض بسهل أو جبل

verses.h1: لغريب قام فيهم سائلا
verses.h2: ولجار جنب جاء فحل

verses.h1: يستخفون إلى الداعي بهم
verses.h2: وإلى الضيف إذا الضيف نزل

verses.h1: هزة النائل فيهم والندى
verses.h2: وثقال عند أطراف الأسل

verses.h1: ولهم سيما إذا ما رئيت
verses.h2: بينت ريبة من كان سأل

verses.h1: حسن أجسام وسرو ظاهر
verses.h2: ورماح وجباب وحلل

verses.h1: وسوام لجب سامره
verses.h2: طلح ذادته يوم النهل

verses.h1: جعلوه دون أحسابهم
verses.h2: فوقاهم كل ذم وبخل

verses.h1: سألتني جارتي عن أمتي
verses.h2: وإذا ما عي ذو اللب سأل

verses.h1: سألتني عن أناس هلكوا
verses.h2: شرب الدهر عليهم وأكل

verses.h1: طلبوا المجد فلما أدركوا
verses.h2: لكتاب وانتهى ذاك الأجل

verses.h1: وضع الدهر عليهم بركه
verses.h2: فأراه لم يغادر غير فل

verses.h1: وأراني طربا في إثرهم
verses.h2: طرب الواله أو كالمختبل

verses.h1: أنشد الناس، ولا أنشدهم
verses.h2: إنما ينشد من كان أضل

verses.h1: Whose abode is this, like worn-out scabbard coverings,
verses.h2: dating from the earliest ages of time?

verses.h1: My people’s abode, before they were overtaken
verses.h2: by time’s hardships and a life of turmoil.

verses.h1: When they were among the finest tribes of common folk
verses.h2: ever to tread the earth, on plain or mountain—

verses.h1: to a stranger who stood among them asking for help,
verses.h2: or an unrelated neighbor who came and settled.

verses.h1: They hasten to anyone who calls upon them,
verses.h2: and to the guest whenever a guest alights.

verses.h1: The impulse to give generously stirs within them,
verses.h2: yet they stand firm before the spearpoints.

verses.h1: They have a distinguishing mark which, once seen,
verses.h2: clears up the doubts of anyone who asks:

verses.h1: handsome bodies and manifest nobility,
verses.h2: spears, tunics, and fine robes.

verses.h1: And grazing herds whose night attendants are clamorous,
verses.h2: whose drovers are exhausted on watering day.

verses.h1: They made those herds a shield for their honor,
verses.h2: protecting them from every reproach and charge of stinginess.

verses.h1: My woman neighbor asked me about my people;
verses.h2: when a person of understanding is at a loss, he asks.

verses.h1: She asked me about people who had perished,
verses.h2: over whom Time had eaten and drunk.

verses.h1: They sought glory; when they had attained it,
verses.h2: by decree, and when that appointed term had expired,

verses.h1: Time pressed its breast down upon them,
verses.h2: and I see it left only a scattered remnant.

verses.h1: I find myself distraught with longing in their wake,
verses.h2: with a bereaved one’s anguish, or like one deranged.

verses.h1: I recite to people, but do not search for them;
verses.h2: only one who has lost something searches for it.

notes.note: الخلل is tentatively understood as coverings or linings of sword sheaths; the precise object in the comparison is uncertain.

سامره is obscure here. The translation tentatively takes it to mean the herds’ nighttime attendants, with لجب describing their clamor. طلح ذادته is understood as saying that the drovers are exhausted.
لكتاب, rendered tentatively as ‘by decree,’ is syntactically awkward. Its connection with أدركوا and the following clause is uncertain, and the text may be defective.

The unvocalized أنشد permits different readings. The translation takes the first as أُنْشِدُ, ‘I recite,’ and the second as أَنْشُدُ, ‘I seek.’ The first could instead mean ‘I seek’ or ‘I inquire of’; ‘them’ is taken to refer to the dead people.

verses.h1: وقالت سليمى: أرى رأسه
verses.h2: كناصية الفرس الأشهب

verses.h1: وذلك من وقعات الزما
verses.h2: ن، ففيئي إليك ولا تعجبي

verses.h1: أتين على إخوتي سبعة
verses.h2: وعدن على ربعي الأقرب

verses.h1: وسادة رهطي حتى بقي
verses.h2: ت فردا كصيصية الأعضب

verses.h1: أصابهم القتل ثم الوفا
verses.h2: ة، هذ الأشاءة بالمخلب

verses.h1: مضوا سلفا ثم لم يرجعوا
verses.h2: إلينا، فيالك من موكب!

verses.h1: غيوثا تنوء على المقتري
verses.h2: ن إن يكذب الغيث لم تكذب

verses.h1: كراما لدى الضيف عند الشتا
verses.h2: ء، والجدب في الزمن الأجدب

verses.h1: إذا أعزب الناس أحلامهم
verses.h2: أراحوا الحلوم فلم تعزب

interludes.text: الربع: الدار، أراد أهلها، وقال أبو عمرو: ربعه: فخذه من عشيرته.

verses.h1: Sulaymā said, “I see his head
verses.h2: like the forelock of a gray horse.”

verses.h1: That comes from the blows of time;
verses.h2: so collect yourself, and do not wonder.

verses.h1: They carried off my seven brothers,
verses.h2: then turned upon my nearest kin,

verses.h1: and the chiefs of my clan, until I was left
verses.h2: alone, like the horn of a beast whose other horn is broken.

verses.h1: Slaughter struck them, then death,
verses.h2: cutting them down like a young palm with a pruning hook.

verses.h1: They went ahead and never returned
verses.h2: to us—what a company of travelers!

verses.h1: Rain clouds rising over the needy:
verses.h2: if the rain failed, they never failed.

verses.h1: Generous to the guest in winter
verses.h2: and drought, in a barren season.

verses.h1: When people let their judgment stray,
verses.h2: they brought theirs home, and it did not stray.

notes.note: ربعي may refer to the poet’s dwelling or household; here I take ربعي الأقرب to mean his nearest kin.
The exact force of تنوء على المقترين is uncertain. I take it as rain clouds rising over the destitute, an image of benefactors coming to their aid.

interludes: [Al-rabʿ]: the dwelling; he means its inhabitants. Abū ʿAmr said: “His rabʿ: his branch of his clan.”
[Al-ashāʾa]: a young palm offshoot. [Al-mikhlab]: a sickle.

verses.h1: دار حي كانت لهم زمن التو
verses.h2: بة لا عزل، ولا أكفال

verses.h1: لا أرى مثلهم ولو قذف الأع
verses.h2: داء فيهم هواجر الأقوال

verses.h1: من كهول غلب ملاويث قط
verses.h2: ساعين قد الأسير ذي الأغلال

verses.h1: وهم مهرب الذليل كما يه
verses.h2: رب من خاف في رؤوس الجبال

verses.h1: هاجروا يطلبون ما وعد الله فبانوا، وجارهم غير قال
فسلام الإله يغدو عليهم
verses.h2: وفيوء الفردوس ذات الظلال

verses.h1: A clan’s dwelling, once theirs in the time of repentance—
verses.h2: men neither unarmed nor unskilled in riding.

verses.h1: I see none like them, though their enemies hurl
verses.h2: scurrilous words against them.

verses.h1: Men of mature years, mighty-necked and stouthearted,
verses.h2: who cut the bonds of captives laden with chains.

verses.h1: They are a refuge for the downtrodden, as one flees
verses.h2: to mountain peaks when afraid.

verses.h1: They emigrated, seeking what God had promised, and departed, though their neighbor bore them no hatred.
May God’s peace come upon them each morning,
verses.h2: and the shades of Firdaws, rich in shadow.

notes.note: التوبة, split across the hemistichs, reads ‘repentance.’ The precise reference of ‘the time of repentance’ is unclear. أكفال is understood as men unskilled in riding, possibly implying cowardice.
قط / ساعين appears corrupt. The translation conjectures قطّاعين قِدَّ الأسير, ‘cutting the captive’s leather bonds,’ with قطّاعين spanning the hemistich break.

prose_translation.intro: He also said, elegizing his people:
interludes: By [Al-tawba] he means Islam.

poems.intro: وقال أبو بلال، مرداس الخارجي، يرثي قتلى من الخوارج:

verses.h1: أبعد ابن وهب ذي النباهة والتقى
verses.h2: ومن خاض في تلك الحروب المهالكا

verses.h1: أحب بقاء، أو أرجى سلامة
verses.h2: وقد قتلوا زيد بن حصن ومالكا؟

verses.h1: فيا رب سلم نيتي وبصيرتي
verses.h2: وهب لي ألتقي حتى ألاقي أولئكا

verses.h1: After Ibn Wahb, a man of distinction and piety,
verses.h2: and those who plunged into deadly perils in those wars,

verses.h1: should I cherish life, or hope for safety,
verses.h2: when they have slain Zayd ibn Ḥiṣn and Mālik?

verses.h1: O Lord, keep my purpose and discernment sound,
verses.h2: and grant me piety until I meet those men.

notes.note: The printed ألتقي is unclear in this construction. The translation conjecturally reads التقى, ‘piety,’ giving ‘grant me piety.’

prose_translation.intro: Abū Bilāl, Mirdās al-Khārijī, said, elegizing some of the slain Kharijites:

verses.h1: أبعد بني الزهر الغطارفة الألى
verses.h2: أرجى رجاء أو نوالا من الدهر؟

verses.h1: غطارفة زهر مضوا لسبيلهم
verses.h2: ألهفي على تلك الغطارفة الزهر

verses.h1: لهم ذكر يعتدن قلبي، كأنما
verses.h2: يلدغنه بين الجوانح بالجمر

verses.h1: يذكرنيهم كل خير رأيته
verses.h2: وشر فما أنفك منهم على ذكر

verses.h1: سقى الله أجسادا ورائي تركتها
verses.h2: بحافة قنسرين من سبل القطر

verses.h1: ثووا لا يريدون الرواح وغالهم
verses.h2: من الموت أسباب جرين على قدر

verses.h1: ولو يستطيعون الرواح تروحوا
verses.h2: معي ومضوا في المصبحين على ظهر

verses.h1: لعمري لقد وارت قبور ضمنهم
verses.h2: أكفا شداد القبض للأسل السمر

verses.h1: وآخر عهد منك يا شغب شمة
verses.h2: بشرج وداعا والمطي بنا تسري

verses.h1: فكان وداعا، لا تلاقي بعده
verses.h2: وبينا إلى يوم القيامة والحشر

verses.h1: After my radiant sons, those noble lords,
verses.h2: can I cherish any hope or expect any bounty from time?

verses.h1: Radiant noblemen who have gone their way—
verses.h2: alas, my grief for those radiant noblemen!

verses.h1: Memories of them revisit my heart, as though
verses.h2: they sting it between my ribs with glowing coals.

verses.h1: Every good thing I see reminds me of them,
verses.h2: and every evil too: I never cease remembering them.

verses.h1: May God water the bodies I left behind me
verses.h2: on the outskirts of Qinnasrīn with streaming rain.

verses.h1: They remained, with no wish to depart; they were overtaken
verses.h2: by the causes of death, running their destined course.

verses.h1: Had they been able to depart, they would have departed
verses.h2: with me, riding among those who set out at dawn.

verses.h1: By my life, the graves that held them have concealed
verses.h2: hands that gripped brown spear-shafts firmly.

verses.h1: My last moment with you, O Shaghab, was a breath of your scent
verses.h2: at Sharj, in farewell, as the camels bore us through the night.

verses.h1: It was a farewell with no meeting after it,
verses.h2: a parting until the Day of Resurrection and Gathering.

notes.note: I read بني الزهر as ‘my radiant sons.’ The unvocalized text could also suggest a group name, Banū al-Zuhr. الألى is syntactically unclear: ordinarily meaning ‘who,’ it has no evident relative clause here and may be misprinted.

شرج is treated as a place name, provisionally vocalized Sharj; its identification is uncertain. شمة literally denotes an act of smelling, rendered here as ‘a breath of your scent’; the precise farewell gesture is unclear.

interludes: (I think it is Ḥāḍir Qinnasrīn):

verses.h1: رمى المحدثان نسوة آل حرب
verses.h2: بمقدار سمدن له سمودا

verses.h1: فرد شعورهن السود بيضا
verses.h2: ورد وجوههن البيض سودا

verses.h1: فإنك لو رأيت بكاء هند
verses.h2: ورملة إذ تصكان الخدودا

verses.h1: بكيت بكاء معولة فقيد
verses.h2: أصاب الدهر واحدها الفقيدا

verses.h1: Night and day struck the women of Āl Ḥarb
verses.h2: with a stroke of fate that left them dazed with grief.

verses.h1: It turned their black hair white,
verses.h2: and turned their white faces black.

verses.h1: Had you seen the weeping of Hind
verses.h2: and Ramla as they slapped their cheeks,

verses.h1: you would have wept like a bereaved woman wailing
verses.h2: whose only child fate had struck down.

notes.note: سمدن له سمودا is understood here as being dazed or bewildered with grief; the verb has several other senses. المحدثان, literally ‘the two bringers of change,’ denotes night and day.
The identities of Hind and Ramla are uncertain.
واحدها, literally ‘her only one,’ is taken here to mean her only child; the relationship is not explicitly stated.

prose_translation.intro: And Ayman ibn Khuraym al-Asadī said:

verses.h1: ألا أيها الموت الذي ليس جانيا
verses.h2: أرحني، فقد أفنيت كل خليل

verses.h1: أراك بصيرا بالذين أحبهم
verses.h2: كأنك تهدي نحوهم بدليل

verses.h1: O Death, who does no wrong,
verses.h2: give me rest, for you have taken every dear friend.

verses.h1: I see you have a keen eye for those I love,
verses.h2: as though a guide were leading you toward them.

notes.note: ليس جانيا literally means ‘is not a wrongdoer.’ This description is unexpected in an appeal reproaching Death; the wording has been retained, though its intended force is uncertain.

verses.h1: هوت أمهم ماذا بهم يوم صرعوا
verses.h2: بحسمان من أسباب مجد تهدما

verses.h1: أبوا أن يفروا، والقنا في نحورهم
verses.h2: ولم يرتقوا من خشية الموت سلما

verses.h1: ولو أنهم فروا لكانوا أعزة
verses.h2: ولكن رأوا صبرا على الموت أكرما

verses.h1: Bereft was their mother! What fell with them the day they were slain
verses.h2: at Ḥasmān—what pillars of glory!

verses.h1: They refused to flee, though spears were in their breasts,
verses.h2: nor did they climb a ladder for fear of death.

verses.h1: Had they fled, they would have remained honored,
verses.h2: but they deemed steadfastness in the face of death more honorable.

notes.note: The place حسمان is unidentified here; the vocalization Ḥasmān is uncertain.

poems.intro: عن شبل بن بشير أنه خرج في سفر وخلف الطاعون في أهله، فلم يدع منهم أحدا إلا أمة سوداء، تحولت إلى بعض الجيران، فقدم شبل فجعل يدق الباب، فسمعته الأمة، فقالت: من هذا؟ فقال: أنا رب الدار، فقالت ما بقى في الدار أحد، فجاء الناس يعزونه على ما افترط من أهله، فقال:

verses.h1: أتى دون حلو العيش حتى أمره
verses.h2: نكوب على آثارهن نكوب

verses.h1: تتابعن في الأحباب حتى أبدنهم
verses.h2: فلم يبق منهم في الديار عريب

verses.h1: إذا ذر قرن الشمس عللت بالمنى
verses.h2: ويأوي إلي الحزن حين تغيب

verses.h1: ونام خلي البال عني ولم أنم
verses.h2: كما لم ينم عاري الفناء عزيب

verses.h1: أضرت به الأيام حتى تركنه
verses.h2: بطول الذي عفين وهو رقوب

verses.h1: وكيف بقاء المرء من بعد أهله
verses.h2: وليس له في الغابرين حبيب؟

verses.h1: وما ترك الطاعون من ذي هوادة
verses.h2: إلينا إذا حان الإياب يئوب

verses.h1: وكنت أرجى أن أؤوب إليهم
verses.h2: فغالهم من دون ذاك شعوب

verses.h1: مقادير لا يغفلن من حان يومه
verses.h2: لهن على كل النفوس رقيب

verses.h1: سقين بكأس الموت من قد أمتنه
verses.h2: وفي الحي من أنفاسهن ذنوب

verses.h1: أريد لأنسى ذكرهم فيهيجني
verses.h2: فؤاد إلى أهل القبور طروب

verses.h1: فلسنا بأحيا منهم، غير أننا
verses.h2: إلى أجل ندعى له فنجيب

verses.h1: Between me and life’s sweetness came—until they made it bitter—
verses.h2: calamities, with more calamities in their wake.

verses.h1: They fell upon my loved ones in succession until they destroyed them,
verses.h2: and not a soul remained of them in their dwellings.

verses.h1: When the sun’s first edge appears, I console myself with hopes;
verses.h2: but grief comes home to me when it sets.

verses.h1: The carefree man slept, heedless of me, but I did not sleep,
verses.h2: just as a solitary man with an empty courtyard cannot sleep.

verses.h1: The days have dealt him harm until they left him,
verses.h2: through the long years gone by, bereft of children.

verses.h1: How can a man go on living after his family,
verses.h2: with no loved one among those who remain?

verses.h1: The plague has left not one affectionate soul
verses.h2: to return to us when the hour of homecoming comes.

verses.h1: I had hoped to return to them,
verses.h2: but Shaʿūb—Death—snatched them away before that.

verses.h1: Decrees of fate never overlook the man whose day has come;
verses.h2: over every soul they have a watcher.

verses.h1: They gave the cup of death to those they killed;
verses.h2: for the living, too, there is a portion of their breath.

verses.h1: I try to forget their memory, but I am stirred
verses.h2: by a heart that yearns for the people of the graves.

verses.h1: We are no more alive than they, except that we
verses.h2: live until an appointed hour: we are called to it, and answer.

notes.note: The referent of عاري الفناء عزيب, literally ‘bare of courtyard, solitary,’ is uncertain. I have taken it as a lonely man whose household is empty.
بطول الذي عفين is obscure and may be corrupt. ‘Through the long years gone by’ is tentative. رقوب denotes someone whose children have died or who has no surviving child.
أنفاسهن literally means ‘their breaths,’ apparently referring to the decrees of fate, but the image is unclear. ذنوب can mean a full bucket or an allotted portion; the latter is used here.

prose_translation.intro: It is related of Shibl ibn Bashīr that he set out on a journey, leaving the plague among his household. It spared none of them but a black slave woman, who moved in with some of the neighbors. When Shibl returned, he began knocking at the door. The slave woman heard him and said, “Who is this?” He said, “I am the master of the house.” She said, “No one is left in the house.” The people came to console him for the members of his household he had lost, and he said:

verses.h1: لحى الله دهرا شره دون خيره
verses.h2: وجدا بصيفي نأى بعد معبد

verses.h1: بقية خلاني أتى الدهر دونهم
verses.h2: فما جزعي أم كيف عنهم تجلدي؟

verses.h1: فلو أنها إحدى يدي رزئتها!
verses.h2: ولكن يدي بانت على إثرها يدي

verses.h1: كأني وصيفيا أخا الصدق لم نقل
verses.h2: لموقد نار آخر الليل

verses.h1: فلست بباك بعده إثر هالك
verses.h2: قدي الآن من وجدي على هالك قدي

verses.h1: May God curse an age whose evil is nearer than its good,
verses.h2: and the fortune that took Ṣayfī away after Maʿbad.

verses.h1: They were the last of my friends; Time came between us.
verses.h2: What can my grief avail—or how can I bear their loss?

verses.h1: If only it had been just one of my hands that I lost!
verses.h2: But one hand was severed, and the other followed it.

verses.h1: As though Ṣayfī, that faithful brother, and I had never said
verses.h2: to one kindling a fire at the end of the night…

verses.h1: After him I shall not weep for anyone who dies;
verses.h2: My grief for one dead is enough for me now—enough!

notes.note: I read وجدا as wa-jaddan, ‘and a fortune,’ continuing the curse. The unvocalized text could also represent wajdan, ‘grief,’ though its syntax would be less clear.
Ṣayfī and Maʿbad appear to be deceased companions; I cannot identify them more precisely.
The force of فما جزعي is uncertain. I have rendered it as questioning the usefulness of grief; it could instead ask about the nature or extent of his grief.
The second hemistich appears incomplete: it lacks the expected rhyme, and the words addressed to the person kindling the fire are missing. The ellipsis marks this apparent omission.

interludes: : “Kindle it!”

poems.intro: وقال الشريف الرضي - رضي الله عنه -:

verses.h1: ما للهموم كأنها
verses.h2: نار على كبدي تشب

verses.h1: أفراق إخوان الشبا
verses.h2: ب غدت مطاياهم تخب؟

verses.h1: فارقتهم، فالعين عي
verses.h2: ن بعدهم، والقلب قلب

verses.h1: ما كنت أحسب أنني
verses.h2: جلد على الأرزاء صعب

verses.h1: أو أنني أبقى وظه
verses.h2: ري بعد إخواني أجب

verses.h1: ما أخطأتك الحادثا
verses.h2: ت إذا أصابت من تحب

verses.h1: Why are these sorrows like
verses.h2: a fire flaring upon my liver?

verses.h1: Is it parting from the companions of youth,
verses.h2: whose mounts have set off at a trot?

verses.h1: I parted from them, yet my eye is still an eye
verses.h2: after them, and my heart still a heart.

verses.h1: I never thought that I was
verses.h2: so enduring under calamities, so unyielding,

verses.h1: Or that I would live on, my back
verses.h2: left maimed after my brothers were gone.

verses.h1: Calamities have not missed you
verses.h2: when they strike those you love.

notes.note: The force of ‘the eye is an eye ... and the heart a heart’ is uncertain. I take it to express surprise that both remain intact after separation, in keeping with the following lines; عين can also mean a spring of water.
أجب means shorn of, or lacking, a hump. Applied here to the speaker’s back, it appears to suggest the loss of his brothers as a source of support; ‘maimed’ renders that apparent sense.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī—may God be pleased with him—said:

verses.h1: أصبحت من حلول قومي وحشا
verses.h2: رحب الجدر جلسها فالبطاح

verses.h1: ولقد ألفيت وفيها كهول
verses.h2: وشباب بيض الوجوه صباح

verses.h1: ومهادير في الندى ولا ينف
verses.h2: ك فيه منهم ندى وسماح

verses.h1: Desolate now are the places where my people dwelt:
verses.h2: the spacious-walled homes, their uplands and plains.

verses.h1: Yet I once found them filled with men of mature years
verses.h2: and handsome, fair-faced youths,

verses.h1: and men of resounding voices in the assembly; never
verses.h2: did their bounty and generosity cease there.

notes.note: The phrase رحب الجدر is uncertain. I have provisionally understood it as ‘spacious-walled homes’; it may instead contain a place-name.
I take مهادير to mean men with loud, resounding voices, and read the first الندى as النديّ, ‘the assembly.’ As written, الندى can also mean ‘generosity,’ so the phrase remains uncertain.

verses.h1: ألم تسل عن ليلى وقد ذهب العمر
verses.h2: وقد أوحشت منها الموارج والحضر

verses.h1: وقد هاجني منها بوعساء فروع
verses.h2: فأجراع ذي اللهباء منزلة قفر

verses.h1: يظل بها داعي الهديل، كأنه
verses.h2: على الساق نشوان تميل به الخمر

verses.h1: فإن تبك في رسم الديار، فإنها
verses.h2: ديار بني زيد وهل عنهم صبر؟

verses.h1: Have you not yet ceased longing for Laylā, though your life has passed,
verses.h2: and al-Mawārij and al-Ḥaḍr lie desolate without her?

verses.h1: There stirred my longing for her, on the sands of Furūʿ,
verses.h2: and the sandy flats of Dhū al-Lahbāʾ, a deserted dwelling.

verses.h1: A cooing dove keeps calling there, as though it were,
verses.h2: upon the bough, a drunken man whom wine makes sway.

verses.h1: If you weep among the traces of the dwellings, they are
verses.h2: the dwellings of Banū Zayd—can one bear being without them?

notes.note: Al-Mawārij and al-Ḥaḍr appear to be place names, but their locations are uncertain; the vocalization of al-Ḥaḍr is provisional.
Furūʿ and Dhū al-Lahbāʾ appear to be place names whose locations I cannot identify. The vocalization of Furūʿ is uncertain.
The particular clan intended by Banū Zayd is uncertain.

interludes: [Al-Mawārij and al-Ḥaḍr]: place names.

verses.h1: ألا ليت شعري! هل يعودن ما مضى
verses.h2: ليالي عيش الأصفياء رطيب؟

verses.h1: وهل عائد قبل الممات، فراجع
verses.h2: إلى عهده دهر إلي حبيب؟

verses.h1: وهل يجمعن شملي من الدهر جامع
verses.h2: بلى، ذاك إن شاء الإله قريب

verses.h1: ولي كبد حرى بما قد تضمنت
verses.h2: عليكم وعين بالدموع سكوب

verses.h1: Ah, if only I knew! Will what has passed return—
verses.h2: those nights when life among dear friends was fresh?

verses.h1: And will there return before death, coming back
verses.h2: to what it once was, a time dear to me?

verses.h1: And will anyone, in time, reunite my scattered company?
verses.h2: Yes—God willing, that will be soon.

verses.h1: I have a heart burning with all it harbors
verses.h2: for you, and an eye pouring tears.

poems.intro: روى أن عبد الله بن عمرو العبلي قال له عبد الله بن حسن بن حسن - رضي الله عنهم -: أنشدني شيئا مما رثيت به قومك، فأنشده: أصعد أنفاسي حنينا إليكم كما حن مقصور اليدين نجيب وقال حيان بن قيس:

verses.h1: تطاول ليلى بالغطاط إلى الغمر
verses.h2: وبات فراشي مشعرا جاحم الجمر

verses.h1: تذكرت من أضحت بحوران داره
verses.h2: وكيف مع الأحداث أصبو إلى الذكر؟

verses.h1: فإن أرهم لا أصدف الدهر عنهم
verses.h2: سوى سفر حتى أغيب في القبر

verses.h1: لعمري لقد أمست إلي بغيضة
verses.h2: نوى فرقت بيني وبين بني عمرو

verses.h1: إذا هبطوا الأدوات، والبحر دوننا
verses.h2: فقل في تناء بيننا آخر الدهر

verses.h1: My night stretched long at al-Ghaṭāṭ, toward al-Ghamr,
verses.h2: and all night my bed was lined with fiercely burning coals.

verses.h1: I remembered those whose home is now in Ḥawrān—
verses.h2: yet how, amid these calamities, can I yearn for remembrance?

verses.h1: If I see them, I shall never turn away from them,
verses.h2: save for travel, until I disappear into the grave.

verses.h1: By my life, I have come to loathe
verses.h2: the separation that parted me from Banū ʿAmr.

verses.h1: When they descend into al-Adawāt, with the sea between us,
verses.h2: think how far apart we shall be till the end of time!

notes.note: الغطاط and الغمر appear to be place-names, but their identification and vocalization are uncertain. The relationship expressed by إلى الغمر is also unclear; it is rendered literally as “toward al-Ghamr.”
The attachment of “until I disappear into the grave” is ambiguous: it may qualify his lifelong refusal to leave them, apart from travel, or describe the exceptional journey as death itself.
الأدوات is treated as a place-name, al-Adawāt, but I could not identify it; the reading may be corrupt.

prose_translation.intro:
It is related that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan—may God be pleased with them—said to ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr al-ʿAblī: “Recite to me something of what you composed in mourning for your people.” So he recited:
“I send up my sighs in yearning for you,
as a noble camel with its forelegs bound cries out in longing.”
And Ḥayyān ibn Qays said:

verses.h1: تخرم الدهر أشكالي فأفردني
verses.h2: منهم، وكنت أراهم خير جلاس

verses.h1: وصرت آلف قوما لا خلاق لهم
verses.h2: والوحش يأنس عند المحل بالناس

verses.h1: Time has carried off my peers and left me alone,
verses.h2: bereft of them, whom I regarded as the best of companions.

verses.h1: I have come to keep company with people of no worth;
verses.h2: even wild beasts seek human company in times of drought.

poems.intro: وقالت ليلى، أخت الوليد بن طريف الشاري، تبكيه:

verses.h1: ذكرت الوليد، وأيامه
verses.h2: إذ الأرض من شخصه بلقع

verses.h1: فأقبلت أطلبه في السماء
verses.h2: كما يبتغي أنفه الأجدع

verses.h1: أضاعك قومك، فليطلبوا
verses.h2: إفادة مثل الذي ضيعوا

verses.h1: لو أن السيوف الذي حدها
verses.h2: يصيبك تعلم ما تصنع

verses.h1: نبت عنك، أو جعلت
verses.h2: هيبة وخوفا لصولك لا تقطع

verses.h1: I remembered al-Walīd and his days,
verses.h2: now that the earth lies desolate without him.

verses.h1: I began to seek him in the sky,
verses.h2: as a man whose nose is severed seeks his nose.

verses.h1: Your people failed you; let them seek
verses.h2: to gain another like the one they lost.

verses.h1: Had the swords whose edges
verses.h2: struck you known what they were doing,

verses.h1: they would have glanced off you, or else
verses.h2: ceased to cut, in awe and fear of your onslaught.

notes.note: الذي does not agree grammatically with السيوف (‘swords’); it may be a misprint for التي. The translation follows that reading.
The line appears metrically uneven as supplied, possibly because of a misplaced hemistich division or textual corruption. I take جعلت ... لا تقطع to mean that the swords would stop cutting.

prose_translation.intro: Laylā, sister of al-Walīd ibn Ṭarīf al-Shārī, said, mourning him:

poems.intro: وقالت فارعة المرية، أخت مسعود بن شداد، تبكيه:

verses.h1: يا من رأى بارقا قد بت أرمقه
verses.h2: جودا، على الحرة السوداء والوادي

verses.h1: أسقي به قبر من أعني، وحب به
verses.h2: قبرا إلي، وغن لم يفده فاد

verses.h1: شهاد أندية، رفاع ألوية
verses.h2: شداد أوهية، فتاح أسداد

verses.h1: نحار راغية، قتال طاغية
verses.h2: حلال رابية، فكاك أقياد

verses.h1: قوال محكمة، نقاض مبرمة
verses.h2: فراج مبهمة، حباس أوراد

verses.h1: حلال ممرعة، حمال مضلعة
verses.h2: فراج مفظعة، طلاع أنجاد

verses.h1: أبا زرارة لا تبعد، وكل فتى
verses.h2: يوما رهين صفيحات وأعواد

verses.h1: Who has seen a lightning cloud that I spent the night watching,
verses.h2: lavishing rain upon al-Ḥarra al-Sawdāʾ and the valley?

verses.h1: With it I would water the grave of him I mean—and how dear
verses.h2: that grave is to me, though no ransomer redeemed him!

verses.h1: A frequenter of councils, a raiser of banners,
verses.h2: a mender of breaches, an opener of blocked ways;

verses.h1: A slaughterer of bellowing camels, a slayer of tyrants,
verses.h2: a dweller on high ground, a breaker of fetters;

verses.h1: A speaker of sound judgments, an unraveler of knotted affairs,
verses.h2: a solver of perplexities, one who holds back those approaching the water;

verses.h1: A dweller in lush pastures, a bearer of crushing burdens,
verses.h2: a reliever of dreadful troubles, a climber of heights.

verses.h1: O Abū Zurāra, be not far away! Every young man
verses.h2: will one day lie captive to stone slabs and wooden planks.

notes.note: Al-Ḥarra al-Sawdāʾ means ‘the black lava field’; it may be a description rather than a fixed place-name. I cannot identify the location.
The printed وغن appears to be a typographical or OCR error for وإن, ‘though.’

The precise force of حباس أوراد is uncertain. Literally it describes someone who holds back parties coming to water; it may refer to keeping enemies from a watering place or to checking advancing war bands.

prose_translation.intro: And Fāriʿa al-Murriyya, the sister of Masʿūd ibn Shaddād, said, mourning him:

verses.h1: أوردتني ومضيت مبتدرا
verses.h2: حز المدى، ولواذع الجمر

verses.h1: وتركتني
verses.h2: والدهر ذو دول أعشى اللحاظ مقلم الظفر

verses.h1: أمري، فلا أصمي، وإن رميت
verses.h2: جهتي رميت معرض النحر

verses.h1: وأصد عن لقيا العدو، وهل
verses.h2: ألقى العدو، ولست من ظهري؟

verses.h1: وإذا مضى من كان يعضدني
verses.h2: ويشد يوم كريهة أزري

verses.h1: ويرد عني كل طارقة
verses.h2: ويخوض كل ردى إلى نصري

verses.h1: فالحظ لي ألا أهيج وغى
verses.h2: حتى أكون مسالما دهري

verses.h1: لا متعة لي في الحياة
verses.h2: فما أحياه بعدك ليس من عمري

verses.h1: You brought me—and hastened away—
verses.h2: to the cutting of blades and the searing of embers.

verses.h1: And you left me
verses.h2: —while fortune keeps turning—with dimmed sight and clipped claws.

verses.h1: I shoot, but cannot strike dead; and if shots are aimed
verses.h2: my way, I am struck with my throat exposed.

verses.h1: I shrink from meeting the enemy; how could I
verses.h2: meet the enemy when you no longer stand behind me?

verses.h1: And when he who supported me has gone,
verses.h2: who strengthened me on the day of battle,

verses.h1: who warded off every calamity from me
verses.h2: and plunged into every mortal peril to aid me,

verses.h1: my best course is not to stir up war,
verses.h2: so that I may be at peace with fate.

verses.h1: There is no pleasure for me in life;
verses.h2: what I live after you is no part of my lifetime.

notes.note: أمري appears to be a transposition error for أرمي, ‘I shoot,’ adopted here. Both occurrences of رميت are read as passive: رُمِيَتْ جهتي, ‘shots are aimed my way,’ and رُمِيتُ, ‘I am struck.’
The unusual phrase ولست من ظهري is read as addressing the deceased, لستَ, with ظهري understood figuratively as support or protection.

prose_translation.intro: And al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, may God have mercy on him, said:

verses.h1: يا دهر قد أكثرت فجعتنا
verses.h2: بسراتنا، ووقرت في العظم

verses.h1: وسلبتنا ما لست مخلفه
verses.h2: يا دهر ما أنصفت في الحكم

verses.h1: لو كان لي قرن أناضله
verses.h2: ما طاش عند حفيظة سهمي

verses.h1: أو كان يعطي النصف قلت له:
verses.h2: أحرزت سهمك فاله عن سهمي

verses.h1: O Time, how often you have bereaved us
verses.h2: of our foremost men, and cracked the very bone!

verses.h1: You have stripped us of what you will never replace;
verses.h2: O Time, you have not judged fairly.

verses.h1: Had I an opponent to contend with in archery,
verses.h2: my arrow would not miss when my honor was roused.

verses.h1: Or if he would deal fairly, I would say to him:
verses.h2: “You have secured your share; leave mine alone.”

poems.intro: وقال أميمة بنت عبد شمس، ترثي قومها:

verses.h1: أبى ليلك أن يذهب
verses.h2: ونيط الطرف بالكوكب

verses.h1: وهذا الصبح لا يأتي
verses.h2: ولا يدنو ولا يقرب

verses.h1: لفقد عشيرة منا
verses.h2: كرام الخيم والمنصب

verses.h1: أمال عليهم دهر
verses.h2: حديد الناب والمخلب

verses.h1: فحل بهم وقد أمنوا
verses.h2: فلم يقصر ولم يشطب

verses.h1: وما عنه إذا ما حل
verses.h2: ل، لا منجى، ولا مهرب

verses.h1: ألا يا عين فابكيهم
verses.h2: بدمع منك مستغرب

verses.h1: فإن أبك، فهم عزى
verses.h2: وهم ركني، وهم منكب

verses.h1: Your night refuses to pass,
verses.h2: and your gaze is fastened to the star.

verses.h1: This dawn does not come,
verses.h2: nor draw near, nor approach.

verses.h1: For the loss of kinsfolk of ours,
verses.h2: noble in character and rank.

verses.h1: Time bore down upon them,
verses.h2: sharp of fang and claw.

verses.h1: It descended upon them when they felt secure,
verses.h2: neither holding back nor turning aside.

verses.h1: And from it, when it descends,
verses.h2: there is no deliverance, no escape.

verses.h1: O eye, weep for them
verses.h2: with tears pouring freely from you.

verses.h1: If I weep, it is because they were my strength,
verses.h2: my pillar and my support.

notes.note: The sense of يشطب is uncertain here; it is rendered as ‘turning aside,’ taking the verb to mean departing or moving away.
The isolated ل at the beginning of the second hemistich appears to complete حلّ (‘descends’) in the first; the divided word is translated wholly in the first hemistich.
مستغرب is understood here as describing copious or unrestrained tears, though its precise force is uncertain.
منكب literally means ‘shoulder.’ In parallel with ‘my strength’ and ‘my pillar,’ it is understood as ‘my shoulder/support,’ although the possessive ending is not written.

prose_translation.intro: And Umayma bint ʿAbd Shams said, lamenting her people:

poems.intro: وقال هلال بن الأسعر، يرثي رجلا من قومه يقال له: المغيرة بن قنبر، كان يعوله ويفضل عليه:

verses.h1: ألا ليت المغيرة كان حيا
verses.h2: وأفنى قبله الناس الفناء

verses.h1: ليبك على المغيرة كل خيل
verses.h2: إذا أفنى عرائكها اللقاء

verses.h1: ويبك على المغيرة كل كل
verses.h2: فقير كان ينعشه العطاء

verses.h1: ويبك على المغرة كل جيش
verses.h2: تمور لدى معاركه الدماء

verses.h1: فتى الفتيان، فارس كل حرب
verses.h2: إذا شالت وقد رفع اللواء

verses.h1: لقد وارى جديد الأرض منه خصالا عقد عصمتها الوفاء
وصبرا للنوائب إن ألمت
verses.h2: إذا ما ضاق بالحدث الفضاء

verses.h1: هزير تنجلي الغمرات عنه
verses.h2: نقي العرض، همته العلاء

verses.h1: إذا شهد الكريهة خاض فيها
verses.h2: بحورا، لا تكدرها الدلاء

verses.h1: جسورا لا يورع منه روع
verses.h2: ولا يثني عزيمته اتقاء

verses.h1: حليم في عشيرته إذا ما
verses.h2: حبا الحلماء أطلقها المراء

verses.h1: حميد في عشيرته فقيد
verses.h2: يطيب عليه في الملأ الثناء

verses.h1: Oh, would that al-Mughīra were alive,
verses.h2: and death had consumed all people before him!

verses.h1: Let every troop of horsemen weep for al-Mughīra
verses.h2: when combat has worn away its mettle.

verses.h1: Let every helpless dependent weep for al-Mughīra,
verses.h2: every poor man whom his giving sustained.

verses.h1: Let every army weep for al-Mughīra,
verses.h2: whose battlefields run with surging blood.

verses.h1: Foremost of young men, horseman of every war
verses.h2: when it rears up and the banner has been raised.

verses.h1: The face of the earth has buried in him virtues held together by loyalty,
and endurance of calamities when they struck,
verses.h2: when misfortune made the wide world narrow.

verses.h1: A lion who emerges from the perils of battle,
verses.h2: his honor untarnished, his ambition set on greatness.

verses.h1: When he entered the fray, he plunged into it—
verses.h2: into seas no buckets could muddy.

verses.h1: Dauntless: no terror holds him back,
verses.h2: nor does caution bend his resolve.

verses.h1: Forbearing among his kin, even when
verses.h2: disputation loosens the knee-bands of forbearing men.

verses.h1: Esteemed among his kin, now lost to them;
verses.h2: praise of him rings sweet in the assembly.

notes.note: عرائكها is uncertain here; ‘mettle’ provisionally takes it to mean the cavalry’s strength or stamina.
المغرة appears to be a typographical or OCR error for المغيرة, al-Mughīra.

I take حبا to be ḥubā, the bands or garments drawn around the knees while sitting. The apparent image is of dispute making even forbearing men undo these bindings and rise in agitation; the unvocalized wording leaves some uncertainty.

prose_translation.intro: Hilāl ibn al-Asʿar said, elegizing a man of his people named al-Mughīra ibn Qanbar, who used to support him and treat him generously:

poems.intro: وقال امرؤ القيس بن حجر الكندي:

verses.h1: تذكرت أهلي الصالحين وقد أتى
verses.h2: على حمل منا الركاب فأعفرا

verses.h1: ولما بدت حوران والآل دونها
verses.h2: نظرت، فلم تنظر بعينيك منظرا

verses.h1: تقطع أسباب اللبانة والهوى
verses.h2: عشية جاوزنا حماة وشيزرا

verses.h1: عشية جاوزنا حماة وسيرنا
verses.h2: أخو الجهد لا نلوي على من تعذرا

verses.h1: بكى صاحبي لما رأى الدرب دونه
verses.h2: وأيقن أنا لا حقان بقيصرا

verses.h1: فقلت له: لا تبك عينك إنما
verses.h2: نحاول ملكا، أو نموت فنعذرا

verses.h1: I remembered my upright kinsfolk, when
verses.h2: our mounts had passed Ḥamal, then Aʿfar.

verses.h1: When Ḥawrān appeared, with mirage before it,
verses.h2: you looked, yet could see nothing with your own eyes.

verses.h1: The bonds of longing and love were severed
verses.h2: the evening we passed Ḥamāh and Shayzar.

verses.h1: The evening we passed Ḥamāh, our journey
verses.h2: was hardship itself; we did not turn back for anyone who pleaded inability.

verses.h1: My companion wept when he saw the mountain pass before him
verses.h2: and knew for certain that we two were bound for Qayṣar.

verses.h1: I said to him: “Let your eye not weep; we are only
verses.h2: seeking a kingdom—or we shall die and be held blameless.”

notes.note: Ḥamal and Aʿfar appear to be place-names, but their locations are uncertain. The wording منا الركاب is awkward and may be corrupt; “our mounts” is a tentative rendering.

The unvocalized نظرت can mean either “I looked” or “you looked”; “you looked” is adopted to agree with بعينيك (“with your two eyes”). The intended force of the following negation—literally, “you saw no sight”—is uncertain.

prose_translation.intro: And Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Ḥujr al-Kindī said:

paragraphs.text: [هذا لفظ ما وجد في آخر الأصل] تم وكمل هذا التأليف المبارك، المسمى بالمنازل والديار، الذي هو بخط كاتبه العالم العلامة مجد الدولة الأمير أسامة، أناله الله الفوز والكرامة في دار المقامة، في جمادى الأولى لسنة ثمان وستين وخمسمائة من الهجرة المصطفوية، على مهاجرها أفضل الصلاة وأكمل التحية، وقد علقها مؤلفها لنفسه في مدينة حصن كيفا في التاريخ الأنور، حسبما بينه العلامة النحرير، المندرج إلى رحمة ربه القدير الإمام محمد أبو المعالي بن أحمد بن محمود الطالوي، الدمشقي تغمده الله برحمته، في بحبوحة جنته في أول هذا السفر الشريف عند ذكر ترجمة المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى، وأجزل عليه نعمه ووالى، ناقلا تاريخ كتابته عن مؤلفه من آخر هذا المجلد الشريف، لكن لتقادم الأزمان ومرور الأيام والأعوام انخرم آخره، فقد نقلنا ما ذكره المرحوم الطاولي في ابتدائه إجمالا في آخره؛ ليعلم أن هذه النسخة المباركة عمرت ليوم رقم هذه الحروف خمسمائة وإحدى وعشرين سنة، وليتحقق أن الخط يبقى زمانا بعد كاتبه، وأنه بعد الآن أيضا يبقى ما شاء الله تعالى.
حرره العبد الفقير محمد أنور بن الموقع، غفر الله زله، وأحسن عمله، في سنة تسع وثمانين بعد الألف من الهجرة النبوية.

[This is the wording found at the end of the original.] This blessed work, entitled Abodes and Dwellings, was finished and completed in the handwriting of its author, the learned scholar Majd al-Dawla, the emir Usāma—may God grant him triumph and honor in the everlasting abode—in Jumādā al-Ūlā of the year five hundred and sixty-eight after the Hijra of the Chosen One, upon him who made that migration be the finest blessings and fullest salutations. Its author wrote it out for himself in the city of Ḥiṣn Kayfā on that radiant date, as explained by the consummate scholar, now departed into the mercy of his Almighty Lord, the imam Muḥammad Abū al-Maʿālī ibn Aḥmad ibn Maḥmūd al-Ṭālawī al-Dimashqī—may God enfold him in His mercy amid the spaciousness of His Garden—at the beginning of this noble volume, in his account of the author’s life—may God Most High have mercy upon him and bestow His abundant and unceasing favors upon him. He transcribed the date of its writing from its author’s statement at the end of this noble volume. But with the passage of ages, days, and years, its ending has been lost. We have therefore copied here at its end, in brief, what the late al-Ṭāwalī recorded at its beginning, so that it may be known that, on the day these letters were inscribed, this blessed copy had survived for five hundred and twenty-one years, and that it may be established that handwriting endures long after its writer, and that henceforth, too, it will endure for as long as God Most High wills.
Written by the humble servant Muḥammad Anwar ibn al-Muwaqqiʿ‘—may God forgive his lapses and make his deeds good—in the year one thousand and eighty-nine after the Prophet’s Hijra.
